en: May there be prosperity! Homage to the beloved of Śrī;
homage to the illustrious Hayagrīva.
In the Śrīpāñcarātra-Īśvarasaṃhitā:
Salutations to the wielder of the discus, the bestower of all auspiciousness.
For the sake of uplifting those submerged in the ocean of sense-objects,
there were great sages devoted to the practice of austerity, skilled in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and longing for the worship of the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
Those who were knowers of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, experts in the Dharmaśāstras,
devoted to the worship of the Lord, and oceans of virtues such as tranquility,
[saw] Nārāyaṇa performing austerities in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly serving with devotion and desiring to know the means to liberation,
all those sages remained devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
After some time, out of a desire to behold Nārāyaṇa, they departed from heaven.
Having descended there, the divine sage Nārada, filled with curiosity,
beheld the god Nārāyaṇa; and having offered salutation with palms joined in reverence,
the sage— his entire body bristling with horripilation and his face radiant with joy— [stood before him].
Having praised him with various hymns and having bowed down again and again,
he worshipped that god, the flawless Nārāyaṇa.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa spoke to that bull among sages.
"For the sages dwell here, seeking the state of Hari;
you ought to instruct them in the Sātvata scripture.
Having spoken thus, the venerable sage Nārāyaṇa then vanished.
Having heard those words of the Blessed One, the sage Uddālaka, his body thrilled with joy,
desired to carry out his command; then that lord of sages departed and beheld the excellent hermitage of the rishis who maintain their vital energy in an upward flow.
Crowded with flocks of various birds, frequented by various wild animals,
rich in trees, flowers, and creepers, and endowed with ponds, wells, and lakes—
having gone there, that best of sages [was met] by the most excellent brahmins residing there.
Honored with offerings of water for the feet, the guest-offering, and so forth, and seated upon a cushion, he spoke these words which bring joy to the sages:
"Since Nārāyaṇa is here constantly served by you... (1.13–1.14)
"Compassion for you indeed flows fully within him;
through this connection with you, I have attained my purpose today.
O lords of sages, I have been commanded by the Blessed One for your sake. 1.15
"O Yogis and sages, having now mastered all these secrets, there is no further [teaching] beyond this. From this day forward, worship the Lord of Gods."
"O Sage, for us who have sought refuge long ago, you are our supreme resort.
Reveal the means for attaining the state of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus spoke Nārada.
"Listen, all you sages, to this Veda called Ekāyana.
This is indeed the path for the sake of liberation; no other is known to exist.
Therefore, the wise proclaim it by the name 'Ekāyana'. (1.18–1.19)
But that which is the great root of the vast tree of the Veda is the sole refuge of the supreme reality known as the True Brahman, Vāsudeva;
[it is established] by means of divine mantras, such as those beginning with *bala*, which directly reveal Him.
"Adorned, free from doubt, and dispelling the darkness of ignorance"—having spoken thus and taught the lords of yoga, he described its majesty:
"This [treatise], known as the *Prakṛtidharma*, has Vāsudeva as its sole object. (1.21–22)
In the Kṛta Yuga it is set in motion, and thereafter, in the Tretā Yuga and the others,
the Vedas undergo modification everywhere, having different deities as their scope.
This great [Purāṇa] is the root of the vast tree of the Vedas.
The Ṛgveda and the others are its trunks, and the practitioners of yoga are its branches.
O twice-born ones, it is established that [this work] is primarily the expounder of Vāsudeva, the root of the world and of the Veda; thus, it is designated as the "Root-Veda. 1.24–1.25

In the Kṛta Yuga, which was the first of ages, men were worthy [of it] and they constantly practiced the Bhāgavata dharma, which was the primary one. Then, in the Tretā Yuga, all [men] were possessed of various desires.
Having become performers of mixed sacrifices, they abandon the primordial and eternal [Brahman].
All this [universe] is withdrawn by Vāsudeva;
thereafter, the Blessed One himself manifests for the sake of the worthy one.
Thus was it previously studied by me on Śvetadvīpa, O lords of sages:
Sanat, Sanatsujāta, Sanaka, Sanandana,
Sanatkumāra, Kapila, and the seventh, Sanātana.
These are the teachers and the promulgators of the religion of the single-minded devotees (ekāntin).
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha—these are the Citraśikhaṇḍins. 1.30–1.31
And Manu Svāyambhuva,
having propitiated the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Master of the World, through great austerity for a thousand divine years, and having studied [the Vedas] at the conclusion of that time—
And those sages were duly instructed in the root revelation (mūla-śruti).
Then those eight sages, desiring the welfare of the worlds,
and having examined the root Veda through hundreds of thousands of verses, [composed the Vedas].
Likewise, having respectfully examined the divine scriptures such as the Sātvata and others,
the twice-born composed another scripture known as Tantra.
In this way, Manu and the others also understood the meanings of the root revelation (mūla-śruti).
They will compose numerous treatises on Dharma according to their own views.
This [work] shall be the source of other treatises as well;
for within it, Dharma, Artha, and Kāma are explained in detail.
And liberation has been indicated later; therefore, this [work] is indeed the most essential.
Formerly, on the peak of Mount Todi, the great sage Śāṇḍilya, having become composed in mind, performed most intense austerity.
At the end of many thousands of years of austerity,
at the conclusion of the Dvāpara Yuga and the beginning of the Kali Yuga,
he received directly from Saṅkarṣaṇa the Veda known as Ekāyana.
In ancient times, he properly taught that Veda to Sumantu, Jaimini, Bhṛgu, Upagāyana, and Mauñjāyana,
as well as to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
In this way, O best of sages, the fundamental dharma is practiced here.
This Veda is renowned throughout the entire world as the single path;
it is difficult to understand and difficult to perform, yet it is pursued by those who have awakened.
O Blessed One, O Knower of All Scriptures, O You who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge!
By Your grace, this great root-Veda has been fully attained.
Its power is known throughout all the worlds, and it is honored by those who have awakened; this eternal Root Veda is to be practiced by them.
How could it be [honored] by those unawakened ones who are submerged in the great ocean of worldly existence?
"O Blessed One, the Dharma is attained by those who practice it with single-minded devotion.
"Nārada, listen; I shall declare [the teaching] of those who desire the welfare of all the world."
Long ago, the Blessed Lord Hari himself, having thus reflected,
[established this path] for those who, having abandoned the supreme dharma, had resorted to a mixed dharma,
yet were desirous of attaining his state and possessed of faith and devotion.
For the sake of favoring the social classes (*varṇas*) and for the purpose of bringing about their fitness,
as well as for the attainment of the desired fruits by all people,
[this work was composed] in accordance with the *Mūla-veda* and in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.

Having spoken that divine collection of true scriptures— namely the Sātvata, the Pauṣkara, the Jayākhyā, and so forth— he caused it to be promulgated on earth by Saṅkarṣaṇa and others who desired the welfare of all the worlds.
In this way, the great sage Śāṇḍilya also, having heard the divine scriptures from the Blessed Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, taught them to the sages;
and those residing on Mount Malaya formerly did so by the command of Rāma.
First, I was thoroughly instructed in the Sātvata scripture,
that scripture which was spoken by the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva himself,
composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter, and distinguished by its concise and expanded sections.
In the same way, O best of sages, that divine [teaching] was set in motion by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the others,
as well as throughout the celestial worlds;
it was promulgated by the gods headed by Brahmā and Rudra, and by the ṛṣis whose wealth is asceticism.
Whatever treatise has been composed by oneself should be known as spoken by a sage.
Know that this is of three kinds, according to the distinction of *sāttvika* and so forth;
having understood the web of meanings exactly as they exist, [the Lord] Puṇḍarīkākṣa [spoke].
That scripture which elucidates this [reality] and is sublime is remembered as *sāttvika*.
Therefore, once the collection of objects has been known, by relying upon some portion of it,
[the scripture] indeed makes known the collection of objects manifested by one's own intellect.
O best of the twice-born, that scripture which was composed by the Lord of all lords, endowed with extensive detail and based on the true nature of knowledge—
that [I shall explain] through the grace of its summary.
"O twice-born ones, that which was composed by Brahmā and others through the expansions of their own conceptual constructions, as well as that which was likewise composed by the sages—
having heard that [teaching], Brahmā and the others [re-stated it] again in a condensed form. (1.60–1.61)
Whatever is produced from one's own conceptual construction is all remembered as *rājasa*.
That is twofold, through the distinction between the Pañcarātra and the Vaikhānasa.
Whatever is performed based solely on what is stated by one's own conceptual constructions is remembered as *tāmasa*.
Whatever has been composed by human beings alone is known as *pauruṣa* (human). O lords of sages, there is no scripture superior to the divine [scriptures],
namely the Sātvata, the Pauṣkara, and likewise the one called Jaya.
These and other divine scriptures were spoken by Hari himself,
in accordance with the root Vedas, out of a desire for the welfare [of beings].
O best of sages, this triad beginning with the Sātvata is all-pervasive.
And just as the wise [worship] the triad of mantras beginning with the eight-syllabled one,
Hari is worshipped in due order at Yādavācala, Śrīraṅga, and Hastiśaila, according to the procedure taught in these three Tantras.
Among these divine scriptures, the Sātvata is the most excellent of the excellent;
its speaker is the Lord himself, and its hearer is the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa.
O lords of sages, how can the majesty of this Sātvata be described?

Therefore, O best of the twice-born, this *tantra* named after the Lord— which is the very essence of the scriptures directly spoken by the Lord, specifically establishing the meaning of the *Sātvata*—
was heard directly from Saṅkarṣaṇa.
"O sages, I shall speak; listen with attention.
Having said this, the yogi Nārada, having bowed to the Lord Nārāyaṇa and paid homage to Saṅkarṣaṇa, began to speak.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Scripture," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the second chapter.
Nārada said:
O best of sages, listen as I describe the procedure for propitiation.
When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, the knower of mantras, being restrained and pure, [should perform the rite].
Having risen from his bed, he should perform the recitation of the names;
having removed all impurities and bathed, wearing clean garments, with his senses subdued,
and having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* marks and completed the rites prescribed for the morning.
Adorned with perfumes, garlands, and ornaments such as bracelets,
and with his hands holding the *pavitra* grass, remaining silent, he approaches the temple of the Blessed One;
outside the door, according to the scriptures, he [purifies himself] with pure water.
Having washed his feet up to the knees and his hands up to the wrists,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should enter within, bow down while reciting the mantra,
circumambulate the abode, and awaken Puruṣottama.

Accompanied by the sound of conchs and the resonance of kettledrums and tabors, O Great-minded One, with the high-pitched and diverse voices raised by throngs of bards, and with the repeated shouts of "Great Victory! Victory! uttered again and again. || 2.6–2.7 ||
Then, having awakened [the deity] from sleep with hymns characterized by awakening,
one should approach the door; standing there, preceded by the binding of the ten directions,
one should then seal it while reciting the armor-mantra with the index finger.
Whether [the deity] is established or imagined there, one should worship him in the *balimaṇḍala*.

Having first [worshipped] the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), one should indeed worship the entire retinue along with Acyuta; having taken Viṣṇu [into account] mentally, one should recite [the names] beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
Homage again and again to the one accompanied by his entire retinue, the infallible one (Acyuta).
Having worshipped Vāstupuruṣa and the others in due order,
[one should worship] either with the root mantra together with its limbs (sāṅga) or otherwise without its limbs (niraṅga).
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the preceptor should then clap his hands three times with the heart-mantra;
then, having opened the door with the root-mantra and the eye-mantra,
he should light the perpetual lamps and wash his hands with water.
Then, for the purpose of entering the interior of the palace, one should mentally divide the door into three parts; having further divided the single middle part into two,
one should then [proceed] with the left side and the right foot.
Having entered slowly within with that very mantra accompanied by tears,
and having struck the earth and bowed to the Blessed One,
he [then] mentally [honored] the lineage of gurus and their mental command.
Having mentally resolved upon his desired fruit, he should bear it upon his head;
then, having offered that to the deity in the center of the sacrificial hall,
he should fashion a palace and an image, [protecting] the embodied armor-mantra.
Then, having meditated upon that Jīva and the Blessed One, he should [enter] the sacrificial hall.
Then, having swept it with Darbha grass together with the śalākās and mixed with the Goddess,
and having washed it with abundant water and smeared it with cow-dung.
Then, having smeared it with the weapon-mantra and having cut off a fragment,
one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow, and then with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra;
having anointed it all over with sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, and camphor.
One should scatter kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains for the purification of the site.
In this manner, the preceptor himself should purify the temple;
he should then sweep and sprinkle the entire area designated as the temple.
The attendants should indeed perform the duties up to the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha),
while recollecting the Blessed One during the preparation of the sacrificial requisites.
Then, he should command the disciplined disciples, sons, and others who have bathed.
The best of the twice-born should also have the purification of his vessels performed by those very same [means]:
he should cleanse gold and copper with the paste of mango and water;
silver, moreover, with house-soot or with extinguished charcoal.
One should purify objects made of metal with water mixed with ashes;
those made of conch or mother-of-pearl, one should purify with salt;
and those made of fruit or leaves, one should purify with earth and water.
Purity is achieved by removing the smell of oiliness;
one should perform the purification of objects in this manner, exactly as prescribed by the rules.
Having thus purified the vessels, the twice-born man, intent on silence, [should proceed]. (2.27–2.28)

Or he may take his place to the south in front of the Lord of the Gods; for the twice-born man should face northward from the eastern side of the Lord. Then, having sat down upon a seat made of darbha grass, wood, or an antelope skin, || 2.29 ||
For the sake of the arrival of the gods and the departure of the *rākṣasas*,
one should cause the sound of bells to be made there— the mark of the deity’s abode—
accompanied by the blaring of conchs and other instruments, and joined with song and instrumental music.
Then, O best of sages, one should perform the purification of the hands according to the rule:
both palms, the two backs of the hands, and likewise all the fingers,
having been thoroughly cleansed with the *astra-mantra* while assuming the meditation mudrā.
Having thus performed the purification of the hands, one should perform the purification of the place.
Having meditated upon the God of blazing form, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns,
surrounded by millions of flames, and vomiting fire from his mouth.
With that, one should fill everything up to the end of the abode of Brahmā;
one should visualize the flood of the quarters blazing with the splendor of the mantra.
One should remember this entire circle of the earth as being cooked by fire.
O best of the twice-born, just as a vessel made of clay is purified by the power of a mantra,
so too does the purification of the site occur through the sprinkling of waves of nectar.
Having thus reflected, one should then perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) with the heart-mantra and the others.
One should perform the binding of the intermediate directions with the Astra-mantra, and from there upwards, the binding of the eyes with the Netra-mantra,
which is as radiant as ten thousand suns and takes the form of a blazing tunic.
Then, for the sake of protection, one should perform the ritual covering (avakuṇṭhana) with the armor (kavaca) while holding up the index finger.
In the evening, one should perform this purification of the elements through the two types of concentration (dhāraṇā).
By means of the mantra alone, accompanied by meditative visualization,
one should contemplate the deity situated at the region of the navel and gather up all impurity.
One should expel [the breath] through the path of the wind until it reaches the limit of the twelve finger-breadths;
having drawn back that which is free from sin and endowed with the wheel of the vital air,
one should then, by means of the nose-tip, recite this mantra for the purpose of filling the body.
One should meditate upon that [Self] residing in the heart by means of the breath with its movement restrained.
For the sake of calming the mind and indeed for the mastery of the vital air (vāyu),
one should then gradually expel the pure wind externally.

Thus, for the others, one should always perform the practice of time and repetition according to one's ability, increasing progressively with each subsequent stage except for the final *recaka*. Then,
at the *dvādaśānta*, one should visualize the Lord of Mantras, resembling molten gold.
Then, having visualized [the self] situated in the center of a circular orb resembling a thousand suns, one should burn away one's own body with those mantras,
starting from the tip of the big toe of the right foot at the location of the syllable of the crest (śikhākṣara).
Having meditated [on him] as being enveloped by flames like the fire at the end of an eon,
one should meditate on one's own body blazing forth on all sides.
One should contemplate the flame born of the body as having dissolved into the Lord of Mantras.
Having mentally presided over that divine and tranquil abode,
one should sprinkle one's own body with a flood of nectar from one’s own mantra.
Then, having drawn that image [of the deity] by means of one’s own mantra, one should place it within the heart.
Thus, having purified his body, he should then perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa),
by the mere performance of which he becomes equal to the God of gods and gains the authority for all rites such as worship.
One should then place the blazing supreme eight-syllable mantra upon both hands,
from the wrists to the tips of the nails, like the heat of the sun; thereafter,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal according to the prescribed rule.

Beginning from the first joint of the right index finger and proceeding through the joints of the fingers up to the end of the last joint, and then down to the end of the joint of the left index finger—this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭi* (emission) placement.
By reversing this order, however, it is *saṃhāra* (reabsorption); while the *sthitī* (maintenance) occurs when both hands are used together.
Beginning from the joint of the index finger and resting at the joint of the little finger,
one should place the syllables of the mantra upon the middle joints of the fingers using the two thumbs; however, one should place them like the vital breath (prāṇa) upon the first and last joints.
One should assign the five limbs, beginning with knowledge and ending with vigor, from the two thumbs to the two little fingers;
and like the root-mantra, one should assign the eye as pervasive over the upward-pointing fingers.
A crown on the right hand, the Śrīvatsa mark in the middle of the left;
the Kaustubha gem on the right side, and likewise a forest garland on the other;
and a lotus, radiant with shimmering rays, in the middle of the right [hand].
One should place a mace, blazing with its own splendor, upon the left palm;
on the right, a discus with the radiance of a thunderbolt, and on the left palm, a conch.
One should place Śrī upon the right hand and Puṣṭi upon the left palm.

First, from the right thumb to the end of the left [thumb], starting from the base of the fingers, one should sequentially place the Gāruḍa mantra upon the ten fingers. By this procedure, one should first perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands. (2.60–2.61)

Having performed the placement of the root mantra pervasively throughout the body from the crown of the head (*brahmarandhra*) down to the feet, one should then perform one of the three— creation, maintenance, or dissolution— placements starting from the feet up to the head. (2.62)

The placement from the crown of the head down to the feet is proclaimed as the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* (creation placement). The placement from the feet up to the crown of the head is intended as the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (dissolution placement).
The placement from the navel up to the heart is declared as the *sthiti-nyāsa* (maintenance placement).
Then, one should place [the fingers] on the crown of the head with the middle and index fingers; on the eyes with the ring fingers together with the thumbs; and in the center of the mouth.
Thereafter, one should place them on the heart with the tips of the index fingers together with the thumbs.
Likewise, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) at the navel with the thumb and the little finger;
with the four fingers excluding the thumb, one should perform it on the generative organ and the knees;
and with all the fingers, one should perform the placement on the two feet.
One should place every mantra-syllable encapsulated by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) everywhere.
Having thus performed the placement of the eight syllables (*aṣṭākṣaranyāsa*), one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
Then, that knowledge which is manifested there, one should place it in the heart.
Since sovereignty (aiśvarya) resides above the region of the head,
the lotus-eyed one is present everywhere, whether in the state of primordial nature (prākṛta) or in the state of ultimate reality (tāttvika).
However, the king of mantras, Śakti, resides in the crest-lock (śikhā), which rises upward from the fire within the heart.
The strength residing in all the limbs, together with the skin and permeating the entire body through the vital air— that which is called *vīrya*— should be placed in the two hands.
That which is the nature of internal consciousness, which brings peace to the darkness of material nature (*prakṛti*), [is to be placed there].
The element of fire is merged into its own fiery locus at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should place the crown upon the head, possessing the radiance of ten thousand rising suns;
and the Śrīvatsa on the left side of the chest, with a luster like the full moon.
Having placed the Kaustubha gem, which has the appearance of the fierce-rayed sun, upon his heart,
and having placed a forest garland made from various lotus-woods and flowers around his neck,
he should then place the lotus, mace, discus, and conch as before.
One should place Śrī on the left side up to the shoulder, and likewise Puṣṭi on the right; then one should place Garuḍa at the end of the two ankles and in the middle of the thighs.
Having thus performed the placement of the mantras, one should then [proceed] with both hands.
Having formed the mudrā, one should recollect the meditation and cultivate the thought, "I am the deity.
Having done this, one should thereafter commence the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga).
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) or others, one should firmly place the Brahmāñjali at the navel.

One should bring the mind to rest and withdraw the collection of senses that remain directed toward external objects. Having cast the mind into the intellect (buddhi), and that intellect into the sphere of knowledge (jñāna),
one should indeed perform actions through the cultivation of knowledge for the sake of the ultimate truth.
Then, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), together with his own name in the vocative case,
one should prepare the seat ending with fire (*vahni*) preceded by the syllable *śeṣa*. Having thus approached him, the visualization of that very [deity] should be performed within one's own heart.

In the past, within this body—a temple of the gods with four wheels and nine gates—there was a heart-lotus that hung downward, mounted upon the support of the throat-well; yet in the center of the ground of its pericarp, there is another which has grown facing upward. (2.81–2.82)
Above that, however, resides the manifestation of sound, characterized by the sun, moon, and fire;
it is the channel known as Śrīdīptibhāsvārā, whose form is unmanifest sound.
O Mahāmati, she exists above the two manifest wheels.
Emerging through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), she went beyond the path of the sun;
having pierced the netherworld (*pātāla*) by way of the gateway of the wind, she reached her own domain.
Everything that is an object of volition is his bondage, and therein it remains established.
Just as a cluster of jewels [is strung], the central channel (nāḍī) is indeed remembered as being thus;
within that very place previously mentioned, which is the locus of the mark,
there is indeed a cavity known as the moon and the sun, characterized by closing and opening.
There, resting upon the lotus and the sun, dwells the bee of Parāvāk—
the Śakti who is the mother of all mantras, belonging to the all-pervading Lord of all selves.
Resounding with the sound born of the phonemes, she is that which is remembered as the Śabdabrahman.
Preceded by the syllable *A* and ending with *Ha*, he assumes the form of a continuous stream;
in the sky at the conclusion of the *Nāda*, the Lord is accompanied by Ananta.
He holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is marked by the conch and the discus.
Endowed with two hands capable of uplifting the three worlds,
he who is peaceful and whose nature is pure consciousness, desiring to bestow grace upon his devotees,
has assumed a formal embodiment through a form that is beyond comparison, though he is in truth formless.
He nourished the entire universe with his splendor, which was equal to ten million full moons,
just as the sun does with its rays or as the ocean does with its waves;
he was accompanied by his own formless manifestations, beginning with Acyuta.
Filled with all the radiant and formless ornaments, abounding in waves of nectar, and possessing a body and feet free from all change;
having then invoked the Lord into the heart upon the prepared seat— 2.93–2.94.

Then one should perform the mantra-installation (mantranyāsa) of the Lord, excluding the hand-installation (hastanyāsa). Then, one should visualize the Gaṅgā falling from the center of the sky-lotus situated above, and [anoint] the head of the Blessed One with that nectar-water.
One should indeed perform an auspicious visualization of the objects of enjoyment that have been offered;
whatever object of enjoyment one may conceive, one should contemplate it as consisting of nectar, falling with speed from the sky and shimmering with moonlight. (2.96–2.97)
Then he should again visualize that king of mantras as nourished, gladdened, and immersed by those various floods of nectar which are themselves the very form of nectar.
Then, having offered the *arghya* to the God of gods according to the rule, [he should proceed].

One should perform the rites of *sannidhi* (presence), *sannirodha* (confinement), and *sāmmukhya* (facing). [Then one should worship] the heart and other limbs along with their ancillaries, as well as the ornaments such as the crown.
The club and other emblems, as well as the powers such as Lakṣmī and others,
Garuḍa, or whatever other forms reside in the body of the Lord—
since He is all-pervasive, they exist in their respective locations as His own radiant essence.
O twice-born ones, all those situated within that body should be worshipped in sequence with their respective mantras and offerings such as the arghya, but without [external] retinues.
O brahmins, this is indeed the sacrifice of dissolution (layayāga) which has been proclaimed regarding the heart and other [centers].
The King of Mantras is in the center of the pericarp, while those beginning with the Heart-mantra are on the eastern petals and so forth.
All these, both with their forms and alone, are to be worshipped;
for this is indeed called the "enjoyment" [aspect], O twice-born ones, through sacrifice performed either alone or separately.
The procedure for their worship is known as the "Chapter on Qualification.
Having thus performed the sacrifice called *laya* (dissolution) as well as that called *bhoga* (enjoyment),
and having meditated upon them with the most purifying enjoyments born of contemplative realization (*bhāvanā*), [one should proceed].
One should worship the deity within one's own heart and address him thus:
"Welcome, O Lord of the gods! O Acyuta, grant me your presence. Accept this mental worship, contemplated according to its true meaning. (2.106–2.107)
Having recognized that the Lord was well-pleased and inclined toward grace,
the best of the twice-born should undertake the mental sacrifice in detail,
with divine, purifying, imperishable, and auspicious offerings produced by mere resolve.
One should worship the God who grants all desires and who assumes the form of the mantra.
First, having offered anointing oil and fragrant unguents, then a bath, and then ointments;
and having presented garments first, followed by fragrant garlands.
One should visualize [the deity] adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and crowns,
and with a variegated waist-belt made of gold and jewels;
one should further adorn him with pure pearl necklaces set with rubies.
One should present to Viṣṇu an umbrella resembling the full moon and provided with a golden handle, as well as an auspicious peacock-feather fan,
fragrant, sweet, and abundant, mixed with camphor powder.
Having offered incense to the Blessed One and a garland of lamps with ghee,
he should then present the honey-mixture (madhuparka) soaked in honey and clarified butter,
as well as various sacrificial animals, images, and purifying birds.
One should first offer personified herbs, rice, dūrvā grass, and trees rich with excellent fruit;
then, having offered various pure foods, both solid and soft, in great abundance. (2.115–2.116)
Having offered heart-pleasing fruits and roots arising from the six tastes,
as well as various drinks possessing the six tastes,
O twice-born ones, all these things intended for his own enjoyment were presented through the power of devotion and faith. (2.117)
One should also present to the God various musical instruments that are not contradictory [to the ritual], accompanied by dance and song,
as well as the sounds of kettledrums and tabors, together with the recitation of hymns of praise. (2.118–2.119)
One should meditate upon all things belonging to the three worlds of the God of gods,
while fanning him with a fly-whisk adorned with a network of small bells,
and [visualizing] canopies, banners, and various kinds of flags.
Having offered [these] with devotion to the Lord with a serene inner self,
he should then remember Him causing those intermediate gifts— elephants, horses, cows, vehicles, and well-adorned fine garments— to be accepted.
Having offered himself, along with his sons, his wife, and all his possessions, bowing his head and filled with tears of joy,
[he should offer] the mudrā consisting of the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) accompanied by the mantra.
One should contemplate Viṣṇu’s bound [mudrā], which fulfills all desires; then one should perform the special worship of Acyuta with both hands joined in añjali, filled with golden flowers.
Having extended [the breath],
one should recite the root mantra with effort through the inhalation (*pūraka*) and other [breath-control techniques],
resembling the sound of a long-ringing bell, for as long as it occurs.

Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who possesses a radiance equal to fire, sun, and moon, and is pervaded by two throbbing rays of light, one should completely suppress ignorance. One should cast that joined palms (añjali) toward the head of that very one whose form is the mantra.
One should again present the *arghya* offering and once more a beautiful handful (*añjali*) of flowers.
Having displayed the mudrā called the *mūla*, one should begin the mental recitation (*japa*),
without a fixed number according to one's capacity, accompanied by the ringing of the bell.

Then, for the heart and other [limbs] located in the places of enjoyment, one should sequentially display the mudrās with the mind and perform the recitation once for each. Having praised them properly with pure hymns and mantras, one should propitiate them.
"Having thus worshipped at the conclusion of the recitation and having brought [the deity] down, one should perform the external sacrifice.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Procedure for the Mental Sacrifice" in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the venerable *Pāñcarātra*.
The second chapter:
Śrī. Now begins the third chapter.
Having performed the mental sacrifice according to the ancient procedure,
one should then worship in the external image with an action joined by devotion.
O best of sages, listen properly to the ritual for the external sacrifice.
The deity, who abides in the form of light within the space of the heart-lotus—
having brought him from that place, one should cause him to enter the center of the eyes;
one should then take refuge in that which was previously described as being named Vāsudeva.
Then, O best of sages, with eyes fixed in a steady gaze and reciting the Locana mantra, one should behold all the requisites for the sacrifice;
by that means, the entire collection of ritual substances is purified.
Whatever great sacrificial implements were previously acquired,
having placed them all at that moment to the left,
one should set down a water-pot filled with strained water; in the center, one should place an auspicious seat (bhadrāsana).
Whatever yellowish leaves, flowers, or other such items may be seen,
having gathered them with one's hand and placed them in a pure location,
[one should use] cow-products, yak-tail fans, peacock feathers, or kusha grass.
Having wiped the auspicious seat with a very white cloth,
or subsequently with abundant water filtered through cloth,
one should wash it with the twelve-syllable mantra, preceded and followed by the *praṇava*.
Having thus washed the support for propitiation with water,
one should then clear it of the hosts of obstructing spirits by means of the weapon-mantra (astra).
Then, having placed the auspicious [liṅga] consisting of mantra upon that which is to be propitiated, one should proceed.
Having fashioned an image made of metal or stone, endowed with all requisites and possessed of all auspicious marks for the sake of self-perfection,
one should then worship the deity with divine offerings of water for honor, water for the feet, and water for sipping.
Therefore, having removed the *arghya* and other offerings that have been consumed, and having saluted [the guest],
O twice-born ones, one should offer them to Viṣvaksena and purify [the mouth] with soft water using a brush made of *uśīra* grass or bamboo. Then, one should wash [the mouth] with water.
Or, while reciting the root mantra, one should perform the three paths for the Lord.
One should cause the God of gods to put on two well-washed garments.
Whatever flowers and other offerings have been consumed by the image of the Blessed One depicted in the painting—
Having removed that [dust], one should wipe away the dust with a cloth;
or else, O twice-born ones, after entering the sacrificial hall,
one should perform various other rites beginning and ending with the placement of the *bhadrāsana*.
Alternatively, having arranged the auspicious seat and so forth at that time,
and having performed the first three paths according to the prescribed ritual,
one should then commence everything as described for the image at the start of the worship of the yoga-throne.
Then, O best of sages, having washed the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, and having filled those vessels with filtered water,
one should place the ritual substances into the primary and secondary *arghya* vessels and so forth, in their proper order.

In one [vessel], he should place sandalwood and the like, as well as dūrvā grass and white mustard seeds; likewise, unbroken grains, tips of kuśa grass, rice, and sesame seeds, along with excellent gems, minerals, and fruits. || 3.20–3.21 ||
In the second [offering], there are four drops of curd, honey, clarified butter, and milk;
with the tip of *kuśa* grass, it includes *bāhlīka*, flowers, sesame seeds, and rice,
as well as *dūrvā*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *śyāmāka*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpaka*.

One should place padmaka and kundareṇu into the vessel for water for the feet (pādyapātra). O best of sages, one should place all the collection of cinnamon, cardamom, and so forth, along with camphor and sandalwood, into the vessel known as the vessel for water for sipping (ācamanīyapātra).
One should cast into the bathing water costus, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, campaka, vacā, kaccora, and mustā; indeed,
one should perform the application of all these substances everywhere with the *hṛdayamantra* alone.
Having placed the vessels upon the support according to their own prior rule,
and having arranged them in the directions beginning with Vāyu (the northwest) with the respective conceptualization mantras,
one should say "Oṃ, I prepare the arghya" and place it in the position of Vāyu.
In the same manner, one should place a water-pot (kalaśa) in the northeast for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana);

in the southeast for the purpose of bathing; and likewise in the southwest for the purpose of the foot-water (pādya). Alternatively, one may place a second vessel for the offering of honor (arghya) either in front or in the middle of those.
Or rather, O twice-born ones, having first placed the vessels upon the support,
he should touch them with his hand while reciting the respective mantras for their visualization,
and contemplate them with the heart-seed syllable using both the right and left hands.
Then, having formed the Kāmadughā mudrā, which flows with the mantra joined to it, one should produce the Sun and Moon arising from the burning of the substance—
[the Moon] in the form of a cow, resembling a mountain of snow, and situated in the supportless state.
With that [mantra], one should transform the entire collection of substances as they are into nectar.
In the eighth group, the third letter situated above the letter *va*,
joined with the vowel *ī* and the anusvāra, and placed between the word *namaḥ* and the *praṇava* (oṃ).
O twice-born ones, this mantra belonging to Saurabheya is joined with his own voice;
thus, by means of these two voices, which consist of Agni and Soma,
having brought it to a state of fitness and the proper stage, he should dispatch whatever has been uttered.
Then, having taken water in a vessel, one should pour into it [the water] consecrated by the heart-mantra.
[One should also place] very white śāli rice together with flowers and fragrance;
this should be consecrated many times with the heart-mantra preceded by the *praṇava*.
Sprinkling with the water drawn from that [vessel], while reciting the Astra-mantra,
one should sprinkle one's own seat, the site, and likewise the ritual implements.
Then, having consecrated the arghya and other offerings with the Astra-mantra and the Mūla-mantra.
With that very [mantra] consisting of six limbs, one should perform the worship with flowers and other offerings.
Having worshipped the incense burner and the bell according to the rule,
one should first ring the bell and then worship the arghya and other items with incense.
Now the worship of the incense burner and the bell is described:
it should be divine, marked with lotuses and wheels, having the form of a supporting lotus-stalk;
it should have a single stem, and the remainder [the base] should be the pervasive Lord with seven hoods.
With palms joined in perpetual reverence, he was constantly meditating upon the Supreme Cause.
The Lord should be depicted with a discus and a plow in his hands, seated upon a lotus throne,
bearing incense, and adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
They know that the discus is the heart of the wheel and the lotus is the hollow of the heart.
Those which are called the spokes in the wheel are known as the twelve *nāḍīs*.
O Brahmins, those *kiṅkiṇīs* that are situated there should be understood as the subtle *nāḍīs*,
among which the central power (*madhyamā śakti*) is like the curve of a serpent.
Having the appearance of a smoke-grey color, she emerged after piercing the egg;
arisen from the heart of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), she dissolved at the end of the Truth (Satya).
Indeed, impelled by her, the Lord and Master, whose form is the mantra, [arose] as the Self.
It remains present nearby and likewise would burn even that which has been utterly destroyed.
O Brahmin-sage, by means of this mantra, grasp that mantra:
having first extracted the syllable *oṃ*, then again the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). 3.46–3.47.
Then, one should utter the word *anantāya* joined with *vyomānandena*,
followed by the word *kālāgnirūpāya* and likewise the word *jagaddhūmapada*.
One should then form the word *sugāndhine* and [the word] *sarvagandhavahāya*.
"O Nārada, the thirty-one syllable phrase consisting of *namaḥ* and *svāhā* joined together is declared by the twice-born to be the mantra for the incense vessel;
when combined with the appropriate mudrā and meditation, it is supreme and bestows all accomplishments."
Having worshipped the incense burner with this mantra immediately thereafter, one should perform the worship of the bell; its procedure is now declared:
first taking the *praṇava*, and after that, *ananteśa*.
O best of sages, having pierced that [point] with fire from above and below,
one should then mark it with five dots by means of that which bestows sovereignty over the three worlds;
thereafter, at its conclusion, one should place the word of the Ṛgveda sound.
The mantra alone is one step, and another is that which is endowed with the syllable *svāhā*.
At its end, one should place the Supreme Self, situated upon the support of wisdom,
joined with the head-syllable *bhū* atop the *bhūdhara*.

O Sage, the thirteen-syllable mantra known as Ghaṇṭā bestows all perfections; it nourishes the universe and grants sovereignty over the three worlds from within. At the time of its ritual placement (nyāsa), one should indeed pronounce its final syllable with a protracted vowel (pluta).
O best of the twice-born, focus your mind upon that meditation joined with dhyāna:
one should meditate on the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as being face-downward and filled with the noise of people;
and above that, one should remember an eight-petaled lotus together with its stalk.
One should meditate upon the goddess in the center of that [lotus], which has scattered petals, is brilliantly white, and possesses beautiful filaments and a pericarp; she is endowed with eight arms,
and in her four principal hands, there are emblems such as the lotus.
She holds a crystal rosary and likewise a book of consciousness;
in her other two pairs of hands, she grants fearlessness and bestows boons.
She is seated in the lotus posture, with eyes as broad as lotus petals.
Resembling the interior of a lotus, adorned with the mark of a lotus,
covered with white ornaments, and embellished with yellow garments;
she vomits forth a flood of mantras and is endowed with the radiance of the flames of mantras.

At the time of every formal worship, one should always properly remember her being well-praised by the gods, by Brahmā and others who discourse on Brahman, and by the ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas who act for the benefit of the worlds, as she is being bowed to.
For the practitioner who worships with this [visualization], accomplishment is not far off.
Having meditated thus, one should worship properly with the water for honor (arghya) and other offerings,
and then recollect that which is the Great Śabdabrahman, situated in the center of the space of the heart-lotus.
"O Lotus-born One, this is the supreme nature of mantras: it is eternally manifest, incomparable, beyond the scope of practice, and therefore cannot be taught to others who lack devotion. (3.66)
That which exists in the tenfold form of the word beginning with the syllable *akṣara* and ending in *visarga*,
abiding in the form of various mantras within the body of phonemes (varṇavigraha)—
the mantra that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation when received from the mouth of a true guru.
It should be known by devotees intent on divine rites as residing in five locations:
in an external image and the like, at the tip of the tongue, in the heart-lotus, in the column of incense smoke, and in the auspicious sound of the bell. (3.68–3.69)
O Great-minded One, know that [the power] which abides in the heart, internalizing the very light of its own nature, is yet severed even from its intermediate form;
furthermore, know that it assumes the body of *vaikharī*, supported by the smoke of incense.
When the bell is being rung, it is experienced without interruption.
Having thus recollected her, whose body is invested with one's own mantra,
and who has been worshipped with offerings such as *arghya* accompanied by incense, while remaining absorbed in meditation— (3.71–3.72)
Then one should properly ring the bell, which possesses an excellent sound, awakens the mantras, causes the three worlds to tremble, and destroys all that is evil.
For this ringing is the awakener of mantras that have fallen asleep.
She is the water that washes away all obstacles and the purifier of all mantras.
Indeed, this resonance at the end of the *praṇava* has gone into dissolution within the power of sound (*śabdaśakti*).
Mantras are known to have the letters as their body, and deities have the mantras as their body.

Those [sounds] rooted in the resonance of the bell are awakened and bestow the accomplishment of karma. O best of sages, the Śakti arising from the supreme sound takes the form of the resonance of the bell; having attained the state of phonemes (*varṇa*), she consists of those very phonemes.
The bodies of the mantras are imagined in thousands of various forms.
Indeed, by this power acting according to its own will, and through its inherent capacity,
it manifests itself here for the sake of bestowing grace upon those devotees whose minds are purified.
O tiger among sages, because they provide protection through contemplation (*manana*) and bestow their own state, they are celebrated as *mantras*. They are likewise unmanifest sounds and formless.
And when the bell is rung, thousands [of emanations] emerge.
For this very reason, O best of sages, she is proclaimed as the Mother of Mantras;
she is the power (śakti) named Ghaṇṭā, and she is Vāgīśā and Sarasvatī.
All mantras reside in speech, and that which is to be spoken is established within the mantra;
therefore, the entire universe, both internal and external, consists of the nature of mantra.
Consequently, everything is contained within the sound of the bell; for that reason, one should ring it first.
At the invocation, the offering of water (arghya), the incense, the lamp, the enjoyment of the food offering (naivedya),
at the conclusion of the recitation and praise, when the libation to the fire has commenced, at the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and at the dismissal of the mantras— || 3.83–3.84 ||
During the worship of Viṣvaksena, in the performance of his ritual service,
and especially at the time of offering oblations to the deities,
one should always employ this [mantra] correctly for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the mantra. (3.85)
Except at the time of worship, there is no benefit in moving it elsewhere.
One who desires success in the rite of worship must not perform the worship without this [bell].
Then, having offered incense, one should do so accompanied by the sound of the ghaṇṭā for the vessels.
One should offer incense at the proper time, just as one offers the *arghya* and other offerings, each once.
However, in the case of a secondary ritual (*anukalpa*), the wise practitioner should perform the repetition using the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).
This applies during the invocation (*āvāhana*), the presence (*sannidhāna*), the confinement (*sannirodha*), and likewise during the worship (*arcana*).
At the time of dismissal, one should always begin by offering the *arghya* from the vessel;
with that water, one should likewise perform the honoring (*arhaṇa*) and the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
One should perform the bringing forward (*praṇayana*), the taking up, the pleasing, and the act of gratification during the rite of propitiation.
The sprinkling of all objects with water from another source should always be performed at the commencement and at the conclusion of all undertakings;
it is for the pacification of deficiencies and excesses, as well as for the pacification of errors in knowledge.
O high-minded one, that offering of arghya must always be performed for the pervasive Lord who is the essence of the mantra; likewise,
it is required for the worship of the pitcher (kumbha), the secondary pitcher (upakumbha), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the weapon-mantra (astramantra), the jar (kalaśa),
and for the propitiation of the spirits (bhūtas) and the teachers (guru) and others.
For the sake of self-worship following the disciple of Dakṣa, one should perform the worship of those stationed at the door,
as well as the temple, the seat, the deities, the gurus, and their lineage, who possess the forms of emblems, limbs, retinues, powers, and ornaments. (3.94)
Likewise, in the worship of the deities residing within the enclosure of the mandala,
one should perform the binding of mudrās, the cleansing of the hands and eyes, their worship,
and the washing [of the vessel], as well as the offering of water for the feet (pādya), always from the third vessel.
But from the fourth [vessel], one should then provide water for sipping (ācamana) at the appropriate time, as well as water for washing the hands, rinsing the mouth, and cleansing the face.
One should also perform the bath with bathing substances; this is the procedure for the officiant.
Having drawn a little water from the second *arghya* vessel,
one should worship the mantras assigned to one's own form in their proper order,
using separately prepared perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Then, having taken up the *arghya* and other offerings, he should worship the deities stationed at the door,
whether standing outside the doorway or remaining seated.
[He should worship] Vāstu, Kṣetreśa, Garuḍa, Dvāraśrī, Caṇḍa, and Pracaṇḍa.

Having worshipped the deities with offerings such as *arghya* and other honors, one should worship those residing in the temples. O Great-minded One, in temples that are divided into many varieties— whether extensive or complete— one should proceed according to their circular or rectangular forms.
I shall describe the arrangement of the deities and the principles (*tattva*) of the worlds above the path of the world,
having firmly established the entire *bhūrloka* upon the surface of the earth as its foundation;
likewise, the *bhuvarloka* is situated within the pedestals of the temples (*prāsāda-pīṭha*).

One should remember [the path] as far as the shins for the heavenly world (svarloka), and that which goes above it; starting from the regions of the sacrificial stones up to the ground of the great peak,
one reaches Janaloka at its altar, and the world named Tapas upon its departure.
One should remember that world known as Satya within the crest-lock (śikhā),
and one should contemplate the pervasion of the seven worlds in this manner.
Then, one should contemplate the upward pervasion in due order.
One should perform the placement while recollecting the sixfold path situated within the stones of the water-jar (kumbha).
One should contemplate the pervasion of the paths situated within that which has become the seed;
having sprouted from the seed, it subsequently attains manifestation.
From the foundation stone of the base up to the pinnacle of the palace,
or from the world-realm as it actually exists, one should meditate upon [the deity] everywhere;
one should observe the path of the feet extending as far as the limit of the height of the womb-chamber.

The path of mantra extends to the end of the *śukanāsā*; the path of reality (*tattvādhvan*) extends to the edge of the altar; the path of power (*kalādhvan*) extends to the end of the throat, while the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) is above that. Having thus established the pervasion of the paths, one should then deposit the principles (*tattvas*).
O twice-born ones, having joined the principle of earth upon the surface of the ground,
one should place the principle of water on the pedestal; one should contemplate the fiery principle as far as the thighs,
and the principle of air up to the region of the neck, and beyond that.
Space should be situated at the peak;
from that point upward, one should sequentially deposit the subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with sound, down as far as the soles of the feet.
On the sides are the two nostrils and the two ears; the eye-fluid is said to be [located] there.
The two eyes should be the windows, the tongue the altar called *bhadraka*,
the nose the *śukanāsa* (gargoyle), and the mouth is declared to be the doorway. The pillars should be understood as the hands, and the pedestals (*pādaśilā*) and *ghaṭas* as the feet.
From the two winds comes the emergence of water; the generative organ (*upastha*) is situated between them.
The internal space (*antarvyoma*) is to be known as the mind (*manas*); pride (*garva*) is located upon the Brahma-stone.
The intellect (*buddhi*) is to be known as the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) would be within that.
The twenty-fifth should be known as the Supreme Man (pratimāpuruṣa).
When the principles (tattvas) have been thus deposited, the deities are to be deposited in sequence.
Beneath the stone that serves as the base for the jar is the king of serpents named Ananta.
It is beautifully adorned by a circle of hoods numbering one thousand.
Above that is situated a wheel graced by a thousand spokes;
know that stone, which is all-pervading, to be designated as the support for the pitcher (kalaśa).
That middle power is the universal, partless, and supreme energy of the Lord.
O twice-born ones, as for those nine jars situated above it,
in the central jar among them resides [the deity] together with his limbs and retinue.
Having worshipped the Lord of Mantras with the root mantra,
the preceptor should then worship Vāsudeva and the others located in the directions starting from the east;
he should also worship Aniruddha and the others located in the intermediate directions according to the method of dissolution.
Within that ninefold arrangement, O best of the twice-born, you— the sphere of Īśa— and the others should be remembered as pervading everywhere in sequence:
Jñānabhāgā, Nivasati, and likewise Ānandabalā and Prabhā.
Sarvagā, Brahmavadanā, Dyotakī, Satyavikramā,
and Sampūrṇā— these are said to be the powers that sustain the universe.
One should place them upon the eight stones set out outside [the maṇḍala] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
From the southeast corner (Agni) up to the northeast (Īśa),
and again from the east to the north, there are four [squares] beginning with Adharma;
on the ground between the stones, there are six by six in sequence.
The [syllables] ending with the final letter should be placed starting from the first letter.
Then, when eight stones have been laid for the purpose of the courtyard wall,
one should place the previously mentioned lords of the directions as before, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should contemplate that wheel of the intermediate grounds revolving like sparks of fire,
pervading the area of the ground as far as the courtyard by means of the syllable *kṣā*;
and outside, the walls of the courtyard together with their foundations and their attendants.
One should install the group of eight beginning with Indra, starting from the east and ending at the northeast corner.
Upon such stones, both those situated within and those embedded in the ground,
this wheel— the support of all— is established, resting upon the root of the branch.
When the two branches, consisting of knowledge and action, are situated as a pair,
the primordial [deity] of the Supreme Lord resides above the door upon the *udumbara* post;
he is established there, pervading all directions, and from his back, in the middle region.
The entire Dharma, in its four quarters, remained established in him, O best of beings.
When the two door-panels of the gate were fashioned, O most excellent of the twice-born, these two—
Kāla-Vaiśvānara and the Lord of Waters— were indeed appointed there.
Positioned by means of the south-north alignment either above the door-panels or on the two sides of that door, or on the two sides of the door of the glorious pavilion,
the two Lords of Treasures known as Śaṅkha and Padma are to be worshipped in due order.
Then, in the assembly of shanks and likewise in the intermediate spaces,
there is the sequential worship of the deities who provide the requisites for existence;
as well as Time, which is the controller, and the scripture characterized by its various limbs.
The lords of knowledge, Śiva together with Rudra and his retinue,
the assembly of Prajāpatis, Indra with his entourage,
the seven ancient sages, and the other planets surrounded by the stars and so forth. (3.139)
Jīmūta, all the Nāgas, and the most excellent host of Apsarases;
the medicinal herbs, animals, and all the sacrifices together with their constituent parts; the higher sciences (vidyā) and other branches of knowledge, as well as the fire and the wind.
Candrārka (Moon and Sun), Vāri (Water), and Vasudhā (Earth)— these groups of deities,
numbering twenty-four, are the immortals who serve as the instruments of worldly existence.
The forms beginning with Keśava are situated above the front of the shanks;
thereafter, these should be installed in sequence upon the surface of the pedestal:
the discus and conch, the mace and lotus, the plow, the club, and the arrows.
The Śārṅga bow, the sword and shield, the staff, the axe, the spear, the noose, the goad, the mallet, the thunderbolt, and the javelin—
these are placed upon the square temple, as well as on the square-and-rectangular one. (3.145)
One should place Garuḍa above the stone slab in the four corners;
above that, on the altar, the lords of sages are to be meditated upon.
These are in the sequence starting from the east, and then the body with its many peaks [is to be visualized].
The god Vāmana, who possesses a dwarf body, is all-pervading Trivikrama;
likewise Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa;
and another Rāma, the wielder of the flaming axe, and yet another Rāma, the wielder of the bow.
The Lord Kalkī, the knower of the Vedas, and the Master reclining upon Pātāla;
then, on the surface of the neck, one should meditate upon the Tortoise who supports Pātāla;
as well as Varāha, Nārasiṃha, and indeed the one who brought back the nectar.
Then Śrīpati, of divine body, the beloved soul, the bearer of nectar;
the conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, the great remover of the Pārijāta tree;
the Lord of the World, the peaceful soul, Dattātreya, the Great Lord.
"O best of the twice-born, [it was said] that the Blessed One lay upon the nyagrodha tree;
then, O best of the twice-born, having divided the summit into three equal parts, [the measurement extends] as far as the altar-base supporting the water-pot."
In the lower portion, the remaining deities of the Vaibhava class are to be meditated upon in succession:
the Lord Ananta, the divine Madhusūdana whose self is Śakti, Kapila the presiding deity of Vidyā, Viśvarūpa, and Vihagaṃgama. (3.153–154)
Kroḍātman, Baḍaka, Vakra, Dharma, Vāgīśvara, and likewise Deva Ekārṇavaśaya— these are remembered as the twelve.
Dhruva, however, is all-pervading and is situated in the station above them.
Above that, however, Padmanābha stands pervading all.
Vāsudeva, the eternal one, is to be worshipped at the mouth of the *śukanāsā* (the gargoyle);
but in that part of the temple where a *śukanāsā* has not been constructed, [he is to be worshipped] there.
There, one should first recollect Vāsudeva at the tip of the nose;
on the remaining three parts of the nose, Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are to be worshipped in sequence.
Alternatively, [they may be] Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Ananta.
They should be worshipped in sequence in the four directions, or alternatively in order:
Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayānana;
or else the four beginning with Nara, or even Dharmamūrti and the others.
Or else, Paraśurāma and the others should be remembered in their sequential order;
all of these may be accompanied by their Śaktis or may be alone,
adorned upon the surface of the altar with trees provided with leaves and creepers.
One should then place the six-spoked wheel upon the *sāmalasāraka* wood.
Therein resides the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the supreme Person and the support of the world,
who eternally sustains the worlds, the multitude of travelers on the path, and even the deities, beginning with the [first] principle (*tattva*).
Having ascended and stationed himself upon the roof of the temple,
he should worship the god Sudarśana, the Lord of Weapons, at its summit. O best of Brahmins, [he should also worship] upon the various parts of the temple in the sequence that has been declared.
Whichever limb has not been assigned among those that serve as the supports for the deities,
or wherever it may be in excess, one should perform it there as well,
by means of the intellect through the collective assignment of the deities to their respective locations.

Or rather, one should avoid performing a sacrifice to the deities when the constituent parts [of the ritual] are incomplete. O best of the twice-born, the seven worlds, the paths, the hosts of beings, and the deities must be meditated upon by practitioners as being formless.
Likewise, when the celestial chariot (vimāna) had been completed and consecrated by the gods, O best of Brahmins,
the emblems and other features of the forms of the deities within that chariot,
as well as their respective positions, were arranged there according to the prescribed rules.
Having carefully scrutinized even the constituent parts of the celestial chariot (vimāna),
one should worship them with a mind full of heedfulness and preceded by meditative concentration (dhyāna).
[This applies] to the marks and so forth of the images, as well as to the components of the temple (prāsāda).
Because its characteristics and so forth are not examined while it exists in an unmanifest form,
O best of Brahmins, one should carefully and thoroughly investigate dreams and the like through the instruction of a supreme teacher, O lord of the twice-born. (3.171–3.172)
O twice-born ones, O best of sages, even if the characteristics and other qualities are deficient or even inverted, one should not perform the rites of characterization and so forth otherwise;
for one should not examine the characteristics with the desire to alter them. (3.173)

However, if for the purpose of altering [the image], the characteristics and so forth are examined, then by performing that [alteration], one's life-span is exhausted; through such characteristics, one goes to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, [one must act] even in the case of self-manifested [images] and the like.
Having examined the characteristics and other features of the forms situated within the celestial chariot (vimāna),
as well as their respective locations and even the constituent parts of the chariot itself,
one should determine the nature of the form exactly as it exists.

One should perform worship with one's own respective mantra, clearly distinguished by its particular characteristic mark and so forth; O twice-born ones, among all [types of shrines], that which is self-manifested (*svayambhū*) in temples is the most excellent.
The Blessed Lord, the God, himself remains there in that very form;
the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward his devotees, is personally present there.
When the defects such as old age have arisen, they never abandon him.
These supreme powers of the mantras each abide in their own respective locations;
even those situated within the temple are preceded by what is self-manifested.
The forms of the All-pervasive Lord are to be correctly understood through the yoga previously described.
Even those whose identity is clearly manifested throughout the three worlds by means of missiles, mantras, and banners, they too bear a multitude of marks upon their feet. (3.182)
On the forehead, the shoulder-cloth, the back, the two palms,
the mass of body hair, and the head— having thus specifically examined each of those various marks for the sake of determining the karma of the practitioners: || 3.183 ||
One should worship them with designators fixed to their respective forms.
O lords of sages, those for whom the multitude of marks on the feet and so forth is not clearly visible, one should worship them preceded by the six-syllable mantra. 3.184–185.
But by means of a single desired mantra among those that are all-pervasive—
having understood this correctly, the knower of mantras who worships in such a manner obtains the fruit of worship; otherwise, he experiences the opposite.

All these [deities] beginning with Loka have been described in sequence for the occasions of propitiating the God of immeasurable splendor. Having performed the worship of the door-guarding deities, one should thereafter perform their worship.

O best of the twice-born, with his own name preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with the word of salutation (*namaskāra*), he should perform the offering of water for honor (*arghya*), touching, and garlands, along with incense,
in front of the God of gods, outside the gateway.
Or, having gone to the location of the inner mandala, one should perform worship in due order.
Thus, O twice-born ones, in whichever variety of temple, the best of practitioners perform worship once, twice, or thrice a day.
There, the omnipresent Lord is always present and constantly performs [his rites] eternally.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born,
a practitioner who longs for spiritual success should perform the worship of Viṣṇu preceded by that adoration.
He who always acts in this way with devotion, directed toward no other,
quickly attains his desires both in this world and in the next;
but he who acts for the sake of liberation goes to the supreme state.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Deities of the Vimāna," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
O twice-born ones, having thus worshipped the gods stationed in the palace, Nārada likewise performed the worship of the deities of the door-surrounds in due order.

O best of sages, one should cause the residence of Viṣvaksena to be established at the end of that which constitutes the limbs of the assembly of deities beginning with the door-keepers (2.2). And for men of small intelligence, [the temple] should end with Viṣvaksena.
For those who are single-mindedly devoted [to other deities], such worship indeed causes mental distress;
it also creates obstacles for the disciples regarding their primary practice.
Therefore, out of compassion for them, one should perform worship with the thought that they are servants of the Lord.
Even that which is performed in this manner, devoid of devotion and faith,
they accept with bowed heads— even if given with indifference—
having reflected in their hearts with their intellects upon the supreme spiritual good. (4.5)
For all of them consist of the Imperishable, and their minds are fixed upon His mind. From this much alone— namely, from the worship of those who are single-mindedly devoted to the Guru—
there occurs the removal of obstacles, since they are indeed servants of Hari.
Having thus performed the worship at the door,
one should then take a flower with the thumb and the three fingers [of the right hand] facing forward;
having consecrated it with the *astra* mantra, one should visualize the *cakra* above it.
One should cast [the weapon] within the sacrificial hall— sharp-edged, blazing in form, raining down fire and thunderbolts, and the destroyer of the multitude of obstacles. Then,
the Brahmin should raise his right index finger with its tip facing upward.
Having remembered that [noose], which is conjoined with the *śikhā* mantra and possesses a radiance flashing like lightning, and while brandishing it, one should enter the sacrificial hall.
Then, having sprinkled one's own seat with the water for the *arghya* and *pādya* offerings,
one should sit upon the seat and, being composed, begin the sacrifice.
At this time, one should perform the inspection of all the ritual enjoyments.

Having placed the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) starting from the base, one should then cleanse it with the hand, or with a ritual grass-bundle (kūrca), using water from the sprinkling and offering (arghya); furthermore,
one should clear it of all hosts of obstacles with weapon-mantra flowers.

There, one should meditate upon this King of Wheels as containing the entire world, the refuge of all the gods, and the support of all, yet internally dissolved within it. One should worship it with the syllable *praṇava*, then with its own name, and finally with the word "namas" at the end.
One should perform the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha preceded by meditative inquiry, using water for the guest-offering (arghya), fragrant unguents, incense, and garlands made of various flowers,
addressing it in due order with its own name, preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ."
Then, one should perform the mental placement (vinyāsa) of all the mantras there,
according to the proper method, preceded by the offering of flowers.
The seat together with the image is declared to be the Yoga-pīṭha.
In the yoga of investigation, one should fashion the Yoga-pīṭha;
that is said to be the seat of the mantra (tan-mantrāsana). O lords of sages, one should perform the placement of the mantra (mantra-nyāsa) everywhere beneath the pīṭha of the deity residing therein.

Above that, one should remember the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti), then the Tortoise (Kūrma) known as the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), and in the center, the Lord Ananteśa, the support of all. In the directions starting from the southeast and ending in the northeast, one should place the fourfold [qualities] beginning with Dharma.
One should place the first [syllable], such as *a*, at the beginning of the east, and the final one, such as *m*, at the end of the north.
Above that, one should meditate on a lotus by means of its own name;
likewise, above that, one should visualize the sun resting upon the petals and the moon upon the ground of the filaments.
Then one should worship the Fire-god situated upon the pericarp with scents and other offerings.
A firm restraint of the mantras is always prescribed therein;
wherever a particular form is appropriate, one should perform that specific placement (nyāsa) in that place.
One should likewise worship in due order upon the seat of Kalabimba.
However, there is a temporary suspension of the mantras therein,
for the Lord of Mantras sits facing [the practitioner] once he has been summoned.
One should therefore arrange the placement of the [deities] such as Dharma and the rest with reference to that [central point],
because the Supreme Lord faces the practitioner;
for that seat is indeed of the nature of consciousness, perfected by its being the vehicle of this [Lord].
And thus, while the Lord is lying upon this immovable seat, one should worship, in sequence, up to the end of Fire below him; then one should worship Ananta.
But when he has mounted his vehicle, one should worship Tārkṣya in the place where Ananta resides.
Below the pedestal of the goddesses Lakṣmī and the others, one should place the Lord of Serpents (Phaṇīśvara);
in its corners, Dharma and the rest; and above that, a manifest lotus.
Then, one should install [the deities] within it for three watches according to the previously mentioned method.
Then one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and the other deities near the pedestal. Beginning from the northwest corner according to the directions of the self,
one should worship while placing bundles of darbha grass like clusters of flowers.
One should worship Viṣvaksena, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and the Gurus immediately thereafter;
likewise, one should worship the Gurus known as the "Supreme" (parama) and all the Gurus,
as well as the assembly of the Primordial Siddhas who are intent on meditation upon the Blessed One.

One should worship with the *arghya* and other offerings, in due order and by their respective names, those who hold the perpetual office, the authoritative ones who know the reality of the Lord, the four other Manus, and the seven ancient sages (4.34–35).
O best of sages, listen to the meditation for all of them in due order:
one should then contemplate the Infinite, which resembles an infinite number of moons, adorned with a garland of a thousand hoods and embellished by a thousand arms. (4.36)
Adorning the surface of his own body with the hollow of his own hands joined as a cup,
he appeared like one possessing white lotuses, a conch, a rosary, and a discus in his hands;
yet his mind was truly terrified by the fear that he might fall.
Saying "Do not fear," he granted fearlessness even unto the realm of Brahmā;
his radiance was like that of the moon, pearl, and crystal clear as ice.
Then Dharmaja and the others, four in number, with shoulders and faces like those of lions—
Resplendent like rubies, coral, fire, and pomegranate fruits,
and inwardly consumed by passion, know that these four, who resemble the sovereign of kings,
are each sixteen years of age and preceded by the Dharma.
All are endowed with fine garments, excellent flowers, and beautiful ornaments;
all hold a conch and a lotus, and indeed have hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
With the lotuses to be placed [upon them] arranged, the practitioners [should do so] for the sake of their own spiritual accomplishment.
With their inner faculties fully surrendered to the Supreme Cause of Mantras,
they meditated upon the inconceivable, unmanifest Lotus, radiant as snow, gold, and fire—
tranquil, eight-armed, gentle, and seated in the svastika posture.

During the three watches [of the night], however, one should remember [the deity] blazing with rays; one should remember Gaṇanātha according to the method that will be described. Except for Gaṇanātha, the others remain well-established with peaceful forms.
Holding counting beads and the gesture of fearlessness, they bestow grace upon all.
All are seated in the lotus posture or adorned with circles of matted hair.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should touch the mudrās in their proper sequence.
One should request permission from them in the proper sequence;
having received that with one's head bowed, one should then invoke the Lord.
Then, one invokes the omnipresent God who has assumed the form of the mantra.
Having been summoned by Sumantu with the words "Come," O Great-minded One,
the Blessed One indeed enters into activity just as the all-pervading wind is set in motion by a fan. 4.49–4.50.
Having indeed caused [the deity] reflected in the mirror of one's own being to emerge from the heart-lotus,
and having restrained it from the external field of perception at the conclusion of the mantra's utterance,
one should contemplate the mantra as it arrives and departs from its own station.

One should always visualize [the deity] as having arisen after the conclusion of the offering of water for the feet and the guest-offering (arghya). Then, one should visualize him being served with enjoyments appropriate to the time,
such as various offerings of food, garments, garlands, gifts, and ornaments.
Except during the worship of the portions (*bhāgapūjā*), one should visualize [the deity] in the lotus posture and so forth;
then, one should again visualize that very same one seated before oneself, full of compassion.
O Mahāmati, in other cases, [this visualization] occurs even upon a support other than a physical image (*bimba*).
Having entered the image by means of its own form as the reflected likeness (*bimbākṛti*), it remains there;
it then assimilates to itself the entire formless power of enjoyment (*bhogaśakti*).
Or else, [it perceives] the Supreme Lord with form (*sākāra*) stationed within the sanctuary.
One should worship Viṣṇu, who bears the conch and discus, who was brought down by gods and siddhas,
or established by seers or men endowed with devotion,
in his image using his own mantra, without the rite of invocation (āvāhana).
Having made his two hands fragrant, he should awaken Him in that manner;
filling them with perfumes, water for honor (arghya), and flowers while reciting the root mantra, he should cast a handful of flowers upon the seat before Hari and onto His head. (4.58–4.59)
One should also meditate upon Him as facing oneself, peaceful and perfectly awakened;
