therein, even without the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa), there are three [other] placements beginning with the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), and likewise the placement of the mantras starting from the root mantra up to the mantra of Tārkṣya. 4.60.

Then, having formed those respective mudrās, one should display them with their respective mantras. One should illuminate [the deity] elsewhere than in the image; in that [space], one should offer a handful of flowers to Hari with the *āgaccha* mantra and the root mantra from the heart-lotus.
O twice-born ones, every day a slight invocation must be performed from the heart-lotus of the primary image into the ritual images; in that regard, the sequence is as follows:
the portion of the splendor (*tejas*) within the primary image (*mūlabera*) that is used for the festival consists of one-sixth part.
But one thirty-sixth part [is used] for the rites of offering (balikarma), worship, and so forth.

Thus, having invoked the deity consisting of splendor through the right channel of the nāḍīs by means of the tip of the nose, one should cast [the essence] into the pedestal, the water-pot, and other [vessels]. 4.64–65.
Upon that sphere whose essence is mantra, which resembles a kadamba flower,

one should assign the limbs (aṅgas) without distinction of location and worship them here within the body. Having thus effected the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa), one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods as having attained manifestation therein.
One should then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) there of the mantras beginning with the root mantra and ending with the Tārkṣya mantra.
Having thus invoked the Lord of Gods and offered the *arghya* with the desire for His presence,
one should again offer *arghya* to Him while employing the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) preceded by the appropriate mudrās.
Having caused [the deity] to be present by offering the *arghya* water preceded by the *mudrā*, and having bound [him] with the *varman* mantra,
one should then face [the deity] while reciting the root and other mantras there together with that *mudrā*.
Displaying the mudrās in that manner, one should offer salutation with the eight limbs.
Then, one should first perform worship according to the procedure taught for the *layayāga*;
this is the complete worship of all mantras, from their root to their points of manifestation.
One should perform the offering with water for the guest (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth, each upon its own respective place.
Then, one should meditate on the heart and other [limbs] as having emerged from the Lord Viṣṇu, their forms radiant with his splendor, like a mass of sparks.
Then, one should place each [deity] individually in its appropriate place of enjoyment.
Having performed the ritual of totalization (sakalīkaraṇa), one should worship there with the water-offering (arghya) and other substances; this is the sequence.
Upon the eight-petaled lotus seat, one should worship the fourfold [mantras] beginning with the Heart.
One should place [the weapons] upon the lotus petals, starting from the east and ending in the north;
one should place the *astra* (weapon) in due order upon the petals in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.
Immediately thereafter, one should place the *netra* (eye) within the mass of filaments.
Outside the petals upon the pedestal, in the northeast corner of the deity’s [mandala],
one should place the crown and the śrīvatsa; then, in the southeast corner,
one should indeed place the kaustubha, the forest garland, and the lotus.
Having placed the mace in the northeast corner and the radiant discus in the southwest,
one should place the Pāñcajanya conch in the northwest in due order.
Then, upon the pericarp of the deity, one should place Śrī and Puṣṭi.
Outside the pedestal, one should place the bird-bannered god (Viṣṇu) at the front.
Having thus bowed, one should then meditate upon the array of mantras as they are situated,
in the center of the womb-ground within the celestial palace.
Having taken his seat upon a lotus, Puruṣottama stands there, his divine form radiant like a mass of monsoon clouds;
he is the God of all gods, the treasury of all splendors. (4.81)
Complete with all the marks of perfection and endowed with qualities such as omniscience,
he possessed a beautiful and divine body that was fully manifested,
emitting from his frame a constant light characterized by primordial wisdom.
For those who meditate, there is a great [attainment] that destroys ignorance without effort—
[an attainment] resembling thick, curled, dark-blue petals of crushed collyrium,
grey as camphor, divine, and with interiors filled with flowers.
His own head was adorned with rising locks of hair crowned by a jeweled diadem;
it was radiant with a tilaka mark rising upon his forehead, resembling the crescent moon;
he possessed beautiful brows and a fine nose, and was peaceful, with lips curved in a playful smile.
His eyes were like slightly reddish cow’s milk and pure blue lotuses;
with his cooling glances, he brought nourishment to the world.
His broad cheeks were radiant, and his earrings gleamed upon his ears.
Adorned with a chin that was graced by the overflow of beauty from his face;
his facial orb shimmering like the stainless autumnal moon;
possessing a neck like a conch shell, broad shoulders, long arms, and a magnificent chest.
Four-armed, with noble limbs and shimmering lotus-hands,
clad in yellow silk garments, with a deep navel and a slender waist; possessing a pair of beautiful thighs and a pair of lovely shanks, resplendent— (4.90)
His lotus-feet shone with ornaments such as jeweled anklets;
his limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, and he was likewise clad in divine garments,
endowed with divine garlands and head-wraps, and adorned with divine ornaments.
Resplendent with a crown and diadem inlaid with many jewels,
he was adorned with the Kaustubha gem resting upon his chest and the Śrīvatsa mark;
[he was further graced] with a forest garland composed of gems, gold, and fine pearls.
The Supreme Lord was adorned with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*),
and with his principal right hand he granted fearlessness to those who were afraid;
while his left hand rested gracefully upon the slope of his hip.
Holding a heavy mace and seated upon the surface of the earth,
he [held] in his right hand a discus with the brilliance of the fire of time;
it was filled with the resonance of the *praṇava* and graced by hundreds of Himalayan peaks.
Holding a conch shell even in his left hand, he possesses incomparable radiance;
he stands in the midst of a circle of flames produced from the splendor of his own body,
his heart filled with compassion and intent upon uplifting the world.

One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Master, who is the husband of Lakṣmī herself— the unborn, eternal cause of the birth and other states of the world, augmented by the undivided and complete majesty of the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), and the object of meditation for yogis. 4.99

Whether he is thus lying down, sitting, or even mounted upon a vehicle; whether he is in a supreme array or manifestation, having two arms, four arms, or eight arms and so forth, and endowed with various ornaments. || 4.100–4.101 ||
Endowed with devotion, one should meditate upon the form of the Blessed One thus joined with various groups of weapons, as well as the network of powers such as Lakṣmī;
indeed, in this very manner, one should meditate on the heart-mantra, white as a water-lily.
One should visualize the head as being deep red, shaped like a mountain of rubies;
likewise, one should visualize the form of the *śikhā* mantra resembling a mountain of collyrium,
appearing on all sides like a mountain of gold scorched by the sun.
Likewise, having meditated upon the armor-mantra at the time of visualization,
one should contemplate it as surrounded by thousands of flames and possessing a luster like that of a magnet;
this is proclaimed as the weapon-mantra, fully endowed with the power of all weapons.
One should meditate on the King of Eye-mantras as resembling smokeless embers. These supreme beings, possessing two arms and endowed with their own natural radiance, should be visualized;
one should meditate on these lords of sages as gazing upon the face of the All-pervading Lord.
One should always indeed meditate upon those standing forms as standing;
likewise, those seated as seated, and those mounted on vehicles along with their vehicles.
One should also mentally recollect those who are reclining, sitting, or standing.
Now, the meditation on the ornaments, weapons, and powers is described in sequence:
He wears a crown, has a gentle face, is golden-hued, and possesses a massive body; he is enveloped by rays of light that take various forms and possess diverse appearances. (4.109–4.110)
Standing in the air by means of the vidyādhara-station,
one should then visualize the Śrīvatsa, resembling a mountain of crystal,
seated upon the bound lotus posture with its hands placed at its own sides. (4.111)
One should meditate upon him as bearing the tortoise-mudrā with his two principal hands,
possessing the Kaustubha gem— the lord of jewels— which has the form of a mountain of rubies and illuminates the ten directions, and as standing with his feet firmly planted.
Bearing [the beads] across the middle of her chest with both hands joined in a hollowed gesture (saṃpuṭa),
and likewise holding another [portion] above her head—
the divine garland, variegated in form and captivating to the mind, is thus to be meditated upon.
Endowed with every fragrance, gentle, slightly smiling, and fresh;
a lotus as white as a kunda flower, gentle, with a face slightly smiling, emitting a sweet sound that is pleasing to the sense of hearing. (4.115–4.116)
[He saw] a mace resembling a mountain of gold, and [he saw] a slender maiden with eyes like blue lotuses,
lovely as if she were sixteen years of age, a young girl in the bloom of fresh youth,
illuminating the expanse of the sky with a network of rays arising from herself.
One should meditate on the Lord Śaṅkha, who stands within a circle of light rays, leaping with vigor;
awaiting the command of the All-pervading One, he has short limbs and red eyes, and resembles the Snowy Mountain (Himalaya). 4.118–119ab.

[He] has the lotus as his mark (kamalalāñchana), and from his own mouths he ever utters the sovereign [teachings] such as the True Scriptures (sadāgama). Those [deities] should be meditated upon as having two arms, resembling men, and endowed with their own respective colors. 4.119–120.
Those who bear weapons, beginning with the crown, and those whose forms are maces, garlands, and women—
all these leaders of weapons stand awaiting the command of the Lord;
they have risen up, moving about, and remain stationed in perfectly balanced postures.
With their hands resting on the slope of their hips, they are intent upon fanning with chowries;
yet, excluding the four [deities] beginning with the Crowned One who hold lotuses,
others have their right hands raised in a threatening gesture toward the multitude of the wicked.
At the time of meditation, one should indeed remember [the deities] upon the heads of all;
each should meditate upon their own respective insignia, which are perfectly awakened and formless.
Lakṣmī, with a lotus and a palm-leaf in her hands, has the luster of a red lotus.

Puṣṭā is remembered as golden-hued and holding a jar of nectar. Lakṣmī is known as the power of the enjoyer, while Puṣṭi is indeed designated as the agent; she has descended for the sake of enjoyment out of a desire to grace the worlds.
Simultaneously with that, the two imperishable powers arose:
the one with a red beak and great vital force, and the one with terrifying frowning eyes;
they were like blazing gold and adorned with circles of lotuses.
O Brahmins, one should remember Garuḍa, who has the face of a vulture and a broad belly;
and one should meditate upon him in due order, endowed with the form as previously described.
The crown is to be known as Agni, while the Kaustubha gem is the sun.
The moon itself, the *śrīvatsa* mark, the garland, the six *Mādhavas*, and others;
the lord of waters (*apāmpati*), the lotus, the mace, and the goddess Sarasvatī;
Time (*kāla*) is to be known as the wielder of the discus, and the sky (*kha*) is said by the twice-born to be the conch.

Know that the king of birds [Garuḍa] is the vital breath (prāṇa); thus, one should worship these presiding deities established within the principles (tattvas) in their proper order with water-offerings (arghya) and flowers.
Thereafter, one should worship the Lord of Gods with enjoyments, beginning with the water-offering, in due sequence.
Having offered an excellent seat to the Lord who had been summoned,
he presented a common footstool covered with a soft rug and adorned with bells;
then, accompanied by the sound of a bell, he offered the *arghya* water at the head of the mantra.
One should offer a golden vessel for receiving the water for the feet (*pādya*) to the Lord, adorned with fine jewels.
(4.134) The water for the feet, the cloth for wiping the feet, and the unguent; the water for sipping (*ācamana*) along with its vessel, the unguent, and the garland. (4.135)
One should worship Hari with unextinguished great lamps fed with ghee and other substances;
one should worship the Lord with abundant, fragrant, and sweet incense.
Immediately thereafter, one should offer the respectful oblation (*arhaṇa*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having offered the cleansing of the private parts along with the vessel, as well as the rinsing water and fragrance;
and then, having presented the finest betel-leaf together with camphor powder, ground nutmeg, and the *śrīgandha* paste, along with areca nuts (4.137–138).
Having first offered himself, along with his sons and wife, by prostrating with all eight limbs and with a mind filled with devotion,
he should then place his hands at the feet of the Blessed One and request the desired object.
"O Lord, I have made this excellent bath manifest for you.
Here is another great and auspicious bathing-seat provided with a footstool;
please take it quickly for the sake of bathing, out of a desire to show me favor."
Having thus requested [the deity] for the purpose of bathing, one should then prepare three paths;
then, having offered two bathing seats for the Lord,
[one should provide] a footstool immediately after he has descended for the sake of bathing.

With his head bowed in devotion, he should offer the *arghya* upon [the deity's] head. Then, having presented a golden vessel adorned with excellent gems as a recipient, he should indeed offer water for the feet (*pādya*) from the *pādya*-pitcher onto the two lotus-feet.
Then, at the conclusion of that, [he offered] auspicious sandals, a bathing garment,
and an excellent vessel filled with fragrant rice for the sake of his mother.
Next, a mirror with the luster of the full moon; then, for the purpose of washing the hands, fragrant water; thereafter, an auspicious footstool;
and following that, a tooth-stick to be used for cleansing the mouth.
The scraping of the tongue, the washing of the mouth,
and again the sipping of water (ācamana), followed immediately by oil for anointing—
highly fragrant— and powder made from wheat and śāli rice.
Next, for the purpose of rubbing the body, a paste mixed with the powder of *rajanī* and slightly impregnated with *padmaka* should be applied; thereafter,
for the purpose of bathing, warm water combined with its own [specific] herbs should be used.
Sandalwood, ground for the purpose of anointing the face and infused with camphor, [should be used].
Then one should bathe the Lord with twenty-five jars;
for the sake of the bath, there should be abundant products of the cow: milk, curd, ghee, and honey.

The juice of sugarcane is pleasing to the heart; in its absence, sugar-water, or water with *dhātrī* fruit, or immediately thereafter water with *lodhra*, water with red sandalwood, or excellent water with turmeric [may be used]. 4.152
Then indeed water with *granthi* sprouts, followed by *tagara* water;
after that, *priyaṅgu* water, and beyond that, *māṃsī* water; then water with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*), and thereafter water with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*).
Then there is water with leaves and flowers, and likewise water with fruits and seeds; after that, scented water, and then water with gold and jewels;
immediately following that, the water of sacred fords and rivers alone.
O Mahāmati, this [mantra] should be employed in sequence, combined with water prepared for the purpose of bathing,
along with arghya and flowers, through the application of intervals between the various baths. || 4.156–4.157 ||
He should perform the washing with the water from the *arghya* jar, accompanied by the offering of *arghya*;
or else, he should consecrate [the image] with twelve or nine jars.
Then, with the remainder of the bathing water, [he should bathe] that which is fashioned from materials such as gold.
A water-pot filled with water, containing turmeric and husked rice that has been well-ground,
smeared on top, and adorned with garlands and the like;
having placed this in one hand, he should hold a small bowl in the other.
Having whirled it while it is smoking with mustard seeds, one should cast it outside over the head;
then, having offered a well-washed, new garment,
another [garment] is worn on the body for the purpose of wiping away the water from the hair.
Having offered two garments, one lower and one upper, scented with perfumes, incense, and the like, as well as a shoulder-cloth made of very fine, unwashed white cloth,
he should then apply a cooling ointment to the head, combined with moon-fragrance and incense.
O Lotus-Seated One, one should fashion the hair on the head of the deity mixed with camphor powder; indeed,
one should perform this for others as well, provided they are of various excellent types and are devoid of the *brahmapāṣāṇa* gem.
For the purpose of bathing, [one should perform] the request for the bath either upon the ritual image (karmabimba), or nearby on a mirror;
having performed the request for the bath, one should place the ritual icon (karmārcā) in its proximity upon the bathing seat and perform everything [the ritual] upon it.
In the absence of that [liṅga], one should offer the baths and enjoyments into a mirror;
likewise, while remaining before a painting, one should offer other enjoyments in due order.
And in the absence of those [images], taking them all with the hand, one should offer them mentally.
In this manner, one should present the offering of enjoyments within the mandala and other such areas.
One should perform the sprinkling with the remaining portions of the *arghya* and other substances.
Furthermore, the ritual bath is performed from the section of the water-spout, while the auspicious seat (*bhadrāsana*) is indeed [prepared] from the other [section]. 4.168–169.
Having purified it with many jars of water and having lowered the image of the Blessed One— whether together with its pedestal or without it— if it has been worshipped,
one should then contemplate the deity as bathed and wash it until it is completely clean.
Furthermore, one should fill four jars with fragrant water;
for the others, excluding the bathing jar, the ritual arrangement should be performed as before.
One should indeed perform the divine union of the four [jars] with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
Having consecrated all of that with the *sāstra* and the root mantra (*mūlamantra*),
one should then prepare the three paths in sequence and offer the seat;
thereupon, the Supreme Lord is situated upon the third [seat], which is inlaid with jewels.
Having meditated upon [the deity] adorned with devotion by means of enjoyments such as garlands and sandalwood paste,
and having worshipped him thoroughly with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), one should immediately offer water for sipping (ācamana) and likewise a footstool.
Having anointed him with fragrant substances such as sandalwood out of devotion,
and having fanned him with a peacock-feather fan smeared with sandalwood paste,
[he should offer] a brush for smoothing the hair, a razor for the beard, and a pair of scissors for flowers and betel.
Having offered two white silk garments to the God of gods,
he should immediately present the sacred thread along with an upper garment, a crown and other ornaments,
and the finest decorations down to the anklets for the feet.
For the head-garland is variegated and provided with a binding,
joined with strings of flower-clusters, extending from the ear down to the foot.
Then one should give a beautiful bracelet and subsequently a *pratisara* (protective cord), made of various metals or of saffron and other pigments, variegated and fashioned from a white thread,
filled with soft cotton and knotted at intervals.
Collyrium with its applicator-stick, betel leaf perfumed with fragrances,
a golden tilaka-mark on the forehead, mouth-perfume mixed with yellow pigment, flower-ear-ornaments, personal adornments, and a large mirror. || 4.181–4.182 ||
He arranged the offering with various kinds of flowers and lamps blazing with the luster of radiant jewels;
these were numerous, possessing great flames, filled with sesame oil and clarified butter,
and fashioned from fresh, unwashed, pure white cloth wrapped around wicks.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship with cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients rolled into pellets (granthi).
Then, one should offer auspicious guggulu incense, which is mixed with camphor powder, highly fragrant, sweet, abundant, and combined with powdered incense.
With his arm being moved by the delightful sound of bells,
he [took] the sandals, the white parasol, the palanquin, and whatever else such as chariots;
the vehicle, extending even to the elephant, together with its banners and its own flag.
Then, having placed the white and black yak-tail whisks and the knowledge of the prosodic measures immediately [before him],
and having knelt with his knees upon the ground, he bowed his head and, taking them with his upturned palms, offered them to the Lord of the World.
And for the fulfillment of these metaphorical enjoyments,
with the sounds of victory accompanied by kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, and the like,
along with various songs, dances, and stringed instruments; 4.189.
One should worship with bamboo flutes, horns, as well as lutes and other instruments that are pleasant to hear.
With hymns, mantras, prostrations, salutations, and circumambulations,
[one should worship] when the ground is narrow and the Blessed One is standing before one.

One should perform a salutation with devotion, joining the palms together at the region of the heart while recollecting Hari, the Lord of All, with gentle movements of the head. [This is done] within the inner sanctum of Viṣṇu, in the half-maṇḍapa at the entrance to the womb-chamber.
One should perform the series of prostrations without the series of circumambulations.
If there is a spatial constraint in that area, one should place the movable images outside in the front pavilion; even if there is a constraint there as well— || 4.193–4.194 ||
Whether in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure,
having made the site very spacious and avoiding the top of a palace and the forbidden directions,
one should perform [the rites] in the three desired cardinal directions and in the desired intermediate directions.

One should install the image for the procession, accompanied by the Goddess, according to the prescribed rite in a training ground (*khalūrikā*) or in a well-situated location that has been thoroughly inspected.
One should never place any other images outside at any time.
Having first worshipped the primary image up to the final rite of lustration (nīrājana),
one should thereafter worship the images situated outside according to the prescribed rule.
Thus, having indeed worshipped the deity up to the end of the circumambulation, one should then proceed.
One should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the God of gods; its procedure is stated here.
The *nīrājana* is threefold, according to the distinction of *sāttvika* and the other qualities (*rājasa* and *tāmasa*).
At the conclusion of the ritual bath and at the conclusion of the sacrifice of enjoyments (*bhogayajña*), the two [types] shall be *sāttvika*.
Every day at evening, one should perform that which is designated as *rājasa*;

in the worship, it should be performed before the offering of lamps and also at the end of the food offering (*naivedya*), while that which is *tāmasa* should be performed in a single temple, but not all three [types] together.

In a temple that is self-manifested, or one consecrated by other wise beings and the foremost of sages, one should perform the rite known as *sāttvika*. In one established by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas, it shall be *rājasa*.
If it is established by Śūdras or women, one should perform what is called the Tāmasa rite;
but listen, O best of sages, to the procedure for the Sāttvika rite,
which was already described previously as that which must be performed at the conclusion of the bath and enjoyment.
What must be done at the conclusion of the *alaṅkāra* rite is now stated here:
having filled a jar made of substances such as gold with water drawn from the *arghya* vessel, or else with water that has been simply filtered. (4.205–206)
Having placed white mustard seeds inside,
one should make an ornament for the neck with *aśvattha* shoots, garlands, sandalwood, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
O twice-born ones, elsewhere one should smear [the image] on all sides with ground turmeric.
Then one should place a flower-filled bowl upon his face.
Having first lit lamps produced from consecrated fire,
O twice-born ones, twenty-four lamps should be offered according to one's wealth and desire.
From the lamp-stand, four finger-breadths above the elevated base,
one should place a lamp within a shallow bowl (mallaka) together with its vessel,
always positioned upon a support in front of the God of Gods.

One should worship it with water for the guest (arghya), perfumes, garlands, and incense using the heart-mantra. O twice-born ones, immediately thereafter, the practitioner should offer arghya with only water and flowers, or else offer arghya at the conclusion of the rinsing (ācamana) of the Lord of Mantras.
The attendant, with both hands, offered the water for honor (*arghya*), the touching of the limbs (*ālabhana*), garlands, incense, and further *arghya*, as well as a lamp and a water-pot;
beginning with the right foot of the deity, he proceeded to the other [left] foot.
One should cause all the limbs to revolve— once, twice, or thrice—
while reciting either the Netra-mantra or the Hṛdaya-mantra according to one's preference; thus, the officiating brahmin should cause the pitcher to revolve.
Or even with a pure woman, one should have [the offering] discarded outside the door;
then, one should offer the *arghya* upon the head of the God of Gods.
When the lamp is brought from the kitchen, it should be half the size of that [offering].
At that time, O best of sages, listen to the procedure for that:
the attendants, having been initiated, well-disciplined, and well-bathed,
shall cover their faces and the openings of their nostrils with cloth.
All wore white turbans and were adorned with white sandalwood;
they had spread out bowls made of gold according to their preference,
as well as those made of silver, copper, and brass.
Or having prepared vessels of bell-metal according to one's means—
whether one, three, five, seven, or eleven;
or two, six, sixteen, or twenty-four in number.
Having reached the kitchen,
O Great-minded One, one should first prepare the fires there; then, in the midst of those [fires], one should again light lamps in vessels with a height of four finger-breadths, filled with ghee.
Having lifted up those vessels with their hands, the attendants should carry them in a single file; in front of them, the women of the courtesans,
devoted to the Blessed One, should proceed while performing dance and song.
In their presence, those intent on sounding conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments,
and in their presence those staff-bearers intent on clearing away untouchable people,
should proceed; and around them, people carrying lamps should go.
Thus, having arrived in succession, they should remain in the presence of the deity.
Then another initiated Brahmin, having brought a water-pot as before, together with a basin,
should light a fire from one of those [fires] and place it above them.
Having brought [the materials] from the kitchen and having placed a lamp,
the best of practitioners should then establish it upon a stable support.
Then, having worshipped the jar as before, he should next worship the Lord of Gods.
O best of the twice-born, at that time one should rotate the water-pot as before; meanwhile,
the twice-born standing in the eastern and other directions should recite the Rigveda and other scriptures,
while the courtesans perform a dance in the presence of the God of gods.
Let all the singers sing auspicious songs,
and let the reciters of hymns praise [him] with exceedingly high voices.
Let them sound kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, and other instruments on every side.
In this manner, one should perform the study of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth in every respect.
Having thus circumambulated the jar and given it to its attendants,
one should then show the lamp-vessels and the other items in their hands.
Having seen [the deity] correctly, one should then offer the *arghya* upon the head of the god.
Attendants carrying vessels, beginning with the water-jars,
should proceed together with the courtesans and others in a clockwise circuit as before.
Or they may throw them outside the door, that is, beyond the outer gate.

Or else, women who have been appointed for this task—having bathed well, wearing clean garments, and whose minds are purified by devotion to the twice-born—should collect those [garments]. (4.235–236)
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead and being adorned with all ornaments,
the best of the twice-born should cast [the fire] by the very path already described.
Or else, prior to its application, even from the kitchen.
Women, taking lamp-vessels according to the prescribed method,
should bring them before the Lord in accordance with the desire of the performer.
In this manner one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and thereafter the rite of the ornaments and the seat.
Alternatively, one should rotate the jar accompanied by eight lamps; or else,
even in that case, one should rotate the jar joined with a small vessel containing fire,
together with *siddhārtha* seeds, while it is emitting smoke, though devoid of lamps.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the *nīrājana* rite for a single form has been described.
In the worship of multiple forms, one should proceed in order starting from the principal form,
offering the *arghya* and other honors individually to all the forms.

Or else, O twice-born ones, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for each [image] individually with a single jar, or for all of them together with a single jar, as previously described. Thus has the lustration ceremony performed for the Lord, the All-pervading One, been explained.
Those people who provide assistance in that rite will undoubtedly become free from passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
Thus has been described the Nīrājana, known by the name Sāttvika.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure Ending with the Nīrājana," in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the venerable *Pāñcarātra*.
May there be prosperity.
Now begins the fifth chapter:
Then the god Nārada sat upon a seat provided with food, along with various kinds of edible delicacies.

One should indeed offer a footstool for the worshipful one, as well as a seat for the meal of the Lord. Having covered it with an excellent cushion made of fine silk or cotton, one should place the Lord, facing eastward, upon that dining seat.
One should offer the *arghya*, the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) together with the vessel for acceptance;
then, having established the libation (*tarpaṇa*),
one should scent it with the *arghya* water.
Then, one should offer clear, fragrant water from the Atharvaṇa, prepared in a vessel,
followed by the *madhuparka* consisting of curd, honey, and ghee.
Alternatively, one may offer all these together as a single item, or even just the curd alone.

Then, cool, refreshing water and the powder previously mentioned should be offered for the purpose of cleansing; thereafter, the Lord should be given the water for sipping (ācamana). Having presented a cow that is well-adorned, beautiful, and decorated with garlands, || 5.5–5.6 ||
One should first present the herbs filled with rice, and the tree rich with garlands and fruit, in embodied form; then, having established the libation (tarpaṇa),
one should offer a garment for covering and the water for honoring (arhaṇodaka).
With divine offerings produced from the six flavors, with purifying fruits,
with many foods enriched with jaggery and sugar-candy and cooked in ghee,
and with those mixed with jaggery, mung beans, milk, and sesame seeds fried in oil at night; || 5.8–5.9 ||
One should offer cakes (apūpa) with fruits mixed with curd, mixed with ghee, and joined with the sweetness of honey; then with eight kinds of foods in sequence,
along with savory rasālās and well-prepared milk.
With purifying, cool, and sweet-smelling drinks,
and with various kinds of foods— those to be chewed, those to be eaten, those to be licked, and those to be drunk—
one should worship that unborn and imperishable one with a mind purified by faith.
However, for each individual offering, one should sprinkle it with the water of the *arghya* while forming the *dhautikā* gesture joined with the mantra using both hands. Then,
indeed with both hands, which consist of the nature of Agni and Soma—

Then, having brought the mudrā that grants all desires to the state of fitness, one should bind it and thereby render the entire array of enjoyments as they exist into nectar. Having offered the arghya water, one should touch [the offerings] from above with the hand of Viṣṇu.
Having touched the forearm of the right hand with the left hand,
he should then offer it with that right hand, the fingers of which are slightly bent,
while bowing his head, O Brahmins.
Whatever enjoyment arises from what is not at hand should follow the state of being an auxiliary limb [of worship].
Having meditated upon each of those with the mind through devotion, one should offer them to Viṣṇu with pure, clear, cool, sweet, and other such purifying drinks. 5.17–5.18
Immediately thereafter, [the deity] should be offered libations with water from a coconut shell, scented with camphor and refined incense such as cinnamon and cardamom,
along with flour made from lentils, black gram, turmeric, and śāli rice.
Having rinsed [the vessel] thoroughly and washed it with much cool water,
one should prepare unsurpassed scented water for the purpose of the food offering and the ceremonial sipping (ācamana),
making it pure with a cloth and white sandalwood paste.
Having anointed himself with well-ground sandalwood paste mixed with camphor,
he should then place sesame seeds and excellent jewels into a vessel made of gold or silver,
and offer it to the God for the sake of his mother.
It was infused with cloves, *takola*, cardamom, cinnamon, and camphor; it was abundant with jasmine and betel nuts, along with fragrant leaves;
and it was mixed with powdered camphor and interspersed with powdered pearls.
At the end, bowing down, he should offer betel leaf to the Lord of the World, accompanied by *mātulaṅga* fruit and provided with coconut fruit.
Having indeed washed [the mouth] with fragrant water drawn from the vessel for the *arghya* offering, [he should perform this].
The pair of hands should indeed be clear and utterly stainless,
not soiled by offerings of food, incense vessels, or other such items; having smeared them with excellent fragrant substances, one should honor each other with the *arghya* water.
Having displayed the mudrās of the root and other mantras in their proper sequence,
and having worshipped again with the offering of water (arghya), fragrance, flowers, and incense,
one should then satisfy the deity through the procedure for the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña).
One should place the vessel either with a crystal rosary or with the joints of one's own fingers. Afterwards, having moistened it with water from the *arghya* vessel,
and having anointed it with sandalwood and other unguents, one should set it upon an auspicious receptacle.
Having worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings, one should then place the mantra there,
along with a seat provided with its base and surrounded by the [deities] preceded by Śakti;
it has four arms and is like another Viraja Nārāyaṇa.
One should meditate on him with hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding a water-pot with joined palms;
situated in the station of Brahmā, one should contemplate that thread as being like a topknot.
"Be present here, O Lord of Gods; be firmly established, O Acyuta! (5.32–33)
In this net of jewels called the Sūtra, as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure— thus, O Sage, having established [the deity] within the mantra known as the rosary,
one should subsequently display one's own mudrā for that which has been consecrated.
One should perform the recitation according to one's ability, either one hundred times or eight more;
having offered that to the All-pervading Lord, followed by speech, action, and mind, [one should say]:
"O Lotus-eyed One, Soul of the Universe, Janārdana, whose form is the mantra! (5.35–5.36)
"O Lord, accept this perpetual recitation from me, a wretched one.
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, he should then place a flower with water in his right hand before Viṣṇu while reciting the root mantra.
Then one should correctly meditate upon the shimmering garland of stars as it enters the mouth of the Blessed One, proceeds from his mouth into his heart,
and from the heart [enters] the tiger among the twice-born, according to the sequence known as withdrawal.
As before, one should unite [the breath] with the Supreme through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Then, for all [the centers] beginning with the heart, this is prescribed individually.
Since it is an auxiliary to the ritual action (*kriyāṅga*), there is no fault; otherwise, it would be without that recitation (*japa*).
Then, having offered incense, prostrated, and praised the Lord of Mantras, [he said]:
"O Eye of the World, whatever has been done deficiently or in excess by me, your wretched servant, whether through ignorance or intentionally, it must be forgiven."
Having thus made this petition to the Lord of Gods with devotion, that best of practitioners,
having worshipped Him with perfumes and incense, and then, being absorbed in the Blessed One, having performed the worship in due order and presented the food offering; 5.43.
At the conclusion of their mantras, one should present the offering of honor (*arhaṇa*) and so forth.
Having given them that which is at the end of the *tanmātra*— which occurs at the conclusion of the sacrifice to the gods—
at this time, one should offer everything from the *arhaṇa* up to the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*).
Then one should offer a bed and a seat, and thereafter satisfy the fire.
Having placed the *astra-mantra* on the seat, one should proceed to the fire-chamber carrying the *arghya* offering.
Then, having performed the door-sacrifice as before, one should enter.

There, having performed the ritual sipping of water according to the previously mentioned rule, being composed in mind, he should construct an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is purified by the proper measurements, adorned with lips, provided with four enclosures, and in accordance with his means. || 5.47–5.48 ||
The width [of the base] is prescribed as three-quarters, one-half, or one-third of the depth;
it may be circular in the shape of a discus, conch, or lotus, or square,
or marked with emblems beginning with the mace and ending with the discus.
O Mahāmati, whatever vessels suitable for the fire-ritual there may be, such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, they too must be marked;
or else, they should bear the marks of the crown, the *śrīvatsa*, the garland, and the *kaustubha* gem. (5.50–5.51)
A wise person should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a water-pot (bhṛṅgāra) or a vessel (karaka), marked with all or some of the symbols of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
One should fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with four tiers, or three tiers,
or likewise two tiers, or even a single tier.
One should make a stationary pit with tiers, but a mobile one without tiers.
If, due to the influence of place and time, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) cannot be constructed,
one who desires success must not interrupt the fire-oblation in its absence.
For on a ground that has been purified, smeared with cow-dung, and provided with immovable clay [the rite may proceed].
The fire-oblations (homa) are prescribed correctly for both the mantra and the consecrated object;
however, a square pedestal (piṇḍikā) is recommended everywhere on the outside.
One should fashion a lotus in the center, with the seat of Śrī situated within the middle of the lotus.
When this has been done, one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) in a clean pit (kuṇḍa);
or else, one may perform the oblation (homa) according to the rules in a hearth or even in a small bowl. Among these, one should choose an auspicious pit that is suitable for the occasion.
Having adorned and smeared [the site] with pure pigments such as lime and the like,
and with fragrant substances such as sandalwood preceded by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [one should proceed];
however, if at the time of commencing the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) have not been performed—

And once you have attained perfection, all of them shall become subject to your command in due order. The preceptor should strike with flowers from the right hand using the weapon-mantra, and perform the digging with a sharp tool while employing the knowledge of the weapon-mantra.

Then, taking a lump of clay from one part within the center of the pit with the thumb and ring finger, he should extract it while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra. Having leveled it with the *astra* mantra so that there is no depression or elevation, [he should proceed].
One should sprinkle it with the Armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and then grind it.
One should smear it with fragrant water and purify it with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*).
This is done with blades of *kuśa* grass consecrated by the Weapon-mantra, provided they are sharp and devoid of tails.
With two blades of *darbha* consecrated by mantras,
and grasping the front portion with the tips of the *kuśa* grass,
one should begin from the southern direction and draw a line extending toward the north.
Upon that [surface], one should clearly draw three lines:
one pointing eastward, one starting from the southern direction and ending in the southwest, and another with an interval between them.
Among those lines pointing eastward, the middle one is named Piṅgalā.
The two [channels] on the south and north, however, have Suṣumnā and Iḍā as their presiding deities;
then, with the fourth [syllable], the Praṇava, one should sprinkle [them] with the water of the arghya offering.
Having worshipped that with arghya, flowers, and so forth, one should meditate upon it as being like the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha).
One should perform its installation with the *praṇava* mantras as previously described.
On a square site, having placed eight full vessels and eight jars outside in the eight cardinal and intermediate directions within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should proceed].
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others, seated upon silken mats, in the four directions of the four girdles, both upper and lower; then,
by means of yoga, one should worship them in the intermediate directions as well, from the top down to the bottom.
In that very same manner, they should be worshipped in sequence with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth.
Furthermore, a bundle of soft *darbha* grass, a sapless stone slab,
and dry cow-dung powder, together with fragrant substances, [should be used].
Having placed a portion measuring one *droṇa* into the pit and having spread it out,
one should then decorate the entire surface of the pit's wall with *darbha* grass whose tips are uncut and which has been consecrated with the *astra-mantra*, using blades held upright.
Immediately after that, having mentally conceived the axle-pit as the armor (*varman*),
and having worshipped it with abundant flowers in the center by means of the *praṇava*,
one should worship the navel, which resembles the moon, according to that same ritual procedure.
Then, one should place a pavitraka made of darbha grass, consecrated with the śikhā-mantra,
and provided with an ointment applied from the east, at the crossroads. Then, one should fashion a yogapīṭha there with the hṛdaya-mantra.

Therein, one should indeed know the power named Nārāyaṇī, who has the characteristic of a flash of lightning; who has attained the state of having Lakṣmī as her form; whose nature is the nectar of immortality;
whose form surpasses all others; and who is endowed with every power.
Having brought down through the path of eternal creation that [deity] who abides within all other things by virtue of her tenderness and beauty, [one should place her] in the lotus of the heart;
previously, indeed, by means of the sequence of meditation and the heart-mantra from the lotus of the heart.
Accompanied by his own name, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the word "salutation" (*namaḥ*),
he should cast [the seed-syllable] into the center of the fire-pit or the heart-lotus by means of exhalation (*recaka*).
Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having displayed the lotus-gesture (*padmamudrā*), || 5.81–5.82 ||
Then, having taken fire— either from the forest, or common (laukika), or produced from a jewel, or from a mirror— in a copper vessel or another [vessel],
and having placed it to the northeast of the sacrificial pit for the sake of the consecration rites now; 5.83.
Having struck him with the weapon-mantra, one should sprinkle him with water from the crest-mantra;
having worshipped him with the heart-mantra, given the meditation on nectar, and then covered him with the armor-mantra,
one should recollect the root-mantra and bring [the nectar] into the interior of the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka).
Having drawn forth from that [source] what was attracted by the wind of the mantra,
there emerged from the multitude of qualities that which is called the sixth quality, namely *tejas* (luster/energy).
This very *tejas* belongs to the Supreme Brahman and is common to all luminous bodies.
Having caused [the substance] to be purified by purgation, one should place it in that previously consecrated fire-vessel.
Then, O twice-born ones, taking up the fire-vessel— which is smokeless and intensely radiant— with the right hand alone or with both hands.
Having whirled it four times, one should then cast it into the interior of the sacrificial pit;
one should then meditate upon it as having attained oneness with the radiance of the mantra.
Then, having kindled [the fire] with dry, sacrificial fuel consecrated by the *astra* mantra.
One should perform the sweeping with the right hand and the heart [of the fire],
moving in a clockwise direction with the palm slightly moistened, held obliquely and facing downwards, without showing the surface of the nails. (5.90–5.91)
One should sprinkle [the area] with the water for the *arghya* offering, consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
Then, one should provide a layer of *kuśa* grass that is even, with roots and tips intact,
extending from each direction up to the northern quarter, starting from the southern quarter, leaving a space between them.
With fourfold qualities, they were likewise covered from top to bottom by one another;
with their front edges reaching from the eastern part as far as the northern region, all the implements for the oblation, preceded by the sacrificial vessels, [were arranged]. 5.93–5.94
Having brought [the materials] down, one should perform the placement of the substances above that, on the right side of oneself,
by means of pairing them in twos:
the enclosing sticks (paridhis), the heap of fuel-sticks (edhma), the basket (karaṇḍikā) with loose darbha grass, and so forth.
Having placed together in one place the four items— the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles,
the garland, the incense, and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*)— and then likewise the seeds;
as well as the silk garment, the *viṣṭara* seat with its hair removed, the clarified butter, and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Immediately after placing the four vessels for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), one should set down another four items in front:
a pair of praṇītā vessels, a water-pot (karaka), and the arghya vessel. 5.98. Having arranged this other quartet in front, [one proceeds].
Fuel-sticks of the measure of a span and abundant dry fuel;
having placed a cloth that removes eye-secretions and fatigue on the left side,
one should indeed bring everything to a state of purification with the *arghya* water accompanied by the *astra-mantra*.

Then, those [blades] situated at the base, arising from the *brahmavṛkṣa* and other [trees], complete with leaves and bark, clearly visible, and not bent downwards, should be more than [the required number].
Those with tips pointing east, west, and north, and those with tips pointing east and north-south [respectively].
One should worship the four enclosing sticks (paridhi) with the *śikhā* mantra.
Then, one should offer seats (*viṣṭara*) to the eight jars with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
therein, one should worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), each situated in their own direction, in due order.
Then, having taken the vessel called *praṇītā* along with water,
one should place within it a *pavitraka* made of four blades of *darbha* grass. Having repeatedly drawn up water with the hand, one should pour it back into that very vessel.
Then, while muttering the eight-syllable mantra,
the practitioner should sprinkle everything again with that water using the ritual grass mat;
he should perform the pouring out of the remainder over the trees in all directions.
Having again filled it with water, having meditated upon the Supreme Lord within it, worshipped him, and established him, immediately thereafter,
when another vessel has been prepared and placed before it—
Having offered the *arghya* there together with the *pavitra*, one should place the *cakra*.
Then, having meditated upon the Lord of Mantras above that and worshipped him in due order,
one should place that vessel in the north and worship it once again.

Then the supreme practitioner should consecrate the clarified butter with the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras). He should perform the placing on the fire (adhiśrayaṇa), the subsequent placing (upādhiśrayaṇa), and the making it palatable (prasādīkaraṇa) with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
The practitioner should perform the immersion and emergence with the *praṇava*;
likewise, purification is performed with the *hṛdaya* mantra and the waving of lights (*nīrājana*) with the *dṛś* mantra.
Then, one should perform the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) with the *kavaca* mantra.

Know that the touching of the clarified butter contained in the vessel with the eyes [of Avalokita] and the armor [of Amṛtīkārī], preceded by blazing *darbha* grass, is the consecration known as "placing on the fire" (*adhiśrayaṇa*). (5.113)
That which is called "relying on an adjunct" (upādhiśrayaṇa) is said to be its liquefaction.
Then, taking the vessel of clarified butter, one should pour into it that clarified butter which was previously liquefied, from the butter-pot, in order to remove any defects. 5.114–115.
For this is the act of making [the vessel] resonant: having taken it up again with the raised hand and placed it before one upon the support,
thereupon [one places] four blades of darbha grass measuring twelve finger-breadths.
Holding [the vessel] with the palms turned sideways and upwards at intervals,
so that the middle [of the vessel] becomes bent by means of the pair of the ring fingers and thumbs,
one should pour the clarified butter four times; one should pour it four times.
By means of repeated intervals, one should indeed cast [the fuel] into the center of the sacrificial pit facing one's own fire with the *praṇava* recited the stated number of times;
having thus performed the sinking and rising [of the ladle], one should place a purifier made of *darbha* grass.

And one should cast that into its midst; it is the act of purification. Taking a firebrand from the sacrificial pit—blazing and free of smoke—the Brahmin should perform a single circumambulation with it; that indeed is known as the *nīrājana* rite.
Having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should thereafter contemplate [the deity] as being within the belly of the armor (*kavaca*).
This is indeed the *avakuṇṭhana* (sealing), which consists of circling with the index finger.
Then, there is the gazing with the splendor residing in the heart, which has reached the eyes.
O Brahmin, having performed this visualization,
one should then meditate upon that which is situated in the center of the lunar disc, accompanied by the *dhenumudrā*,
the *saurabheya* mantra, and possessing the radiance of a hundred shimmering moons.
One should visualize the Lord of Mantras situated within that [liṅga], resembling the Himalaya mountain.

One should contemplate the clarified butter (ājya) as being purified and endowed with all consecratory rites, by means of the floods of nectar flowing from it— both that produced from the moon and that produced from the celestial cow (dhenu).
This rite called Amṛtīkaraṇa has been fully revealed to you.
Then, taking the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with a bunch of *darbha* grass,
one should perform the removal of dust by washing them with warm water.
Having purified it with the *kūrca* and heated it thoroughly with flames,
and having sprinkled it with the *arghya* water, one should strike it with fragrant flowers.
Then, for the sake of the success of the ritual, the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) should be known as immeasurable.
Ananta, whose nature is the hundred-petalled lotus, is the fist that holds infinite faces.
Having remained within as the essence of the internal seed, he then faces upward;
he is the sevenfold aggregate of the inner self, consisting of the elements, the vital breaths, the winds, and the Great Principle (mahat).
Impelled again by his will through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
he entered the seven netherworlds and the serpent realm by means of the earth-lotus;
for when the nectar-essence remains within the water, it flows along the path.
Situated within the web of the arrangement of the wheel of consciousness, he bears the splendor of the three forms;
then there is Vāyu, who assumes the form of the conch, and the treasury of sovereignty which is space (kha).
That [space] is seedless, unborn, unshakeable, and primordial, whose presiding deity is he.
Listen now to how it should be known regarding the other *sruva* so that it may be produced:
Varuṇa himself, the very embodiment of nectar, exists in the form of the *kalaśa*,
while that weapon exists in the form of its stalk, removing the fear of obstacles.
The moon, which brings nourishment to the world, is [visualized] as a lotus in the foremost position.
Indeed, that sovereign power of the Supreme Lord known as bliss (ānanda) should be understood;
it is the truly existent, immeasurable object of knowledge (prameya) here described. || 5.135–5.136 ||
But at the time of ritual preparation, having invoked [the deity] constantly during the satiation with excellent mantras—

[using formulas] endowed with their own names and the *praṇava*, and joined with words of salutation (*namaskāra*)— O Brahmins, one should worship all [the deities], either by means of the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

Having worshipped with offerings of water for the feet (*arghya*), perfumes, and so forth, one should then take up the group of mantras that have been assigned. Then, having taken four *kuśa* blades— with many branches, unbroken tips, and roots, and which are perfectly even— with the left hand as a purifier (*pavitraka*), [one should proceed].
Then, having fashioned a ring-like form consisting of four segments upon the right ring finger,
he should immediately touch the fuel and other materials with drops of consecrated clarified butter.
Then, for the sake of pacifying all defects without exception,

he should offer oblations of sesame seeds sprinkled with ghee along with pure sacrificial food— either one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations, according to his own capacity— using the fire that has been brought forth. (5.141–5.142)
Understand correctly that the oblation must be offered for the sake of accomplishing the rite;
when the offering has been drawn out, one should recite the word ending with the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by "Purify Agni, purify! at the conclusion of the root mantra. (5.143)
Then, with that very [substance] in its established form, the wise one should subsequently offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and four fruits with clarified butter; thereafter,
the fire-oblation (*homa*) must be performed for the sake of accomplishing all purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
Having encased the fire within the heart, one should utter the name of the rite;
ending with "I accomplish, svāhā"—this is the procedure for all rites.
O twice-born one, [one may offer] flowers sprinkled with clarified butter, or even with ghee, through the power of the mind.

One should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) beginning with conception and ending with marriage. O Sage, know that the entry of the external [soul] into the hollow of the illustrious womb is indeed the first purificatory rite, namely conception.
And from the union with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that power which resides within the belly as the splendor of fire—
which is insentient in form yet subtle— possesses an expansion of consciousness (*cit*) through the gradual efficacy of the Lord’s power and consciousness. (5.149)

Having remembered this, one should offer clarified butter with the aforementioned mantra. Through the directing of the power of consciousness (cicchakti) into the fire, the *puṃsavana* rite is accomplished;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the sacrament known as *sīmantonnayana* in the fire.
And all those unmanifest [limbs], such as the head, hands, and so forth,
which abide within it, resort to their respective limits of action once they have awakened;
because of the calculation of their divisions, that is called the "sīmanta" (the parting of the hair).

One should offer oblations once into the fire as before for the sake of the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) of the child who has emerged from the womb; that is declared to be the *jātakarma*. O twice-born one, [the rite includes] the feeding of the breast and the consumption of gold, honey, and clarified butter.
Thereafter, one should diligently give a name to the newborn fire;
indeed, one should mark it with a well-known name such as Vāsudeva.
Thus, for that which has been purified by the consecrations of the Vaiṣṇava fire, [one should proceed] with diligence.
That which was previously the giving of mantra-food is known as the *annaprāśana*;
that which is the binding of the crest-lock (*śikhā*) before the fire is called the *caula*;
and that which one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) into the fire is remembered as the *upanayana*.
Having performed the Vedic vow, the gift of a cow, the return home, and the marriage,
one should again meditate upon the seven tongues of fire within the sacrificial pit,
where the nine sections are kindled and the flames have been raised.
Likewise, Dīptiprakāśā, Marīci, and Tāpinī,
as well as Karālā and Lelihā, are situated pervading the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The triad beginning with Prabhā is recorded as being located in the direction between the northeast and the southeast.
In the south-west, west, and north-west are those three beginning with Marīci;
situated from the center of the northern direction toward the south is the one named Lelihā.
They are red, white, blue, black, yellow, and likewise ruddy.
One should meditate upon the seven tongues of fire, resembling flashes of lightning, in their proper sequence.

O best of the twice-born, one should contemplate them in order using these mantras: either with their respective seed-syllables (bījas), or with their individual names, or with their own seed-syllables and names. 5.162–5.163.

The embers, the flames, and the power whose nature is burning—this is the substratum characterized by these three qualities; the pervasive consumer of oblations is that which is supported therein. But the eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, is the fire of the Self.
Having thus previously understood correctly the supreme Vaiśvānarī who is indeed attached [to the fire],
one should visualize the fire within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as having the form of the *ādheya* (the object to be supported),
and then [visualize] her mother arriving from the pit by way of the path of flames.
One should contemplate her, who possesses the radiance of supreme bliss, as residing in the nose-tip up to the distance of twelve finger-breadths;
then, by means of the descent-yoga, one should meditate upon her as having entered the heart.
For that person whose body has been thus completely purified, one should perform the practice once again in this manner.
Having recited the root mantra accompanied by two *praṇavas*, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) that produces perfect awakening and grants the pacification of the state of dullness,
offering either a thousand or a hundred oblations.
In the same manner, having heated it with clarified butter (ājya), one should likewise offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, one should perform the worship of the consecrated fire with devotion,
using flowers, incense, curd, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
O twice-born one, having thus worshipped the fire according to the prescribed rite with food, edible fruits, and clarified butter in due order, he should then satisfy it with sesame seeds,
clarified butter, and other offerings as far as his ability permits, following the proper sequence.
Or, having offered a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to Agni with clarified butter alone, numbering one hundred thousand times,
ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*,
one should then perform the worship of the god Agni in the center.
And as before, one should remember the Fire-god, possessing form yet radiant with the unmanifest (*niṣkala*), pervasive and extending in all directions through the power and vigor of one’s own yoga;
having the shape of a *kadamba* flower and resplendent with its own effulgences. (5.174–175)
Filling the entire pit from all sides with every form,
it is thus extended, pervasive, formless, and intensely radiant.
Then, within the center of the fire-pit, upon the support of a mass of flaming locks—
One should mentally investigate the seat exactly as it was described.
One should perform its worship below with flowers and incense mixed with sandalwood.
Then, one should perform the binding of the mudrās for the host of deities on the pedestal.

Then, having brought him down into the center [of the mandala], one should offer a handful of flowers to the Lord, the most beloved of the heart, from the waterless [state] with his own mantra. One should meditate upon Him as the manifest (sakala) one, together with His limbs and His distinctive marks.
One should perform the facing toward the Supreme Lord, the presence, and the complete absorption. 5.180
One should perform everything as before, preceded by the offering of *arghya*;

just as the meditation is performed upon the primary image (*mūlabimba*), so it should be performed within the fire. One should meditate on the one who is in a vehicle within the vehicle, and likewise upon the one established in the place within the fire.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon him as seated when he is seated, and likewise when he is reclining;
he is pure and as red as a ruby, to be remembered in the abode of fire.
And having displayed the respective mudrās for all the mantras beginning with the root-mantra, [one should worship].

Having worshipped with water for the guest (arghya), fragrance, and other offerings, one should fully honor the Lord according to the previously mentioned procedure, by means of the nature of dissolution and enjoyment. Then, having placed the collection of sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) in a vessel and honored them with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra), [one should proceed].
Then, having made his submission to the Lord with his head bowed low,
that best of the twice-born took eight pieces of fuel-sticks produced from the *brahma* and milk trees, sprinkled them on both sides with clarified butter, and divided them into two parts.
Having placed [the first] in the south and the one facing the southeast (āgneya) in the center,
one should place the one resting in the southwest (naiṛta) position and the other in the north;
these should be deposited within the two Āghāra lines, occupying the positions of Vāyu and Īśa.

Then, having taken [the ladle] from the base of the fuel, and having placed it upon the fuel with the fuel above it, one should fill the *sruva* with clarified butter and contemplate the thousand-rayed sun within it; one should place it to the south of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 5.188–5.189 ||

Having meditated upon the other ladle as the full orb of the moon by means of the syllable named Soma, one should then offer it to the north. One should indeed offer clarified butter and sacrificial fuel sticks according to the prescribed number.
Know that the two eyes of the fire are of the nature of the sun and the moon.
That which is indeed between these two is remembered as the mouth of the fire;
there one should first offer seven pieces of fuel in succession.
One should offer into the fire four pieces of wood, each well-prepared and soaked in ghee; having first smeared them with saffron and other substances, they are to be known as "wood" (kāṣṭha).
Then, one should offer garlands, incense, honey-mixture (madhuparka), seeds, and clarified butter in their proper sequence.
In that regard, this specific rule is prescribed for the offering of the fuel-sticks of food (annasamidh):
having first placed the prepared sacrificial porridge (caru) before the consecrated fire,
one should open it, look at it, and first sprinkle it with the water of the arghya-offering.
Then,
with four blades of *darbha* grass together with fire, he should touch that [spot];
in the middle of it, he should deposit four *sruva*-ladles of clarified butter while reciting the mantra.
Then, taking the *sruk* ladle there, one should offer four [oblations] in the same manner;
then one should take a morsel of food measured by four finger-breadths.
Having placed that within the hollow of the *sruva* ladle, one should [pour] clarified butter over it as before.
One should offer four oblations into the fire, and then cast an oblation of food.
Again, having carefully taken four ladles of clarified butter (ājya) into the fire,
one should then make another oblation of food sprinkled with clarified butter, as before.
One should give [the offerings] in this very same manner four times according to the previous procedure;
having offered the oblations of food, one should then offer those called clarified butter (ājya).
One should offer one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds mixed with ghee.
One should perform [the rite] a hundred times, fifty times, or a quarter of that, according to one's ability.
Then, one should likewise offer oblations with unbroken rice grains and sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter;
half [of the portion] should be combined with a half-share, and more should be given to those at the head.

At the time of recitation as well as during the fire-oblation, one who desires success should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* rite once with a mouthful of food. This should be done with those offerings that yield desired fruits when performed according to the specific place and time.
With sesame seeds, ghee, milk, or curd, or with milk-rice;
with prepared foods, well-cooked delicacies, seeds, parched grain, and rice; and with roots, fruits, shoots, and very excellent tender sprouts. || 5.204–5.205 ||
With fragrant flowers such as the *sthalapadma* and others, as well as white and other varieties;
with *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter, or properly with *śrīveṣṭaka*;
and with fresh *dhātrī* fruits and auspicious blue lotuses.
With lotuses that were white, black, and red, and with beautiful *bilva* fruits;
with blades of *dūrvā* grass whose tips were unbroken and as pure as the fine tusks of an elephant;
and with fuel-sticks produced from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree as well as from milk-exuding trees.
[One should offer] branches of the *audumbara* tree joined with nectar and milk, drenched in honey, with uncut tips, unbroken, and free from thorns;
all of them should be combined with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) or, alternatively, with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (5.209)

All these, along with the various kinds of food, sandalwood and the like, as well as tooth-sticks and betel— provided it is free from excessive alkaline substances— are always to be offered into the midst of the fire together with the fuel sticks. (5.210–5.211)
In the Lakṣahoma, however, the seats and other such items should be provided;
they must be free from honey, salt, drinks, garments, pungent substances, and oils.
With sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, all perfections (siddhis) are likewise accomplished.
An oblation of clarified butter, milk, and curd bestows satisfaction.

O twice-born one, through milk-rice, prepared foods, and edible delicacies, there shall always be nourishment; and when propitiated with seeds, grains, and rice, the King of Mantras is satisfied. (5.213–5.214)

When pleased, the Supreme Lord always bestows the highest good; an oblation performed with sprouts, fruits, and roots grants satisfaction. It causes one to abandon untimely death and brings diseases to a state of pacification.
When propitiated with land-lotuses and other flowers such as the white ones,
O Brahmins, she bestows incomparable good fortune before long;
likewise, with guggulu resin and clarified butter, she grants health to the twice-born, as does she with auspicious dhātrī fruits.
With sugar, pieces of *bilva* fruit sprinkled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
offerings of ghee and rice, and lotus seeds, one quickly bestows prosperity (*lakṣmī*).
One who desires subjugation (*vaśya*) should offer blue lotuses (*utpala*), while one who desires enjoyments should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).

By performing a fire sacrifice with *dūrvā* sprouts, one shall obtain an increase in longevity. A fire sacrifice with auspicious fuel-wood brings prosperity, while a sacrifice with *māṣa* beans bestows peace.
A fire sacrifice of sesame seeds is highly commended when performed with the "deer-face" (*hariṇānana*) mudrā.
An oblation of clarified butter is one karṣa, and that of milk is likewise, with special preference for the latter;
an oblation of curd is the measure of a śukti, or a handful (prasṛti) of milk-rice;
and of solid foods and edibles, the measure is half a mouthful according to their own natural size.
One should perform the oblation with a handful of all seeds.
For parched grains, one should offer five grains using the tips of the fingers;
for fruits, the offering should be of their own natural measure, and the same applies to sprouts. (5.222–5.223)
One should always offer pills of guggulu the size of a jujube fruit;
or, if available, one may offer them the size of an emblic myrobalan fruit.
O best of Brahmins, one may also offer blades of dūrvā grass measuring four or eight finger-breadths.
The fuel sticks should be of equal size, measuring a span (prādeśa) in length, and covered with bark. Furthermore, the colors, smells, sounds, shapes,
transformations, and the direction of the flames of the fire must be observed for the successful accomplishment of the ritual action.
O twice-born one, the fire that possesses the brilliance of a ruby, which is excellent and resembles lac or liquid lac,
or has the color of the rising sun or the sacrificial fire (hutabhuj), is praised for the sake of victory.
Or, the fire that resembles the wrath of Indra or has a crimson luster [is likewise auspicious].
The best [fire] resembles a wheel or a bow, and likewise has the hue of saffron.
Here, fire is said to have the color of red flowers;
it is fragrant with the scent of substances and possesses the auspicious fragrance of clarified butter.
Āyurda has the fragrance of a lotus, while Suvrata has the fragrance of a bilva fruit;
Agragandha is prescribed for malevolent rites (abhicāra), as is Sarvadānala.
Jīmūta has a sound like that of a lute, a conch, or a drum.
Sound is the reason for the accomplishment of fire; anything other than this would fail to grant success.
When the fire appears red, with its flames diminished, or when it has the luster of a ruby or the brilliance of crystal, it is auspicious. (5.231–5.232)
If that fire which was previously described should attain circumambulation [of the practitioner] and undergo a mutual transformation, then it is the fire that brings about accomplishment. However,
if it possesses a proud color, such as pigeon-grey (kāpotaka) and so forth—
O Brahmin, fire likewise undergoes such reversals;
for that reason, at the conclusion of the *homa*, one should perform more than a hundred additional oblations.
Furthermore, irregular flames of the fire and its rising [in various directions] bring about auspicious results. (5.234–5.235)
A flame that is short, not short, high, or long is known to bestow success (*siddhi*).
One that is glossy, turning to the right, and whose sound covers [the ears] like the *śruti* [of a lute],
is always auspicious, even when it lacks other qualities.
One who desires prosperity should offer oblations into a fire that is blazing, flickering, smokeless, endowed with its natural qualities, pleasant to the heart, and gratifying;
[but not into one] that has little luster, little form, and is accompanied by sparks. || 5.237–5.238 ||
A fire that is devoid of flames and smoke does not grant success at all;
if one should offer oblations into a fire that is unawakened and smoky,
there will be a loss of ritual efficacy for him, and he experiences only the results of malevolent magic.
If the mantra— foul-smelling, yellow in color, licked by [the tongue], and inauspicious—
is satiated while residing within the light-form, O best of beings,
that lord, established in radiance and bestowing the earth, will grant the vidyā before long. (5.240–5.241)
By remaining above the light, the pervasive Lord quickly scorches the enemies;
ascending through the Marīcī [channel], he swiftly brings about the destruction of the foes.
Ascending through the Tāpinī [channel], the mantra bestows the pacification of all curses.
If one performs oblations while established in the Karālā posture, one shall effect the eradication of opposing forces.
O Sage, if the mantra is propitiated while established in the Lelihā posture,
it shall grant whatever is desired and, at the end of the body, the supreme state.
One should always use *svāhā* in the fire-oblation (*homa*), and *vauṣaṭ* in the full oblation (*pūrṇā*);
one should employ that same [term] in rites for pacification (*śāntika*), and likewise *vaṣaṭ* in rites for nourishment (*āpyāyana*).
One uses *svadhā* in rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkriyā*), and the syllable *phaṭ* in rites of destruction (*kṣayakarman*).

"Huṃ" is for inciting enmity; "namas" is for the subjugation of women and for the attainment of liberation. At the conclusion of the ritual fire-offerings (karmahoma), one should fill the ladle with clarified butter;
in its absence, one should fill it with an abundance of other sacrificial substances.

Thereupon, one should place ghee above; then, beginning from the base, one should worship the *sruk* ladle together with the *sruva* spoon using water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth.
That substance mixed with ghee is then placed within the bowl of the *sruk*'s receptacle.
One should meditate on [the deity] resembling a flowing moon; then, one should draw it forth in its fullness.

Having restrained it at the base of the handle of the sacrificial ladle—that is, at the navel of the body—one should contemplate the Lord of Mantras in his partless form, whose body is like the full, cool-rayed moon.
One should draw it up from its very root by means of the power of the vital wind (marucchakti) from one's own body;

having established it in the support of the Lord (Īśvara), one should contemplate that great stream of nectar falling into the lotus of the sacrificial ladle (srukpadma) through the path of the junction of the nostrils.
One should pour forth an unceasing stream of clarified butter like a shower of wealth;
one should then visualize it entering correctly into the center of the mantra’s mouth, or into the aperture of Brahmā,
having fully entered within the heart-lotus.
In that way, one should indeed split apart the fortified mantra with the stream of Brahman;
[the mantra] becomes satisfied, nourished, gladdened, and truly contented above the practitioner.
Indeed, it is accompanied by the utterance of the mantra and endowed with the formation of the body.
O best of the twice-born, this [offering] is proclaimed as complete when accompanied by meditation;
it eternally grants all perfections and increases the fortune of liberation.
For the accomplishment of ritual acts, one should offer oblations even into a fire with many dry logs.
One should not perform multiple applications for each individual ritual action;
rather, one should worship the Lord of Mantras with water for the guest, perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Then, one should display all the mudrās in sequence, beginning with the root mantra.
One should perform the satiation of the limbs with a fourth part of the root [mantra],
and that of the insignia, ornaments, Lakṣmī, and so forth, with half of that.
Alternatively,

O best of the twice-born, one should offer all the marks, ornaments, and so forth, in sequence: half of those [measures] for the Heart-mantra and others in all [the rites], and half of that again for the beloveds of the Supreme Lord.
Or else, one should offer oblations for each of the mantras beginning with the heart-mantra.
Then, having offered the *arghya* together with incense, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*).
