Those mantras residing in the stations of enjoyment, which have been worshipped in their proper sequence, [should be dismissed].
And one should contemplate them as having entered the body of the principal mantra, just as rivers enter the ocean or as flames merge within other flames.
O twice-born one, that gross embodiment of the mantra is the locus of all mantras. || 5.262-5.263 ||
One should meditate upon that which has entered the subtle, the presiding principle consisting of the heart— the supreme,
previously described form, which is both subtle and dual-natured (5.264)—
that supreme, throbbing form resting in the supportless state.
One should visualize [the breath] having entered the heart-lotus through the path of the joint; then,
by means of the inhalation accompanied by mantra and mudrā, for the seventh time, one should visualize the body illuminated by that [light], from the feet up to the head.
O twice-born one, when the mantra has entered [the body], even without effort,
the body of that person whose mantra is pleased begins to tremble.
Having thus dismissed the Lord of Mantras together with the binding of the mudrās, [one should proceed].

O best of the twice-born, for the mantras of the shared seat and of Gaṇeśa, as well as for the Guru and the others, an oblation (argha) is prescribed from the mirror of the [spiritual] mark (lācchanadarpaṇa). O Brahmin, one should perform their dissolution (laya) according to the sequence of creation.

One should offer half [of the portion] each, in due order, starting from the Guru, to those stationed at the gates of the guardians of the three worlds and to those who serve Hari while standing upon the ramparts;
or else, one may offer it once, or according to one's own capacity, into all of them simultaneously.
Then Viṣvaksena should be gratified with devotion using sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains.
O twice-born one, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ.
Having worshipped him according to the rule, one should perform his dismissal (visarjana).
Having worshipped the fire according to one's ability, one should then offer libations;
with the mantra, one should pour out a full oblation that makes [the rite] flawless.
Then, one should display the mudrā of the fire accompanied by the mantra.
Having cast a handful of flowers into the vessel while recollecting the fire-mantra,
and having offered forgiveness and paid obeisance according to the rule, he should dismiss it; then,
having smelled [the flower], he should deposit it into the square (koṣṭha) according to the sequence of descent.
Having wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and placed the *sruk* into the fire,

he should fill it with water from the *arghya* vessel and, outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), perform a circumambulation starting from the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*) with an unbroken stream of water.
Having cast [the remains] with the *pavitraka* from below to above, or else with the hand, one should place the remainder on the head; the garland should be placed below the mouth, and it,
together with the sacrificial seat (*viṣṭara*) and the flow [of the offering], should be on one's own left side.
Having discarded the water contained in the two vessels after it has been worshipped,
and having likewise withdrawn that [deity] with ashes produced by churning the water, one should then apply four vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks.
One should form the shape of a lamp flame on the heart, the shoulders, and the forehead.
Then, taking the vessel for the arghya offering and going to the house of the Blessed One,
one should pay homage to the Lord of the World by prostrating with the eight limbs.
Having filled both hands with flowers placed upon them,
one should recollect the partless mantra augmented by nectar;
then, one should cast it, shimmering with abundant radiance, onto the head of the mantra.
"You have been gratified by my devotion, O All-pervading Lord, through this oblation within the midst of the fire.
Accept for yourself this potency that resides in the sacrificial substances.
Having performed the worship according to the rule, offer the oblation as a dedication to the Lord."
One should meditate upon that which has been received with a serene inner self.
Having thus completed the rites up to the fire-oblation (homa), one should worship the Lord with water for honor (arghya), perfumes, and other offerings,
and then perform the distribution of portions for the ancestors.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Seat of Food and the Fire-Rite," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Śrī. Now begins the sixth chapter. O sages!
"What is the procedure for the distribution among the ancestors, and what is its fruit?
O tiger among sages, let all of that be described by you now. (6.1) Nārada.
O Brahmins, that which is performed daily before the one worthy of worship should be known as the supreme *saṃvibhāga* among all ritual acts.
Through this *saṃvibhāga*, a man becomes free from debt to his ancestors.
By that [act], they attain incomparable satisfaction even through the power of their past karma.
Now, it is explained how the distribution for the ancestors should be performed:
one should spread *kuśa* grass with the tips pointing south near the base of the *kuṇḍa*.
Either on the ground near the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) or above it, having scattered sesame seeds along with water containing silver upon a layer of grass,
one should then sequentially visualize the fathers and the grandfathers there.
Then, for the satisfaction of all, having offered [the food] to the deity,
one should place four vessels of food— or four morsels— upon the seat (staroḥ) after sprinkling them with water; then, one should worship them with the arghya and other offerings.
Then, in due order, through the dissolution-yoga by means of the fourfold mantras belonging to himself,
he should offer water with sesame seeds preceded by the [deceased's] name and lineage, along with the mantra. Furthermore,
he should present the *arghya* jars for all [the ancestors] in their proper sequence.
Then, for that purpose, he seated four Pāñcarātrika brāhmaṇas who had attained the supreme reality as their goal upon their seats—
two facing east and two facing north.
Even in the absence of [all] the [deities], having placed at least one facing north,
one should then perform their worship in sequence, as in the *Cāturātmya* rite,
with offerings such as water for the guest (*arghya*) and unguents, up to the concluding oblations (*mātrā*).
With all things appropriate for those respective times, excluding what is not to be accepted,
they should remain established in silence and well-restrained;
with speech controlled and their focus fixed, even upon Janārdana in the form of food.
Through that, the ancestors attain eternal satisfaction.
Therefore, silence that is subject to deviation must be avoided by those intent on ritual action. That which is auspicious and free from deviation should be practiced in all matters.
That silence which is produced by indistinct nasal syllables consisting of bodily gestures and signs, and which is bound by the *mokṣapuṭa* [technique], causes the loss of its own accomplishment.
That which operates upon all objects by itself through one's own intellect—[that is true silence]. (6.15–6.16)
Know that silence to be perpetual which is not accompanied by words.
Therefore, during a divine rite for the ancestors or at a Śrāddha feast,
one should place everything before the recipients within the prescribed boundaries, as if it were an offering (naivedya).
Restraining their speech, they remain thus until the time for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). By this very rule, men must always, and especially at a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice,
perform the distribution of portions for the ancestors with those riches.

Or, if one is unable, having performed [the rites] ending with the water-offering of sesame seeds, one should offer half of that— just a single morsel— with fruits and roots to a cow-path mendicant (*goṣpathabhaikṣuka*). For when Acyuta has been worshipped, whatever is given with divine great mantras [becomes immensely fruitful].

Whether it be small or abundant, that which is offered for the sake of the ancestors shall become inexhaustible for them. Having worshipped that omnipresent Lord, who resides in the root-mantra and the central image, with offerings of water, perfumes, and other articles,
[one should worship] in all courtyards, palaces, and hermitages.
When the forms of the arrayed manifestations have been installed for the sake of beauty,
as well as those at the gate-towers, the gates, and the directions within the pavilion,
one should perform their constant worship according to one's capacity, so that they may remain ever present.
One should perform [the worship] with sixteen services, or thirty-two, or even more than that; likewise, in the occasional rites (*naimittika*), one should do so using the mantras of those forms.
Then, the practitioner should perform the concluding recitation (*japa*) or the concluding fire-oblation (*havana*), as well as the bathing and other [rituals]. (6.24–6.25)
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) situated at the foremost point of each respective image.
However, there [in that pit], one should not perform ritual worship of the deity, bathing, festivals, and so forth,
nor the offering of oblations (bali), in all cases such as the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) and others.
One must especially not perform [the full ritual] upon forms that are dependent on others;
rather, one should perform there only the daily consecration (nityābhiṣeka) for those [images],
or else the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) or the offering (nivedana) for those endowed with colors such as white and so forth.

The teachers should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) as an ancillary part, together with the worship of the Root Abode (mūlālaya), in the case of the dependent [deities], using threads that have been consecrated;
and likewise in all the *pūraka* offerings, as well as in the *āgrayaṇa* and other rites.
Even among the hosts of attendants such as the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and Viṣvaksena,
when they are established in temples, they are to be worshipped like the foundational forms (āśrayamūrti).
However, this applies to the formless Lord of Birds, Viṣvaksena, and the others.

One should offer the bali-oblation three times a day before the daily festival worship to the lords of the Kumuda and other gaṇas who dwell in the gates and enclosures, as well as to the other members of the retinue residing in the great sacred seats (mahāpīṭha).
Whether with form or formless, Viṣvaksena, together with his hosts,
should be worshipped with the remaining materials at the conclusion of the offering;
thereafter, one should perform a perpetual festival endowed with all ornaments.
O best of sages, listen as I describe the procedure for the offering of oblations (bali) to the deities of the walls and gates,
by performing which the desired fruit arises for devotees. (6.35)
For the purpose of perpetual festivals, the image should be made of gold or silver, or else of copper or bell-metal; it should not be too tall, should have four arms,
and must correspond in form to the original primary image that was previously installed.
Having adorned [the image] with garments, ornaments, and garlands according to its beauty,
and having not yet ritually installed the Śakti residing in the original image into it by means of mantra (6.38),
one should then worship it thoroughly with offerings beginning with water for the guest (arghya) and flowers, and ending with incense.
When the deity has been propitiated by trusted attendants in self-manifested shrines and similar locations,
one should choose another officiant for the rites such as the offering of oblations (bali),
whether at the door of the inner sanctum or likewise in the front pavilion.
Having worshipped those stationed at the door with a lamp ignited together with the sound of a bell, and having honored them with offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with incense,
one should then present the water for *arghya*, followed by food and the water for libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having offered betel-leaf in due order with the respective mantras in succession,
[he should place] a vehicle made of gold or other materials in the first courtyard in front,
adorned with the luster of fragrant flowers and silken garlands of white and other colors.
Having adorned it as beautifully as possible with auspicious offerings and festive decorations,
and having placed it facing the east on the courtyards while circumambulating from left to right, [they honored it] with white and other parasols, and with banners featuring peacock feathers.
With banners, yak-tail whisks, and beautiful palm-leaf fans; with courtesans, temple-maidens, and singers, accompanied by a multitude of musical instruments;
and with the sounds of kettledrums and tabors that filled the range of hearing.
In a mandala measuring one cubit, smeared with cow dung and adorned with such ornaments as these, preceded by the offering of bali,
one should [worship] the deities of the door-enclosures who have been visualized in their respective directions.
One should perform a fixed festival according to the procedure to be described.
Having performed the worship of Viṣṇu and the beings along with their attendants upon the pedestal,
one should scatter the remaining offering, together with water, as a *bali* for the sake of satisfaction.
Having circumambulated the pedestal four times or twice,
and having gratified [the deity] with dance, song, and other offerings, one should cause the Lord to enter within.
With reverence, [this should be done] in the spacious outer courtyards.
Having placed [the deity] upon a decorated chariot, one should perform a circumambulation. Then, having removed [the deity] from the vehicle and other such means, and having offered the sandals,
one should seat [the deity] upon an auspicious throne situated on the ground of the main pavilion.
Having honored him with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and water for sipping, as well as with ointments such as sandalwood,
various kinds of garlands, incenses, and concluding with betel leaf,
one should settle him in his own place for the sake of allaying fatigue.
Having first established the Śakti and then joined it to its base,
one should worship it with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and perfumes, and bow down preceded by hymns of praise.
Where this is performed according to rule three times a day, there a constant festival takes place.
In that case, there shall be constant prosperity for both the king and the kingdom,
provided that the image of the deity is brought into proximity by means of an offering of food.
Alternatively, one should perform the daily festival with a tuft of grass or a figure made of grain.
Having performed the withdrawal of everything without exception, including the *arghya* and other offerings,
and having bowed to and praised the Lord of Gods, one should then take the water for the feet (*pādya*) from the vessel and sprinkle it over one's own body. (6.57–6.58)
One should place upon one's own head the leaves and flowers that have been consumed [as offerings],
once the sacrifice to the gods has been performed with flowers, water-offerings, and perfumes, and when devotees who observe the mantras have respectfully presented their offerings.

By constantly holding [the breath] at the crown of the head, misfortune comes to an end; one attains fame, splendor, prosperity, health, and spiritual perfection. Afterwards, for the sake of maintaining the body's journey through life, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
Having indeed received permission, he should perform the concluding sacrifice according to the rule;
taking all the food, beginning with the *naivedya*, and placing it in a vessel,
he should offer it to the deity and purify it with water.
For it is of the nature of truth, unperceivable, and it brings about the destruction of the defects of food.
This meditation, which pertains to the fourfold self, should be cultivated with the mind;
thus, one becomes established in the state of goodness within food, known as the direct perception of the Self.
The Lord Pradyumna resides in form, while Lāṅgalin (Balabhadra) resides in this heroic power;
the high-souled Lord Vāsudeva himself, however, is the unborn enjoyer.
Then, one should drink a handful of water consecrated with the four *praṇavas*.
Having offered four oblations of food into the mouth-kuṇḍa with that very [food],
he should then eat the desired morsels according to his liking.
Having sipped water again, he should go back to the house of the Blessed One, purified in mind.
Having placed the mind, along with the intellect and the sense of ego, upon the surface of the earth—
with the four legs like those of a tortoise and the head as the fifth—
one should always perform circumambulation in this manner.
One should perform prostration with eight limbs, preceded by the eight-syllable mantra. Thus, the worship with eight limbs has been described as ending with the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga),
beginning from the internal sacrifice of the mind up to the self-offering (ātmanivedana).

O Sage Nārada, know that the first part of the limb-sacrifice (aṅgayāga), which is called Abhigamana, consists of all the worship with offerings such as water for the hands (arghya) and flowers, as well as all the enjoyments (bhoga) performed through external services. 6.71b–72a.
With honey, ghee, curd, and with animal sacrifice, one performs worship;
that is indeed the third limb of sacrifice, O Sage, while the fourth is worship with food, which is the giving away of what has been offered according to the previously mentioned rule.
The fifth is traditionally known as the gift (sampradāna), which is an auxiliary of the sacrifice;
the sixth is the satiation of the fire, and the seventh is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyāga).
The eighth of these is the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga) known by the name Prāṇāgnihotra.
In this manner, one should perform the worship endowed with its eight limbs according to the prescribed rule,
wherein twelve offerings are to be made at the [twelve] times of the day with great elaboration.
Therein, one should perform the morning worship endowed with eight limbs;
however, two limbs are omitted after completing the *ghāta* and performing the distribution to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) as prescribed. (6.76–6.77)
The teacher should always perform his own worship during the midday rite;
at the three times of day, he should offer one [type of worship] with eight limbs and the other two with six limbs.
For those seeking yoga, there is self-study (svādhyāya), and for those seeking enjoyment, that which is known as the adhyātma [worship].
One should perform one's private study at those respective times; this is now being described.
Having prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation and sat down before the Lord, one should engage in the study of the scriptures and the investigation of the meaning of their statements. (6.79–6.80)
Then, when the time for twilight has arrived, having bathed up to the hips or having washed them,
one should then perform the changing of clothes.
One should perform the evening worship consisting of six limbs, concluding with the offering of oblations.
At those respective times, one should perform [the rites] according to what is declared in the scriptures.
Having performed the recitation (japa) to the best of one's ability, and then having attained one's bed,
one should withdraw the external deity and establish it in the state of the supportless (nirālamba).
With a mind that was indeed neither strained nor slackened,
he remained thus until sleep came upon him at that very moment.
Then, rising at midnight, his sleep conquered and his fatigue overcome, [he sat up].

Having sipped water from the very water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and having paid homage to the Guru and the Deity, one should sit upon a seat of antelope skin and then practice yoga according to the rules, O lords of sages.

Having thus abandoned the act of recitation and composed the self within the self, one should remain until, through the dissolution of the distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation, one attains absorption in That;
then, one gains stability in a state of samādhi that is forever free from any perceivable object.
Then, through practice, the yogi of the Blessed One attains Brahman.
There, having abandoned the meditation seat, one should gradually achieve mastery over fatigue;
thereafter, one should offer a bed and seat following the primary form (mūlamūrti).
One should not project the deity onto that [liṅga], which is endowed with powers such as Lakṣmī and has assumed the form of the sacrifice, even though it is adorned in all its limbs.
[One should offer] the arghya, pādya, and ācamana, together with the ritual implements for acceptance.
Having given [these], he should afterwards anoint [the image] with ointments such as sandalwood;
and having offered fragrant flowers, garlands, and the like, as well as lamps and incense, [he should offer] foods beginning with cakes, along with milk and fruits. (6.91–6.92)
Then, having offered water for libation, betel-leaf prepared with fragrant substances, and all the ritual accessories according to one's means to the God of gods,
one should afterwards place everything— including whatever rites have been performed— within that [liṅga].

One should contemplate that right hand as satisfied, grasped, and full. In its center, one should meditate upon the partless mantra, which is entirely filled with rays of light, and the attainment of the fruit arising from yoga in the form of Lakṣmī.
Having recited the root mantra, one should likewise visualize it in the center of the palm;
furthermore, one should contemplate the partless (niṣkala) mantra above that.
Placing both knees upon the ground with the head [bowed], one should offer it to Viṣṇu.
Then,

O best of the twice-born, with a mind inclined toward faith and being thoroughly satisfied, he respectfully made that his own; having properly performed either renunciation or the accumulation [of merit] for it.
And by means of the mudrā, which conforms to the form of the mantra,
that which brings forth fruit for the sake of the result [of those] who have performed renunciation must be sealed;
and at the conclusion of the fruit, let there be as much as is enjoined by the Āgama.
That by which [the rite] is performed for our Lord is not suitable for those seeking fruits through Siddhas and the like.

Therefore, one should perform the dismissal after offering the *arghya* together with incense, provided that the image has been permanently installed and is independent of [specific locations such as] land or water. (6.100–6.101)
One should remember that the mantras residing in the places of enjoyment, having been worshipped in their proper order, have entered into the body of the principal mantra,
just as flames enter into other flames or as rivers enter into the ocean. (6.102)
O twice-born ones, one should contemplate that mantra as a gross body, having entered the state of all mantras; indeed, it enters the subtle, the presiding deity who possesses both natures,
and finally the supreme reality of the previously described form— that subtle one which consists of both.
Therefore, having shown a stainless mirror that reflects the supreme, radiant form and rests upon the supportless state,
one should meditate on the heart-lotus as having entered through the path of the junction (sandhi) in front of it.
Having recollected that [deity] as both other and self within the sky of one's own consciousness in the heart,
one should meditate upon the God who pervades the universe, endowed with his own nature,
within the six images such as the ritual worship and so forth, for the sake of attaining the eternal state and the rest.
When the [deities] have been duly and permanently installed in the worship according to the sequence beginning with the east,
one should worship that Power (śakti) joined from the primary image (mūlabimba) according to the rule,
using offerings such as water for honor (arghya), flowers, and the aforementioned betel leaves and so forth.

One should again project [the deity] onto the root [icon], having assigned it to its respective place for the sake of worship in the action-icons and so forth, during the daily, occasional, and other rites. When that particular rite has commenced, the knower of mantras should invoke [the deity] from the root [icon].
Having completed those rites undertaken therein according to the truth,
and having concluded them at the primary image, one should dismiss [the deities] from there;
having dismissed the mantras residing in the vessels of arghya and so forth, according to the preliminary procedure.
Having offered all the remaining portions, beginning with the *arghya*, together with what was previously eaten,
to Viṣvaksena with a hand purified by water,
and having mentally withdrawn the two-fold placement (*nyāsa*) from his own body, [he should proceed].
One should perform the disposal of everything without exception— the *arghya* and so forth—
by means of the sacrificial vessel, the fire-pit, the sacrificial grass-mat, and whatever else there may be. Together with the ritual smearing, one should cast it all into the water.
One should secure the door-panels while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca),
having stationed the Wheel and the Lord of Birds there for the sake of protection.
Then, the practitioner, having risen in the morning as before, may depart at his own will.

One should perform everything as described, including the awakening, the sacrifice, and so forth, for one day, three days, seven days, a fortnight, or even a month. Whoever performs [the rite] according to this rule, endowed with devotion and faith, [attains the fruit]. 6.117
Even he would go to the supreme state, how much more so one who is firmly established therein;
the high-minded one, having girded his loins, [remains] for a period of time lasting as long as life.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedures from the Distribution of Offerings to the Ancestors up to the Festival of the Reclining," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
O Blessed One, tiger among sages, you who are proficient in all the scriptures!
Immediately after the worship of the Pradhānamūrti,
the worship of the installed images in all courtyards, temples, and shrines is prescribed.
In that regard, O divine sage, we wish to hear specifically about the worship of the goddesses Śrībhū and the others; please reveal it to us in detail. (7.3) Nārada said:
Listen, all you sages, to the supreme worship of the illustrious Goddess Bhū,
by the mere knowledge of which a man obtains his desires.
Lakṣmī is remembered as the power of the enjoyer, while Puṣṭi is indeed designated as the agent.
For him who has descended for the sake of enjoyment out of compassion for the world,
that imperishable pair of powers arose together with him; indeed,
it is through their diversity that his transformation is manifested.
In that regard, three forms of the goddesses beginning with Śrī have been described:
Yogalakṣmī resides upon the Śrīvatsa mark, while Bhogalakṣmī stands at his side;
Vīralakṣmī, however, is established independently in a separate location.
Thus, three forms have been described for the other goddesses.
One should worship Yogalakṣmī and Bhogalakṣmī together with the Lord;
however, one should worship Vīralakṣmī separately in her own chamber according to the prescribed rite.
Wherever that goddess is worshipped, there prosperity shall become immovable.
O best of sages, listen as I explain the procedure for that;
it may be performed either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure.
Or, at the beginning of the third enclosure,

one should arrange the station of Śrī; O lords of sages, one should likewise arrange Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Sāvitrī, and Vāgdevī in the four directions of that celestial chariot, as well as the deities of the cardinal points.
In the corners, one may place either Vainateya or a lion according to one's preference;
within that, in the divine Brahma-section, one should install Śrī,
who has four arms, noble limbs, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
Seated in the lotus posture, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
she grants fearlessness and boons with her two principal hands,
while holding divine lotuses with her two lower hands.
O best of the twice-born, one should worship the Goddess three times a day with her mantra,
having first extracted the *praṇava* (Om) and immediately thereafter the seed-syllable of Śrī (*śrīṃ*).
This six-syllabled mantra, "Śriyai namaḥ," bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
One should join [the syllables] *śrāṃ śrīṃ śrūṃ śraiṃ śrauṃ śra* with the heart and other limbs.
Having first bathed with this mantra, the best of preceptors,
having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rule, [should proceed].
Then, having entered the palace, he should perform everything as is appropriate,
sitting comfortably on his own seat, facing either the east or the north.
Having completed the purification of the hands, the binding of the directions, and the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), [he should proceed].
Then, having purified one's own body with the two types of *dhāraṇā*,
one should thereafter place the venerable mantra, along with its limbs (*sāṅga*), upon the hands and the body,
as well as the crown, the forest garland, and the pair of lotuses.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and other limbs as before, and having formed the lotus-gesture (*padmamudrā*),
one should then assume identity with the Supreme Self, the Lord who abides in the abode of his own bliss within the lotus of the heart.
From the Śrīvatsa, however, one should bring forth the goddess Śrī, endowed with all auspicious marks;
having brought her down, one should worship her until the end of the recitation with nectars and enjoyments as previously described.
Then, outside, one should worship the goddess with the collections of enjoyments mentioned before.
For that purpose, the knower of mantras should prepare, as before, the five vessels beginning with the *arghya*;
having worshipped the mantras placed upon his own body as previously described,
he should then perform the rite of the gateway (*dvārayāga*) with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with incense (*dhūpa*).
Having likewise worshipped Vāstvīśa, Kṣetranātha, and Dvāralakṣmī,
as well as Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī on both sides of the entrance to the sanctum,
one should perform the worship of the temple structure (vimāna).
One should perform the arrangement of the principles (tattva) of the world-path exactly as before;
however, listen here to this specific detail regarding the seats of the deities:
one should worship the fourfold group beginning with Dharma upon a base of lentil-shaped cushions (masūraka).
The forms [of the Lord] beginning with Vāsudeva and the forms beginning with Keśava;
likewise Padmanābha and the others— wherever these lords of sages are to be worshipped, one should worship their respective Śaktis there, or worship those very forms themselves in due order.
Or else, one should worship them together with their respective powers in due order.
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are declared to be the powers of the Vyūhas.
Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, and Vibhūti are the [powers] of the [other] forms.

Desire, Affection, Delight, Illusion, Intellect, and Greatness—these are proclaimed as the powers of Keśava and the others in their respective order. Intellect, Tārā, Vāruṇī, Śakti, Padmā, and likewise Vidyā [are the powers of the others]. || 7.32–7.33 ||
Sāṅkhyā, Viśvā, Khagā, Bhūḥ, Gauḥ, Lakṣmī, Vāgīśvarī, as well as Amṛtā, Hariṇī, Chāyā, Nārasiṃhī, Sudhā,
Śrī, Kānti, Vīrā, Kāmā, Satyā, Śānti, and Saroruhā.
I am she who sits upon the lotus, the dwarf, and the valiant stride born of man;
I am Nārāyaṇī, the delight of Hari, Gāndhārī, and likewise Kāśyapī;
I am Vaidehī, the Vedic lore, Padminī, and she who reclines upon the serpent.
And these thirty-eight goddesses are the powers (śaktis) of Padmanābha and the others;
where there is another auspicious form of the Lord, there one should worship Śrī.
One should worship the other deities of the celestial chariots (vimāna) exactly as they were previously described.

One should especially worship Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Sāvitrī, and Vāgdevī, who are stationed specifically at the four directions of the celestial chariot (vimāna). Then, at the door of the front pavilion, one should worship Balākinī on the right.
Having performed the worship of the gateway in this manner on the northern side of Vanamālī,
one should then prepare the seat;
beneath the pedestal, one should [visualize] the Lord of Serpents, the support of all, for this deity.
And in its corners, one should worship Dharma and the others; above that, a manifest lotus.
Then, for three watches of the night, one should worship within that [lotus] in sequence with water for the hands (arghya) and other offerings.
Then, having worshipped Gaṇanātha and the others according to the prescribed rule— || 7.41–7.42 ||
Then, having invoked Śrī, one should perform the ritual procedures beginning with the placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*).

Having performed the rites of presence (*sannidhāna*) and so forth, one should display the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*). One should worship the mantras assigned to the limbs according to the procedure prescribed for dissolution (*laya*).
And the sacrifice of enjoyments (bhogayāga) should be performed upon the surface of the lotus-seat.
On the lotus petals starting from the east, the heart-mantra and the others are to be placed as before;
on the petals in the intermediate directions, the weapon-mantra and the eye-mantra, along with the cluster of filaments.
Outside the petals upon the pedestal,
one should place the crown and the forest garland in the southeast and northeast corners, and the two lotuses in the southwest and northwest corners; immediately thereafter, one should install them.
Thereafter, I shall explain meditation; listen, O best of the twice-born!
[One should meditate on her] seated within the divine celestial chariot upon a lotus throne, sitting in the lotus posture, with the luster of the interior of a full-blown lotus.
Endowed with all the primary marks and adorned with every ornament,
her mass of curls was overspread by swarms of hovering bees.
Adorned with a crown embellished by shimmering jewels,
her forehead graced by a radiant crescent moon;
her wide eyes like blossoming blue lotuses, her face lit with a gentle smile.
She who brings nourishment to the world with side-glances full of compassion;
whose round cheeks shine like the surface of a mirror;
whose nose-bridge is radiant with pearls, and who is ablaze with the creeper-like eyebrows.
Her teeth were like pearls, her lower lip was glistening coral, and she was enchanting with her two ears adorned by sparkling gem-studded earrings;
her face resembled the full moon, and her neck was like a conch shell.
Adorned with a jeweled neck-ornament and decorated with auspicious gems,
she has four arms and broad shoulders, and is embellished with pearl necklaces;
her breasts are very firm, solid, high, full, rounded, and thick.
Adorned with a variegated bodice and embellished with various ornaments,
she grants fearlessness to the frightened with her principal right hand,
and bestows boons upon those who seek refuge with her lotus-like left hand.
In her right hand she holds a lotus bud,
and likewise in her left she holds a full-blown lotus;
she is adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and various gem-studded rings.
Adorned with divine garments and decorated with girdles and other ornaments,
she possessed a deep navel and a slender waist graced by the three folds of skin;
her sprout-like feet shone with anklets set with various jewels.
Her limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, and she was adorned with celestial garlands.
One should meditate upon this Vīra-lakṣmī, who bestows all desired objects, whose luster is equal to ten million full moons, and who is an ocean of the nectar of beauty.
Having thus meditated on the goddess Śrī, one should [worship] the heart and other limbs as before.
Having meditated upon the crown, the forest garland, and likewise the pair of lotuses,
one should then perform the worship with the prescribed seats and other offerings,
O twice-born ones, using either sixty-four or thirty-two subordinate services.
One should offer the oblation to the Goddess, either separately or as that which has already been offered to the gods.

One should worship the Goddess at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*) or at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homa*), according to the prescribed rule. Because of her state of dependence, one should never perform the *bali* offering there;
rather, it should be performed by the most excellent of teachers together with the worship of the primary abode (*mūlālaya*).
The rite of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa) should be performed as an ancillary part with the [threads] consecrated [for the purpose];
one should perform the bathing and other festivities on his birth-star and so forth. Even though Lakṣmī is dependent [on another], there is indeed a festival during the nine nights (navarātri).
Preceded by the offering of the sprouts and followed by the binding of the protective thread,
one should perform the worship of the four locations for the sake of the prosperity of the kingdom;
however, one should avoid the offering of oblations (*bali*), the hoisting of the flag, and the ritual bathing (*tīrtha*) therein.
This procedure applies when [the site] is dependent on others; now, however, it is described for when one has independence.
Whether in a village, a city, on a mountain, or on a riverbank, one should construct a place of fortune (śrī-sthāna) complete with a wall and a celestial palace (vimāna).
Having established Śrī there according to the ritual with her mantra,
one should then invoke Śrī from the Śrīvatsa mark of the God of gods into the lotus-heart of the image by means of the mantra, together with its limbs, and perform the rite of sakalīkaraṇa.
Having performed [the rite], one should worship the Goddess with offerings ending with the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Then, one should gratify Śrī in the midst of the fire with fuel-sticks (samidh) and other materials.
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules, one should likewise generate the fire.
One should sprinkle the fuel and other materials with drops of consecrated clarified butter (*ājya*). Likewise, one should perform the satiation of the fire and the placement of the mantras upon it.
Then, having invoked the Goddess from her heart into the center of that [fire] according to the prescribed rite, || 7.73–74 ||
One should likewise offer oblations with both the regular (nitya) fuel-sticks and those for specific desires (kāmya),
as well as the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt and the expiatory oblation (prāyaścittāhuti).
Having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and so forth, one should then [place] Lakṣmī within the lotus of the heart.
Having dismissed his attendants and performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite,
he then entered the temple of the Goddess, the site of sacrifice;
there he performed the dedication of the oblation and also the libation for the ancestors.
The offering of oblations to the spirits and to those who are beloved and well-disposed;
the giving of gifts to those devoted to sacrifice, to artisans, and to those of purified soul;
and the performance of the secondary sacrifice according to rule, including the consumption of the sacrificial food (naivedya) and so forth.
One should perform everything as previously described for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(7.79) In this very context, the sequence for the worship of the retinue in the offering of oblations (*bali*) and so forth is as follows:
in the first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), Kumuda and the others are to be worshipped, starting from the east. (7.80)
One should worship Vibhīṣikā and Śāṅkarī on the two sides of that door;
subsequently, in the second enclosure (āvāraṇa), one should worship Upendra and the others.
And on the two sides of that door, one should worship the treasure-deities Śaṅkha and Padma.
In the third enclosure, one should worship Indra and the others behind [the central deity].
Nalakūbara and Jṛmbhala are to be worshipped on the two sides of its door.
And in the fourth enclosure, one should worship Vajra and the others.
Then, on the right side of that door, one should worship Śibi-kuṇḍala;
and on the north, Maṇibhadra—in the fifth enclosure.
Having worshipped Lohitākṣa and the others, one should then [worship] at the sides of that door.
One should worship Jayā and Vijayā according to the proper sequence.
One should duly worship Kumuda and the others at the great seat (mahāpīṭha).
One should worship the four-armed Sumukhī in the place of Viṣvaksena.
Holding a cane in her right hand and also displaying the threatening gesture (tarjanī),
she holds two lotuses with her two right hands behind [her].
In this manner, one should worship all the attendants with offerings of oblations and other rites.
One should perform the rites such as the mounting of the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa) separately according to the prescribed rule.
Having raised the Garuda-banner, one should likewise hold a great festival;
and one should carry out the worship of the four locations and other rites with the Śrī-mantra.
O best of sages, having been thus addressed, this is the sequence for the worship of Śrī and the other goddesses;
in this manner, one should worship Puṣṭi and the other goddesses with their respective mantras. (7.90) O sages!
O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge,
we have heard from you, O Lord of Sages, the worship of Śrī and others;
now, O Lord, you ought to tell us the worship of Sudarśana.
Nārada said: "Listen, all you sages, with attentive minds,
to the procedure for the worship of the Sudarśana [discus], which bestows benefits both in this world and the next."
The mantras of the *Saudarśana* and its various forms are destroyers of manifold evils.
Therein, one should worship with a chosen mantra a chosen form,
whether in a divine temple or elsewhere, such as in a painting or in the courtyard.
In a village or elsewhere— on a riverbank, in a forest, or even on a mountain—
one should construct a temple or a pavilion, decorated with paintings and facing in all directions,
or perhaps facing the east, provided with latticed windows and doors.
Provided with a single tier of stories, marked with the emblem of a wheel,
endowed with auspicious entrances, and equipped with stairways; having reached it, which was likewise surrounded by a wall, within that palace— (7.96–7.97)
Having installed the Bimba image of Saudarśana there according to the prescribed rite,
the disciplined preceptor should worship it three times a day with its mantra.
Therein, mental anguish, physical disease, famine, spirits, vetālas, and evil grahas [are subdued].
They do not afflict any people, and auspiciousness prevails forever.
Listen now to the procedure for worship there, preceded by mantras:
on a pure and well-concealed spot of ground, one should spread out a mandala of colors.

One should draw the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center as the cause of all mantras, which consists of the form of all letters from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', and is adorned with spokes, a hub, a rim, and a felloe. || 7.101 ||
The vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga* are situated in the limb of the navel.
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha* are in the twenty-four spokes;
those beginning with *ma* and ending with *ha* are in the rim, while the syllable *kṣa* is situated in the central hub.
First, this wheel of the Śabdabrahman, consisting of the collection of phonemes, was then [established] by the preceptor,
the Guru, who has duly performed the placement of his own Mātṛkā-yantra, using the names beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ" in their proper sequence.
Having worshipped thoroughly with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), flowers, and other articles that which is the embodiment of the *mātṛkā* mantra,

one should then extract the mantras that grant all desired accomplishments— those mantras which, by their very nature as power (*śakti*), are intent upon creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and are capable of being conquered through the self.
In ancient times, Kriyā-śakti was designated as the mother of perfect ritual action;
presiding over the form of Time, by her this world was expanded.
Therefore, the wheel of time is the wheel of the world; that is the body of Sudarśana.
Presiding over that [body], that power remains as the individual soul (jīva).
Deprived of it, this entire world would become like something non-existent.
Therefore, one should uplift that power, which possesses a splendor equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
The axle-rod (*akṣadhārā*) is indeed eternal and without beginning or end, belonging to Viṣṇu.
First is the pair ending with the rim (*nemi*), then that which begins with it and has two fires (*analadvaya*).
The nave (*nābhi*) consists of four, and the final part is adorned by two; this is the *piṇḍa*.
The great spear of the Sudarśana is the bestower of all accomplishments;
it is the life-force of the six-syllable mantra, consisting of the nature of light and bliss.
This *piṇḍa* [mantra] is formed by the syllables excluding the vowels, for the sake of accomplishing the limbs beginning with the heart.
One should differentiate the last of the eyes by means of the three long vowels and the final [syllables];
these [mantras] begin with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and end with the fourth [state], together with the heart-mantras and so forth,
along with the classes [of mantras] beginning with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *vauṣaṭ*.
They should be applied in sequence along with the qualities beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Then follows the extraction of the six-syllable mantra, which is the nature of *śakti*;
having brought forth the two final syllables as before, [one takes] the very last one.
Therein, the third of the eighth measure should ultimately proceed to the last;
one should make it end with the fifth note and adorn it with the rim and so forth.
Subsequently, one should form the syllable *avimukta*, which consists of eleven spokes and twice that number of rims, using other syllables; this is for the fifty-sixth [and sixty-first] positions.
This six-syllabled mantra of the Sudarśana has thus been declared.
The third, fifth, and sixth [syllables] are each remembered as having three syllables.
The other three syllables, joined with the phonemes, consist of two syllables each.
This is the designator of Viṣṇu, who is Time itself and whose form is the universe.
By means of the syllables *sat* and *tārayā*, as well as by *śakti*, the eight-syllable mantra is proclaimed;
for just as the Person (Puruṣa) resides within Prakṛti through the union of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*),
so too is Hari, in his form as Sudarśana, to be meditated upon as consisting of both the gross and the subtle.
May there be the vision of the supreme reality, which is the vision of its exposition. For those established in that [reality], this [vision] is eternal and removes the darkness of ignorance;
it cuts away their doubt so that they may proceed by means of the true path.
This transformation of his is surely the cause for cutting away doubt;
indeed, through the power of his own knowledge, it severs the creatures who revile those devoted to the conduct of their castes and stages of life from their very mouths.
By this, the hearts of devoted ones whose souls are purified are swiftly marked.
Victory shall be in one's hand, both in this world and in the next;
how much more so when it is placed and worshipped in a sacred site?
Now, the characteristics of the heart-mantras and the others are being stated.
One should first of all place the seed-syllables of the heart-mantra and the others in their proper order; then, at the end of each, one should add the *tāra* (OM) followed by the *bindu*.
At the end of the life-force syllables (*prāṇasūna*) in sequence, it should be done as with the two syllables of the Sun (RAVI).
And at the end of the two words *mahāsudarśana* and *jvālā*,
one should sequentially append the word *cakrāya* six times at the end of each [syllable], ending with the head (the letter *ha*).
These are joined with the heart and other [limbs] ending in the fourth state (*turya*), endowed with qualities such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth.
One should write [the mantras] according to the previously stated procedure, beginning with *namaḥ svāhā* and ending with *adinetra*.
The forms of the female attendants (*ākārapattī*) are to be meditated upon in the places of enjoyment as being like the primary deities,
in terms of their colors, ornaments, garments, weapons, arms, postures, and gestures.

Having thus understood the greatness of the mantra, whoever worships according to the prescribed rule— with the binding of the directions (*digbandha*), the fire-wall (*vahniprākāra*), the invocation of Gāyatrī, and so forth;
with the ritual implements and mantras that are devoid of [worldly] enjoyment and giving— [that person attains the fruit].

Gradually, the attainment of all fruits and the perfection of mantra arise. First, the characteristics of the mantras for binding the ten directions will be explained: preceded by *oṃ*, followed by *puruṣāya*, and ending with *svāhā*.

"I bind with the weapon-mantra, svāhā"— this six-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā* is declared to be the mantra for binding the directions, which removes the faults of the wicked. Having first extracted the *praṇava*, [one should place it] before the mantra and the wife of Agni (*svāhā*).
One should place the wheel known as the "Fire-Wall" as it approaches.
O best of sages, listen to the proclaimed Cakra-Gāyatrī: having placed the [specific] caste-name first, one should utter the word "to the Wheel" (cakrāya). 7.135–136.
The second [mantra] consists of the three syllables from the beginning of the *Nṛsūkta* and the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*;
having taken the word [from the Gāyatrī] with the two eyes (*netrābhyām*), it is joined with the end preceded by the rim (*nemi*).
At its conclusion, "dhīmahi" is to be placed, while "naḥ" is excluded.
Having extracted the Gāyatrī up to its end, there are four syllables at its conclusion.
This is declared to be the Saudarśanī Gāyatrī, consisting of the syllables of the Tāraka.
Originally, this [Gāyatrī] was with the Tāraka, but it became increased by one syllable.
Now I shall declare the three mantras common to all worship:
having first extracted two *tāra*s (oṃ), one should extract the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*).
Then, having established "yāmye," one should take the [syllable] beginning with *nemi*, which consists of eighteen [units].
The syllable situated on the twelve spokes reaches from the navel to the fifth [cakra] at the crown of the head.
Then one should extract the five-syllable mantra *gṛhakāmyāyaḥ*,
joined with the second consonant of the rim (the letter *kha*), having proceeded through it nine times; then,
having reached the syllable on the sixteenth spoke, it is conjoined with the second vowel (*i*).
Furthermore, the fifth [mandala] has the rim as its fifth [element], possesses sixteen spokes,
and is connected to the third gate; it extends from the third rim-circle to the end of the rim,
and the intervals between the spokes are endowed with the vowels up to the end of the vowels.
Having joined the third vowel to that which stands on the sixteenth spoke from the rim, and then to that which goes to the eighth from the rim,
one should place it above the nineteenth spoke, at the top of the two-ninth syllable.
(7.145) Then, having joined the third vowel, [one places it] upon that which goes to the two-ninth spoke.

Furthermore, regarding the "body of the mantra": it consists of [the deity's name] ending with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), followed by *namaḥ*. Moreover, the mantra joined with *namaḥ* is suitable for invocation (*āvāhana*).
This mantra is revealed for the bestowing of all enjoyments.
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, which is the sole cause of all enjoyments,
and then this threefold word ending with the rim (*nemi*) and joined with the *bindu*;
"gṛhāṇa" (take), ending with the head (*śiras*), is the designator of the giving of enjoyment.
In the rites of invocation, worship, and likewise in the procedure for dismissal,
one should first utter the *praṇava* (oṃ), then address [the deity] as "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*),
then provide the word "mantramūrti," and finally the word for oneself in the accusative case.
One should utter "Āsādaya kṣamasva" ending with the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
These are the mantras I have thus declared for the purpose of worshipping Sudarśana.
O lords of sages, I shall now explain the procedure for worship here.
Having performed the ritual bathing and other rites as before, he enters the sacrificial hall;
having washed his feet and sipped water for purification, wearing an upper garment and well-adorned,
and having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark, he worships the door-keepers with flowers as previously described.
Having opened the door and entered within, he should prostrate before the Lord with the Gāyatrī mantra and perform the washing of the hands and other preliminary rites. Then,
having established the three paths upon the image, the seat, or the yantra;
Having purified the temple, [he should place] a wooden board or similar object before it;
having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, he sits facing it upon a beautiful seat,
with the sacrificial materials for the consecration (adhivāsana) placed at his side.
Having performed the purification of the hands and the purification of the site with the *astra* mantra as before,
one should [ward off] the obstacles residing in the place of worship, whose forms are visible outside, by means of the two hands joined with the aforementioned mantra and the *astramudrā*.

Having performed the purgation, one should establish bonds in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Then, having enveloped [the self] with the Kavaca mantra and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) as before,
one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and carry out the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).

First, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā*— the mother of mantras, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with *kṣa*— upon the hands and then upon the body, while bathing the *cakra*. Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*), which possesses a radiance like the heat of the sun, [one should proceed].
In the same sequence as for the right hand, [one should perform it] on the branches and also on the two palms;
from the thumb to the little finger, four times for each [finger],
thus having placed twenty-two [units] on the fingers, one then places ten on the two palms.
Having thus performed the placement upon both hands— five [syllables] in the middle, five in each of the four [fingers], and likewise five in the other four, all situated between two *praṇavas*—
one should then perform the placement upon one's own body, preceded by the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*).
Having pervaded [the body] from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet with both hands like the rays of the sun,
one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) separately:
at the hairline, around the face, at the two eyes, and at the two ears.

One should place the vowels, followed by the others along with the visarga, in the two nostrils, the two cheeks in order from right to left, in the upper and lower positions, in the two teeth, and in the two lips, and finally on the head. (7.166)
The *ka*-group is located sequentially at the five joints of the right arm;
likewise, the *ca*-group is on the left [arm]. The *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups are at the joints of the feet, starting from the right, on both sides as before.
One should place the *pavarga* on the back, the navel, and the heart; the letters from *ya* to *sa* in the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and the letter *ha* within the heart.
Having thus first deposited the *mātṛkā* alphabet, one places the letter *kṣa* in the space of the heart.
Then, one should perform the six-syllable placement upon the hands and the body by means of the Śakti-mantra.
O lords of sages, first perform the hand-placement (karanyāsa); listen to that:
it is done with the mantra together with the Śakti, enclosed between the two Tāra-mantras.
One should wash both hands from the wrists to the tips of the nails as before;
at the beginning and end, one should perform this with the syllables of Śakti, including the nasal bindu, preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ).
Then, leaving aside the thumbs and ending with the little fingers, one should [anoint] the middle joints of the fingers.
And one should place the final syllable upon the tips of the fingers.
Having thus placed the vowels, one should then place the heart and the other [limbs] on the joints of the roots and the tips, according to the sequence of the placement of the syllables.
One should touch the body with both hands from the head down to the feet;
having thus performed the *vyāpaka-nyāsa*, one should perform the *aṅga-nyāsa*:
[placing the mantras] on the head, the mouth, the heart, the navel, the private parts, and the feet.
The placement beginning with the feet and ending with the head is called the *saṃhṛti-nyāsa*.

One should perform the placement in sequence upon the heart, the crown of the head, the crest-lock, the two shoulders, the center of the palms, and the two eyes, using either the seed-syllables (*nissva*) or the aforementioned mantras.
Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) of the heart and other [limbs], one should thereafter place upon the two palms the crown, the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the Śrīvatsa mark as before;
then, one should place the eight weapons, beginning with the lotus, in their proper order.

Having placed the power of will (icchā-śakti) on the right and left shoulders, and the principle of mind (manas-tattva) at the base of the thighs on both sides, he should recite his own mantra and meditate within himself as Hari,
whose body is the Sudarśana [discus], thinking "I am He."
The best of those who know mantras, O Brahmins, should rotate the Gāyatrī outside with the wheel-mudrā, [visualizing] a garland of wheel-flames all around his own self;
he should then perform the sacrifice born of meditative visualization as enjoined from the beginning.
Having restrained the collection of the senses as before within the sphere of knowledge,
one should conceive of a seat in the heart, beginning with Ananta, as previously described.
From the supreme reality of the Lord, one should [conceive] that which is of the nature of consciousness and is the supreme Self.
Having mentally recited the mantra and lowered it above the seat,
and having performed the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth, as well as the worship of dissolution and enjoyment,
one should visualize the lunar orb above the head of the God of gods.
And with the streams of nectar flowing from that, one should perform the preparation of the *arghya* and other offerings.
One should worship either with the sixteen or the thirty-two services (*upacāra*).
Having thus performed the mental sacrifice according to the rule, ending with the recitation (*japa*), [one should proceed].

Then, outside [the shrine], the best of preceptors should worship the deity Hetīśa with the formal offerings (arghya) and other enjoyments (bhoga) presented according to the rules, along with the [deity's] forms.
As before, he should then perform the placement and worship of the vessels for the arghya and other offerings.
For those who have deposited mantras upon the body, there is the worship at the entrance of the womb.
One should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the entrance of the womb;
likewise, one should sacrifice to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the door of the front pavilion.
Having thus performed the sacrifice at the door, one should then enter the interior;
beginning with the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), one should arrange the Yoga-pīṭha,
and having worshipped Gaṇanātha and the others according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having invoked the god Sudarśana as before,
one should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), beginning with the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) and the other two;
likewise, one should place the heart-mantra and the others, as well as the ornaments, in their respective locations.
Then one should also install the eightfold group of the best of weapons;

and one should install the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*) as if they were one's own body. Having performed the rites of dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*), one should then meditate upon the god Sudarśana.
The great thousand-spoked wheel, fierce with a mass of ten-thousand fires,
whirling through the six paths and manifested by the power of the Lord;
[he beheld] the Supreme Self, the flawless Nārāyaṇa, situated within the axle.
The all-pervading Lord Īśāna, who has the form of a discus, resembling divine saffron, with tawny eyes and abundant tawny hair, wearing red garments,
possessed of great majesty and a massive body, endowed with eight arms.
It was filled with the tumultuous roar of the terrible flames of fire spat from his fangs;
its bees were the curls of hair distorted by the knitting of his curved eyebrows;
and the quarters of the sky were set ablaze by the flames vomited from the eye in his forehead.
Adorned with a crown kissed by a mass of upward-flaming tongues of fire,
his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, and decorated with divine garlands;
he stands in a most beautiful posture with knees raised, wielding many weapons.
The mace, the goad, the club, and the wheel of most fierce splendor;
the conch, the bow with arrow, the noose, and the Kaumodakī— these [are held] in sequence,
beginning from the primary right hand and ending with the primary left hand.
Beholding that incomparable hero, adorned with divine ornaments,
who terrified the multitudes of Daityas and Dānavas with his own boisterous laughter,
seated in a place of blazing splendor like ten thousand times ten thousand fires;
One should meditate upon the supreme wheel of the Wheel-bearer within the wheel consisting of the six paths;
one should thus meditate on the God who bestows the fruits of whatever is desired.
And one should meditate upon the heart and other limbs, as well as the crown and other ornaments, as before.
Now listen, O best of the twice-born, to the meditation on the weapons:
the supreme preceptor should meditate upon the discus, conch, mace, and lotus as before.
He was lean-limbed with long arms, tawny-eyed, and holding a goad;
his face was formidable and fierce, possessing the luster of a mountain of split black collyrium.
With a slender belly, a pestle encircled by rows of flames, resembling a heap of glowing coals, long and exceedingly harsh;
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, he was the very embodiment of arrows and weapons.
He brandished his bow, which was of various forms, sharpened, and possessed the power to bind the farthest reaches of the quarters;
it was golden-hued and adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
Then, clapping his hands together, he produced a sound like that of a great rain-cloud.
A noose filled with hosts of serpents, with lightning-like tongues, terrifying,
white as a row of golden bees, with a fierce mouth and red eyes—
these Supreme Persons (Puruṣottamas), endowed with their own respective splendors, are to be meditated upon as having two arms.
All these attendants of the Lord wait for his command;
they have risen up, moving about, and stand in perfectly balanced postures,
with their hands resting upon the slopes of their hips, holding yak-tail fans raised aloft.
Excluding the four [mudrās] beginning with the crown (kiriṭa) and including the lotus,
one should remember that all others have their right hands threatening the host of the wicked;
furthermore, at the time of meditation, they should be visualized upon the heads of all.
Each one’s own well-known insignia is formless as the object of meditation (dhyeya).
O best of sages, the sequence of their presiding deities (adhiṣṭhātṛ) is now told:
the goad is to be known as Kāma, and the mace as Nāganāyaka.

Know that sound and the other sense objects are the arrows, the weapon; know the wind to be the bow; and the noose is to be understood as illusion (māyā). Having meditated thus, one should perform worship with the seat and other offerings, ending with those that touch the heart.
One should propitiate [the deity] according to the prescribed rule, ending either with the fire-oblation (homa) or with the recitation (japa).
In this very same manner, one should worship a self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) image, a divine (divya) one,
a Siddha-made one, or even one established by humans, whether it be made of stone, clay, or metal.

One should worship the God— who wards off all that is undesirable— three times a day, having installed him as one with eight arms, four arms, or sixteen arms, according to one's preference and the distinction between mobile and immobile [forms]. (7.219)
The occasional rites, those performed for specific desires,

and the obligatory sacrifices must be performed with particular care, except during sleep or a great festival; this applies especially to rites for peace, prosperity, as well as the study of the Vedas and so forth.
"By means of meditation, worship, burnt offerings, and recitation,
the desires of devoted ones whose souls are purified are fulfilled.
(7.222) Thus has the supreme worship of the Sudarśana been correctly explained.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of Lakṣmī and Sudarśana," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Īśvara-saṃhitā.
Now begins the eighth chapter:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, O you who are skilled in the scriptures of the Blessed One!"
And the worship of those headed by Garuḍa was previously mentioned.
O treasure of compassion, reveal specifically that ritual procedure.
Nārada.
Listen, all you sages, to the ancient method of worshipping Garuḍa,
by the mere knowledge of which a practitioner attains his desired goal—
[the worship] of Viṣṇu, known as Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is endowed with the power of supreme knowledge.

The form known as Jñānabala, which is the very nature of the support of all, is the majesty (mahimā) of the Creator of the world; he is to be known as Vihageśvara. He is the destroyer of all diseases and fears, and the repeller of all enemies.
Then, the knower of mantras, having established [the deity] in a temple, should worship it daily—
either in the first courtyard or in the second from the main shrine.
One should construct a temple in the form of a pavilion (maṇṭapa) at the front location.
Equipped with four gates and endowed with three groups,
or else accompanied by six groups, and adorned with all ornaments;
it should be one-third the height of the main building, or half its height, yet broad in extent.
Having installed an image made of metal or stone as prescribed, whether it be divine, celestial,
or human, one should worship it constantly at the three times of day, concluding with the worship of the primary form.
The specific procedure for that, preceded by the mantra, is now declared here:
having first extracted the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed immediately by the word "bird" (*pakṣin*),
this five-syllabled great mantra is proclaimed to end with *svāhā*.
O twice-born ones, these syllables of the mantra, accompanied by the *bindu* and preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,

should be uttered together with the [six] limbs beginning with the Heart, ending with the Fourth (*turya*), and starting from Knowledge (*jñāna*) up to the Eye (*anetra*) and ending with the Weapon (*astra*). || 8.11–8.12 ||
By reversing the beginning, middle, and end of the root mantra, it becomes a destroyer of poison;
this very mantra has been proclaimed as one difficult even for the gods to obtain.
O best of sages, it is known as the five-syllabled Gāruḍa mantra.
The five limbs should consist of the syllables as before, accompanied by the nasal bindu.
By means of this mantra together with its limbs, [the deity] is to be installed according to the ritual procedure,
whether the image is situated in the root-abode or established upon a vehicle.
The form of Garuḍa remains standing in the vehicle, or is poised for flight;
likewise, it may be seated on the bed or the throne, or otherwise well-established.
This was taught specifically in the chapter on meditation regarding the deities of the door-panels.

Even when the banner is raised, its characteristic shall be clearly explained. O twice-born ones, having understood this, one devoted to its mantra should bathe at the proper time with that mantra and perform the washing of the feet.
Having sipped water according to the rule and having entered the temple,
he sits comfortably on his seat, facing either the east or the north.
Having performed the purification of the hands, the binding of the directions, and the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), [he proceeds].
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the rules, with his body invested by the mantras,
he then forms the mudrā of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) within the lotus of the heart;
[he meditates] upon the fourfold Self, the God who abides in the abode of his own bliss.
Having brought down [the deity] from the portion of Saṅkarṣaṇa, which is filled with complete wisdom and power,
and having worshipped as before until the end of the recitation with nectar-like offerings,
one should then worship the external forms with the previously mentioned collections of portions.
With the food of the gods remaining in the vessel, or prepared separately,
one should arrange five vessels as before for that purpose— the *arghya* and so forth—
and then two [vessels] in one: water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and water for bathing (*snānīya*).
In the *arghya* and *ācamana* vessels— or in one or the other—
the knower of mantras, having worshipped the mantras previously assigned to his own body with all [the offerings],
then [proceeds] at the four doors with the offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with incense (*dhūpa*).
One should then invoke Vāstvīśa, Kṣetranātha, and Dvāralakṣmī with their respective mantras,
as well as the host beginning with Caṇḍa, arranging their seats as previously described.
Thereafter, one should sequentially install the eight deities beginning with Dharma, starting from the remaining [corner].
Above that, one should worship the manifest lotus together with its three watches (yāmas),
as well as Gaṇanātha and the other deities, using offerings rich in fragrance;
these were previously worshipped mentally within the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
Having invoked [the deity] by means of one's own vidyā from its own abode into the heart-lotus of the image,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa according to rule with the limbs, ornaments,
and marks, one should thereafter place the crown and the forest garland.
One should assign the lords of the *nāgas*, beginning with Ananta, to the left hand and the other [limbs],
along with the one called Satya on the right, who is the power (*śakti*) of Bala and whose form is [that of] Svara.
Likewise, [one should assign] the rosary and the cluster of *mandāra* flowers.
One should [place] the jar, the vessel of nectar, and the Lord of Serpents starting from the south.
His power (śakti), previously described, consists of the nature of strength and dharma.
Having displayed the mudrā of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), one should perform the sacrifice of dissolution (layayāga).
And the sacrifice of enjoyments (bhogayāga) should be performed upon the surface of the lotus-seat;
on the lotus-petals starting from the east, the Heart-mantra and the others are to be placed as before,
and on the petals in the intermediate directions, the Weapon-mantra, their colors being as before.
With ornaments such as beauty and grace, like the body of the root mantra,
the best of preceptors should place the crown and the forest garland;
while [the deity] stands before him, he should place them respectively on the right and left sides.
In the same sequence of four, one should place the remaining lords of serpents, beginning with Śeṣa,
in the corners of fire, northeast, southwest, and northwest of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).
Furthermore, one should install the group of four beginning with Gaṇitra in their respective order.
To the south of Vihageśa, upon the pericarp, is the one named Satī.
Outside the central Khageśa, starting from the east and proceeding in order, are those whose forms are the vital breaths: Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna.
Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya are the lords of birds. This fivefold manifestation of the five-fold vital breath (prāṇa) is as follows:
Satya and the others occupy the four cardinal directions, while Vihageśvara is in the intermediate corners.
Now, their meditation is specifically described in brief:
He whose limbs extend down to his feet, whose body is human, who has two arms, and who is white as snow—he is Satya, the presiding deity of the vital breath (prāṇa). (8.41–8.42)
Suparṇa was the color of a ruby with eyes of pure gold;
Garuḍa was golden-hued with curved, tawny eyes.
Tārkṣya indeed had squinting eyes and resembled a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
The fifth was Dravatkanakanetra, who had a variegated luster.
(8.44) Suparṇa and the others all had four arms, possessed gentle forms, and were undisturbed; they all moved with feet like birds and were adorned with circles of feathers. (8.45)
Hanging-bellied, with very stout limbs, adorned with earrings and other ornaments,
possessing curved eyebrows and large round eyes, with diamond-like snouts and white faces,
they abide as the presiding deities over the vital airs such as the *apāna*.
Possessing great strength and large bodies, the fifth among them has a red beak.
All these foremost of birds hold handfuls of flowers with both hands, which grasp their respective two thumbs extended forward. (8.47–8.48)
With his two hind hands, starting from the right, Suparṇa holds a cluster of Mandāra flowers and a ring of wonder;
Garuḍa, however, holds these same objects with his two hands in the reverse order.
Tārkṣya always holds Kadrū on his right and the jar of nectar on his left; likewise, the fifth lord of birds holds the jar of ambrosia with his right hand and the lord of serpents with his left.
He bears the names of the five winds— prāṇa, apāna, and the rest— as well as those of the eternally risen (*nityodita*) manifestation and the tranquil-risen (*śāntodita*).
Garuḍa serves as his retinue and especially as his emblem on the banner.
The same should be applied to other states such as deep sleep and so forth. These [qualities],
beginning with Satya and ending with Tārkṣya, belong respectively to the four forms beginning with Vāsudeva, and likewise to their various internal manifestations.
Among each triad of Keśava and the others, the [first] three—Satya and so forth—are to be accepted;
for the forms beginning with Padmanābha, the fifth is Vihageśvara (Garuḍa).
Of the all-pervading Lord, who possesses the bodies of the Parātpara, the Para-vyūha, and the Antar-vyūha...
And also of the Lord who manifests himself, desiring to protect the world.
And because he is the cause of the birds, he is called Khageśvara as previously stated.
Thus, the power of the Garuḍa array has been fully revealed to you.
Then, outside [that] are Kumuda and the others; beyond them, in sequence, are Śakra and the others.
Outside of that, Kumuda and the others, as well as Bhūteśa and Utkaṭa and the rest,
should be worshipped; or else, Gaṇeśa should be worshipped in the offering pavilion (balimaṇḍapa) in front of that,
or the followers of Garuḍa should be worshipped upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).
And protecting his devotees as well as the divine abodes,
one should perform worship by means of meditation, using the seats and other requisites as prescribed,
either with the sixty-four services or with the thirty-two others.
Or else, with sixteen types of offerings, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior;
that food and other items thus offered always cures diseases for men,
as well as barren women and kings who desire victory.
One should distribute and offer [the food] to those whose garments have been affected by poison;
one should especially worship in this manner during the month of Ārdrā.
During festivals, one should especially carry the image in procession as part of the festival worship.
Thus has been correctly explained the supreme worship of Garuḍa.
Now, however, the worship of Viṣvaksena as taught in the Pauṣkara is being told;
listen, all you sages, with attentive minds.
Pauṣkara said: For what purpose did the Blessed One speak [to] the Lord who destroys obstacles,
he who is the supreme cause of all the lords of obstacles?

By what substances, by what rite, and what does he accomplish when he is fully honored? By what substances, by what rite, and what does he accomplish when he is fully honored? [Śrī Bhagavān] said: 8.67 Śrī Bhagavān: "When Acyuta has gone to the realm of enjoyment, Viṣvaksena is to be worshipped.
For those who possess existence, there will be obstacles that obstruct the true Dharma;

I believe that for those in the cycle of rebirth, there is no auspiciousness to be found through sacrifices, rituals, or religious duties. Indeed, those obstacles that arise when one engages in such practices are what prevent one from being encouraged [to follow the true path].
And they all flee, afflicted by the fear of the flaming wheel; moreover,
through some previously accumulated karma,
he now experiences the various fruits of his sacrifice standing before him.
Indeed, for the sake of its protection, Viṣvaksena should be worshipped at that very time,
or on the second day at the conclusion of the sacrifice,
having made one's mind free from agitation, for the attainment of the fruit.
With the unfading remnants of the sacrificial offerings, beginning with the *arghya* water;
with all the enjoyments consisting of ritual services, such as ornaments and the like; and with food offerings, the *madhuparka*, and so forth, presented to the principal image. (8.72–8.73)
With those remnants of the gift of food that had been set aside, which were not consumed by himself,
as well as with other offerings presented by those residing within the inner apartments—
refined, endowed with savory heat, and drenched in honey and clarified butter.
Who indeed is this Pauṣkara of incomparable prowess,
