from whose mere distance even those obstacles that are capable of uprooting the three worlds flee away in a mere twinkling of an eye?
The form of the all-pervading Lord known as Kālavaiśvānara, which belongs to the Fourth Self (turyātman),
is indeed that very Viṣvaksena who is celebrated as the god of the twice-born.
Established through the distinctions of the Āhavanīya and other fires for those who sacrifice in the ritual,
it takes up the oblation purified by the Ṛgveda and satisfies the entire world.
Thus, from the sattvic sacrifice consisting of mantra, which is permeated by Brahman— (8.77–78)
Having indeed attained the transmission from the form of the Guru, consecrated by mantra,
he himself quickly distributes it— without being summoned by the immortals or the inhabitants of all the worlds— out of a desire for his grace.

Having thus understood his majesty, one who abides by their prescribed conduct should worship him for the sake of attaining the fruits [of practice] during the daily worship at the three junctions of the day, ending with the offering of oblations;
likewise during the festivals at the end of the year and on other special occasions.

O Lotus-born One, having first performed worship according to one's ability or wealth— either briefly or extensively— upon the supports such as the pedestal and so forth, in due order, or even ending with the fire-oblation (homa), one should then proceed constantly.
Having placed water in a leaf-cup, or in a vessel or a flawless jar,
one should worship it with oneself in the northern part and offer it; then,
in another vessel consecrated with that weapon-mantra, [one should place the remainder].
Taking a portion from the food offering (*naivedya*),
and likewise a portion of rice extracted from within the *caru*, together with curds, clarified butter, and condiments,
he should consecrate it with the water of *kuśa* grass that has been infused with the *samālabhana*, flowers, and the *arghya* offering.
O Lotus-born One, having consecrated it many times with the mantra of that [deity's] vision, [one should proceed].
Having recited its root mantra while endowed with meditative visualization (*dhyāna*) and contemplation (*bhāvanā*),
one should pour it into the vessel previously prepared and cover it;
O Pauṣkara, it may also be consecrated by reciting the *praṇava* eight times along with the name [of the recipient].

One should always and everywhere, even in a sacrifice performed without the previously mentioned ritual, prepare a single vessel containing water, along with an offering of food (naivedya) submerged in water. That [offering] one should then pour out upon the ground, into a well, or into a pond and the like.
Having understood this, the practitioner of mantra should worship with effort using that mantra;
now I shall explain the mantra along with its ancillaries—listen attentively as it is correctly described.
The lord of seed-syllables, known as Prāṇa, is indeed conjoined with the fire element (Ra).
That [mantra], endowed with the sovereignty of the three worlds and situated above the *ūrja*, is then followed by the boar (*varāha*), adorned by the earth, the mountains, and the sky;
thereafter, one should place the foot accompanied by a salutation for Viṣvaksena. (8.91–92)
This mantra of Viṣvaksena is proclaimed to begin with the *praṇava*.
Its original seed-syllable (*bīja*), when deprived of the vowel *ū*, should be joined with the six long vowels beginning with *ā* to produce the collection of limbs (*aṅga*). (8.93)

Accompanied by the *praṇava*, one's own name, and the six *jātis*, as well as the words "namas," "svāhā," and so forth—this is the designator (*vācaka*) of Viṣvaksena. Having installed [the deity] according to the rules with this mantra together with its limbs (*sāṅga*), [one should proceed]. || 8.94–8.95 ||
Whether in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure,
situated between the directions of Īśāna and Soma (the northeast and northwest), in a temple facing south,
with the sanctum (*garbhamandira*) designed to be lower than the height of the main structure; 8.96.

Alternatively, in the Brahma-sthāna, according to the measurement of the portion of the primary image (mūlabera), worship may be performed with materials such as stone, wood, or metal; this constitutes the primary ritual (mukhyakalpa) in the Ugra-maṇḍapa. || 8.97–8.98 ||
Having brought [the deity] down from the sky— whether formless or indeed embodied— onto a pedestal fashioned with three tiers in the previously mentioned corner of the ground,
one should satisfy [the deity] solely with the offering of oblations and with water.

In the case of the deity who has entered the four locations within the activities such as the maṇḍala, and who consists of the supreme manifestation (paravyūha) and other forms during the limit of worship—
even when situated inside the temple or in the pavilion at his own place— || 8.100–8.101 ||
Worship should be performed according to the rules, beginning from the day of the commencement; however,
at the conclusion of all rites, when the Lord has entered the mandala and so forth,
and each deity has been dismissed to their respective abodes, one should meditate [on Him] from the center of the mandala.
On the second day as well, the practitioner of mantra should worship according to the rules,
especially that [image] situated in the temple for the purpose of worshipping the Blessed One;
having worshipped it duly with food offerings presented to it.

One should constantly satisfy with all offerings such as *arghya*, as well as betel and other items, those beings residing in water, on land, and elsewhere, as well as those belonging to them. Then, for that [deity] situated in the temple, according to the measurement of its body—
Having performed a special worship according to the ritual rules with divine materials such as gold and other substances—
[worship] to [the goddess] who is capable of destroying obstacles, whether she be fierce or peaceful in form, four-armed or two-armed, seated or standing firmly— 8.106–107.
Whether he is conceived as having two arms or four hands— or otherwise—
whenever special occasions arise, one should worship him with festive offerings.
When an occasion for sport, hunting, or other festivities arrives, wherever the Lord may go, [he should be worshipped].
In each and every place, one should lead her forward for the sake of accomplishing the fruit without obstacle.
O best of beings, listen as I describe his meditation exactly as it is:
he has the luster of fresh *dūrvā* grass shoots and possesses a slightly yellowish radiance.
He had four tusks, four arms, and measured four cubits; he possessed the four states of existence, with all his limbs complete, lion-like shoulders, and a chest adorned with a broad surface.
He was graced by a navel cavity that was deep and spiraled to the right.
With arms reaching to his knees, majestic, wearing matted locks with tawny flames,
his eyes were tawny like molten gold; he was flat-nosed with a broad nose,
adorned by rows of long white nails, and possessed crooked eyebrows.
His face and cheeks were broad, his body was fully developed with body hair resembling young crescent moons and having the appearance of fresh *kiṃśuka* flowers;
he was graced by beautiful, long, wide, and prominent [limbs].
Adorned with two ears enriched by ruby earrings,
he was graced with a lofty crown and embellished with necklaces and other ornaments;
he wore variegated silken garments and was decorated with diverse garlands and jewels.
His radiance was like that of twelve thousand suns at the time of universal dissolution;
his eyes were cast slightly upward and sideways;
his teeth possessed the luster of jasmine and the moon; and his face was graced with a gentle smile.
Naturally gentle and stainless, yet colored by illusory wrath.
Standing in a posture with the placement of his feet moving gracefully,
he thus meditated upon the supreme state with his own inner mind;
[he visualized] three creepers on his left hand, beginning from the thumb and ending at the little finger.
Bending one [hand] which was raised, it is applied to the tip of the nose.
Accompanied by this mudrā, which bestows fearlessness from all obstacles,
[he beholds the Lord] holding a discus and a conch in his hands, and bearing a mace hanging down.
With his hand resting nonchalantly upon the slope of his hips,
one should thus meditate upon this god Rūpadhara, who possesses a body of many wonders, fierce in form, and radiant like fire with a fiery luster.
With his fangs bared in a gesture that is nevertheless free from threat, he displays the mark of peace;
with his primary right hand, he bestows fearlessness upon his devotees,
while his left hand likewise holds a hanging mace.
Holding a discus and a conch respectively on his right and left rear arms—thus has the four-armed form been described; now understand that of the two-armed form.
[This latter] is as previously described in its fierce and peaceful aspects, but without the discus and conch.
Alternatively, one may employ the two previously mentioned [mudrās], or the second [alone], or the *cittatantu*;
or else, free from the mace, resting upon the left hip,
placed upon the region of the left thigh by means of the standing or sitting posture.
Either with the *gopanī-mudrā* or with the *kaṭaka-ākāra-mudrā*,
resting both hands behind the seat and grasping the upper end of the mace, which has the shape of an elephant’s club.
Having stepped upon the petals of the lotus with both feet, one should occupy the seat of the pericarp;
or else, remaining well-established upon the pericarp as before, adorned by others.
Thus, having established one [deity] according to the ritual procedure during these specific meditations— || 8.129–8.130 ||
One should perform worship at the times previously mentioned with one's own mantra,
for the purpose of worshipping the four locations in the center of the mandalas; then,
when the mantras have been worshipped and assigned to their respective abodes.
Either within a square city situated between the directions of Īśāna and Soma,
or outside the door-ornaments and adorned with three lines;
in the space between them, upon a half-moon, there is a lotus endowed with eight petals.
When this [deity] has been appointed to universal sovereignty by Acyuta,
and is constantly worshipped according to the rule, the practitioner attains his desired goal.
Therefore, having first bathed according to the prescribed rite with mantras belonging to him, [one should proceed].

Having washed one's hands and feet, or having sipped water (ācamana), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa). Having purified one's own body through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇā) by means of its presiding deities, and having performed the placement once more, beginning with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) starting from the hands.
As before, having brought down the Lord likewise from the abode of bliss,
and having worshipped Him within the lotus of the heart as the partless Self according to one's own requirement,
one should meditate upon Him as having attained the state of possessing parts and worship Him externally.
Having established the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings as before,
and having worshipped the mantras assigned to one's own body, [one should worship] those resembling Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, known by the names Bala and Prabala, at the southern and northern doors.
Having worshipped Vāyuvega, Mahāghrāṇa, and Garuḍopama at the front of the door as before, and having first offered a lotus-seat (kamalāsana),
[one should worship] the group of five beginning with Dharma and ending with Ananta, or the group of nine.
Afterwards, one should cover that lotus with the *satva* alone, according to one's own rite.
Having invoked that deity into it, impelled by meditation within the heart,
and having performed the rites of presence (*sannidhāna*) and so forth, preceded by the binding of mudrās.
Having worshipped thoroughly with water for the guest (arghya), flowers, and other offerings according to the procedure of the dissolution-sacrifice (layayāga),
the knower of the principal mantra [should worship] that which resides in the center of the pericarp, beginning with the Heart-mantra and so forth;
and those situated within the petals of the lotus, though lacking its specific form and luster.
However, meditation on the limbs, beginning with the white [syllable] and so forth, is prescribed everywhere.
One should meditate upon the power called Kriyā, which is of the nature of fire and is synonymous with Svāhā;
she bears the form of Lakṣmī, is joyful, and is adorned with all ornaments.
She is always seated or standing comfortably in a manner suited to her beloved,
holding two chowries in the right and left hands respectively.
This mantra is proclaimed as ending with "Oṃ hrīṃ kriyāyai svāhā."
By this [mantra], having brought [the deity] down from the luminous body of the Lord, the destroyer of obstacles,
onto his left side at the conclusion of the sacrifice of enjoyment—
[there appear] Gajānana, Jayatsena, Harivaktra, and Mahābala.
And the fourth, O Lotus-born One, is known as Kālaprakṛti;
these four are the lords of the hosts of Gaṇas, possessing fierce forms,
awaiting his command with white chowries raised aloft.
And likewise Vināyaka and the others who are the foremost among the lords of obstacles— one should place these lords of the hosts, who are ever obedient to his command,
situated outside the lotus in the corners beginning with Īśāna.
Gazing at the face of the Lord, they stand in positions corresponding to His;
all are marked by those same hand gestures, yet they are devoid of ritual mudrās.
Observe their distinct meditative absorption, which is embodied.
He has the face of a formidable lordly elephant, four tusks, and three eyes;
he has a neck like a conch shell, four arms, and the splendor of ten thousand full moons;
he is adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, girdles, and strings of gems.
One should meditate upon the elephant-faced one, enriched with various garlands, perfumes, and garments, and possessing incomparable prowess; thereafter, one should remember Jayatsena,
who has the face of a great horse and the luster of a mountain of rubies.
And one should meditate upon him with eyes like molten gold, possessing a manifold form of elemental beings; with the face of a lion, his head covered by a mane,
resembling refined gold, and making a terrible, gurgling sound.

O Brahmins, one should meditate upon him who has the face of the king of beasts, who possesses the speed of the fire at the end of an eon, whose name is Kālaprakṛti, and who resembles a mountain of collyrium;
his face is terrifying with fangs, and his beard and eyes are tawny.
Fierce, wearing shark-shaped earrings, with a nose as sunken as that of a fish—
these lords of the hosts of Gaṇas, O Brahmins, are endowed with all the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) from the feet up to the neck.
One should remember whatever object serves as an ornament, as previously described, in relation to these three;

one should perform their worship with their own names preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with "namas," for the sake of attaining the fruits of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*). (8.161) O Lotus-born One! [I bow to you] for the attainment of the fruits of various accomplishments.
One should worship with eight times eight, or half of that, or half of that again, according to one's preference;
or, for the sake of the swift accomplishment of the rite, one should worship with eight.
One should offer the food and other items presented there, such as the *arghya*, garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth.
The wise should not give anything to anyone for the sake of attaining gains in this world or the next;
rather, by that [act], it is permitted for those who depend upon them and for all living beings.
For they always move with their hopes blocked by that [refusal]. 8.164
For this very reason, it brings about the loss of wealth for those who consume it.
Indeed, it always utterly destroys the entire multitude of hopes;
therefore, he who eats it himself after giving it to others is the lowest of men. (8.165–166)
If he neglects it out of delusion, that base man goes to hell;
therefore, one who seeks his own welfare must always take precautions against it.
Furthermore, one should throw it into a pit, a well, a pond, or similar place on the surface of the earth.
For the lotus-born [soma] does not become fit for consumption when among crows and the like;
because it increases primarily through purification by sacred mantras, its use is forbidden for the sinful, and especially so for those who are sinless. (8.168–169)
Thus has been correctly declared the supreme worship of Viṣvaksena;
Or else, one should perform worship according to the rules with [images] made of gold and other materials, whether they are movable or not,
three times a day, twice a day, or once a day in times of distress;
this worship should be performed with the respective mantra using the eightfold offerings (aṣṭopacāra).
Thus, the entire worship of the host of attendants, such as Vainateya and others,
has been declared, which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
O best of sages, if you wish to hear anything else beyond this, let it be told.
O Blessed One, sages who are worshipped by the world have been established in the temple of Viṣṇu.
How are those devotees of Viṣṇu to be honored? Tell us the procedure for that.
Nārada said:
"The highly fortunate Ekāntins, led by Śaṭhakopa,
who have descended upon the earth for the sake of reviving the world," || 8.175 ||
And Śāṇḍilya and others, as well as those other founders of the Pāñcarātra system.
Prahlāda, Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa the son of Vāyu,
and others such as Sanaka and his brothers, who are devoted to the five-fold ritual cycle (pañcakāla)—
these are to be known as the supreme devotees; they [should be worshipped] in divine abodes and other sacred places.
According to the distinction between mobile and immobile beings, [they may be fashioned] from metals or even from stone;
they should have forms and gestures corresponding to the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life,
and be marked with the discus and the conch.
On the two arms, starting from the right [and continuing leftward],
they are seated upon lotus-thrones, or else well-positioned,
or standing upright as is appropriate for beauty, or according to the Paiśāca arrangement.
Having fashioned [the image] according to the prescribed rite on the courtyard floor, or on a pedestal,
or in suitable palaces prepared in front of the Lord—
either to the left, the right, or the rear, according to the available space.
Having installed them with their respective mantras, one should worship them according to the rules with faith.
Now listen to those mantras for the rites of installation and so forth,
beginning with Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Īśa, Aja, Tāraka, and Brahmā.

They should be joined with the name by means of the *ahaṃsa* syllable, together with the *tāraka*, and with the final *visarga*; either with the first, the second, or both combined as a triad. Now, the sacrifice with its constituent parts (*sāṅgayāga*) is described.
Having combined one of the two [mantras] beginning with Tārā and Ādyā into a *ṣoḍhā*,
one should utter at its end the [mantras] of Knowledge and so forth, as well as the Heart and others, ending in the dative case;
indeed, these very limbs must first be joined with the support of the *praṇava*.
With this mantra, one should indeed worship the devotees according to the prescribed rule;
having performed the bath and other rites as before, wearing the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark and well-adorned,
one should wash one's feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and enter the sacrificial hall.
One should perform the opening of the door-pivots preceded by the worship of the deities stationed at the doorway.
Then, having prostrated with that mantra and likewise performed the purification of the image and so forth,
as well as the purification of the temple and other rites, one should proceed on its southern side.
Then, having sat down at the side, one should perform the purification of the hands;
likewise, having completed the binding of the directions (*digbandha*), the *sāyāmā*, and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*),
the knower of mantras [should proceed] with the mantra of the devotee, enclosed by the two *tāra*s (the syllable *oṃ*).
One should wash both hands from the wrists to the tips of the nails as before;
then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs according to the previously stated rule,
one should likewise place two rosaries made of *tulasī* and lotus seeds.
Having placed the wheel and the conch on the two palms respectively, and having thus performed the placement of the hands, then while reciting that mantra,
one should touch the body with both hands from the head down to the feet.
Having thus performed the pervasive nyāsa, one should place [the mantras] on the heart and the other limbs.
Then, having placed two garlands on the neck and the discus and conch on the two arms,
and having formed the *hārdadhī* mudrā, one should take recourse in identity [with the deity].
Then, having meditated upon the consciousness of the Supreme Lord within his own heart, situated beneath His feet,
and having subsequently invoked that consciousness from there, one should worship Him with mental offerings.
Then, outside [the mandala], one should worship the food with the previously mentioned accumulations of offerings.
For that purpose, having prepared five vessels— or four, three, two, or even just one—
one should then worship the mantras deposited upon the body.
Then the supreme preceptor should perform the door-consecration (dvārayāga) with offerings such as the arghya and so forth;
having worshipped Sāvitra and Savitṛ on the two sides of the womb-door,
he should likewise worship them within that temple in the four directions in due order.
O best of sages, having worshipped the deities of the food offering with water for the guest (arghya) and other offerings,
one should then worship Durgā and Gaṇapati at the door of the front pavilion,
and Indra and the other world-protectors in the first enclosure and the others.
Having performed worship at the door of the enclosure, one should sacrifice to Indra and Indrajaya;
or else, at all the doors as well as in the enclosures,
one should designate the respective groups of disciples themselves as the retinues.
Then, one should worship at the great seat (mahāpīṭha) with the mantra "Obeisance to all beings" (sarvabhūtebhyo namaḥ).
Having entered the inner sanctum (garbhageha), the Guru should prepare the seat;
having worshipped the four [principles] beginning with Dharma in the corners of the seat as before.
Afterwards, one should worship the lotus alone, which has been covered by the *satva* [element];
having caused that devotee to descend there, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*).
Then, according to the prescribed method for dissolution, one should do so in the image just as one does in the body.
Then, having performed worship thoroughly, one should perform the sacrifice of enjoyment according to the rule:
on the lotus petals starting from the east, one should place the heart-mantra and the others as before;
and on the petals in the intermediate directions, the weapon-mantra and the eye-mantra, located upon the mass of filaments.
Outside the petals upon the pedestal, in the southeast and northeast corners,
one should worship the two previously mentioned garlands, as well as the discus and the conch.
Then, one should meditate upon a devotee of Viṣṇu, endowed with all auspicious marks.
With forms and gestures corresponding to the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama),
with palms joined in reverence (añjali) or endowed with the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā),
they are seated comfortably in the midst of lotus-thrones.
Indeed, his body, from the forehead and other parts, was adorned with vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
and marked on his two arms, beginning from the right, with the discus and the conch.
Adorned with two garlands of *tulasī* and lotus seeds,
having thus meditated upon the devotee of Viṣṇu, one should then perform his worship with the seat and other offerings as previously described, after first meditating upon the heart and other limbs.
One should perform worship with thirty-two services, or eight, or sixteen,
as before, ending either with recitation (*japa*) or with fire-oblation (*homa*), using the respective mantra for each.
Because of their lack of independence, one should never perform the *bali* offering there.

On each of their respective birthdays, one should perform their special worship together with the God of Gods; likewise, on occasions such as the sun’s passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti) and the solstices (ayana),
festivals, processions, and other rites must be performed during these times.

Alternatively, a festival may be held separately, excluding the hoisting of the banner (dhvajārohaṇa). There are no fire-oblations (homa) nor ritual offerings (bali); this is the rule for a pilgrimage site (tīrtha) when it is under another's authority. However, in cases of independence—such as at a land-grant (agrahāra), in a forest, or on a riverbank—the following procedure applies.
Having diligently constructed it with its various features, level, and adorned with floors as desired, and embellished with carriage-roads,
[he should provide for] those who have come from other lands or for the inhabitants of the world of the Blessed One.
Whether visible or invisible, having attained a form identical to that of the deity,
one should install [the image] according to the prescribed rite in a temple, on a human site,
or in a divine or human location that is either celestial or terrestrial. || 8.219–8.220 ||
Having brought down the consciousness from the sentient being situated within the unmanifest lotus of Viṣṇu’s seat of mantra into the lotus-heart of the devotee's image,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the mantra together with its limbs (aṅgas), one should always worship it.
This is the specific procedure for the invocation, whether for those who are living or those who have passed away.
In all cases, one should worship with the eightfold offerings beginning with the unmanifest lotus (*avyakta-padma*), or with sixteen,
using the abundant enjoyments previously described, ending with betel.
Having fashioned a banner with a lotus or likewise one with a swan,
and having raised it according to the scriptures, one should perform a great festival there.
One should carry out all the rites for the sacred ford (tīrtha), such as the offering of oblations (bali) and so forth.

One should cause the Lord to hear, according to the prescribed rule and with devotion, verses that are composed in a devotional style, profound, and augmented by the meaning of the Upanishads, preceded by songs. One should then cause the food and other offerings presented to Him to be given to the singers.
Thus has been correctly explained the supreme worship performed by Viṣṇu;
it must be guarded with effort, especially from atheists,
but it should be revealed to devotees whose souls are devoted to their daily duties.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Retinue Beginning with Garuḍa," in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the ninth chapter: Formerly, during the rites for the perpetual festival, the sages [spoke] regarding those residing at the gateway enclosure.
"The worship of the gods has been proclaimed, as well as their meditations and so forth in due order. O tiger among sages, you who are learned in all the scriptures, please speak [further].
Nārada said:
Listen, all you sages, with attentive minds,
to the characteristics of the deities of the door-panels according to the prescribed rule,
beginning from the deities of the palace entrance and proceeding in due order.
Outside the door of the palace, at the base of the final udumbara tree,
Vāstvīśa and Kṣetranātha stand in the order from right to left.
Vāstvīśa has a white face and a black body, possesses two arms, and has eyes like jeweled vessels.
With his right hand alone, he is the refuge of all the immortals;
O Brahmins, the Vāstupuruṣa should be meditated upon as having a complexion like a white lotus, adorned with garments, garlands, and unguents, and with a mace raised in his hand. || 9.5-9.6 ||
One should meditate upon Kṣetreśa, who has two arms, is golden-hued, wears garments and garlands, resembles a dark blue cloud, holds a staff in his hand, possesses a massive body,
and protects the sacrificial field with his left hand formed into a fist. (9.7)
With their bodies adorned by earrings and other ornaments, these two gazed upon the face of the Lord, which was exceedingly replete with splendor;
it possessed the luster of molten gold and was clothed in garments resembling coral. (9.8–9)
Adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, armlets, caskets, and crowns, she whose eyes resembled white lotuses possessed a face like the stainless,
perfectly full autumn moon.
One should meditate upon Lakṣmī, holding a lotus and a water-pot, seated upon a lotus above the door-post (udumbara). Seated in the lotus posture,
he [Viṣṇu] resembles the rising sun, possesses a broad chest, and has four arms.
He was lofty with high shoulders, his limbs full yet not excessively fleshy;
he had a slender belly and a deep navel, adorned by a line of body hair.
His face was formidable with fangs, and he bore tawny moustaches and matted locks.
With eyes honey-tawny and endowed with curved, creeper-like eyebrows;
with long, swaying ears and a broad nose, his face was graced with a smile;
he was adorned with earrings and embellished with necklaces and armlets.
With his uṣṇīṣa tied upon his forehead and adorned with a tilaka mark,
wearing white garments and garlands, one should visualize a raised discus in his right hand and a blazing mace in the other.
Seated upon her hips and resting on the surface of the earth,
she holds a conch in her former left hand and a rosary in the other;
thus is Caṇḍa, the Lord of the Gaṇas, unconquered through his prowess.
Enraged and capable of destroying tens of thousands of obstacles in an instant,
he should be meditated upon at the base of the southern door-jamb of the inner sanctum.
In that very place, on the opposite side, one should likewise worship Pracaṇḍa.
However, there may be a reversal by means of the right and left arms.
That which is proclaimed for Caṇḍa on the left [arm] of the pair of arms should be meditated upon or assigned as belonging to Pracaṇḍa on the right.
One should meditate upon Garuḍa at the entrance, possessing a golden luster,
with curved eyebrows and large, round eyes adorned with rows of eyelashes;
he has a protruding belly, well-filled limbs, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Resplendent with ornaments such as a crown and anklets,
wearing blue garments adorned with various garlands,
he stood before the God of gods on the ground with his palms joined in reverence.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Birds, known as Satya, who has two arms, possesses the luster of snow,
and is the presiding deity of the vital breath (prāṇa); he is stationed in the center of the circle of offerings (balimaṇḍala),
embodied in human form with all his limbs complete.
With a protruding belly, adorned with rows of wings,
holding a rosary with his right hand alone, his other hand turned upward, and decorated with earrings and other ornaments. || 9.26–9.27 ||
Clad in blue silk garments, with blue garlands and unguents,
he was constantly gazing at the Lord with steady eyes.
Then, [the two gatekeepers] stood at the pair of door-panels of the front pavilion.
Resembling the interior of a lotus and possessing exceedingly terrifying prowess, they were like Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, adorned with arm-emblems and ornaments;
they wore red garments and were anointed with red garlands and unguents.
Having meditated upon and worshipped the two Gaṇas, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, with single-minded devotion,
one should worship the lords of the Gaṇas, Kumuda and the others, in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
Furthermore, two leaders of the Gaṇas are to be worshipped in the eastern direction and in the south-eastern quarter.
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa, with serene faces and eyes,
resembled the snowy mountain and stood in the prime of youth;
their limbs were smeared with various ornaments and they were adorned with diverse earrings.

O twice-born ones, the right hand of the Lord of Gaṇas named Kumuda should be meditated upon as adorned with various garlands, wearing various crowns, its limbs smeared with various perfumes, and decorated with various garments. (9.34)
Resplendent with a fly-whisk resembling a ray of the moon,
one should meditate on the second right hand as extending the teaching of virtues to others who have sought refuge from the destruction of worldly existence. (9.35–9.36)

One should meditate on his very first left hand as raised with a blossoming lotus, silently indicating fear; and the supreme hand among those situated outside [the others] should be meditated upon in silence.
Indeed, one should contemplate this for Kumudākṣa in its reverse order.
Indeed, for the others as well, it is exactly the same with two hands each.
Both Puṇḍarīka and Vāmana have the splendor of fire;
they hold the Garuḍa-bannered [Viṣṇu] in their hands, while the rest is as previously described.
Having performed [the ritual], meditated, or having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in the south and also in the southwest—
[there are] he who is named Śaṅkukarṇa and he who is designated as Sarvanetra;
these two are the color of campaka flowers and are intent upon raising peacock-fan whisks.

Of the god Mahāvibhūti, [the attendants] Sumukha and Supratiṣṭha are situated in the west and northwest directions; they should be meditated upon as standing in the direction of Soma and Īśa (the north and northeast),
holding a shield and a parasol in their hands, dark-complexioned like mung beans.
But know that for those who perform what remains unsaid, O Kumuda, it has arisen;
these, O Brahmins, are the internal [devotees] of the Blessed One whom I have described,
whose minds are absorbed in Him through action, mind, and speech.
They were crowded by millions of supreme beings endowed with the sixfold qualities beginning with knowledge,
as well as by infinite *siddhas* who were seeking the highest state;
all of them, adorned with garments, ornaments, and unguents, resembled white water-lilies (*kumuda*).
Indeed, adorned with the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) fashioned from white clay placed upon their foreheads,
all the lords of the hosts such as Kumuda and the others—
likewise, O twice-born ones, all the other attendants beginning with Bhūta— are thus adorned.
In this same way, the Āvṛti deities and likewise those stationed at the gates [are adorned];
so too are his Brahmins, as well as those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes,
by means of vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) fashioned from either clay or sandalwood.
The twice-born should always be adorned with twelve or four [ornaments]. Dark as the flax flower, they should be clothed in yellow garlands and garments;
wearing yellow turbans, they are fierce, adorned on their arms as before.

One should worship the two attendants named Jaya and Vijaya at the sides of that door; they bear fierce forms, are difficult to behold, and are hard to overcome. Beginning from that point and extending outward until the end of the gateway, one should worship them.
Having divided the field of the second enclosure into six parts, O brahmins, one should place Garuḍa in the fifth part, or else having fashioned and meditated upon him—
one who has the appearance of glowing gold and eyes with fierce, knitted brows.
With large tusks, a broad nose, a massive body, and a vast belly;
with a chest adorned by the sprouts of his wings and graced by a circle of feathers;
and further embellished with ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, earrings, and crowns.
Adorned with blue garments, decorated with various garlands,
his limbs smeared with various perfumes, and embellished by eleven serpents.
O twice-born ones, he held his hands joined in añjali, filled with clusters of flowers,
having raised his right knee and made the other rest upon his seat.
Seated upon a comfortable throne, awaiting the command of the Lord, he was one who had attained perfection and beheld the true nature of ascetic practice, ritual action,
and the self; he was endowed with qualities such as omniscience and power equal to that of the Blessed One.

O best of the twice-born, he is separated from ordinary suffering yet joined with the Lord; for, by virtue of being the savior from worldly existence, he is established in due order within this enclosure. Upendra is stationed in the eastern quarter.
In the southeast is the one called Tejodhara, who is difficult to overcome;
in the southwest is Mahākarmā; in the west is Mahāhrada;
in the direction of the wind (the northwest) is Agrāhya; and likewise in the north is Vasuretā.
One should remember the witness in the northeast, who is increasing, whose domain is the sky,
and who is named the Abode of the Support (Ādhāranilaya), situated below all things;
these [deities] possess the luster of crystal and are adorned with white garlands and garments.
Holding a rosary, a discus, a conch, and likewise a mace,
with their four hands extending from the primary right hand to the primary left hand; they are perfectly symmetrical and adorned with crowns and other ornaments.
Driving away the nets of obstacles with their splendor,
those of great majesty all stand in their respective positions with eyes opened in meditation.
Alternatively, these may have two arms, holding the ten [implements] beginning with the thunderbolt in sequence.
In their right hands they hold the Lokapāla [image],
while with the left hand they hold a rosary, or else they grant the boons of *vara* and *abhaya*.
Likewise, by means of their complexions, bodily ointments, and so forth, they may be made similar to Indra and the other [guardians].
On both sides of the second gopura door, situated within,
one should place these two groups known as the gatekeepers, starting from the left:
the two lords of treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, who stand upon vessels containing jewels.

O twice-born ones, they have thick tusks and are well-tamed; they possess two arms and are permeated by the Blessed One. They are endowed with curved creeper-like eyebrows and slightly elevated chests. Their bellies hang down, their limbs are very plump, and their hands and feet are short.
Resplendent like a conch and a lotus, they were adorned with blue and white garments and garlands.
Adorned with various ornaments such as crowns and the like,
they both held a lotus with their right hands;
with their other hand, indeed, held up their own treasure-trove with the palm turned upward.
Alternatively, O twice-born ones, they may be endowed with the gestures of granting refuge and fearlessness in their left and right hands; or they may hold a conch or a lotus with both hands;
or the two Lords of Treasures (Nidhīśvarau) may hold a lotus in the left hand and a conch in the right.

Alternatively, one should visualize them holding a conch and a lotus, or else holding a conch and a discus upon their crowns above their heads, according to the wish of the practitioner. One should then remember them stationed at the door-panels, starting from the right.
White as milk-jars and dressed in blue silk garments,
their bodies adorned with flowers having the hue of blue lotuses,
resembling the previously mentioned hosts, they were named Bhadra and Subhadra.
Outside that door, on the two sides at the gate-towers (gopura),
one should install these two lords of the Gaṇas, either by meditating upon them or by visualizing them;
or else, if these two are two-armed, then [one should place them] to the right of Bhadra.
The right hand, joined with the index finger, is slightly bent;
it rests upon the tip of the mace while the left hand remains upon the base of the mace. The right foot is crossed over, while the left foot is firmly planted on the ground. (9.78–9.79)
O Brahmins, that which was described for the left hands and feet of Bhadra is for the right hands and feet of Subhadra; what was stated for the right side becomes the left side [for him].
However, his left hand is joined in the gesture of wonder (vismayamudrā).
Or else, O best of the twice-born, he is auspicious, endowed with the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) mudrā in his right hand; his left hand rests upon a mace above,
and subsequently, he holds a discus and a conch in his two hands respectively.
Subhadra, however, has his right hand resting on a mace, and the others likewise;
he is endowed with the gesture of fearlessness (abhītimudrā) and possesses the discus and conch.
In the case of Caṇḍa and the others as well, there should be exactly the same, including the state of having two arms and so forth.
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and likewise Jaya;
Vijaya, Bhadra, Subhadra, and Gaṇeśvara—
these are indeed the eight lords of the hosts (gaṇeśvaras), though they were without splendor, flowers, or garments.
Equal in their bodily forms and facial features, and likewise in their ornaments and weapons,
they were prepared to sever the net of obstacles for their devotees— obstacles situated in every direction and bestowing the fruits of worldly existence. (9.86)
All stood facing one another, positioned in equal postures.
They were surrounded by many tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of Gaṇeśas, who bore bodies of various colors and were devoted to the worship of Acyuta.
O twice-born ones, in the third enclosure, one should place the ten world-protectors beginning with Indra, starting from the west and proceeding in order toward the east.
One should meditate upon Purandara, who resembles the sun and possesses four arms.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god (Hutāśana), who stands upon a great elephant, brandishing a very sharp thunderbolt; he is mounted on a goat, red in color, holding a spear in his hand,
filled with thousands of flames, and as radiant as a thousand suns.

One should meditate upon that god, the Lord of the Ancestors (Pitṛīśvara), who is seated upon a great buffalo, whose splendor is like a mountain of collyrium, who holds a terrifying staff in his hand,
whose face is formidable with fangs, and whose radiance is like a black cloud. 9.92–93ab.
One should meditate on the terrible lord of the rākṣasas, holding a sword and seated upon a corpse;
[one should meditate on] the formidable lord of the waters, possessing the luster of pearls, holding a raised noose,
rich with thousands of serpent-maidens, and seated upon a makara.
One should meditate upon the god Vāyu, resembling a dark blue rain-cloud, marked by a great banner-cloth, and seated upon a deer;
and [one should meditate upon] Soma, accompanied by hosts of stars, white as a conch shell or cow’s milk.
One should meditate upon Īśāna, the wise one, seated upon the back of a large hare, holding a cooling weapon in his hand;
his limbs smeared with white ashes, three-eyed, riding a bull,
and bearing a trident in his hand.
One should meditate upon Halāyudha, who resides in the direction of Pātāla and is mounted upon a tortoise;
he is white, and the king of serpents named Ananta, possessing a thousand hoods, supports him.
One should likewise meditate upon Prajāpati, who brandishes the discus of the planets and holds a staff in his hand.
One should meditate upon the eternal, unborn, and all-pervading Lord, seated upon a swan and established in his own nature.
All these [deities] have four arms, are adorned with rosaries,
contemplate the supreme reality, and hold their hands raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
With their limbs smeared with divine ornaments, endowed with celestial garlands and garments,
possessing divine forms, and wafting divine fragrances, O twice-born ones,
they shone with the luster of red, white, black, yellow, and blue campaka flowers.
Likewise, they were adorned with garlands, unguents, and garments resembling the sky, crystal, and the sun-stone (mārtāṇḍarājopala), all of great value;
they were further embellished with various ornaments such as caskets and crowns.
"Among these, he whose banner is the bull should be known here as four-armed;
or alternatively, the others may be two-armed, granting boons and protection from fear. Thus it was said regarding the Lords of the World, O best of the twice-born."
At the root of the branch on the southern side of the third enclosure gate is Sudarśana, four-armed and short-statured, with blazing radiance;
his eyes are red with wrath, and he is smeared with the blood of Daityas and Dānavas. || 9.105–9.106 ||
Dancing and intoxicated with pride, he stood within the hub of the thousand-spoked wheel;
his face was terrifying with its fangs, and his eyebrows were curved like creepers.
He had the appearance of the fire at the end of an aeon and was encircled by his own rays of light.
In his two right arms, he holds the Sudarśana discus with the first,
and with the other, a mace resting upon the ground;
in his principal left hand he holds a conch, and in the other, a rosary.
Adorned with various ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, earrings, and crowns,
and further embellished with white garlands, garments, and the like,
he dispels obstacles by means of his own blazing splendor.
Then, O twice-born ones, at the root of another tree branch,
he should remember Garuḍa well-established there, O brahmins— resembling molten gold,
with a face like a hawk, wide-open eyes, a red beak, and most terrifying. || 9.111–9.112 ||
With a broad belly and a long tail, adorned with a circle of feathers,
wearing red garments and anointed with red garlands and unguents;
his face was formidable with fangs, and his eyes were crooked with a frown.
Wearing a variegated tunic,
adorned by the lords of serpents,
and decorated with various ornaments such as a crown.
Regarding the two arms, that which is proclaimed for the left side of the Cakra should be on the right of this [deity],
and what was stated for the right should be on the left.
[The remaining implements are] the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the banner.
The trident named Śiśira, as well as the plow and the mace,
are situated in the fourth enclosure according to the sequence starting from the east;
O twice-born ones, their visualization is now described in order.
The vajra, resembling a diamond-stone, marked with long white claws;
his face terrifying with fangs, his eyes blazing like gold;
the spear possessing the brilliance of lightning, its tip like the flame of a tranquil fire.
One should visualize the staff as having a body and eyes that are red, with its fist clenched, repeatedly emitting a deep and gurgling roar;
it is the very embodiment of wrath, biting its own lower lip with its teeth.
One should meditate upon Nandaka, dancing and adorned with rays of light;
resembling the autumnal sky, biting his row of teeth,
holding a noose strewn with a multitude of virtues, with a tongue like lightning, and terrifying.
With a complexion pale like a row of gold, a terrible mouth, and blood-red eyes;
resembling an autumn cloud, with a banner and crooked eyes;
illuminating the entire world with his own splendor, he was preeminent in strength.
Cool as the moon, with full limbs and a broad body,
he was gentle, wearing a mass of matted locks, with eyes like white lotuses;
he possessed the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and held a trident of terrifying form.
Resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, encircled by its own rays,
resembling a twilight cloud, with a tail and terrifying eyes;
with a slender body, elevated shoulders, a diamond-like frame, and preeminent strength.
A pestle, white as a jasmine flower, gentle, with a face slightly smiling,
uttering a sweet sound that was pleasing to the faculty of hearing;
[with hands] resembling blue, red, white, yellow, fire, and collyrium.
They were adorned in due order with garlands, unguents, and garments that shone like gold, snow, and the sky, and were appropriate for them. 9.129

Adorned with divine ornaments and their heads marked with their own respective signs, they stood in a perfectly balanced posture, leaning their left hands upon their hips while threatening the multitude of wicked beings with their right hands.
Having meditated upon the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā on the southern and northern branches of the door of the fourth enclosure, one should worship them in sequence.
She was like the Gaṅgā born from the feet of the Blessed One, resembling a white water-lily,
and endowed with the qualities of fresh youth, beauty, and delicacy.
Clad in blue body-unguents and garments, adorned with blue garlands,
two-armed, with a gentle countenance and eyes like lotuses,
she is graced by necklaces, anklets, armlets, earrings, and other ornaments.
She washes away with her own splendor the mud of latent impressions and karma from those scorched by the heat of saṃsāra who desire to ascend to the supreme state;
she carries a water-filled pitcher in her very right hand.
With her left hand she was threatening ordinary people;
Yamunā had the luster of a blue gem, with dark, curly hair,
and was adorned with white unguents, garments, and white garlands.
The right hand is known to hold the tarjanī mudrā, while the left holds a water-pot (kalaśa).
O lords of sages, everything else here should be as described for Gaṅgā.
Lohitākṣa is of great heroism, immeasurable, and most beautiful.
Vīrahā, Vikrama, Bhīma, and Śatāvarta as the eighth—
these are stationed in the fifth enclosure according to the sequence of the directions starting from the northeast (aiśvarī).
One should meditate upon him who resembles the moon, has red eyes, and is preeminent in strength.
Wearing blue garments, with blue garlands and blue unguents,
possessing great heroism, a massive body, yellowish complexion, and mighty arms;
wearing garments the color of coral, with red garlands and red unguents.
One should recollect him known as Immeasurable, preeminent with immeasurable power;
one should meditate on him who has a greenish form, wearing yellow garments, garlands, and ointments,
most beautiful, with handsome limbs, resembling a pearl.
One should meditate upon the slayer of heroes, known as Vīrahā, who resembles the *atasī* flower in his garments, garlands, and ointments, yet is like a *caṃpaka* flower in appearance.
One should meditate upon Vikrama, the abode of valor, adorned with garments and garlands dyed red by the artisans of Vāhlīka, resembling the belly of a blue jay,
wearing clothes as white and beautiful as jasmine and the moon, and anointed with white perfumes and garlands. 9.145–146ab.
One should meditate upon Bhīma, of terrifying form, resembling molten gold.
One should meditate upon Śatāvarta as having a pale-red silken garment, likewise endowed with perfumes and garlands, and dark-complexioned like the flax flower;
[one should meditate upon him] wearing yellow garments and adorned with yellow garlands and perfumes.

Indeed, these beings possess two arms and have hearts filled with inner joy. All of them hold a blazing axe with their right hands, and with their left hands they bear a radiant, excellent conch; they are adorned with beautiful earrings.

They were all equal, with limbs symmetrically proportioned, and possessed of tranquil appearances; they stood in various postures, resplendent with their own radiance. With serene faces and gentle countenances, they were capable of uplifting the three worlds.
Adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, and armlets,
they awaited his command and brought about the pacification of the faults of the wicked;
by their great power, they cast down the gods, asuras, and great serpents.
And you, as a solitary hero without companion,
are able to constantly overturn everything up to the realm of Brahmā effortlessly and with ease.
One should install the door-deities at these four doors using the method of pairing, starting from the eastern door in sequence:
Vajranābha and Karīśa in the east, [to its] south and north.
One should meditate upon the one named Vajranābha, whose radiance is equal to a hundred suns;
who, with his primary right hand, displays the gesture of prohibition (*niṣedhābhinaya*),
holds a cane-staff with the second, and a sovereign wheel (*cakrarāja*) with the third.
With his primary left hand resting upon the region of his hip,
he holds the king of conchs with the second, and likewise a vajra with the third;
he is adorned with various ornaments of gold.
Wearing red garlands and garments, and adorned with red perfumes and unguents—
thus [he visualizes] Hari on the left, devoid of the gesture of prohibition (niṣedha),
but rather marked by the hand known as the gesture of entry (praveśa). || 9.158–9.159 ||
For here, indeed, there is one who effects the exclusion of those who are not devotees.
And another indeed grants entrance to the devotees.
Such is the purpose of the pair of doorkeepers at every gate;
as stated by Dakṣa, they belong to Vajranābha on the right and to Hariśa on the left.
Everything on the left side of the first [hand] is different from that which is on the right hand.
One should fashion the two [deities] Dharmādhyakṣa and Nityatrīśa on the right and the left [of the central deity],
resembling Antaka (Yama) and adorned with arms as before.
Clad in yellow silk garments and adorned with yellow garlands and unguents,
they hold staffs and maces in their hands, but are devoid of the thunderbolt and the discus;
[they bestow] the bliss of the pure nectar of immortality from the west, starting from the south.
In one hand he holds an arrow and a bow, and in another a noose;
that first set of four hands should remain active as before.
Indeed, in form, he is always similar to the Lord of Waters.
Clad in blue silk garments and adorned with blue garlands and unguents,
[the two deities] Vasunātha and Sudhānanda are situated in the north-east and north-west respectively;
both hold a sword and a mallet in their hands, and the remaining four [deities] are as previously described.
The function of these two hands was equal to that of the moon in form; they were dark like flax flowers, clad in silk garments, and adorned with garlands and ointments.
Indeed, they were decorated with various ornaments like those of Vajranābha.
O best of sages, now hear in truth the meditation upon the deities of the sixth enclosure, specifically those stationed at its gates,
situated from the east up to the northeast. 9.169–170.
And these deities, O Brahmins, are endowed with the form of splendor;
as is Time, which is the controller, and the scripture characterized by its various limbs;
likewise the lords of knowledge, together with Rudra and his hosts, and Viśva.
Indra, together with his retinue, is the assembly of Prajāpati.
At the four principal gates, however, they are stationed in order as before:
the discus and conch, the lotus and mace, the plow and pestle, and the arrows.
And these [five] Śārṅgas should be meditated upon in sequence, possessing the luster of lightning,

snow, and jasmine; they are resplendent with garments, garlands, and ointments that resemble yellow, blue, white, red, black, and the color of cow's milk, as well as the hue of yellow orpiment and the dawn.
They are adorned with ornaments made of every kind of jewel;
they possess great strength and great heroism, having one face and two arms.
All these leaders have their heads marked with their respective insignia.
Threatening the wicked flood with their right hands,
while resting their left hands upon their hips, they stood in perfectly balanced postures—
firm in their vows, many-headed, massive in body, and possessed of great strength.

He who has conquered anger, who is invincible, possessed of great energy, and who strides with the three steps; who is incomparable, the destroyer of the wicked, radiant, all-seeing, and impossible to overcome;
who is formidable, profound, unfailing, and the bestower of the sixteen entrances.
Starting from the middle of Śakra and Agni and extending to the interval between Śakra and Īśāna,
[the colors are] white, crimson, golden, black, tawny, red, white, and dark blue;
[alternatively] red, yellow, flaxen, golden, crimson, bright white, and dark blue.
Wearing fine garments, garlands, ointments, and ornaments appropriate to their respective castes (varṇa),
and possessing conduct consistent with their names, they carry conch shells and mallets,
acting as those who permit entry and prohibit exit according to the sequence of right and left.
One should worship these aforementioned [deities] in their proper sequence, as before, who are capable of performing the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world in an instant.
The seven sages and others previously mentioned are surrounded by the stars and other celestial bodies.
All the clouds, the Nāgas, and the most excellent hosts of Apsarases;
as well as the medicinal herbs, the animals, and all the sacrifices together with their constituent parts—
these remain in a subtle form during the seventh envelopment, just as before.
Sambhava, Prabhava, Pūrṇa, Puṣkara, Ānanda, Nandana, Vīrasena, and Suṣeṇaka—
these two each stood at the main door-frames on the right and left.
Sambhava is white in color, while Prabhava resembles a kunda flower;
Pūrṇa has the appearance of red, and Puṣkara is intensely red.
Ānanda is yellow in color, while Nanda is said to have the luster of gold. Vīrasena has the appearance of black, and Suṣeṇa resembles collyrium.
They have two arms, their limbs are adorned with variegated crowns and armlets, and they hold maces in their hands.
Or, O best of Brahmins, they may have four arms, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
with another hand as before, they prevent entry.
Their faces are formidable with fangs, and they are capable of both restraint and grace.
The maker of security, the maker of auspiciousness, the wise one, the performer of oblations, the creator of beings;
the fire at the end of the eon, the devourer, Saṃvarta, and likewise Bhīṣaṇa;
the thunderer, the unblinking one, the hundred-jointed, and the hundred-faced.

Audumbara, Prakṛtika, Virāma, and Aṃśumālin—this group of sixteen, beginning with Dṛḍhavrata, is respectively like [the preceding] in color and possesses six arms. Each of these is associated with the office of an attendant (aupadauvārika). 9.193.
By means of the union of the left and right, [he faces] west and east from behind.
He is endowed with the conch, mallet, lotus, rosary, boon-granting gesture, and fear-dispelling gesture;
he possesses various colors, garlands, a turban, garments, ointments, and ornaments.
Rich in the previously mentioned virtues and heroism, and capable of performing all actions, Virocana,
the lord of a hundred cities, [acted] for the sake of protecting his eightfold splendor.
He was indeed inconceivable, unassailable, and possessed of an immeasurable name.
Amarṣin, Mahābhūta, and likewise Cakorākṣa as the eighth;
stationed one by one in order on the beauties of the side-entrances between Indra and Agni, these heroes stand there to prevent anyone from entering.
Having the luster of blue, yellow, japā, dark-blue, black, and vermilion,
they were of great strength and great heroism, possessing a prowess that was very difficult to overcome;
they were adorned with various kinds of garments, garlands, ornaments, and ointments.
Adorned with other ornaments as was fitting,
they were endowed with the majesty of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya); they had four arms, and in sequence,
their right and left backs were equipped with the discus and the conch.
One should worship these lords who grace the main doors and side-entrances in sequence— those who possess two principal hands resting upon the tops of maces—
as well as Vidyā, Aparavidyā, Pāvaka, and Māruta. 9.202–203ab.
The Moon, the Sun, Water, and Earth—these indeed are the deities of saṃsāra.
They abide in subtle form upon the surface of the outer enclosure.
Amareśa, Virūpākṣa, Sudharmiṣṭha, and Niyāmaka [are there].
And Sarvasattvāśraya—immediately after him—is Gahana;
likewise Mahārājeśvara and Dhanādhyakṣeśvara.
These eight are the lords of the Gaṇas, the primary gatekeepers at its entrance.
All [the deities] are to be meditated upon as four-armed; however, Amareśa and Virūpākṣa hold a thunderbolt and a cane-staff with their two principal hands,
while with their two rear hands they shine with a discus and a conch.
Resembling saffron and collyrium, with faces distorted by fangs,
they are joined respectively to the south and north, endowed with reversed markings;
stationed at the right and left of the door, they are the ones who permit entry and forbid it.
The most righteous one was the restrainer, while the two of them possessed a very white and dark luster respectively;
they held formidable staffs in their hands and were devoid of the thunderbolt weapon,
maintaining the other [implements] in due order according to the prescribed rule.
The support of all beings is extremely deep, dark, and white;
however, these two [deities] holding nooses have their arms adorned as before.
Mahārājeśvara is red, and Dhanādhyakṣeśvara is black.
Joined with the weapon Śiśirāyudha, they were another triad just as before—
possessing great strength and great heroism, causing the destruction of the faults of the wicked,
difficult to behold, unassailable, and destroyers of Daityas and Dānavas.
Adorned with various costly garments, ornaments, and unguents,
[they beheld] the Great Bull— abundant, profound, within the range of the vital breath,
the limb of yoga, the abode of yoga, eternal, and unshackled.
*Tārakāntarita*, *tāra*, *virāma*, and likewise *viṣama*;
*duratikrama*, *durgaha*, *sudhūmra*, and *anilāśana*—
these he should place at the gates of the *sālakopa* according to the previous method.
This group of sixteen attendants, equal in color to the previously mentioned gatekeepers and resplendent, is endowed with four hands;
[the sequence of their attributes] begins from the secondary left hand and ends with the primary left hand.
He holds a thousand conch shells marked with the gesture of prohibition (niṣedha),
and is marked by the gesture of entry (praveśa); he wears garments and garlands of various colors,
is joined with various postures (sthānaka), and is adorned with various ornaments.
O best of sages, one should distinguish between him who bears a rosary and grants entrance to those who have sought refuge, and him who likewise bars others;
as well as Devavrata, the fearless Bhīṣma, and the Puruṣa.
O best of sages, [he is] Ugra, Vīreśvara, Ramya, Ariṣṭa,
Nirviṣaṇṇa, Yugāntāṃśa, Śatānanda, Śatānana,
Tejodhara, Viśālākṣa, Yugāṃśa, and Devanandana.
One should place this group of sixteen deities individually within the beautiful [enclosures],
resembling the lords of the secondary gates (upadvāreśa) in color, but without their emblems (lāñchana). They should be depicted with four arms, positioned from the back, the right, and the front.
Holding the conch, discus, and mace, he extends his primary right hand to its full length.
He is the repeller of evils and the usher-in of those who are sinless;
adorned with various garlands, garments, turbans, ornaments, ointments, and the like,
he possesses infinite and inconceivable majesty and is the refuge for all beings.
Skilled in various weapons and missiles, endowed with diverse forms of knowledge,
having cast out many lords of the Daityas, and intent on protecting the virtuous—
both of them stood at the main gate of the wall which possessed two entrances.
While remaining in a subtle form on the other side of the gate,
one should place [the deities] at all the corners of the enclosure wall, starting from the southeast (vahnikoṇa).
These are the fourfold forms whose nature consists of origin and dissolution.
Likewise, one should sequentially recollect the forms of the other manifestations and their consorts,
as well as the mantras of the collection of weapons and so forth,
for all four corners outside the temple, which are unmanifest.
One should indeed perform the sacrifice with the name "Bhava," for no other is known as Bhava.
Having established them outside [the maṇḍala] according to the sequence of the directions by means of their own mantras, [one should place] the Lord of Weapons (Hetirāṭ),
who illuminates [all] with his own multitude of rays.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one should perform the worship with offerings such as the water for honor (arghya), garlands, and sandalwood paste, purified by the rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa), accompanied by mantras and mudrās.
The deity named Vāsudeva is the embodiment of the six divine qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).

For the sake of assisting those who perform ritual actions, the Lord, residing within the eternal image, always bestows grace upon them after having entered the temple— a massive form rich in all knowledge and action, and the refuge of all principles (tattvas).

Therefore, one should sequentially place the eight external principles (bāhyatattva), culminating in the cognition of earth and the other elements, within the eight walls that constitute its limbs. And the temple, together with its constituent parts, is the primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa).
The image therein is the individual soul (jīva), and the Supreme Person (parama-puruṣa) resides therein.
Therefore, these principles (tattvas) are the presiding deities (adhidaivatas) here in their respective order.
Having meditated upon them as pervading everywhere, one should then perform worship.

Having enclosed the palace together with its ramparts from above by means of the lotus of Kālacakra— which consists of the support of all, which is the refuge of all sentient beings, and which destroys the poison of all defects— [one should meditate]. || 9.238–9.239 ||

Having worshipped [the deity] and displayed the heart-mudrā together with the discus-mudrā, one should enclose [the deity] from all directions with the armor-mantra (kavaca). This applies likewise when there is the arrangement of a single form and it is adorned with a single door.
In this abode, once the arrangement of the array of directions is completed,
[one should perform it] in a house provided with four gates, in a pavilion situated at the front of the directional gates,
in a Sarvatobhadra hall, and also in a place that releases one from suffering.
In the ritual known as the Sadadhva-deśa-dharma, which is endowed with two pairs of doors,
this specific procedure for the placement (nyāsa) of the hosts of door-keepers is now revealed.
[The deities] beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Subhadra are located at the four doors of the temple.

They should be installed in due order, as before, through the union of pairs. Located respectively upon the two *udumbara* beams above the doorways are the goddesses Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā, whose characteristics have been described previously.
Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya are established at the forefront;
Anivartin, Mahāvṛtti, Darpahā, Sarvajit, Sthira, Jayanta, Bhayakṛt, and Mānī are the eighth, O best of the twice-born. (9.246)
They stood at the sides of the door-frames of the pavilion at the edge of the quarters:
Anivartin, Mahāvṛtti, Kṛṣṇābha, Śukasannibha,
Darpahā, Sarvajit, Pāṇḍu, Rakta, and Suvarṇabha.
Sthira, Jayanta, Śyāma— who has the luster of collyrium— and Añjana; Bhayakṛt, Mānin, Piṅgala, and Pāṇḍurojvala—
all of these have two arms, and with their right hands— || 9.249 ||

Holding the conch Nandaka with another hand, these lords of the Gaṇas possess fierce prowess. When they are to be meditated upon as four-armed, then these lords of the Gaṇas hold a sword and a cane in their primary right hands.
Likewise, they hold a conch in their left hands, while on their backs, starting from the right,
they bear a discus and a lotus in both hands; they possess a blazing radiance and are adorned with various garments, garlands, turbans, ornaments, and unguents.
With hands and feet reversed and endowed with inverted marks;
the Exalted One, whose body is nectar, who possesses all limbs and faces in every direction;
the one of radiant form, the bestower of boons, the Lord of Speech, and whose prowess is sound.
Indeed, two specific forms of Pāñcajanya are established in pairs in succession,
as before, at the four gates of the Sarvatobhadra Sāla temple;
they are to be remembered as having two arms, with [the conch] in the right hand.
All of them held maces in one hand and conchs in the other; four were like the color of the bandhūka flower,
while the others resembled cuckoos and were adorned with every ornament.
By their great power, they could effortlessly and playfully cast down the gods, asuras, and great serpents; alone and without companions,
they were capable of constantly overturning everything up to the realm of Brahmā.
Viśveśa, Viśvakṛt, Viśva, Viśvātman, Viśvalocana,
Viśvapāda, Viśvabhuja, and likewise Viśvakarmakṛt—
these are the presiding deities at the directional gates of the second sāla grove.
They are to be known as having two arms, joined by the left and right [hands], equipped with maces, swords, and missiles, and adorned with crowns and caskets.
They are red, tawny, white, and dark; and red, yellow, white, and black.

Resplendent with all colors, garments, unguents, garlands, and ornaments; solitary heroes without companions, they ward off all defects. They are situated at the inner portions of those gates, according to their left and right positions.
One should install the lords of the treasures (nidhinātheśvaras) in sequence facing the palace:
Śaṅkha, Padma, Mahāpadma, and the one named Śatadhāman;
then Akhaṇḍita, Santata, and the one known as Anantadhāra.
The first two are proclaimed as "Sarvadvāra" (All-Gates) and were described previously.
Now, the colors, forms, and other characteristics of the remaining six will be stated in order:
they are red, black, gold-hued, white, crimson, and the color of tamāla.
Marked by all the characteristics described for the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures,
they are the lords of wealth, gems, gold, the eight metals, grain, and riches;
they are the masters of all medicinal herbs and treasures, seated comfortably upon them.
Adorned with all ornaments, they bestow the desired objects upon those who take refuge in them.
Then, at the doors of the third enclosure, one should arrange [the deities] in pairs,
sequentially on the southern and northern branches.
In front are the discus and Garuḍa; on the right, the plow and the palm tree; on the west, the Śārṅga bow and the Makara; and on the north, the sword Nandaka and the Ṛśyaka.
[Furthermore, there are] the discus, the lord of birds, and the plow, as well as the conch and Nandaka.
O twice-born ones, the previously described colors, forms, and other attributes apply to their respective positions.
Now, the three others beginning with Tāla will be described:
Tāla is the banner (dhvaja), and he possesses the conceit of being the form of a child such as a Bhūta and so forth.
The fish (jhaṣa) is declared to be the seed of the universe, with all its limbs restrained;
the deer (ṛśya), accompanied by all calamities, is the world (saṃsāra) characterized by a fickle nature.
Having meditated upon these in their subtle form, one should worship them in sequence.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Godāvarī, and likewise the great river, as well as the Vitastā, the Narmadā, the one named Jambū, and the Sarasvatī—
these rivers stand respectively at the gates of the four quarters of the Sāla tree.
The color, form, and other qualities of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā were described previously; other rivers are equal to them, though they lack their specific beauty of hue.
They are white, reddish, and possess a luster like that of white gold and the white kunda flower.
And they possess the mature attire of those who are intoxicated, adorned with various ornaments;
their limbs are variegated with all kinds of minerals and they shine with every sort of jewel.
As before, they hold jars of nectar with two of their hands.

Thus has been described the stationing at the gates of the directions and the gates of the palaces; likewise for those with a single form, the placement of the directional deities within the enclosures and above them. Their gates and so forth are declared to be common [to all].
Both [deities] should be visualized or installed at the side of the branch of the *sarvasāla* door-keeper,
if they are located outside the food-offering;
they should be installed in their proper order, endowed with the characteristics as previously described.

Having thus meditated upon or established the lords of the enclosures (āvaraṇeśas), one should worship them in their respective seats, within dwellings that are the embodiments of their own forms arising from meditation. For that purpose, one should divide the courtyard area into three or five parts.

Having set aside one-third or one-fourth [of the space], one should construct a pedestal (*pīṭha*) or a sanctuary (*āyatana*) either outside from the middle of that [space] or within it, in all directions; or else,
as previously stated, [it may be constructed] with the lower and upper parts established as before.
Platforms constructed from stone, brick, and other materials, one cubit in width and half that height, all adorned with every ornament—
whether square or perfectly circular, or even worshipped alone— are to be prepared. (9.285)
One should offer the *bali* to the deities of the village and other local spirits upon mandalas smeared with cow dung and the like, situated in the directions and sub-directions.
There are two types of pedestals (*pīṭha*), previously described by their characteristics, according to their dimensions of width and height.
Alternatively, they may be made half that size, provided it does not conflict with the chariot procession.
Thus, the lords of the enclosures (Āvaraṇeśas) are situated upon their respective pedestals in their own directions,
facing the temple in order to dispel the faults of the wicked.
O best of sages, listen to the installation of the lords of the Gaṇas at the gate and in the sacrificial hall of one who has entered the four stations:
two, known as Vāstu and Kṣetreśa, are situated at the eastern gate as before.
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā stand in sequence above the doors;
the deities Vajranābha and the others are in pairs at the two door-panels of each cardinal direction.
In the pitchers at the eastern and other doors are Sambhava, Prabhuva, and the rest.

And the supreme group of eight elements, beginning with Kumuda, which is internal, O twice-born ones, has taken recourse to the region of Bhramaṇī by means of the arrangement of pairs within the doorways: Suparṇa, he who is named Cakra, Satya, and Kaumodakī. (9.292–293)

O twice-born ones, they should be arranged in due order upon the ground in front of the doors; Satya is positioned on the golden staff, but he is located in the western direction. Furthermore, the deities beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Subhadra are placed two by two in the directions starting from the east.
By means of the southern and northern alignment, they reach the base of the archway pillars.
The Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) stands upon the archway between two wheels;
on either side of him stand wheels adorned with banners of various colors.

The tetrad beginning with Truth (satya) is situated on the eight banners of the central altar; it is to be worshipped according to the sequence starting from the east, through the conjunction of origin and dissolution.
Vihageśvara.
"Those world-protectors,
Indra and the others, preceded by hosts of Siddhas,
and their weapons such as the vajra, stood outside in their respective directions. (9.298)
One should proceed in this manner during the primary ritual or during other [auspicious] occasions;
likewise during the secondary ritual (anukalpa), one should first worship Caṇḍa and the others, beginning with the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha).
Having installed them alone at the gates, ending with Garuḍa, one should perform the worship.

Or he may be worshipped at all the doors, together with his weapons, the Lord who is the protector of birds (Garuḍa). [This applies] in various rites of installation, as well as in the procedure for the restoration of ruined temples,
in all great festivals, and in the rite of hoisting the banner.
In the planting of the auspicious sprout, in the rite of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) and so forth,

as well as in the ritual of consecration with the infinite jars (*anantakalaśa*) and others, in occasional penances (*prāyaścitta*), and likewise constantly in rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*). (9.302)

One should perform [the rite] according to the procedure prescribed for the primary ritual; otherwise, it should be done differently. (9.303) Likewise, the hosts of Siddhas, Indra and the others, and their weapons, as well as these world-protectors of the directions, are surrounded by their own armies. (9.304)
By virtue of their well-known former abodes, they have eternally occupied their own places;
for because they are the guardians of the directions, their station has remained firm since the beginning of creation,
O lords of sages, as they are the infinite embodiments of the Lord’s mantras.
Established in their own abodes, they pay homage, worship, and recite [his name];
they also attend upon him perfectly with offerings such as banners and the like,
for the sake of attaining absolute liberation, together with many of their own followers at all times.
They protect their devotees and bestow strength;
they incessantly destroy the flood of obstacles for those who perform sacrifices with mantras.
They preserve the fruit of the mantra, which increases in two ways.
The power-seed (*śaktibīja*) of the Lord of the World is an authority that has no beginning.
For the sake of establishing the directions, it possesses a tenfold nature; for its manifestation, it consists of the eight directions.
The deities of existence, such as Kāla and the others, reside upon the ground of the three external pillars. (9.309–9.310)
Because they accomplish that [task], the gods Vajranābha and others, who are the guardians of the world’s cardinal directions, are eternally stationed in the previously mentioned regions.
Likewise, there are Amareśa and others, as well as Sambhava, Prabhuva, and so forth.
Established in the directions and gates according to the well-known sequence:

the group of eight beginning with Kāla and ending with Rudra, starting with Indra; the Controller (Niyantr) at the end of the principle of Time (Kālatattva), and beyond that, the well-established Ether (Viyat).

One should sequentially place the two, Vidyā and Avidyā, in the northeast and southwest corners respectively; indeed, these two reside in their own positions in the southeast and northwest. Having likewise established Candra and Āditya in their northern and southern locations, one should assign them.
