One should place the water situated in the western portion onto the earth in the eastern portion. Likewise, one should place the lords of the enclosures beginning with Kumuda, as well as those beginning with Lohitākṣa,
excluding the gatekeepers beginning with Vajranābha— these three groups of eight.
These groups of gatekeepers likewise stand at the corners of the walls, positioned according to the stated sequence with respect to the east of the Blessed One.
The lords of the hosts, Kumuda and the others, reside in the dwellings of cities, villages, and so forth.

And they remain in the dwellings of the *pālikās* according to the directions prescribed for the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas). One should perform the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) to the gods at the three junctions of the day (trisandhya) within the consecrated halls for those who reside at the entrances and enclosures.
One should not perform an offering for deities whose temples were built without prior intention; rather,
having installed them according to the prescribed rite at the time of their respective construction,
one should perform the offering of bali when they are included in a procession of the gods.
Having thus prepared everything, including the ground above the great seat (mahāpīṭha),
one should ascend it after it has been washed. Facing either east or north,
one should then place the kumuda and other lotuses upon the petals of the water-born directions above that.
Having summoned all the spirits known as *grahas* who serve as his attendants,
and having honored them there with water, he should scatter the remainder of the sacrificial offering (*bali*).
Afterwards, having sipped water (*ācamana*) according to the rule or having bathed, he should enter his house.
In the worship of the lords of all the door-panels situated in the corners,
the mantra is said to be their own name joined with *namaḥ* and the *praṇava*.
[This applies] to the attendants (*pārṣadas*) who are spirits residing in the great seats (*mahāpīṭhas*) and whose nature is that of planetary deities (*graha*).
One should apply the word "Viṣṇu" at the end of "Tārā" according to the stated sequence.
All mantras located in the corners are declared to end with "phaṭ.
All mantras combined together for the rite of fire-offering (homa) should end with "svāhā."
Having meditated thus and worshipped with their respective mantras and services such as the *arghya* offering,
one should display the mudrā known as *tarjanī* to the lords of the enclosures (*āvṛti*).
Immediately thereafter, one should perform [the worship] for the hosts of gatekeepers, beginning with Caṇḍa.
If, due to obstacles such as [hostile] deities and so forth,
it is impossible to offer bali-oblations above that point by any means whatsoever, one should perform the rite for those located there in due order,
doubling the offerings in the directions starting from the Sarvatobhadra.
In the primary ritual as well as elsewhere, according to one's capacity, on the ground of the enclosure,
one should satisfy the deities of the outer enclosures by repeatedly offering oblations;
one should present [the offerings] to the guardians of the gates and sub-gates at that very gate.

And for those [deities] arisen from the great seats (*mahāpīṭha*) within the circle at the tip of their respective doors, there is no fault in not moving from their positions during meditation; for what reason?
Because they have been assigned to the locations of the doors of their respective enclosures according to the stated sequence.
Furthermore, there would be an undesirable movement of those [deities] residing within the physical form.
Thus, one should perform the bali offering for the deities of the enclosure at the three junctions of the day;
for the sake of the daily festival, one should perform it in the presence of the image.
Accompanied by dance, song, and the like, and endowed with the resonance of the Vedas—
thus has the meditation on the deities of the doors and enclosures been revealed. Indeed,
one should perform the worship in this manner, ending with the offering of bali.
Therein, the presence of the deity is accomplished through uninterrupted continuity.
Thus, the best of teachers should perform worship during the three periods of time;
worship performed less than three times is never prescribed.

O best of the twice-born, in palaces that were previously self-manifested, the primary [period for construction] should be the three times; beyond that, it may be according to the builder's desire. Furthermore, one should increase [the dimensions] in due order in accordance with one's wealth.

O best of sages, among the twelve periods of time, the dawn is indeed the most excellent; furthermore, among the three times, it is the best. One should perform the ritual placement of mantras upon oneself, on the hands, and on the body according to the rules.
Then, in the morning, one should perform the heart-sacrifice (hṛdyāga), the purification of the locus, and the ritual of the elements;

this is the daily practice at dawn, while at other times it may be performed according to one's desire. One should always perform the ritual bathing and the offering of oblations (bali) at the three periods of the day.
The worship of the seat (āsana-pūjā) of the form [of the deity] should be performed during the four periods;
at five periods, the ritual placement (nyāsa) should take place; at six periods, the act of oblation (havana-kriyā);
and from seven periods onwards, the worship should conclude with the recitation of mantras (japa).
The ornaments, the seat, and so forth, should be performed according to the sequence as previously described;
indeed, one should not act otherwise than by the manner stated.

In the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*), however, up until the end of the fire-oblation (*homānta*), [one performs] that which consists of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
One should indeed perform the worship in sequence, concluding each with the respective oblation (homa).

However, in the case of a secondary rite (anukalpa), it ends with the recitation of mantras; likewise for sacrifices that have been omitted, and for all obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites where the sacrifice concludes with the oblation.
Having performed each respective sacrifice, ending with the recitation of mantras (japa),
in due order, thereafter the best of sages should perform the corresponding fire-oblation (homa) in sequence according to the prescribed rule,
even in the case of secondary sacrifices (anukalpa) mentioned for times of adversity.
Then, having offered a seat, the water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamana) along with a vessel for the gift;

and having given, in due order, perfume, a garland, a lamp, incense, and the sacrificial fee (mātrā); one should then, according to the prescribed rule, offer the food at the conclusion of the sequence.
"Thus has the procedure for worship, with all its primary and secondary limbs, been demonstrated.
O best of sages, if you desire to hear anything else beyond this, let it be told.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
The ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Characteristics and Other Attributes of the Deities Guarding the Doors.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, O omniscient one, best among speakers,
we have heard from you in full detail everything concerning the daily worship and other rites.
"Now you should speak of the great festivals and other celebrations.
Nārada replied: "Therefore, I shall now explain the sequence of the ritual for the great festivals. 10.2
"O bulls among sages, the wise declare that *sava* is suffering;
since that *sava* has been removed from it, it is therefore called a festival (*utsava*).
That great festival is of three kinds: obligatory, occasional, and optional. (10.3)
That which is performed year after year is the obligatory (nityaka) rite.
When there is an earthquake, the burning of the quarters, or during great portents; when there is famine, disease in the kingdom, or likewise a crisis caused by enemies—10.5.
O virtuous ones, [these are the signs] when there is drought everywhere, when stars fall from the sky,
when the image of the Blessed One laughs, when its limbs move,
when it weeps, or when the image wanders from its seat.

Whatever one performs for the sake of pacifying such events as the reversal of the moon and sun, or other similar occurrences, that is called *naimittika* (occasional rite). This is directed toward any one of the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) as its fruit.
The optional festival was performed, which bestows the fruits intended by one's resolve;
the preceptor, together with Brahmins skilled in the sciences of astrology, first determined the auspicious time and lunar mansion according to the scriptures. (10.9)
One should arrange the hoisting of the banner according to the procedure for a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā).
O lords of sages, at the very time of the consecration of the mantra-form,
the banner of the king of birds (the Garuda banner) is installed at the tip of the spire of the temple.
O twice-born ones, wherever the festival is always joined with the King of Weapons (hetirāja),
one should arrange the festival even without the hoisting of other banners; however,
if there is the means, one may also perform the hoisting of other banners there.
One should perform the festival elsewhere, preceded by the hoisting of the banner (dhvajārohaṇa).
A nine-day festival is declared to be divine; a seven-day one is middling;
and a five-day one should be known as inferior—thus the festival is remembered as being of three kinds.
In that regard, I shall first explain the sequence of rites for the nine-day festival.
On the day prior to the consecration of the banner, the preceptor, most skilled in mantras,
should bathe after first shaving his head, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice to the Blessed One.
When the onset of night had begun, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images,
performed his daily obligatory rites such as bathing according to the rules,
adorned himself with various ornaments and new garments.
Wearing a white turban and upper garment, adorned with variegated garlands,
and accompanied by the patron (yajamāna),
he enters the temple at the conclusion of the daily worship, [addressing] the best of the twice-born Vaiṣṇavas.
Having duly honored those who are devoted to the six duties and dedicated to the five times, and having received permission from them,
he should then worship Viṣvaksena for the pacification of obstacles to the sacrifice.
Thereafter, for the purpose of purifying his own body, the Guru should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
having prepared a seat of grain upon a pure surface according to the rules,
he should place an auspicious jar filled with scented water.
Adorned with jewels, gold, a brush, garlands, cloth, and sprouts,
and smeared with sandalwood paste and other substances, and sprinkled all around with *arghya* water—
one should station four guardians of the form (*mūrtipā*) in the four directions of that jar.
Having gratified all of them with water, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, sacrificial fees, and so forth, he should then invoke Sudarśana into the pitcher,
worship him thoroughly, and meditate upon Acyuta within his heart.
Touching the water-pot with *darbha* grass while together with the Brahmins,
the preceptor should cause them to recite the first four mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *pavitra*,
accompanied by the declaration of a meritorious day (*puṇyāha*) and joined with three repetitions of the *gāyatrī*.
Then, being thus composed, one should recite the self-praise (*ātmanuvāda*) and likewise the self-manifestation (*ātmavyūha*), as well as the purity-mantras (*śuddhimantra*):
"May the supreme deity Vāsudeva be for the sake of my purification. (10.27)
May Saṅkarṣaṇa be for the sake of purity, and may Pradyumna be for the sake of purity;
may Aniruddha also be for the sake of purity, and may Keśava be for the sake of purity;
may Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe, be for the sake of purity in all rites.
May Mādhava, who is devoted to the welfare of all worlds, be for our purification;
may Govinda, the eternal Supreme Self, be for our purification.
May the primordial Viṣṇu be for our purification, and may Madhusūdana be for our purification.
May the Lord Trivikrama, the benefactor of all the worlds, be for our purification.
May Vāmana be for our purification, and may Śrīdhara be for our purification today.
May Hṛṣīkeśa be for our purification, and may Padmanābha be for our purification.
May the divine Dāmodara, the Lord of the world, ever be for the sake of purification;
may Padmanābha be for the sake of purification, and may Dhruva ever be for the sake of purification.
May Ananta be for the sake of purification, and may the one whose self is Śakti be for the sake of purification.
May Madhusūdana be for the sake of purity in all rites;
likewise, may Kapila, the presiding deity of knowledge, always be for the sake of purity.
May Viśvarūpa be for the sake of purity, and may Vihaga be for the sake of purity.
May the Boar-natured Lord be for purification, and may the Horse-headed One (Aśvavaktra) be for purification;
may Dharma always be for purification, and likewise may the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśvara).
May the God who reclines upon the single ocean be for purification without interruption.
May the god Kūrma, the sustainer of the netherworld (pātāla), always be for the sake of purification.
May Varāha be for the sake of purification, and may Nārasiṃha be for the sake of purification;
and may he who brought back the nectar (amṛta) be for the sake of the purification of all actions.
May the Lord of Śrī be for purification; may the one of tranquil soul be for purification.
May the conqueror of Rāhu be for purification, and likewise the slayer of Kālanemi.
May the remover of the Pārijāta tree be for purification, and may the Lord of the World be for purification.
May the great lord Dattātreya be for the sake of purification everywhere.
May the Blessed One who reclines on the banyan tree be for the sake of purification at all times;
and may Vāmana, whose body has but a single horn, also be for the sake of purification.
May Trivikrama be for my purification; may Nara always be for my purification;

may Nārāyaṇa be for my purification; and may Hari and Kṛṣṇa be for my purification. May the wielder of the flaming axe, Pradyumna, be for my purification; may the wielder of the bow be for my purification.

And may the Lord Rāma, the knower of the Vedas, be for the sake of purification; thereafter, may Kalki, who brings about the destruction of all defects, always be for the sake of purification. May the Lord, the Master who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla), always be for the sake of purification.
May all these gods, when worshipped, always bring peace to everyone everywhere at all times for the sake of purification;
may they also lead to prosperity, nourishment, accomplishment, and devotion.
May they always lead to auspiciousness, liberation, and the increase of all undertakings—
namely, the mantras, the teachers, the sacred sites,
as well as sons, friends, wives, female and male servants, and cattle. || 10.46–10.47 ||
May there always be the attainment of the Vedas, scriptures, and traditions; of vows, desired prosperities, and all cherished aspirations that are beneficial.
May there be long life, health, intelligence, and the abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches.
Of merits such as the *aṇimā* powers and other qualities, as well as of blessings—
for the king, for the realm, for the patron, and for the ministers, and especially for the Vaiṣṇavas who desire the welfare of the hereafter— (10.49–50).
May there be well-being and auspiciousness for those who are purified by the five times, established in truth, and virtuous in nature; may there be prosperity again and again.
May there be freedom from obstacles at all times, and may there indeed be long life.

May the mind be composed, and may there be ever-increasing prosperity. May this be an auspicious day for purification; [I take refuge in] the forms of Vāsudeva and the others—the Lord of all lords, endowed with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.

May the blessed Lord, the wielder of the plow, be ever pleased; may Pradyumna be eternally pleased, as well as Aniruddha, the lord of the gods. May Nārāyaṇa, the lord of the gods, also be pleased for the fulfillment of all actions.

For the sake of pacifying any deficiencies or excesses, may the All-pervading Lord be pleased, may He be pleased! (10.55) Having proclaimed "Auspicious Day," "Welfare," and "Prosperity" together with the guardians of the images, [he should perform the rite] with those waters using the *śatadhāra* vessel and the *sthānāni* hymn and so forth. (10.56)
Thereafter, the preceptor should sprinkle himself for the sake of his own purification.
In this manner, he should perform the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) in all yogic rites.
Then, having attained purity through gifts of cows, gold, and other such things, the preceptor—

Having approached the presence of the deity and seated himself upon the throne, he should perform the purification of the elements through the concentrations (dhāraṇās). Then, with the mantras placed upon the body, he should perform the mental sacrifice.
Then, having worshipped the deity according to the ritual rules upon the mantra-seat,
one should lead him to the bathing-seat and bathe him with nine jars. Then,
for the purpose of the bath, [one should prepare] the ground in front of the deity according to the ritual rules.
O best of the twice-born, having divided the nine chambers into three groups,
having prepared the seats for the grains and so forth, and having consecrated the jars,
[one should offer] water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and likewise water containing all medicinal herbs.
One should place [the substances] in the four compartments starting from the east and ending in the north;
one should then place curd, milk, honey, and ghee in the directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
Immediately thereafter, one should place a pitcher of pure water in the center.
One should place a jar of turmeric powder before them;

having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle them with those waters from the jars placed in the directions starting from the east, in the order of their origin.

One should worship the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva in the pitchers located in the intermediate directions— from Īśāna to Agni— by means of their dissolution (apya-aya). In the center, in the pitcher of pure water, one should worship the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa.
O best of sages, one should worship the goddess Śrī with *arghya*, water for touching, flowers, and incense;

and within a jar of turmeric powder, one should worship her in sequence with the enjoyments prescribed for the bathing and seating rites, ending with the application of facial ointment. || 10.67–10.68 ||
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods, one should then bathe him with water-pots;
first with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī and then with the three-verse hymn beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," followed by the mantra beginning with "trīṇi padā" concerning the deeds of Viṣṇu.
One should bathe [the deity] in due order with water for the feet and other offerings placed in the directions starting from the east.
Then, one should use the mantra *dadhikrāvṇo* and the mantra *āpyāyasva*;
thereafter, one should use the mantra *madhu vātā* and the verse *śukram asi*.
One should bathe the Lord with jars placed in the intermediate directions containing curd and other substances;
then, one should smear the God with turmeric while reciting the Śrīsūkta.
After that, one should do so together with Brahmins chanting the Puruṣasūkta.
One should consecrate the deity with pure water from a vessel of a thousand streams. Having worshipped each substance with a cloth, with offerings of water (arghya), unguents, and garlands,
and having honored it with incense, one should then perform the consecration with that [water].

Or else, one should offer the arghya, the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and the food offering (naivedya); or indeed, offer everything as a single arghya alone.
Then, having performed the waving of lights (nīrājana) and other rites for the deity as before, [one should proceed].
Having brought the seat of ornaments, one should worship according to the sequence beginning with the seat,
honoring it duly with various enjoyments— both those involving touch and those consisting of ritual services— as previously described, and with those known as "heart-pleasing."
Having praised the Lord with hymns such as the *Jitantā*, the preceptor should prostrate before the All-pervading One.
Then, the preceptor, most skilled in mantras, should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
O best of sages, listen to its procedure in detail.
And there are three types of vessels for planting the auspicious sprouts,
distinguished as *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvas*. Now,
the height of the *pālikās* should be twenty-five finger-breadths.
The width of its mouth should indeed be sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula),
its height eight finger-breadths, and from that, the rim should be one finger-breadth. O Brahmins, the cavity of the throat should then be eight finger-breadths wide.
O twice-born ones, starting from the circle of the mouth up to the cavity of the throat,
one should gradually reduce that twelve-finger-width stalk;
it should be six finger-widths in diameter at its middle, measured both in height and in width.
Below [the neck], the width should be four finger-breadths;
from there, one should decrease it proportionally down to the opening of the throat.
The height of the footstool below should be known to be four finger-breadths.
Its width shall be ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and its joint shall be one finger-breadth;
O twice-born ones, the circumference of that joint shall be one and a half finger-breadths.

The face should have the form of a *unmatta* flower, and the shape of a lotus. The *ghaṭikās* are said to be equal in height to the *pālikā*, or else three finger-breadths less; above that, it has the shape of a jar (*kalaśa*).

The *ghaṭikās* should have five faces; their central face should be six *aṅgulas* wide, and there should be four [other faces] in the four directions. The width of the belly of the jar (*kalaśa*) should be four *aṅgulas*.
One should perform the remaining rites as previously described for that which measures sixteen finger-breadths;
however, when it is three finger-breadths less than that, then—
The height [of the face] is seven finger-breadths;
that face and its stalk are ten and a half finger-breadths.
The pedestal is three and a half finger-breadths; as before, this is the width in all cases.

O lords of sages, the shallow bowls (śarāva) should be equal in height to the pedestal (pālikā), measuring five finger-breadths; or they may be less than that, starting from the width of the mouth and decreasing gradually down to the width of the footstool (pādapīṭha). || 10.91-10.92 ||
In all cases, the width [of the pedestal] should be one-quarter less than that previously mentioned;
however, the width of the footstool (pādapīṭha) should be three-quarters less.
When the shallow bowls (śarāva) are deficient by five finger-breadths, then—
The mouth [of the vessel] should be six finger-breadths in height, and its neck ten finger-breadths.
The footstool should be three finger-breadths; the width in all cases is as previously stated.
O twice-born ones, this is declared to be the supreme measurement for vessels.
O best of sages, this very same [measurement], when reduced by one-quarter, is called the middle;
when reduced by half, that measurement is proclaimed as the lower.
Therefore, those who desire spiritual success should never construct anything smaller than this.
All [vessels] made of gold and other metals, or even those made of clay according to one's wealth—
for each of the *pālikā* and the others, twelve should be the best;
or, if one has the means, one should arrange thirty-two, which is twice eight.
For each *aṣṭaka*, there should be four of medium size, and four of inferior size.
For all purposes, the *pālikās* are as before—sixteen, eight, or according to one's capacity, or even four. Then, upon them, the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*) are arranged.
In rites for humans, the *pālikās* should be odd in number; in rites for the gods, they should be even.

This applies likewise during great festivals, at consecrations, during the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), in the procedure for restoring what is decayed, or at the rite of the thousand jars.
O best of the twice-born, it should consist of three groups, or perhaps five as the highest number, or even seven as the middle number; it should not be otherwise.
In all other rites, however, it should be according to one's wealth and according to one's inclination.
One should construct a pavilion for sowing the seeds of sprouts either in the first enclosure,
or in the second enclosure,
or in the third enclosure, or even in the fourth enclosure. || 10.103–10.104 ||
In an auspicious, secluded, and pleasing location, the supreme instructor [should prepare] a site with four gates and four rows of salutations in the four directions;
it should be encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass and adorned with strings of pearls.
It was covered with spread fine linen, its floor smeared with cow dung,
strewn everywhere with rows of lamps and unbroken grains of rice,
and its interior ground decorated with white lime powder.
Having thus prepared a pavilion, or else in the bathing pavilion,
or even in the pavilion called the sacrificial hall, one should perform the sowing of sprouts.
One who desires the increase of the kingdom should offer the sprouts at night.
Soma is the lord of seeds, the sovereign of plants, whose very nature is nectar.
If the sowing of the seed is performed during the day, he does not always grant satisfaction therein;
therefore, with every effort, the sowing of the seed should be done only at night.
One who is endowed with devotion to the Blessed One should perform [this rite] according to the correct procedure.
When that moon, beloved by the world and the life-sustainer of living beings, is pleased,
there shall be a great abundance of all crops in that region.
If one should, out of ignorance, sell sprouts during the day— whether for cows, the mothers of the world, or for human beings in every respect—
the kingdom will become ill-fated, filled with people lacking prosperity.
O Brahmins, for a rite performed at that very moment, it may even be during the day;
whatever is required there, all of that he should collect.
Having gathered all the necessary materials, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), [should proceed].
Having offered that for his sake, accompanied by the sacrificer,
and having worshipped you, the source of the world, according to the prescribed ritual,
he should then [place it] in a new vessel made of gold or silver.
Sesame, mustard, nīvāra, śāli rice, mung beans, priyaṅgu, horse gram, green gram, flat beans, barley, wheat, and bamboo seeds—
these twelve seeds, O twice-born ones, [should be placed] individually in separate vessels.
Having gathered [the materials], O best of sages, and having placed them upon his head,
the preceptor— holding a handful of flowers and unbroken rice grains in his joined palms— should enter together with the initiates who are absorbed in the Blessed One. || 10.118-10.119 ||
O Brahmins, one should place the seed-vessel upon its support inside the temple; then, having worshipped it with the arghya water, perfumes, flowers, and incenses,
[one worships] that which resides in the primary image as well as that which has entered the festival image.
Then, having worshipped the seed-vessel, one should present it to the deity,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs, auspicious songs,
various sounds of trumpets, and the chanting of Vedic hymns on all sides.
Having placed that vessel upon the head of the initiate himself,
O Brahmins, the preceptor, accompanied by the practitioners, goes outside,
circumambulates the temple, and should place it in the pavilion for the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Alternatively, having especially adorned Viṣvaksena, Tārkṣya, or those headed by Hanumān—
or even Hetīśa— with garments and other ornaments,
one should place them upon a vehicle or similar conveyance, and wash the spade with water.
Having clothed him in a new garment and adorned him with garlands,
O twice-born ones, the preceptor should have him carried by initiated Brahmins or Śūdras,
accompanied by variegated banners, flags, and vessels containing sprouts.
Together with three kinds of vessels and the like, along with conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments; accompanied by devotees of the Lord intent on proclaiming the sacred tradition,
by singers, courtesans, and likewise by other auspicious elements.

Having circumambulated them all in due order, including all the surrounding enclosures, and having reached a spot not far from there in that charming grove— either toward the east, the north, or the northeast— (10.129)
Or, in a purely clean place, he should collect pure clay.
First, the Guru, having sprinkled the earth with the Astra-mantra,
should touch it while reciting the Mahīsūkta, meditating with a one-pointed mind.
Having worshipped the earth with flowers after adoring the Varāha-form of the Lord,
and having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and honored with flowers,
one should dig the ground facing east while reciting the Krodha-mantra using a spade.
Having taken earth from a vessel made of iron or one made of cane, according to his preference,
and having wrapped it with a cloth using the root mantra,
he should likewise take fresh sand or cow dung from a river.
Having taken [the vessel] from Gokula as before, covered it with a cloth,
and placed it upon a vehicle or the like— or alternatively, upon the head of the initiated one—
he should go and circumambulate the village, and then enter the pavilion.
Having purified the pavilion according to the prescribed rite, O twice-born ones, one should then stretch out the lines within the pavilion in sequence;
first, one should cast seventeen lines extending toward the east in due order. (10.136–10.137)
One should lay down fourteen threads extending from north to south;
the distance between each thread should be measured at sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
There shall be exactly thirteen rows from east to west.

Thus, sixteen rows are numbered for the south and north. For the purpose of installing the seed-vessels, three rows should be established in the east and west; one should clear two [rows] in the middle for the sake of the central path.
Furthermore, one should establish three rows on both sides;
however, four rows should be established in the south, north, and middle.
One should then again clear away two by two on the sides for the sake of the central path (*vīthī*).
One should arrange four rows of four in sequential order.
In the eight directions and in the center, twelve bowls, jars, and small vessels each should be placed; thus, there will be one hundred and eight.
The *pālikās* are placed in the south-eastern, southern, and south-western [directions];
the *ghaṭikās* in the western, central (Brahma), and eastern directions;
and the *śarāvas* in the north-western, northern, and north-eastern directions, according to the rule.
Each of the *pālikā* vessels and so forth is prescribed to be sixteen [in number].
One should lay down five threads extending from south to north;
one should lay down the threads extending eastward as before.
O Brahmins, one should perform the arrangement of the rows facing east and west as before;
there, one should place sixteen *pālikās* in order within the four rows on the south side,
starting from the front in the middle of the four rows.
Having placed sixteen water-clocks (ghaṭikās), one should arrange them in the north. Then, for the twelve-fold arrangement, one should also place that same number of shallow bowls (śarāvas).
Here, one should cast four lines running from south to north. || 10.148–10.149 ||
One should lay out the preceding and following lines as before;
indeed, there will be forty-eight squares.
Having established twelve squares in the southern direction, one should then erase them.
Then, for the purpose of piercing, one should place six squares in the middle.
After that, one should eliminate twelve squares behind and six squares [in front].
Furthermore, twelve squares situated in the northern direction should be established in sequence.
One should place the *pālikā* vessels and the others in three sets of twelve parts,
starting from the southern direction and proceeding in order up to the northeast, from the southeast to the north.
This is done when calculating eight for each of the *pālikā* vessels and the others.
One should indeed apply three lines running from south to north.
All else should be as previously described, and one should likewise drop three lines running from east to west across each of the four groups of four squares.
One should lay down eleven threads for the east-west lines in the preparation of all the sixteen *pālikās* for every purpose.
Likewise, one should cast five southern threads and eastern threads.
From the previous sūtra, one should cast five [lines] and three lines for the eight [pots].
In the arrangement of twenty-four *pālikās*,
one should cast seven and five lines of the eastern and southern sūtras.
One should cast four [lines] for the enclosure, adding three and three [squares] each time;
the laying of the lines should be as before, starting from the first five numbers.
Having thus stretched the lines, one should divide them according to the extent of one's wealth.

In the various sections, one should fashion a pedestal (pīṭhikā) for the *pālikā* and other vessels, using *śāli* and *vrīhi* rice measured in *āḍhaka*s and so forth, as previously described, according to the distinction between the superior (*uttama*) and other grades; it may be circular or square, arranged in due order. || 10.160–10.161 ||
One should wash the vessels, such as the *pālikā* and others, with the root mantra,
together with *sahadevī*, *dūrvā*, and the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree,
as well as the sprouts of the *śirīṣa* and the leaves of the *niśā*.
Immediately thereafter, one should tie neck-threads (pālikās) and so forth around their necks.
One should fill the openings of their roots with kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and other blades of grass;
first the openings with clay, and subsequently with sand.
One should fill the cavity above with cow-dung powder,
or, O Brahmins, one may fill it by mixing all the materials such as clay and so forth.
One should then place those vessels, beginning with the *pālikā*, in their proper order within the compartments.
O best of the twice-born,

one should place nine out of the twelve [syllables] upon each shoulder, starting from the southeast (Āgneya) and ending with the northeast (Īśa), according to the prescribed sequence beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna, within the one hundred and eight [syllables]. || 10.166–10.167 ||
In the last of those places, upon a heap of grain,
one should place the jar of Soma, which possesses the auspicious marks, wrapped in a new cloth,
and provided with perfumes, all medicinal herbs, gems, a bundle of kusha grass, and young sprouts.
Having thus completed everything with the initiated attendants,
and having accomplished all those various tasks that were not previously acquired,
the preceptor, facing eastward, should then commence the rite upon the pedestal.
Having sat upon an auspicious seat to the west of the place for the water-jar,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the prescribed method and prepare the sprinkling water and the offering (*arghya*).
One should then perform the worship with the *arghya* and other offerings for the mantras placed upon the body.
Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers according to one's means and capacity,

the preceptor, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) according to the previously mentioned procedure, should worship the archways (*toraṇa*), the banners (*dhvaja*), and the pitchers at the doors.

Thereafter, one should worship the presiding deities of the *pālikās* and other vessels with offerings such as *arghya* and so forth. O Brahmins, one should worship them in sequence upon the three sections of the vessel's shoulder: the supreme Añjanābha, Padmanābha, and Dhruva.
In the group of twelve *pālikās*, [the deities] beginning with Vahni (Agni) and ending with Īśāna are in the west;
then, in the group of twelve *ghaṭikās*, the twelve beginning with Ananta;
and in the group of twelve *śarāvas*, the twelve beginning with Kūrma.
One should worship the twelve [deities] beginning with Ekaśṛṅga in sequence,
for each of the sixteen arrangements starting with the *pālikā*.
And [one should worship] the thirty-six [deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Pātālaśayana.
One should worship the twelve Śaktis, beginning with Lakṣmī and ending with Mati.
When arranging the thirty-six [deities] for each of the Pālikās and so forth,
there is a group of four Mūrtis situated in the stage called Svapna.
Through the yoga of origin and dissolution, there is the waking form consisting of eight; likewise,
the twelvefold group of other forms, the thirty-four [forms] of the Śaktis,
and the thirty-six beginning with Ananta and ending with Pātālaśayana.
And one should worship the thirty-four powers beginning with Svadhā,
followed by the Discus and the Conch, in sequence, with offerings such as water for honor (*arghya*), perfumes (*gandha*), and so forth;
and in the eight [petals], one should worship Keśava and the others, along with their respective powers.
In the fourfold [arrangement], one should worship Keśava and the others alone;
for all purposes, however, one should worship sixteen [deities] in the pitchers (pālikā) in sequence:
the four beginning with Vāsudeva and the twelve beginning with Keśava.
In the group of eight, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others according to the sequence of their manifestation and dissolution;
in the group of four, however, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the order of their origin.
Having worshipped in this manner, one should then perform the ritual worship of the Soma-vessel.
One should worship the god who is of the nature of Soma in the large jar (kumbha), and Sudarśana in the small vessel (karaka);
and one should worship Indra and the other deities in the jars placed in the eight directions.
Having thus performed the worship of the jars, one should perform the washing of the seed-syllables (bīja).
O twice-born ones, having properly worshipped the seeds with cow’s milk using the root mantra,
and having honored them individually with their respective names in the dative case along with offerings such as *arghya*, one should then wrap them in a cloth.
Having established the fire according to the rules in either a fire-pit or on a sacrificial mound,
and having performed the satiation of the fire, one should arrange the seat for the mantra and so forth within it;
then, having invoked the deity into its center as before, [one should proceed].
One should perform all the preliminary rites, such as the preparation of the site and so forth, exactly as before.
Then, one should offer oblations with the perpetual fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and those intended for specific desires (*kāmya*),
using the mantras of the presiding deities of the *pālikā* vessels and other items, in their proper sequence.
The twice-born should offer eight, four, or even just one oblation of clarified butter;
having offered with the mantras beginning with "Soma," they should collect the residual drops of the ghee.
This may be the ghee remaining from the offering, or another that has been consecrated.
Taking a vessel made of iron or clay according to his preference,
and grasping a blade of dūrvā grass by its root with both hands,
he should dip the tips into clarified butter and sprinkle them into the *pālikā* vessels and other containers.
By the path of transposing the hands, from Agni to Īśāna and then to the West;
for each shoulder, the application of ghee is proclaimed to be a distinct type of *dūrvā*.
Having performed the application of ghee in this manner, [one honors] the presiding deities of the shoulders once again.
Having worshipped all the seeds, he should consecrate them with the root mantra (10.196).
Having obtained permission from the preceptor and others, the lord of teachers, facing north or east,
should [place them] in the *pālikā* vessels and so forth during an auspicious moment (10.197).
O twice-born ones, one should sow all the seeds with the eight-syllable mantra, or with the *jita* mantra ending in *-tā*, or indeed with both. This should be done in sequence,
branch by branch, starting from the southeast and extending to the northeast.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, drums, and cries of victory,
one should sow the twelve seeds in sequence upon the twelve [squares];
or else, having mixed them all together, one may sow them according to one's desire.
But if even seeds cannot be obtained, one should sow a single mung bean;
other teachers, preceptors, and practitioners who follow the master should sow it while joined with meditation, or the master alone may do so.
O Brahmins, the preeminent teacher should sprinkle [the image] many times in sequence with water mixed with turmeric powder and scented with flowers; then,
above each section (skandha), he should [visualize it] as being situated within the orb of the moon.
Having meditated upon the deity, who resembles that splendor and is incessantly sprinkling the seeds sown on all sides with floods of nectar arising from his own body,
one should worship him with new, flawless, and auspicious vessels.

Having covered [the deity] with garments, one should worship Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, above all [the others] in successive order for each shoulder. O best of the twice-born, one should offer a bali-oblation of meat to the spirits in the eight directions.
From that time forward, all those beings— Kumuda and the others— protect, according to the sequence starting from the east,
the teachers, the elders, the preceptors, and the Vaiṣṇava practitioners. (10.207)
The diligent patron should satisfy the preceptor with abundant betel leaves, flowers, fruits, and wealth; then,
having gradually lifted all those [images], he should place them in a well-protected location.
Either in the northeast corner of the pavilion or in another place according to one's preference;
there too, around the *pālikā* vessels and so forth, in the eight directions starting from the east (Indra’s direction) in due order,
[one should place] the *bhūta*s, such as Kumuda and the others.
One should present the bali offering in the pavilion according to the ritual for the Bhūtas and Krūra deities.
One should illuminate many lamps around the area so that they do not go out. To pacify any deficiency or excess, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations.

Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* and other rites according to the rule, the preeminent teacher then dismisses the deity who resides in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) into the interior of his own heart; thereafter,
he likewise [dismisses] the presiding deities of the four gates with their respective mantras in due order.

Then, having offered oblations with clarified butter, he should dismiss the fire according to the prescribed rule. Around the *pālikās* and other vessels, he should offer a *bali* offering separately every night, either during the day or at night, or even at both times.
On the day of the ritual, the best of preceptors should offer the bali offering in the morning;
from the moment the seeds have been sown,
no one whatsoever should enter there or touch anything in any way.
Only the teacher or his disciple, being composed in mind, should enter.
One should avoid all things such as food remnants from afar;
and without having offered some *bali* oblation, one should not perform the rite of the *pālikās*.
One should sprinkle the sprouts with water infused with turmeric for their growth.
O best of sages, one should diligently avoid those sprouts that are dark, red, black, or growing horizontally, as well as those that have not yet fully developed.
In the case of dark [spots], there shall be loss of wealth; in red ones, there will be quarrel.
In black ones, there is mental anguish, and for one who is ill, it occurs when they are situated on the side of the body.
If they are not fully developed, death shall occur therein; of this there is no doubt.
If the [lines] are auspicious, yellow, white, straight, and upward-pointing,
there shall be the attainment of all prosperity for both the performer and the one who causes it to be performed.
The Guru, at the outset, should plant the sprouts for the sake of the ritual action.
He alone, and no other, should perform the rite in its entirety, even if he is wise;
or else, with his permission, his son or his disciple may perform it.
In this manner, the planting of the sprouts shall take place in all sacrifices.
Having understood the place, the time, as well as the wealth and one's own capacity,
and having duly reflected upon everything that has been prescribed, one should perform the primary rite.
Having thus performed the sowing of the seeds, one should go into the presence of the deity.

Having worshipped the deity with the *arghya* and other offerings according to the ritual procedure up to the presentation of food (*naivedya*), one should complete the remainder of the night like a lamp that is not extinguished. On the following day at dawn, one should fetch the cloth for the banner (*dhvaja*).
One should obtain, according to one's means, either a new and beautiful *dukūla* cloth,
a divine *paṭṭa* garment, or even a variegated linen (*citrakṣauma*),
or else a cotton cloth that is free from blue wool and other such defects. (10.228)
A cloth that is well-characterized, firm, and smooth is said here to be "measured.
It should be nine, seven, or five cubits in length; its measurement should be equal to the height of the principal image (mūlabera) or the height of the doorway. || 10.229–230 ||
It is as wide as half its length, with its crest formed by one-fourth;
the tail is equal to the crest, and the ear-tail is half of that.
The cloth for the banner known as "hair" is measured according to the standard of the "cloth."
The width should be equal to that of a cloth, and the pinnacle should be as described previously.
Having washed, bleached, dried, and ensured it possesses the proper characteristics, the wise man should have the cloth decorated by a truly skilled artisan.
One should place a parasol at the summit and white fly-whisks on both sides;
below that, a multi-petaled lotus, and beneath that, a full water-vessel (pūrṇakumbha).
On the sides of the vessel, one should depict a group of flower-pots (pālikā) along with sprouts.
One should place two beautiful lamps on either side of the *pālikās*.
O best of men, for the single-formed [deity], the banner should be in the shape of Garuḍa;
for the fourfold self, they are Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya.
Of the five-fold form (pañcamūrti), however, four are joined with the Lord of Birds (Vihageśvara); or for the Four-Selfed One (Caturātman), they are Suparṇa, Tāla, Makara, and Ṛśya.
Above that, for all the emanations (vyūhas), Garuḍa is the banner.
On the center of the cloth, however, one should depict Garuḍa with two arms, his hands joined in the añjali gesture;
or else, with his palms cupped in a handful of flowers, resembling a mountain of gold,
moving through the sky, and endowed with the effortless flapping of his wings.
His left foot was drawn in while his right stood behind;
his eyes were slightly elongated and round, and his nose had a long, dark tip. He wore an exceedingly peaceful garb and possessed a smiling countenance.
Having a form like the young moon, adorned with two fangs,
with a curved knitting of the eyebrows, beautified by curling locks of hair,
with a neck like a conch shell, large arms, a stout body, and a firm chest.
With a broad belly, a deep navel, and adorned with a line of body hair;
endowed with a pair of thighs as thick as well-rounded golden pillars;
with shanks like golden plantain trees and two beautiful feet.
His head was adorned with a flower-garland resting upon a crown-shaped hair-ornament;
his eyes were round and wide like lotus petals;
his pair of eyebrows rose like the arching mane of a lion; and the tip of his nose was shaped like the beak of a parrot.
The middle part is like a lion's [mane], while its lineage is like the back of an elephant;
thus, by the long reach of destiny, it is expanded like the wings of a swan.
Its tail, possessing hundreds of branches, is characterized by qualities such as the measure of its own wings.
Now, that which is common to all and is called the "particular" is described:

[the body] from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet, adorned with various jewels, and embellished with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and the sacred thread (brahmasūtra). || 10.247–10.248 ||
With beautiful earrings resting within the loops of his long, pendulous ears;
adorned with a tilaka on his forehead and flower-ear-ornaments;
wearing jeweled rings and having his feet colored by the girdle-string.
Adorned with other divine ornaments and decorated with snakes,
he wore blue garments and shone with a blue breast-cloth;
his neck was embellished with garlands of blossoming red lotus petals.
Likewise, he is radiant with other various flower garlands;
Ananta is his left bracelet, while Vāsuki is his sacred thread (yajñasūtra).
Takṣaka is his waist-band, and Kārkoṭaka is his necklace.
Padma is on the right ear, while Mahāpadma is on the left;
Śaṅkha is on the region of the head, and Gulika is between the arms.
He is adorned by these eight foremost serpents, the best of nāgas.
Ananta has the luster of white; Vāsuki is red in color;
Takṣaka has the luster of yellow; Kārkoṭaka is likewise smoky gray;
Śaṅkha has the luster of frost; and Gulika is like the color of a bee.
Padma is the color of a lotus, while Mahāpadma is tawny;
one should thus draw the god with five colors, as well as his five weapons:
the discus with its beautiful rim, the arrow, the conch, the Śārṅga bow, and the mace.
Above the cloth, one should indeed draw on both sides according to the prescribed rule;
below that, on the right side, one should draw the circle of fire (vahni-maṇḍala).
Likewise, on the left side, one should draw the sign of the svastika, endowed with its characteristic marks.
One should have the remainder of the cloth coated with dark green or black pigment,
adorned with various flowers and provided with leafy creepers;
thus should the best of artists have it executed by the supreme master of the directions.

Or, O best of the twice-born, a consecrated Śūdra may do so according to the rules; or else, the mantra-practitioner should have it made by a skilled potter. Having thus completed everything, the preceptor, being well-composed, [should proceed].
When evening has arrived, accompanied by those who bear his forms,
he should enter the artisan’s workshop; then, having gratified the craftsman and taken that cloth, he should place it upon the head of the disciple.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, as well as the blare of trumpets,
various songs, and diverse vocal resonances,
one should bring the banner-cloth from there into the front pavilion.
Having entered the interior and saluted the Supreme Lord residing in the primary image,
one should worship him with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), perfumes, and so forth, as well as with flowers and incense.
Afterwards, having dismissed the artisan, one should sprinkle [the image] with the water from the *arghya* vessel.

[He should prepare] a cloth [painting]. 10.266 The best of practitioners should strike it with flowers accompanied by white mustard seeds while reciting the *astra* mantra, and he should show it face-to-face to the God of Gods. 10.267
One should perform the acts of burning and nourishing according to the ritual procedure;
then, having worshipped the Supreme Lord again with water for honor, perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
one should recite this mantra with palms joined in reverence while ascending the mountain peak.
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, Lord of all, who pervades the universe!
(10.269) It is not possible for me to act exactly as you have instructed, due to a lack of independence, a lack of capability, and the absence of faith and other such qualities. (10.270)
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying all [defects] such as pride, whether deficient or excessive, look with your two cool eyes at [the image of] Garuḍa situated upon the cloth;
O gracious one, [look] with those [eyes] which remove all faults! Oṃ.
Then, having placed that cloth in the hands of the initiated brahmins,
the preceptor, having circumambulated it four times together with them,
[should place it] either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure.
The sacrificer should enter the pavilion situated at the top of the palace;
having placed a *bhadrapīṭha* there, he should construct an altar with rice grains (*śāli-taṇḍula*) upon it,
and on its surface, he should draw the mandala named *bhadraka*.
When there is sufficient wealth, one should spread out a cloth and scatter a heap of sesame seeds upon it; in the center of that, one should draw a svastika.
Upon that, one should place the painting facing toward the temple.
Having sat upon his seat, the preceptor, being well-composed, should perform everything previously described— beginning with the purification of the hands and ending with the worship of his own body—
using the Khageśa mantra together with its ancillaries.
One should perform the worship of the door-keepers, the archway, the water-pots, and so forth, as before.
Then, O twice-born ones, one should cause the proclamation of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) to be made as previously done;
and in front of Garuḍa, as before, one should place the water-pot together with the ritual vessel (karaka).
One should place a vessel such as a wooden water-tub, well-filled with fragrant water, upon a grain-mat prepared merely for the sake of support. Then,
one should set it down there to the right of the water-pot.
One should immediately perform the consecration by shadow of Garuḍa;
then, one should perform the ritual bathing according to the lowest-of-the-low method,
while [the image] is situated upon the altar in front of Vainateya.

Thereafter, at an auspicious hour, the Guru should perform the opening of the eyes of all the serpents according to the procedure to be described. (10.283) He should carry out the opening of the eyes for every one of them.
But once his body has been thoroughly purified as before, the artisan should bring it forth into manifestation.
He should perform everything according to the rules, beginning with the filling of the eyes,
having prepared the seat for both the *kumbha* and the *karaka*.
Having invoked Garuḍa into the pitcher and the Astra-mantra into the water-pot,

and having worshipped them with offerings such as *arghya* and *gandha*, one should then worship Indra and the other world-protectors in the eight directional pitchers, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Having sprinkled the wall and once again established [the deity] there,
one should then, as before, prepare a seat upon the banner-cloth (dhvajapaṭa);
then [one should recite] the Garuḍa-mantra, radiant as a thousand suns.
It pacifies all diseases, destroys all calamities,
bestows all perfections upon men, and eliminates all poverty.
O best of Brahmins, having drawn [the mantra] from the heart, one should place it upon Garuḍa depicted on the cloth.

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa, one should effect the presence (sannidhi). O best of the twice-born, one should likewise perform the complete confinement (sannirodha), the facing [of the deity] (sāṃmukhya), the binding of mudrās, as well as the sacrifice of absorption (layayāga) and the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga) according to the rules.
One should perform everything with the Garuḍa mantra along with its ancillaries,
according to the sequential method for the water-pot, the small vessel, and the cloth;
one should perform the worship with great magnificence.
O Brahmins, having performed the worship of Garuḍa up to the ornaments and the throne according to the stated sequence, thereafter,
within the temple, with the permission of the preceptor, O Brahmins— || 10.293–10.294 ||
One should properly cause the worship to be performed by another preceptor or by a distinguished practitioner for the primary image,
as well as for the Lord’s processional image, up until the conclusion of the distribution of gifts.
Then, for the sake of Vainateya, [the offerings] were presented with various foods preceded by seats and food, including diverse *madhuparka* preparations, heart-pleasing fruits and roots,
and other exceedingly abundant and manifold varieties.
Having worshipped with offerings and performed the recitation (japa) at the end according to the sequence as before,
one should separately perform the distribution of gifts to the artisans according to the rule.
Then, one should give what was offered to the mantra-weapons and the water-pot to the preceptors.
Having taken some of the food offering (naivedya) from the vessel, even that which pertains to the deity on the cloth-painting (paṭa),
the Preceptor himself should take it and indeed offer it to the Guru and others;
this applies also to the deity residing in the primary image (mūlabimba) and the one residing in the processional image (yātrābimba).

Having presented the food offering (naivedya) to the God with honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other substances, one should cause it to be given to the preceptor (deśika) and others; thereafter, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa).
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics in the eastern part of Garuḍa’s [temple], [one should proceed].
There, having consecrated the fire and invoked the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa),

one should offer seven pieces of sacrificial wood; then, for the sake of pacification, having offered sesame seeds and clarified butter one hundred and eight oblations, one should present the final full oblation.

Or else, the preceptor should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in an occasion-specific sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Having thus performed the consecration of the banner (dhvajādhivāsa), he should proceed to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
Then, O lords of sages, he should perform the binding of the protection-thread (rakṣābandha) according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped the deity residing in the primary image with water for honor (arghya) and other offerings,
and having placed his hands at the deity's feet, he should address the deity thus:
"O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, I shall perform the rite of the marriage-thread (kautuka)."
"O Lord of Gods, for the sake of the great festival, be gracious to me for that purpose.
Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, he invoked him into the festive image,
worshipped him with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), perfumes, and so forth, and with various auspicious garments.
Having especially adorned it with ornaments and divine fragrances,
and having placed it upon a golden vehicle accompanied by conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments,
and provided with parasols and other regalia, [he should proceed] in a clockwise direction.

Having led him to the assembly pavilion and seated him according to the prescribed ritual upon a golden auspicious throne, which was adorned above with pearl canopies and other ornaments, and provided with all necessary implements; || 10.310 ||
Having worshipped the Lord of the World and offered abundant food,
and having completed the concluding rites of satiation, one should cause him to enter the temple;
then, one should bring forward a vessel made of gold or silver.
O Brahmins, it should be well-filled with *śāli* rice— either a full *bhāra*,
or half of that, or a quarter, or a sixth, or even an eighth part.
Above that, there should be a cord made of gold, or of linen, or of cotton.
Having placed a cloth made of silk, woven with five, four, or seven threads,
and having set down a vessel containing betel together with the other items,
one should then place that vessel upon a seat prepared with rice grains in the inner pavilion.
On a pedestal made of rice, measuring one *bhāra* or half of that,
one should place [the vessel] in another container together with cakes;
having worshipped it properly with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should cover it completely with a cloth.
O twice-born ones, having placed two vessels upon the heads of the two initiated [disciples], or having established them upon a vehicle or similar object according to his means, the preceptor,
accompanied by those two vessels and joined with dance, song, and other such arts— || 10.317–10.318 ||
Having performed circumambulation around all the enclosures,
or four times around even a single one, or having performed circumambulation around the village and so forth once, O Brahmins, he should then enter the root temple.
Or, O twice-born ones, having mounted upon a vehicle such as the Sudarśana, or Viṣvaksena,
or the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), or Hanumān accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa,
one should cause it to be paraded according to one's desire.
Then, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhageha) into the presence of the God of gods,
one should place two vessels upon the support (ādhāra) and worship them with the eight-syllable mantra, as well as with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, and other articles.
Having made the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-ghoṣa*), one should worship the deity with offerings such as the *arghya* and so forth.
Then, having performed the rite of the protective cord (*pratisara*) and having perfumed it with fragrant scents and incense,
[one should first offer it] to the primary form of the God of Gods who resides within the root image.

One should bind the *kautuka* with threads made of gold or of silk; having taken a golden thread, one should anoint it with fragrance and bind it upon the right hand of the deity who has entered the processional image.

Having touched the thread with the right hand while reciting the mantra known as *jitaṃta* accompanied by the sounding of conchs and songs, one should mutter the weapon-mantra (*astra*) one hundred times.
One should then place the auspicious knot upon the left hand using a silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*).
O best of the twice-born, while reciting the Śrīsūkta or its mantra,
one should tie a protective amulet (kautuka) on the left hand for the sake of nourishment using a linen thread;
one should also perform the tying of the bathing image with a silk thread.
Having thus performed the rite of *kautuka* for the images of the deities and so forth,
the preeminent teacher should then bind the *kautuka* on his own right hand with cotton while reciting the root mantra. || 10.329–10.330 ||
In the same manner, one should sequentially tie the *kautuka* for the performers of the ritual.
If resources permit, the thread for all of them should be made of gold.
Having worshipped the deity with the *arghya* offering and other rites, one should present cakes and other such offerings.
Then, having offered betel leaves and other items, he should satisfy the twice-born with betel;
likewise the initiated Vaiṣṇavas led by the preeminent teacher (deśikendra).
The preceptor himself should take for that purpose rice and other such offerings.
In this manner, the tying of the *kautuka* (protective thread) should be performed in all sacrifices.
Having thus performed the binding of the protection (*rakṣābandha*), one should conclude the remainder of the night.
Then, at dawn, the most excellent preceptor, having bathed well and sipped water for purification, [should proceed].
Having performed the daily worship of the Lord as well as the special sacrifice,
one should then worship Vainateya and the [deities] beginning with Kumbha according to the rules;
then, having offered the great oblation and performed the fire-sacrifice (homa) as before.
Then the most excellent preceptor should perform the installation of the flagstaff (dhvajastambha),
either in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) or in the second enclosure and so forth;
he should install the supreme staff either inside or outside the gateway (gopura).
Alternatively, O lords of sages, one should construct the pedestal for the banner (dhvajapīṭha) either in front of the pedestal for the offerings (balipīṭha) or behind it;
the distance between these two should be made one cubit (hasta) or even one palm-span (tāla).
O twice-born ones, one should lay down the flagstaff, together with the flagpole, either to the north of the pedestal of the banner or in the eastern direction;
it should have its tip pointing east or north, be endowed with auspicious marks, and be very beautiful.

A tree is of three kinds: having internal essence, having external essence, or being without essence. (10.341) O Lords of Sages, sandalwood and the like are trees with internal essence and are praised for the construction of pillars; betel-nut trees and the like have external essence, and they too are praised. (10.342)
One should avoid wood that is sapless, such as that of the *kiṃśuka* tree, for the work of making a staff.
[The ideal wood] should be fresh, straight, smooth, free from cracks at the ends,
have an odd number of joints, be oily, possess its bark, and be well-stable.
One should have the flagstaff erected after examining it according to the perspective of the scriptures;
it should be one hundred *tālas* at most, or even twenty less,
or measuring sixty *tālas*, according to the measurement of the *mānāṅgula*.
One may also determine the measurement by means of finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*),
whether it be the height of the pinnacle at the top of the temple, or the height of the temple itself;
or one may determine the height of the corner-tower or the height of the gatehouse according to one's capacity.

One should divide the pillar into four parts; the capital (mastaka) shall consist of exactly one part. Then, the three pedestals (pīṭha), which serve as its support and are perforated at their three bases, are to be fixed upon the top of the pillar.
One should join the flagstaff through the two holes at the top of the pedestal;
above that, one should bind a handful of *darbha* grass together with a bell.
One should wrap the flagpole with garlands of *darbha* grass in a clockwise direction.
Having done this, one should sprinkle the flagstaff with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra.
Into the pit situated at the base of the flagpole, the preceptor should deposit gems and grains,
accompanied by the *tārkṣya* mantra and the most excellent Brāhmaṇas.
O Brahmins, having been consecrated by Śūdras, or even by temple-servants (devadāsa),
one should place the flagstaff upright in that pit, accompanied by the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, as well as songs and instrumental music.

Having placed it facing the temple, one should fill it with sand so that it becomes very firm by means of hands, feet, and other such efforts. At the base of the pillar, one should construct an altar five cubits high.
One should construct it as three cubits high, or even one cubit high,
and with the same dimensions in width, making it square.
Above that, in the middle, there should be a lotus endowed with eight petals.
Just as a pillar stands upon its capital, so should the wise one act.

Then, having entered the interior of the temple, he should worship the Lord residing in the primary image with offerings of water, fragrance, and other articles; thereafter, [he should perform the rites] for the festival image.
Then, having invoked him along with the two goddesses,
and having worshipped the Lord of the World and offered the two sandals,
he subsequently placed him upon a vehicle endowed with golden luster.
In this very manner, having performed the worship with offerings,
the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should proceed to the presence of Garuḍa;
having mounted the banner with care upon a chariot, an elephant, or a vehicle.
One should adorn the banner with a garland made of variegated flowers and its radiance;
one should further adorn it with garments, ornaments, and diverse wreaths.
Then, one should provide it with parasols, chowries, and peacock-feather fans.
With variegated palm-leaf fans and enchanting parasols,
with diverse flagstaffs adorned with fine silk cloths,
and accompanied by the loud chanting of the four Vedas along with the sounds of hymns of praise.
With various songs and musical instruments, with the sounds of conchs and trumpets,
with the resonance of kettledrums, clay drums, and other auspicious sounds,
and with groups of Brahmins carrying clusters of pots containing sprouting seeds.
Accompanied by groups of well-dressed courtesans and always with devoted followers,
[they marched] with shouts of "Ha! and slapping sounds, joined by cries of "Victory!",
placing the image of the Lord at the front, with a banner-cloth in the center.
Thereafter, one should gradually carry the procession image around,
starting from the first enclosure up to the western side of the street enclosure;
having preceded it with the offering of oblations, one should perform the circumambulation of the village.
Thereafter, he should lead the procession image to the assembly pavilion;
having seated it upon a golden throne facing the base of the banner,
the preceptor, together with the guardians of the forms, takes up the Garuḍa-banner.
Accompanied by the sounding of conchs and other instruments, having brought the flag-pedestal around in a clockwise direction according to the yoga, one should wash the pillar with pure water;
and if resources permit, one should wrap the flag-staff with a cloth.
Then, having taken a very firm rope made from triple-stranded cotton threads,
the best of teachers subsequently fastened it to the apparatus situated at the tip of the staff.
Then, O brahmins, one should fasten the top of the banner very firmly;
together with all his attendants, he should take his place beside the pitcher. Having lifted that pitcher up, he should place it upon the head of the disciple.
And he should have the "Eight Verses on Non-apprehension" recited together with the Brahmins.
Then the preceptor, taking the *vardhanī* vessel in his own hand,
should pour it with an unbroken stream, preceded by the sound of musical instruments.
Having circumambulated the temple, one should take refuge at the base of a pillar;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, one should indeed consecrate the banner with the *astra* mantra.
One should worship Garuḍa as depicted on the cloth using the very mantra of Garuḍa.
Then one should offer water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), perfume, garlands, and incense;
furthermore, cakes, flattened rice, drinks, and refreshing refreshments.
Immediately thereafter, having offered water for rinsing the mouth mixed with coconut water,
and having given excellent betel-leaf prepared with camphor and other ingredients,
one should then display that mudrā while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
Then, having sprinkled Garuḍa with the water from the great pitcher,
one should place the Garuḍa residing in the great pitcher onto the cloth-painting.
With the eight subsidiary pitchers, one should likewise [place] the eight nāgas in their proper order.
In the same manner, it is said for weapons with water from the *karakāstra*;
having thus sprinkled [the objects] in sequence, the best of preceptors then performs the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth, preceded by an offering of handfuls of flowers.
One should perform the acts of bringing near, restraining, and facing [the deity];
then, having worshipped with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should present many sacrificial gifts (*upahāra*).
Having offered mung beans and the like, one should then offer betel leaves and other items.
With palms joined in reverence, the preceptor should praise Garuḍa with hymns for the sake of becoming the vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu: "Obeisance to you, O Tārkṣya of immeasurable splendor,
to Garuḍa, the death of all the lords of serpents."
Homage, homage to you, O Lord of Birds; homage to you whose body is sacred study!
O King of Birds, homage be to you, who have uprooted the world-destroying age!
Homage to the one who brought back the jar of nectar and liberated his mother from servitude.
Salutations to You, the conqueror of the lords of gods and asuras, who are adorned by the lord of serpents;
salutations to You, whose support is that upon which all this rests.
You, whose two wings are the Bṛhat-sāman and the Rathantara—these two.
The two eyes are the Gāyatrī, and the Trivṛt-sāman is remembered as the head;
the Stoma is the self—homage to that perfection of limbs consisting of the Vāmadevya.
Salutations to Garuḍa, the lord of the vital breaths and other winds!
Drive away all defects without exception and bring forth virtues from every side.
Destroy all obstacles and make even me your own.
Having thus offered praise, he should cause [the disciple] to hear the Bṛhatsāman and the Rathantara;
at that time, the preeminent teacher, meditating on the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and being a knower of mantras, should consume the food offering while reciting the mantra.
By means of human and Gāruḍa mantras, one should cast [the medicinal substances] into the cupped hands of even barren women, while meditating upon Garuḍa and Acyuta Hari;
having consumed these balls, the women shall give birth to many sons.

Then, having honored the astrologer at the head of Garuḍa with betel leaves, perfumes, and garlands, and having obtained an auspicious moment, he performed the ceremony at a favorable hour and a propitious conjunction,
preceded by benedictions.
Accompanied by the sound of bells, drums, and the noise of all musical instruments,
one should carefully cause the rope to ascend with the mantra "Suparṇo 'si" (You are Suparṇa). Then, one should fasten the rope to the pillar in a clockwise direction.
One should place the Garuda-banner upon a pillar facing the temple.
Whether in the forenoon or at midday, the great hoisting of the banner takes place;
thereafter, the preceptor, having placed the processional image upon the vehicle, [proceeds].
Having led [the image] near the flagstaff,
he should show the flag to the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) for the purpose of summoning all the devotees;
having thus appointed him, the deity should thereafter proceed to the site of the pavilion.
Then, one should pray for the presence [of the deity] within the interior of Garuḍa’s banner:
"O Lord of Birds, from this day until the final day of the festival, remain present here for the sake of the king and his realm."

For the satisfaction and nourishment of the village, of the sacrificer, and especially of the Vaiṣṇavas, and for victory over all enemies, and for the sake of overcoming untimely death— O Vainateya, be gracious! Om!
Having thus addressed the Lord of Birds, one should scatter a handful of flowers.
Having gone into the presence of the God of Gods, one should cast a handful of flowers, saying:
"Whether through knowledge or ignorance, that which was prescribed has not been performed by me."
May all that be fulfilled; may you always be well-satisfied.
Om! Acyuta, Lord of the World, embodiment of mantra, Janārdana!
Protect me, O Lotus-eyed One; forgive me today, be gracious, Om!

Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, the omnipresent one who had assumed the form for the procession, they led him to another pavilion; there, after performing special worship and offering abundant food,
they performed everything up to the final oblation.
Having constructed it according to the proper sequence, one should cause [the image] to enter the temple.
One should fashion a water-shed (*prapā*) above the pedestal of the banner, provided with four pillars;
or else, it may be devoid of eight pillars and endowed with sixteen pillars.
It should be provided with four archways, adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass,
decorated with banners and the like on the outside, and enclosed by a curtain;
one should light lamps there on all sides so that they remain unextinguished.
Starting from that day until the end of the day of the flower-sacrifice,

one should perform worship at the three junctions of the day with special care, accompanied by recitation. At the time of the offering, one should present the oblation for this [deity] every single day.
Thus has the daytime ritual ending with the hoisting of the banner been described.
Thus ends [the chapter] titled "The Procedure for the Great Festival Ending with the Hoisting of the Banner" in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
The Tenth Chapter;
now the Eleventh Chapter: Nārada.
When the onset of night has arrived, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images,
having performed his daily obligatory rites such as bathing according to the prescribed rule,
should go into the presence of the deity and perform the daily worship.
Having led the deity, who has assumed his processional form and is accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi,
to the pavilion of the assembly hall, one should place him upon the bathing seat.
Then follows the bathing ritual, whether inferior or superior, which is about to be described.
With that, one should bathe the deity with full elaboration according to one's means;
having worshipped him on the ornamented throne with supremely purifying offerings,
one should then present abundant food-offerings (naivedya) in due order.
Having concluded the recitation, one should perform the striking of the drum (bherī). Then,
the preceptor, having sat upon a seat to the right side of the deity,
should proceed to the front of the Lord of Devas for the purpose of installing the drum.
Having recited the *caraṇam pavitram* mantra and washed the ground with water,
the preceptor should sweep it with *darbha* grass while reciting the *viṣṇorarāṭa* mantra; then,
he should smear it with cow dung while reciting the *gandhadvārā* mantra.
One should perform the decoration with sudhā powder while reciting the *āpa undantu* mantra.
One should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) on the ground while reciting the *devasya tvā* mantra.
One should prepare a seat of grain while reciting the *grīṣmo hemanta* mantra.
With the mantra "devasya tvā," one should surround [the area] with upright *darbha* grass;
