with the mantra "śanno devī," one should place a hundred-petaled lotus in the four directions;
and with the mantra "trātāram indram," one should draw a lotus in the center. || 11.10 ||
One should spread darbha grass upwards with the mantra "dhananāgeti";
then one should pay homage to the earth with the mantra "mūrdhānam".
There, one should place four lamps in the four corners.

Then the best of preceptors should cause the *svasti* and *puṇyāha* rites to be recited. With those waters, he should sprinkle the drum with the mantra "āpa undantu," and with the "agnir āyuṣmān" mantra, he should sprinkle all the musical instruments.
With the mantra "To Aryaman," one should place the drum upon a seat of grain; to its east, a collection of conch shells, and in the southeast,
a multitude of kāhala trumpets.
In the south, however, a mardala drum; in the direction of the Yātus (the northwest), a lute together with a flute;
in the west, a mṛdaṅga drum, ḍuḍḍukas, and small mardalas;
and in the northwest, a jhallarī cymbal accompanied by bronze cymbals.
The large drum (paṭaha) and the small drum (hrasvapaṭaha), along with the ḍuḍḍuka, are for Soma;
in the northeast (aiśānī) are the ḍuḍḍuka and the jhallī, together with hand-bells.
Outside of those, O best of Brahmins, one should place the courtesans on the south.
One should station mantra-singers at his side for the purpose of singing auspicious songs;
having placed dancers in front and groups of panegyrists to the north,
one should establish the others who are skilled in instrumental music in their respective places.
Having thus established [the deities] in sequence according to their respective origins, O twice-born ones,

one should first worship Garuḍa— who has reached his station— using offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), and then take one's place beside the drum.

One should wrap the drum with cloth according to one's means; having consecrated the space within the drum as the embodiment of sound, one should worship it. Then, in the center of the drum, one should worship Viṣṇu with the Viṣṇu-mantra.
Having worshipped Brahmā in the south and Rudra in the north,
one should place Vāyu in the corner to the right of that and worship him there well;
having worshipped Viṣṇu in the conchs and Sarasvatī in the kāhala drums.
One should worship Indra upon the mṛdanga drums, and worship the Gandharva upon the string;
having worshipped Rudra upon the mṛdaṅga, one should also worship Ṣaṇmukha upon the ḍuḍukka drums.
One should likewise worship Medinī upon the small mṛdala drums.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu in the jhallarī drum, Brahmā in the bronze cymbal (kāṃsyatālaka),
the goddess Śrī in the paṭaha drums, and Sarasvatī in the bell,
one should worship Viṣṇu alone in all other musical instruments.
In this manner, the Guru himself should worship all musical instruments, such as the kettledrum (bherī) and others.
At that time, courtesans, accompanied by handfuls of flowers,
should joyfully scatter those flowers upon the drums from above.
Then, having placed before him a Pāraśava who has bathed, whose hands hold Darbha grass, who is adorned, equipped with the sacred thread and other regalia, endowed with the five purificatory rites,
and possessed of devotion to the Lord, one should cause him to gaze [upon the deity].
Afterwards, one should sprinkle it with water from the *arghya* vessel using the Astra-mantra.
When an auspicious moment has arrived,
the Guru himself, meditating upon the three forms [of the deity], should strike the drum— thus worshipped— with the corner of his hand.
The first striking should be performed with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ";
the second striking should be performed with the mantra "brahmajajñānam";
and the third striking should be performed with the mantra "kadrudrāya". (11.31–32)
One should strike the drums three times at the three locations and so forth for the gods;
then Pārāśava, carrying that decorated drum,
should perform the triple striking first with his left hand.
Then, one should properly strike it three times with the right hand.
First is the sound of a conch, second is the blast of a trumpet, and the third is said to be the striking; indeed, one should perform them in this sequence. (11.34–35)

At the time of invoking the deities, one should cause all musical instruments to sound; then one should cause the Lord to hear a verse for the invocation of the deities— whether refined (saṃskṛta) or vernacular (prākṛta), or even in the Dravidian tongue—
just as one desires.

At that time, for the complete satisfaction of the deities, the preceptor should display the dance of the gods accompanied by various songs and other performances for the God of gods. Then, the preceptor [should place] the festival image together with the two goddesses.
Having mounted [the deity] upon a very sturdy vehicle and having adorned it especially,
one should then circumambulate the image of the procession (yātrāmūrti), preceded by the image of the offering (balibimba),
in due order, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments.
Together with all his attendants, preceded by the offering of oblations (bali),
he then took a vessel containing a *droṇa* measure of milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
as well as the water for honor (*arghya*), perfumes, garlands, incense, and betel.
Beginning from the door of the palace and ending at the outer gate,

and likewise in all the enclosures, one should offer the sacrificial oblation according to the ritual rules, accompanied by song, dance, and other such performances, at the western end of the path that obstructs the enclosure.
Then, having entered the village and stationed himself in the eastern direction,
the preceptor himself, facing eastward, should perform the invocation of the deities;
his son or his disciple should do so with a loud voice.
"May those hosts of spirits who dwell in the eastern quarter—both the deformed and the beautiful—come and accept this prepared offering.
Having received it, may they, being satisfied, protect us as followers of Kumuda. (11.45)
"May the Great Ones approach this [place] with joy; homage be to you all.
Having invoked Kumuda along with his retinue by means of this mantra, one should then offer the guest-water (arghya), ointment, garlands, incense, and water in their proper order.
One should then cause milk-rice, water, and betel-leaf to be offered;
afterwards, one should gratify [the deity] with beautiful and great sounds produced by conch-shells,
and thereafter with his own rhythmic music, song, and dance.
"O Arhaṇas, come;

you who dwell upon the hope of being worthy ones—may those who are formidable, with terrifying faces, fierce, and followed by Kumudākṣa, accept this prepared worship and protect us, being well-satisfied. (11.49–50)
"May the Great Ones approach this [place] with joy; homage be to you!
Having thus invoked Kumudākṣa, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and having gratified him as before, one should then proceed to the southern direction."
"Come, O hosts of ancestors who dwell in the southern quarter! May you,
who are fierce and of fierce conduct, accept this prepared offering and,
being satisfied, protect us— you who follow in the wake of Puṇḍarīka."
"May the Great Ones approach this [place] with joy; homage be to you!
Having invoked the Lord of the Gaṇas, named Puṇḍarīka, by means of this [mantra], and having worshipped him in due order, one should then go toward the direction of the Yātudhānas."
"Come, O hosts of spirits who dwell in the quarters you have traversed!
You flesh-eaters of cruel intent, accept this prepared offering and, being satisfied, protect us, O followers of Vāmana! (11.55–56)
"May the Great Ones approach this [place] with joy; homage be to you!
Having thus invoked Gaṇeśa, one should worship Vāmana in due order.
Then, having gone to the western quarter, one should worship Śaṅkukarṇa, the Lord of the Gaṇas.
May those great venomous serpents who dwell facing the west come first; having accepted this prepared worship,
may they, being satisfied, protect us along with their followers, the Śaṅkukarṇas.
"May the great ones come here with joy; homage be to you!

Having thus invoked them, one should worship as before. Then, having reached the direction of the wind (the northwest), [one should say]: "May the hosts of Gandharvas come, who dwell in the quarter of the wind."
May they— Sudarśana and Bhīmavega—
who follow all the eyes, accept this offered worship and protect us with satisfaction.
"May the Great Ones approach this [place] with joy; homage be to you all! (11.62) Having invoked Sarvanetra along with his retinue by means of this [mantra], one should gratify him.
Then, having gone toward the direction of Soma, [one should invoke] Sumukha, the lord of the Gaṇas. (11.63)
"Come, O hosts of Yakṣas who dwell in the north!
You who are deformed and carry staffs in your hands, accept this prepared offering and, being satisfied, protect us as the followers of Sumukha. (11.64)
"May the great ones come here with joy; homage be to you!"—having invoked them with this mantra, one should satisfy them according to the previous procedure.
Then, having gone toward the direction of Īśa (the northeast), [one should worship] Gaṇeśa, who is well-established.
May the hosts of Piśācas who dwell in the northeastern quarter come here,
holding tridents and weapons in their hands; having accepted this prepared offering, may they, being satisfied and well-established, protect us as our followers.
"May the Great Ones approach this [place] with joy; homage be to you all!
Having invoked them with the mantra and worshipped them, one should go to the center of the village and there invoke Gaṇeśvara, who contains the fire (praśnigarbha), above."
"Come, O hosts of Siddhas who dwell in the sky!
You who are pure-minded and pure, accept this prepared worship.
Having taken it, may you, being satisfied, protect us—you who follow the thunderbolt-wielder."
"May the great ones come here with joy; homage be to you!
Having invoked and gratified them, [one should then invoke] the human [beings] below;
may the hosts of lower beings who dwell upon the earth come forth. (11.71–72)
May those of many forms and great wisdom, having accepted this prepared offering,
protect us with satisfaction; may they come to this great [sacrifice] as followers of Mānava,
and may there be salutations to you.
Having invoked [the deities], one should satisfy them in the prescribed order as before, concluding with the final rite.
Then, for the satisfaction of all beings, one should cast the remnants of the *bali* offering.
In the ritual of giving the *bali*, however, the sequence begins from the east and ends in the direction of Vaivasvata (the south).
The preceptor, standing facing the east, should perform the invocation and other rites;
for the triad beginning with Yāmya, he should do as previously stated while facing north.
In the two directions of Someśa (the northeast) and the village center, he should face the east.
Samatāla, likewise Baddhatāla, and Śṛṅgiṇī;
Mallatāla, Maṅgala, Jayatāla, and Bhadraka;
the tāla known as Ḍhakkarī, and likewise Brahmatāla. || 11.77-11.78 ||
O twice-born ones, these ten *tālas*— Ananta and the rest— are proclaimed as belonging respectively to the ten lords of the *gaṇas*, Kumuda and the others:
*ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, and likewise *pañcama*.
Dhaivata, niṣāda, dhaivata, madhyama, and likewise pañcama—these are said to be the ten notes in their proper sequence. Gāndhāra-rāga, that called Kaula, Kauśika, and Naṭabhāṣika; || 11.81 ||
Śrī, Kāmada, its hair-like Keśī, Dakṣarāga likewise,
the one called Cālāpāṇi, and Megharāga as the fifth—
these are proclaimed as the ten rāgas of Kumuda and the others.
The *vilāsa*, the *sarvatobhadra*, the *kheṭaka*, the *cakramaṇḍala*,
the *kāntārakuṭṭima*, the *pṛṣṭhakuṭṭima*, the *kaṭibandhana*,
and the *vāmajānūrdhvanṛtta*; furthermore, the first two [of these] again.
These specific dances of Kumuda and the others are recorded in their respective order;
indeed, these rhythms (tāla) and so forth are recorded as belonging to the surrounding deities in their proper sequence.
For all other deities, O Bhadra, the rhythm known as Bhadra is recommended.
The *garuḍatāla* should be used for the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), while the *madhyama* scale is for him;
the *gauḍa* melody should be employed, and the dance is indeed the *viṣṇukāntaka*.
For the Enemy of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), the *jayatāla* should be used, and the dance is said to be the *svastika*.
The musical note is declared to be Ṛṣabha, and the rāga is Varāṭī;
preceded by the striking of a drum, one should perform the invocation of the deities.
One should cause the Gāruḍa rhythm to be proclaimed in the intermediate directions.
At that time, by the Lord of Teachers himself, in a refined Sanskrit verse:
"The hosts of Maruts, headed by the Four-faced One (Brahmā), as well as other attendants of the Blessed One, must be summoned for the service of the God's festival. (11.89–90)
Likewise, other devotees of the Blessed One, people who serve at his feet,
or those approved by their guru and strengthened by devotion to the Blessed One—
O twice-born ones, those brahmins should be summoned by them with a divine song.
Having thus wandered through the village and entered the palace,
one should reach the station of Garuḍa and satisfy the one whose banner is the bird;
then, with cymbals and other instruments, one should satisfy Viṣvaksena.
Then, one should cause the festive image to enter the sacrificial hall,
endowed with all the characteristics in the manner to be described,
either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure.
Or else, starting from the third enclosure, [one may place her] facing whichever direction is desired;
likewise, she may face east, or face whichever direction is preferred.
She may have one door, four doors, or be provided with two doors.
Whether it be joined with walls or not, or provided with corner walls—
for the sake of the swift accomplishment of the rite— one should construct a pavilion that is either simple or complete,
equipped with a smoke-vent and a central altar.
Above that, there should be a fire-pit (homakuṇḍa) provided with four girdles;
or it may be furnished with three girdles, or even two, or even a single girdle;
it should be square and endowed with the proper characteristics.
To its east, it should be provided with a mandala; in the southeast, it should be equipped with lamps and jars;
in the west, it should be joined with a lamp (or image); in the north, it should be furnished with sprouts;
and in the northeast, it should be provided with a water-pot and all necessary implements.

Having entered such a sacrificial hall, adorned with canopies and the like, and beautified by arched gateways and banners, the most excellent of gurus should station those composed of the *Ṛgveda* upon their seats, facing west while positioned toward the east.
And on the south, he should station the followers of the Yajurveda facing north;
on the western side, he should settle the chanters of the Sāmaveda facing east,
together with Brahmins belonging to the Ekāyana school who are characterized by the name Mūrti.
Then, having established in the northern quarter all those devoted to their daily rites who were learned in the Atharvaveda, numbering two by two,
the sound of the Vedas and the sound of musical instruments resounded outside.

Having entered the place of the jar, one should sit upon an excellent seat nearby facing the east and recollect the mantra as before, while contemplating its pervasive presence. Having sat down according to the rule, one should perform the rites up to the end of the internal sacrifice.
First, having performed the purification of the hands and so forth, one should subsequently prepare the *arghya* and other offerings.
Having performed [the rites] as before, one should then worship the assembly of mantras residing within the body.
Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle all the ritual implements.
Two pairs of water-pots should first be placed— either made of gold or silver,
or of copper or clay— provided with lids and sprouts of leaves,
filled with fruits, gems, and other such items, and encircled with a thread.
Having placed [the deities] upon Śālipīṭha on both sides at each door,
one should then perform the door-sacrifice (dvārayāga) starting from the east and proceeding to the north and west,
using water for honor (arghya), ointments, garlands, and incense mixed with guggulu resin. || 11.110–111 ||
Then, having taken a firm, bright, uniform, and flawless jar—
either made of clay, or beautiful gold, or silver—
provided with jewels, gold, garlands, perfumes, fruits, and all medicinal herbs; (11.112)
Rich with branches of auspicious trees, adorned with silken garlands and fragrances,
filled with filtered water and provided with a stream of fresh water;
anointed with sandalwood paste and the like, and honored on all sides with unbroken grains of rice.
Having encircled it on all sides with threads, one should scatter [flowers] and place it upon [the vessel];
then, one should perceive that body of the deity as possessing stainless luster.
Then, one should consecrate the *vardhanī* vessel with the *sāstra* and the *cakra* mantra.
Combined with the previously mentioned substances and wrapped all around with thread,
one should invoke [the deity] and, having placed it to the right of the Lord of Mantras and to the north of the jar,
one should establish eight jars there surrounding it.

Having placed a jar with sprouts, a lid, and wrapped with thread in the center [of the area], and having subsequently prepared a seat for the Lord, one should then duly invoke the Lotus-eyed One into its midst according to the prescribed rite.
The sequence beginning with storage and ending with enjoyment and sacrifice, starting from complete restraint.

Having performed everything as before, one should meditate upon [the deity] situated in the southern direction, having the form of the personified Weapon (astra), and worship him according to the rules—
[him who is] destroying the multitude of obstacles until the completion of the rite.

When those eight jars have been placed there around [the central one], Vāsudeva and the others are to be worshipped according to their connection with the origin and dissolution [of the world]. Standing with palms joined in reverence, one should address this prayer to the God while holding a weapon.
"O Lord of All, please accept this sacrificial hall constructed by me;
O All-pervading One, grant success to these [rites] and be present as the presiding deity of the ritual components.
Then, one should lead an unbroken stream of water from the weapon-mantra (astra) along the wall.
One should remember that [the vessel] reaches the edge of its base by proceeding clockwise from the eastern side; or else, O best of the twice-born,
one should rotate the vessel behind it from the northeast direction to the edge of its base, either simultaneously or separately.
Having placed the *kalaśa* together with the *vardhanī*, scattering the *vikiroddhva-gama* [offerings],
and having performed the offering of *arghya* for those two, one should again fill them with flowers and other such items.
Then, having consecrated a pair of unwashed garments with the *astra-mantra*, indeed—

Having perfumed both of them with incense and wrapped them [in cloth], one should then place a *bhadrapīṭha* (auspicious seat) upon which the upward-moving *vikira* (scattering grains) has been strewn. One should then set down the mantra-vessel (*mantrakalaśa*) together with its weapon (*sāstra*) upon that base.
Or, when a seat has been made of four, three, two, or one *bhāra* of *śāli* rice,
one should place upon it that same quantity or half of it of *taṇḍula* rice;
and above that, one should arrange sesame seeds in the same measure or equal to them.
Having spread a pair of unbleached, auspicious cloths upon that,
one should place a water-pot together with a *vardhanī* vessel above it; then,
as before, one should worship the Lord of Gods along with his weapons, following the sequence beginning with the seat.
One should perform the divine activity while recollecting the All-pervading Lord during the *kumbhaka* [retention of breath];
since one cannot remain engaged [in this] without cease, this is the remedy.
Thus, for the sake of protection, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate the *kaumbha* weapon.
Then the preceptor, having reached the mandala altar,
should smear the ground with water and cow dung;
there, having laid out the lines according to the rules, the mandala is to be drawn.
O best of sages, listen specifically to the procedure for that:
having first established the east and west from the center by means of the staff-method,
one should place four threads on the two sides within the interval between those two directions.
Having divided the center into two equal parts,

one should produce two crossroads from the eastern and western sections by means of a thread established with the previously calculated half-measure, extending from the center to the end. (11.136–11.137)
Having made the cord equal at both ends, one should cast it upon that;
then, having laid it out equally in the cardinal directions, one should form the four corners.
By means of the fourfold intersection of the paths, one should indeed bring it to clarity by stretching it out.
One should draw four equal lines for the sake of achieving a perfect square.
Having divided that [space] into eighteen equal squares in the four directions,
one should cast there a collection of threads marked by the maker of the jar (the architect).

One should fashion Padmāvanī in the center across three successive rows of squares; outside of that, one should construct a pedestal (pīṭha) consisting of a row of squares and endowed with the eight directions. Then, having arranged four directions enriched by four squares each, [one proceeds].
A group of four [squares] at each intermediate direction, three squares in a row for the circumambulation of the pedestal;
from the outside of the circumambulatory ground, a group of four in each of the four cardinal directions;
and from the outside of those four, two squares further out on each side.
Having purified that [area], one should then purify, with effort, a group of four outside of it for the sake of establishing the gates;
furthermore, one should purify step by step in each direction a set of four,
extending both outward and inward.
Furthermore, having cleared away six groups of six from each of the two outer squares,
one should place eight red lotuses there for the sake of perfect beauty,
positioned according to the directions, for the worship of the gods.
One should erase three [units] each from the outer *pada* and *padma*;
that which stands between the three *padas*, one should bring to a state of oneness (*ekātmatā*).
Know that to be the *upaśobhā*; one should adorn it with blue lotuses.
Having first brought the five-fold [lines] from each corner to the middle line into dissolution,
one should then complete the corners with the remaining [lines], including the intervals, and outside of that, one should apply three threads; then, one should draw a lotus in the center.
Its characteristic is said to be a wheel with eight spokes.
Having carefully fixed a peg in the center of the thirty-six squares,
one should fashion five perfectly level mandalas by means of the rotation of the measuring lines.
Among those, the first mandala in the center shall indeed be the location of the pericarp (karṇikā).
Having again divided the second mandala into three parts by means of rotating the threads,
among those, the first is the place for the filaments (kesara) and the second is the petal-mandala (dalamaṇḍala).
That third [circle] should again be divided into three, and one should draw three naves;
outside the navel, one should arrange twelve spokes in the two circles.
Outside that, one should designate a single circle as the place for the nave.

Having done this, it should be filled with pure and most brilliant pigments. Know that the pericarp is yellow, high, wide-spreading, and endowed with the seed-syllable; all the petals, moreover, are white and marked with lines.
One should fashion three filaments on each petal, possessing a reddish glow;
the space between the petals should be black, white, yellow, and pale-red.
There should be three naves in sequence, while the spokes are red in color.
The eastern portion should be dark-colored and the final [portion] white.
The corners of the pedestal are white, and the four directions thereof are red.
The pathway has the luster of lapis lazuli and is adorned with leaves, garlands, and so forth.
Except for the western portion, all the doors should be like lotus petals,
black and possessing all beauties, situated at the locations of the doors. The secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) should be equal to half their size, like the interior (garbha).
The corners should have the luster of filaments and be adorned with white conch-shells;
one should likewise create a series of lines outside in colors such as red and gold in sequence.
Having thus performed this, one should contemplate [the mandala] as being identical with one's own self, like the body itself.
Know that the dust particles are the elements, as well as white, yellow, and so forth;
the subtle elements (tanmātras) are the ornaments, and the organs of action are the decorations.
Thus are all the corners, along with the doors and the sense organs.
The outer enclosure is indeed that triad beginning with *sattva*;
the mind is the well-spreading path, and pride is declared to be the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
The intellect (*dhī*) is the lotus, and its presiding deity is the Person (*puruṣa*), whose essence is consciousness and who consists of the seed-syllable.
And here dwells the formless Lord, whose characteristic is bliss;
by the mere sight of whom one's very being becomes eternally serene.
This occurs for both those with attachments and those without attachments once the body has fallen away.
For those who possess liberation and have but one birth remaining in this world, the Lord dwells both outside and within them, having abandoned ignorance;
otherwise, how indeed could they attain such joy from the mere sight [of Him]? (11.166–11.167)
Whatever reality is a specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) that establishes existence through internal awareness is established everywhere.
Having thus grasped the previously constructed mandala as a real entity, [one should proceed].
[He should worship] by name the world of the Lotus-navelled One (Viṣṇu), which brings about the destruction of all suffering.
Then, having prepared a seat for the Lord there as before,
he should duly invoke the God of gods into its center.
Having performed everything as before, beginning with the *sannidhi* (invocation) and *sannirodha* (confinement), and ending with the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*),
the Guru should worship the Lord of Gods within the mandala using the previously mentioned seats and other offerings, up until the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*).
One should perform the ritual bath during the mandala ceremony, the jar-offering, and the sprinkling rite.
Then, having gone into the presence of the image together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās),
one should worship the deity there with great magnificence.
Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the best of preceptors,
having consecrated both the pit and the fire there according to the rules,
should perform the libation into the fire for the Lord according to the prescribed ritual.

One should perform all the rites, beginning with the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), in the same manner as before, using both the regular fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and those for specific desires (*kāmya*) in their proper order.
One should not discard the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) nor the *darbha* grass, and one should not dismiss the deities from that point.
One should maintain the sacred fire every day until the end of the tirtha-day;
one should offer oblations every day for a full day and night according to the prescribed method.
Then, having gone near the image and performed the offering of the oblation, [one should proceed].

Having performed everything ending with the act of giving in due order, and thereafter, if one possesses the means, one should again perform the worship of the Lord. Then, one should offer the door-oblation (dvārabali) in the four directions according to the prescribed rite.
Then, one should cause the deity to enter within the sacrificial hall;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods there, one should complete the remainder of the night.
From the day of sowing the sprouts until the final day of the flower-sacrifice—
The supreme preceptor should perform the vow over a period of twelve days in sequence.
Having performed the ritual bathing, worship, and other rites, and having drunk the water from his [the deity's] feet mixed with kuśa-water, he should recite the eight-syllable mantra.
O twice-born ones, one should first consume the food offering (naivedya) and then observe the practice of eating only at night;
one should recite the twelve names in sequence while keeping them in mind. When the second day arrives, the preceptor, who is most skilled in the knowledge of mantras, [should proceed].
Having completed the daily obligatory rites such as bathing, together with the image-keepers (mūrtipās),
and having performed the daily worship of the Lord,
the Guru should then perform the special sacrifice after entering the sacrificial hall according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having completed the worship up to the doors, one should go to the vicinity of the water-pot (kumbha) and worship the deity according to the prescribed rule, both in the pot and in the mandala—
wherein the worship was previously performed in both the pot and the mandala.
One should perform the worship on that very same day even if it is another;
for there is no fault of the offerings having become stale for those two, O lords of sages.
If performed previously on ground resembling ash, the worship would be fruitless.
Having joined [the ritual], one should then draw the maṇḍala within the water-pot (kumbha).
Then, with white and other purifying pigments, one should worship [the deity] within the pot.
Thereafter, one should duly worship the Lord of the Gods of gods within the maṇḍala.
In this way, O best of sages, even when defects have arisen in the water-pot,
one should purify the pot once more and worship it with pure water.

There, the Guru should unite the God of gods, who is situated in the mandala, having adorned him as before; he should worship the Lord there. Then, having gone to the temple of the god, [he should worship] the lotus-eyed Acyuta.
Having paid homage with the eight-limbed prostration, one should worship Puruṣottama with offerings of water for the guest, unguents, garlands, and incense, together with the ancillary rites.
All that is suitable should be brought forth and presented during the course of the worship.
Having first taken up flowers and honored them with his head,
he should offer them to Viṣvaksena; then, having consecrated the image of the Lord along with its pedestal with water empowered by weapon-mantras, he should wipe it clean.
Having purified the temple, one should worship the God of gods with baths consisting of milk and other substances, or with *dhātrī* fruits and so forth,
as well as with other unartificial offerings presented in the prescribed order.

One should perform a special festival ending with circumambulations and prostrations. Then, having gone to the sacrificial hall, one should satisfy the Lord in the fire by means of the fire consecrated according to the previously mentioned procedure. || 11.197-11.198 ||
One should cause a *caru* oblation to be cooked on the hearth with milk, ghee, and rice while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having then extracted it and purified it with ghee, one should offer it in due order;
thereafter, one should sacrifice one portion of the jars, the pedestals, and the images.
Alternatively, having prepared the *caru* before the commencement of the sacrifice,
and having performed the worship of the jars, the site, and the images in due order,
one should then offer everything, ending with the gifts to the twice-born, into the fire as a libation.
After offering the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should likewise perform the *dvārabali* offering; then,
having gone near the image and performed the announcement of the *homa*,
one should take the image of the offering and place it upon a vehicle.
One should especially adorn [the image] with garments, ornaments, and garlands.
The Brahmins, meditating upon the Lord of Birds (Vihageśvara), should carry the vehicle,
beginning from the first circumambulation and ending at the western enclosure of the street.
Having circumambulated the Lord of Gods in a clockwise direction preceded by the offering of the *bali*, one should then proceed as before into the village,
according to the arrangement of the directions starting with Indra in the cardinal and intermediate quarters.
And in the center of the kumuda and other [lotuses] together with their attendants, one should offer oblations (bali) in due order upon pedestals that have been prepared beforehand,
or on the ground smeared with cow dung and other substances as desired.

O best of the twice-born, one should offer water for the guest (arghya), fragrance, garlands, and incense— preceded by scented water— to the group of ten Gaṇeśas beginning with Kumuda, using their respective names preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ."
One should further offer the bali-oblation, water, and betel-leaf in due order.
One should arrange all the performances, such as dance and song, as previously described.
Having thus performed the village bali-offering, the Guru [should proceed] before the image of the bali.
O lords of sages, having said "Salutation to all those not mentioned here" and "Salutation to the attendants," one should cast the remaining offering in the middle of the village.
Then, O lords of sages, one should cause the image of the offering to enter within.
Having worshipped them for the sake of pacifying fatigue, one should establish them in their own places.
In this manner, one should perform the *bali* offering at two times: on the final day of the pilgrimage (*tīrtha*) and on the night of the commencement day and the day of the completion.
One should offer one *bali* at midday and two *balis*;
thus, preceded by the daily worship, both by day and by night,
the best of preceptors should perform the special sacrifice ending with the *bali*.

The mounting of the vehicle at night or by day may be done according to one's preference. The preceptor should perform the *balidāna* (offering of oblations); the procedure for that is now described here.
The deity situated in the image for the procession, whether together with the two goddesses or without them—
Having specially adorned it with variegated garments,
as well as with various ornaments and many kinds of garlands;
[he saw] a vehicle specially decorated, constructed of gold and other precious materials.
Having brought [the vehicle] together, sprinkled it with water, and meditated upon it in the form of Garuḍa,
he should then worship it with its own mantra using the arghya and other offerings;
and having performed the proclamation of a "meritorious day" accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas.
Having placed the Lord— who has assumed the form for the procession— upon the vehicle there in a clockwise direction, accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments,
one should especially secure him and adorn the Lord of the World.
Having honored him with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites, one should present betel leaves and other offerings.
The Brahmins, meditating upon the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), should carry the palanquin;
or else, Śūdras who are Vaiṣṇavas should carry it, filled with devotion.
In a village, a city, or even a town, O lords of sages,
one should perform circumambulation by following the path of circumambulation alone,
while Brahmins are being carried [in palanquins] and wearing cloaks and turbans.
With pearls, parasols, and beautiful peacock-feather fans;
with palm-leaf fans likewise provided with golden handles;
and with various fly-whisks made of silk, both white and black.
With various flagstaffs adorned with victory banners,
with staffs made entirely of jewels, and with other auspicious objects;
and with diverse throngs of bards, accompanied by the sounds of lutes and flutes.
With the sounds of golden horns and other auspicious cries,
with courtesans, temple-servants, and citizens,
and with Brahmins holding cane-staves in their hands, adorned with tunics and turbans.
Likewise, with hundreds of extremely brilliant lamps being carried by attendants on either side,
[he placed] the two sandals, inlaid with jewels and fashioned from gold and other precious materials, into a vessel.

Having placed [the image] before the deity, with attendants carrying it while standing behind and reciting the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with Brāhmaṇas on the right side likewise reciting the Ekāyanī Śruti; || 11.230–231 ||
By those reciting the *Saṃhitās*, the *Sātvatas*, and so forth, endowed with devotion,
and by those constantly narrating the majesty of Vāsudeva;
by the *Sāttvika* followers of the *Pāñcarātra* who are intent on the worship of Vāsudeva.

On the left, however, were devoted Brahmins who investigated the meaning of the three Vedas, reciting the Purāṇas along with their histories and hymns composed in various languages that indicate the supreme nature of Viṣṇu. (11.233–234)
Accompanied by grammarians, logicians, astrologers, and others, who were full of humility as they expounded the tenets of their respective scriptures,
[the attendants] sang the supreme Drāmiḍa Śruti before the Lord.
Likewise, there are compositions in the vernacular language consisting of both prose and verse (11.236).
And likewise, by the best of Vaiṣṇavas— Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras— who speak with Vaiṣṇava devotion and are devoted to the Blessed One (11.237).
With hearts intent on beholding the Blessed One, bowing in prostration,
and accompanied by an army rich in the fourfold forces in all directions, together with other various attendants befitting a king— || 11.238 ||

One should cause the deity to circumambulate the village and other processional routes clockwise. While the festival is underway, one should devotedly offer mouth-fresheners and betel leaf many times to the God of gods.
One should offer sandalwood, well-perfumed with camphor and other substances, for the sake of pacifying fatigue,
as well as various garlands to the God of gods. One should also offer cool water for libation mixed with coconut water.
One should also report other signs of the pacification of fatigue.

In the eight directions of the village and its surroundings, and especially in their center, [one should perform worship] with various songs and dances accompanied by stringed instruments. || 11.242–11.243 ||

One should gratify the Lord of Gods with conch shells, kettledrums, clay drums, and other instruments. Having thus circumambulated the God, one should lead him to the outer pavilion; and having seated the Lord of the Worlds upon a golden seat, [one should proceed].
Having offered the water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), as well as perfume, garlands, a lamp,
incense, and the waving of lights (nīrājana) according to the prescribed rite,
he then presented clear water for worship, cakes (apūpa), and flattened grains (pṛthuka).
Having offered libations of coconut water as well as water for sipping (ācamana),
along with betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfumes,
in due order to the God of gods, one should then present the various offerings.

At all times during worship, one should offer ornaments, garlands, and garments; likewise, at the time of dismissal, one should perform the honoring of those [deities] with food offerings and other enjoyments,
while remaining unobserved by others.
For its accomplishment, one should spread a curtain around the deity;
then, one should lead the deity from that pavilion into the interior of the temple.
In front of the great pedestal, one should worship the deity with the arghya offering and other rites.
One should offer cakes, sacrificial offerings, betel leaves, and so forth.
Immediately thereafter, one should have the four Vedas recited before the deity;
furthermore, one should have the *Drādiḍī* hymn and praises recited by the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs and mridangas, as well as by dance, song, and other performances,
one should circumambulate the temple of the Lord of the Gods in a clockwise direction.
Then, one should lead him very slowly up the path of the stairs.
At that time, one should offer betel leaves and other items to the God of gods.
One should fan him with chowries, palm-leaf fans, and the like, to alleviate his fatigue.
One should praise the Lord of gods with hymns, whether in Sanskrit or in the Dravidian language.
With lutes, flutes, and drums, and with auspicious sounds of rhythmic clapping,
the most excellent Vaiṣṇavas sang songs of praise in the Dravidian style;
likewise, at every step, there were courtesans singing auspicious songs.
Accompanied by the loud-sounding cries of panegyrists and hymns of praise,
one should lead the deity inside with various kinds of ritual services;
this should be done with devotion at the gateway of the temple of the God of gods.

Having offered the guest-water (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana), perfume, garlands, and incense to the Lord of the Gods, one should establish him in his own place.
One should thus perform the mounting of the vehicle for the God constantly.
On the first day there is a palanquin; on the second, the remaining seats;
on the third, the lunar disc, and if it be by day, the solar orb;
when the fourth day arrives, there is the vehicle of the flower-pavilion.
When the fifth day arrives, there shall be the mounting upon Garuḍa;
when the sixth day has arrived, whether by night or by day,
having performed worship ending with the offering of oblations (bali) to the God in the assembly pavilion.
Having placed [the image] upon an auspicious seat, one should set down a jar of powder on a purified ground or a pedestal of grain in front of it;
having sprinkled it with water for the "merit-acclamation" (puṇyāha), one should worship Śrī there.
Having covered the wheel with a cloth containing sacred grass (darbha), one should install it there;
then, for the sake of protection, the preceptor, having worshipped the deity with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*),
should take turmeric powder.
Reciting the Śrīsūkta, one should consecrate the deity with powders.
In a portion of the pavilion prepared with rice grains,
upon a seat, one should place a golden or silver water-vessel.
Or made of copper, according to availability, it should be four, three, or two cubits in length;
half that in width at the top, and one-fourth of that in width at the base;
it should be circular and elongated at the lower part, provided with a drainage channel.

Or rather, O twice-born ones, having placed within it that [image] which resembles the form of a madman's flower— possessing a bimba-like measurement and endowed with all auspicious marks— and having filled it with filtered water; 11.269–270.
Having brought the deity to his side with sandalwood mixed with saffron paste and camphor powder,
and scented with flowers,
he should worship him with the arghya and other offerings.
Accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, musical instruments, and conchs,
and further endowed with the resonance of Vedic hymns through the chanting of praises and auspicious verses,
he performed the ritual immersion for the Lord with the Puruṣasūkta.
Having placed the deity upon a vehicle together with one whose garment is still damp from the bath,
and having anointed [the deity] with saffron according to the ritual from the feet to the head,
one should circumambulate the courtyard and the street for the pleasure of Varuṇa.
And for the sake of purifying all people as well,
those twice-born who behold the Lord of the Gods with devotion at that time—
all of them become cleansed of sin and free from affliction.
Then, having seated the deity upon a seat within the pavilion,
the preceptor himself should personally bring all the requisites for the bath, such as the garments and other items.
Then, having adorned the deity, he should properly perform the Gajotsava festival.
When the seventh day had arrived, having performed the worship ending with the offering of oblations,
he first set out the chariot, which was endowed with all auspicious characteristics and adorned with clusters of golden blossoms and strings of pearls.
With various flower garlands accompanied by strings of pearls,
with a golden canopy, and especially with its particular luster;
likewise, with a noble throne made of gold situated in the center.
One should decorate the chariot-vehicle on all sides with various beautiful banners and flags, as well as with the Garuda emblem;
thus the chariot is adorned with golden pinnacle-jars.
Having sprinkled [the chariot] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as well as with the waters of the auspicious day (puṇyāha),
one should worship the deities stationed from the base of the chariot up to its top.
First, in the wheels of the base, starting from the southeast (vahni) and ending in the northwest (īśāna).
Having worshipped Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya in their proper order with their respective mantras, one should worship the Lord of Birds elsewhere;
[one should worship] Māyā on the two parts of the discus and staff, and the Moon and Sun upon the discus.
And that [universe] is infinite within its support, the two staff-like pillars known as Bhāra;
there Viṣṇu, assuming the universal form, and Śaktīśa—both of these—are situated.
Around them, in a network of rows, Keśava and the others are arranged in succession.
One should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Dharma on the limbs and the parts of the limbs.
One should place the collection of weapons, beginning with the discus, from one limb to another;
and one should always place Hari upon the pinnacle of the stūpa at the top of the chariot-palace.
In the peaked halls (kūṭaśālā), one should worship Vāsudeva and the others previously mentioned;
having placed Kūrma and the other eleven [forms] around the base of the altar, one should likewise worship them all around the neck.
Then, on the summit, one should worship Ananta and the others in their proper sequence.
O Brahmins, above all of them, one should worship Padmanābha and Dhruva.
Having worshipped these in order with water for the guest-offering (arghya), garlands, perfumes, and incense—‖ 11.290–11.291 ‖

One should worship Caṇḍa and the others, ending with Subhadra, two by two in the cardinal directions; likewise, one should worship Kumuda and the other Gaṇeśas, as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas), in their respective places in due order.
Having worshipped them in those locations, one should worship the chariot in the form of Garuḍa.

Having meditated and worshipped with offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the Guru then offers the *bali* to Caṇḍa and the others around the chariot; thereafter,
the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, reaches the temple.
Having placed the Lord of Gods, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi, upon the vehicle and led him to the pavilion of the assembly hall, he seated him upon a throne; then,
having worshipped the God with water for the feet and other various ritual offerings, he honored Him.
O twice-born ones, for the sake of the unimpeded success of the journey, the best of guides, having offered various seeds,
fruits, gold, and curd-rice to the Brahmins in the presence of the deity, [proceeded].
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction of stars as determined by the astrologers,
having diligently worshipped the God for the purpose of ascending the chariot,
and having offered the two sandals, he was placed upon the vehicle as before.
With the sounds of Vedic recitations, as well as the ringing of bells and auspicious chants; with shouts of "Victory! Victory!", the blare of trumpets, and the sounding of conchs;
together with the beating of kettledrums, tabors, and musical instruments, and amidst dancing and singing.
Together with the parasols, fly-whisks, and other requisites for the procession,
starting from the first enclosure and proceeding as far as the outermost street-enclosure,
he should circumambulate in a clockwise direction just as before.
Having circumambulated the chariot at an auspicious hour and a favorable moment,
one should have the deity placed upon the chariot with great care by the Brāhmaṇas;
and having seated the deity on a cushion upon the upper surface of the chariot.
There, for the God of gods, he offered water for the hands (arghya) and likewise water for the feet (pādya),
water for sipping (ācāma), as well as fragrance, garlands, a lamp, and incense;
furthermore, the ritual honors (arhaṇa), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and various kinds of food offerings (naivedya).

Having offered the *pṛthukā* (flattened rice) and other items, as well as the beverage, the satiating drink (*tarpaṇa*), and the water for rinsing the mouth; and then having presented betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfumes—
at that time, for women desiring sons and wishing for health— (11.305–306).
Having consumed the sacrificial offering (naivedya), the preceptor and the practitioners should present it in the presence of the deity while standing upon the upper surface of the chariot.
Below that, on the ground, the umbrella-bearers should be stationed to the west.
There, on his two sides, should be stationed the two bearers of the peacock-feather umbrella;
on the right and left flanks, and in front, the two bearers of the fly-whisks;
and the charioteer should be stationed in that place directly in front, in the middle.
Then one should cause that chariot-vehicle to circumambulate all the streets,
proceeding clockwise through the village, the city, or even the town.
Then, having carefully descended the Lord of Gods from the chariot, [one should proceed].
Having placed it upon another vehicle, one should settle it in its own place.
On the eighth day, during that night, there should be the mounting of a swing and the mounting of a camel;
thereafter, one should have him mount a horse and also engage in hunting.
The play of protecting his devotees, the purification of the city in the realm of Brahmā,
affection, and a quarrel between the two goddesses with the Lord;
he should effect a reconciliation between both and say, "May it be forgiven."
On the ninth day, one should perform the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and on that night, the festival of the palanquin (*śibikotsava*).
Thus has the sequence for the mounting of the vehicle been correctly described;
[the deity should be adorned] with unprecedented ornaments, garlands, and likewise with unprecedented garments.
Just as curiosity arises from unprecedented things such as gardens and vehicles,
so too should special preparations be made until the day of the pilgrimage site.
O twice-born ones, the procedure for the concluding ritual (avabhṛtha) is now being described.
The preceptor, having entered the temple of the Blessed One together with the image-protectors (mūrtipa),
should worship the deity according to the rules and perform everything up to the offering of the bali.
The preceptor, accompanied by the patron and the practitioners, [should proceed].
Then, having entered the temple and prostrated like a staff at the feet of the primary image, one should bring the sacred bathing image there.
O best of sages, in its absence, one should bring the image used for the daily ritual bath.
O twice-born ones, even in the absence of this original image,
one should place an image made of sacrificial offerings (balibimba) before the original image, invoke it, and worship it;
then, having lifted up the sacred image (tīrthabimba), accompanied by musical instruments and the ringing of bells— || 11.320–11.321 ||
Having brought [the bathing image] near the base of the banner according to the prescribed rite,
one should place the bathing image facing the principal image upon a bathing seat within that pavilion which has been purified and adorned.
Having established that [image] in front, the lowest of the low bathing rite is performed.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front, one should place a mortar there;
having placed mortars in the four directions, one should place [pestles] upon the mortar.
Taking stalks of *dūrvā* grass, one should tie them to the pestle and mortar;
having wrapped them with a new cloth, one should pour powder into them—
gold mixed with the powder of turmeric and combined with fragrant substances.
O twice-born ones, one should have the threshing performed by four Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas or by Vaiṣṇava women while auspicious songs are being sung;
it should take place either to the east or to the north of the area where the installation and bathing have been performed.
Having made a pedestal with rice grains and placed a jar upon it,
one should deposit the powder there along with the thread and wrap it with a cloth.
Alternatively, one may use five or nine jars filled with the powder.
Having worshipped with the root mantra, one should then bathe the Lord.
Having anointed the Lord of Gods with oil and performed an exfoliation as before,
one should then bathe him according to the ritual procedure using the vessels for water for the feet and so forth, in their proper order.

Having worshipped the deity with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites, and having taken up the pitcher filled with gold dust and other substances, one should consecrate [the deity] with those powders while reciting the Śrīsūkta. Having performed the bath with a thousand streams and having purified [himself] with the water, [one should proceed].
Having clothed him in two new garments, one lower and one upper,
and having adorned him most excellently and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
he should thereafter offer him food such as mung-bean porridge and milk-rice.
Having placed the consecrated image upon a palanquin or similar vehicle,
and likewise the festive image accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi,
one should indeed place them upon the palanquin or similar vehicle after having adorned them especially.
Placing the image of the Tīrtha before him— the Lord who has entered the form for the procession—
equipped with all the ritual implements such as the parasol, fly-whisks, and conch shells,
one should circumambulate it, doing so even through all the surrounding enclosures.
Having reached the vicinity of the sacred ford (tīrtha), or else at its bank in a pavilion,
or at a water-station (prapā), one should establish the Lord of the Gods upon a seat;
then, having placed the bathing pedestal in front of the processional image (yātrābimba).
Having installed the image of the deity at that sacred site, the preceptor should perform the consecration with twenty-five jars,
or else with twelve or nine pitchers;
having performed the ritual powder-bath for the deity according to the rules.
Having worshipped with the *arghya* and other offerings, and having then wiped the image,
one should cause the powder remaining from the meal to be placed upon the heads of the devotees.
This powder, which destroys all sins, yields the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Even if one wears that powder on the head merely as a plaything,
the sin residing in his body perishes at that very moment.
Having made the proclamation of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha), the preceptor should sprinkle the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Having invoked all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) into that particular ford, one should worship them;
then the preeminent teacher, having approached the Lord residing within the processional image (*yātrāmūrti*),
should prostrate at His feet and, with His permission, [proceed].
When an auspicious moment has arrived and the sun has reached midday,
having taken up the image of the Tīrtha along with the sounds of bells and conchs,
one should place it upon the palm of the left hand while oneself remains seated within a mandala drawn on the ground.

Having first bestowed blessings upon the king, the kingdom, and others, the eminent preceptor, composed in mind, should reach the bank of the sacred ford and hold [the vessel] with his right hand at its middle portion.
Having reached the middle of the water and standing in water reaching up to the navel,
the preceptor, together with the image, should indeed mutter the root mantra; filled with devotion and meditating on Acyuta within his heart, he should immerse himself.
At that time, all the devotees and even the Bhāgavatas would immerse themselves;
those people who immerse themselves along with the Lord at that moment shall indeed be freed from all taints and attain the supreme goal.
One should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) for the Lord at a naturally manifest site or the like, either at midday, in the afternoon, or during the first part of the night;
no fault arises there from the passing of the auspicious moment (muhūrta).
Then, having placed the image of the deity upon a seat on the bank of the water,
and having offered two pieces of cloth and discarded the bathing garments,
the preceptor himself should take those two cloths and hold them over his head.
Having worshipped them with offerings of water for the hands (*arghya*) and having adorned them especially well,
he should then present a great sacrificial oblation and feed the Brahmins.
He should feed the Brahmins every day, either a thousand or even a hundred.
Having placed the deity upon the vehicle, one should then lead him into the temple;
one should then dismiss the Śakti residing in the image at the sacred site (tīrtha) back into the primary icon (mūlabera).
When evening has arrived, [one should worship] the God of gods, the Lord of the World.
Having especially adorned [the image] with garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth,
the preceptor, having placed it upon a palanquin or similar vehicle together with the two goddesses,
proceeds amidst the auspicious sounds of conchs and other instruments, accompanied by umbrellas, chowries, and banners.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village together with all his attendants— the royal insignia, the retinue, the courtesans, the temple-servants, and the entire household—
he then entered the interior of the palace near the sacrificial altar.
Having offered the *madhuparka*, one should then offer cakes and other foods.
One should offer cool water for libation, betel leaves, and so forth.
After circumambulating the temple of the deity, one should take refuge in the great pavilion.
Having offered [the deity] upon that seat, the preeminent teacher, composed in mind, should worship the God with the *arghya* and other offerings, performing the rites up to the *nīrājana*.
[This is for the sake of] the site, the king, the kingdom, the patron, and the ministers.
Then, gazing at the face of the Lord, he should offer blessings to the subjects, their retinues, and especially to the Vaiṣṇavas.
In the presence of the God, they should all respond with "Om."
Then, one should cause the Lord of the gods to enter the sacrificial hall;
having installed the God there upon the western altar as before,
one should [install] the omnipresent Lord situated in the four locations, beginning with the water-jar (kumbha), in due order.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with abundant food,

he should then offer the bali-oblation to the deities presiding over the doors according to the rules, and having dismissed the deity residing in the sacrificial pit and the one in the mandala into his own heart.
And one should duly dismiss the deities presiding over the doors,
while the preceptor, taking the *karaka* weapon in his own hand, leads forth the festive image preceded by the great water-pot (*mahākumbha*).
Having performed the circumambulation of the house with the [water] held in an unbroken stream,
one should reach the temple and place the festive image facing the original image; then, having worshipped it with offerings such as the *arghya* and other rites.
In due order,
one should sprinkle the pervasive Lord residing in the primary image with water from the pitcher while reciting the Puruṣasūkta; thereafter, one should sprinkle the image for the procession.
One should offer the Śakti residing in the great pitcher (mahākumbha) to the primary image (mūlabera);
one should offer the Śakti residing in the hand-vessels and weapons to the implements.
In the same manner, one should join Vāsudeva and the others to the pedestal (pīṭha) in successive order.
At that time, however, one should especially show honor to the Guru.

With garments such as fine silk (*dukūla*) and other cloths previously offered to the Lord, as well as with various excellent garlands and fragrant substances such as sandalwood, [one should worship]. || 11.372–11.373 ||
The teacher as well, O best of the twice-born, having taken up an unsurpassed garment such as fine linen and having bound it upon his own head like a turban,
and wearing garlands and other ornaments as appropriate, should prostrate himself.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers and having prostrated again and again:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Master, you ought to forgive all that has been previously done by me, whether deficient or excessive. (11.375–376)

Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, he then released the auspicious thread (*kautuka*) from his hand; having mentally transferred the pervasive Lord who had entered the processional image (*yātrāmūrti*),
he then established him in his own place and worshipped him with offerings of water for the feet (*arghya*) and other honors.
Having then offered cakes and sacrificial oblations to the Lord,
and having provided a bed and seat, one should conclude the remainder of the night. On the following day, when dawn has broken, having performed one's bath and daily rites, [one should proceed].
The preceptor, having entered the temple together with the guardians of the images,
and having performed the daily worship of the God of gods up to its conclusion,
[should then perform] the ablution which will be described, whether it be the lowest or the highest.
Having bathed the Lord of Gods with that [water], one should worship Him until the end of the oblation (havis).
When evening has arrived, at the conclusion of the daily worship,
one should stand before the Lord of Gods and perform this petition.

O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, whatever rite has been performed by me for your pleasure, O All-pervading Lord, beginning from the offering of the sprouts and ending with the final purificatory bath of the festival— [11.383]
Likewise, whatever has been performed by other teachers authorized by me,
as well as by other practitioners and various attendants—
for the sake of completing those respective rites and for the pacification of deficiencies or excesses.
"Today, on this day, I have begun to sacrifice to you according to the ritual of the flower-offering; please grant me leave, desiring to show me favor.
Having thus informed the God and obtained his permission, [he proceeded].
The preceptor, having led the Lord— who resides within the festival image— along with the two goddesses to the assembly pavilion, and having placed the Lord upon a golden auspicious throne there,
should adorn him with special ornaments.
Then, one should draw a mandala of flowers before him,
using white, yellow, red, pale-pink,
white, and black flowers— thus with flowers of five colors— and with dark-blue *tulasī* leaves.
Having filled the mandala according to what is pleasing to the eye,
one should place a great pitcher in the northeastern part of the mandala;
and in the four directions of the pavilion, one should place eight door-pitchers.
Having beautifully adorned the pavilion with canopies, banners, and arches,
the preceptor should then perform the rite of the flower-sprout according to the prescribed rule.
Having stretched the lines on the northern part of the mandala as before, he should proceed.
One should place the *pālikā* vessels and other receptacles upon the *śālipīṭha*. According to one’s wealth and desire, one may use either the full set or the *pālikā*s alone.
Having washed the *pālikā*s and other vessels and having adorned them according to the prescribed rule.
One should fill their hole-bases with *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and grass;
one should fill the holes with rice grains according to the prescribed rule.
Having sprinkled them with water for the "hail" (*puṇyāha*), one should worship the presiding deities of the vessels.
One should scatter flowers upon them according to the sequence previously described.
In this case, the preceptor should avoid the worship of the Soma-vessel and the fire-oblation;
thereafter, he should perform the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) upon the primary image and the others in due order.
Having taken the festive image and placed it facing east in the center of a flower mandala adorned with a soft carpet,
O Brahmins, one should place Śrī and Puṣṭi on either side of it.
Having approached the side of the water-pot (kumbha), the best of teachers, as before,
should perform the door-consecration (dvārayāga) after completing the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga).
He should then invoke [the deity] slightly from the primary image (mūlabimba) into the great pot (mahākumbha) and worship it.

One should perform all the worship of the *karakāstra* and other implements as before; then, one should perform the worship of the image (*bimba*) as previously described, ending with the *nīrājana* rite. Having offered the sacrificial gifts (*upahāra*), one should then perform the worship once again.
The water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), as well as the water for sipping (ācāma), perfume, garlands, and a lamp;
then incense, the water for honoring (arhaṇajala), cakes (apūpa), and parched grain (pṛthuka);
the libation (tarpaṇa), the juice extracted from coconut, and likewise the water for sipping again.
One should offer betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume.
Having thus performed the worship of the Lord of the World twelve times,
one should then present the great sacrificial offering and perform the ritual perfuming (*adhivāsana*) with flowers.
One should fill a vessel made of gold or silver with flowers.
Having placed that vessel on a pedestal of rice in front of the deity,
and having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the *puṇyāha* mantra, one should worship it with the root mantra.
Having covered that vessel with a cloth and gone to the sacrificial hall,
one should consecrate the fire-pit and the fire, and worship the Deity in its midst with the perpetual and optional fuel-sticks according to the prescribed rule. 11.407-408ab.
Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* and other rites, he should dismiss the gods and others.
Then, taking the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*), the preceptor, most skilled in mantras, goes into the presence of the deity and offers the oblation to the god. (11.408–409)
Having sprinkled the flowers with the *sampāta* clarified butter immediately thereafter,
one should offer a flower at the feet of the Deity while reciting the *Puṃsūkta*.
Then, one should [offer] the eight-syllable seed-mantras and those beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*), in their proper sequence.
And one should offer divine ornaments, such as the crown and so forth, in due order; likewise, one should offer divine weapons, prosperity, nourishment, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa),
and his retinue, according to the sequence.
The best of preceptors should offer a flower at the feet of the deity;
then, having carefully placed the Lord of the gods of gods upon a vehicle and having adorned him especially with garments, ornaments, and garlands.
Accompanied by all auspicious rites, having circumambulated the Lord of Gods through the first enclosure and so forth, as well as through the village streets,
one should lead him into the temple near the base of the flagstaff.
Having worshipped the deity with the *arghya* and other offerings, and having then presented the sacrificial oblation (*havis*),
one should proceed to the place of the banner and worship the Lord of Birds (*patatrīśa*).
Then, having offered the great oblation, one should worship the Lord of Birds stationed upon the banner.
Having dismissed [the deity], one should lower the banner into one's own heart.
The preceptor himself should take up the banner-staff, the banner-cloth, its pole, its support, as well as the sacrificial implements.

Then, having seated the Lord of the Gods of gods— either in the first enclosure, or in the second enclosure, or in the pavilion upon an auspicious seat— facing either eastward or northward; ||| 11.419 ||
Those gods who had previously arrived for the purpose of attending the festival of the Lord— namely,
the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, the lords of the hosts such as Kumuda,
as well as Brahmā, Rudra, and others, along with the best of the divine sages (11.420–421).
Thus indeed, the devotees of the Blessed One, residing in other lands,
have come to contemplate the welfare of the God of gods.
For their return to their own country, preceded by the permission of the God—
Having performed the dismissal, one should afterwards cause the deity to enter within.
Then, having seated the deity together with the two goddesses facing the primary image,
one should place the great jar between the two.
Having performed the rites beginning with the sprinkling of the pitcher and ending with the removal of the protective cord (*kautuka*),
as previously prescribed according to the scriptures, one should cause the deity to enter within.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the *arghya*, perfumes, and other offerings, one should dismiss [the deity] into the primary image (*mūlabimba*).
Having provided a bed and seat, he should then pass the night in vigilance.
When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, the preceptor, the most skilled in mantras,
should offer the dismissal-oblation (udvāsana-bali) together with his silent attendants.
In the village, having first invoked the groups beginning with Kumuda along with their retinues,
and having gratified them with the offering of oblations, he should dismiss them with special ceremony.
Then, at a great lake, a river, or similar site, the preceptor, most skilled in mantras, [should proceed].
Together with the officiating priests, attendants, and all his followers,
having performed his bath according to the rules and then gone to the temple,
he should perform all the daily worship and other rites in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
The patron, having adorned and worshipped the preceptor with golden ornaments such as bracelets and the like,
with garments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
should give an excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of a hundred gold niṣkas.
Or one may give even more than that, according to the extent of one's wealth.
Or one may give half of that for a middling gift, or half of that again for an inferior gift;
indeed, one should give in accordance with one's resources or according to one's faith.
One should give half of that to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and half of that to the attendants; likewise,
one should satisfy with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) those beginning with the Veda-reciters as well as the most excellent singers, and others according to one's ability.
A sacrifice devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) would be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a fee, however small, should be given according to one's wealth.
At that time, the patron, having adorned the preceptor, [should give it].
Having placed [the image] upon a vehicle adorned with garments, garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings,
accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kāhala trumpets, drums, kettledrums, and paṭaha drums,
provided with parasols and lamps, and attended by singers and others; 11.437.

Having remembered the preceptor as a god, one should cause him to enter his own home. Indeed, he who causes such a festival for the God of gods to be performed attains happiness in this world and is glorified in the next world.
Thus, O twice-born ones, the procedure for the great festival has been correctly declared.
Thus ends [the chapter] titled "The Procedure for the Great Festival" in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
The eleventh chapter;
now the twelfth chapter: Nārada.

Henceforth, O best of sages, I shall proclaim the festivals of the fortnights, the months, and so forth, as well as the spring festival and others; listen! On every twelfth day of each fortnight, and likewise at the beginning of every month, [the rites are performed].
O twice-born ones, on the new moon day, the full moon day, and the following day after the Śravaṇa constellation;
likewise on the days of the incarnations of the God of gods,
on the birth asterisms of the sacrificer and others, and during the two equinoxes of Caitra and other months.
O twice-born ones, at both solstices as well as during the transits [of the sun],
the preceptor should perform a special worship of the God of gods;
this is especially fruitful when performed even before the change of the lunar mansion has occurred.
If there are ten *nāḍīs* on the following day, it will be supremely auspicious;
likewise, when a change of lunar days (*tithi*) occurs, it bestows the highest fruit.
O twice-born ones, this applies whether it be on the eleventh, the new moon, or the twelfth day and so forth.
If even for a mere moment on the following day, that very time shall be auspicious;
O twice-born ones, during the six transits occurring in the northern course [of the sun],
one should worship the Lord within the interval of sixteen nāḍīs after [the transit].
And during the six transits that precede the winter solstice,
one should worship the deity even before the sixteen-nāḍī interval; however,
according to the secondary rule (anukalpa), one should perform it after the sixteen-nāḍī interval.
Having thus understood the constellations and so forth, one should perform the respective worship on those days.
Now, the festival to be performed on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions is described.
O best of men, in ancient times, after performing the daily worship of the God of gods—
Having bathed the Lord according to the rules— whether he is the omnipresent one residing in the primary image (mūlamūrti),
or the one residing in the processional image (yātrāmūrti), or the one whose festive attire is for the ritual bathing—
having led him to the seat of ornaments and having worshipped him according to the prescribed method.
Having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis), one should perform everything— whether ending with the fire-offering (homa) or the recitation (japa)—
especially from the root-mantra onwards for the festival image (utsavakautuka).
Thereafter, having invoked [the deity] slightly into the mobile image (yātrāmūrti) of the Lord...
Having placed him upon a golden vehicle endowed with the splendor of flowers,
and having adorned it most excellently with the aforementioned riches,
they performed a festive circumambulation, duly circling the village.
In front of the temple of the Blessed One, or even before the offering altar,
the Guru should perform worship for the sake of pacifying the exhaustion of the deity:
[offering] water for the guest (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), as well as fragrance, garlands, and lamps.
One should offer incense, as well as water for worship, cakes, and parched grain; likewise, one should present the libation, the juice extracted from coconut, water for sipping,
and betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfumes.
Then one should gratify the Lord with various forms of dance, song, and the like;
likewise, courtesans, temple-servants, and those skilled in instrumental music;
as well as panegyrists and all others, endowed with devotion.
Having circumambulated the deity together with the offering pedestal,
they should bow down with devotion two or four times;
thereafter, they should lead the Lord of the gods of gods into the interior of the temple.
Then, having caused [the deity] to descend from the vehicle and having offered the sandals,
and having seated [him] upon an auspicious throne in the area of the front pavilion,
one should worship with the arghya and other offerings as before and establish [the deity] in his own place.
One should first unite the Śakti that was employed [in the preliminary rite] with the primary image (mūlabimba).
Thus has the festival to be performed on the twelfth day and other such occasions been described, especially during the bright fortnight of the months of Madhu and Mādhava. || 12.23–12.24 ||
O twice-born ones, even on the fourteenth day when the lunar phase is incomplete,
the best of preceptors should perform the water-play for the Lord;
following that water-play, it may last for seven or nine days.

One should observe the festival for five days, or three days, or even for a single day. On the eve of the day the festival begins, at night, the preceptor shall perform the sowing of sprouts and the binding of protective cords according to the prescribed rite.
Starting from the day the festival begins,

one should perform worship at the four locations every day, both morning and evening, according to the prescribed rule. One should also offer the bali offering at both times of day, following the rite described for the daily practice.
O twice-born ones, at midday, after the offering of the bali, they place the Lord, who has entered the processional image,
upon a palanquin together with Śrī and Puṣṭi;
having carried him to the great pavilion, they seat him there upon an auspicious throne.
Having placed [the deity] upon a seat of grain before the Lord,
the most excellent of instructors, having performed the perfuming with powders as previously described,
should worship the Lord with the water for honoring (arghya) and other offerings up to the sacrificial oblation (havis), according to the ritual rules.
Then, having consecrated the Lord, as well as Śrī and Puṣṭi, with the *Śrīsūkta* and with turmeric powder according to the prescribed rite, the preceptor should cause the Lord of Gods,
together with his two goddesses, to be paraded through the streets of the village.
Proceeding clockwise with the aforementioned equipment for the procession,
one should then cause the battle-play of the God and the two Goddesses to take place.
First there shall be a battle of perfumes, and secondly a battle of flowers.
In the third [round] there shall be a powder battle, and in the fourth a battle with oil;
in the fifth there shall be a milk battle, and in the sixth with camphor and saffron;
