in the seventh, however, one should carry out a battle with coconut water.
In the eighth [round], there is a battle with scented water; in the ninth, a water-battle.
From the house to the center of the village, one should engage in playful combat with devotees and followers of the Bhagavata, as well as with courtesans and temple-maidens.
Having thus performed the sport of battle, one should cause the deity to enter within.
During a seven-day festival, one should perform the seven [contests] beginning with the powder-battle;
during a five-day festival, one should perform the five [contests] beginning with the milk-battle.
During a three-day festival, there may be battles with coconut juice and the like;
however, during a one-day festival, one should perform only water-battles.
O best of sages, listen now to the rules for the performance of water-sports.
Or at the beginning of the third enclosure, or even outside the gate-tower,
O best of sages, having dug into the earth to the depth of a man's height and having made it firm on all sides with stones or bricks, || 12.41-42 ||
One should construct a water cistern provided with a series of steps,
or a pavilion (maṇṭapa) or a water-shed (prapā) furnished with four pillars;
having done so, one should fill that cistern from above with pure water.
Having filled the cauldron as before and perfumed it with musk, saffron, and other fragrant substances,
the Guru should thereafter scatter auspicious flowers over it;
having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the separate powders in the sacrificial hall, he should proceed.
Having invoked Śrī into either a sacrificial pit, a consecrated mound, or the fire, the knower of mantras,
having there gratified her according to the rule, should sprinkle [the area] with the residual clarified butter.
Taking that vessel of powder, preceded by the sound of musical instruments,
and having approached the water tank while reciting the declaration of a meritorious day (puṇyāha),
he should pour the powder therein and worship Vasanta there.
Having especially worshipped the world-protectors on all sides,
one should offer oblations in the eight directions preceded by song and instrumental music.
O lords of sages, the consecration in the water-vat is thus described.
One should worship the Lord of Gods together with the two Goddesses in the pavilion as before;
having performed the rites up to the powder-consecration near the water-tank,
one should bring the God there and worship him along with the two Goddesses with the water-offering (arghya) and other offerings.
Accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, musical instruments, and conchs,
and with the chanting of hymns of praise, auspicious recitations, and the sound of the Vedas,
one should perform the immersion there with the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Or else, O Brahmins, the knower of mantras— the most excellent of preceptors— having invoked the deity into the ritual grass-bundle (*kūrca*) or the sandals (*pādukā*), should then cause [the image] to be immersed therein. At that time, the patron, the guardians of the image, the Brahmins, and the foremost Vaiṣṇavas [should perform this].
Ascetics devoted to Brahman should sprinkle them with auspicious water;
likewise, all men and women born of the four castes,
courtesans, temple-servants, and others who play musical instruments.
And they should all sprinkle one another with auspicious waters;
having obtained the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā, they shall attain union with Viṣṇu.
Having placed the Lord upon the vehicle along with those whose garments are still wet from the bath—
Preceded by water-sports and accompanied by the requisites for the procession,
he should cause [the image] to be carried around the village streets for the pleasure of Varuṇa and for the purification of all his subjects.
Then, one should cause the Lord of the gods to enter the interior of the temple; there,
having bathed the deity according to the scriptures with twenty-five jars,
one should worship him especially until the offering of oblations is complete.
And likewise, at the conclusion of each day’s battle, one should perform the ritual bathing in this manner.
On that night, one should perform the rites as before, ending with the sprinkling from the water-pot;
thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
One should satisfy the deities of the images and others with wealth according to the prescribed rule.
Thus has the excellent Vasantotsava been described in brief.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the Damanikotsava.
One should perform the worship of the four locations and so forth, as in the Pavitrārohaṇa rite.
Likewise, one should provide the ornaments, beginning with the most excellent, using *damanaka* flowers;
these should be arranged according to their number and in accordance with what is beautiful.
Having placed twenty-five jars, one should perform the consecration:
first with the jar [inscribed] "Nārāyaṇa alone," and second with the jar [inscribed] "of him who abides within meditation."
Then again, "Nārāyaṇa" is for the third [vessel];
then again, "Nārāyaṇa" is for the fourth;
and "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads" is for the fifth jar.
"Lord of the universe, the Self-sovereign"—thus indeed from the sixth pitcher;
"Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman"—thus indeed with the seventh;
and "Whatever there is in this world"—thus indeed from the eighth pitcher.

One should worship with the ninth verse, "The infinite, imperishable sage" (anantam avyayaṃ kavim). Then, with the tenth verse, "And thus, [the earth] a span thick," and with the eleventh verse, "Continuous with its veins."
With the twelfth [verse], "In its midst is a great fire," he indeed causes his own body to heat up;
with the thirteenth, "He torments his own body";
and with the fourteenth, "Standing in the midst of dark clouds."
"In the middle of that crest" is with the fifteenth [verse];
"of the whole of Viśin" is with the sixteenth.
One should perform the consecration with the jars situated in the outer enclosure.
By that which is situated in the east, it is said that there is no external covering;
by that which resides in the fire (southeast), it arose from the navel-lotus;
by that which is situated in the southern direction, one who has applied the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) attains the Supreme.
On the right arm, however, it was taken up by Viṣṇu in the form of a Brahmin, saying "O Brahmin," while he was situated in the west,
saying "They eat what has been taken by me";
and in the form of the wind, saying "Viṣṇu is the Lord whose essence is the Puruṣa."
"Imām mahopaniṣadam" (This Great Upaniṣad) is uttered by the one situated at Soma;
"Om" is the first name, uttered by the one situated at Īśāna;
and "Puruṣo ha vai Vāsudevaḥ" (Vāsudeva is indeed the Supreme Person) is uttered by the one situated in the center.
Or else, having consecrated him in sequence with the sixteen mantras of the Puruṣasūkta using the pitchers situated in the outer enclosure,
one should [consecrate him] with the previously mentioned mantras from the Brahma-sūkta, in groups of two.
Having consecrated [the deity] in sequence with the jars situated within the inner enclosure,
one should finally sprinkle [him] with the three remaining jars and the central jar.
Having set out nine jars mixed with the powder of *rajanī* (turmeric), [one should proceed].
Having honored them with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should visualize heaps of powdered *rajanī* possessing a radiance equal to the rays of the [deity's] wheel,
and consecrate [the disciple] with them for the sake of dispelling all obstacles and for the fulfillment of all [attainments]. (12.81–82)
On his right arm, O Brahmin, he [inscribed] with the mantra facing eastward, "iti";
with the mantra facing the fire (south), "suṣaṇam iti"; and with the mantra facing the south, "prate viṣṇo abjacakre."
With the verse beginning "By these, we [serve] Urukrama," he should apply [the mark] with his hand moving toward the south;
with "He who has assumed the upward-mark" and "He who has made the wheel," toward the west;
and with "The purifier" and "Agni," toward the northwest.
With the mantra "The foot is pure, spread out," addressed to Soma;
and with "The radiant gate of the world," addressed to Rudra—
by means of these eight mantras and others likewise belonging to Sudarśana.
Having bathed him with the central pitcher and sprinkled him with pure waters,
[he performed the rite] with the *Brahma-sūktas* previously mentioned found within the *Mahopaniṣads*,
as well as with the four mantras of the *Puruṣasūkta* and likewise with the sixteen [mantras].
With the two Brāhmaṇas of the six syllables of Vāsudeva,
and with the four pervasive mantras beginning with Oṃ and ending with the purifier (pavitra),
one should bathe the Lord with a thousand streams according to the prescribed rite.
Or else, O twice-born ones, one should perform the entire ablution with the eight-syllable mantra;
then, having worshipped in sequence with all other enjoyments as before,
using all the previously mentioned mantras or the root mantra.

Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) especially with sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) soaked in the three sweets (trimadhu), one should then perform the offering of *damanaka* flowers according to the prescribed rite.
Whatever has not been mentioned here shall be exactly as in the ritual for the sacred thread (*pavitrāroha*).
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme Viśākhā festival.
O best of the twice-born, when the sun is situated in Taurus, that which occurs on the full moon day—whether it be joined with the Viśākhā asterism or not—is [the occasion for this]. 12.93–94.
On that fourteenth day, provided it is not pierced [by the fifteenth], one should perform the festival;
[offering] mango fruits and the like,
as well as coconut fruits, grapes, dates and so forth, and even citrons.
And other suitable items, O twice-born ones, whether obtained as they were found,
having brought all of them together and placed them in vessels, O twice-born ones,
he should set those vessels upon the heads of his attendants.
Placing Viṣvaksena at the head, accompanied by the sound of musical instruments,

one should circumambulate the village and cause [the deity] to enter the interior of the temple. Thereafter, having placed the vessels of fruit in the kitchen and other such areas, [one should proceed].
By pure Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas, filled with great joy,
their mouths covered with cloths and free from the fickleness of the tongue,
one should have the skins removed so that they are fit for the removal of the outer skin.
One should clean those things that require cleaning according to their actual state;
likewise, one should wash those things that require washing with pure water.
Mango fruits [should be cleaned] with milk mixed with jaggery.
One should cook it with pieces of coconut and black pepper;
likewise, one should mix it with the powders of cardamom and camphor.
One should thus prepare the great sacrificial oblations, such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and cakes (apūpa).
Whether by day or by night, at the conclusion of the daily worship,
one should lead the Lord— who is preceded by the mantra-seat— to the bathing seat.
Having bathed Puruṣottama with twenty-five jars, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped [the deity] on the ornamented seat, one should then lead him to the food seat.
Having offered the great oblation— such as milk-rice, mangoes, and other fruits—
to the God of gods, one should present betel leaves and other such items.

One should cause that prasāda to be given to the artisans and the devotees of Viṣṇu. Then, having placed the festival image together with Śrī and Puṣṭi upon a vehicle, one should especially adorn it with garments and other ornaments.
Having led [the image] clockwise around the village accompanied by all auspicious rites, one should then bring it inside the temple and install it in its proper place. Thereafter,
the patron should satisfy the preceptor and others with sacrificial fees and other gifts.
Thus has the procedure for the Viśākhā festival been proclaimed.
Now, O eminent sages, hear the ritual for the Plava festival;
one should perform it during any one of the three seasons beginning with Śiśira.
On either the bright or the dark fortnight, during the festival of the Lord of Gods' boat,
on the birth-star of the sacrificer or even on the birth-star of the gods,
one should perform the ascent of the boat, which brings about the prosperity of the king and his kingdom.
In accordance with that lunar mansion, the festival should last for seven days, nine days,
five days, three days, or even a single day.
On the day before the commencement of the festival, one should perform the ritual of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having performed the binding of the protective thread according to the rules,
the best of preceptors should perform the worship of the four locations, accompanied by the offering of oblations, every day at two times starting from the day of commencement.
At the beginning and at the end, one should bathe the Lord of Gods daily according to the lower or higher path;
on the final day, the mounting of the boat (uḍupa) should be performed.
And every day at midday, having placed the God together with the Goddess upon a vehicle and having especially adorned them with garments and other ornaments,
one should circumambulate the village and bring them to the shore of the lake.
There, having specially placed the God of gods upon an auspicious seat within that beautifully fashioned, divine, and most enchanting pavilion,
and having worshipped him with abundant offerings of water for the feet and with a great sacrificial oblation; || 12.119 ||

Then, one should cause the Lord of the Gods of gods to enter the interior of the temple. On the day of ascending the boat as well, having especially propitiated the Lord of the universe on the shore of the lake with offerings ending in the oblation, [one should perform the rites].
On a Svastika, a square, a circle, or even a lake-like reservoir,
provided it is surrounded by stairs and adorned with four gates,
and further embellished in the four directions with very lofty gate-towers (gopuras).
In the divine central pavilion, filled with pure water,
a celestial raft had been prepared, reinforced with wooden planks,
equipped with numerous pillars, and made secure with iron bolts.
Having a form like a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) or indeed in the shape of a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*),
consisting of two, three, or even four or five stories,
and adorned with various canopies and flower garlands.
It was adorned all around with mirrors, chowries, and various kinds of banners;
with coconuts, clusters of betel nuts, plantains,
and fragrant roots, as well as with bells.
O twice-born ones, having sprinkled the lake water with the *puṇyāha* water,
and having purified it through the rites of burning and nourishing so that it becomes pure water,
the preceptor should invoke the Ocean of Milk and worship it with the *arghya* and other offerings.
Having invoked the Lord of Serpents upon the raft and [the deities] such as Kumuda and others all around,
and having worshipped them thoroughly with offerings of water (arghya), perfumes, and so forth, one should invoke and worship [the deity] within the pitcher.
Then, having offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Ananta-mantra, one should proceed.
The most excellent preceptor should sprinkle that raft with water from the pitcher;
having thus consecrated the raft during an auspicious moment,
the Guru should cause the Lord of Gods to ascend the raft together with the two Goddesses.
The preceptor, the practitioner, the initiated attendants,
those devoted to service, as well as other Vaiṣṇavas and Vedic reciters,
should stand around the deity; for others, however, there shall be a separate boat.
But others who do not touch that raft which consists of the remainder— namely,
the bards, the courtesans, and those others who are players of musical instruments—
they, each mounted on separate rafts, should likewise perform dancing and other such acts.
Then, with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, and with the chanting of the Vedas on all sides,
one should gladden the Lord with showers of flowers and various entertainments;
one should perform three, five, or seven circumambulations.
Then, the best of teachers should bring the deity to the pavilion in the middle of the lake;
having worshipped the deity there with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites,
he should likewise present the offering of parched grain, cakes, and coconut juice.
Having offered libations, betel-leaf,
and mouth-fresheners to the God of gods, and having satisfied the attendants with betel and other offerings thereafter, [he should remain] until the setting of the sun.
Having gratified the God with various diversions and led him back to the boat,
and having reached the shore, he should then help the Lord of Gods descend from the boat;
he should then lead the God, after circumambulating the village, into the interior of the temple.
Having first performed the daily worship as well as the special sacrifice,
one should carry out everything according to the rules up to the sprinkling of the jar, just as before;
the patron and the preceptor should likewise satisfy each other with sacrificial fees and other offerings.

Thus, O twice-born ones, the ritual for the festival of the boat has been declared in brief. Now, the procedure for that known as the Āgrayaṇa is briefly described. Specifically, it should be performed in the month of Āṣāḍha under the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī, and especially under Puṣya.
O twice-born ones, on the fifth or the seventh day of the month of Māgha,
when an auspicious moment has arrived, one should carry out the collection of grain;
for that purpose, one should appoint a commander of the army, such as Tārkṣya or Māruti.
Having placed [the image] upon a palanquin together with all his attendants,
the preceptor and the patron, preceded by the sound of musical instruments,
reached the sacred precinct; there the Guru caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made.

Having worshipped the field with the *arghya* and other offerings using the *bhū-mantra*, the knower of mantras should also sprinkle the sacrificial blade (*lavitra*) and worship it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). Then, he should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapālas*) on all sides.
For the increase of the field, the preceptor,
observing silence at an auspicious moment, should offer curd-rice or milk-porridge with the root mantra; thereafter, the harvest of grains should be carried out by the farmers in this manner.
Having caused loads of grain and various fruits to be prepared, and having gathered many people, he then, accompanied by the sounds of divine drums and other instruments,
placed Viṣvaksena at the head and performed a circumambulation of the village.
Having reached the temple of the deity and entered within the palace,
one should show a small amount of grain in the right hand of the deity.
Afterwards, one should dry it in the sun and then perform the threshing.
In that place, having smeared it all around with cow-dung and water,
and having adorned the pestle and the mortar with lime powder,
one should wash them with pure water and worship them with the *arghya*, scents, and other offerings.
Having placed the grains in the mortar at an auspicious moment,
one should have them threshed along with the singing of auspicious songs and the sound of all musical instruments,
accompanied by Brahmin women whose husbands are living, or by groups of temple maidens.
Having removed the husks with a winnowing basket, one should wash them with pure water.
Having cleansed them all once more, they should be mixed with molasses,
combined with black pepper and cumin, and provided with coconut fruit.
Having prepared the primary image and other icons, and having worshipped them especially,
one should then offer them to the fire and satisfy the Lord.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should then offer seven fuel-sticks (*samidh*) along with rice grains.
Afterwards, having reported everything, one should cause it to be offered to the Guru and others.
Thus, one should perform annually for the God of gods this rite called Āgrayaṇa, which is superior to a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Now, O best of sages, listen to the ritual for the swing festival (ḍolotsava),
whether during the period of the sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa) or even its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana),
especially on the fifth or the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
One should commence the festival on the eleventh, the tenth, the twelfth, or the full moon day; it may last for seven days, nine days,
five days, or even three days, according to one's available means.
On the night preceding the commencement of the festival,
the most excellent of preceptors should duly perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) and the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha),
whether in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure and so forth.
Or outside the city gate, in some very beautiful place,
one should construct a pavilion for the sake of the swing festival (ḍolotsava),
provided with thirty-two pillars or twenty-four.
One should beautifully decorate a pavilion provided with sixteen pillars and equipped with four doors, using canopies of various colors,
as well as variegated silken cloths and strings of pearls.
With various flower garlands, mirrors, chowries, and the like;
with diverse and beautiful banners, as well as clusters of blossoms;
with bells, heavy loads of fruit, and rows of lamps.
Having smeared the ground inside the pavilion with musk, saffron, camphor, and the like,
and having especially adorned the ground with lime powder and other materials,
as well as with flowers and auspicious unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having scattered divine incenses and perfumed [the area] on all sides,
he should prepare a swing made of gold, silver, copper, or wood, according to his preference,
possessing the characteristics as prescribed, whether circular or square.
Or even one resembling a celestial chariot (vimāna), adorned with floors according to one's desire,
provided with four pillars or perhaps endowed with two;
likewise decorated with various canopies, garlands, mirrors, and banners.
Having adorned it most exquisitely, one should suspend it within the pavilion with ropes fashioned of iron,
or with threads of linen or cotton,
as appropriate; then, the best of preceptors [should proceed].
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having consecrated the swing with mantras,
the knower of mantras should worship Ananta in the middle of the plank of the swing;
and likewise, he should worship the group of eight beginning with Dharma, or the group of four, upon the feet [of the swing].
Having worshipped the array of Garuḍas upon the pillars in the proper sequence,
one should likewise worship the four Vedas upon the cords in due order,
as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and the Vedāṅgas.

O best of sages, one should worship the pervasive four mantras in the eight directions upon the surface of the board, and one should fully worship them at the feet [of the image]. Having worshipped Sāvitrī on the banners and likewise the Vyāhṛtis on the umbrellas, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped the Praṇava on the banners and likewise the vowels and consonants on the arches, and having fashioned a swing consisting of speech,
one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the directions around the swing in their respective quarters.
On the front part of the swing, or elsewhere as prescribed by rule,
having placed a great jar upon a seat of grain accompanied by eight smaller jars,
one should invoke and worship the deities mentioned for the swing there.
And one should worship Indra and the other deities in the eight secondary jars (upakumbha).
Having consecrated the fire in either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as before,
one should invoke those gods there in their proper sequence with their respective mantras.

Having offered eight separate oblations of clarified butter and other substances, the most excellent preceptor performs the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and other rites; then the Guru dismisses the fire and,
at an auspicious moment, sprinkles that cradle with the clarified butter from the residual drops.
Having sprinkled [the swing] with water from a pitcher, one should worship it especially.
One should offer an oblation (bali) to Indra and the other deities in all directions around the swing.
Having thus consecrated the swing, one should perform the festival of the swing for the Lord.
Accompanied by worship at the four locations and provided with the offering of bali,
and endowed with the previously mentioned ablution (snāna) both at the commencement and the conclusion;
having performed the daily evening worship as well as the special sacrifice (viśeṣayajana).
Having placed the Lord, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi, upon the vehicle,
one should circumambulate the temple and lead him to the side of the swing amidst the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, and the resonant music of auspicious instruments.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction of stars, one should place the Lord upon the palanquin;

there, one should worship the Lord of the World with offerings presented on the decorated throne, including all enjoyments up to the rite of *nīrājana*. Then, one should place the Lord upon the seat for the meal.
Having brought the divine Mahāhavis and the sacrificial cakes (apūpa),
and having presented the offerings such as the libations (tarpaṇa) ending with betel (tāmbūla),
the best of the twice-born should take hold of the ropes of the swing from the four directions.
Then the supreme teacher should move [the vessel] very slowly,
praising the God of gods with loud voices using the Puruṣasūkta and other hymns; meanwhile,
[the vessel] should be infused with musk, saffron, camphor, and other fragrances.
Having especially offered divine fragrance to the god,
they should fan him particularly with palm-leaf fans and chowries,
as well as with various flower garlands and showers of gold and jewels.
O best of the twice-born, at that time one should adorn the God of gods with various offerings and likewise provide water for sipping (ācamana).
One should also present betel leaf accompanied by mouth-perfumes.
Then the courtesans should perform various dances;
at that time, they should gratify the Lord of the God of Gods with the sounds of lutes and flutes, with various songs, and likewise with diverse hymns of praise.
Let all the panegyrists, strengthened by devotion to the Blessed One, offer praise;
thus one should satisfy Him with various other services as well.
Those who behold the Lord of Śrī at the moment the swing is being moved—
Having attained their desires here, they shall reach the supreme goal.
Then the preceptor, having placed the deity upon a vehicle together with the two goddesses,
and having performed a circumambulation of the temple, should cause him to enter the interior of the palace.
Having thus performed the festival for one day, three days, five days, seven days, or nine days, always at the evening hour according to the rule, he should,
as before, perform at the conclusion of the festival the final consecration with the water-pot (kumbha).
"The patron should worship the teacher as before, in the same manner as previously described.
(12.204) Thus, the procedure for the swing festival has been briefly demonstrated.
Now, one should perform the festival of sleep on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha. (12.205)
From that day until the same day of the month known as Kaumuda,
the Lord of the World, gratified by his asceticism, enters into yogic sleep for the sake of protecting the world. (12.206) He resorts to yogic sleep for the purpose of guarding the universe.

One should perform the occasional rites (*naimittika*) month by month, as well as the annual festivals accompanied by special sacrifices, provided they do not conflict with the completion of all [other] obligations; one should not perform any other occasional or optional (*kāmya*) rite during the four-month period.

Having undertaken their chosen vow, those four should be conducted [there] by those proficient in devotion to the Blessed One; regarding this, it is said: "O lords of sages, [this should be done] in front of the temple or elsewhere. (12.209)
One should construct a bedchamber provided with all ornaments,
equipped with all necessary utensils, and adorned with couches and the like;
or else, it may be in the inner sanctum of Viṣṇu, to the right of the primary image.
O Brahmins, having gathered all the necessary materials on the tenth day, O best of the twice-born, one should prepare the bed along with all its appurtenances.
On the night of the eleventh day, one should worship the Lord in four locations.
Having reached the sacrificial pavilion, one should pass the night in vigilance.
When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, having performed his bath and daily rites,
and having first performed the regular worship as well as the worship of the four stations (catussthānārcana).

Then, having bid farewell to the Lord of Gods, he should worship the primary image— from the water-pot, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit— with the offering of water (arghya), with fragrant flowers, and with most auspicious incense;
and from that [image], [he should transfer the deity] to the couch-throne.
Or, having invoked the deity together with Śrī and Bhūmi upon the pedestal (kūrca),
and having bathed, adorned, and worshipped him with the final oblation,
one should perform the daily worship of the Lord when the onset of night has arrived.
Then, having led him to the bedchamber and performed the auspicious rites for the bed,
one should seat the Lord facing east upon a golden throne in the western part of the sleeping area and worship him with offerings until the end of the oblation.

Having performed the fire sacrifice according to the rules and having completed the offering of the oblation, he should invoke the Infinite One (Ananta) upon the couch and, having laid the deity there according to the ritual,
[he should recite] before him the observances enjoined by the scriptures.
Having resolved upon four months until the time of the deity’s awakening,
one intent on the performance of the vow should worship the deity every day.
All Vaiṣṇavas indeed should then perform this supreme vow from that time onward.
And he should daily gratify the Lord with services for His bed and personal attendants.
Thus, O twice-born ones, when two months have passed and it is the month of Bhādrapada,
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, at the onset of night, the preeminent teacher [should perform the rite].
One should first perform the special sacrifice and then carry out the ritual turning over;
thereafter, O twice-born ones, one should perform the awakening of the Lord who is lying on his bed,
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika.
On the tenth day, having gathered all the necessary materials as before,
one should especially worship the Lord stationed in his four places on the night of the eleventh day, and pass the night in a vigil.
During the *brāhma-muhūrta* on the twelfth lunar day, one should awaken the Lord in his form as Mantra,

having first performed the daily worship (*nityārcana*) as well as the worship of the four locations (*catuḥsthānārcana*). Then, one should especially worship the Lord in his form as the Reclining One (*śayanamūrti*).
One should cause the rites beginning with the bath and ending with the oblation to enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
One should dismiss the mantra residing in the bed-chamber image (śayanamūrti) back to the primary image (mūlamūrti).
Then, the festival image (cautsavabimba), adorned together with the two goddesses, [should be brought forth].
Having placed [the deity] upon a chariot or similar vehicle along with the requisites for the procession,
and having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should settle [the deity] in its own place.
Then, one should dismiss the deity from the water-pot, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit.

Then all those dwelling in the hermitage should perform the ritual dismissal of their vows. O best of the twice-born, the patron should then satisfy the preceptors and other practitioners, as well as the Brahmins, with gold according to his capacity.
Thus has been described the sleeping and the awakening of the Lord;
while the Lord of the World remains in sleep during the middle of the four-month period,
one should perform the Pavitrārohaṇa rite, which brings supreme satisfaction to Ananta.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fortnightly Festival," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
O best of sages, listen to [the account of] Nārada and the birth festival of Kṛṣṇa.
This birthday of Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed to be of two kinds:

Janmāṣṭamī and Jayantī; the distinction between them is now described. Jayantī occurs when the eighth lunar day is joined with the rising of the moon, provided it is not touched by even a fraction of the seventh lunar day.

Even if it is devoid of Rohiṇī, that is indeed remembered as Janmāṣṭamī; it is considered primary when the sun enters Leo, or even if it occurs in the month of Śrāvaṇa alone. On that day, the worship of Viṣṇu bestows the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha.

If one is free from desire, it certainly bestows the fruit of liberation. O best of the twice-born, even at sunrise, a Rohiṇī that is not pierced by the seventh lunar mansion (Śravaṇa) or by Kṛttikā, even by a single digit, [is auspicious].
Whether accompanied by the eighth lunar day or even without the eighth,
likewise whether joined with Wednesday or even without it—
that [day] is called Jayantī, for it conquers all that is inauspicious.
If, on the eighth, ninth, or even the tenth lunar day,

even a single minute fraction of Rohiṇī is found unpenetrated (by the preceding nakṣatra), it must be accepted by the Vaiṣṇavas; however, if it is penetrated, it must never be accepted by the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
Or rather, Mṛgaśīrṣa should be taken, since there is an absence of a pure lunar mansion;
for Jayantī is primarily in Bhādrapada, or even when the moon is in Leo.
O best of sages, when two lunar mansions occur in that month—
One should perform the festival on that very [lunar day], which destroys great sins.
If Rohiṇī is pierced by [the previous nakṣatra] later [in the night], one should perform it on the preceding [day] alone.
In this very manner, the avoidance of the piercing of a saṅkrānti is also recommended.

If the yoga of the transit occurs during the day, one should abandon the Jayantī occurring before it; but if the yoga occurs at night, one should abandon even that which is endowed with the yoga [if it occurs after].
O best of sages, if there is a piercing of both transits on the two Jayantīs—

Or one should perform the festival even earlier, under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa. Thus is the determination for the Jayantī of Rāma, as well as for Narasiṃha and Varāha; the same decision applies to the Jayantī of Vāmana and the others as well.
Having especially fasted there on the day of Jayantī, one should perform worship at night; the procedure for that is stated here:
having completed the daily rites in the evening, the best of teachers [should proceed].
Having reached the temple of the Blessed One and first performed the daily worship,
one should construct a pavilion in front of the palace;
or, if a pavilion has already been constructed previously, one should especially decorate it.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with banners and archways,
and beautified on all sides by various and variegated canopies;
it was surrounded by great curtains of exquisite, patterned silk.
It was resplendent with strings of pearls and various flower garlands;
it was beautifully adorned with plantains, rose-apples, citrons, coconuts, and other fruits, as well as with pillars of banana trees and clusters of betel-nut fruit.
Adorned with mirrors and rows of lamps, perfumed with incense,
and its floor anointed with saffron, agallochum, and musk;
it was beautifully decorated all around with various patterns made from lime powder and other materials.
In the center, it is beautified by a seat adorned with shimmering divine jewels.
Having thus first decorated the pavilion,
one should then bring the image of Kṛṣṇa and place it upon an auspicious seat.
Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly with the *arghya* and other offerings, and then, by his permission,
one should place a flower-sprout and perform the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandha*).
One should then set down a great water-pot (*mahākumbha*) in the northeast quarter of the deity.
Having drawn the maṇḍala in front according to the prescribed rule,
one should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front of the pavilion.
Having thus completed everything, the preceptor [should remain] until the rising of the moon.
Chanting the eight-syllabled mantra on the right side of the Lord,
he should cause the majesty of Kṛṣṇa and other Vaiṣṇava narratives to be sung;
with songs, dances, and diversions, he should gratify the Lord of the worlds.
When the lord of the night has risen at the time of the world-lord’s birth,
one should worship Kṛṣṇa in the water-pot and the mandala according to the prescribed rite;
then, having worshipped the God in the image, [one should perform] the final part of the mantra-seat.
One should bathe the deity with eighty-one jars, preceded by a fire oblation (homa),
or one may bathe him with twenty-five jars according to the prescribed rule. Having brought him to the seat of ornaments, one should worship him especially.
Having performed the rites ending with the *nīrājana* ceremony, one should then lead [the deity] to the seat for the meal.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should present the formal honor (*arhaṇa*).
Then, having offered the *madhuparka*, as well as fresh butter and sugar.
Cow’s milk mixed with ghee, various kinds of fruits,
and offerings such as flattened rice (pṛthuka) along with jaggery and sugar-candy; likewise,
with black gram, mung beans, sesame, barley, curd, honey, clarified butter, and milk.
Especially prepared with turmeric, cumin, cardamom, and other spices;
various kinds of edible foods cooked with cow’s ghee; the eight types of food in their proper order; and excellent, well-boiled milk. (13.34–35)
Having offered cool, refreshing water, especially various drinks, as well as food to be chewed, eaten, licked,
and drunk in great abundance to the God of gods, the best of preceptors should offer it up to the measure of the Mother.
Having offered betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume,
and having then completed the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña), one should go near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and,
upon the fire established there, arrange the yoga-seat (yogapīṭha).
Having invoked Kṛṣṇa into the center of that [fire] and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the knower of mantras,

having performed seven oblations of sacrificial fuel (samidh), should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Then, the preceptor, having dismissed the deity, should dismiss the fire of the fire-altar.
Then, having performed the offering of the oblation to the God of gods,
one should especially perform the offering of the *arghya*, which bestows all fruits.
I shall now describe that procedure on the ground before the Lord.
Then, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should fashion a very beautiful circular shape,
decorating it with lime powder, perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and fruits.
Within that mandala, one should worship the Moon together with Rohiṇī.
Then, O twice-born ones, one should indeed pay homage to him with this mantra:
"O Lord of the Moonlight, salutations to you; salutations to you, O Lord of the luminaries. Salutations to you, O beloved of Rohiṇī; salutations be to you, O jar of nectar. (13.43-44)
Having thus paid homage to the Moon, one should thereafter offer the *arghya* oblation;
having filled a conch with water mixed with cow’s milk,
one should worship the Moon at the front of the conch and worship Kṛṣṇa at its base.
Taking a conch shell along with flowers, fruits, and sandalwood paste in his two hands, and touching the ground with his knees, he should present the *arghya* offering to the Moon:
"O you who were born from the Ocean of Milk, O you who arose from the eye of Atri! (13.46–47)
"O Moon, together with Rohiṇī, accept this water-offering from me.
Thus is the offering of water to the Moon, which causes the satisfaction of Kṛṣṇa,
delights all the gods, and brings about the growth of all crops.
Then, O twice-born ones, one should indeed offer the *arghya* to Kṛṣṇa with this mantra:
"Born for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa, for the removal of the earth's burden, for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas, and for the establishment of Dharma. (13.49–13.50)
"For the destruction of the Kauravas and for the slaying of the Daityas,
O Hari, together with Devakī, accept this *arghya* offered by me.
Thus is the offering of *arghya* to Kṛṣṇa, which bestows prosperity upon the king and the kingdom.
It brings about all prosperity and accomplishes the welfare of the entire world.

Or rather, the sacrificer should likewise offer the *arghya* to the Lord of the Universe for the sake of attaining all desired goals in this world and for the attainment of happiness in the hereafter.
At that time, for the satisfaction of the deity, the patron should especially give cows, land, gold, and other gifts many times to the preceptor and the others.
Then, with various offerings such as betel-leaf and the like, the preceptor—
One should propitiate the Lord of Śrī with recitations, hymns of praise, and other such acts. Then, one should divide the offered food, edibles, and so forth into four parts.
The preceptor himself should take one part, and from the remaining three, [the others should take their portions].
Having satisfied the image-worshippers (mūrtipās), the Vaiṣṇavas, and other devotees who are the best among the Bhāgavatas,
one should then satisfy them all with betel leaves and other offerings.
One should then dismiss the deity residing in the jar and the deity residing in the mandala, as previously described.
Then the preceptor should have a bed prepared for the God of gods;
having fashioned a beautiful swing made of jewels in a lovely pavilion,
it should be provided with soft pillows and cotton, and suspended by golden ropes.
Adorned with golden bells, draped with hanging strings of pearls, scented with musk, saffron, and other perfumes, and fumigated with incense—
there, having worshipped the Lord Ananta, the preceptor should cause [the image] to be mounted.
One should worship the Lord there with beds, seats, and enjoyments.
Having thus performed the festival lasting for one day ending with the laying down on the bed,
the preceptor should then perform the concluding sacrifice (anuyāga) together with the Vaiṣṇavas.
"O twice-born ones, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) for Vaiṣṇavas is prescribed at the conclusion of the festival;

or rather, the breaking of the fast should be performed on the following day with the desire for its fruit. Then, during the remainder of the night, the preceptor [should act] in the presence of the deity."
Accompanied by devoted Vaiṣṇavas, he should cause the Vaiṣṇava stories to be sung;
he should pass the night with songs, dances, laughter, and keeping a vigil.
Then at dawn, the preceptor, having performed his bath and completed his daily rites, [should proceed].
Having raised the deity according to the rules, one should perform the daily worship;
one should especially honor the deity with rites beginning with the ritual bath and ending with the offering of oblations (havis).
Then, having adorned Kṛṣṇa with various garments and ornaments, [one should proceed].
Having mounted [the image] upon a divine elephant, or a horse, or in a palanquin, or even in a chariot— having secured it and adorned it especially—
one should perform a festival for the God of gods by circumambulating the village.
With four pillars made of various carved woods, enchanting,
adorned with canopies of variegated cloth, and provided with fruits and sprouts;
with milk-pots suspended from their centers and accompanied by vessels of fresh butter.
Then there were various arched gateways adorned with vessels of curd,
along with variegated banners and flags, hundreds of flower garlands,
canopies, clusters of fruit, plantain trunks, and the like.
Adorned and sprinkled with divine water of saffron,
decorated with powdered lime, and strewn with flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
O best of the twice-born, when the pathways have been perfumed with divine incenses,
one should then lead the God of gods slowly and gracefully,
accompanied by umbrellas, banners, and flags, as well as by bards, courtesans, and others.
With the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas, by devoted and most excellent devotees of the Lord,
who were scattering oil and the powder of turmeric upon one another,
as well as fresh butter, curd, milk, flowers, and so forth.
Some were throwing [objects], some laughing, and some devouring;
others were satisfying supplicants with fresh butter, ghee, and the like,
while giving betel-leaf and lime-powder to the city women.

With the scents of flowers and saffron being scattered by the crying cowherd boys who had raised their hands, and while breaking vessels of curds and other foods on the ground before Kṛṣṇa, [they honored] the imperishable Kṛṣṇa.
Drinking milk, curd, and other such things, splashing one another,
tasting fresh butter, and throwing it about in many ways among themselves;
climbing upon the pillars of the archways and dancing with repeated roars.
By those born of the Ābhīra clan, who were engaged in the service of Kṛṣṇa’s attendants,
[the cows] were repeatedly struck with sticks as they stood at the vessels;
and at every step, they drank the streams flowing from the vessels.
Thus, with devotees delighted in play through such diversions as these,
having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should cause [the deity] to enter within the temple;
having led the Lord to the assembly pavilion, [one should place him] upon a golden throne.
Having installed [the deity] and worshipped it with various offerings,
and with services such as betel and other articles, one should cause the Lord to enter within;
this may be done for one day, three days, five days, seven days, or nine days.
For a fortnight or even for a month, one should thus satisfy the Lord with festivals;
whether independent or dependent, one should worship Kṛṣṇa in this manner.
In the absence of an image of Kṛṣṇa, [one should worship him] as situated in that particular temple.
One should worship the Lord with devotion, especially on the Jayantī day;
likewise, one should properly worship Nṛsiṃha, Rāma, Varāha, Vāmana,
and the others on their respective birthdays with special ablutions.
One should worship the Lord with a great oblation in four locations:
in the water-pot, in the mandala, in the image, and in the fire.
One should perform the sacrifice according to the primary ritual procedure; however, in the secondary procedure, one may use the mandala alone.
One should perform the sacrifice in the pitchers and other vessels, or one may perform it in the image and the fire.
He who thus causes this supreme Jayantī festival to be celebrated with devotion shall, having accomplished all desired objects in this world, attain the state of union (sāyujya).
Furthermore, O best of sages, I shall describe the ritual for the festival of Vīra-lakṣmī, which grants all perfections and should be performed in the month of Āśvayuja. Indeed,
it may be observed even on the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of that month.

One should perform the festival of the Śrīdevī on the unpenetrated ninth day; or, according to the requirements of that day, one should perform the festival of the new moon. Indeed, if the lunar day is lost, one should begin the festival on the new moon (amāvāsyā).
O twice-born ones, during the festival of Vṛddhi, one should perform the celebration for nine days beginning from the second day,
or for seven days, five days, three days, or even just one day;
one should perform this festival of Lakṣmī with the desire for its fruits.
The Vaiṣṇava festival is said to last nine days, while the Ārṣaka lasts seven;
the Aindraka is said to last five days, and the Śaiva is declared to last three. The Brāhma festival lasts one day; thus it is proclaimed as being of five kinds.
The Brāhma [festival] is indeed for the sake of attaining Brahman; the Śaiva destroys disease;
the Aindra is for the purpose of destroying famine; the Ārṣa bestows the prosperity of the kingdom;
and the Vaiṣṇava is declared to be the festival that grants the fruits of devotion and liberation.
On the night preceding the commencement of the festival,
the most excellent of preceptors should duly perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) and the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha),
both at the beginning and at the conclusion, according to the inferior and superior methods respectively.
The preceptor should bathe the goddess Śrī with the Śrī-mantra itself;
he should perform the special worship every day at the conclusion of the daily ritual,
according to the rules, upon the water-jar, the mandala, the image, and also in the fire.
In this regard, O twice-born ones, that specific distinction which is now being described:
one should worship the goddess Śrī in the central pitcher during the worship of the jars (kumbha),
and one should worship Sudarśana in the vardhanī vessel exactly as before.
O twice-born ones, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, Māyā, and Upakumbhā— these eight should be worshipped in order, starting from the east, according to the principle of origin and dissolution.
O best of sages, listen now to the procedure for the worship of the doors therein.
One should worship Vāstvīśa and Kṣetrapāla at both sides of every door.
At the doors, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are stationed above in due order;
likewise Sṛṣṭi, Lajjā, Jayā, Māyā, Sāvitrī, and Kṣamā.
Likewise, the pure and impure [energies] are in pairs on the door-frames of the east and the other directions;
similarly in the pitchers at the doors, and likewise in Jyeṣṭhā and Vidyā;
and in Śraddhā and Kānti, Kriyā and Sṛṣṭi, and those known as Kṣamā, Mūrti, and Jayā.
One should perform the worship in sequence by means of the dual application [of mantras].
One should worship Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī at the eastern gate,
located at the bases of the two pillars of the archway according to the southern and northern positions.
One should worship Balākinī and Vanamālinī in the south;
likewise, one should fully propitiate Vibhīṣikā and Śāṅkarī in the west, and at the northern gate, one should worship the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.

O Brahmins, one should likewise worship Satya and the others, as well as Indra and the others, upon the banners in their proper order, just as before; this is the sequence for the worship of the doors. At the conclusion of the special morning sacrifice, one should perform the festival.
Having placed the goddess Śrī upon a golden palanquin or within a pavilion of flowers, and having adorned her most exquisitely,
one should lead her in a circumambulation of the village with all the requisites for a procession.

Having thus performed the festival, he should afterwards place the Goddess upon a golden throne in the assembly pavilion; having worshipped her in due order with enjoyments arising from the ornaments and the seat, he should then lead her to the dining seat.
One should offer the guest-water (arghya) and other honors, as well as the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
one should present various kinds of foods, such as mung-bean rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), and so forth,
along with offerings of flattened rice (pṛthuka) and the like, to the Goddess Śrī.
Having offered cool and refreshing coconut water,
one should present betel leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) with the Lakṣmī mantra.
Whatever substance has been offered, one should then divide it into four parts; taking one portion from among them, one should cause it to be given to the preceptor.
Likewise, one should cause all the remaining portions to be given to the devotees.
Then, with various hymns, dances, songs, and the sounds of musical instruments,
one should gratify Lakṣmī, who bestows the fruit of all desires.
Having done this, one should then cause Lakṣmī to enter the interior of the temple.
In this manner, one should perform the great festival daily until the ninth day,
accompanied by worship at the four locations in the evening and morning.
When the ninth day arrives, having performed the festival and other rites as before, [one should proceed].

At night, at the conclusion of the special sacrifice, having dismissed Śrī who was situated in the center of the sacrificial pit and mandala into his own heart, and having brought the pitcher— which is the presence of the Goddess—
nearby and worshipped it while reciting the Śrīsūkta; 13.122–13.123.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with water from the pitcher and having removed the protective thread (*kautuka*),
one should worship until the end of the oblation, prostrate, and ask for forgiveness.
The patron (*yajamāna*) should satisfy the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the others with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Thus, whoever should cause this Mahānavamī festival to be performed with devotion shall obtain longevity, health, sovereignty, splendor, fame, and progeny;
and having attained all desired objects, he shall reach union with Brahman.

On the following day, the tenth, he should perform the festival of the god’s hunt according to the procedure to be described, which brings about the prosperity of the kingdom. On the ninth day itself, he should especially [prepare] the horse for the god.
Having brought the horse, the weapons, and the rest— including the god’s bow and the multitude of missiles— which were thus adorned, to the bank of a river or the shore of a lake,
he should then bathe the horse and the weapons.
Having adorned [the image] especially with garlands, garments, and the like,
as well as with umbrellas, banners, flags, and so forth, accompanied by the sounds of dance and musical instruments,
one should lead it on a circumambulation of the village and then cause it to enter the temple.

There, the preceptor, knowing the mantras, having worshipped the horse of the deity with the Tārkṣya-mantra using offerings such as arghya and perfumes, should worship it up to the final oblation; likewise, he should worship the weapons with their respective mantras.
Having first performed the daily worship of the God of gods on the tenth day,
one should lead the Lord, who has entered the processional image, to the assembly pavilion.
Having bathed that Lord there with twenty-five water-pots, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped him upon the ornamental throne and presented the great sacrificial offering,
he placed the god upon the horse; then, having adorned him with ornaments suitable for the hunt, together with the requisites for the expedition.
Together with devoted bhāgavatas and armed soldiers clad in armor,
he brought [the relics] to the great forest; there, in various places especially,
they were offered with devotion by forest-dwellers, ascetics, and others.

Having offered roots, tubers, fruits, and various flower garlands to the God of gods near the sacred fire-tree, and having led [the deity] around and circumambulated him there at the water-shed; || 13.137–138 ||
Having seated [the deity] upon the auspicious throne at the base of the fire-tree (vahnivṛkṣa),
and having worshipped the weapons preceded by the proclamation of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha),
the preceptor should take hold of a śamī leaf with the root mantra.
Having offered [the oblation] upon the head of the deity and worshipped him with arghya and other offerings,
the preceptor, having then presented betel-leaf with the deity’s permission,
took up the bow and arrows for the sake of victory over all directions.
For the destruction of all enemies and for the increase of the king and his kingdom,
one should discharge four arrows in the four directions and two arrows above and below,
using the weapon-mantra or the verse beginning with "dhanvanāga."
Then, when evening has arrived, one should worship the God of gods with various offerings, having mounted the Lord of the World upon the horse,
accompanied by a hundred lamps and various musical instruments.
Having circumambulated the village, the preceptor should cause the Lord to enter the interior of the temple; having bathed the Lord of Gods with nine jars and adorned Him,
he should worship the All-pervading One together with Śrī and Puṣṭi until the conclusion of the oblation.
Thus, the festival to be performed on the tenth day has been proclaimed.
Hereafter, O twice-born ones, I shall describe the unsurpassed Festival of Lamps (Dīpotsava), which occurs on the full moon day when the sun is situated in Scorpio.
O lords of sages, even if the fourteenth lunar day is pierced by a single moment of the *bharaṇī* nakṣatra at dawn, the day joined with *kṛttikā*— whether it is so joined or not—
is [the proper time]. On that day, during the hour of Taurus (vṛṣabha), one should perform the offering of lamps.

If there is a conjunction of two days, it should be on the final day of the *parvan*; however, for occasions such as the Festival of Lamps (*dīpotsava*), the *parvan* may be accepted even if it lasts for only a brief period of time. One should offer lamps on the first day (*pratipad*) if the pure *parvan* cannot be obtained.
O best of the twice-born, when both lunar fortnights of that month have arrived,
one should perform the Festival of Lights specifically on the final lunar day (parvan) of the month; however,
if that [final day] is defiled by a solar transit (saṅkrānti), one should perform it on the preceding day.

O best of sages, on both occasions of the transition [of the sun], one should perform the offering of lamps specifically on the full-moon day when it is conjoined with the Kṛttikās. O twice-born ones, if both of these lunar festivals are not joined with the Kṛttikās, then—
One should celebrate the festival on a full-moon day conjoined with Rohiṇī;
even if it is not conjoined with Rohiṇī, one should do so on the full-moon day at the end of that month.
Even when the conjunction is defiled by a solar transit (saṅkrānti), one should perform the lighting of lamps.
Moreover, O twice-born ones, if an inauspicious lunar day occurs during a lunar eclipse,
one should light a lamp within the night, excluding seven *nāḍikās* before and after the eclipse; this brings happiness to the king and the kingdom.
Having thus reflected correctly, the wise man should then perform the Festival of Lamps (Dīpotsava).
O best of sages, I shall describe its procedure in detail.
On that day, O twice-born ones, the temple of the God of gods [should be adorned] on all sides.
Beginning from the section of the palace and extending outward to the edge of the enclosure,
one should have it washed with pure water by Brahmins and attendants using *darbha* grass together with wooden rods and mixed with *sahadevī*.
One should sweep that area on all sides and smear it with cow-dung and water;
afterwards, one should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water mixed with kuśa grass.
Having adorned it with lime powder, one should scatter unbroken rice grains upon the ground.
Having decorated [the area] on all sides with canopies and flower garlands,
one should fumigate it everywhere with incense made of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
Then, when the afternoon has arrived, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), [should proceed].

Then, having entered the temple, he should worship the Lord residing in the primary image with offerings such as water for the hands (*arghya*) and perfumes; thereafter, having invoked [the deity] into the festive icon (*utsavakautuka*),
he should worship it together with Śrī and Puṣṭi.
Having placed the procession image upon the auspicious throne in the assembly pavilion,
the best of preceptors, O twice-born ones, should then apply flower-sprouts to the primary image and others, and perform the binding of the protective thread according to the rules. (13.164–13.165)
Then one should perform the worship of the four locations according to the prescribed rite;
at that time, one should bathe the deity with twenty-five jars,
as well as with a great oblation of sacrificial food, cakes, and offerings.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Gods of gods, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the lamp.
In front of the primary image, one should prepare a pedestal of grain made of gold,
silver, copper, or even clay.
Taking a lamp-vessel,
one should fill it with cow's clarified butter measuring one *āḍhaka*, and place a wick in its center;
the wick should be made either from pieces of new cloth or from cotton threads.
O best of sages, having placed that vessel upon a pedestal of grain,
one should place eight bowls filled with ghee and provided with wicks around that vessel, starting from the east and proceeding in due order.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle [the area] with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
At nightfall, having carried forth the lamp-vessels by the initiated twice-born,
one should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and, there, with the fire situated in the pit...
Then, having lit lamps and leading [the image] with the eye while Brahmins recite the Vedas,
together with the sounds of musical instruments, one should perform a circumambulation of the temple and place it upon the pedestal as before, in front of the deity.
One should worship the lamp with the *netra-mantra* and the *agni-mantra*, as well as with the *arghya* and other offerings.
Then, at an auspicious moment during the hour of Taurus (*vṛṣalagna*), the most excellent preceptor,
having worshipped the deity with *arghya* and other offerings, [should place] the brightly blazing lamp-vessel.
Having taken [the lamp] with the Netra-mantra or with the verse "uddīpyasva," and having shown it to the God of gods while it is endowed with all auspicious things,
the Guru then places that lamp into the hand of the attendant.
Then, the best of the twice-born should light all the lamps placed at every door and within the pavilion enclosures.
At that time, the festival image, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi, [should be brought forth].
Having mounted him upon a vehicle and especially adorned him with garments and other ornaments,
together with the requisites for the procession and thousands of lamps,
the best of the twice-born should recite the mantras dedicated to the fire-gods.
O twice-born ones, one should cause the Lord of the Gods to circumambulate in a clockwise direction within all the enclosures, beginning with the first enclosure;
this should be done everywhere during the time of the deity’s festival, throughout the enclosures and so forth.
Lamps of various forms should be arranged on all sides;
likewise in the directions of the palace, in the pavilions, at the gate-towers,
in the temples of Śrī and the others, and in the dwellings of the retinue.
Then one should offer lamps in houses containing wealth and grain, as well as in flower gardens and the like, in the presence of the processional image.
Thereafter, one should lead the Lord of the gods to the gateway of the gopura.
There, O twice-born ones, one should prepare the Viṣṇu-lamp as it will be described:
made of stone, metal, or wood according to one's preference;
its height being equal to that of the temple, or even a hundred palm-trees.
One should fashion the lamp-pillar to be either half of that [height] or half of that again.
One should divide the pillar into four parts: one part shall be square;
the three parts above shall be sixteen-sided, eight-sided, or circular.
One should construct a square pedestal at the top of the pillar, one, two, or three cubits in thickness and adorned with a lotus;
likewise, one should decorate the pillar with clusters of leaves, flowers, and creepers.
Having thus brought such a pillar, one should place it outside the outer door; there shall be an intermediate space between the pillar and the gopura.
Its measurement should be either thirty-two cubits or twenty-four cubits.
Or, without obstructing the chariot procession, he may even erect it higher than that;
O best of sages, he may place a pillar within the gateway,
or he may fashion a pillar between the pedestal and the gateway.
O twice-born ones, at the base of the pillar, there should be a square pedestal (pīṭhaka) measuring four cubits or three cubits in length,
O twice-born ones, and of the same measure in width, rising two or three cubits,
or even one and a half cubits in height.
O best of sages, one should construct [the temple] with stones or bricks.
Beneath the pillar, on the eastern side, one should depict a lion; on the south, Māruti;
on the west, Vainateya; and on the north, a swan.
When the lamp-pillar has been thus beautifully constructed according to the scriptures,
it should first be consecrated at an auspicious moment with the Tārkṣya mantra.
Then, the brahmins should place the previously described lamp-vessel upon it.
Thus has the ritual procedure for the Viṣṇu-lamp been fully proclaimed.
Having performed this, one should then lead the deity on a circumambulation of the village;
at every point along the village streets, one should perform the offering of lamps.
O twice-born ones, one should perform the lighting of lamps at the banks of sacred fords, in gardens, at the edges of wells and other such sites, in public squares, and everywhere;
likewise, one should do so in every house while passing through all the processions.
Then, one should cause the Lord of the Gods to enter within the temple;
having seated him upon an auspicious throne in the assembly pavilion,
one should worship him with the *arghya* offering and other rites, as well as with cakes and sacrificial offerings.
One should offer milk-rice and the like, parched grain, betel-leaf and so forth;
likewise, one should gratify the deity in the fire with oblations for atonement.
The most excellent preceptor should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter.
Then one should dismiss the deity situated in the center of the sacrificial pit and the maṇḍala.
One should perform the sprinkling of the water-pot and other rites exactly as before. Thereafter, one should cause the festive image to enter inside the temple.
And there, one should re-engage the invoked Śakti back into the root [mantra].
The patron should satisfy the preceptor and others with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
He who thus causes this unsurpassed Festival of Lamps to be performed with devotion—
Having attained happiness in this world, one is glorified in the next world.
Indeed, this festival should be performed on the full moon day of Kārttika;
it has been proclaimed in detail as that which brings satisfaction to the God of gods.
O best of Brahmins, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika,
having fasted and kept a vigil through the night, one should please the Lord of the World with songs arising from the aesthetic emotion appropriate for that occasion.
When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, one should especially worship the All-pervading Lord.
One should cause songs, hymns, and various sacred narratives to be recited;
indeed, one should perform everything at the conclusion of the fire-oblation with particular care.
Who is able to fully describe the attainment of the fruit of merit for those people who sing at that time and those who listen to it?
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme festival of Mārgaśīrṣa.
O twice-born ones, when the sun was situated in Sagittarius at that time of the transit,
they bathed the Lord of the gods according to the lower and higher paths,
led him to the decorated throne, and worshipped him with water for the hands and other offerings.
Having adorned the Lord of Gods, as well as Viṣvaksena and the others, with garments, ornaments, garlands, and fragrances such as musk,
and likewise having bathed the images of the devotees with nine jars, [one should proceed].
Having adorned [the deity] with special ornaments, one should worship him in due order with the *arghya* and other offerings.
Then, having led the Lord of the Gods to an auspicious seat for the meal,
[one should offer] rice with mung beans and milk-rice mixed with sugar and ghee.
Having offered various kinds of edible foods, diverse fruits, betel leaf, and mouth-perfumes according to the prescribed rite, [he should offer] the food,
edibles, and so forth that have been presented to Viṣvaksena and the others.
Then, having offered [the oblation] to the devotees and to the God of gods, the Lord of Śrī,
he should circumambulate him and prostrate according to the prescribed rite,
and then satisfy the Lord with various kinds of Vaiṣṇava hymns.
Whether in Sanskrit or Dravidian, using words that indicate the supreme deity,
mental meditation is thus described, as is bodily action;
vocal praise is likewise described— one should satisfy the Lord through these three kinds.
Then, one should offer food and other gifts to the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas who sing praises of Viṣṇu at the holy site in the presence of the Lord.
Having accepted these with humility, the Vaiṣṇavas, the devotees of the Blessed One, [should partake].
Having drunk from the sacred bathing place and partaken of the prasāda in the presence of the deity,
those foremost of sages, beginning from the very day of the transit [of the sun] until the end of the month,
should worship according to the prescribed rites before the rising of the dawn.
Day after day, he should offer to the God and to his devotees various kinds of foods, such as dishes made of mung beans and milk-rice;
and with deep, heartfelt hymns composed by his devotees, he should praise Puruṣottama.
In that month, especially in the presence of the God of gods,
one should perform the offering of lamps with clarified butter or sesame oil.
Furthermore, he who offers a lamp specifically on the thirtieth day [shall attain great merit].
Having enjoyed all pleasures here, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus one should perform the worship at dawn for thirty days;
on that final tenth day, one should conduct a special festival.
On the night preceding the commencement of the festival,
the most excellent of preceptors, having performed the ritual planting of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) according to the rules,
[should perform] the rites from the day the festival begins until the final day.

One should perform the worship of the four locations in the evening and in the morning according to the prescribed rule. At the beginning and at the conclusion, one should perform the ritual bathing as before,
either at the start of the second enclosure or outside the gateway (gopura).
One should construct an excellent great pavilion for the God of gods, and should especially adorn it with canopies, fruits, flowers, mirrors, chowries, and so forth,
in such a way that it is exceedingly pleasing to the eye.

At midday, having specially adorned the Lord of the Gods of gods together with Śrī and Puṣṭi, and having placed him upon a palanquin along with Viṣvaksena and others, as well as the images of the devotees and so forth; || 13.233–234 ||
Having made a circumambulation of the village together with the requisites for the procession,
he brought [the deity] to the great pavilion; there, having placed the Lord upon the lion-throne along with the two Goddesses, Viṣvaksena, and the others.
Having placed [the image] facing the deity and having worshipped the Lord with enjoyments arising from the decorated throne, the preceptor [should worship] the images of the devotees,
as well as the Vedas beginning with the *Sadāgama*, and the divine *Siddhāntas*.

At that time, he should cause the Lord to hear the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, hymns addressed to the gods and those concerning humans, as well as other works that augment the Vedas, whether in Sanskrit or Prākṛt, or even in another language.
Then, however, there were eight kinds of grains and various types of foods—
puffed rice, coconut, sugarcane, plantains, chickpeas, and so forth;
as well as coconut water and the like, betel, and offerings.
Having offered [the food] to the God of gods and to the devotees in due order,
one should cause the Vaiṣṇavas to receive the offered food, edibles, and so forth.
Then, [one should worship] the Lord of the God of gods, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi.
O best of the twice-born, having placed [the image] upon a palanquin along with the devotee-images and other items, one should carry it gracefully to the pavilion;
at that time, one should also perform the honoring of the devotee-images.

Having circumambulated the pavilion twice with the sounds of the Vedas, with the sounds of hymns, with praises consisting of prose and verse, along with the resonance of lutes and flutes, and together with dance, song, and the like, he [placed] the Lord once again upon the lion-throne.
Having installed and duly worshipped [the deity], especially at the time of evening,
one should have the Vaiṣṇavas chant there day after day, at the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya), the supreme *Drāmiḍī* hymn consisting of four thousand verses.
Then, O twice-born ones, having led the Lord of the gods around the temple according to the previously mentioned rite, one should cause him to enter within the shrine;
having led him to the assembly pavilion and performed the daily worship of the Lord.
Having also performed the worship at the four locations, he should bring [the deity] back to its own place.
O best of sages, one should thus conduct the festival for ten days.
At the conclusion of the festival, however, the deity residing in the pitcher and other vessels should be [dismissed] according to the prescribed rite.

Then one should dismiss the deity, prostrate, and ask for forgiveness; the patron should satisfy the teacher and the others with gifts that do not cause regret. Thus has the ritual procedure for the Mārgaśīrṣa festival been fully proclaimed.
O twice-born ones, when the sun is situated in Capricorn at that time of its transit,
one should bathe the Lord of the gods with twenty-five jars,
adorn him with special ornaments, and offer oblations and other gifts.
At that time, the patron should likewise offer cows, land, gold, and so forth,
as well as an offering of *kūśmāṇḍa* rice, for the satisfaction of the God.
On the following day, having especially worshipped the God of gods—
Having placed the Lord, who has entered the festival image, upon the horse-jewel,
one should perform the supreme hunt festival according to the previously mentioned rite,
bringing the Lord of the World with playful grace to forest after forest.
O lords of sages, having worshipped the various [deities] in their respective places according to the prescribed rites, he should thereafter engage in hunting for his amusement,
[seeking] boars, elephants, tigers, black antelopes, hares, and the like.
Having placed the armed army in a circle around him and keeping him in the center,
the most heroic warriors, having stationed themselves there in the middle with great effort,
should capture the deer alive and lead them into the presence of the god.
Then he should release all the deer one by one in succession;
or, for those deer that have been killed, there will certainly be a meritorious rebirth.
Then, [he should worship] the Lord of the Gods of gods in a pavilion or at a water-shed.
Having placed [the deity] upon the auspicious throne and having worshipped it especially,
when evening has arrived, one should lead [it] around the village with the aforementioned riches and cause it to enter the temple.
Having bathed the Lord of the gods and adorned him according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship the All-pervading Lord together with Śrī and Puṣṭi until the conclusion of the oblation.
Thus indeed is the festival of the hunt for the God of gods described.
O best of Brahmins, he who thus causes all the festivals of the God to be performed every year, being endowed with universal sovereignty,
shall enjoy desired pleasures for a long time after experiencing happiness in this world.
"At the time of casting off the body, one attains the state of the Blessed One.
Thus have the festivals of the God been correctly proclaimed.
O best of sages, if you wish to hear anything else beyond this, let it be told.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fortnightly Festival and Other Rites," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter: While the Lord of the World was lying down in the midst of the Cāturmāsya [observance], the sages [spoke].
"You have previously stated that the Pavitrāropaṇa rite should be performed.
O best among speakers, explain its procedure in detail.
Nārada said:
I shall describe the procedure for the Pavitrāropaṇa rite for the benefit of the world.
Listen with attentive minds, O best of sages,
for without the realization of its essential nature, even the enjoyment of worldly pleasures is impossible.
He who, due to a lack of capacity, falls away from the *kṛcchra* and other penances;

he whose daily observance is impaired by the affliction of diseases such as fever; or he who, without independence, fails to perform the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifice— [for these, there is a different rule]. (14.4)
O one of great intelligence, hear what is ordained as beneficial for each of them:
the filling of the measure of tangible enjoyments,
and food that reaches the heart, though devoid of consciousness, saturated with sacrificial oblation.
The seeds of secondary enjoyments have indeed been ordained;
he is the fulfiller of vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa,
joined with special worship and the self-restraint of the Cāturmāsya.
The daily rite (*āhnika*), which is based on the Sūtras, variegated, auspicious, and like a string of pearls, always brings tranquility to devotees;
one should perform it on an auspicious day within the four-month period. (14.8–14.9)
From the fifteenth day of Āṣāḍha until the full-moon day of Kārttika—
that entire period is the final lunar month.
[It lasts] from the transit into Cancer until the end of the portion of Libra.
That time consisting of eight fortnights is known as the middle solar period.
Know that the time at the end of the eleventh day, characterized by the Cāturmāsya [observance], is the supreme Vaiṣṇava period, which bestows all perfections.
If this period cannot be reached due to some obstacle,
