another period must be completed by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances; furthermore,
within that interval, [the vow] must be accomplished according to rule, preceded by sacrifice.
O twice-born ones, one should construct a pavilion for that purpose in front of the temple,
either in the first enclosure, or in the second,
or in the third, or even in the fourth or fifth.
Upon obtaining the best site, otherwise it should be situated in whichever direction is desired;
it may be square or even rectangular, elongated toward the east and west,
or elongated toward the north and south, according to the builder's wish.
Likewise, it may face east or face whichever direction is desired. A pavilion measuring twenty-two *dhanus* in size shall be the best;
a pavilion measuring eighteen *dhanus* shall be the middling one.
O twice-born ones, the smallest [measurement] should be twelve *dhanus*, or alternatively,
starting from five cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time up to twenty-one cubits,
it shall be of nine types according to these measurements.
Alternatively, one should know that the best is ten cubits, the middling eight cubits,
the inferior six cubits, and the smallest three cubits in length;
or [the lengths] range from six cubits up to thirty cubits, ending at twenty-five.
Having selected one among these [types of] pavilions according to one's wealth—
whether it be a base together with a pedestal, a foundation alone, or a mere *masūraka* seat—
one should place a pillar upon the foundation and a three-part entablature (*prastara*).
It may be associated with the pigeon motif, or it may be devoid of the aforementioned forms;
it may be enclosed by one, three, five, seven, or more varieties of walls, and it may be endowed with the ornaments mentioned for its subordinate parts, or it may be devoid of them. || 14.23–14.24 ||
Whether constructed of stone, brick— either fired or unfired—
and whether it has one door, four doors, or is provided with two doors;
whether it is enclosed by walls, unenclosed, or possesses corner walls.
Or, for the sake of the swift accomplishment of the rite, one may construct a simple water-shed (*prapā*) devoid of the aforementioned characteristics— auspiciously made of reeds and wood,
provided with latticed windows, and adorned with doors. || 14.26–14.27 ||
One should construct a pavilion above, covered with a canopy;
its contraction or expansion of the site shall be according to the desire of the builder.
O twice-born ones, having thus constructed the maṇṭapa in accordance with the treatises on architecture (śilpaśāstra), [one should proceed].
O Brahmins, for the sake of the sacrifice, one should then prepare a very beautiful site in the midst of that [area]:
a pedestal (*masūraka*) as the foundation of the building, a level ground-surface as the support of the site,
which is firm, even, shaped accordingly, and slightly sloping toward the northeast.
And the ground should be especially elevated and mirror-like,
so that the earth beneath the pavilion is not level;
it should rise by two, three, or up to eight finger-breadths.
For sacrifices involving few participants, the sacrificial ground should increase by one [unit] at a time;
its height should be nine finger-breadths, extending up to fifteen finger-breadths.
This is the prescribed elevation for sacrificial grounds of moderate dimensions.
The height for those of measured self-restraint should be made from sixteen finger-breadths up to twenty-four finger-breadths, according to the previously mentioned progression;
thus has the measurement of height been described for the various sites.
One should first construct the platforms in all directions with bricks and other materials, measuring one foot, half a foot,
or a cubit in width; then, having filled their interior with earth mixed with a small amount of sand.
Having carefully examined it for hair, insects, and the like, and having struck it thereafter,
one should thoroughly inspect that ground— which is elevated in the center and beautiful— for seven days, until it possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, especially. (14.37)
When she does not give way, then she becomes fit for sacrifice.
Above that, one should construct an altar provided with many steps and equipped with archways,
according to one's means.
With purifying sacrificial wood— firm, straight, and even—
the O Brahmins, one should fix archways (toraṇas) endowed with the proper characteristics at the four directions, either outside the doors or within them.
Alternatively, one should correctly place three [deities] in each of the directions.
Having ascertained the extent of the pavilion, there should be five or seven [mandalas];
these should be decorated with gold, jewels, and so forth, provided that one has the means.
O twice-born ones, one should then construct four archways (toraṇas) made from the wood of the śrīvṛkṣa, udumbara, vaṭa, and plakṣa trees, extending from the east to the north; or else,
there may be four in the four directions, or even just one for each.

The height of the archways (toraṇas) is prescribed to be equal to the length of the pillars. Their width, however, should be measured by the distance between two pillars, always being slightly greater than the measurement from the top of a pillar.

O best of those who know the Vedas, one should place those staffs on the ground; their position must always be within the pillars for those whose nature is vision. O Brahmins, when the position of the arches is outside the doors, [the staffs should likewise be placed accordingly].

Then, the measurement from the base up to the pinnacle in terms of height should be equal to, or one and a half times, or twice that [of the base]; and its projection on the ground should be equal to those same proportions.
It should be situated between two wheels and adorned with a circle of feathers.
At each gateway (toraṇa), one should place a Garuḍa standing upright;
on its two sides, one should set up two banners bearing the mark of the discus and possessing various colors.
Then, according to the distinctions of white, red, and so forth, one should place eight banners starting from the east.
Having established [the central deity] upon the middle altar according to the principle of origin and dissolution,
one should depict the incarnations beginning with the Fish (Matsya) and numerous other manifestations in the four directions, following the procedure described in detail.
By hosts of sages, Siddhas, and immortals who perceive many beings;
by numerous islands, mountains, forests, and groves;
and by many herds of deer intent on sporting in the waters of lakes filled with cranes and white lotuses.
By sky-dwellers accompanied by women, by kings who were lords of the Vidyādharas,
by Brahmins of tranquil mind devoted to meditation on the Self,
and by such others— by these and countless other activities arising from various sources.
One should diligently make that entire sacrificial hall pleasing to the sight;
one should either coat it with lime-plaster or, immediately thereafter,
adorn it with mirrors, chowries, cloths, and various brilliant silk garments.
With bells, crescent moons, and other ornaments, with beautiful parasols, with lofty plantain trees and clusters of bananas, with sacred and sturdy wooden pillars,
and with vessels filled to the brim with honey, clarified butter, curd, and excellent milk.
With bronze vessels,
bowls of śāli rice, auspicious fruits together with gold, parched grain, white mustard seeds, and vessels of seeds provided with the six flavors. || 14.57–58 ||
With six fragrant substances such as cinnamon and cardamom, with betel leaves and areca nuts,
with madhūka, jujube, grapes, sugar cane, and the three myrobalans—
along with many seasonal flowers gathered in abundance.
With various such pure offerings of abundant enjoyments,
one should further adorn the area above with a sacred canopy that is very white, brilliant, and marked with the signs of the wheel and the lotus.
Thereafter, one should wrap the pillars individually with various kinds of fine silk cloths (*dukūla*),
starting from the eastern and northern directions up to the northwestern corner (*māruta*).
One should then attach banners there, produced according to the distinctions of colors such as white and so forth.
Thus, by means of the division according to passion (rāga), and again from the western side as far as the southern limit, a second set of four [colors] is formed;
and on the canopy at the navel, there should be one [deity] of all colors (or golden).
Outside the altar platform, in the eight directions of the pavilion,
beginning from the southeast corner and extending to the northeast corner,
one should make four [lines] of white, red, yellow, and black.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, from the northern region as far as the western direction,
there is likewise proclaimed a set of four banners:
one with the luster of the color of royal stone (rājapāṣāṇa), and one approached by the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) upon his discus.
One should fashion three Vaijayantī banners on the arch situated in the eastern direction;
on the southern [arch], one resembling crystal; on the western [arch], with the luster of vermilion;
and on the northern arch, one with the brilliance of gold—one should thus fashion the triad of banners.
It should be provided with four banners, white and so forth;
and each archway here should have either three or five [banners].
The length of the banners shall be half the width of the archway.
O twice-born ones, having thus newly constructed a pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice,
one should then decorate it— whether it be a pavilion previously prepared for the specific assembly [of deities] beginning with the ritual bathing and ending with the festival.
When this has been done, thereafter one should anoint the altar together with the archways in due order with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, radiant with color;
and one should likewise smear the altar itself with pure sandalwood.

With that very same [substance] prepared by the Bāhlīkas, one should smear the first archway with musk and place it facing the southern direction. Then, one should have the western [archway] made white with frost and dust.
One standing in the northern [quarter] should be anointed with pure saffron alone.
[One should prepare] a surface made of milk, sandalwood, and saffron,
together with water containing the powder of *rajanī* and *hrīvera*.

O twice-born ones, one should then fumigate the area of the pavilion at the doors with meritorious fragrant herbs and with many various kinds of incense. Then, one should enclose that [area] on the outside in every direction with a curtain.

One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the north of the pavilion beforehand; or else, O twice-born ones, it may be elsewhere, provided it is not in a direction forbidden at the commencement of the sacrifice. One should construct the fire-pavilion in whichever of the three desired directions is preferred.
It should be equipped with an exit for smoke, adorned with various sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
and provided with archways and the like made of thick, well-leafed wood;
or else, one should construct a pit endowed with the proper characteristics in the kitchen.
Or it may have been previously arranged for some specific purpose.
One should perform the layout of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) in this manner everywhere;
O twice-born ones, when this has been done, one should then undertake the gathering of the necessary materials.
Now, first of all, the fashioning of the purifiers (pavitra) is described.
Their form is twofold, distinguished as subtle and gross;
for they always protect devotees with their entire being. (14.83)
The entire auspicious activity born of mind, speech, and heart must be fully understood;
therefore, one should know its true nature as it is, and the fruit that results for devotees through the completion of that [practice]. || 14.84–14.85 ||

Know that to be the thread of the world, which is uncut, white, and of infinite extension from the source of the universe; it undergoes division through its own manifold nature for the sake of those who are ignorant, just as a golden thread [is divided] by gold ornaments and the like.
For it assumes the majesty of the sixfold policy through its nature as a protective amulet (pratisara);
yet, being colored by knowledge and passion, it is joined with activities born of vigor,
enveloped by fiery mantras, and thoroughly infused with power.
Sovereignty, however, is in ritual service; it is imperishable through power when there is prosperity.
Thus should the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) of the Lord of the World be understood—established in Viṣṇu, the sovereign of Brahman, who is its very form. (14.89)
And that which is given with devotion and according to the rules bestows the state of the Blessed One.
Herein is described the procedure for that [offering], which is to be conceptualized by means of gross, distinct objects existing within the sphere of worldly convention.
The thread should be fine, firm, white, and smooth, prepared by a girl born of the Brahmin caste,
or by a disciplined young woman or an old woman,
or even one who is pure or a widow.
Having taken whatever is available— whether linen or silk— that is free from hair, body hair, and the like, and having thoroughly washed it with water,
one should first effect its purification by means of burning and moistening.
O twice-born ones, having contemplated and brought to completion the fourfold root-mantra,
one should then employ the eightfold mantra when there is a requirement for the fourfold nature;
however, when characterized by the distinction of the intellect regarding origin and dissolution, it is perceived as distinct.
In Keśava and the others, one should avoid the three or fourfold [thread] by means of the presiding nature;
for Viṣṇu, who is equanimous, one should avoid uneven threads,
because the act of purifying the sacred thread is rendered uneven for no one.
O best of sages, the sacrificial purifiers (*pavitraka*) should be made from those white and black threads for all the mantras, beginning with the root mantra.
O twice-born ones, one should first fashion the ornament for the mantra-form residing in the pitcher.
With threads produced from one hundred and fifty [fibers], having the form of continuous streams,
the first [coil] should be made with one hundred and eight, the second with twice that,
and the third with three times that; in this manner, one should extend its width.
The first [mandala] should have thirty-six knots; the second is remembered as being double that;
the third the wise one should make triple;
and likewise for the Lord residing in the mandala as well as for Him who has entered the fire.
Let the specific distinction of the purifiers (pavitra) placed upon the image also be observed:
one is in the form of a garland upon the head, tied with knots as desired; the second hangs from the shoulders down to the circle of the knees. || 14.102–14.103 ||
It is well known that [the measurement] from the head down to the feet constitutes one-third;
from the head down to the pedestal is the sacred forest-garland (*vanamālā-pavitraka*).
One should fashion the pedestal separately, making it beautiful according to its own proportions.
The width of the *bimbapratisaraṇa* is also recorded as being indefinite;
its length, O best of sages, should be double or triple the previously mentioned measurement of the thread, provided it is possible, for this ornament known as the *vanamālā*.
It should be provided with one thousand and eight threads,
or alternatively, one may make half or a quarter of that number according to one's means,
O twice-born ones, when the primary image is situated on a plastered wall or a cloth painting.
One should prepare five ornaments for the festival image;
at that time, one should also arrange the original ornaments of the primary image as before,
but on the protective cords (*pratisara*) of the images, they should be the very first ones used.
In the case of the Lord of the Gods of gods, it should be joined with five necklaces;
the threads should be of various forms and provided with pearl necklaces.
Knots should be placed at intervals of three finger-breadths for all of them, and they should be uniform.
Without counting, these auspicious [garlands] are like citron fruits;
they are forest garlands consisting of one hundred and eight knots, intended for the invitation of the All-pervading Lord who has descended into the four stations. || 14.111-14.112 ||
A purifying thread, equal to the primordial one, whether single or double,
is for all ritual images as well as for the gate-towers and other structures; it always brings about the presence of the mantra-images that reside therein for those who worship them.

One should indeed perform the highest and other types of rites according to the primary rule (mukhyakalpanā). In the secondary rule (anukalpanā), one should arrange two similar [rites] with either a middling or a highest [substitute], or even one of each pair.
O twice-born ones, one should likewise fashion the purificatory thread (*pavitra*) for the limbs, the ornaments, the marks,
and the spears of the Lord of Birds;
it may consist of three, or two, or two each, or even one by one, as before.

One should fashion the collection of ornaments with the inner sanctums (garbhas) provided with the rotation of threads, using threads arising from a number according to one's desire; this applies to the other components of the mandala for the deities, provided there is the means to do so.
One should prepare the collection of purifiers (*pavitraka*) with threads knotted according to one's desire;
likewise for the retinue beginning with Viṣvaksena.
There should indeed be two for the mantra-vessel and the weapon-vessel, and one for the mandala.
And there is a pair consisting of the sacrificial pit and the fire, and a pair consisting of the Teacher and the sacred seat (14.120).
There is also [a pair] of the script and the Lord who is the Word-principle— the essence of speech—
and of the great-souled ritual implements beginning with the bell and the rosary, which are limbs of the rite (14.121).
[This applies] to the presiding deities of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) who reside in other lands,
to the four beginning with the Guru who lament their desire for Hari,
and to the best of the twice-born and other castes who constantly contemplate Acyuta.
Of householders, celibate students, ascetics, and forest-dwellers;
of the elders such as Janaka and others who know the true nature of the Blessed One;
and of kinsmen, brothers, and sons whose souls are devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
[He was pleased] by his wife, who was humble with devotion and intent on the worship of Hari;
by his kinsmen and friends who dwell in the abode of the Lord; and by those who assisted him in that [practice], who desired the realization of the fourfold Self.
For the prosperity, the fitness, and the purification of his servants who were well-disposed toward him and performers of the Puruṣottama sacrifice,
[he provided] with threads and knots according to their desired measures.
Or else, O best of sages, one should prepare a collection of purifiers for the four types of persons beginning with the guru— namely, ascetics and householders—
using twenty-four threads for the former and sixteen for the latter, respectively. (14.128)
Then, one should prepare sacred threads (*pavitraka*) with twelve, eight, and thirty-six knots according to the number of the threads;
and for the worshipper and the preceptor, one should indeed fashion two ornaments.
This has been declared as the gross method; now the subtle method is being described here.
The first ornament for the image is traditionally prescribed according to the measurement of the head, consisting of four hundred and thirty-two threads.
Having fashioned it beautifully with well-proportioned spiral turns,
and having applied twenty-seven knots to it according to the measurement,
one should place the purifying cord (pavitraka) above the ear, reaching down to the level of the navel.
O best of sages, having conceptualized a second [arrangement] of the sūtras by means of three hundred and twenty-four collections of knots,
that is remembered as being "with internal compartments" (anugarbha).

O best of the twice-born, starting from the region of the shoulders down to the limit of the two feet, one should fashion it with eye-threads reduced by one-third and with clusters of threads, and then with triple-knotted groups of cords. 14.135–14.136.
With one hundred and eight threads and likewise with knots,
starting from the head and the previous descent down to the Vaiṣṇava pedestal,
it is [adorned] with threads, collections of knots, and various internal chambers.
One should construct another four [circles] according to the measurement of the mandala:

the first according to the measure of the lotus, the second according to the measure of the nave (nābhi), the third should be equal to the spokes (ara), and the fourth equal to the rims (nemi). || 14.138–139 ||

O best of the twice-born, the wise man should fashion three ornaments according to the requirements: one consisting of eighty-one coils of thread, another with knots equal in number to the measurement of the fire-pit, and likewise [the third]. 14.140.

With one hundred and eight threads, or half that number, and likewise with their knots, one should fashion a very even and most auspicious ornament for the best of the twice-born— the eminent Brāhmaṇas— with half that [number] of threads. (14.141–14.142)
This is remembered as the primary ritual procedure (*kalpa*); now the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*) is being stated. This first [type] consists of one hundred and eight threads;
the second is less by a quarter; the third is half of that.
Then, one should fashion the fourth [part] by means of a quarter of the first;
moreover, one should make the ornament for the fire three-quarters of the fourth part.
For the foremost of the twice-born, one should prepare [the thread] consisting of twenty-seven strands.
O twice-born ones, one should fashion the sacred thread for Brāhmaṇas with nine threads;
it must never be made above the breast or below the navel. For others who are devoted to the Teacher of the World, however, it should consist of three threads.
This has been declared as the subtle ritual procedure; now the supreme ritual procedure is being described here.

O twice-born ones, for the all-pervading Lord whose principal mantra has descended into four locations, it is performed with one hundred and eight repetitions, or indeed with half that number, or even with a quarter.
One should make an ornament of the threads, either one by one or three by three.
For great-souled ones, the number [of recitations] such as japa and homa may be complete or empty; for this very reason, it equalizes the devotees who are practitioners of mantra.
One should fashion a collection of those knots, marked by the number of threads;
then, having fashioned others at will for the patrons,
one should provide a collection of ornaments consisting of inner chambers accompanied by the confusion of threads.

Then, O best of men, O brahmins, one should perform the construction of the womb for that entire collection of purifiers (pavitraka) belonging to the God of gods who resides in the four stations, as previously described in its entirety.
With gold, excellent jewels, camphor, sandalwood powder, and saffron;
with all kinds of medicinal herbs combined with cinnamon, cardamom, and other ingredients;
with various purifying substances, along with a sacred thread and a cotton wick.
Having the appearance of a citron, or like a mango, an emblic myrobalan, or a conch shell,
the spaces between them should then be strung together with an unbroken thread nearby,
for the purpose of clearly discerning their divisions.
For all other images, one should fashion the interior arrangement according to one's wealth, using the previously mentioned collections of materials;
and for the worshipper and the Guru, there should be two sets of ornaments together with the interior contents.
O Blessed One, [this] has been prescribed through the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and the cultivation of identification (*tādātmyabhāvanā*).
Therefore, for others, the "ungarbed" (*agarbha*) arrangement should be composed according to the sequence.
One should make the intermediate group "garbed" (*gārbha*), adorned with the Bāhlīka [style].
And having adorned it with gold above and with silver,
or else with [ornaments] made of gold from the root down to the tip of the sacrificial grass (pavitra),
[marked] with conch shells, lotuses, maces, discs, garlands, the śrīvatsa, and other such symbols; || 14.159–14.160 ||
O best of the twice-born, having thus prepared the purificatory threads (*pavitra*) for one person or for many according to their means,
and having placed them in a wide vessel made of metal and covered with a cloth, [one should proceed] in due order.

Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, having placed the collection of ritual ornaments intended for the mantras in one beautiful vessel made of split bamboo or clay, or even in a single vessel made of *pālāśa* wood, and having placed all the worldly [ornaments] in another, [one should proceed]. || 14.162–14.163 ||
Having covered it afterwards with a well-washed, new, and pure white cloth,
and having bound it with a firm, well-white thread,
one should place those two vessels in the midst of the sacrificial materials.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, having prepared all the necessary materials,

one should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropa*) for the God of gods on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight during any one of the four-month periods (*cāturmāsya*). (14.166)
One should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the tenth or eleventh lunar days;
or, as an alternative, one should perform the consecration on the eleventh day. Or, due to a lack of capacity, one may perform the immediate consecration on the twelfth day.
Having performed the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the day prior to the day of consecration (adhivāsa),
the preceptor should perform the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) on the day of consecration.
O best of sages, listen to all [the details] regarding the consecration and so forth.
On the tenth day, at the onset of night, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images,
having gone into the presence of Mantreśa and having worshipped him in due order with offerings such as arghya, [should proceed].

Therefore, having obtained permission and reached the auspicious sacrificial pavilion situated on the roof of the palace, one should perform worship as before— beginning with the adoration of the door—
at the ritual pitcher and upon the site of the mandala.
Then, having entered, one should perform the worship of the primary image (mūlamūrti) as before,
carrying it out with special care until the end of the circumambulations and prostrations,
O twice-born ones, when the primary image is situated on a plastered wall or a cloth painting.
Then, one should perform everything especially in the occasional image (*naimittika-bimba*);
O Brahmins, having performed even the mere ritual bathing (*snāna*) in the presence of a single [image],
whether it be the image intended for daily rites (*nitya*), occasional rites (*naimittika*), or even the bathing rite itself.

One should perform all other rites ending with the purification (*pavitra*) upon the primary image (*mūlabimba*). For the purpose of the daily festival (*nityotsava*), one should then hold that festival for the image itself. O Brahmins, in their absence, one should perform it upon a mirror placed near [the image].

One should perform merely the ritual bathing; then one should perform that festival upon a tuft of hair made from *dūrvā* grass, or on a wheel, or even in a water-pot (*kumbhaka*). All other [rites] should be performed as before upon the primary image (*mūlabimba*).
Then, having gone to the fire-chamber and consecrated the sacrificial pit as before,
he should consecrate the fire there and perform the libation with mantras.
Then, having entered the temple and performed the dedication of the oblation, [he should proceed].
Having prostrated before the Lord of the gods, he then [offers] a single purifying thread (pavitraka),
purified by burning and moistening, sprinkled with the water of the arghya offering,
and perfumed with fragrant scents and incense, for the deity stationed in the four locations.
Having offered [the oblation] in due order and presented incense preceded by the *arghya* offering, [he says:

"O Imperishable One, though You are eternally satisfied by enjoyments consisting of Your own bliss, nevertheless, being myself satisfied by devotion, I worship You for the sake of my own spiritual perfection. (14.181–182)
Having thus informed the Lord, he then sprinkled the entire collection of materials, beginning with the ornaments, with the water of the *arghya* consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Then, having brought the entire collection of ornaments to a state of fitness by means of both hands— which consist of the nature of Agni and Soma—
and having sprinkled them with the root mantra, touched them, and gazed upon them;
O best of the twice-born, some [vessels] are suitable for the *kumbha* rite, others for the *maṇḍala*;
some are suitable for the *bimba*, others for the *agni* rite;
and others are suitable for the *mantra* rite, each in its respective place.
Having placed each one separately in its own vessel according to the size of the vessel obtained,
and having subsequently covered them with a well-washed,
new cloth, those ornament-vessels [should be arranged] individually and in due order.
They should be bound with a firm and well-whitened thread,
using either *śāli* rice, *taṇḍula* rice, or sesame seeds— either all three together or individually—
upon a pedestal or on the ground, weighing four, three, two, or one *bhāra*.
Having placed those vessels containing the ornaments before the Lord,
and having worshipped them with the *praṇava*, one should again cover them with the *varman* mantra.
[One should likewise consecrate] the temple, both outside and inside the sanctuary known as the sacrificial hall (*yāga*).
Having wound it four times with a white thread of that same quality,
he should then request the assembly of Vaiṣṇava ascetics who are devoted to the five-fold ritual time and dedicated to the six duties.

"Tomorrow, out of devotion, I shall worship the Lord in your presence; therefore, please grant your presence out of a desire to show me favor. Having thus petitioned them and received their permission, [he proceeded].
One should spend the night in vigil in the presence of the God of gods.
Then, on the morning of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), having performed his bath and daily rites,
the preceptor, together with Brāhmaṇas and the most excellent Vaiṣṇava ascetics, [should proceed].
Those devoted to their own duties, who are devotees of Viṣṇu and firm in their vows,
having entered the temple of the Blessed One and performed the daily worship of the Lord,
should also perform the special worship of the four stations.
In the same way, one should perform the rites during the night as well, even more specifically.
Having completed the ritual section ending with the fire-oblation, one should then be intent on recitation and praise;
standing before the object of worship, one should pass the night in vigil.
Then, having bathed during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the preceptor, together with the Vaiṣṇavas,
enters the temple of the deity and performs the daily worship of the Lord.
Having worshipped the God established in his four stations according to the prescribed rite, [he proceeds].
Then, having placed the festive image, accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi, upon a vehicle and having adorned it especially with garments and other ornaments,
one should bring it to the pavilion and seat it upon a cushion.
One should cause the four Vedas to be taught in the four directions according to the prescribed rule.
Then, O twice-born ones, having gone into the presence of the vessel of ornaments,
one should worship it, open the protective amulet-vessel, and [proceed].
O twice-born ones, having observed and taken up everything from the beginning, one should meditate [upon it].

Whatever ritual action belongs to the year, from dawn until the end of night—that which arises from meditation, which is partless and perfectly bestows liberation—[that is what should be meditated upon]. || 14.203–204 ||
Having recollected the partless mantra through the sequence of pure pronunciation,
one should join that thread with the mantra and likewise the mantra with the thread;
having unified them with one's own self, one should indeed place [the mantra] upon the head of the mantra.
Having undertaken another sūtra, both in its entirety and in its parts,
one should meditate upon the nature of the ritual of meditation for a year;
and having remembered the mantra in its dual form, it is worshipped in the water-pot (kalaśa).
Having performed the connection [of the ritual] as before, one should offer the purificatory thread (*pavitraka*).
Then, O Brahmins, one should perform the third [rite], the *pratisara*.
One should remember all the external annual rites in their entirety and in full.
One should worship one's own self, from the foundation up to the supreme limit,
by means of the sequence known as dissolution, enjoyment, and authority, with the nature of the Sakala;
indeed, one should worship the Lord of Mantras in his entirety, whose form consists of dissolution, enjoyment, and the rest.
Having recollected [the mantra] and performed the reconnection (*sandhāna*), one should then offer the *pratisara*.
O twice-born ones, with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), flowers, perfumes, garlands, and incense,
one should worship and enclose the various ornaments individually.
At intervals, it should be accompanied by the sound of bells;
it should be provided with all kinds of jewels, excellent minerals, flowers, unbroken grains, and fruits;
it should be enriched with fragrant substances, water for honor (arghya), and *darbha* grass, and joined with parched grain and white mustard seeds.
One should joyfully shower many handfuls [of flowers] held in the hands,
or even a rain of flowers alone, while sounding conch shells and other instruments.
Having thus first offered the *pavitraka* to the jar situated [there], O Brahmins, [one should proceed].
According to this procedure, O Nārada, one should first offer three auspicious *pavitraka* threads to the one situated within the maṇḍala; and at the place of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*),
one should offer three, or one, of all the mantras as desired.
Having worshipped the deity residing in the image (bimbastha), one should present ornaments;
specifically, the ornament known as the forest garland (vanamālā) according to the very sequence prescribed for the water-pot (kalaśa).
Having performed the entire meditative contemplation (anusandhāna) as before, one should offer it.
When the separate placement is prescribed for the fourfold set beginning with the crown, O brahmins, one should invoke them in sequence upon the four ornaments. First,
one invokes the ornament called the crown of the Lord of Gods, which is endowed with a radiance equal to the sun.
"Stay here, surrounded by your retinue, upon this crest-ornament which is equal to the Śrīvatsa and the full moon, O beloved of the Blessed One;
it has been fashioned by me as an ornament for the chest of the Source of the World."
"O Kaustubha, come! You are the lord of jewels, beloved of the Blessed One.
You have been fashioned by me as an ornament for the chest of the Source of the World, which is strewn with minerals and flowers and adorned with coral gems. (14.221–222)
"O Vanamālā, come hither, O auspicious one, beloved of the God of gods!"—
with these four mantras, the twice-born should invoke [the deity] in due order.
Likewise, [they should invoke] the weapons, the ornaments, and the emblems.
O best of sages, one should likewise offer the purificatory substances for the powers (śaktis) of the Lord of Birds (Vihageśa), and then for the sacred seat (pīṭha) in due order;
in this very same manner, one should offer them for the Lord as he resides within the primary image (mūlabimba).
In the same manner for all the primary images, such as Lakṣmī and others,
as well as for other subsidiary images, the retinue,
the teacher’s throne, the script, and the Lord who is the essence of sound.
O best of the twice-born, [this applies] to the bell, the rosary, and the like, as well as the water-offering vessel and so forth;
to the parasol, the fly-whisk, and all other ritual implements;
and to all the deities of the door-panels.
Having bestowed the ornaments in due order, he should proceed to the abode of Agni.
To the Lord residing in the fire, he should offer the ornaments as before.
O Brahmins, he should present the ornament to the fire, but he must not perform a *homa* offering with it.
Since the disposal of the ornament is prescribed for what has been burnt, it is not proper to take it away without the defect having been removed;
likewise, one should then provide a replacement for the *sruk*, *sruva*, and other implements.
Having placed [the deity] upon the heart of the preceptor who has been worshipped like a god,
and likewise having placed it upon the hearts of each of the other preceptors and the practitioners,
one should then bestow [the offerings] upon the limbs of the sacrifice in due order.
O twice-born ones, when one performs the rite of consecration (pavitrāropaṇa) for the primary image,
one should first offer the protective thread (pratisara) to that primary image;
after having worshipped it thoroughly up to the offering of food (naivedya), one should thereafter perform it for the festive image (utsavakautuka).
Having brought [the deity] to the sacrificial pavilion or else to the assembly pavilion,
and having seated him upon an auspicious throne according to the previously mentioned procedure,
O twice-born ones, one should then bestow the *pratisara* upon him as he stands in the four positions.
Thus, for the God of gods who is established in the four stations,
having bestowed the ornaments according to the rule starting from the head downwards upon the Ornamented Throne with either the root mantra or the *praṇava*, [one should proceed]. (14.236–237)
Then, having brought the food and the seat, and having honored the Lord of Gods with various kinds of edibles and enjoyments, one should, with palms joined in reverence, say this:
"Neither out of arrogance nor out of delusion have I abandoned my duties."

"You alone know everything, O Lord of All, for you abide within the heart. Even though I lacked the desire, O Supreme Lord, I have performed this action according to my ability for that purpose and for your pleasure."

Having spoken thus and having honored the four Pāñcarātrikas with devotion toward the Blessed One, according to his ability, with garments and wealth; likewise, he honored the Brahmachārins, Yatis, and Gurus with Pratisaras and other offerings.
Then, having gratified [the deity] with various kinds of pure food,
the preceptor should subsequently place the image of the deity, which has been praised, upon a vehicle,
accompanied by all the auspicious rites prescribed for the rules of a great festival.

One should cause [the disciple] to enter the temple by way of circumambulation; then, O best of the twice-born, the preceptor, accompanied by his kinsmen and brothers, should perform the meal preceded by the offering of food (naivedya) with special care.
Every day, at dawn and dusk, until the removal of the ornaments,
one should worship the Lord stationed in the four locations according to the prescribed rites; furthermore,
one should worship the festival image in the pavilion with special care.

O twice-born ones, one should perform the festival of the God of gods during both [the morning and evening] periods; one may carry out the mounting of the vehicle at night or during the day. On the day of completion, there should then be a special sacrifice in the morning.
Even for one established in the four stations, having performed worship at intervals,
he should remove the purificatory threads (*pavitra*) during the night, cast them into the fire of the mandala,
and according to the rule, perform the sprinkling of the ritual jar (*kumbha*) and other rites.
Having established the *pavitraka* for one night, three nights, five, or seven nights, he should then perform the renunciation (*sannyāsa*).
Or else, O Brahmins, having placed the ornament upon the image for that duration, [he should proceed].
This should continue until the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika arrives;
or alternatively, one may offer garlands and other items day by day,
removing them so that they do not wither until the appointed day has come.
Having taken it with devotion to the guru or having offered it to a brāhmaṇa who is engaged in the five daily observances (pañcakāla)— in his absence, O Nārada—
to one who is truly devoted to Viṣṇu and intent upon the six duties (ṣaṭkarman).
At the conclusion of the special sacrifice and oblation, having performed the worship of the preceptor,
the Vaiṣṇavas should be honored as before; then one should give them clothing, O Nārada, according to one's ability, or even if such means are lacking.

One pair of garments or at least one garment must certainly be provided for one [ascetic]; for the others, he should provide upper garments along with sacred threads (upavīta). Then, a request should be made to the self-restrained ascetics (yatis).
"By the power of your grace, may there be fulfillment for me.
May there be no lapse in my observance of the rules regarding all the constituent parts of the ritual.
"So be it," they should all reply in unison with the rhythmic beat of the *tāla*.
The fault incurred through what was done or left undone during the year is swiftly destroyed by the Pavitrāropaṇa rite performed according to the prescribed rules;
for it protects the flawed practitioner from falling, thus guarding him from ruin.
Especially for the twice-born, he performs the rite that fulfills all [desires].
Even when the practitioner is devoid of ritual action, therefore this great sacrifice called the *pavitra*, characterized by the previously stated definitions, has been described by me.
O best of sages, another subtle form will be described:
[the deity] either in the solitary image, or situated in the sacrificial temple,
or situated in the temple, having been consecrated on the tenth day.
One should arrange the placement of ornaments in the mandala of the water-jars (kalaśa), excluding [the central one].
Then, even when [the deity] resides in the fire, one should perform that [rite] as previously described once it has been consecrated (adhivāsita).
At that time, one should offer one, two, or three purifiers (pavitra) to the Lord.

O best of the twice-born, whether these [rites] have been performed according to the distinctions beginning with the "excellent" (uttama) or others, if there be an absence of materials or if one should be incapable,
one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) immediately on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), carrying it out according to one's ability.
O best of the twice-born, while fasting, one should perform the decoration of the Lord’s image according to one's desire, using threads fashioned as one wishes and knots made at will,
or with the ointment of the night (turmeric), or with the substances used for purificatory rites.
O Brahmins, one should duly honor the Great Ones with someone [as a medium],
having filled their bellies with flowers, or otherwise with only [the flowers];
O Brahmins, having worshipped the Lord as present in the image as before.
Having presented the ornament, he should give it and utter this speech:
"Please cause me to take up the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) which was prepared by me,
for the sake of completing my rites, so that no fault may befall me."
Having spoken thus, one should then place the *pavitraka* upon the object of worship;
and having praised the Lord of the Gods of gods on the second day with diligence,
and having worshipped the Lord of gods, one should perform its ritual withdrawal.
Now, this specific rule for the Pavitra sacrifice in the home is declared:
whether [the deity] resides in the image, in the mandala, or even in the four locations, one should offer three pavitras, or one each, according to one's desire. || 14.272–14.273 ||
Thus it was said by the best of yogins: "The supreme *pavitrārohaṇa*—when this is performed, then eternal perfection (*siddhi*) arises;
and then all goals of the practitioners, whatever is desired by their minds, [are attained]. (14.274)
Having performed the completion of the penances, gifts, vows, the prescribed daily rites,
and the full enjoyment of all sacrifices,
one should perform [the rite] on the following day, or indeed on the fourth or even the seventh.
The ritual bathing (snapana) of the worship mantra should be performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), at a confluence,
in a river flowing to the ocean, or in a natural pool or lake,
for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord and for the destruction of one's own suffering.
For the delight of the immortals and for the satisfaction of the ancestors; for the nourishment of all beings and for the welfare of the worlds;
for the pacification of regional calamities and truly for the benefit of cows and Brahmins.

One should perform the ritual bathing according to the rules, especially for the *tīrtha*-image; however, for the daily-bathing image, one may perform it in its absence. Indeed, for the image used for the daily festival, one should perform it when that [original] image is not present.
In the absence of those [lotus stalks], there are auspicious purifiers (*pavitra*) made from clusters of *darbha* grass;
listen to my instructions on this matter with full concentration.
[The grass] should have many branches, with unbroken tips, including the roots, and should be free of flowers.
Facing east and taking up a blade of *darbha* grass with the *praṇava*, he should first [draw a line] before the earth;
then, with that very same [blade], he should establish its base as before.
That middle stalk of it which remains turned downwards—
Having propitiated him through the lord of mantras, one should remember that he is pervaded by the Great-Souled One. Know him to be the manifestation of the Supreme Self,
called the "Direct Witness," who is like a lofty stalk with many blades of darbha grass, the most excellent among all stalks.

The *puṃstattva* (the principle of the individual soul) is conceived as endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest; its designator (*vācaka*) should be employed, consisting of two syllables joined with the *haṃsa*. Outside, preceded by the *citta*, there is a fourfold group within the four sections.
Then, one should string together the downward-facing [mantras] whose ends are unmanifest, using their own words;
[these should be] pervasive, characterized by subtlety, beginning with *praṇava* (om) and ending with *namaḥ*.
In this manner, one should then string together the five [senses], beginning with hearing, by means of their own names.
Thereafter, having bound the organs of action, then the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra),
and then the pentad of gross elements ending with earth—
having bound these with their undifferentiated stalks like a basket.
Then, from the limit of its arising, without the mass of flames,
and from a certain region above that, the multitude of shafts does not indeed go forth again; thus it is conceived in many ways.
Through the enumeration of reality,
by the breaking apart of the various sections and the unification into a single essence,
another element arises; therefore, one should cultivate that firmly.
Having thus prepared the *pavitraka* made from a cluster of *darbha* grass at the outset, one should there contemplate the Mother as she truly is.
Having worshipped her with offerings of water for the hands (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth, and having adorned her, one should recite this: [14.293]
O Blessed One, you alone are the sacred ford; you alone are the supreme sanctuary.
I know this entire world to be truly presided over by you alone;
and therein, you have taught the ritual section that bestows auspiciousness.
"Whatever I shall now carry out, desiring to show you favor—
having thus informed the Blessed One, who is the supreme embodiment of mantra,
whether he has been placed within the vessel of that [disciple] or has ascended to the vehicle of Brahman (Brahmayāna)..."
Preceded by the sounds of Vedic chants, songs, conchs, and auspicious music,
they led it to the vicinity of the sacred bathing place; having placed it there in a spot shaded by clouds,
they took up that vehicle facing eastward along with the purificatory materials.
One should form [the mudrā] as if it were situated upon the earth-maṇḍala on the palm of the left hand,
and then hold it in the middle with the right hand.
Having descended into the midst of the water, one should indeed submerge oneself along with that [mudrā].
Indeed, at that time,

they remain present there without ceasing; and all the holy fords (tīrthas) situated throughout the three worlds abide for a moment in that reservoir of water, in the form of mantras, for the sake of protection.
In that place, there shall be a gathering of all the sacred sites and pilgrimage centers;
how much more so where the Blessed One, whose form is mantra and who is born of the lower eye,
bathes at the request of the practitioner with a mind intent on bestowing grace upon all.
The wise man who, knowing the truth, reaches a sacred ford (tīrtha) by this rite and bathes his kinsmen and others, they shall,
through the grace of those whose forms are the mantra, obtain the fruit of the ford without effort and before long.
However, the ritual procedure should be performed excluding vehicles and musical instruments;
the one of great intelligence should understand this distinction in this rite.
That which is common, indestructible, consisting of consciousness, and devoid of form—

Having visualized the swan of the individual soul (jīvahaṃsa) as connected with specific knowledge, and having remembered the purifier (pavitraka) in that same form, one should then bathe it with water;
in this manner, by means of that very [purifier], either for oneself or for many others, using many [purifiers].
Indeed, for those situated at a distance, the bathing on the seat is always performed first;
once the bathing has been completed in this manner, on the second day, the high-minded one,
having placed him upon a consecrated chariot, should worship him according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the festival known as the *yātrā*, preceded by the gift of food,
accompanied by dance, song, and instrumental music, and joined with a vigil for one night, two nights, or three nights, performed with devotion. (14.309–14.310)
At the end of one year, he should perform a festival consisting of the ritual bathing and other rites for the mantra-deity; he shall obtain supreme accomplishment (siddhi).
Alternatively, in the temple, [he should worship] the deity according to the most excellent of the superior paths.
Having bathed and adorned the Lord of the worlds, and having placed him upon a chariot or similar vehicle,
one should then perform a particularly grand festival procession;
thus is the ritual procedure for the Pāvitrika correctly proclaimed.
"O twice-born ones, if there is anything further to be heard, let it be told.
Thus ends [the chapter] titled "The Ritual for the Pavitraka Festival and Other Observances" in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the venerable *Pañcarātra*.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Now begins the Fifteenth Chapter. The Sages:
O Lord of Sages, please correctly explain the procedure for ablutions,
by the knowledge of which all daily and occasional rites become complete. (15.1)
— Nārada.
Listen, all you sages, with attentive minds,
to the procedure for the ablutions, which is composed of many varieties.
For that purpose, one should construct a pavilion in front of the temple.
Whether in the first enclosure, or even in the second enclosure;
or in the third enclosure, or even in the fourth or fifth;
whether in the southeast, the south, the southwest, or the west. || 15.3–15.4 ||

O twice-born ones, one should perform all the measurements and so forth in the northwest, the north, or the northeast, according to one's preference, just as in the case of a sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa). However,
this is done without a sacrificial ground in the center or an altar above it.
The placing of the jars, as well as their consecration and bathing,
should be performed by inferring how it is done in one case to apply it to all;
there should be four Brahmin preceptors, or six, eight, or even twelve.
The patron, together with his preceptor, should choose those who are learned in the scriptures;
if there are many, their number has been fixed at seven.
In the absence of such qualified persons of the prescribed number, [the following should be done].
He should choose such Brahmins— four, three, two, or even one;
he should choose four, six, eight, twelve, or sixteen practitioners who are skilled in the scriptures and proficient in the prescribed rites.
Thus, in all sacrifices— whether obligatory, occasional, or for self-perfection—
the prescribed number of preceptors and practitioners has been declared.
One should never accept [an offering] that lacks the proper number, even in times of distress.
If one should take [the property] out of delusion, there will be danger from the king and the kingdom.
(15.12) In the western third of the pavilion facing east, one should prepare a bathing pedestal by relying on the central line. (15.13)

When one performs the ritual bathing upon the bathing image or other such objects, [the deities] situated in the east should be placed facing west, those in the north facing south, and those situated in the north facing south— each according to their respective characteristics. (15.14) When one performs the ritual bathing upon the main image, [the same applies].
O best of the twice-born, one should construct the pavilion in this manner at that time. When one constructs it in front of the primary image, then,
O most excellent of the twice-born, one should not construct a bathing pedestal at that time.
O best of sages, O twice-born ones, on the seventh, the fifth, or even the third day prior to the day of the ceremonial bath, or indeed on that very day,
one should first offer the ritual sprouts and then commence the bathing ceremony.
When one performs the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the water-pots on the preceding day,
then one should perform the tying of the protective thread (kautukabandhana) during the first part of that night.
If it is obstructed on the previous day, one should perform it on that [following] day.
When the Brahmins perform the preliminary consecration of the water-pot (kumbhādhivāsana) on the day of the rite,
then on that very day he should perform the binding of the marriage-thread (kautukabandhana).
Thereafter, at dawn, the preceptor, having bathed and with a serene mind, [should proceed].
Having entered the cremation ground along with a caravan of people intent on performing the service,
O Brahmins, one facing either the east or the north should sprinkle [the site] on all sides with *darbha* grass together with *śalākā* sticks and mixed with *sahadevī*.
O Brahmins, one should smear the ground from the east to the northeast and west with fresh cow dung,
and then sprinkle all directions with filtered water mixed with the five products of the cow and kusha grass.
One, two, or even many guides are prescribed for the ritual bathing.
All of them should wear new garments, be adorned with all ornaments,
have upper cloths of new fabric, wear turbans, and be approved by the preceptor.
Many who were established in their religious observances as well as attendants,
O brahmins, gathered whatever was suitable for the bathing ceremony in each respective place;
having collected all of that, they brought it into the pavilion.
Thereafter, the preceptor who has mastered the scriptures should commence the ritual ablution (snapana).
Know that the ablution is of two kinds, distinguished as the higher (para) and the lower (apara).
The higher is said to be tenfold, according to the distinctions of the primary [deity] and so forth.
Know the first to be Pradhāna; the second is remembered as Para;
the third is Parasūkṣma; and the fourth is Parasthūla. The fifth would be Sūkṣmapara, while the sixth is Sūkṣmasūkṣma.
The seventh is subtle-coarse; the eighth would be coarse-superior.
The ninth is coarse-subtle, and that which follows is coarse-coarse.
Thus, through the distinctions of superior and so forth, the other is established as ninefold.
This common ritual bath for all these [deities], distinguished as superior and inferior, is known by the name Anantakalaśa; it fulfills all [desires].
For these [deities] beginning with the principal one, preceded by the laying of the foundation lines (sūtrapāta) [the rite is performed].
O twice-born ones, listen in due order to everything up to the conclusion of the extraction.
Having placed a very beautiful water-vessel made of metal, wood, or even clay in the north-eastern direction of the pavilion (maṇṭapa), [one should proceed]. 15.33–34.
Having washed the altar with water and covered it with new cloths,
one should then perform the laying out of the lines (sūtrapāta) in accordance with the number of ritual jars (kumbha),
within the sacrificial field (kṣetra) and pavilion (maṇṭapa) of the prescribed dimensions.
O best of Brahmins, having taken up the eastern part of the pavilion,
one should lay down four lines— three from west to east and one from south to north—
and then establish five lines running from south to north. (15.36–15.37)
When this has been done, O twice-born ones, there are twelve squares here;
the extent of each one should be either a *tāla*, a *prādeśa*,
a *hasta*, or an *aratni*, according to the dimensions of the pavilion.
And for the large jars, in this same manner everywhere and upwards;
having adorned them on all four sides with flour-dust,
one should prepare a pedestal in the enclosures using either rice or grain.
For each of those rooms,
O Brahmins, one should prepare [the offering] with three *prasthas* plus half a *prastha*, or simply with three *prasthas*,
or with two *prasthas* plus half a *prastha*. (15.41)
Or else,

O twice-born ones, having constructed a pedestal (pīṭhikā) of such proportions— measuring two prasthas, or one and a half prasthas, or one prastha, or half a prastha, or even a quarter of that, or a fourth part of that— according to the prescribed rule; || 15.42–15.43 ||
The jars should be made of gold, silver, or copper, free from flaws, smooth, and without holes; they should be twenty-four finger-breadths in height.
Their width at the middle should be the same, and their necks should be three finger-breadths high.
The width of its mouth is known to be three finger-breadths;
O best of the twice-born, the girdle should be understood to be three finger-breadths all around,
or else half that measure, with all dimensions determined first by the height.
Or else, the most excellent of the brahmins, who fill a *droṇa* measure,
are less by one-eighth [of that amount] in successive order down to two *prasthas*.
But the lowest of the low pitchers are those that hold only one *prastha* of water.
Thus, these [images] should be fashioned according to one's means, endowed with these characteristics:
they should be situated upon the base of the discus, broad, with bellies like those of tortoises, necks marked by the lines of the Pāñcajanya conch, and faces like lotuses. 15.48–49.
The twice-born [gods], adorned with garlands of moonlight above and below,
carry forth streams of nectar-water from the mouths of the serpent Śeṣa, who has the face of a sea-monster.
Adorned with river-pearls, ocean-pearls, auspicious trees, and various garlands— or,
if such things are unavailable, even without the discus-supports and so forth—
these [liṅgas] may be made of clay in the secondary rite, provided they are free from cracks, fissures, or holes. (15.51)
They should not be double-heated, but well-heated, being of a single color and possessing a beautiful luster.
Having grasped them, one should wash them thoroughly on all sides with pure water;
one should then carefully wrap them with thread, leaving an interval of one finger-breadth between each.
In the western direction, from the location of the water jar, one should consecrate the jars.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with *śāli* rice, or on a bare sacrificial mound,
one should spread *kuśa* grass there with the tips pointing eastward and northward.
Having placed the jars there with the *tāra* [syllable], one should worship them with the *puṣpa* [mantra]. Then,
having placed those very same jars facing downwards in a row,
and having spread *kuśa* grass over them, one should face eastward with the *parameṣṭhin* [mantra].
Then, having displayed the darbha-mudrā and having sprinkled everything all around with scented water, one should scatter unbroken grains (akṣatāni) with the *pums* mantra and the *viśva* mantra,
O best of sages; and having turned [the vessel] upward with the *nivṛtti* mantra and the *sarva* mantra.
Having set aside the individual jars, one should place them in their respective positions in due order.
One should perform all the rites, such as the placement of the jar (*kumbha-nyāsa*), with the root mantra;
however, having purified them through inspection and other means, one should do so with the *sahṛdaya* mantra.
One should consecrate them one by one with the eight-syllable mantra;

thereafter, one should worship them with that same mantra using offerings such as water for honor (arghya), garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth. Then, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for their extraction according to one's capacity.
Then, having completed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should sequentially apply the ritual substances.

In the three rows, starting from the west and ending at the east, there are four [substances] in each. Therein, in the row of the southern direction, in the pitcher situated in the west— || 15.61–15.62 ||

Then one should likewise place in the middle row water from *dhātrī* fruit, followed by water from *lodhra*, water from red sandalwood, and the excellent water from turmeric. 15.63. Then, however, one should arrange them in the middle row in that very same manner.
Then there should be water with *grandhi* sprouts, followed by *tagara* water;
after that, water with *priyaṅgu*, and beyond that, water with *māṃsī*.
Likewise, these four should be placed in the northern row.
Then one should place water with white mustard seeds, water with all medicinal herbs,
water with all gems, and thereafter pure water.
One should also place a *kūrca* made of *kuśa*, *darbha*, or *udumbara* grass, sixteen finger-breadths in length.
The knot should measure one finger-breadth (aṅgula), while the root is indeed twelve fingers;
one should know that the remainder is the tip—this is the characteristic of the *kūrca*.
Alternatively, the knot may be half a finger, and the tip should be two fingers.
O best of Brahmins, one should prepare a base (mūla) measuring twelve finger-breadths;
for a Brāhmaṇa it should consist of four darbha blades, for a Kṣatriya three darbha blades, and for a Vaiśya two darbha blades; such should also be the kūrca for women and Śūdras.
Alternatively, one should prepare a *kūrca* for each of them, repeating it twenty-eight times;
then, O best of sages, one should worship the jars in sequence with the root mantra, using water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), touch, flowers, and incense.
Having covered them in sequence with lids wrapped in thread,
one should wrap each jar with cloths if one has the means; then,
having covered [the whole] on all sides with a new cloth, one should face the east or the north.
Having performed the worship as before, one should then commence the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of fuel sticks (*samid*) and other materials individually,
and having then offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should consecrate the water jars (*kalaśa*) with mantras.
O twice-born ones, the bathing of all [the deities] is prescribed with the root mantra,
using jars filled with pure water in successive intervals. One should perform both the bathing and the offering of *arghya* with the ritual substances.
Its extraction is proclaimed to follow the very sequence of the deposition of substances (*dravyanyāsa*).
This is declared to be the primary [practice], consisting of twelve jars;
O virtuous ones, this is the cause of all things, while others are the effects. || 15.76–15.77 ||
Then with water, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and subsequently with milk,
curd, ghee, honey, and the water of all medicinal herbs;
then with the water of seeds, fruits, and fragrant flowers.
Then, twelve jars— this is what is declared to be the supreme number— should be filled in due order with water containing gold and jewels,
and with the five products of the cow, curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugarcane juice.
It was filled in succession with the scents of all medicinal herbs, jewels, fruits, flowers, and water,
and even with pure water alone;
this set of twelve jars is declared to be most subtle.
And in both of these cases, O twice-born ones, the laying of the lines and so forth should be performed as in the primary rite.
Likewise, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for rinsing the mouth, water with all medicinal herbs, curd, milk, honey, ghee, and pure water [should be offered]. (15.82–15.83)
This group of nine pitchers is declared to be "thick at the top";
its [method of] laying out the lines and so forth has already been fully described.
When the field is divided fivefold, there shall be twenty-five parts.
Outside, by means of the arrangement starting with the east and so forth, in the sixteen jars [are placed]:
milk, curd, ghee, honey, and indeed sugarcane juice;
as well as the ten items beginning with the *dhātrī* fruit and ending with all medicinal herbs.
Thereafter, within those eight jars, [one should place] leaf-water; then,
starting from the east, flower-water, fruit-water, seed-water,
and then scented water, as well as water containing gold and jewels.

One should place pure water in the midst of the waters of sacred fords and rivers. The extraction [of the deity] is declared to follow the very sequence of the placement of the ritual substances. Thus, O best of the twice-born, with the jars containing the substances in their proper order, || 15.88–15.89 ||
This *snapana* [ablution] with twenty-five [substances] is known as the subtle and supreme.
Having arranged twenty-five compartments as before,
one should place pure water in the center and [the other substances] outside according to the sequence beginning with Indra.
The first was filled with milk and water; the next with pure water; the third with water containing jewels; another with golden water;
and others mixed with scented water and provided with water from fruits and flowers.

The eighth [vessel] is proclaimed to be filled with water and śāli rice seeds; these eight jars are situated outside, resting upon the eight directions. In the east, there is water with dhātrī fruits, and in the west, water with pathyā.
In another [vessel] powdered *gulūcī*, in another water of *vibhītaka*;
water boiled with *kumārī* and likewise water of *vyāghrī*;
in another water of *nāgara*, and similarly in another water of honey.
In this case, the extraction is prescribed by means of the sequence for depositing substances,
using only water consecrated with the Nṛsiṃha mantras,
followed by the five mantras beginning with Satya and the three beginning with Siṃha, respectively.

O Lords of Sages, having consecrated each one of the jars situated within the inner enclosure seven times with the mantra of the wheel (*cakramantra*) and those beginning with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should then consecrate the jars standing outside that [enclosure] starting from the east. || 15.97–15.98 ||

The Brahmins should bathe [the deity] in sequence with water-pots containing the *gāyatrī* mantra; however, for those situated in the second enclosure, the ritual services (*upacāra*) are prescribed to be performed with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, one should sprinkle [the deity] with pure water consecrated by the recitation of the *astra-mantra*.
Or rather, one should perform everything according to the very path previously described.
This [rite] is remembered as being performed with ten or seven jars, on a field of four cubits, three cubits, or two and a half cubits—each [measurement] becoming increasingly subtle. 15.100–15.101
Having prepared a space of two cubits, half of that should be divided into two parts;
with one part one should fashion the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and with the second part the sixteen petals.
Then, O Brahmins, one should arrange the petals upon the pericarp.
A set of four jars, situated in the four cardinal directions,
should first be filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then with clay and water, then with water containing all medicinal herbs, and finally with pure water alone. || 15.103–15.104 ||
Beginning from the eastern leaf and extending as far as the domain of Īśāna,
one should install sixteen other jars there in sequence;
first, one should fill [the initial jar] with the five products of the cow alone.
The second [application] is with cow urine, the third with cow-dung water,
O Brahmins; the fourth is with the ashes of the three sacred fires,
and the final one with earth from the horns of an elephant, a cow, or a bull, and from an anthill.
O twice-born ones, the sixth jar should then be filled with earth from rice fields, from the middle of a river, from a cluster of lotuses, and from a mountain;
the seventh with water and mustard seeds; and the eighth with all medicinal herbs.
Know that the ninth is with milk; the tenth is said to be with curd.
O twice-born ones, the eleventh is with clarified butter, and the twelfth is with honey.
The thirteenth is with all [these] seeds, and the fourteenth is with all fruits.
Another [type] is with all grains, and the sixteenth is with all fragrances;
here, the extraction is performed according to the sequence of the placement of substances.
Having first consecrated each individual jar with the heart-mantra, [one should proceed].
"Then one should bathe [the image] with each individual root-mantra in due order.
(15.112) Thus, O best of the twice-born, this rite accompanied by twenty jars has been described; now another, both subtle and gross, is told, O brahmins. (15.113)
Having laid down five threads extending from east to west,
one should then lay down eleven threads for the south and north.
When this is done, there will indeed be forty squares.

There, beginning from the western row and proceeding in due order, having placed four jars each from south to north, one should fill them with substances; listen as I describe them in sequence. (15.115–15.116)

The three [substances] are prepared with the materials for the water for the feet, the respectful offering, and the water for sipping, as previously described; they are obtained from a mountain— at its beginning, end, and middle— from a river, from clay, and from sand, from a pool,
from the crest of an anthill, and from a place scarred by the tusk of an elephant.
Cow-dung arises from fields, from the horns of bulls, and from rice-paddies; likewise, it arises from clusters of lotuses, or else from a single [spot],
or from a forest fire, and similarly from a kitchen.
Others, having placed the ashes of the three sacred fires within one jar,
and in another, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) together with kuśa-water;
and [yet others] a jar of oil along with ghee, filled with the water of the camasa-vessel.

Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, śamī, and red sandalwood [are used] in one [mixture]; in another, however, there is decoction water made from the three myrobalans (triphalā). Vacā, śatāvarī, kanyā, vyāghrī, siṃhī, and kṛtāñjali [are the herbs]. || 15.121–15.122 ||
O best of beings, in another jar [should be placed] golomī, siṃhalomī, kuṣṭha, bhūmyañjana, and mahāgaruḍavegā;
likewise mahānīlā, gulūcī, sahadevī, and śatāvarī.
Viṣṇukrāntā, Kārkoṭā, Sāhvā, and Vahniśikhā are [used] in one [preparation];
Yaṣṭī and Varāhakarṇī, as well as Gajapippalī, are in another;
and Śrīphalā and other purifying fruits are in yet another. || 15.124–15.125 ||
One should place jars of curd, milk, and ghee, along with two jars containing honey and sugarcane juice;
and one should place the roots of lotuses in another pair of jars,
especially those of purifying trees that contain milky sap.
A cluster of blossoms on a single branch provided with leaves, flowers, and fruit;
or else, a collection of flowering creepers such as the *jāti* and others on a single [branch]; as well as the two—*rocanā* and the pair of *rajanīs*—*balā*, *moṭa*, and *padmaka*.
Thus, in one [vessel] there are the five [grains], and in another, sprouts of *darbha* and *dūrvā*;
in yet another vessel, indeed, there is a heap of rice sprouts along with *āsya*,
and white *siddhārthaka* and the like, as well as *priyaṅgu* known for its fragrance.
One should place [the herbs] together with *nāgakeśara* into another jar.
Seven village herbs and seven forest herbs should be placed in the two jars;
likewise, *bāhlīka*, sandalwood, juice, and camphor.

Others, however, place this tetrad in another location; the pure elements, such as copper, Jāmbūnada gold, and so forth, are a great mass of jewels (ratnacaya). One should place a network of coral and pearls in two locations.
Then there is the water for the guest-offering (arghyodaka) in one vessel, and river-water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in two;
furthermore, a jar of all medicinal herbs, a jar of very cool water,
and a pitcher of fragrant flowers— these are recorded as being forty [in total].
This extraction of the sequence for the deposition of substances is remembered as both gross and supreme,
O twice-born ones; it consists solely of forty jars filled with cool water, and thus the gross and subtle [system] is revealed.
Accompanied by forty jars filled with scented water, this is proclaimed as the "very gross" [level of practice]. Likewise,
there is the procedure for laying out the lines and the sequence for the placement of the ritual vases (kumbha).
O twice-born ones, one should perform the redemption for these two in a manner dissimilar to the gross [offense] and so forth—
either by the power of devotion and faith, or in accordance with one's wealth.
One should perform the threefold gross distinction, however, doubled.
In the secondary rite (anukalpa), O best of Brahmins, one may use half of that [measure], or a quarter, or even an eighth part;
or there may be four jars, or two each,
or even just one each, containing all the ritual substances.

Regarding the nine complete [types], other requirements besides those mentioned should be performed by inferring them all according to the path taught for the primary [type]. (15.141) Thus, O Brahmins, the tenfold subdivisions of the supreme [mantras] have been proclaimed.
O twice-born ones, listen now in due order to the subdivisions of the other [mandala]:
when the field has been made square and divided into thirty-one parts, there are nine hundred and sixty-one squares. (15.142–15.143)
Having established three rows in the middle, one should erase two on its exterior; then,
for the sake of the paths (vīthī), having again established three rows on the exterior,
one should erase two for the sake of the paths and establish seven more.
Or, O twice-born ones, having divided each [section] into three or nine parts, one should sprinkle [the site];
in a narrow place, for the sake of piercing [the ground], one should arrange the jars as before.
One should place the jars in those compartments in sequence, as previously described.
Clarified butter, warm water, jewel-water, fruit-water,
iron-water, cleansing-water, scented water,
and water with unhusked rice— these, ending with the Ishana [quarter], should be offered starting from the center in the middle vessel. || 15.147 ||
One should offer water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācāma), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in sequence.
This is done in the center of nine squares enclosed by two [lines] on each side,
and likewise in the center of those situated at the intermediate directions, starting from the east and ending with the north.
Curd, milk, honey, and likewise a decoction, in the order of the directions starting from fire (the southeast)—
thus seventeen [substances] are declared, combined with the principal materials.
The remaining others are sixty-four, accompanied by pure water.
"Thus, O twice-born ones, eighty-one jars are situated in the center.
Then, there are forty-nine jars in those eight directions;
one should sprinkle those located in the directions into the central jars."
O best of sages, one should sprinkle molasses-water, sugarcane juice, coconut water,
and likewise the water of peace (śāntivāri) into the Brahma-pitchers located in the intermediate directions, following the sequence starting from the east, using the auspicious water.
O best of the twice-born, there are three hundred and eighty-four remaining jars, starting from the southeast and extending to the northeast,
likewise increased by four;
these are filled with fragrant, cool waters.
Thereafter, in the central group of nine, one should worship the nine forms beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Varāha, starting from the center and proceeding to the northeast and west,
using water for the guest-offering (arghya), anointing, garlands, and incense, in due order.
Outside of that, one should worship [the deities] within the nine Brahma-pitchers,
starting from Keśava up to Vāmana, in groups of two and four according to the sequence of the directions. Then, O lords of sages, there are forty-nine pitchers.
O twice-born ones, one should worship the four beginning with Śrīdhara in the Brahma-pitchers,
starting from the east and ending in the north, and from the southeast to the west; likewise,
one should worship the group of four beginning with Nara and ending with Kṛṣṇa.
Having arranged the tufts of grass as before and covered them with small lids,
he should then cover each one individually with new cloths.
Thereafter, he should worship the god Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe.
One should bathe the Lord with water-pots accompanied by verses beginning with "pādya" and ending with auspicious words,
using either the eight-syllable mantra, or the twelve-syllable one,
or the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, or even the mantra of His specific form.
O twice-born ones, the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) may be performed with all the jars; or else,
