one should bathe the deity with water for the feet (*pādya*) using the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī,
and bathe him with the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) using the mantra "Tad Viṣṇoḥ."
One should perform the bath with the verse beginning "prati viṣṇo" followed by the sipping of water (ācamana);
the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be performed with the mantra "viṣṇoḥ karma".
One should bathe the Lord with curd using the mantra "dadhi krāvṇaḥ".
One should perform the consecration with cow’s milk using the mantra "āpyāyasva";
the bathing of the Lord with honey should be done with the mantra "madhu vātā";
and the bathing with decoctions should be performed with the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ."
One should perform the bathing with plain water using the mantra "tvaṃ viṣṇuḥ";
one should bathe [the deity] with water containing fruit using the mantra beginning with "phalinī";
and one should perform the bathing with purificatory waters using the mantra "śanno devī".
With the *Sāvitrī* mantra and water containing unbroken grains (*akṣata*), one should sprinkle [the image] with the mantra "O Agni, come hither" (*agna āyāhi*).
With water containing jewels and the mantra "May it be for you" (*iṣetva*), one sprinkles with metallic water.
One performs the bathing with barley-water using the mantra "Gandhadvārām" (*gandhadvārā*). || 15.169–15.170 ||
One should perform a bath with fragrant water using the *śatadhāra* mantra;
then one should bathe the deity with ghee while reciting the verse *śukram asi*.
Alternatively, one may proceed from the *pādya* offering up until the final water-offering.
Then, with the verses of the Puruṣasūkta and the verse beginning "śukram asi," [he offers] the fourfold oblation of clarified butter, molasses-water, and so forth, ending with the Śānti hymns;
and with the mantra "tvaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and "viṣṇor nukam," O twice-born ones. || 15.172–15.173 ||
O best of sages, one should bathe [the image] with water called *maṅgala*; indeed,
with that same principal jar (*pradhānakalaśa*) with which one would sprinkle the Lord of Gods,
one should consecrate it with jars of pure water using that same mantra.
For each substance, having worshipped with a mantra using water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), touching, garlands, incense, and so forth, one should then consecrate [the disciple] with that.
Whatever *arghya*, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for rinsing the mouth (*ācāma*), fragrance, garland, incense, and lamp there may be— || 15.175–176 ||
One should offer everything in due order, or simply the *arghya* alone;
this bathing of the jars, joined with four hundred, seventy, and three [verses], is called the most excellent of the excellent.
It was inferior, with its interior waters purified by eight times eight [sixty-four] drops.
That which is performed with water-pots (kalaśas) would be either superior or middling;
likewise, a row of four [pots] would be inferior compared to what was previously determined.
This aforementioned bathing [rite] is joined with eighty-one [pots] in the middle.

O twice-born ones, it was accompanied by pitchers placed in the cardinal directions— forty-nine in each set— and in the intermediate directions, as well as those situated in the portions belonging to Brahmā and the gods,
numbering one hundred and sixty in total.
O Brahmins, that [rite] which is devoid of pure waters and jars would be the lowest of the superior;
whereas [that which is performed] with two hundred jars stationed in the four directions is the highest.
O Brahmins, when it is joined with eighty-one [verses] minus four— that is, with seventy-seven—
it becomes the middle-superior bath, as before.
It is performed with sixty-four pure waters for internal purification.
If it should be deficient by [the number of] pitchers, that would be the "middling-middling" [type].
And when it is endowed with eighty-one pitchers from the center, with forty-nine in the directions and nine in the middle; 15.184–15.185.
Devoid of the remaining pure water-pitchers, it is considered middling or inferior;
one should designate this as a low-quality site when it lacks eight rows [of pitchers].
O twice-born ones, it consists of eighty-one pitchers alone, just as before.
This is proclaimed as the lowest and highest form of the ritual bathing (snapana).
However, that bathing which is devoid of the thirty-two pitchers located at the corners and filled with pure water would be of the lowest-middle grade.
O best of the twice-born, that which is devoid of the sixty-four jars filled with pure water situated in all directions is the lowest of the low.
Having divided the field here into nine or seven parts, one should then press it.
"Two or four [measures] remain for the purpose of placing the jars.
Thus, O best of sages, another [method] has been declared in nine ways;
however, one should perform everything prior to the consecration of the jars (*kumbhādhivāsa*) as previously described.
The deity of clarified butter is remembered as the supreme god Vāsudeva;
of hot water, Saṅkarṣaṇa; and of jeweled water, Pradyumna.
O twice-born ones, the blessed Aniruddha is the deity of fruit-water.

Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is mantra, is the deity of the metallic water; Hayagrīva is the deity of the cleansing water, and Viṣṇu is the deity of the fragrant water. Nṛsiṃha is the deity of the water used for washing the [image], and Varāha is the deity of the barley-water.
Keśava is declared the deity of the water for washing the feet; Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the deity of the arghya offering; Mādhava is the presiding deity of the water for sipping (ācamanīya);
Govinda is the deity of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), while Viṣṇu is the deity of the curd.
The deity of milk is known as Madhusūdana;
the one named Trivikrama is the deity of honey, and Vāmana is the deity of astringent honey. The Blessed One named Śrīdhara, however, is the deity of molasses-water.
Hṛṣīkeśa, the God of gods, is the deity of sugarcane juice;
Dāmodara, O twice-born ones, is the presiding deity of coconut water.
The Blessed One Padmanābha, however, is the deity of the water used for propitiatory rites.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa are the deities from Agni to Īśa for the auspicious waters;
they are also the deities of the eighty-one Śuddhodāna [pits].
The group of eight beginning with Kānti and ending with Unnati [is placed] in each direction;
outside, in the forty-nine pure waters,
there are in sequence the Śaktis beginning with Svadhā and ending with Gāyatrī as their presiding deities (adhidevatās).
There are eight [deities] each in the directions starting from the east, and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast.
Garuḍa is the deity of the water-pots (kalaśas), Śeṣa is the deity of the cord (sūtra),
the Supreme Brahman is the deity of the grass-bunches (kūrca), and the King of Cakras (cakrarāj) is the deity of the small discs (cakrikās).
Vāsudeva alone, or he himself,
[performs] the cleaning, the sprinkling, and the smearing with cow dung of all the garments;
as well as the laying out of the lines and the decoration all around with flour-dust.
The knower of mantras should perform [the rite] with the eight-syllable and other mantras;
the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the jars with the five Upaniṣads.
There, he should place the jars in the compartments with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
There, one should fill [the vessels] in sequence with the designations of the presiding deities of the respective substances;
one should then cast *kūrca* grasses into them with the *Dviṣaṭka-Brahmavidyā* mantra.
One should worship each of those presiding deities of the substances within their respective substances.
Afterwards, the practitioner should establish the wheels with the wheel-mantra (cakramantra). Then, the knower of mantras should cover them with cloths using the twelve-syllable mantra.
The knower of mantras should then perform the removal of the cloths with the root-mantra (mūlamantra).
Having cut the threads with the *praṇava* and having honored them with that same [mantra],
he should lift them up with the *viṣṇugāyatrī* and likewise place them in the hand of the preceptor.
O twice-born ones, whatever mantra has not been prescribed here for a particular rite—
The wise practitioner should perform each of those [rites] with the eight-syllable mantra;
or else, O best of the twice-born, one should perform all rites with the root-mantra alone, as previously described for the various types of ablutions.
The collection of materials for the *arghya* and other offerings is now described for the others:
*viṣṇuparṇī*, *dūrvā*, lotus, and *śyāmāka*.
O best of the twice-born, these four are the constituent parts of the water for washing the feet (*pādya*).

Fragrant substances, flowers, unbroken rice grains, fruits, barley, white mustard seeds, sesame seeds, and the tips of *kuśa* grass—these eight indeed constitute the components of the *arghya* offering. Cloves, nutmeg, and *kakkola* are the ingredients for the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). || 15.214–15.215 ||
Cow dung, cow urine, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter—
these five are the constituent parts of the *pañcagavya* in their entirety.
[The wood of] the *śamī*, *udumbara*, *bilva*, as well as the *palāśa* and *vaṭa* [trees are used].

Likewise, from the *khadira*, the *aśvattha*, and the *vikaṅkata* tree, the bark-essence (*tvaksāra*) is an astringent that removes all sins. Also, the *kadalī*, *bimba*, *cūta*, *panasa*, and *mātuluṅga* [are used]. (15.217–218)
Coconut, emblic myrobalan, and citron— these eight fruits are indeed said to be the constituent parts of the fruit-water (phalāmbhas).
Sahadevī, śirīṣa, turmeric, and sūryavartinī.
The *sadābhadra*, *kuśāgra*, and the six parts for cleansing are the [six] twice-born [gems].
Likewise, the sun-stone (*sūryakānta*), ruby (*padmarāga*), moon-stone (*indukānta*), lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), emerald (*ayas-kānta*), sapphire (*indranīla*), and coral (*prabālaka*). (15.220–221)
The *gāruḍa* gem, the *puṣyarāga*, crystal, and *brahmarāga*,
as well as diamond and pearl— these, O twice-born ones, are the limbs of the giver of jewels;
furthermore, the *maṇi*, the pearl, the diamond, coral, and likewise the *puṣyaka*.
O best of sages, these five are the ingredients of the jewel-water:
bāhlīka, sandalwood, camphor, and likewise agallochum;
or else, O best of sages, there are four fragrant ingredients.
Sandalwood, saffron, spikenard,
nut-grass, *mura*, vetiver, costus, and agallochum— these are the eight ingredients for fragrant water for the body.
Gold, silver, copper, and likewise iron and tin;
The five limbs of the water of iron have indeed been described.
Sesame, white mustard, wild rice, barley, bamboo-seed,
and Tulasī leaves combined— these are the six limbs of the water for pacification.
The sprout of *indravallī*, a lotus, and likewise the sprout of the *aśvattha* tree,
as well as a single lotus— these are the four components of the auspicious water (*maṅgalavāri*).
All the jars of pure water are joined with a single portion of sandalwood.
Having thus stated the subsequent varieties of ablutions in their proper order, the collection of substances and all the medicinal herbs and so forth are now described:
*kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, the two types of *haridrā*, *murā*, *śaileya*, and *campaka*. (15.229–230)
Vacā, kaccūra, and mustā are proclaimed to be all-purpose medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhyaḥ*).
Also, the tender leaves (*pallavāḥ*) produced from the palāśa, bilva, vakula, kadamba, āmra, śirīṣa,
nyagrodha, and aśvattha trees constitute *patravāri* (leaf-water).
Flowers arising from the *ketakī*, *mallikā*, *jāti*, *nandyāvarta*, and *utpala*; flowers produced from the *padma*, *campaka*, *kunda*, and others—these constitute the "flower-water.
[Likewise, there are grains such as] barley, wheat, *kava* rice, *vrīhi* rice, *śāli* rice, mung beans, and *priyaṅgu*. (15.232–15.233)
Māṣa, nīvāra, krauñca, and aṅga are said to be the seeds for the seed-water;
then there is the vessel named Anantakalaśa, which fulfills everything.
O best of sages, listen now to the procedure for this.
One should construct a pavilion as before, forty cubits in length,
thirty-two cubits in width, provided with four doors and so forth,
and well-adorned with banners and other decorations as previously described.
Or, having constructed a mere water-station (prapā) at a location as desired,
one should fashion a pavilion (maṇṭapa) nearby for the sake of the sacrifice, as previously described.
On the day mentioned, prior to the day of the ritual, one should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having gathered all the necessary materials for that purpose, being well-composed,
the preeminent teacher, having bathed thoroughly on the preceding day and performed his daily rites,
shall adorn himself with various ornaments and new garments. || 15.238–239 ||
Wearing a white turban and upper garment, and adorned with variegated garlands,
he was accompanied by four or eight attendants of similar appearance who were likewise practitioners,
skilled in the sciences, and adorned with tunics and other finery. (15.240)
With many attendants whose faces and noses were covered with other very white garments,
and who were skilled in various specific applications,
one should enter at the time of afternoon, having performed the worship of the door-keepers.
For the sake of the sacrifice, one should worship the deity there in a pavilion (maṇṭapa) within the ritual pitcher and other vessels;
or else, one should worship the image (bimba) in that very place after having gratified the fire as before. Then, O best of sages, having obtained permission, [one should proceed] in due order.
But in the case of a secondary rite (*anukalpa*), having entered the temple and worshipped the primary image (*mūlabimba*) with offerings of water (*arghya*), unguents (*ālabhana*), and garlands,
and then having received permission with incense, one should then begin.
Having first worshipped the two door-keepers, one should enter the bathing pavilion;
one should sprinkle it everywhere with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the root mantra.
One should also scatter various kinds of flowers in all directions.
And having placed white mustard seeds in the center of the pavilion,
one should divide the field into five parts, each measuring twenty-two and a half cubits;
furthermore, each of these should be divided ninefold, resulting in forty-five sections.
There shall also be twenty-five rows of squares;
then, in the center of those two thousand [squares], for the purpose of installing the vase,
one should set aside eighty-one squares and sweep them clean.

Around [the center], there are two rows of paths; outside of that, one should again arrange eighty-one squares in the four directions starting from the east. Alongside the path, there should again be two rows.
One should arrange forty-nine squares in the four corners there,
according to the sequence of eighty-one;
having established a group of nine in the center, one should omit one entire row around it.
Outside, having established six squares in each of the cardinal directions and six in each of the intermediate directions,
as well as four in each of the corners, one should erase the remaining [squares].
Then, one should erase two rows all around that outer boundary to form the enclosure (vīthī).
One should carefully construct sixteen squares for the corners;
then, on each side, one should erase one row in each of the four directions.
In the two rows of the gates, there are three internal parts and three external parts.
On the five sides, however, for the sake of beauty, there are four [squares] and two outside of that.
Within that, in the three rows, there are thirty-three squares;
having brought them to unity with the central path (vīthī), one should place each one on the exterior.
O lords of sages, having established twenty-five squares on each side in the middle of the corners of the doors, one should erase each row in mutual alternation.
Having thus prepared the positions for the jars for the purpose of their placement,
O twice-born ones, one should then fashion straight lines with white fragrant powder, equal in width and height to a thumb. || 15.259–15.260 ||
Having scattered powder upon the inner chambers, one should subsequently fill the doorways with that same yellow powder, adorned with various flowers.
O best of sages, one should everywhere decorate the pathways with clusters of creepers.
Then, having taken up one hundred and eight jars marked with all the auspicious characteristics, and having offered clarified butter with the root mantra or with the Gāyatrī,
he should [proceed] to the four doors in the order starting from the eastern direction.
Having established the water-jars in pairs and worshipped the *kumuda* and other [deities],
one should honor the compartments with flowers consecrated by various mantras; then,
with great care, one should arrange the pathways using all kinds of grains.

Into those [vessels], O twice-born ones, one should place two blades of *kuśa* grass at the tips using the root mantra (15.265). Having wrapped the jars with thread as before, and having washed them with the *gāyatrī*, one should then place them in their respective compartments (15.266).
One should place kusha grass with its tips pointing downward upon the back [of the image], identifying it with the nature of Parameṣṭhin.
Then, one should sprinkle those kusha blades with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Puṃs-sūkta.
Having sprinkled them, one should scatter unbroken rice grains over them while reciting the Viśva-sūkta.
Then, by means of the rite of withdrawal, he should indeed gradually and with effort turn them face upwards.
O Brahmins, he should then fill them all in sequence with filtered water scented with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like.
In the middle of the eighty-one [squares], situated within the central group of nine, in the central pitcher,
are: sunstone, ruby, lapis lazuli, moonstone,
magnetite, sapphire, coral, and likewise emerald.
Having placed the puṣyarāga, crystal, brahmarāga, and mecaka,
as well as the diamond, silver, pearl, and copper—
all these— outside that [structure] within a new enclosure of eight wooden pieces.
From the east to the northeast, one should place these sixteen substances in order within the central jars in pairs;
in the remaining seventy-two [jars], one should place pearls.
In the previously mentioned group of nine situated in the center, within the central region—consisting of the plantains, jackfruit, and mangoes; those known as *kṣīrikā* and *badara*;
the *mātuluṅga* and *kesara*; and also the *bhavya* and *jambīra*—(15.274–15.275).
Thereafter, one should place fruits outside that [mandala] upon nine wooden planks,
extending from the east to the northeast: the citron (*mātuluṅga*), the pomegranate (*dāḍima*),
the orange (*nāraṅga*), the lime (*jambīra*), the *takkola*, and likewise the jujube (*badarī*).
Kṣīrikā and āmalaka, as well as drākṣā and kharjūra; the āmra and sahakāra, and likewise the fruit of the panasa; the small-panasa, and likewise the kadalī and mocaka. || 15.277–15.278 ||
One should place them in the central jars by means of pairs in successive order;
one should cast jujube fruits into the nine jars and the eight jars,
as well as uśīra, saffron, māṃsī, and sandalwood.
One should place murā, haribera, kuṣṭha, and agaru in the eighty-one squares in the southern direction; these are all the Viśvas.
In the center, in the central jar, they should be placed according to the sequence starting from the east.
In the remaining middle jars, one should place a pala each of [the aforementioned substances],
and one should also cast in sandalwood (*malayaja*) among these groups of eight.
[This applies] to the oceans, ponds, wells, tanks, and lakes.
One should place the waters of rain and of rivers in the central jar dedicated to Varuṇa; one of each [of the remaining substances] in the other middle jars;
and in the remaining groups of eight, one should pour pure water.
Barley, wheat, *vrīhi* rice, *śāli* rice, mung beans, *priyaṅgu*,
black gram, and wild *nīvāra* grain— these should be placed in the ninth central jar;
and in the remaining jars, as well as in the middle jars, one type of grain each should be placed in due order.
And in the groups of eight, one should offer pure waters;
in the group of forty-nine, one should fill [the vessels] with clarified butter according to the Āgneya method;
and in the groups of six, one should likewise place cow’s urine and cow dung through the application of Indra and the other deities.
Having poured milk and curd [into the central nine], one should place warm water in the corners;
having placed oil in the ninth square in the southwest (nairṛta), outside of that,
in the remaining forty jars, one should place molasses-water.
In the center of the ninefold [array] of the Vāyavya direction, one should place mustard oil;
and in the remaining jars, one should place sugarcane juice.
In the forty-nine-fold [array] of the Īśāna direction, one should place honey.
In the remaining [vessels], one should place coconut water or its milk.
In the twenty-five [vessels] beginning with that of Indra, [one should place these] in the first and middle jars.
[These substances are taken] from sacred fields, pilgrimage sites, oceans, and mountains; from the cave known as Sūkara; and from an elephant.
One should fill [the remaining parts] by taking earth from an anthill and from the horn of a bull;
for each of the other eight [parts], and for the sixteenth, one should add fragrant water.
[The herbs are] sahadevī, vacā, śatamūlī, and śatāvarī.
Kumārī, gulūcī, siṃhī, and likewise vyāghrī—
one of each— should be placed in the second middle pitcher on the outer eightfold [array],
following the same sequence as before up to the sixteenth.
Having filled the middle jar with the tips of shoots produced from the nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, jambu, bilva, palāśa, śirīṣa, and madhuka trees,
one should fill eight jars in the third [round] individually, and sixteen as before.
Having cast into a jar the sprouts produced from *palāśa*, *bilva*, *vakula*, *kadamba*, mango, and *śirīṣa*, as well as those from *nyagrodha* and *aśvattha*,
one should place sixteen [other items] separately in the middle and in the eight [surrounding jars], as before.

Having filled the central pitcher with flowers born of the *mallikā*, jasmine, *vakula*, *nandyāvarta*, and *priyaṅgu*, as well as with *padma*, *campaka*, and *kunda* flowers, arranged separately in the fifth [pitcher], and filling the remaining eight as before. || 15.298–15.299 ||
One should place Siddhārtha mustard, Māṣa beans, Gorocanā derived from a cow,
Indrayava, Veṇuyava, and the seeds of Śamī and Śyāmāka, respectively,
into the sixth pitcher situated in the center and into the eight others in sequence.
Those substances are to be distributed individually as previously stated, along with the remaining sixteen:
sesame, wild sesame, cumin, black cumin, linseed, dill, and likewise *kuṭhāracchinna*. (15.301–302)
O twice-born ones, having deposited the seed-syllables of the sages into the seventh central jar, one should likewise place them individually in the sixteen [jars] on the outside as before;
[and one should place] the grain of ṣaṣṭī, śyāmāka, śāli, and nīvāra rice.
One should place sprouts of dūrvā, kuśa, indravallī, and pippala in the center and in the eight [directions] on the eighth day, distributed as before in the others;
likewise [sprouts] of kuśa, udīcī, ikṣu, kāśa, uśīra, and śarapuṅkha.
And one should place the roots of *agaru* and *pāmārga* in the ninth jar;
in the central jar, they are placed in the eight [surrounding jars] individually as before.
[One should also place] the leaves of *tulasī*, black *tulasī*, and *granthiveṇu*.

Of *bhṛṅgarāja*, *bilva*, *śamī*, and the two species of *ketakī*—in the tenth [case], in the middle [of the group], and in eight [cases] they are distributed; in the remaining [cases] it is as before. Of *mustā*, *nāgara*, the tuber called *mustā*, and *kuvalaya*—[the same applies]. (15.307–308)
One should also place the root of the *śītalīyaka* plant from the white and blue lotuses,
as well as the tubers of the *kalhāra* and *kaśeru*, into the eleventh [vessel].
These should be placed in the central jars in this sequence, and in the others as before.
O twice-born ones, one should place sprouts of mung beans, black gram, flat beans, peas, rice,
barley, and *āḍaka* and *kuluttha* lentils into the twelfth vessel;
and in the eight middle jars, they should be placed separately as before in the sixteen [vessels].
One should place the sprouts of *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *sadābhadrā*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *ekapadma*, *balā*, *kharamañjarī*, *sahā*,
and likewise *sahadevī* within the thirteenth pitcher in the center.
Having assigned them to the eight [directions], one should perform the rite for the others separately as before:
white *arka*, *brahmadaṇḍī*, and likewise *brahmasuvarcalā*;
those that are with blood and those that are without blood, *praśniparṇī*, and *sthirā*.
Having also placed an *eraṇḍa* plant in the middle of the fourteenth jar,
one should place those [other plants] individually upon the eight [remaining jars] as before, and in the others [the following]:
*surabhi*, lotus filaments, and *nāgakesara*.
One should likewise place *patra*, *melā*, *tvac*, *latā*, and *kastūrikā*,
as well as *jātīphala* as the fifteenth, into the central pitcher; having thus distributed them among the eight pitchers, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
O twice-born ones, having placed gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, brass,
and bronze— distributed individually in the sixteen jars situated in the eight directions and collectively in the central jar on the sixteenth— as previously described.
Having thus arranged the ritual substances in due order with a well-composed mind,
one should then, for the purpose of worshipping the deity, place the collection of materials such as the *arghya* offering and the *madhuparka* in the southeast corner.
Then, in the southwest corner, one should place turmeric, rice flour,
*dūrvā* grass, an *aśvattha* leaf, white mustard seeds, unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
garlands, and a full water-pot for the purpose of the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*).

Likewise, for the purpose of massage, there is powder made from wheat flour mixed with the powder of *rajanī* (turmeric) and slightly infused with *padmaka*; as well as *camasī* and *khalī*, O best of sages. (15.322–15.323)
Sandalwood, ground and infused with camphor,
combined with *campaka*, *mura*, *māṃsī*, and *haribera*, should be used for smearing the face; likewise, one should apply ground *āmalaka* for the purpose of bathing the head.
Then, in separate vessels in the north-western corner,
[place] a washed cloth, a basket, and a container for flowers, garlands, and so forth.
Then, in the north-eastern corner, however, [place] iron rods.
O twice-born ones, one should likewise place iron balls and tongs,
as well as whatever else may be useful, according to one's preference;
this has been stated either in its entirety or according to the desired arrangement of the corners.

In the ninth square situated in the middle of the eighty-one central squares, one should worship Vāsudeva within the pitcher (kumbha). Then, according to the sequence starting from the east and so forth, one should worship in the centers of the nine squares located in each of the directions, following the order of their manifestation.

One should worship the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva in the middle of those situated in the intermediate directions— from Īśāna to Agni— by means of their dissolution (apyaya) into the pure water-pitchers (śuddhodakumbha) located in the center, which represent Truth (satya). All of these should be worshipped.
But for the nine [deities] of the outer directions, they are in the Śuddhodas, according to the sequence of the directions:
Suparṇa, Garuḍa, Tārkṣya, and Vihageśvara,
within the four groups of nine extending from Agni to Īśāna.
And one should worship those very same [deities] in sequence within the Śuddhodakas;
in the eighty-one located in the cardinal directions according to the order starting from the East,
and in the thirty-six central jars in due order.
The Brahmins Padmanābha and others, who are the foremost among those who know the Vedas,
are to be worshipped by means of the ninefold method, starting from the center and proceeding to the northeast and the west.
One should worship him in the form of Kalki within the pure water-pitchers at the center.
One should worship the Lord in the nine jars of pure water outside; then,
starting from the southeast direction, in the four corners and in the forty-nine groups of nine, one should worship the one known as Pātālaśayana.
In the middle [group] among the triads and tetrads of Keśava and the others,
[one places] the first [syllables] in the jars situated at the cardinal directions, the second in all four [intermediate jars],
and the third in the jars situated at the intermediate directions, following the sequence for the group of six and the group of sixteen.
One should worship the sixteen weapons beginning with Akrūra and ending with Vajra;
thereafter, one should place the Śaktis in the four groups situated in the corners.
Then, among the twenty-five [deities], one should first worship [the Śakti] to the south of Aindrī.
One should worship Lakṣmī, the bestower of all prosperity, in the central jars, and outside of those.
O twice-born ones, one should worship Puṣṭi in the eight [petals], Kānti in the sixteen outside of that;
likewise, in the first and the other [groups] of twenty-five,
one should worship the triad of triads of powers beginning with Prabhā in due order.
There too, one should place [the ornaments] on the fifteenth [digit], and on the sixteenth externally.
On the final twenty-fifth [digit], one should worship the triad:
the *kirīṭa* (crown), as well as the *śrīvatsa*, the *kaustubha*, and likewise the forest garland (*vanamālā*).
Having offered clarified butter twenty-eight times in sequence with the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Vanamāla, according to one's preference,
and having then offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should touch the jars while following the procedure for the residual offering (sampāta-vidhi).
Having covered [the vessels] with lids according to the sequence previously mentioned,
one should afterwards cover them individually with new cloths.
Then, having again offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should present the bali-offering to the spirits in the various directions.

O lords of sages, the sequence for the extraction [of the deity] is held to begin with clay and end with all the jewels; first, one should consecrate [the site] from the east to the northeast using water-pots of clay while reciting the mantra "viṣṇor nu kam. (15.347)
Then, outside that, with a single jar made of clay situated in the center,
O Brahmins, [one should proceed] with sixteen jars according to the sequence starting from the east;
O twice-born ones, this same sequence applies to all twenty-five [jars].
One should sprinkle him with water from the root [mantra] "pratadviṣṇuḥ";
with water mixed with astringent decoctions [using the mantra] "pratatte viṣṇo vāsaḥ";
and with jars provided with sprouts [using the mantra] "yasya tri-pūrṇā".
With the mantra *tad asya* and jars filled with flowers;
with the mantra *tāvām* and [jars] provided with white mustard seeds and other substances; and with the mantra *pravo pāntam* and waters mixed with sesame seeds and the like.
Then, with the mantra *paro mātrayā*, one should [sprinkle] with water containing sixty-fold substances;
with the mantra *nate viṣṇoḥ*, with water mixed with the roots of *kuśa* grass;
and thereafter, with the mantra *irāvatī*, with water from *tulasī* and other plants.
Then, with the mantra *ato devā*, using water mixed with musta roots and other ingredients;

with the mantra *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, using water filled with sprouts of mung beans and the like; and with the mantra *trīṇi padā*, using water containing śaṅkhapuṣpī flowers and other substances. || 15.354–15.355 ||

Then, with the mantra "Viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi," one should bathe [the image] with water from white Arka flowers and the like; then with the mantra "Tad viṣṇoḥ," with fragrant waters and the like; and then with the mantra "Tad viprāsaḥ," one should bathe it with water infused with iron.
First, one should perform the bath with eighty-one jars according to the sequential method.
The sequence for the ninefold bathing, beginning from the east and ending in the center, is as follows:
first, with the group of nine jars in the northeast, using the verse "purūyajñāya" (RV 10.9.4).

With the hymn "indrāviṣṇū dṛṃhitā" situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast), and with the nine verses beginning with "yaṃ manīṣā" in the southern direction, one should perform the consecration;
thereafter, with the hymn "vaṣaṭ te viṣṇo āsa" in the direction of Nirṛti (the southwest).
O lords of sages, by means of this Vāruṇa hymn beginning with "tisro vācaḥ," [the rite is performed]; likewise,
by the nine Vāyavya verses and the nine Saumya verses beginning with "starīḥ," the [rite] called *starī* is accomplished.
With the verse beginning "yasmin viśvena" while standing in the northeast direction,
he should bathe [the deity] with the middle vessel using the mantra "parjanyāya idaṃ vacaḥ. Then, with eighty-one jars from the southern direction, he should bathe the Lord.

O best of sages, with the eight mantras beginning with "The thousand-headed god" (sahasraśīrṣaṃ devam) and ending with "with continuous veins" (santataṃ sirābhiḥ), one should proceed in order from the east and the other nine directions.
One should bathe [the deity] with all of these together, but with the middle one;
or one should consecrate [him] with the eighty-one Vāruṇī jars,
using the nine [mantras] beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhā" starting from the east.
One should perform the consecration with the mantra "yā āpo divyāḥ" using waters drawn from ponds, wells, and tanks, or those arising from lakes and rain; then,
having bathed [the image] with river water, one should do so with the verse beginning "yāsāṃ rājā".
Then, with the mantra beginning with "yāsu rājā," he should indeed sprinkle [the king] with cold water;
then with the four mantras beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭha," and then with the middle one.
Thereafter, O gentle one, he should consecrate him in due order with eighty-one jars.
With the hymn beginning "yad imā" (Śākara, nine verses),
with "yasyauṣadhīḥ" situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast),
with "sākaṃ yakṣma" in the south (Yāmya), and with "anyā vaḥ" in the southwest (Nairṛta).
With the mantra "yāḥ phalinīḥ," one should perform [the rite] in the western direction (vāruṇī) with nine [verses];
with "muñcantu mā śapathyāt," in the northern direction (vāyudik) with nine [verses];
and with "avapatantīḥ," situated in the direction of Soma (the north).
With the mantra "The herbs whose king is Soma" (yā oṣadhīḥ somarājñīḥ), [he should sprinkle] in the northeast;
with "The herbs whose king is Soma, which are distributed" (yā oṣadhīḥ somarājñīr viṣṭhitāḥ), in the center.
Then he should consecrate him with forty-nine jars of water, including that of Agni.

With the Gāyatrī and the six verses beginning with "aindra," [he should worship] from the south; with the six verses beginning with "gandhadvārā," in the west; and thereafter, with the verse "dadhikrāvṇo" and the six verses beginning with "payasvatīr oṣadhayaḥ," in the north.
With the *sūkta* "samyaṅ sravanti saritaḥ" and with clarified butter,
one should perform the consecration with forty-nine jars for Nairṛta;
then, one should bathe [the image] with oil while reciting the *yajus* beginning with "tejo 'si."
With the twelve-syllable mantra in the forward order, one should perform [the rite] with molasses-water;
with the mantra beginning "Tejo 'si," one should do so in the northwest with mustard oil;
and then, with the mantra known as the twelve-syllable one, one should do so with all types of sugarcane juice.
With the mantras beginning with "madhu vātā," using jars filled with honey,
and with coconut water using the previously mentioned mantra, one should proceed in sequence;
thereafter, with warm water, from the southeast (vahni) to the northeast (īśāna) and ending in the west.
Then, at that very moment, one should rub the deity with the warm paste produced by throwing well-heated iron balls [into water], using the mantra beginning with "drupadād".
One should then apply *āmalaka* fruit to the head using the mantra beginning with "mā nas toke".
Having washed [the image] with many pure and fragrant waters,
one should then bathe it in succession with eighty-one jars,
using the verse beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā" and nine jars for each of the hymns dedicated to Indra.
With eight [verses] situated in the eight directions, with the middle one and the second,
and likewise with two Ṛg-verses each, in the sequence of groups of nine and seven;
and then gradually with the entire Pauruṣa Sūkta.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with the central group of nine [mantras],
or else sequentially with the mantras beginning with "yad vā sarvasya vaśinaṃ," located within the *Mahopaniṣad* and situated in the eight directions using the eight pitchers.

O best of the twice-born, with the eight-syllable mantra "Eka eva Nārāyaṇa" recited by one standing in the center, he should bathe [the image] in sequence with all the jars, beginning with clay and ending with all types of gems.
Thus the extraction has been described; now the sequence of ritual action is stated here.
At dawn, having performed his bath and completed the auspicious rites for protection, the preeminent teacher, accompanied by other teachers, [proceeds]. (15.387–15.388)
Then, having entered the temple and performed the daily rites as before,
he should reach the sacrificial pavilion and fill the mandala with colored powders.
Having worshipped the pitcher and the mandala, and having entered the temple once more—
Then one should worship the primary image with offerings such as the *arghya* and other enjoyments. Thereafter, having likewise invoked [the deity] into the bathing image,
one should worship it and adorn it with various garments, garlands, and ornaments.
O Brahmins, having placed [the image] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, adorned with all ornaments, one should lead it to the bathing pavilion according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having placed it upon the bathing pedestal, one should perform the rites according to the method stated before.
Having worshipped them in due order up to the offering of self-surrender (ātmanivedana),
one should then perform the binding of the auspicious thread (kautukabandhana) for the God of gods,
provided that the ritual for the jars was not already performed previously.
By what reasoning, then, should one perform all of that?
Having worshipped in sequence with the enjoyments beginning with bathing and seating and ending with the smearing of the face,
one should then bathe [the deity] with water-pots according to the prescribed method.

One should fill all the jars with the remainder of the bathing water. Having bathed the space between the jars with pure water by means of the successive application of substances, one should worship it with a cloth, the *arghya* offering, and so forth.
Having thus bathed [the image] according to the rules with jars filled with the powder of *rajanī* (turmeric),
which have been consecrated (*adhivāsita*) beforehand, one should place it upon a pedestal of grain (*dhānyapīṭha*) that has been adorned,
using twenty-five, nine, or five jars.
Or, O best of the twice-born, one should apply that powder to the head of the deity while reciting the Śrīsūkta; furthermore, one should worship with arghya and other offerings.
Then, having rubbed it over all the limbs, one should cause it to be placed upon the heads of the devotees.
Then, O twice-born ones, having offered [the oblation] to Viṣvaksena with his mantra,
one should perform the ritual bathing with a thousand streams of pure water.
Having offered sandalwood paste and other items, one should then place the Lord upon the pedestal.
Having brought the seat of ornaments, one should worship according to the sequence beginning with the seats,
using various enjoyments involving touch, as before, along with diverse, heart-pleasing, and captivating offerings that are beyond description. || 15.402–15.403 ||
Having thus performed worship up to the point of giving gifts to the twice-born or up to the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa),
one should place [the image] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle and enter [the temple] as before;
then, by way of circumambulation, one should proceed into the interior of the temple.
Having installed that image there and settled it in its proper place,
and having worshipped both the original image and that one with offerings such as water for honor (*arghya*) and other enjoyments,
and having offered the ritual performed, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*).

O lords of sages, this procedure has been proclaimed for the primary image made of clay and similar materials; however, when the primary image is made of stone or other substances suitable for bathing,
one should bathe that very image according to the previously mentioned rite, along with this *kautuka* [protective cord].
Having worshipped with offerings ending in oblations, one should perform everything up to the conclusion of the fire sacrifice. Then, one should adorn the festival image with various garments,
many beautiful ornaments, and highly fragrant garlands.

Having adorned [the body] and placed it upon a palanquin, one should bring it into the assembly pavilion according to the path prescribed for festivals. Having then lowered it from the vehicle onto a beautiful, spread-out golden [seat], [one should proceed].
Or else, O Brahmins, on an auspicious seat provided with various coverings,
one should perform worship according to the very path described in due order,
especially with various objects of enjoyment, beginning with those of touch.
Then, having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis) and performed everything in due order up to the gift to the twice-born, one should satisfy the fire in sequence.
Having performed everything including the formal dedication (samarpaṇa), [one honors] the God, the Lord of the Universe.
Having placed [the deity], together with all the limbs, upon the vehicle and so forth,

one should cause it to enter the palace; then, having removed it from the vehicle and so forth, one should settle it in its own place and worship it with water for the guest (arghya), perfumes, and other offerings.
Having thus worshipped the primary image,
one should offer the performed ritual action with the water remaining from the bath, which is contained in the pitcher,
in due order to all the deities stationed at the doors as well as those situated in the surrounding enclosures.
Having sprinkled [the deity] according to the procedure for the offering of the *bali*, and having worshipped him thoroughly,
and having offered the *bali* and consecrated Gaṇeśa with the remainder,
one should then worship him with *arghya*, perfumes, and so forth; or else, indeed, according to the secondary alternative (*anukalpaka*).

O twice-born ones, at the conclusion of the worship, the sacrificer should then perform, in the proper sequence, the bathing and the manifestation of the deity, the sprinkling of the deities, and the consecration of Gaṇeśa. 15.419.

One should satisfy the teachers and the practitioners with various kinds of wealth; likewise, one should satisfy all other Vaiṣṇavas according to one's ability. One should cause food and other provisions to be distributed freely to all people without restriction.
In this very way, the sequence of ritual actions for all ablutions is as follows:
one should omit the sprinkling of the attendants and the offering of the bali-oblation;
however, if one has the means, one should perform the rite of the great oblation (mahāhavirvidhāna).
O brahmins, one should perform the five ablutions in the sequence beginning with *pradhāna* (primordial matter) during both the daily (*nitya*) rite and the occasional (*naimittika*) ones;
thereafter, the five beginning with the subtle-subtle (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma*) and ending with the gross-gross (*sthūla-sthūla*).
The rite of bathing for deities such as the Cāturātmya and others should be performed during the solstices,
the equinoxes, and during lunar and solar eclipses; indeed,
one should carry out this most excellent bathing according to the primary ritual manual.
But in the case of a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*),

O best of sages, one should arrange that middle [period] and the four [periods] beginning with the one less than that, according to the sequence of the two cycles, during the four transits situated between the two solstices.

One should commence [the rite] on the day the festival begins and at its conclusion; however, in the case of a secondary alternative (*anukalpaka*), one may perform it either in the middle of that period or in the intervals between them. In the performance of the *mahāhavis* sacrifice, one should perform it even if it is somewhat less than that.
In all matters concerning expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), one should apply all these [rules]. However, I shall describe their various types of ablutions (snapana) in detail further on,
according to the procedure for ablutions as taught in the divine scriptures.
"What has been correctly explained as it truly is— what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Procedure for Ablution" in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the venerable *Pāñcarātra*.
Fifteenth Chapter;
now the sixteenth chapter: The Sages.
O Blessed One, tiger among sages, omniscient one, best of speakers:
how should the consecration of a mantra-image be performed by the most excellent of men?
And what are the characteristics of the temple, the image, the pedestal, and so forth?
"Tell all of that now, out of compassion, in full detail.
Nārada said: "Listen, all you sages, with attentive minds."
The procedure for the consecration of the mantra-image, including its characteristics and other details—
all that has been proclaimed by the God of gods in the Sātvata and other scriptures.
Having extracted the essence of those [teachings], I shall explain it in brief.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, one who is filled with the Blessed One,
endowed with faith and devotion, possessed of a peaceful mind,
a believer, true to his word, and endowed with virtuous conduct— (16.5)

First, one should choose a preceptor who is learned in the scriptures of the Blessed One, who knows the reality [of the teachings], who is a devotee of the Blessed One, and who is born of the lineage of the Blessed One. Having consulted together with the craftsmen, both the preceptor and the patron [should proceed]. (16.6–16.7)
In a meritorious region that is favorable, pleasing, and frequented by holy men;
rich in soft water, fruits, and flowers, and provided with *kuśa* grass and fuel; blessed with cattle, crops, and rice, and free from small creatures. || 16.8 ||
On a mountain peak, or in its midst on a plateau suitable for the twice-born;
or in a delightful forest situated on the ground, thick with trees and medicinal herbs;
or indeed in a noble, excellent grove, abundant with lotuses.
On the banks of rivers and at their confluences,
near sacred fords, in stable places teeming with cranes,
free from predatory beasts and devoid of the fear of robbers.
In a divine and charming region, entirely free from all defects,
one should first examine the ground there according to the method prescribed in the scriptures;
thereafter, O best of the twice-born, one should perform the ritual demarcation of the site.
At the commencement of all undertakings for the acquisition of land,
the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All, should first be propitiated with devotion by means of mantras beginning with the twelve syllables, either upon an altar, in a water-pot, or on the ground.
Then, having gratified [the deity] with devotion through offerings such as clarified butter and by means of mantras consisting of the Vedas,
the Blessed One, whose self is Viśvakarman, should perform the sacrifice for Gaṇeśa along with his retinue,
using various services such as flowers, incense, and unguents.
O Lotus-born One, once the dismissal of Viṣṇu has been performed along with the fire-offering,
those artisans who are skilled therein are to be honored thereafter,
so that they may always carry out their work with a cheerful mind.
Even they, being purified and bathed, must offer libations to their own husband.
Thereafter, O twice-born ones, a field should be accepted that is desirable,
whether it be uncultivated or cultivated, and characterized by the virtues of the earth.
Free from thorns, favorable, and approved by architects, he took it for the purpose of establishing [the city], as extensive as desired.
In the directions of Mahendra, the Lord of Waters, Vāyu, and Vittapa (Kubera), and in the direction of Śāna (Nairṛta) as well... [16.20]

Having attained the *pada*, one should indeed construct a great and auspicious temple for the deity, based on a divine abode and preceded by the five *āyatanas*. For success, it must follow its own path; from a wrong path, there is no success.
Thus much has been stated regarding those who are liberated; for others, however, it results in fault.
For those whose minds are constantly illuminated by Hari—whether their own path or the supreme path—who is omnipresent, they should themselves [recognize] that Guru through the scriptures.

O twice-born ones, when an auspicious and favorable constellation is present, one should pay homage to the all-pervading Lord Acyuta; having performed the daily rites beginning with the worship of Vighneśa,
one should then proceed with the ritual worship together with others who follow the single path and recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
[He was surrounded] by those wearing ornaments, turbans, and white garments; adorned with ointments, garlands, and finger-rings;
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and musical instruments, and by auspicious songs.
O twice-born ones, having taken fruits, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), parched rice (lāja), white mustard seeds (siddhārthaka), and so forth, the pure performer, together with the preceptor,
should reach the site while remembering Vāsudeva in his heart.
Then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day according to the previously mentioned procedure,
the preceptor remains standing outside the sacred field, either in the northeast or the east, O best of sages, while reciting the eight-syllabled mantra.

Having constructed a beautiful leaf-hut there that is capable of withstanding wind and rain, one should prepare flowers, water for honor, incense, and so forth, and place [the deity] upon an auspicious seat. Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) together with various extraordinary mantras.

Having brought Nārāyaṇa— the embodiment of the waters— into proximity within a beautiful golden vessel filled with the water of a river-tīrtha, and having worshipped him with all kinds of medicinal herbs,
gems, darbha grass, garlands, and fragrances; (16.32) [he should place him] in that auspicious vessel.
Then, having prepared the arrangement with the mantra-weapon and the water-pot (kalaśa),
one should meditate upon a seat together with its base using those two and perform its worship;
having worshipped the Lord of Mantras along with his weapon in the heart according to the rule, [one should proceed].
The Praṇava, together with the word "namas," should be placed upon the golden seat;
then, by way of the lunar channel, the King of Mantras, the Astra-mantra,
[should be placed] by the right-hand path in the southern jar of the Lord.
Having brought down [the deity] in a blazing form, burning away the multitude of obstacles—
O twice-born ones, the three mantras common to all rites are prescribed everywhere:
namely, the six-syllable, the eight-syllable, and likewise the twelve-syllable mantra.
That thousand-spoked weapon, Hetīśa, which is to be fully understood as a divine armament,
obtained by one who has undergone initiation from a most gracious guru—
that auspicious and extraordinary weapon must be acquired as a constituent part of his body.
Having worshipped the Lord together with his limbs (the retinue) with offerings ending with the *mātrās*,

one should then perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) for the Lord of All, using true *sūktas*, *yajus* verses, and *sāman* chants characterized by their appropriate occasions, as well as the expressive [mantras].

The preceptor should perform this in a sacrificial pit that has been purified by mantras, weapons, and the directions, using a full measure of one hundred thousand [offerings] made with unbroken palm-leaves;
or alternatively, he should place them upon surfaces such as sand, beginning from the east.
And four attendants of his own, experts in mantra and adorned with ornaments, [should be present].

(16.42) The four [Vedas], beginning with the Ṛgveda, which extend from Īśa to Vāyupatha, should be joined with this supreme devotion for the sake of the fire-oblation during the gathering of the sacred site. (16.43)
One should offer abundant clarified butter and other substances with those mantras characterized by the syllables *bhūḥ*,
using the four mantras pertaining to the fourfold self that begin with the sixteen-syllable [formula],
while other Brahmins should also offer oblations, remembering Hari, the Lord of All.
Having appointed one supervisor for each of the four corners,
[he should appoint] those who are pure, self-controlled, skillful, and trained in the science of architecture to perform the oblation in all the fire-pits, their bodies consecrated by mantras.
Having summoned those born of the lineage of Viśvakarman and seated them in front,

and having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, they were indeed clothed in white garments and adorned with garlands, sandalwood paste, turbans, and finger-rings.
Having inspected it and purified it, and having taken a very strong cotton thread along with a water-pot, consecrated with the *sahasrāra* mantra,
he should place it in the hands of the architects together with a single rod.
Having sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated with a thousand recitations of the Sahasrāra mantra,
he should scatter seeds mixed with parched grain and accompanied by white mustard;
while muttering the Astra mantra along with the Cakra, he should perform the circumambulation three times.
From the initial point up to that [final] point, accompanied by auspicious sounds from bells,
one should then take the measurement of the site using the desired cubits,
whether established by the disciple, the preceptor, or the architect who is a portion of Viśvakarman.
Having extended that thread from the northeast corner and so forth into the four directions,
one should seal the eight directions with stakes made of sacrificial wood.
Then, the wise practitioner should offer a bali-oblation to the spirits while proceeding clockwise.
Sesame flour, powder of turmeric, parched rice, curd, and roasted barley—
this is called *bhūtakrūra*. With it, one should offer the *bhūtabali* wherever any spirits or *rākṣasas* may reside.
"May all these [obstacles] depart; I shall prepare this place for Hari.

Let the trees be cleared away with thorny shrubs, cane-sticks, heaps of hides, and the like, as well as the dwellings of deer and the forms [of other creatures], making it fit for the collection of pale clay."

One should not perform the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*), nor should one worship sharp spades known as *kuddāla*, nor digging-tools made of very hard sacrificial wood, nor elephant’s feet. Standing upon the sacred spot of the field (*kṣetrabrahmapada*), facing whichever direction one desires, [one should proceed]. (16.57–16.58)
Having recollected [the mantra] with its twelve syllables, the Blessed One, the creator of beings,
should meditate upon that which is characterized by the adhyātma, known as the adhibhūta and adhidaiva.
Therein, he should contemplate the earth consisting of seven continents, complete with the oceans and other features.
[He saw it] together with the seven netherworlds, joined by spirits such as humans and others,
and surrounded by powers (śaktis) established in sound and omnipresent,
[all] accompanied by the letter *la* with the nasal bindu, which is conjoined with the seed-syllable of Brahmā.

Having first honored him who is himself appointed by knowledge, and having meditated upon his nature as the *adhibhūta* (the elemental), one should thereafter remember the *adhidaiva* (the divine). Whatever power belongs to the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Lord of All—
And the supreme form of the inner self is indeed the great Vārāha of Viṣṇu.
This much has been stated as the general meditation regarding the acceptance of the earth;
however, one should here also recollect the specific [form] according to the particular temple.
Having meditated upon the manifestation of the fourfold form within the square,
one should contemplate the divine, elongated square known as the Vidyāgama.
Within the circle, one should remember the wheel of the tranquil and the arisen, with its parts fully enclosed.

One should meditate upon the Lord who reclines on the infinite [serpent] within the circular and elongated abode. That stainless "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), which bears the body of the lotus of time, arises from the navel-cavity of Viṣṇu and is situated within those whose nature consists of the eight directions.
Likewise, in the temple, one should meditate upon the eight-cornered abode of the earth;
having thus contemplated it repeatedly with the twelve-syllable mantra,
and having restrained it with the six-syllable mantra, one should likewise form the mudrā of Acyuta.

Having performed meditative absorption and concentration, and having reached the vicinity of the water-pot as before, one should then worship with extraordinary offerings using the eight-syllable mantra.
Together with the Brahmins, one should personally offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire once again.
When the site has been consecrated for the purpose of completing all the ritual works,
one should indeed perform the laying of the foundation on another most auspicious day.
Then, skillful workmen should be appointed in due order.
Just as people attain satisfaction when they have gratified others with food, drink, and other necessities,
so too, when a portion of the earth has been accepted that is free from thorns and well-compacted,
even though it contains pebbles, that young girl— the Earth— becomes a bestower of wealth upon the donor.
Did you abandon that purity which requires some degree of artifice,
as long as the grove was not crowded with great trees grown there for a long time, nor pervaded by their dense, spreading roots? (16.74)
The childishness of that [river] has also been recognized; indeed, its purity is traditionally held to be future.
It has not been abandoned by the currents of rivers because it serves cities, villages, and regions;
for it has been enjoyed many times and thus beholds great purity.
Having dug and extracted the wealth, the heir approaches the auspicious clay;
he should bury it at the edge of the water, white, free of grit, and smooth.
Having seen the water, he should worship it and offer libations to the Lord of Aquatic Creatures.
Then the host of gods, accompanied by the tears of the Nāgas, stood there.
For the sake of stability, it was filled with all kinds of stones and earth;
and having been filled with earth and stones, it was made smooth with that [earth] throughout its various layers.
Having repeatedly pounded [the ground] by watering it with water,
having leveled and smeared it, one should then cause the herd of cows to dwell there—
along with their young calves and accompanied by groves of lordly trees. (16.80)

Having scattered water there along with wet rice and a large heap of grass, and after the cow dung and other materials have been discarded, he should drive away the herd of cows; then, at the end of three days, [he should plow] the earth again.
Having purified it, on the fourth day it was turned over with plows;

then, after being touched everywhere with a glowing brick, the dust consisting of gold, copper, and silver [was removed]. 16.83. Then, the dust produced from gold, as well as that made of copper and tin...
One should sprinkle everywhere upon the ground that which is produced from jewels, enriched with perfumes and garlands, endowed with crops, rice, and fruits,
abounding in flowers, parched grain, and parched rice, and joined with white mustard seeds and sesame seeds;
this brings prosperity when sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Whether it has not been performed or has been performed, whether it has been dug or not, it attains purity at that very moment;
therefore, one should properly perform this rite wherever one may be. Then, having leveled the ground and smeared it with cow dung...
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform the accomplishment of the directions (diksiddhi).
Having established the gnomon and so forth by the path seen in the scriptures,
one should begin the construction of the temple according to the stated injunctions.
When the palace was being constructed, there were indeed spirits, dānavas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas who created obstacles; for their pacification,
the God of gods was installed according to the prescribed rites in the inner sanctum.
One should worship [the deity] with various enjoyments as far as the root temple.
At its conclusion, having invoked the power (śakti) residing in the child-image (bālabimba) into the water-pot (kumbha), one should offer it into the root image of the God of gods.
O best of sages, when Viṣṇu has been worshipped in this manner in the house of the child,
all those who create obstacles perish; thereafter,
on an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion, and with the planets propitiated, the Guru—

When the ascendant is fixed and in a fixed degree, when it is cleared of malefic aspects, and during the northern solstice; when purified of divine and other portents, during the bright fortnight, and when the sky is stainless;
once a pit has been dug down to the water-level and filled as before. || 16.93–16.94 ||
On a ground free from defects, marked with all the auspicious characteristics,
well-smeared after being filled and leveled,
and divided into sixty-four squares as before by means of a cord in every direction— || 16.95 ||

Having bathed, wearing white garments and garlands, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), and with a perfectly tranquil mind; equipped with all the necessary implements and provided with an *arghya* vessel,
he should take up an auspicious jar while meditating on Acyuta within his heart.

Together with Brahmins who follow the single path and are devoted to the sacred scriptures— as well as those whose origins are rooted in the Ṛgveda and who are permeated by the Lord from their very foundation—
he should enter the area of the palace grounds after placing that water-pot in the center.

One should perform the inspection of the ground, as well as its striking, sprinkling, and irrigation with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) along with water consecrated by weapons (astravāri).
The first four mantras should begin with the syllable Oṃ and end with the word "pavitra. (16.99–16.100)

And he should have the Brāhmaṇas—those who know the Ṛgveda recite the Śākuna hymn; those who know the Yajurveda, the Bhadra hymn; those who know the Sāmaveda, the hymn beginning with "iḍāmayā"; and those who know the Atharvaveda, the hymns beginning with "śānti" and others, while performing the auspicious rite (puṇyāha) and having performed the auspicious ceremonies. (16.101)
Beginning from the northeast corner and proceeding eastward in each row,

one should worship the deity according to the characteristics of the body, at every step, using the twelve-syllable mantra combined with one's own name, encased within the *praṇava* and the word of salutation (*namaḥ*). || 16.102–16.103 ||
The Vāstupuruṣa should be worshipped with curd, garlands, sandalwood, and other such offerings; thereafter, one should satisfy him in the fire with a *sāttvika* oblation.
Or rather, O best of sages, listen further to another procedure.
Having divided the ground of the sacrificial hall into nine equal parts in all directions with threads smeared with lime,
one should diligently arrange it so that it consists of eighty-one squares.
In each square, one should fashion a lotus with one-fourth of that [space],
provided with eight petals and endowed with a pericarp and filaments; likewise,
in the outer corner squares of the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.
That which is a group of four lotuses is simply called a *caturdula*.
One should perform worship beginning from the lotus-foot of Īśāna,
[placing] the gods, asuras, and sages in order within the external rows of lotuses.
Within the pericarp of the lotus-feet of the Bull-bannered One, one should place Brahmā;
likewise, one should place Īśvara, Tapana, Diti, and Aditi,
beginning from the eastern petal and proceeding as far as the northern one.
Thus, having worshipped the pentad upon that lotus-foot,
one should then properly sacrifice to the seven deities above the pericarp of the seven lotuses situated at the successive steps.
Vāyu, Apavatsa, Jayendra, Samarīyaka,
Ravi, Satya, and Ātmadeva— these should be placed in the lotus-feet of Vahni; then,
one should again place Pitāmaha in the center and Bhṛgu on the eastern petal.
For Pūṣan [is worshipped] in the south, while Gaganavibhu is in the west and north.
Having thus worshipped the four [deities] situated on the petals within the corner lotuses,
one should then worship seven [more] in the lotuses up to the corner of the Rākṣasas.
The one called Savitṛ is Sāvitra, and Gṛhakṣata is with his army;
Vivasvat is Dharmadeva, who is remembered as the lord of the Gandharvas.
When the lotus is situated in the southwest corner, Brahmā is again within it.

Then Bhṛṅga, Bhṛṅgarāja, and the Lord of the Pitṛ-gaṇas; then the one called Devadauvārika—this quartet is on the eastern petal and the others. Then, upon the eight-petaled lotuses, there is a group of seven deities in sequence.
Having placed [the seed-syllables] within the pericarp, extending as far as the station of Vāyu:
Indra, the one called Indrapada, Sugrīva, Kusumadvija,
the one called Mitra, Varuṇa, and again the Lord of the Asuras.
In the lotus of the northwest direction, one should place Prajāpati in the center;
on the eastern petals, Śeṣa and Adharma;
and immediately after that, Yanmaya and the Lord of Serpents (Nāgendra).
Then one should worship the group of seven deities as before:
Pūrvākhya, Rudradāsa, Mukha, Bhallaka, Somaka, Dhārādhara, and the one named Matsya; such is this host of deities.
Having performed worship, one should thereafter, in each individual lotus,
worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) situated within the middle of the petals by means of his own name;
and one should also worship him beneath the filaments of the lotuses located in the corner sections.
Having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning and the word "namas" at the end, one should worship [the deity].
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule with flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as with curd, milk, water, and various foods including fruits and roots— || 16.125 ||
Having thus worshipped the host of deities in the outer enclosure previously,
one should again fill the lotus-squares within that [enclosure], starting from the northeast corner up to the central lotus-square, with the eight syllables.
According to the sequence of the letters of the *mātṛkā*,
beginning with the letter *a* and continuing up to the letter *ha*, one should worship the host of deities upon the petals of the lotus within that very lotus by means of that same sequential method.
And now learn of those in the second enclosure and the intermediate space:
Dhātṛ, Yātṛ, Dhruva, Kāla, Kāma, Kartṛ, Jayantaka, Jīva, Prāṇa, Tara, Yajña, Ravi, and Mṛgayāmyaka. (16.129–16.130)
Lokanātha, Vidhātṛ, Bhṛgu, Sraṣṭṛ, Niyāmaka, Manojava, Kalyāṇa, Parjanya, Draviṇas,
and then Sraṣṭṛ Viśvakarmā— these, O bull among sages, [are the creators].
And the deities within the intermediate [spaces] are to be worshipped, numbering twenty-four. Furthermore, within these, in the third enclosure likewise,
one should duly worship the group of sixteen deities in their proper order.
The oceans, the mothers, the islands, the months, the rivers, and the stars;
the Viśvedevas, the Apsarases, the Manus, and likewise the Ṛṣis;
the Vasus, the Maruts, the Siddhas, the Nāgas, the Sādhyas, and the Planets—in this order.
One should place Indra and the other world-protectors in the fourth enclosure (16.135).
Starting from their respective quarters up to the northeast, within the middle of the lotus petals;
one should worship the Lord Viśvarūpa, seated upon a lotus, in the central lotus (16.136).
In the body of that great-souled one who possesses such a wheel of deities, complete with mounts, weapons,
and attendants, [the mantra] consisting of the *praṇava*, his own name, and a salutation should be employed.
One should worship each deity individually, as well as each syllable here.
Having thus worshipped the deities, one should then satisfy them in the fire as before; let it be understood how one should perform the consecration of the water-pot.
One should adorn the area of the ground with archways and other decorations as before,
outside that earth [of the altar] in front of the cleansed face of the temple.
One should construct an excellent mandala there, provided with the previously mentioned requisites.
The area situated between the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) there shall measure eight cubits.

The pits, together with their pedestals (piṇḍikās), shall be two cubits in size and possess the characteristics previously described. The pathway (vīthī) surrounding them shall be three cubits wide; thus, the measurement is eighteen cubits [in total].
As before, having placed the ritual implement (*sādhana*) within each fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should construct another pit to the north of oneself on level ground. Then,
having brought down the deity to the south as before, one should worship him in the proper sequence.
On a raised spot on the ground above the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), as before,
having offered libations according to desire and then extracted the group of fires,
he should deposit them into the consecrated fire-pits in the cardinal directions, as previously described.
In the same manner, having extracted and worshipped those situated in the intermediate directions in due order, one should then,
by means of their origin, install the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva in the four cardinal directions, O twice-born ones, according to their names as Ekāyanas.
Having described their respective tasks as being beyond numbering with each of their own [mantras],
one should perform the concluding rite of the ritual with oblations of sesame and rice mixed with clarified butter,
extending thus by this method of progression from the region of Vāyu up to Īśāna.
Having first consecrated the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, one should likewise place them there;
and with those [mantras] which have Acyuta as their deity, as well as the purifying mantras prescribed in one's own Vedic branch,
the fire-oblation (havana) should be performed according to the rules with a mind full of devotion.
Then, having reached the northeast corner together with other Brahmins,
he should place there the bathing implements previously specified,
beginning with the five products of the cow, each in its own separate jar.

Having honored them with water for the feet, the guest-offering, and so forth, and having consecrated them with the twelve-syllable mantra, one should bring forward the previously prepared jars together with the stone slab—
either nine made of precious minerals or those fashioned from stone.
In the absence of those [earthen vessels], one should use earthen ones that are well-baked, very dense,
twelve finger-breadths in width, and of the same measure in height;
or, if one has the means, golden ones of double that size are beneficial for kings.
One should collect a mass of stone blocks that are square, measuring twelve *aṅgulas* in width,
and having a thickness equal to one-third of that;
then, having duly established the water-jars according to the previously mentioned sequence.

Then, that neck should be one *tala* or even one *kara* in height, measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in its excavation; it should be broadened by those same proportions, or else it may be a large, very white conch-shell, excluding the ears on all sides. (16.156–157)
The nose having been struck, it is prescribed that it be internally purified and intact;
for thus, having touched [the image] both inside and out, and having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa),
one should then [worship] with fruits such as gold, with gems, and with those consisting of all medicinal herbs.
One should adorn [the deity] with perfumes, seeds, grains, coral and the like, pearls, eye-cloths, ornaments, and excellent, auspicious garlands;
one should perform this for each individual item with the twelve-syllable mantra.
For the sake of perfecting the form, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of those whose essence is consciousness using the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).
Then, one should worship with various offerings, beginning with the water of honor (*arghya*) and ending with the sacrificial oblation (*bali*).
Once this has been done for the stones in this manner, one should subsequently lead them into the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
One should place the group of pitchers together with their stone bases upon the supporting slabs;
then, one should consecrate that base-stone there, or outside the pavilion,
and likewise meditate upon it with the *praṇava*.
Blazing like a thousand cows and radiant as the orb of the sun,
one should then worship the mantra and satisfy it a hundred times; thereafter,
having placed that jar in the center along with its limbs and its retinue.
But the knower of the reality of Brahman [perceives it] as all-pervading, containing within its womb all powers without exception.
From above, across, and by means of these powers— speech and the rest—
accompanied by the forms of the vows, they are indeed non-different from it in essence.

There, the King of Mantras should cause the Brāhmaṇas to recite the *Ātmavyūha* as well as the *Ātmānuvāda*, beginning and ending with the *praṇava*. Having worshipped him according to the rules, he should immediately thereafter offer libations.
One should install Vāsudeva and the others in the pitchers situated in the cardinal directions;
likewise, one should install Aniruddha and the others in those placed in the intermediate directions.
One should cause [the disciple] to recite the fourfold mantra of the fourfold self (cāturātmīya), consisting of the four designatory mantras (saṃjñāmantra).
Then, through the yoga of origin and dissolution, he should devoutly cause them to recite the Puruṣa-sūkta from the Ṛgveda; and others,
who are wise in the Sāman and absorbed in the Blessed One, he should cause to recite the Yajus known as the Rathantara.

Then, O best of sages, one should recite the mantra "sahasraśirasam" from the Atharvaveda; alternatively, all that has been prescribed should be placed beneficially within a single water-pot. Likewise, the oblation in the central sacrificial pit is ordained by the Lord himself.
However, one should cause the mantras to be recited in their proper order as they stand;
having thus performed the *sampāta-homa* up to its conclusion with the *pūrṇāhuti*,
there arises the supreme collection of great powers characterized by efficacy.
And he who clearly abides as non-different from the forms of the Mantra and so forth,
should be joined with the stones by means of their own names and the *praṇava*.
Likewise, the radiance of Nandabalā dwells there as the light of gnosis.
The powers that sustain the universe are said to be Sarvagā, Brahmavadanā, Dyotakī, Satyavikramā, and Sampūrṇā.
Know that the stone known as Kalasādhāra is Sarvagā.
Having gratified the partless, supreme power of the Lord, which is common to all capacities and potencies,
with the root mantra and the *śikhā* mantra, O wielder of the plow; and then,
with the single mantra of the one goal, within the navel of the Unborn.
However, for that purpose, one should indeed offer oblations with earthen vessels;
likewise, this speech of his should be offered with *gāyatrī* verses and not with others.
It should be properly offered by Brahmins who are indicative of its pervasion.
Having offered the full oblation and performed the worship himself,
he should again perform the offering of bali to the spirits; then, having sipped water for purification,
he should proceed to the area of the Brahma-pada of the temple and place the great foundation stone there.
Recalling the wheel-mantra together with Ananta by means of the *praṇava*,
and remembering the six paths situated within that which has arisen from the seed-syllables,
he should worship her immediately after the *arghya* and other offerings with the entire collection of mantras.

While looking toward the directions at the doors, one should place the mantra-pot in the center. One should install the other pots in their respective directions according to their positions, using their own respective mantras.
Then, one should cover each pot individually with stones empowered by one's own śakti.
Then, one should fill the spaces between the jars with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
For the sake of achieving immovability, one should fill them with soft earth, soft sand, and lime.
Then, having wrapped them in cloths over the eyes, one should cause them to recite the *Ṛgveda*.

The Sāma-singers should chant the hymn beginning with "ā tvā hārṣa" as the Pratiṣṭhā-sāman. Furthermore, those established in Brahman who are well-disciplined should repeatedly recite the mantra of power consisting of twelve syllables, ending with the Praṇava.
One should meditate upon that [Supreme Reality] which has attained a single form by means of the *praṇava*,
established in the powers of the forms and so forth, and consisting of name, form, and action;
furthermore, by means of the twelve-syllable mantra and those [mantras] that reach the heart.
One should meditate upon the one to be propitiated by mantra, whose form is space and who is a treasury of splendors.
Then, with the words "Oṃ Bhagavan," one should cause the followers of the Pāñcarātra to recite the *arcāmita* hymns from the Ṛgveda and those from the Sāmaveda who are experts in the *arcā*.
