Then, once the site belonging to the deity has been taken possession of,
one should place eight [lines] measuring twelve finger-breadths each in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having been properly bathed and worshipped, it possesses auspicious characteristics for the disciples.
Within that, the qualities of the intellect (buddhi-dharma) should be restrained in succession.
From the southeast corner up to the northeast, and again from the east to the north, one should place the fourfold group beginning with dharma and beginning with adharma.
Within the gaps between the stones upon the ground, one should place six by six in sequence,
starting from the first letter and ending with the final letter of the alphabet.
Having thus fashioned the snare of the intellect, permeated by the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), [one should proceed].
One should properly lay down the foundation, situated upon the floor of the palace.
Likewise, one should lay down eight stones for the purpose of the courtyard walls;
within them, one should correctly station the previously mentioned lords of the directions.

One should contemplate that wheel, which rotates like sparks from a fire, pervading the ground within its perimeter; with the syllable *Kṣā*, one should meditate upon the courtyard area as being completely filled. Below that is the expanse [of the earth], below which is Śeṣa, and above that is Gaganīśvara.

Outside, against the walls of the courtyard, one should install the eight deities beginning with Indra, together with their weapons and retinues, starting from the east and ending at the northeast corner (Īśa). One should likewise do so upon the stones that have been laid within the ground.
Having honored him by his own name, one should then have him recite the Ṛgvedas. Then,
thinking "he is neither impotent nor unlearned," those gods who consist of the Yajus,
having entered the interior of Devavrata who knows the Sāmans, [should do so].
Standing before the form of the mantra, one should contemplate the pervasion of the paths.
Having emerged as a sprout from the seed-syllable, it attains manifestation in front,
extending as far as the palace and the pedestal, indeed from the stone base of the jar.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā), in its actual state, should always be meditated upon;
one should observe it as far as the path of the levels (padādhvā), which extends up to the height of the womb (garbha).
The path of mantras (mantrādhvā) ends at the parrot-nose (śukanāsā), and the path of principles (tattvādhvā) extends to the altar (vedikā).
The path of time extends to the end of the throat, while the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is above that.
Having first equalized everything, one should then begin the temple (prāsāda),
for the sake of achieving the stability of the temple and for the attainment of the deity’s presence.
For the sake of pacifying all defects and for the accomplishment of all prosperity,
one should first perform the ritual placement of the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*) in the womb-chamber according to the prescribed rule.
[The chamber] should be filled with jewels, metals, seeds, bulbs, and mung beans.
One should prepare a chest made of gold, silver, or copper according to one's means,
provided with nine cavities and fitted with a lid;
having consecrated it by sprinkling water empowered by the Astra-mantra, one should wrap it in a pair of cloths.
Having placed [the deity] upon a heap of grain with the root mantra, the preceptor,

having worshipped [him] with the water-offering, scents, and so forth, should worship the deity according to the rules in either the fire-pit or on the sacrificial mound with seven fuel-sticks in succession.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the preceptor, having fasted,
wearing a white upper garment and adorned with ornaments,
his body decorated with perfumes and garlands, [performs the rite] at night during an auspicious conjunction.
Taking that vessel, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, auspicious hymns,
and the sound of musical instruments, he circumambulated the house;
having entered the inner chamber, he stood there to the right of the door.

Having filled the pit with the five products of the cow and sprinkled it on all sides, he should then worship the ground there with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites; then, having meditated upon her as having bathed after her menses and remembering himself as Hari, [he should proceed].
"O beloved bearer of all beings, adorned with mountain-breasts,
clothed in the ocean— O Goddess, take up this embryo! Having said this, he then placed the vessel in a chasm and [filled it] with nectar.
Then, having made the pit firm and filled it completely with earth,

O lords of sages, one should maintain protection for three, four, or five nights. This, O brahmins, is the ritual of depositing the embryo (garbhanyāsa), which brings prosperity to the temple of the deity.
It is taught that if the placement of the embryo is not performed, a great transgression occurs;
therefore, one should perform the placement of the embryo with every possible effort.
O best of sages, I shall now describe the characteristics of the temple.
From a base that is either less than or more than two cubits, by means of appropriate finger-breadths,
up to a height of twelve cubits— whether the base is deficient or excessive—
one should construct the interior of a temple for the sake of auspiciousness and spiritual success.
Having first calculated the cube of the fields, finger-breadths, or cubits,
one should properly subtract eight from that; having reflected upon what remains,
[one should know that] the numbers beginning with one and ending with eight correspond respectively to the banner (dhvaja), smoke (dhūma), deer-lord (mṛgeśvara), and so forth.
Then, a dog, a donkey, an elephant, and crows are auspicious;
those numbered one, three, five, and seven are prescribed everywhere.
Thus, by means of the internal rotation together with the count of the walls, [the directions are determined].
The area of the temple's sanctum (garbha) should be twice as wide as the temple building itself;
however, in the case of a single-walled structure, the measurement of the area is prescribed as being increased by one-third of what was stated for the sanctum,
provided it is joined by a suitable passage.

In that case as well, one should examine the purity of the income through its decrease and increase. Thus, having determined the measurement of the temple site— including the ground, the portioned pedestal, and the exclusion [of certain parts]— let it be understood as being properly joined together.
Then, [the projection] is by one-sixth, one-fourth, and one-third; it is of both natures.
In the four directions, it is increased by half, and indeed by three-fifths.
In the center, the projection is prescribed by one-third.
One should cause the remaining portion to enter from corner to corner.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be high, equal to the inner sanctum (garbha), or it may be made with petals corresponding to that pedestal.
This is the conceptualization of the proportions for the placement of the characteristics of the pedestal as prescribed for the temple.
In the four directions, one should indeed construct many [structures] beginning with the Ananta;
then, one should determine the height of the temple from the site as either one and a half times,
twice, or according to one's desire.
One should first divide that [measurement] equally into twenty-two parts;
subsequently, it should be fashioned like a pedestal (pīṭha), and with one part, the masūraka (pedestal-base) is to be made.
Above that, the jaṅghā (shaft) is constructed, elevated according to the measurement of the interior (garbha).
Adorned by deities who provide for existence,
with the pair of shoulders on the shanks indeed either deficient or excessive;
the pinnacle-base (śikharapīṭha) should be made as characterized by the previous marks.
However, the entrance and the exit there are each measured by half a part.
And here, a pinnacle (śikhara) is fashioned, provided with nine storeys (bhūmikā);
having first contracted that thread, one should take it up to the height [of the structure].
From this single-syllable [mantra], having extended the *jaṅghī* upward,
one should touch the pinnacle and the pedestal, immediately restraining it;
O Amalekṣaṇa, [this is done] on that pure ground outside the temple.
O lords of sages, one should lead the cord from the corner (karṇa) upwards, marking it gradually until reaching the height of the pinnacle;
in this very manner, one should traverse all four directions,
marking from corner to corner.
As long as that Śikharamañjarī has the luster of a white water-lily petal,
it should be prepared through the method of viewing the drawing and by the application of threads.
Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the ground-section (bhūmikāṇḍa), it should be made tenfold.
Above that, however, the *āmalasāraka* (dome) should be formed by one part.
One should then apply the measurements of the parts to the successive tiers (*bhūmi*s), according to the rule of decrease and increase;
the construction [of the dome] is measured by twice eight parts [sixteen parts].
The arrangement of the seats (pīṭhas) should be made according to their respective positions,
with various lotuses accompanied by wheels,
or with all the manifestations, or with all the embodied emblems (lāñchanas) abiding in the aesthetic sentiments of dance and song. || 16.242 ||

The *uṣṇīṣa* should be made from the upper portion by one-ninth, extending out by its own quarter; it should be fashioned from the upper ground and devoid of ornamentation. Having divided the remainder into three parts, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is to be established as before within the mandala.

Then, with the second [line], one should fashion the neck; with the third, which goes upward, one should make the egg (aṇḍa) perfectly level and endowed with beauty, like the egg of a wood-apple (dhātrīphala).
Having fashioned the nine-fold uṣṇīṣa with four [lines], one should rotate the altar-platform (vedikā).
It should be made with a width of three parts, provided with pillars, or even without them; it is elevated by half the height of the pinnacle, resembling the petals of a lotus,
and should be fashioned above the pedestal of the pinnacle, adorned with divine craftsmanship.
Then one should construct an even more auspicious pavilion provided with pillars,
adorned according to the measurements of the fire-altar and the sacrificial mandala.
Likewise, three pavilions should be prepared at the four gates and in the cardinal directions.
In the pavilion, there should be a pavilion endowed with three entrances;
or one may construct a pavilion without [such] openings, according to one's desired exit.
However, the *ratha*, *uparatha*, and so forth are prescribed from their inner sanctum (*garbha*).
The *niryāsa* [should be made] with a tenth part, the *lāṅgalin* with a twelfth part, or else with a sixteenth part; these should again be fashioned like a rim (*nemi*).
They are smeared on the four sides and the wings, and adorned with the work of pedestals (*pīṭha*).
One should complete [the structure] upon the pedestal (pīṭha) at the four directions of the pinnacle (śikhara).
With the chariot-ornament (rathaka), one should fashion the group of spires (nāsikā) and floral clusters (mañjarī) evenly;
likewise, one should fashion the group of doors (dvāra) evenly at the four directions of the central region.
Then, from the center, it is prescribed as three, four, five, or six parts;
it is twice as high [as wide], and possesses three, five, or nine branches.
It is provided with two door-keepers, or else with jars and elephant tusks.
One should perform its installation according to the rules, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Having bathed it with the root mantra and worshipped it with the *arghya* offering and other rites using the *hṛdaya* mantra,
one should establish its presence in the form of minerals and gems within the base of the branch.
Having indeed suppressed the mantra consisting of the support of all within that [place],
and having meditated there upon the eternal [deity] whose nature is knowledge and action, one should place the pair of branches by means of the right and left sides using the *śikhā* mantra.
Having obstructed the primordial Supreme Lord above that with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) and having brought him into presence,
one should worship him while he resides in the sky within an udumbara fruit;
[one should offer] the two kinds of metallic substances, gems, white mustard seeds, and sesame seeds.
Having taken the fragrances such as sandalwood, milk, curd, ghee, honey,
śāli rice, all seeds, all medicinal herbs, and coral,
and having placed them in the eyes with the *netra* [mantra], one should fix them above the door.
The visible [form] is for the attainment of enjoyment, while the invisible is for the accomplishment of liberation.
Having completely restrained [the breath] above that, one should then cause the four-footed,
complete Dharma to be recited as "catvāri śṛṅgā" consisting of the Ṛgveda.

Having performed the accumulation of the ritual fire-offerings (karmahoma), one should pour the full oblation (pūrṇā) with the root mantra. This should be performed after the consecration of the image, as previously described;
indeed, it depends upon the stability of the abode of the All-pervading Lord.
Know that the temple named Anantabhuvana, which bestows all worldly desires and liberation, is indeed of four types like the pedestal (pīṭha);
it is likewise manifold through the distinctions arising from its construction and arrangement.
It was provided with pitchers resembling the lords of birds and the kings of beasts, as well as the treasures and the bhūtas;
it was further endowed with rows of steps marked with conchs and lotuses,
according to the requirements of the gates and likewise according to the requirements of the pedestals.
The extent of Aruṇa, situated in every direction, is thus prescribed.
O wielder of the plow, the designation "womb-born field" (garbhortthakṣetra) belongs to Jagatīka;
it should be known that for him, along with Jagatīka, [the extent] in all directions is according to that measure.
From these [dimensions], one should fashion the base and so forth, omitting the portion corresponding to the base and so on;
having understood this, and having previously established the courtyards for the sanctuaries,
there shall indeed be four sanctuaries with palaces situated in three directions.
Together with the first [deity] and those situated in the corners, that is known as the five-shrine (pañcāyatana) system.
The eight-shrine (aṣṭāyatana) system is to be understood as consisting of the other three located in the cardinal directions, together with the one situated in the center;
however, [the four-shrine system] consists of two by two [deities] located in the cardinal directions, excluding the one situated in the center.
That ten-fold arrangement becomes increased by one when joined with the two palaces situated on either side of the gateway;
indeed, this constitutes the twelve-fold arrangement together with that which stands in the center.
That very [structure] is designated as *adhika*, while others are designated as *ananta*.
One should construct two palaces facing each other at the location of the entrance;
furthermore, those situated in the three directions facing the palace [should be arranged accordingly].
Facing forward is prescribed by means of two [lines] situated at the corners, each pair being directed toward one another;
furthermore, one should face the appropriate direction by means of two desired [lines].
O lords of sages, in the case of temples with infinite doors, two [doors] should be placed facing each other, situated at the corners;
the other doors may be constructed without hesitation in whatever directions are desired.
Therein, no defect of mutual obstruction occurs among them,
because they have become subordinate members of the primary sanctuary. Furthermore,
it is beneficial that [the courtyard] is reduced from the open space by half, one-third, or one-quarter.
The height of the *paraṇḍaka* should be equal to its width,
and it should be made like a pedestal, smooth, or even with a crown (*uṣṇīṣa*). It should then be joined with a multitude of millions of various deities.
O lords of sages, when there is only one sense-base (*āyatana*), that is the courtyard;
it may be joined with a small pavilion, or it may be a pavilion alone.
When there are from two sense-bases up to twelve sense-bases, [the same applies]. (16.280–281)
And [one should worship him] while looking toward a single direction in a courtyard that is either square or oblong, or in a spacious temple possessing the aforementioned characteristics;
for [this is especially appropriate] for temples and courtyards.
O lords of sages, for altars that are square and so forth,
there is always either mutual conformity, or what is beneficial, or indeed what is relative,
depending on the nature of the ground and likewise depending on the specific form of worship.
Furthermore, by virtue of various fruits and likewise by virtue of its beauty:
from a square [altar] there is gain of land; from a long square, density;
from a circle, the attainment of all desires; and from a long circle, liberation.
For those who desire both seen and unseen fruits, the worlds beginning with Mahat [are the goal]; however,
for Vaiṣṇavas free from desire, there is the Vaiṣṇava abode— health and supreme prosperity— and at the end of their descent, the highest state.
O Lord of Sages, we sages have heard from you this definition of a palace;
now please explain in detail the procedure for its consecration.
Nārada said: Listen to the supreme ritual for the consecration of temples and other structures.
Having constructed a pavilion in front of the temple as previously described, [one should proceed]. (16.289)
The Guru should construct eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around the temple, provided with every necessary implement and endowed with all auspicious characteristics; however,
in the absence of such materials and the like, they may be fashioned at the front of the temple.

One should prepare a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) on the ground area of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇṭapa*). One should perform the *homa* offering there for all the deities (*mūrti*) as well. This should be done either on the third or the fifth day after the commencement of the installation of the temple (*prāsāda*).
On that day, one should perform the planting of the sprouts according to the prescribed rite;
having fashioned a pitcher made of stone or, as before, of metal,
in accordance with the measurement of that [deity's] image, together with the mantra-image.

On another auspicious day, in a sacrificial pavilion possessing the previously described characteristics, having performed the preliminary consecration according to rule and provided with all necessary implements,
and having duly completed for those two the entire sequence beginning with the ritual bath; || 16.294–16.295 ||
Having placed the image within that jar endowed with jewels and other [precious materials],
and having covered it with cloths, ornaments, and flowers— just as one would with the *arghya* offering—
one should slowly ascend to the couch in the temple together with the guardians of the image.

In that regard, one should perform the preliminary striking and so forth, carry out the cleansing and other rites, and arrange all the gems as prescribed for the invocation; thus the image, together with the ritual pitcher, is to be installed. (16.298)
O wielder of the plow (Lāṅgalin), having first performed a single contemplation there with the root mantra restrained from the heart onwards and joined with the supreme (parā),
one should thereafter [contemplate] the previously mentioned general characteristic consisting of the kalās.
Having worshipped it and covered it with cloth, one should bring it to manifestation with white plaster.
Then, above that, one should fashion the *piṇḍa* together with its pedestal (*āṇḍa*) as prescribed.
Afterwards, one should bathe the temple with the six substances beginning with white mustard seeds.
If one should perform a ritual bath in a mirror that consists of nectar,
one should then anoint it, worship it with garlands and other offerings, and decorate it;
furthermore, on the panel of the temple, one should [work] with twenty-five threads.
After tying the sacred thread (kautuka), one should then perform the preliminary consecration of the shadow (chāyādhivāsana).
The most excellent of preceptors should perform the ritual bathing (snapana) upon the mirror as before,
provided that the deities (mūrtis) have been assigned to the four directions of the temple.
The lords of sages, having opened their eyes according to the prescribed rite,
should perform all other [rites] as appropriate by the path that will be described;
they should also perform the consecration of the door and the *kūrca* for the temple.
From the stone supporting the pitcher up to the very top of the temple,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the worlds, the paths, the principles (*tattva*), and the deities as before.
Likewise, one should place the root-mantras and the others upon the limbs of the directional forms (*diṅmūrti*).
One should worship those stationed in the temple within both the water-pot (*kalaśa*) and the mandala;
having consecrated Vāsudeva and the others according to the rite of their manifestation and dissolution, one should establish the fire in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) prepared around the temple.
One should satisfy [the deities] according to the scriptures, or else [perform it] while standing before that [deity].
The preceptor himself should perform the entire fire-oblation (homa) in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
he should cause the Brahmins to recite the mantras and indeed bring that [rite] to its formal conclusion.
Having personally restrained the armor-mantra there with a mind fixed in meditation,
and having performed everything up to the final *pūrṇāhuti* according to this rite,
one should indeed cause the Sāman-chanters to recite the Sāman: "kṣuro hare."
One should place the discus of pure essence in the center,

having a form according to one's desire, with its face turned toward the directions and its mouth facing the sky; it should rest upon a staff colored by one's own power, as fierce and radiant as the sun.

One should place the wheel-mantra upon that [deity], along with the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) previously described, by means of the practice of going and returning, characterized by the prior knowledge of the object of cognition. Having first understood the Lord as residing within the form of the substance, one should not proceed otherwise.
Then one should perform the connection of the paths, and not otherwise, O lords of sages.
Indeed, he who knows in truth that single wheel—the stainless one known as "the peaceful," as well as that which is both peaceful and arisen—is the very embodiment of it. (16.315–16.316)

In this wheel of saṃsāra, he shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all those dwelling in the various stages of life (āśrama) and all who delight in their respective duties (dharma).
His power, established through the very form of Brahman, is manifest and independent of any external support.

It is known as stainless, bestowing liberation upon all, and existing both within and without. Like the ocean of milk, resembling a thousand suns, it is indeed partless and possesses a sharp edge; through yoga, it is called "Peace" (Śānta).
But that which, by its very independence, exists as itself without being a constituent part of anything else,
proceeds by its own internal activity extending in all directions—
like the slight curvature of the navel, or like the spokes within the space of a wheel.

Know that this wheel, which bestows the fruit of one's desires, is both quiescent and arisen. That which remains after having established all connection within its quiescent form is the sovereign wheel called "arisen," proceeding from the navel.
In that [mandala], the mantra is not merely propitiated; it is indeed considered fully worshipped.
When recited and gratified with devotion, it accomplishes everything for everyone.
Thus, this desired wheel brings about the destruction of all obstacles.
Having installed and duly worshipped it, immediately thereafter,
the King of Birds (Garuḍa), having consecrated the flagstaff— which is one-third higher than the pinnacle and well-adorned— should set it in place with the *śikhā-mantra*.
Then, there is the tip of the pinnacle of the flagstaff, which is of various colors, adorned with clusters of small bells, long, and unartificial;
it is extended by one-twelfth or one-ninth of its length.
Having first established the presence of the weapons upon that cloth bearing the sectarian mark,
one should then place it at the tip of the flagstaff and worship it with perfumes and other offerings.
O best of sages, this is the procedure for the installation of images made of plaster and other materials.
O Brahmins, the simultaneous installation of both the image and the temple occurs;
thus has the consecration of the temple been briefly described by me.
Now, O best of sages, listen to the consecration of the pavilion and other structures.
First, the foremost pavilion for the Paṇṭas, and likewise the pavilion for the assembly;
the enclosure wall, the kitchen, the treasury, the storehouse for garments,
the hall for flowers and water, and the sacrificial pavilion.
Having thoroughly washed the granary and all other structures with abundant water,
and having caused the best of the twice-born to perform the rites of circumambulation with fire, sweeping, and smearing, they should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow.
Having especially adorned the pavilions and other structures with canopies and the like,
having perfumed them with aloe-wood incense and lit lamps on all sides,
and having decorated them with lime powder, one should scatter unbroken grains upon the ground.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should worship the Vāstupuruṣa.
Then, having prepared a pedestal of grain, one should place there a water-pot (*kumbha*) possessing the proper characteristics,
along with a secondary pot (*upakumbha*) and a small vessel (*karaka*), each endowed with the aforementioned characteristics as before.
There, having worshipped the deity together with his limbs and retinue,
the best of teachers should then establish the fire either in a sacrificial pit or on a sacrificial mound; there, he should satisfy the deity until the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
When the auspicious moment has arrived, the preceptor, the best among those who know mantras, should sprinkle [the image] with water from the pitcher using the root mantra in every case.
Thus has the ritual for the installation of the Pañcapāda and others been described.
In the consecration of pavilions and the like, as well as in the erection of gate-towers (gopura),
one should first perform the ritual acquisition of the ground and then carry out the laying of the foundation (garbhanyāsa).
One should deposit the foundation in the south-east corner of the pavilions and other such structures.
O lords of sages, the placement of the womb (garbhanyāsa) should take place to the south of the gopura;
the wise man should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the gopura just as he would that of the temple (prāsāda).
Now, the specific procedure for the installation of the deities therein is being described.
One should worship the deities beginning with Cakra and ending with Dharma upon the branches, roots, and so forth.
On the two door-panels, Kālāgni and Varuṇa are likewise to be worshipped;
one should place the great equipment of Bhava upon the collection of the lower legs.
One should place the forms beginning with Keśava situated above the upper part of the shanks;
and upon the area of the pedestal (prastara), one should arrange the collection of weapons beginning with the discus (cakra).
As before, [one should do so] on the ground areas of the neck and the pinnacle of the altar (vedikā).
O twice-born ones, O best of sages, one should install the deities of manifestation, ending with Padmanābha,
on each level of the gateway (gopura), as well as the directional deities (diṅmūrti) according to their original order,
following the procedure prescribed for the temple (prāsāda).
Then, O twice-born ones, one should worship the six-spoked Sudarśana on the floor beneath the pedestal supporting the water-pots (kalaśas);
when the group of six pots has been prepared, Vāsudeva and the others are to be worshipped.
When eight jars have been prepared, one should worship the group of six beginning with Keśava;
when twelve [jars] are used, one should worship the group of eight beginning with Keśava and then worship the twelve.
For one who desires liberation, the installation of the jars should be performed in pairs.
One should perform the installation of the other pitcher by means of the odd-numbered method.
When one pitcher has been installed, one should worship Vāsudeva;
O best of the twice-born, one should worship Keśava and the others starting from the third.
Having thus assigned the host of deities at the gateway, one should worship them.
O lords of sages, such is the procedure for the consecration of temples and other structures.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the venerable *Pāñcarātra*.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of Palaces and Other Structures.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Then Nārada shall describe the characteristics of the pedestal and other components for the image, O twice-born ones;
it may be fashioned from clay, wood, stone, or even from metal. (17.1)
The image, which is beneficial for the twice-born who seek its fruits, appears distinct [from the wall];
yet for those free from desire, it is attained as non-distinct and causes no contradiction.
Know that here, the painting is supported by the wall, the wood, and the sky.
Furthermore, according to the sequence of colors, that which arises from the sky is of four kinds:
namely, made of cotton, silk, linen, and hemp;
likewise, that produced from clay, such as white [chalk] and so forth, and various types of bark-cloth.

Know that for the twice-born, there are these pairs of materials in their respective order: the *āśvattha* originating from the *brahmavṛkṣa*, and that produced from *śrīparṇī* and *suradāru*; likewise, those made of *sāla* and *tāla*, and those produced from *śāśa* and *vāntīndusāra*. (17.5)
Other than these, those who are firmly rooted and possess substantial strength are indeed fit for sacrificial rites.

(17.6) But those that are common to all four [classes] are used in the initial acts such as the making of images; they are considered equal to stone or clay for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (17.7)
Likewise, those made of silver, gold, copper, and brass;
indeed, the various grounds, cloths, stones, minerals, trees,
and all gems such as diamonds, characterized by white, red, and other colors.
For those who desire fruits, [the mantras] are not common due to the influence of gain and loss;
however, by means of one's own form-mantras through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth,
one should bring them to a state of common manifestation, just as it occurs through the worship of their respective causes.
One should worship the Earth together with Indra using clay from a mountain during the rite of laying the foundation;
likewise, for the sake of cloth and trees, one should worship Varuṇa along with the Lord of Forests (Savanaspatis);
and for the connection of gems and minerals, one should worship the Moon and Fire.
Without the meaning of the *dhātu* based on the *ratna*, and indeed without the substitution of the [deity] through worship,
likewise without worship, a seat consisting of a wheel, lotus, or similar forms,
an image made of jewels is not recommended for the success of meditation by those who meditate. || 17.12–17.13 ||
She alone is the light of measure, devoid of the constituent parts of proof;
and because she is the weightiness of the castes and stages of life, because she is the sovereignty over all,
and because she is the divine form of the primordial elements, she resides within the highest and most excellent of things.
Indeed, a king who occupies a position of special distinction deserves this constantly;
how much more so one who desires no fruit, who is always devoted to faith and devotion?
Having understood this, one who seeks the goal as clearly as a reflection in a mirror should practice this with effort.
Having first worshipped the Guhyakas and the household deities with the heart-mantra and offerings such as *arghya*,
one should [discard] dirt, ashes, husks, charcoal, hair, insects, nails, straw,
radishes, thorns, leather, bones, common stones, and wall-scraps on that day.
Therefore, one must certainly leave a space of four finger-breadths before [the image];
having set aside a portion of the earth from the wall that is slightly more than the size of the image,
it should then be cleared of the aforementioned defects and purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water.
Having further filled that portion of the wall with well-kneaded clay,
he fashioned a wooden panel with a tool, making it as smooth as deerskin;
then, for the sake of purification, he removed the outer coating and placed a jar released from its binding-cloth.
Having washed [the vessel] seven times with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra,
using the Hṛdaya-mantra together with the Astra-mantra and the Mūrti-mantras,
[one should take water] from sacred sites, riverbanks, holy fields, and mountains.
Having discarded the earth mixed with impurities and having taken up fresh clay from above,
one should grind it, dry it, and then, on a well-smeared surface of the ground,
[prepare] flax, wool, cotton, and likewise silk thread.
Having first fashioned a stone vessel, one should place it there along with sand.

One should then consecrate it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the ash of the khadira tree, using a mixture of abundant milk, ghee, and so forth, combined with a small amount of cow dung.
Indeed, together with mustard oil, *tala* oil,
and sesame oil, one should soak it for twenty-one days in a vessel made of iron or similar material,
even without exposure to wind, fire, sun, or moon.
Having completed that image with that [clay], and having encased it within auspicious wood as if with cloth,
he should then perform a washing of the metals,
followed by a further wiping with sacred ash consecrated with mantras.
One who proceeds with devotion in the rite of preparing the image should perform the recitation of the weapon-mantra everywhere for the sake of pacifying obstacles.
One should perform worship, fire-offerings, and the offering of oblations to the spirits, accompanied by ritual fees.
At the time of correct grasping, this indeed concerns the general rule alone;
however, the specific [procedure] regarding the taking of stones and wood is now being stated.
But in every case at the time of commencement, one must observe the underlying cause.
During a pilgrimage for special worship, there is the arising of auspiciousness through an auspicious [sign];
through an inauspicious omen, the pilgrimage will be beset with obstacles.
However, by means of cessation, recitation, propitiatory rites, blessings, and so forth, [the obstacles are removed].
By turning back from that [place], one burns away [the effects of] misdeeds;

therefore, having worshipped the mantra, requested permission for the journey, and offered salutations, one should eat the remains of the food offering, maintain conduct on the left, and keep the senses restrained. (17.33–17.34)
Facing the east, having risen at the dawning of the nectar [of dawn], he should recollect the mantra; then,
having recognized either the supreme form or another form of that [deity], he should proceed toward its direction, or,
in its absence, toward another direction.
Accompanied by vigilant attendants and artisans,
he should proceed surrounded by jars of parched grain, curd, and consecrated rice, with flowers placed at the front.
A cheerful disposition, great enthusiasm, and the throbbing of the right limb are auspicious signs.
Auspicious speech, a banner, a conch, the fruits of stringed instruments and the like, cows, elephants, horses, brahmins, a maiden, new vessels, clay,
curd, fresh meat, ornaments, wine, fire, clarified butter, and milk. (17.38)
From a perfected being (siddha), [one obtains] rice seeds and the like, as well as *darbha* grass; the blossoms of excellent trees;
an umbrella, clothing, a banner, a vehicle, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), honey, a mirror, a chowrie, a necklace, and minerals, excluding weapons. (17.39–17.40)
Jewels, the image of a deity, wine, a fearless person, living fish, and whatever causes no weariness to the mind—
all that is excellent for the sight; however, that which causes weariness is not so.
From the threshold of one's own house up to seven steps on the path, as he proceeds, an omen yields its fruit; for indeed,
having departed from the city or the village, [the result is determined] by a half-krośa or even a full krośa of his stride.
Therefore, one should take an auspicious omen consisting of a mongoose or similar creature;
likewise, seeing a deer from within a full or more than half a *krośa* brings benefit.
Success will especially come in whichever direction the face is clear.
The sky is clear and brings about success; the sun and other luminaries are brilliantly radiant.
The wind is pleasant, gentle, moving in a clockwise direction, and steady;
free from divine portents and calamities, that time indicates the attainment of success.
The swan, the parrot, the bharadvāja crane, the cuckoo,
the wagtail, the peacock, the bee, the ruddy goose, and others such as these are auspicious birds that move through the sky.
Among those that move on the ground, the mongoose is gentle, as are the white snake, the lizard, and the monitor lizard.
The sight of the gandha, the khura, and the jackal is auspicious for all [the castes].
Among deer, the hariṇa, the lion, the tiger, the hare, and the leopard—
all these are indicators of success and are indeed ordained for all.
A jackal is especially auspicious when it circles to the right, even when the situation is reversed;
the affectionate cry of the twice-born (or the lowly) brings about success and bestows happiness.
When such an omen has arisen during the performance of the rite for the withdrawal of the elements (dhātusaṅkṣepa):
When it is no longer appropriate to wait, one should then practice peace.

Having entered the sacred field according to the rules, one should examine it with one's own spiritual luster, performing the previously mentioned special rites along with sacrificial fees for the sake of purifying the mind. (17.51–52)
One should look for a stone that possesses good qualities or a tree suitable for the task;
one should avoid one that is excessively old, as well as one whose bark is withered,
broken, scorched by forest fires, silent, or rough in texture.
One should examine a vein that contains sand, is perforated, marked by drops, and carries a pulsation;
one that resembles a mouse, a frog, a fish, a snake, a cat, or a rabbit;
and one that is covered with a network of veins arising from both its own color and other colors.
Because of the absence of the previously described forms, the perception of these [qualities] is beneficial.

That which resembles a pigeon, a parrot, or a lotus; that which has the luster of honey, madder, or black gram; that which is heavy, pleasant to the heart, auspicious, and unctuous—therefore, it is praised as being favorable for the wind (*vāta*).
O friend, she is submerged in the earth, situated at the bottom of a reservoir;
she is hidden by a great tree, dwelling amidst rows of forest trees;
she is entwined by a multitude of creepers and likewise surrounded by medicinal herbs.
Rising from the region of the knees, [the vein] is formed as a single mass and is soft.
The one with a sky-like face (khavaktrā) bestows liberation, while the one with a face like the netherworld (sutalānanā) bestows enjoyment.
The one with faces turned toward the directions (diṅmukhī) and two hands, whose head is directed eastward, grants prosperity and long life.
Therefore, one with the head facing east is considered to increase fame and renown.
That which faces north bestows the growth of the lineage, health, peace, nourishment, prosperity, and excellent intelligence. (17.60–17.61)
Having thus previously understood [the requirements],
he— by means of his powerful self endowed with vigor— together with artisans, lifted up the back, thighs,
feet, and head; facing eastward, [he placed it] in the northern part, with its face toward the north.
Having brought the Lord of Mantras down onto dry land and worshipped him with garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings,
one should meditate upon him as being confined within the stone, worship him thoroughly, and then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
This should be done either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on dry ground in one of the two directions previously mentioned.

Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should spend the day engaged in meditation and recitation. At the arrival of night, he should perform worship and satisfy the spirits with offerings (bali). Having projected his own body through the placement of mantras, he may eat the remains of the food offering (naivedya).
To the south of that, upon darbha grass, he should lie down with his head toward the east, reciting [mantras].
Having risen at the end of the night as before for the sake of obtaining a dream,
he should perform his own duties and offer oblations for the pacification of inauspicious dreams.
Having rejoiced at that auspicious dream which was clearly heart-stirring,
he would see himself as that mountain, his own place,
with its rocky terrain, resembling pure crystal or like molten gold.
Then he quickly attains that auspicious state which resembles a mass of smokeless embers. Then, taking up a weapon and a mallet consecrated with mantras,
facing the east, he should strike it four times, ending at the top of the head.
Having first examined the result from the location of the feet or from the center,
and having made it square and elongated,
one should bring it— either as a separate structure joined with a pedestal or as a machine-like frame— to the auspicious workshop for the work, which has been covered over by a pedestal.
Having first performed the ritual placement according to that procedure,
one should then extract the stone for the pedestal— either of a different color or of the same form as desired—
provided it possesses the qualities of the relationship between the primary and secondary parts and grants the vision [of the deity], O lords of sages. (17.72–73)
Indeed, even when wood, metal, or gems are unavailable, it is auspicious;
yet when they are available, one should certainly not create inequality or substitution.
Having brought at that very moment a beautiful stone serving as a base for the jewels—

One should know that the triad known as the *bimba* is beneficial when made from stones originating from male, female, or neuter sources. Indeed, everything [is acceptable] except for a stone from a *bimba* tree; furthermore, an image of the Lord made from a gemstone or a stone from a gemstone pedestal is prohibited.
Those stones that have the forms of deities such as Lakṣmī and others grant all accomplishments; however,
that stone which emits sparks like struck fire accompanied by sound is indeed a male stone, while one that is lusterless yet resonant is female.

That [mantra] in which there is neither the letter *agni* (ra) nor the sound (*dhvani*) at its beginning, middle, or end, should be known as "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*). It bestows fruit when established in its own proper place.
Having understood this regarding the God of Gods, and likewise for Lakṣmī and the others— || 17.78–79 ||

Having likewise worshipped all the retinues, the seats (pīṭhas), and so forth, as well as the stones for the temple and other structures with their respective mantras in due order, one should collect all the stones and place them upon carts and similar conveyances.
Having installed and brought [the materials], the Guru should have the images and so forth fashioned.

(17.81) It has been stated that this refers to the selection of stone; now the selection of wood is described: [one should take wood] that extends from within the mountains, which is free of wounds, straight, and large. (17.82)
It was free from disease, not scarred by the claws of lions or other beasts,
its potency unimpaired by wind, lightning, or forest fires, and not situated on the outer edge; rather,
it stood upon a raised plot of ground that was well-proportioned and very fertile.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) as before, one should then worship on the following day while reciting:
"Salutation to you, the Lord of All, who are the self residing here, whose true nature is unknown. (17.84–85)
"Forgive me; descend elsewhere and remain here as the conscious self (cidātman).
Then, with a tool purified by water and smeared with ghee and other substances, while reciting the supreme mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ," one should indeed cut [it] with a saw or similar instrument.

If it falls facing toward the east, the north, or the northeast, it should be understood as auspicious; if it falls elsewhere, one should perform worship and other rites. Having brought the portion for the deity, one should do so without taking anything that is not to be taken.
If one indeed wishes to make an image out of wood that is very large,
adorned with many arms, faces, and weapons,
it does not constitute a fault provided it is measured according to the remaining intact parts of the tree from which it arose.
And because everything consists of syllables through the power of devotion and faith;
thus, having first performed the collection of even a single object preceded by devotion, one should fashion the desired form. (17.90–91)
For that purpose, the general measurement known as Saumya is first described;
it is straight, free from modification, pervasive, and possesses a single form.
Having indeed carved out the measurement upon a level and smooth portion of ground by means of that [line], || 17.92 ||
Having examined the characteristics of the parts in detail, [it is stated]:
that which is one hundred and eightieth part of its own height is one *aṅgula*;
two *aṅgulas* are a *kalā*, and the eye, the globe (*golaka*), and the *bhāva* are likewise [measured in these units]. 17.93–94.
That which is one-eighth of a finger-breadth is proclaimed to be a barley-corn (*yava*).
In the work of making images and the like, a *tāla* should be understood as six such units.
Furthermore, the face, the navel, the genitals, and the ground [of the feet] are measured in *tālas*, as is the pair of thighs.

Furthermore, for those with two time-units, the shanks, the ankles, the knees, and the neck should each be known as three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure; this is declared to be the measurement according to the length or shortness of the images of those who wear matted hair. 17.96–97.
One should cast out the measurement of four units and three units from the base of the head;
the crown (*mauli*) has five, seven, or eight peaks and rises eight units in height.
For those without matted locks (*nirjaṭānām*), there should be a forehead above, or a very beautiful diadem (*makuṭa*).
In this matter, however, the decrease and increase should be performed according to the specific requirements of the work by means of the *tāla*.

As has been stated regarding the proportions, one should divide the portion of the face—consisting of the mouth, nose, and forehead—into three parts, each measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). || 17.99–17.100 ||

Then, in front of that, the nose should be one *kalā* in measure, like a sesame flower; its width is half a *kalā*, and there is a depression in its two nostrils. The space from the tip of the nose to the seat is four barleycorns in measure, equal to a *gojī*.
That [space] is separated from the tip of the nose by a measure of four barleycorns.
The upper lip is half a finger-breadth, while the lower lip is one finger-breadth.
The chin is a *golaka* [in measure], and the two corners of the mouth are four finger-breadths apart.
One should fashion the two eyes within the openings of the ears and eyes, situated in the middle portion of the first part of the nose; they should be one *kalā* apart from each other,
equal to one *kalā* in length, and half a *kalā* in width.
That which has the shape of an utpala petal is increased by two barley-corns;
one should make it in the shape of a lotus petal for the purpose of the eye, with a circular pupil.
The length of the pupil for the first and the other [eye] is increased by one-third of its own length.
O lotus-eyed one, that [measurement] for the light is one and a half barley-corns, and it is also prescribed as three-fifths of that;
the socket of the eye is twelve barley-corns in width, with an additional barley-corn.
The two eyebrows are known to be two and a half finger-breadths in length and two *kalās* in thickness;
in the middle they are two *yavas* wide, shaped like the crescent moon, tapering gradually,
with an interval of half a *kalā*, and their tips aligned on the same horizontal line.
The two ears are two finger-breadths wide and twice the size of a golaka in length;
the circumference of the neck is two yavas, and the two joints are four yavas each.
Know that the middle part between them is likewise [measured], while the droṇī is indeed one and a half finger-breadths.
That hole, which is the measure of the noose, should be made with half a *kalā* according to one's preference;
it may range from one finger-breadth up to two *kalās*, and there may even be some irregularity therein.
It should be understood as being four *yavas* in width and free from any internal cavity.
The two ears are thus remembered as being endowed with six ornaments.
The forehead is four *kalās* [in width], while the two *śikhara*s (temples) are two *golaka*s [in height].
They are three *aṅgulas* in height and one *aṅgula* in width at the front.
One should fashion the mass of hair, arising from the region of the hairline and situated above the forehead,
measuring half a kalā; and one should make the circumference of the cheeks extend evenly from the ears to the neck.
In the middle of that, the two cheeks are rounded and well-defined as previously described;
know the circumference of the head to be thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
which is the distance from the two tips of the ears to the back of the head.
Know that [the distance] from the forehead to the cavity of the ears is sixteen *aṅgulas* and likewise three *tālas* behind; it should be understood as one and a half *tālas*.
The neck, resembling a fine conch shell, is indeed [proportioned] at its base, middle, and tip.
The circumference [of the base] is twelve kalās and twenty-one aṅgulas at its tip;
it is eighteen aṅgulas wide, expanded by one-third of its own part.
Its base is likewise in width, while the two shoulders are elevated, circular, elongated, and symmetrical.

The thickness of that [forearm] is six *aṅgulas*, and thus the measurement of the arm is stated. The portion from the shoulder to the head is three *kalās*, while up to the end of the joint it is recorded as six *kalās*.
Indeed, the measurement from the joint to the wrist is recorded as four *kalās*.

The hand up to the middle finger-joint of a jewel is considered to be seven *aṅgulas* in measure; that measurement for the middle finger should be understood as reduced by one *kalā*. Furthermore, the index finger (*pradeśinī*) is equal in name [to the middle finger] when it is reduced by four barley-corns (*yava*).
The little finger together with the thumb should be known as two kalās;
the thumb is remembered as having two joints, and all the fingers are extended.
One should shorten them by a barley-corn at every joint from the base to the tip.
The nails should be shaped like a phallus according to the measure of half the first joint;
the measurement of the base of the thumb is four finger-breadths in circumference.
And that [circumference] minus four barley-corns should be known for the three fingers;
for a finger less than that, the reduction is one and a half kalās, and the decrease due to the wrapping is as before.
The thumb is one finger-breadth from the tip; the other three [fingers] are said to be six barley-corns [in length];
they are not less than half a finger-breadth from the tip; the palm is diminished in sequence from the middle.
One should not have a hand that is water-like (unsteady) at the tip, nor one that is deficient by a finger-breadth.
The palms are slightly depressed and adorned with the lines of Lakṣmī.
From the base of the fingers to the wrist, the girth of the hands is two barley-corns per finger-breadth;
from the wrist downwards, it is remembered as being four barley-corns greater.
In the middle, however, its width is said to be reduced by one-sixteenth part (*kalā*).
From the wrist as the limit, the circumference of the upper arm is recorded as six *kalās*.
Know that at the joint it is seven *kalās*, including a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) and also three *avamas*.
The nine spheres from the base are indeed diminished by half a finger-breadth;
likewise, the width above the joint is as previously described here.
Here too, by the same principle as before, the earth itself is to be placed within the field of vision.
Having abandoned the *tāla* at the limit of the neck, and having made an interval of that same measure,
one should fashion the two breasts equally; their ridge should be fleshy,
and the depression [between them] should be half the size of the heart-sphere (*hṛdgolaka*), topped above by a row of jewels.

The two sides of the breasts are three *kala*s; the circle of the breast is three *yava*s. The nipple is raised by one *yava* and its width from the tip is likewise [one *yava*]. The eye is three and a half *yava*s; this is declared to be the measurement for the armpit.
Free from the pride of the aggregates (*skandha*), it was level from the shoulder-blade to the back;
resembling a trough and full of flesh, it was like the sacrificial altar.
Behold the chest-enclosure, five *tāla* spans wide and possessed of eyes.
When two *tālas* are doubled and increased by three *yavas*, know that to be the measurement for the girth of the belly;
the navel region should be understood as having a measurement of one *kalā* less three *yavas*. || 17.137–17.138 ||
That measurement is three *avinas*, and its depth is prescribed as such;
the three-eyed Lord [Śiva] has a circumference (*paridhi*) of three *tālas* at the center of the navel.
Six *golakas* is recorded as that measurement for the purpose of the girdle (*kaṭi*).
The two buttocks are fleshy, resembling the frontal globes of an elephant, and each is surrounded by five *golaka*s.
The line of the loincloth (*kaupīna-rājī*) is prescribed to be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) from the base;
it is one *aṅgula* in width all around, while the penis (*meḍhra*) is prescribed to be three *kala*s in length.
That sheath is four barley-corns [in width], while the covering is six finger-breadths [in length].
The two testicles are two finger-breadths in length; from the base to the end, they are equal in width.
Know that it is two finger-breadths all around, and the aperture for the wind is perfectly circular.
The measurement of the thigh should be known as nine aṅgulas for the middle ground.
From the base to the tip, it is recorded as six kalās, and the top portion is remembered as three kalās.
The knee-pan is one aṅgula less, measuring two kalās.

In width and height, it should be equal to four barleycorns; at the base of the shank, the circumference is known to be nine golakas. In the middle, it is two times seven (fourteen) aṅgulas, and from there, it is five and a half kalās.
In this case as well, O Wealthy One, one should determine the width by one-third of the circumference;
[the width] from the middle, the base, and the tip should be proportionate,
as should that of the two arms, the middle region, and the number of finger-joints.

The pair of thighs should be joined with the shanks, reaching down to the feet; the length of the foot is traditionally held to be one-sixteenth of a tāla. The heel has a surface of two golakas, and in its middle, there is a space of one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
At the three joints and at the front, it is generally equal to one *kalā*.
The foot is said to be three *yavas* less than the measure from the base of the big toe;
the *bāhula* is the measure of one *kalā*, and from the region of the ankle, it is one *aṅgula*.
From the base of the fingers to the ankle, the circumference of the calf is one *piṇḍikāṅgula*;
from the terminal point of the shank, the circumference is seven eyes (*saptalocana*). At that very time, the circumference at the top is prescribed to be reduced by one *kalā*.
Having completed the foot according to that rule upon the back of the tortoise,
O wielder of the plow, its length should be three finger-breadths, and the length of the thumb should be five finger-breadths; this is to be understood as its circumference.
The forefinger should be made two *yava*s longer than that [middle finger] in length;
furthermore, the middle of the foot should be made equal to the length of the thumb.
The middle finger is reduced by two-eighths [of its length];
the one following it is likewise, and that which follows it has three joints, all as described before.
They are joined with a network of nails resembling the back of a tortoise.

The wrapping of the big toe should be two units of time (dvikala), less half a barley-corn (yava); for the remaining toes, it is proclaimed to be four barley-corns less [at each subsequent one]. The width of all of them is to be known as three parts of their respective circumferences.
All [the limbs] are fleshy, gentle, and symmetrical; the individual parts are auspicious.
When the two canine teeth are positioned outside the row of other teeth, they should be seven barley-corns high. The measurement for the four central teeth is two barley-corns high.
The measurement and wealth of all those belonging to that class [should be known];
the width of the two front teeth is three *yavas*, and from the tip to the root it is two *yavas*.
From the middle part, each of those teeth is one and a half *yavas* wide, and all the teeth are without gaps.
This auspicious mark, arising from a birth that has turned clockwise like a flame consuming its own fuel,
is most certain, beneficial, and unfailing in its measurement.
It possesses a captivating charm, uniquely adorned with beauty and grace.
And always understand the existence of these two as being established in mutual dependence:
beauty sometimes exists by encroaching upon pride,
while in other cases pride remains by completely covering over beauty.
Just as in the world a handsome man attains honor even if he is poor,
whereas one who is ugly does not attain it even if he is exceedingly wealthy;
so too, a physical form devoid of both qualities becomes unacceptable.

Because the lords of sages are always endowed with a single quality that is worthy of being accepted— namely, perfect dignity and beauty— and because, through their desire to bestow grace upon devotees,
the power of the mantra’s presence truly remains fruitful.

For one who has correctly entered the path, that [image], being formless yet standing within the range of vision, quickly brings delight; knowing this, one should apply effort for the sake of perfecting its beauty through measurement, weighing, and sizing. (17.167)

For one with straight and well-aligned feet, the distance between the feet is three finger-breadths (aṅgula). For one with uneven feet, that distance from the front is considered equal to a tāla; however, measured from the middle of the two heels, it should be known as two golakas.

For the sake of stability, one should mark the central Brahma-channel as well as the two pathways with a perfectly straight thread extending from the body, from south to north. From the forehead of the image standing with feet even, [one should measure] down to the top of the genitals.
Having extended the cord and covered it, [one measures] the interval between the navel and the heart;
likewise, the success regarding the tip of the nose and the forehead belongs to him whose tilaka-mark extends upward.
In this manner, one should lead [the cord] from the tip of the right big toe of the uneven foot.
Having brought about the symmetry of the limbs by means of a thread extending from one part of the body to another, for the sake of eliminating all irregularities in the images,
[the form] is auspicious because it is completely pure with four, three, or two corners on all sides. 17.173.
But the impure [meditation] is the state in which the limbs of the image arise in full clarity.
17.174 The forehead of the horse-faced one is twelve finger-breadths in width; it has eight eyes in length, and four finger-breadths at the front. 17.175
In the nostril-aperture, which has a hollow of half a *kalā* and is separated by another part,
there are two corners of the mouth (*sṛkviṇī*) at the jaw, measuring eight finger-breadths and equal to that [width].
In the middle, there are two ear-conch shells (*śrotraśukti*), measuring two finger-breadths and raised by two units.
The bridge of the nose is two finger-breadths wide, and above that, it is recorded as being two kalās.
One should fashion the expansion of the mouth with two *yava*s in sequence from the front;
indeed, one should bring that very [expansion] to a thinness at the edge of the jaw by a single *yava*.
The two sides of the bridge of the nose should be depressed in the middle and joined together.
With two and a half barleycorns [of space] between the eyes and the nostrils;
then, the petal of the eye-socket is accumulated with the measure of a barleycorn.
The forehead, together with its hairline, is as before; the middle of the eye is one-sixteenth of a finger-breadth.

One should place the face of Nṛsiṃha with eight eyes all around; then, from the region of the eight segments, one should fashion two ears arising therefrom. Again, by the measurement of those two ears, one should extend [the line] to the edge of the forehead.
From the previously established measurement, the nasal cavity, characterized by its vigorous expansion, should be provided with a nasal septum and possess blossoming, wide-open apertures;
those apertures, moreover, should exceed the previous measurement by three *yavas*.
The temple (sagola) should be placed upon the upper parts [of the face], and the eye should possess all its proportions.
The lower lip is to be known as one finger (aṅgula) and four barley-corns (yava).
The mouth is four kalās and a half; the remaining length is recorded as that of the jaw (hana).
Its expansion should be understood as one *netra* measure plus one *yava*.
In front, it decreases by one *aṅgula* up to the corners of the mouth.
The entire circumference of the pair of eyes, including the area of wonder, is half of that [measure]. 17.185–17.186.
The ear is extended as before; its elevation is equal to half a *kalā*.
The brow, joined by a pair of *indrakalās*, consists of three globes (*trigolakā*).
The space between them is one *kalā* in measure, large and resembling a conch-shell spiral.
That measurement of the portion should be clearly applied to its head.
The face of the mountain-support (kṣmādhara) is recorded as being one and a half tālas in length;
in width, from the forehead, it is that same measure minus two aṅgulas.
The width of the *potra* (the lower lip) of the Lord, who is of gentle form and arisen [in manifestation],
is four parts of that [measurement] minus one *kalā*.
Above that, its thickness is equal [to the width], and below it is one *aṅgula*.
The measurement of the two jaws is traditionally held to be seven and a half finger-breadths.
As for the remaining space of the mouth, which is the interval between the two corners of the lips,
its expansion at the front edge is one and a half kalās.
That [measurement] should be understood as one finger-breadth from the two corners of the mouth;
the opening for the arrow [the nostril] is curved in the case of eloquent speech, while the two fangs are raised by half a *kala*.
The bridge of the nose is as described before, like the back of a plantain stalk.
In the *Vājimukha*, it is said that the ears should be seven *kalās* apart;
the eyes should be equal to those [ears], yet with sharp outer corners and devoid of the *yava* measure.
Their necks, however, are prescribed to be two finger-breadths [in width].
That which is joined at each individual point, arising from a gentle form,
and which corresponds to the measurement of whichever limb of Nṛhari lacks its height—
that very same [measurement], through its circumference and breadth, shall be greater by half a *kalā*.
His chest, waist, belly, shoulders, and buttocks are free from any deficiency;
likewise, his nails and palms are well-formed, and his body is fleshy and full, with extremely curly body hairs that curl to the right.
For a deity with three, four, or five faces,
one should effect a reduction of two *golaka*s by means of the right and left faces, excluding the upward-facing face;
therein, the expansion is said to be that of the lion-faced [upward] face.
However, for the sake of attaining liberation, the alignment of the gaze of the four [faces] should be equal;
and for the sake of attaining health, enjoyment, and isolation (kaivalya), one should perform the alignment of the gaze by half a finger-breadth to the left and to the right.
Together with the aforementioned [measurements], for one who is correctly facing westward,
the [distances] from the nose, the eyes, the ground, and the ears to the corners of the mouth and the width [of the face] are as follows:
then, the auspicious right side has a slightly lowered face with the gaze cast toward the earth.
And like that, the aforementioned face of the [deity] facing north brings about all accomplishments (siddhi).
Indeed, because it indicates its own function, there is the presence of that mantra. Otherwise, if one relies on a different [direction], the King of Mantras is neither peaceful nor auspicious.
And because of his constant presence, spirits, vetālas,
and rākṣasas flee from sight and enter [him] upon being seen.
Taking the minister’s command upon their heads, they depart.
Therefore, one should perform that by which the presence of the *bimba* (the reflected image) may be attained;
for indeed, no one undertakes anything auspicious merely because of its proximity—such as [a face] with the tusks of a boar, the eyes of a lion, or a flat nose. (17.206–207)
The western face of the five-faced Lord is indeed to be fashioned;
its equality with the upper and lower lips should be maintained.
By half a finger-breadth less than those two, the [central] face situated between them is clearly defined.
The row of teeth should indeed be made level from the root to the middle to the tip.
Then, the pair of cheeks should be prominent and circular by half a *kalā*.
The beard at the front should be two *kalās*, and the [chin] should be one *kalā* and a half *kalā* respectively.
The *sambandhaveṇī* (the weaving of connections), when measured according to the previously stated proportions, will bring about auspiciousness;
one should bring gentleness to the primary faces, which are like those of a lion or a boar.
This measurement indeed arises from the perspective of the visible, yet it consists of conventional practice.
And the expansion of the gentle-natured Bhūbhṛt was spoken of as having the horse's face (Aśvavaktra).
However, one should practice that which was previously mentioned for Nṛhari and so forth;
likewise, this applies to the state of being permeated by the faces and limbs of the Lord Śaktīśvara.
Adorned with necklaces, anklets, garments, garlands, bracelets, and armlets,
and graced by flower wreaths, sacred threads, upper-arm ornaments, crowns, and other finery—
an image fashioned in this way for those whose forms are composed of mantra bestows spiritual accomplishment.
Regarding that vehicle, the deity of the vital breath, which was previously described as fivefold:
the facial circle [of the deity] is equal in measure to the *tāla* arising from its image;
the forehead is said to be two *aṅgulas*, and the matted locks are bound above the two eyes.
The ear is elevated by two finger-breadths; the chest is known to be five kalās;
that belly is eight finger-breadths; the waist is elevated by five finger-breadths;
the thighs are elevated by nine finger-breadths; and the knees are known to be two finger-breadths.

The shanks are eight finger-breadths in height, and the two masses of the feet are two finger-breadths [each]. One [unit] is equal, while that [other] is diminished by one *kalā*; such is the circumference of the neck. The total extent of all the limbs should always be understood as being equal to the [height of the] image.
Know that the girth of his belly exceeds its width,
and the circumference of his waist is indeed more than four times the measure of his eyes.
Know that the girth at the base of his thighs is like that of a *bimboka* fruit.
That same [measurement] applies to the middle of the shank and the end of the shank;
for the foot is five kalās in length and four aṅgulas in width.
From the region of the heel, the big toe is three aṅgulas long and equal to one and a half kalās.
The fingers should be known from the region of the feet by means of barley-corns in successive order.
The navel cavity is very extensive, measuring two and a half eyes (two and a half finger-breadths) in width.
From the wrist to the tip of the middle finger is nine finger-breadths.
The span of the hand is three *kala*s; its nails are sharp and prominent.
Know that the height of the head of the arm is two *locana*s.
That pair consisting of the upper arm (*bhuja*) and the forearm (*upabhuja*) is recorded as being equal to two *tāla*s.
The girth of her arms was greater than half a *kalā* more than the diameter of her face;
for she possessed lips like the bimba fruit, well-formed breasts, and prominent eyes.
Her eyes were as round and expansive as lotus petals.

The pair of eyebrows, arising from the form of Narasiṃha, should be like the tip of a parrot’s beak; the bridge of the nose should be one-sixteenth of the measurement in length and long like the back of an elephant;
and the pair of flanks reaching the region of the belly should be neither too short nor too long.

That very [body] is expanded by half its length, like the wing of a swan; its tail, consisting of a hundred branches, is twice the measure of its own wings. This true extent, including the wings and endowed with its constituent parts, is thus established.
The common proportions for all [images] have been understood; now the specific [proportions] are being described.
One should reduce the two thighs by three finger-breadths;
one should likewise determine the height of the shank-shafts and perform the wrapping with the shanks.
O Mahāmati, from the root of the wrist-joint known as the *bimba*,
at the region of the webbing, the web on the foot should be understood to be half of that [distance] plus half a finger-breadth; in width, it is six finger-breadths.
Know that everything else spoken by Satya is always true for all beings.
However, the two wings are devoid of feet; due to their length, they are as wide as those petals.
And this is the extent of the wing-span of those who are flying.
And for the five [limbs] that remain to be fully known, their measure is half [of the previous];
taking this as the measure, O wielder of the plow, know it to be the characteristic of the dwarf-form, excluding the tail, eyebrows, and wings. (17.235)
Taking [the material] three finger-breadths from the forehead, nose, and mouth,
one should fashion the binding of matted locks (jaṭābandha) above the head, such that the length from the base of the matted locks to the end is five tālas.
Now, however, the specific distinctions regarding the ritual images (karmabimba) are being described:

the image for ritual action (karmārcā), the image for festivals (utsavārcā), the image for offerings (balyarcā), the auspicious eye-opening ceremony (tīrthakautuka), the image for the ceremonial bath on special occasions (nimittasnapanārcā), and the image for the period of rest (śayanārcā); thus they are of six kinds.
O Brahmins, these images should be fashioned according to the various rules for multiple *beras*.

However, in the case of a single *bera*, one should arrange five [images] excluding the ritual image (*karmārcā*). If the primary image (*mūlabimba*) and the *kautuka* are joined with all these subsidiary images (*aṅgabimba*), [then this rule applies]. 17.239–240.

That which is endowed with three [of these] is the best; it is proclaimed as middling when endowed with two; and that which is endowed with one is the lowest—this is here called their respective measurement. The height of the primary image should be divided either into two parts or even into three.
Or, having divided [the height] into four parts, one should arrange it with one part. Having divided the height of the festive image (utsavārcā) into two, three,
or even four parts, one should determine [its proportions] with one part.
O best of the twice-born, one should likewise fashion all five images, beginning with the karma-image and the arcā-image,
as well as the group of six images together with the two goddesses; or else, one may fashion the festive image (cautsava-bimba) and the image for the bed-chamber (śayanakautuka).
O best of the twice-born, the rite accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi should be performed upon the primary image (mūlabimba),
whether it is standing, mounted on a vehicle, or even seated, O twice-born ones;
and likewise, the group of six beginning with the action-image (karmabimba) should also be in a standing position.
O twice-born ones, while the primary image (mūlabimba) is reclining, the ritual images (karmabimba) and others should be made to stand;
O lords of sages, even when [the primary image] is standing, they should be made to sit.
However, the image for the daily festival (nityotsava) should be standing in all cases.
O tiger among sages, by what signs is the oneness and multiplicity of the form to be known? O best of speakers, tell me that in its entirety.
That [image] which is made of stone, or even of jewels, or of metals,
is always devoid of the scope for all daily rites such as bathing and the like. (17.249)
Even by means of the ritual worship (karmārcā), the deities may remain standing or assume a seated posture. Know that the single-form image (ekabera) is established as a solitary form;
however, that image made of clay or wood is provided with the ritual worship and other such features.
For the purpose of all daily baths and so forth, [the image] may or may not be accompanied by the Śaktis;
it should be made of materials such as gems, vajra, or stone, and be capable of undergoing occasional ceremonial baths (nimittasnāna).
However, that which is intended for the daily bath (nityasnāna) must always be accompanied by the ritual image (karmārcā).
The large image, whether accompanied by Lakṣmī and the others or devoid of them,
is capable of all types of ablutions prescribed for daily and occasional rites;
it is that image which is always endowed with Lakṣmī and the other Śaktis.
O lords of sages, know that this threefold wealth consists of many images;
namely, those made of variegated materials which rest upon walls, wood, or cloth, and are provided with ritual icons for the daily rites of bathing and other ceremonies. (17.255)
Furthermore, an image made of clay, or even one produced in three ways from painting,
equipped with a mirror and other such items for the daily and occasional baths,
is suitable for the lineage of ritual images according to one's wealth.
Know that this fourfold wealth is distinguished by its many forms;
it exists in many forms according to its application, whether standing, seated,
lying down, or even moving in a vehicle, as desired.

The distinctions regarding the many images (*bahubera*) and so forth are proclaimed to be fivefold. Other ritual images (*karmabimba*), preceded by the image for processions (*yātrābimba*), are intended for the specific purposes of those respective rites, whether they consist of many images or a single image.
And for two [deities], they should be fashioned according to one's means. Thus has the characteristic of the image been stated in brief; now the pedestal (pīṭha) is described.
For images that are seated, that [pedestal] should be square.
For those that are always raised up, the shape is indeed square and long; otherwise, the form of these two is circular or elongated,
measured by finger-breadths arising from atoms or by those consisting of the worshipper.

From the *dhāttrī* tree, or from a door, or from a temple structure, the length of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be measured; its width shall be half that measure. Furthermore, above the door, there were formerly three *ranta*s, with one at the front.

Having subtracted twelve parts, the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be three [parts]; by the remaining collection of parts, the image (pratimā) should be raised. Alternatively, it may be mounted upon a vehicle, or it may be of inferior, middling, or superior size.
The height of the seated [image] is prescribed as four-twelfths (one-third) of that;
its width everywhere is made to be half of it.
Alternatively, it may be reduced by one-third or diminished by one-fourth.
Furthermore, by the power of the retinue alone, there is the fourfold nature;
and for that which has not lost its parts and whose seat and extent are established in every direction,
it belongs both to that which is situated within the view of the four directions and to that which is situated within the view of a single direction.

That same length is doubled for one that is covered with markings, and it is increased by a half for one that is uncovered; its thickness has been described previously. A set of four [images] on a single pedestal is entirely devoid of auspicious marks.
Know that each one is distinguished by its specific mark, and they are as many in number as those marks.
The first is Anantāsana, the second is Pakṣamandira,
the third has the lotus as its emblem, and the fourth is adorned with the discus.
Thus, indeed, the commonality of all the seats (pīṭhas) consists of sixteen;
understand them again in brief as they are divided by their distinctions.
Know the marks of the seats in the directions and those situated in the throat.
Furthermore, due to their mutual arrangement, they possess a manifold nature; moreover,
