because of the presence of the wheel and the lotus situated therein, or their absence,
and through their mutual conjunction, they serve as the support for infinite birds in all directions.
Let the plurality be determined by means of two-fold natures or a dual nature;
by an upward-pointing lotus alone, the pair [is indicated], and by a wheel outside of that.
Thus, indeed, by a downward-pointing one alone, each pair is to be fully understood.
Above, however, there are two lotuses, and below, two wheels.

O Lords of Sages, the other [arrangement] should be understood through the reversal of these pairs, according to whether the pair of wheels and lotuses is situated internally or externally. (17.277–278)
Know that from the reversal of these two, there is a group of four from the upper portion;
likewise, there is another group of four from the lower portion.
This is the octad of seats, whether below or above.

It is proper that one should perform [the rite] with either a single discus or a lotus. For many pedestals may also be fashioned in the shape of discs, resting upon a single pivot; likewise, they may be provided with a slight pericarp.
Thus has the movement of the marks been described by me in many ways.
Now, that which pertains to the *pīṭha* which serves as the fundamental ground is being explained.
Having first divided the *pīṭha* into twenty parts by means of equal squares according to its original extent—
One part is for the feet and the shanks; three parts each for the calves and the thighs; one part for the neck-protrusion (*kaṇṭhavīdhī*); six parts for the neck and that which is above it;
one part for the neck-line (*kaṇṭhasūtra*), and three parts for the *śuktikā*.
And one should indeed fashion the *uṣṇīṣa* above that with two parts;
the projection of the base is prescribed by its own portion alone.
In the four directions, the Great Beings are remembered as being superior in terms of their field (*kṣetra*).
One should fashion the entire vessel from a single mold, provided with sprouts and *vāraka* ornaments.
One should cause the ear-base (*karṇapīṭha*) to enter [the interior] by means of two parts on all sides,
and the internal entry of the neck by one part of the path (*vīthyaṃśa*).
One should effect an equal emergence of the thread for its entry into the throat;
fashioned with one-quarter [of the length] below the shell,
from the portion of the neck-thread to the edge of the mouth, one should briefly perform the contraction of the power.
The symmetry of the head, the pitcher-shaped calves, and the shanks should remain as they naturally are.
One should adorn them like a jar with pearl-ornaments, emeralds, or lotus sprouts.
There, having left a space above the enclosure measuring four parts, one should bury the trough (droṇī) on all sides with a slope of one part; then,
at the midpoint of its width, there should be an outlet measuring one-third of itself.
That measurement shall be square and extend outward from the field of the pedestal (pīṭha).

Having divided that [measurement] into three parts at the front, one should eliminate two side-portions. Then, by means of the remaining part, starting from the base, it should be properly shaped like the face of a plough.
Having first divided it threefold and again threefold from the front and the base,
one should then bury it from the middle so that the water flows out quickly; thus,
O lords of sages, it becomes exactly like the face of a boar.
One should indeed fashion the water-egress [of the pedestal] resembling a conch or like the snout of a sea-monster;
this is the characteristic described for pedestals.
One should not, however, fashion the ritual images of those whose nature is limited by hope and so forth.
But for those made of variegated materials, clay, or wood— especially for those that are movable—
as well as for the square [image] and for that which is situated as a fourfold form,
the water-channel must be positioned at the front of the image, since [otherwise] it causes the destruction of its perfection.
Without a purpose, there is no loss for that [universal] without it;
for the universal, however, there is specifically a need for a substratum. Thus, the pedestal would be with a channel, and the seat would be the channel itself.
Wherever the practitioner performs a bath with abundant water and other substances,
a clear transgression occurs there every day if it is done without that [ritual].
In this very same way, the procedure for the large image is prescribed for those who are adorned.
And for the purpose of bathing the images originating from stone monuments according to their signs,
one should perform the rite upon the ritual image (karmabimba) seated upon a throne;
and one should constantly offer curd, milk, ghee, and so forth, as they may be obtained.

One should diligently lead that water away to a plot of ground or a receptacle, so that it is not stepped upon by feet; for that bestows great merit. Therefore, a drainage channel has been prescribed, and for this very reason, [standing water] is prohibited.
Whether it extends to the end of birth, the end of the world, the end of the night-lily, or the end of the throat,
or reaching the end of the blade of a sword— these five varieties exist in all abodes.
At the time of their installation, they are beneficial for the gods in two directions.
For those facing east and west, that which is situated in the northern direction is auspicious;
for those facing north and south, it is always prescribed in the eastern part.
Furthermore, to the left of the deity on the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha), it brings about the attainment of one's goals.
"But for those who always worship [it], it bestows the opposite through its contrary nature.
Thus, the characteristics of the *pīṭhas* have been briefly described by me.
(17.307) Thus ends [the section] in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
The seventeenth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Images and Other Objects," followed by the eighteenth chapter.
Henceforth, I shall explain the installation of the mantra and the image,
which bestows what is desired in the present for those castes who seek worldly enjoyment (bhoga),
and which grants liberation (kaivalya) through tranquility for those who follow the four stages of life (āśrama).
And he should provide assistance for those devoted to sacrificial rites, along with their fruits;
as before, in front of the temple, in a particular direction, there should be a pavilion,
square-shaped, with four doors, and enclosed by a garland of *darbha* grass.
But if that is not available, one should face whichever direction is preferred;
[the image] may range from fourteen cubits up to thirty cubits,
or even ending at six cubits, depending on the measurement of the physical form.
In the center of those [structures], a platform (sthalī) should be constructed with fourteen parts [of the total height] and then eight;
it should be Samantabhadra, very smooth, and paved with baked bricks and the like.
Indeed, in this general procedure, one should begin from a height of one tāla.
By increasing the height by one finger-breadth [per section], it is gradually reduced to that same [original] diminution;
through two, three, or eight parts in the middle, the mandala of all [the deities] is formed.
It is square, with four gates, and adorned with wheels and lotuses.
The bed is to the south and the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) to the north, as before.
It should be auspicious, measuring two cubits with a girdle (mekhalā), marked with a wheel and a lotus;
below that, it is square, provided with a front-frieze and a girdle.
Then, one should fashion a circle marked with a wheel in the southern quarter;
in the west, a charming lotus-marked [circle]; and in the north, a conch-marked [circle]. In all corners, the measurement of these should be according to that of the upper [mandala].
All the pavilions (maṇṭapa) measuring ten cubits on each side have four altars with a single girdle (mekhalā). However, in this case, all those extending upwards have girdles on every level;
consequently, all the pavilions situated below consist of a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Among these, the first [type] with its girdle (*mekhalā*) shall be twenty-two finger-breadths;
by decreasing by two finger-breadths at a time, it should reach sixteen finger-breadths.
In a six-cubit house, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or the girdle may be made larger.

It should first be eight cubits high; thereafter, it may be increased by one cubit at a time. There shall be no reduction in height for those [temples] ending with six cubits, nor for those that are less than that.
Then, one should subtract four [units] starting from thirteen cubits;
[the reductions are] eight finger-breadths, followed by seven, five, and four [finger-breadths] in sequence.
Thus is the width of the bathing houses, together with their heights.
However, they should indeed be adorned in the middle with sand platforms,
measuring two, four, or two cubits in width, and elevated as previously described.
The bathing materials should be brought from the front house to three auspicious and desired directions.
One should construct the primary hall for the gift of sight, equal in measure to the *arghamāna*, provided with an excellent pedestal and a bed,
along with auspicious jars;
it should be adorned on all sides of the site with corner pillars.
One should have it surrounded by beautiful pillars and adorned with wheels and other ornaments as before;
it should be well-situated, with firm legs, and capable of withstanding the pressure of bathing.
Or, half of its length should be a sand pedestal, according to the initial sequence.
It should be increased by half a cubit and decreased by four finger-breadths;
having made it half as wide as its own length,
one should thus provide it with a spout and adorn that central sand-platform with it.
In the cardinal directions of the sacrificial hall, as well as in the intermediate spaces, for the purpose of the doors,
there should be an increase of half a *śama* in one place and a decrease of a *kalā* and so forth in the other.
One should construct archways outside with sturdy, well-consecrated timbers.

They increase by half a cubit up to five cubits; they do not undergo reduction except when there is a change in the ritual procedure. One should not cause them to enter the ground unless they are equal to five cubits.
And for those increased for the sake of peace, one should increase each by two units at every stage.
The distance between them should be one-third of the remainder left after subtracting the width from the length.
All the wheels and banners should be made together with cloth garlands and flower clusters.
Smeared with yellow pigments such as lime and with sandalwood paste and the like,
this entire broken-limbed [image] is joined together as one, just as a ritual act in a sacrificial hall is performed constantly without the use of ashes or fire. (18.27–18.28)
The field, measuring thirty-five [units], is expanded by one-fourth of itself;
in its center, one should establish seven platforms, each four cubits in size. One should indeed leave a space between these platforms equal to one tāla.
One should indeed make the courtyard area two cubits in width by reducing it by one unit at a time;
according to the measurement, it should be reduced successively by eight finger-breadths, then by two finger-breadths, and then by two finger-breadths again.
The interval between the platforms and the narrow passages is two *golaka*s.
In this very manner, the height of all [the elements] is proclaimed;
here, the measurement for the *vīthi* (pathway) surrounding them is derived from its own pedestal.
Or, in such a constriction, one may construct two pavilions as prescribed;
the central mandala-pedestal shall be to its southern side,
and nearby shall be the place for the bed and the installation of the ritual jars (kumbhas).
For in this way, there is the satiation of the mantras with enjoyments in the vicinity of the Dwarf;
the supreme [offering] consists of the oblation of the Vedas beginning with the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāma,
as well as the gift of the gaze and the place of rest, which is beneficial on another bed.
Then, for the guardians of the eight directions of the temple, as previously described,
one should perform the oblation either upon sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) or in fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), or else personally in one's own pit dedicated to that purpose,
within the supreme [mandala] consisting of the four Vedas.
Or he himself may perform the drinking from all the images;
O twice-born ones, this is appropriate due to the lack of ritual materials and the absence of qualified image-attendants.
Thus, having constructed a new pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice, O brahmins... (18.37–18.38)
Having adorned it with the various ornaments previously mentioned,
one should first place eight banners— distinguished by colors such as white, red, and so forth—
on the central altar; and then, once again, [arrange them] in that same manner as before.
Having gathered all the necessary materials for that purpose with a well-composed mind,
on the seventh or fifth day prior to the day of the ritual,
one should offer the sprouts and then commence the rite.
On the day before the principal day, the best of preceptors—
having bathed, wearing white garments and garlands, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and being of perfectly tranquil mind—
having completed his daily rites and adorned with all ornaments, prepares for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
Equipped with all the ritual implements and provided with the vessel for the *arghya* offering,
he should take up the auspicious jar while meditating on Acyuta within his heart,
accompanied by Brahmins who follow the single path and are devoted to the true scriptures. || 18.43–18.44 ||
Likewise, O Blessed One, [the rites are performed] beginning from the root with those consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth, which are permeated by the Lord,
together with the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, musical instruments, conchs, and the like;
while reciting the sacred scriptures, they are praised when preceded by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers and entered the sacrificial hall,
one should recall the pervasive presence [of the deity] on one's own seat, worship it,
and sit down facing east near the central pedestal at the western step.
One should place an auspicious vessel at the front upon the base; and having seated the Brahmins as before, beginning with those versed in the Ṛgveda,
the auspicious collection of ritual substances should be arranged with the previously mentioned materials plus additional ones.
And whatever is to be employed in a particular place, one should introduce that there.
A teacher of mantras who is well-disposed, highly intelligent, and skilled in ritual action should be appointed for all occasions. (18.49–18.50)
For the wise man, with a single-pointed and concentrated mind,
having himself investigated the substance for the acts of offering and worship,
remains focused on nothing else as he performs the rites beginning with their origin and ending with their formal dedication (nyāsa).

Having performed everything in sequence, beginning with the purification of the hands and ending with the placement (*nyāsa*) of the wheels (*cakra*) and so forth, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*). Then,
according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the worship of the water-jar (*kalaśa*) accompanied by fire-oblations (*sahoma*).
Then one should perform the installation of the archways and the banners.
One should worship the four [principles] beginning with Truth upon the eight banners on the central altar, according to their origin and dissolution, starting from the eastern direction.
Furthermore, the gods, being attentive, should then cause those composed of the *Ṛgveda* to recite [the texts].
(18.55) In the four directions beginning with the east, at the fourfold archways (*toraṇa*), one should worship, in sequence, Suśobhana, Subhadra, and Sugandha. (18.56)
O best of sages, one should worship the Sugotra-cakra, joined with the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), above each archway;
or alternatively, their worship may take place first together with those stationed at the doors.
Then, one who knows the Sāman chants should cause the *Sāma* to be recited at the gatekeeper’s station.
Thereafter, carrying the *arghya* and flowers, he should proceed surrounded by those bearing the [divine] forms,
to where Viśveśa resides together with the pedestal and the Brahma-stone.
There, one should perform the inspection of them, as well as the striking and other rites;

then, one should bathe them with bathing jars consecrated by the *cakrāstra* mantra. Likewise, one should bathe them with white mustard seeds, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), earth, and ashes mixed with water.
Then, having washed [the image] with ant-hill earth and water, and with the water of the *cakrāṅka* herb,
and having honored it and rubbed it [with unguents], one should wash it again with the water of the *astra*.
Having worshipped it with the *arghya* offering, one should then place those consecrated [flowers] in one's hand.
Having tied white mustard seeds on the right side, one should cause him to recite the verse at the outset.
Likewise, having fastened all the protective amulets (*pratisara*) and gems,
and having wrapped [the patient] everywhere, one should place him upon an excellent chariot.
While he recites the commencement of the ritual, he should place [the Brahmins] in the southern direction;
four each of those versed in the *Ṛgveda* and *Sāmaveda* in the north, and the Brahmins in front, while himself destroying obstacles according to the prescribed method of the weapon-mantra.
Accompanied by dancers, singers, instrumentalists, panegyrists, and readers of auspicious hymns,
and together with reciters of Vedic verses such as "idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame," at the conclusion of that [rite], they performed the "ekāyana" [chant] beginning with "oṃ namo brahmaṇe."
In the same manner, having recited the Śākuna Sūkta together with the Śrī Sūkta,
he should satisfy those who seek gold and other gifts according to his capacity and settle them there.
Then, having brought down the image from the chariot or other vehicle, he should proceed to the sacrificial ground.
Having seated him upon an archway made of solid wood in the bathing area,
one should then perform oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds with the Astra-mantra.
Alternatively, having first brought a pedestal accompanied by the Brahma-stone...
Having placed [the deity] upon a blessed seat situated on the ground at the altar,
one should then bring the image and install it upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
O twice-born one, a specific procedure is now described for when a large image is being installed.
As before, having established [the image] in the workshop for the sake of purifying its form,
and having bathed it according to the rite, one should then perform the opening of the eyes; thereafter,
one should carry out either the extensive consecration bath or simply a bath with abundant water.
Having performed the bathing ritual for the stone [image] and others, together with a brief act of worship,
they should raise it up with many attendants carrying water for the feet and so forth,
and then, with great care, bring it into the interior of the temple.
Having first arranged the jewels according to the prescribed manner and seated the large image upon the pedestal, one should then perform all the rites in the ritual image (karmabimba). Indeed,
the "complete restraint" (sannirodha) of the mantras is traditionally taught to occur there at the rising of the [auspicious] conjunction (lagnodaya).
O lords of sages, having understood that everything up until the completion of the full ablution must be concluded before the *bṛhat-snāna*,
you should act in such a way that the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) does not pass away. 18.76–77.
O best of sages, in this manner one should complete the rites beginning with the bath for other images that were previously painted, provided they are devoid of precious gems and Brahma-stones;
these rites— starting with the bath— should be performed upon the image itself, or otherwise upon a mirror placed near it.
In the case of others, one should perform the rites beginning with the induction of sleep (prasvāpa) upon the pedestal, excluding the ritual image (karmabimba),
starting with the entry and ending with the festival.
This applies when [the rite] is performed together with the Śaktis, the ritual images, Garuḍa, and the rest.
One should indeed perform the installation of the primary image together [with the others];
at that time, one should cause those images to enter the sacrificial ground.
Having thus caused that image to enter, one should place the jars for the purpose of bathing.
Alternatively, on the third day prior to the day of the ritual action,

the preceptor, having performed the worship of the water-jar along with the oblation according to the previously stated procedure, shall enter the ritual hall together with the guardians of the images.
When the afternoon hour has arrived, having bathed the image according to the ritual for the sake of purifying its form, and having subsequently consecrated the image in water; then,
when the following day has arrived, the preceptor, having performed his daily rites—
Having lifted that image from the water, one should cause it to enter the sacrificial ground.
O Lord of Sages, how should the ritual procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the water be performed?
"O best among speakers, tell me that procedure in detail.
Nārada replied:
"O bulls among sages, listen to the ritual for the preliminary consecration of the water."
For the sake of the purity of the temple and for the very purity of the image; for the pacification of any deficiency or excess in measurements, proportions, and dimensions;
and for the nourishment of the world and for the accomplishment of all things in their full perfection.
On an auspicious day, prior even to the commencement of the installation and ritual activities,

one should perform the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, as well as worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and the recitation (*japa*) of one's own mantra— provided that this has been done previously in such a manner. (18.89)
For some specific reason, one may dwell in water there.
(18.90) Whether in rivers, long ponds, lakes, mountain springs, or pools, if such places are available, one should practice dwelling in water according to the prescribed rule. (18.91)
In the absence [of water], one should do so in a wooden tub, a cauldron made of metal,
or, as the case may be, in another vessel such as one made of clay;
with a small amount of water at the edge of a cremation ground, submerged in salt water.
In that which is pungent, astringent, or bitter, and defiled by froth;
near a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), or near a low dwelling; mixed with other colors, small, saline, or covered with moss. || 18.93–18.94 ||
In the presence of such defects as these, one should not cause the image to dwell in water;
rather, one should have it dwell within the water for one, three, or five nights, or perform the water-dwelling immediately according to the requirements of place and time. (18.95)
On the third, fifth, or seventh day prior to the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
having entered the ritual hall (karmaśālā) during the afternoon,
one should then sprinkle the image with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and strike it.

Having bathed [the image] for the sake of purifying its form with long white mustard seeds and sesame seeds consecrated with the *astra* mantra— using the six substances beginning with white mustard seeds—
and having adorned it with ornaments such as garments, jewelry, and flowers; || 18.98 ||
Having tied the auspicious thread as before and having mounted [the image] upon a chariot or similar vehicle,
accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas as before, along with conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, and with various dances, songs, and other auspicious rites; || 18.99–18.100 ||
Having circumambulated the village, or the city, or even the palace, he should, together with the image-keepers, lead [the deity] to a body of water. Then,
having dismounted from the chariot or other vehicle at a water-shed near the water's edge, [he should proceed].
Then, having seated him upon a seat facing either east or north,
one should construct an auspicious pavilion in the middle of the water, capable of withstanding wind and rain,
provided with four pillars and adorned with four archways.
It was provided with canopies and banners, encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass,
and adorned with various fruits as well as purifying branches of trees;
it was further furnished with strings of pearls and decorated with wreaths of flowers.

Having first caused it to be prepared with a lamp placed in a corner and adorned with chowries, one should then have the proclamation of the "day of merit" (puṇyāha) made. Having performed the purification of the waters as before, one should then place [the vessel] in the center of that area.
One should prepare a throne (bhadrapīṭha) appropriate to the image, provided with a covering and a pillow;
above that, one should arrange the seat (āsana) according to the mantra.
Having visualized Ananta above, one should worship him with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, and so forth.
With the root mantra, one should offer the arghya and likewise the pādya for the image; then the ācāma, scented water, fragrance, the sacred thread and upper garment,
ornaments, garlands, a lamp, and incense, in due order.
Having offered [the oblation] and performed the anointment with clarified butter (ghṛtāropa), one should contemplate the process of withdrawal (saṃhṛtikrama).
O twice-born ones, listen as I describe the sequence of withdrawal:
having visualized oneself as the all-pervading, omniscient, and imperishable Viṣṇu.
The practitioner, endowed with meditative absorption, should perform that consecration (*adhivāsana*) of Viṣṇu.

Having established the life-force (*jīva*), which identifies with the image, by means of the *praṇava*, and having caused it to ascend and achieve oneness with himself—Hari, the Lord of All—he should [proceed]. (18.111–18.112)
Having purified the defiled earth and burned it with fire containing seeds,
having flooded it with water and dried it with wind, and having dissolved it in fire;
having withdrawn the fire by means of the wind, one should lead the wind to the state of space.
But having gradually withdrawn the internal and external organs, together with their objects,
which abide as mere subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the teacher dissolves space into the mind, and the mind into the ego (*ahaṃkṛti*). Then that [ego] again— || 18.114–115 ||
One should lead that [individual self] into oneness with the unmanifest within the Great Self—
that which is peaceful, infinite, the supreme ether, partless, and whose form is knowledge.
One should meditate upon Him who is established in supreme bliss and possesses a peaceful form.
In that state where the indeterminate is dissolved, which possesses its own essential nature—
that very state is to be known as Vāsudeva, the soul of all, the Lord who creates all.
Having withdrawn the earth and the other elements into that very [state], the Teacher—
Having meditated in this manner according to the rule, one should wrap the image in a cloth;
having covered it with divine silks, with all the *darbha* grasses, garlands, and so forth,
the preceptor, together with the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipa*), [should recite] the four pervasive mantras.
While others recite the Śākuna Sūkta and other Vedic hymns,
intent upon the proclamation of the sacred tradition (Āmnāya),
one should take that image from the bank and lay it upon a pedestal in the midst of the water.
With the mantra beginning with "ambhasya," having caused various kinds of drums to resound in the ten directions while facing north with his head toward the east,
and accompanied by shouts of victory, songs, and other music preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day—
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon oneself in due order, one should bind the directions with the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having looked about with the eye-mantra (netra), one should conceal [the site] with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Then, having meditated on the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside this place on all sides, [one should proceed].
Having reached the riverbank, he should place a water-pot wrapped with a cord,
encircled by two new cloths, provided with a lid, and adorned with sprouts;
and likewise, he should place a small vessel to its right.
One should place the jars all around, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna;
they should be provided with cloths, lids, gold, and *kūrca* grass-bundles.
One should place the *viśākha-yūpa* in the large jar (*kumbha*) and the *sudarśana* in the small vessel (*karaka*).
Having invoked and worshipped Indra and the other deities in the eight jars with water-offerings (arghya) and so forth,
one should place the primary jar and the ritual pitcher (karaka) at the region of the head of the image.
One should then arrange the eight worshipped jars in sequence around it.
In the corners, one should place small lamps that are not extinguished.
One should display the wheel mudrā as well as the protection mudrā.
Thereafter, one should indeed perform the worldly rite in that water.

For images made of wood, metal, or stone, the consecration by water is performed directly; for others, it would be the consecration by means of their shadow. O best of sages, I shall describe that procedure there exactly as it is.
One should perform the bath for the sake of purifying the form upon a mirror; O Brahmins, all other rites should be performed as before upon the image,
in front of the deity’s image, for the purpose of consecrating the shadow.
One should place a water trough or a cauldron made of iron,
or even a vessel made of clay or wood, for the collection of grain;
one should fill it with fragrant water that has the luster of pure crystal.
Having prepared a seat as before with auspicious darbha grass,
O best of the twice-born, the preeminent teacher fashioned a kūrca from twenty-eight blades of darbha and,
according to the prescribed rite, invoked the Teacher of the World there.
Having worshipped with *arghya*, perfumes, and other offerings, and having indeed recalled the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*),
one should lay the seat (*viṣṭara*) within the water with its head facing east.
Then, having displayed the *cakra*-mudrā, one should install the *kumbha* and the other vessels as before.
O best of Brahmins, for the Śaktis as well, there should be a seat as before.

Alternatively, one should fashion a *kūrca* according to the rules using three blades of *darbha* grass; for them too, there should be a separate ritual of shadow-consecration (*chāyādhivāsa*) for each individually.
Having covered the entire body of the image on all sides with a new cloth,
one should scatter white mustard seeds upon the ground all around while reciting the mantra "rakṣohaṇā" (O slayers of demons). One should thus provide protection on every side.
Whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform all of it as previously described.
Regarding an image made of clay or situated on a wall, the preeminent teacher, having entered the temple, should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the shadow. 18.141–18.142.
For others, having constructed a pavilion or a hut for the sacrificial hall as before,
the Guru should perform the preliminary consecration of the image in the shade;
this applies when there is the means to provide images made of wood, metal, or stone.
One should perform the consecration of the water in a vessel such as a wooden trough;
at that time, one should also perform the consecration of the water within a pavilion,
or one may perform it in the pavilion prepared for the purpose of the ritual bath.

Alternatively, that may take place at the sacrificial site or on the bathing ground. Having thus performed the preliminary consecration of the water (jalādhivāsana), the most excellent of preceptors should employ whatever materials have been acquired for the installation ceremony.
Having gathered all of that together, one should cleanse the palace and other structures. One should also have the ritual circumambulation with fire performed by a Brāhmaṇa;
having purified the temple with sweepings and smearing it with cow-dung, one should then proceed.
Having adorned it on all sides with lime powder, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings,
one should then sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and place lamps everywhere.
Having decorated it with canopies and the like, one should fumigate it with fragrant substances.
Those who are nihilists, those who have broken the bounds of propriety, those who revile the gods and Brahmins, others joined with sinful practices, as well as the censurable, the treacherous,
heretics, those of base conduct, those born in the inverse order, and those full of envy— [these he should avoid].
He should then expel from there those who are greedy, foolish, or ignorant.
On the day of the ritual, during the afternoon, the Guru himself,
having reached the site for the ritual immersion in water along with the image-keepers (mūrtipāḥ), [should proceed].
Having lifted the image from the water, along with the mouth-vessel and the jars,
and having dismissed the deities residing therein, one should then place that image upon a seat on the bank facing east and wash it with waters.
O lords of sages, if iron objects are purified with water infused with *tintriṇī* fruit, having first performed the sequence of creation according to the prescribed rule,
one should adorn them with beautiful garments, ornaments, flowers, and other such items. (18.155)
Having placed that image upon a vehicle, accompanied by conch shells, drums, and other instruments,
one should circumambulate the village or lead it back to the temple; then,
having removed it from the vehicle and so forth, one should install it in the sacrificial hall.
In the previously mentioned place, the Guru should afterwards begin the ritual bathing;
having first entered the temple with the image-keepers (mūrtipāḥ),
he should then lift the cushion (kūrca) that was previously consecrated from the water.
Then, one should remove the garments, ornaments, and garlands from the image.
O twice-born ones, one should then place upon the pedestal— which has been prepared for the setting of the bathing jars— the previously mentioned elaborate (sthūla) supreme ablution.
Wherever a separate bathing pavilion has been established, extending from the east to the western limit,
one should place the station of the Yātudhāna to the left of the God of Gods,
starting from the southeast corner.
The bathing known as *sthūlaparā* is gross, while that which follows is both gross and subtle.

Beginning from the northeast corner (*īśakoṇa*) and extending as far as the southeast region (*āgneyagocara*), [the rite is performed] on the right side of the deity, starting from the northeast and ending in the west of the northwest (*vāyu*).
One should establish the bath called *sthūlasthūla* according to the sequence of the ritual;
on the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), one should perform the bath called *sthūlapara*;
and on the day of the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), one should perform the bath that is both *sthūla* and *sūkṣma*.
On the fourth day, there shall be a bath known as Sthūlasthūla.
Then, on each respective day, the Guru should install the corresponding ablution-vessels.
Thus, having installed the bath-pitchers in sequence as before, [he should proceed].
Then, at the conclusion of that offering, one should prepare two types of beds;
first, one should prepare a bed for the purpose of opening the eyes.
Thereafter, one should consecrate the pedestal with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having spread out abundant darbha grass with its tips pointing either eastward or northward,
one should then place upon it a circular or square woolen cloth, weighing five bhāras or half that measure, covered with fine śāli rice.
One should arrange variegated pillows as parts of the bed,
having placed auspicious jars situated in the eight directions.
Then, for the purpose of consecrating the image, one should prepare a bed;
for that purpose, one should draw a svastika maṇḍala upon the altar with powders or with flowers of four brilliant colors.
Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward across that [surface],
one should thereafter scatter rice there in the measure of five bhāras;
half of that [measure] should be pure rice, and likewise half of that should be sesame seeds.
Having placed [the items] one above the other, one should then arrange parched grains (lāja) on top;
[and place] a very firm, smooth wooden [seat] provided with four limbs,
equipped with four legs, square and elongated, and well-spread out.
Then, one should place a couch known as a *khaṭvā* above that; upon it,
one should spread a soft mattress made of fine silk, together with its necessary furnishings.
O twice-born ones, one may then place merely the mattress, or else,
having removed the cotton from the bedstead, one should place a jeweled blanket over the parched grain;
thereafter, one should place a fresh garment made of new cotton.
One should place a linen cloth in the center, and upon that, a multicolored cloth,
provided with a pillow for the head and footrests;
all [the items] should be fresh, bright, and equipped with pillows for the cheeks.
Garments perfumed with fragrant incense and imbued with the scent of flowers;
water-pots filled with water, equal in size, smooth, provided with lids and cloths, and wrapped with threads, extending from Indra to Īśāna. || 18.179–180 ||
One should place [the vessels] adorned with jewel-sprouts upon heaps of grain;
and [one should place them] with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, along with banners, in the directions of Indra and the others, in due order.
One should place a golden Śrīvatsa, Garuḍa, and a tortoise upon them;
and between each pair of jars, one should set auspicious objects atop the grain.
[These include] a conch, a discus, as well as Lakṣmī, a jar, and the Śrīvatsa itself.
A mirror, a svastika, and a pair of fish—these indeed constitute the eight auspicious symbols (maṅgalāṣṭaka).
Likewise, one should place the pitchers (pālikā) covered with cloths in the corners. Having thus prepared the pair of beds, one should worship beneath them.
One should worship the support of all, which is infinite, and above that, the all-pervading Lord,
through the yoga of origin and dissolution, according to the sequence beginning with the east.
One should cause [the disciple] to recite the Sarpasāman and so forth, which consist of the nature of the power of knowledge and its designations.
Having offered oblations one hundred and eight times, one should then prepare the root-mantra;
[one should draw] a mandala with purifying colors such as white and other auspicious hues.
Then, for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess therein, one should offer oblations into the collection of fire-pits (kuṇḍas).
One should consecrate [the vessel] situated within the *kumbha* near each individual *kuṇḍa*;
one should then perform the sacrifice to the fourfold self (*cāturātmya*) through the union of origin and dissolution.
Alternatively, [one may worship] the [deities] beginning with the Heart in those located at the cardinal directions, and the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) in those located at the intermediate directions.
Having given that for its purpose, one should recite the *Pūrṇā* [mantra] and then teach the *Pūrṇāt-pūrṇa*;
then the *Ekāyana* texts consisting of the *Yajus*, followed immediately by the *Āśrāvita*.
Having thus completed everything, one should proceed to the presence of the *Bimba*.
Having worshipped the image with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites, the Guru should begin the ritual bathing;
first, however, with the water from the auspicious jar using the Astra-mantra.
Having sprinkled the image, one should then bathe it with water mixed with that clay.
Immediately thereafter, one should cause the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras to be recited there, following the *Bala* mantra.
Then, with a jar of cow-dung, one should cause the *Gāvaḥ* [mantras] to be recited here.
While the mantra "bhūtis tvam" is being recited by Vibhūti,
he should thereafter cause [the disciple] to recite the *pañcagavya* and then the *śākvara*.
Then, having worshipped as before according to the rules with water from the *camasa* vessels...
Having washed it with pure water and then consecrated it, one should worship it;
this is declared to be the bath for the purpose of destroying defects caused by the artisan.
Then, O Brahmins, having put on two garments, an upper and a lower one...
O twice-born ones, the image should be laid to rest upon that bed which has been prepared for the purpose of opening its eyes, with its head facing the east;
thereafter, one should cover the image on all sides with blankets and other such materials.
Having placed a golden and a silver vessel,
each filled with an āḍhaka of grain, at the front of the heap of grain, one should fill them in due order with honey and ghee; thereafter, [one should prepare] a vessel for the honey-mixture.
Situated in the center of a solar orb, resembling ten thousand suns.
Having meditated upon and worshipped the Lord of Mantras, O lords of sages,
[one should worship] another [form] situated in the center of the lunar disc, endowed with the *dhenu-mudrā*,
possessing the *saurabhīya* mantra, and shining with the luster of a hundred shimmering moons. (18.200)
One should meditate on the Lord of Mantras situated within that, resembling the Himālaya mountain.
One should meditate on the image as well-consecrated by the floods of nectar flowing from it— nectar born of the moon, born of the *dhenu* [cow], and [born of] the mantra "madhuvāta" (RV 1.90.6).
One should consecrate the ghee and other substances with mantras and then cover them with a cloth.
O best of the twice-born, there should be a golden or silver rod eight finger-breadths long,
or it may be a golden rod alone.

One should place the eight grains all around in the vessels. Then, the worshipper, joined with meditation and with a focused mind, should correctly recite the supreme mantra "Yātavya" to the Brahmins who are single-mindedly devoted.
I shall invoke the Lord of Lakṣmī, the cause of the universe, who is immeasurable, whose pair of feet is bowed to by the hosts of other gods.
The primordial, eternal thread, seated upon the throne of the Praṇava, possessing the brilliance of a thousand full moons, suns, and fires;

He is the supreme object of meditation for those who know all principles, and the one to be known; his form is gentle like that of the Boar, Kapila, and the Man-lion; his limbs are adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha jewel, and great gems;
and his hands hold the mace, the conch, the lotus, and the discus.
O Blessed One, although you are indeed all-pervading, I nevertheless invoke you just as one summons the wind with a fan;
for just as fire, though hidden, emerges through friction, so too do you approach the image when invoked.
O Wearer of the Garland, O Acyuta, O All-pervading Lord, O Embodiment of the Ultimate Truth, O Omniscient One, O Protector, O Supreme Sovereign, O All-powerful One!
Come to me, show me compassion, accept this image, and receive my worship today out of a desire to bestow grace upon me.

Then, having wiped [the image] with a cloth, one should worship it with the previously mentioned offerings, beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thereafter, one should cause those who recite the *Ṛgveda* to chant the mantra "arcāmi te," and those who sing the *Sāmaveda* to chant "arcitas tv asi."
Then, with the mantra "Oṃ Bhagavān," he should satisfy those wise ones in the fire. Thereafter, the preeminent teacher should offer seven fuel-sticks into his own sacrificial pit,
followed by one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds and rice mixed with clarified butter.
Having performed the libation until completion, one should then extract a spark from the fire and cast it into the directional pits that were previously consecrated;
likewise, having extracted [the fire] from those situated in the intermediate directions, one should worship them in due order.
Then, by means of the yoga of emanation, one should establish in the four directions four twice-born men of the Ekāyana tradition, known by the names Vāsudeva and the others; and with them,
each according to their own [mantra], an incalculable number [of others] should be employed through those [mantras] beginning with Abhidhā.
With seven previous offerings of fuel-sticks, along with sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with clarified butter,
and likewise by means of this sequence of dissolution, one should consecrate the four Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda and place them starting from the northwest (Vāyu) up to the northeast (Īśāna).
With those [mantras] possessing the marks of Acyuta, as well as the purifying ones prescribed in one's own Vedic branch,
the oblation (havana) should be performed according to the rules with a mind endowed with devotion.
Having thus offered oblations into all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in this sequence, the preceptor (guru) then—

O lords of sages, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the rules in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for the previously mentioned guardians of the directions, such as those stationed at the gates,
in the northeastern quarter of the temple that was prepared for that purpose.
Having offered praise with the *jitantam* mantra, he should again cause the chanters to recite it.
Having muttered the twelve-syllable mantra together with the *gāyatra* and the *rathantara* sāman, and having formed the mudrā and prostrated, [he should proceed].
Then, by means of this very form with its distinct manifestations, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, should be informed through the eightfold path; indeed,
he should now gladden the citizens of the city, whose true nature remains unknown.
By entering within [the heart], even for a short time,
they indeed attain liberation from the sins arising from thousands of other births;
for such is the Blessed One, the Lord who acts for the benefit of the worlds.
Having offered the arghya, perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and food offerings,
and having presented the water for sipping and the arghya once more,
one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) accompanied by the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory," as well as the sound of the Vedas.
With the sounding of conch shells, drums, and paṭahas, along with songs,
the preceptor, having placed his hands upon the feet of the God of gods, should then cause him to recite the mantra consisting of the Ṛgveda, beginning with "Arise. || 18.251-18.252 ||
Having performed the ritual with the implements for the journey, once the Brahma-chariot is firmly established,
well-secured, and provided with milk, ghee, curd, and rice,
as well as excellent food and fruits, for the sake of abundance, security, and peace; (18.253)
Immediately thereafter, one should cause him to recite the *Asyavāmīya*, which consists of verses;
then, O lords of sages, the *balamantra* consisting of five [verses].
One should personally mutter the *kavaca*, which is enclosed at its beginning and end by the *hṛdaya*.
One should cause the offering of the sacrificial oblation (bali) to be whirled in all directions;
as before, one should perform the scattering of jewels, gold, and diamonds.
And worship should be performed as is appropriate for the divine sense-bases (āyatana) and others,
as well as for those who know the Pañcarātra, for ascetics (yati), and for celibate students (brahmacārin).
One should also give gifts to those devoted to the six duties and even to the wretched.
As long as one proceeds for a hundred steps while the mantra-image is situated upon the chariot, the worshipper—
steadfast in his vows and possessed of his desires— obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices through that chariot accompanied by the sound of musical instruments. || 18.258-18.259 ||
Then, having positioned the chariot at the gateway, one should worship the Lord with water for the feet,
the arghya offering, flowers, and incense; and having prostrated,
one should recite the entire twelve-syllable mantra, "uttiṣṭha," together with the *jita* syllable.

Reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, he should cause [the image] to enter the sacrificial hall. With the heart-mantra, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should lay the image upon the bed with its head toward the east, and then complete the *yātrā-homa* sacrifice.

Then, at the location of that head, one should worship [the deity] encased within the Netra-mantra in a jar placed upon the wheel-base (cakrādhāra), possessing the characteristics previously described.
One should worship the eight auspicious objects (maṅgalāni) starting from the east with their respective names.

When those eight jars have already been placed there, Vāsudeva and the others are to be worshipped according to their connection with the origin and dissolution [of the elements]; or else, Hṛdaya and the rest are worshipped in the jars situated in the cardinal directions, while the Weapon-mantra is worshipped in those situated in the intermediate directions.
Alternatively, Vārāha is in the east, Nārasiṃha in the south,
the god Śrīdhara in the west, and Hayavaktra likewise in the north; Bhārgava Rāma is in the southeast, and Rāma is also in the southwest.
Then, having worshipped Vāmana in the northwest and Viṣṇu in the domain of Īśāna by their respective names with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), perfumes, and other articles,
one should thereafter worship the Lord as he rests upon his bed with *arghya*, perfumes, and the like.

Having given a protective cloth (varmaṇā) that has been fumigated with incense, one should then perform the rite of nourishment (āpyāyana) for the one situated on the bed by means of the root mantra (mūla). Then,
the preceptor (deśika), seated in a place near the feet of the deity, [should proceed].

O best of the twice-born, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the deity’s form according to the mantra, whether it be on a painting or other such [support], or on a mantra-image situated in a temple; and having likewise prepared a festive rite for the action-image (karmabimba) or upon a seat (viṣṭara).
Having put [the deity] to sleep on the bed as before, and having entered the temple,
one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and other rites according to the procedure that will be described.
O best of sages, listen to that extensive procedure.
Having offered a handful of flowers along with sandalwood paste and unbroken rice-grains upon the pedestal,
one should place the eight-syllable mantra as before, from the top down to the feet.
One should then place the six mantras, beginning with the heart-mantra, in their respective locations starting from the heart.
One should place the crown on the region of the head, and the Śrīvatsa below the throat;
immediately after that, one should place it on the left side of the chest.
Then, having placed the Kaustubha on the heart and the forest garland (vanamālā) around the neck—
In the god’s right hand is the discus and in the left the conch;
or else, the mace and sword are in the left hand, while the discus and other emblems are in the right and left hands respectively,
according to the sequence of the emblem-mantras.
One should place Śrī on the right side and Puṣṭi on the left; then,
one should place Vainateya at the base of the thighs— now, listen further.
Regarding the placement of the discus and other attributes of the four-armed deity:
one should place the lotus in the primary right hand and the mace in the left hand;
the discus in the other right hand and the conch in the other left hand.
Furthermore, one should install other insignia-mantras according to their appropriate application.

In the other [deities], such as the six-armed one and others, one should place all the insignia-mantras (lāñchanamantra) in their respective positions, starting from the primary right hand and proceeding in order.
O Blessed One, the image to be installed bears the marks such as the discus;
one should likewise place those marks upon the hands in their proper sequence.
One should also install the mantras, beginning with the *kirīṭa*, everywhere as before.
Then, within the twelve limbs beginning with the feet, one should meditate upon Dāmodara and the others,
as well as their respective powers and mantras, characterized by pervasiveness,
using the Īśvara seed-syllable according to its specific state.
By means of that same excellent mantra consisting of the feet and so forth,
according to the previous method of dissolution, [the practitioner] becomes one with that very supreme state— the pervasive Lord whose nature is speech and who consists of inner light.
Having realized that which is perfectly peaceful, all-pervading, and like an ocean without waves;

he should then teach the Pāñcarātrikas the *Vidyā* beginning with "Gadā," and immediately thereafter the mantra known as *Dhāraṇā*, which pertains to the placement of the body (*dehasānyāsika*). || 18.286–18.287 ||

"O lords of sages, having offered sesame seeds and clarified butter with these mantras in this sequence, according to the number of one hundred items, beginning with the *jīmūta* [hymn] from the Ṛgveda and then reciting 'Non-being was not' (*nāsadāsīt*). (18.288)
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* as before, characterized by the ritual withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*),
one should then remember that supreme Brahman as previously described,
by means of one's own nature which consists of all powers.
Just as vitality exists in the form of strength, as fragrance exists in the form of a substance,
as a seed exists in the form of a tree, and as the ocean exists in the form of bubbles;
even so, that power which is indefinable resides within its own mirror of power.
O lords of sages, having taken hold of Viśveśa who abides [therein] by virtue of his own sovereignty,
he assumes a body in the form of mantra for the sake of perfect propitiation;
and he himself [experiences] the expansion of that [mantra] which has attained manifoldness.
And when the seed of consciousness (*cid-bīja*), having reached a state of lusterlessness and its own restrictive rule (*niyama*) has been manifested as distinct by a powerful, formless [agent],
it is indeed by the dense thicket of ignorance— which is itself eternal, non-eternal, and pure in nature— that this occurs. (18.294)
Having thus recollected the root mantra, one should visualize it as residing within the heart-lotus of the [deity's] image.
One should meditate upon that body composed of those very substances, endowed with the six powers and instruments,
as it withdraws [the universe] by the very path previously described;
then one should again meditate upon that stainless essential nature through the form of the image.
When that Supreme Lord, having attained sovereignty through the nature of mantra according to the aforementioned rule, leads [the disciple] in this manner,
then one should cause him to recite all [the scriptures], beginning with "The God of a Thousand Heads."
One should cause the Brahmins to recite the mantra beginning with "dhātary adha kṣe," as well as "yo 'viśvataś cakṣuḥ" and "dhyātavyo bhavati.
Following that, one should recite "dvā suparṇā" and then "ato devā."
"The Puruṣa-sūkta consists of Ṛg-verses; beyond that [is] 'tataḥ paratamāni'";
"from the eternal [comes] time (kāla), so one should declare";
"this is the sevenfold intellect"—thus one should recite here now. (18.300–301)

Then, O twice-born ones, having worshipped the Lord of Mantras upon his couch according to the ritual procedure for the image— with various tactile offerings such as seats and other services, with heart-pleasing items, and with the "honey-mixture" (madhuparka) and so forth, even if they lack consciousness— 302.18.302.
With supreme foods such as *paramānna*, as well as with pure and purifying offerings,
and with various other enjoyments in their proper sequence,
one should perform everything up to the final gift, and afterwards [worship] in the mandala.
Having brought [the materials] together and worshipped them with great magnificence,
one should satisfy the deity along with his limbs (sāṅga) in the fire, preceded by seven pieces of fuel-wood.
The guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should also offer oblations in their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in due order.

In the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) located in the directions starting from the east, the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) are prescribed in sequence [from the Palāśa tree]. In the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, there should be those originating from the Khadira, Bilva, Udumbara, Pippala,
and Plakṣa trees.
Those originating from the *nyagrodha* tree and likewise those originating from the *kaśmarya* tree,

as well as *palāśa* fuel-sticks, are prescribed for use in other extensive ritual preparations. However, in the absence of all those mentioned, *palāśa* fuel-sticks are considered appropriate in every case.
Four milch-cows should be stationed in the south, facing north:
Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Godāvarī, and Yamunā in embodied form.
With their milk, one should perform the cooking of the sacrificial porridges (caru) as well as the oblations (āhuti).
One should first cook one āḍhaka of śāli rice with milk;
then, in the southern fire, one should cook kṛsara mixed with jaggery;
in the northern fire, turmeric-rice; and in the other fires, pure rice.
There should be one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] with fuel-sticks and other materials;
or half of that, or even a quarter, according to the requirements of place and time.
With sesame, rice, barley, bamboo, and oblation-seeds, they should be offered in sequence.
One should prepare [the offerings] with sesame seeds in the other *kuṇḍas*, or with those [seeds] everywhere.
Having drawn up water from the jars representing one's own forms (*svamūrti*) by means of the mantra into a vessel,
it should be offered in succession upon the head of the image by all [the officiants], beginning with the Ekāyana and the others.
Immediately thereafter, with a *kūrca* made of four blades of *darbha* grass,
the image-protectors (*mūrtipās*) should properly sprinkle [the deity] with water from the pitchers placed upon the altar, using branches of *palāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, and *bilva*.
The preceptor, having gratified the mantras situated in the corner regions with a branch of the *vetasa* reed,
and then [having gratified] the mantra together with its retinue by means of abundant clarified butter and other substances, should thereafter offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Even for the sake of sustaining the earth and other elements— which have proceeded in the form of reflected images (*bimba*) as the constituent parts (*aṅga*)—
and for the sake of the physical body (*piṇḍa*),
there is indeed the pacification of the apertures (*chidra*) that arise from the very beginning of their undertaking. (18.318–319)
For the purpose of nourishing the mantras, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with ritual substances;
[using] twelve oblations for each of the four *hṛdaya* mantras.
Having first touched the clarified butter from the base of the feet up to the knees, one should offer it into the fire.
One should likewise offer curd from the navel down to the region of the knees;
milk from the navel up to the throat; honey from the throat up to the head;
and one should offer all mixed together, having touched the entire body.
Having first offered [the oblation] with ghee,
and thereafter having consecrated the pedestal (pīṭha) and the Brahman-stone (brahmaśilā)— which may be separate— as if they were the [central] image,
one should then install the deity who presides over the vital breaths (prāṇābhimānadeva), whichever one has been prescribed for that [deity].
Then, having enveloped it with variegated cloths, the oblation for the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) should be performed with the Cakra-mantra one hundred and eight times;
and half that number [of oblations] should be offered separately by the Bahvṛcas and others using the Gāyatrī mantras.
Then, by means of the *ekāyana* mantras beginning with "In the navel of the Unborn" (ajasya nābhau),

one should establish the seat (*pīṭha*) as the locus of the deities— conceived through the intellect— as consisting of the path and so forth, whether as a formal image or as a separate object of enjoyment. || 18.326 ||
One should offer oblations with the *praṇava* alone, and then with the *vyāhṛtis* oneself;
thereafter, one should cause the offering to be made with other mantras ending in the *praṇava*.
Then, indeed, one should likewise perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the *havana-mantra*.

One should perform the rite of confinement (saṃrodha) for those who have been gratified with their own names, with the *praṇava*, and with others ending in *svāhā*; indeed, it should be performed up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
accompanied by water, a seat, devotion, and recitation.

Of the Lord who is the sovereign of all, within his own embodied forms consisting of sound, and likewise of that which consists of the Vedas; having thus performed [the rites] and then stationed the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) in the various directions.
Then, by the side of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should offer libations with milk-rice (pāyasa);
thereafter, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of gold and other items according to one's ability.
Having received the sacrificial fee, the mantras should then be propitiated by them.
Then, having praised the Lord while He was sleeping, having veiled Him,

having worshipped Him, and having fixed Him in the mind, one should cause all the Brahmins to enter there— both those who follow the Ekāyana Veda as well as those who study the Ṛgveda and other branches.
One should cause them to recite the mantras prescribed in their respective Vedic branches according to their devotion,
as well as those who recite hymns of praise and are devoted to dance and song;
one should also introduce lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments.
During the recitation of the *praṇava*, one should station the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipas*) in the intermediate directions.
O Brahmins, during the twelve-syllable mantra, one should employ the guardians of the forms stationed in the cardinal directions.
Then, having performed the protection-gesture (*rakṣāmudrā*), one should display it in all directions.

Then, O twice-born ones, the sacrificer, having fasted, should be made to lie upon a bed of *darbha* grass on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with his head toward the east, for the sake of attaining success in his dreams. Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), he should spend the night in a vigil.
When the night has turned to dawn, having performed the rites such as bathing and so forth,
the preceptor, most learned in the scriptures, should then commence the consecration.
He should ask the awakened patron about his dream, whether it was auspicious or inauspicious.
There, O twice-born ones, for the sake of pacifying inauspiciousness, the Guru should then perform oblations— either one hundred, one thousand, or eight hundred, according to his ability—
with sesame seeds mixed with honey, clarified butter, and milk, along with fruits.

With the name itself enclosed by *asra* (the weapon-syllable) and joined with *svāhā*, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homayet*) using the mantra of the Lion (*siṃhamantra*), consisting of the phrase "Destroy the fault! Destroy! (*doṣaṃ jahi jahi*), ending with the name. Or else, one may do so with that sentence alone.
Having thus performed the pacification of bad dreams, one should carry out the ritual installation (*sthāpana*).
One should cleanse the temple both inside and out with branches of *darbha* grass.
Having scattered flowers along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should again fumigate it with *guggulu*.
Then, O brahmins, the preceptor, accompanied by artisans bearing his own image and holding arghya, flowers, and unbroken rice grains in their hands, should proceed to the edge of the temple. There,
he should strike away the obstacles situated there with white mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra.
First, one should dig a pit in the middle according to this rule,

or else one should divide the womb-chamber (garbhagṛha) for that purpose by means of the laying of the lines (sūtrapāta). In a temple with a single door, the measurement of the womb-chamber is determined.

One should properly divide the area extending from the door to the western wall into seven parts, running north to south; the first is known as the Paiśāca portion, the second is the Mānuṣa portion, and the third is designated as Daiva. || 18.348–18.349 ||

The Brāhma [form] is to be known as the fourth; likewise, the other three—the Daiva, Mānuṣa, and Paiśāca—are to be known in their respective order, O best of the twice-born. In a palace with four doors, one should proceed toward the four directions with equal steps.

One should divide [the area] into seven parts; the middle portion shall be designated as Brāhma. The divine, human, and piśāca [deities] are situated respectively in order within the three abodes at the four gates, in the central position known as Brāhma.
O twice-born ones, for a temple with a single door, one should install the deity of the fourfold self while looking toward the four directions;
this may be done according to the portions assigned to Brahmā and the gods, or between the divine and the human.

Whether it be in the Brāhma, the Daivika, or that which is based on the Divine (divya), [the results differ] indeed by virtue of the distinction of fruits according to that which is based on the Human (mānuṣa) and the Divine. In the Brāhma portion, there is liberation; the Divine brings about the increase of one's station.
The attainment of the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation occurs when one relies on the divine within the Brahmanical [system];
the attainment of the fruits of divine portions occurs when one relies on the divine within the human [system].
And from the divine-human portion, there arises fruit pertaining to both this world and the next.
And from the portion belonging to Vibudha-Brahmā, there is the eightfold quality of Saiṃhika.
Then, at the front part of the image, upon two portions, an altar (vedi) should be constructed;
for the purpose of worship, O Brahmins, stones should be installed there.
Or else, O twice-born ones, one should always worship the Lord upon a pedestal;
having placed a gemstone in the center of the pedestal, one should install Him thereon,
together with the Goddess, where the installation takes place.
Having left a space for the pedestal on either side of the principal image,
one should perform the installation of the goddesses together with their pedestals;
one may be installed on the left or the right, or two may be installed on both the right and the left.
However, the four [deities] should be established in due order on the right and left;

an excellent guide who desires the welfare of the king, the kingdom, and others must not, whether through negligence or intentionally, cause a displacement of them from their respective positions. (18.362)
If, due to the influence of a divergent view, [the ritual] should again be performed in the middle,
one should wash [the site] with the water of the weapon-mantra and smear it with sandalwood and other substances while reciting the heart-mantra.
This is the method for obstructing the chasms and for the suppression of the mantras held within the jars.

Having performed the worship as prescribed, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*, according to the previously stated procedure and with focused mind upon each respective vehicle, one should deposit [the offerings] there,
measuring approximately six, five, or four *golakas* in quantity.

One should cause [the officiant] to recite: "The stone that emerged slightly from the pedestal for the sake of prosperity, which was firmly established, and which was previously fashioned with nine apertures by the Pīṭha for the sake of liberation—may it be consecrated there as well with its own mantra. (18.366–367)
Then, one should place five items each, starting from the east in order of their origin,
upon the stone-pits for the materials; therein [should be] diamond and gold,
as well as yellow orpiment and uśīra root, while rice grains are placed in the south.
Sapphire, green vitriol, sandalwood, and sesame; pearl, silver, mercury, and likewise the rest; saffron, ushira root, and mung beans, and then the ruby in the north. (18.369–18.370)

One should place bell-metal, a royal stone, and a king-cowrie together with chickpeas—twenty in total—in the center; first [these], and then outside them. Likewise, by means of this same arrangement, one should place the other items separately in the intermediate directions.
Likewise, in the east is lapis lazuli, as well as the *cakrāṅka* and *abhraka* stones;
in the northeast and the direction of the wind (the northwest) are the *ṣāṣṭika* stone, the *puṣyarāga*, and *harītikā*;
in that same place are *gairika*, *śārikā*, and *masūra* stones; now let one go toward the [next] direction.
Mahānīla, vaṅga, and likewise ākṣika stone;
barley and sāgaruka in the southeast, as well as crystal;
copper, realgar, wheat, and śaṅkhapuṣpikā.

Then, having covered all those things in the middle and that entire group of pits with plaster, one should worship the mantras along with their limbs at every step and cause the Yajurvedic sections and the *camasatka* formulas to be recited.
Above that, O Mahāmati, one should place the pedestal, having set it into its cavity; and above that, a wheel made of the eight metals,
which has its own specific support arising from the twelvefold distinction.
Beyond the winter [layer], one should place either a lotus made of that [same material] or copper;
for these five, situated in their proper order within the fourfold self,
one should install Ananta at the center of the wheel, while Mīna and Kūrma belong to that [wheel].
For the Fish [incarnation], however, Kūrma and Ananta [are placed]; for that one (the Tortoise), Mīna and Ananta;
for every [other incarnation], the lotus is prescribed, and for that [lotus], one should install Ananta.
And for the powers such as Lakṣmī and the others, in the rite of installing the wheel, [Ananta is likewise installed].
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) up to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),

one should likewise perform the rites and the libation (tarpaṇa) here in the pavilion of the Lord of Birds (Khageśa). Together with the image-bearer (mūrtidhara), the rite of darbha-water should be performed as before.
One should encircle the temple of the deity with a cord four times its length;
one should likewise cover it with a new cloth and a garland of *darbha* grass.
Then, together with the presiding priests (*mūrtipas*), one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.

One should wait for the auspicious moment (lagna), and as long as it does not arrive, one should pass the time with diversions, fire-offerings (homa), laughter, and recitations. O Brahmins, when the rising of the auspicious moment has arrived, one should awaken the one lying upon the bed.
Having worshipped him with water for the guest-offering, fragrant unguents, garlands, and so forth, one should recite this:
"O you whose nature is mantra, withdraw your own fiery form;
O Supreme Lord, assume gentleness for the sake of stability."
Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; arise, O Supreme Lord! For the sake of showing me grace, take your seat upon this pedestal. Then, having awakened the mantra-form with his heart, he cast off sleep.
Having forcibly raised [the image] together with the bearers of the form by means of the Mūrti-mantra,
he likewise [raises] the jar situated upon the base of the wheel at the location of its head,
as well as the jars situated in its eight directions along with their auspicious [accoutrements].
Having raised [the image] with the attendants of the form (mūrtipāda), the preceptor (deśika) should go in front,
leading the way while scattering many various jewels,
as well as many kinds of flowers mixed with parched grain (lāja) and other offerings. || 18.390–18.391 ||
Others immediately following were bearers of the image, who carried the physical form so that no others might pass between the preceptor and the statue;
others carried eight water-pots, and there were those who recited auspicious verses.
They too should go along reciting the *Śākuna* [treatise].
The sacrificer, however, should remain silent, holding *kuśa* grass in his hand and bowing;
behind them, other attendants should indeed follow.
Having emerged through the archway, one should perform four circumambulations of the pedestal of the temple, blocking the entrance at the front of the door. Then,
having offered water for the feet, the guest-offering, and water for sipping, one should cause [the deity] to enter with the heart-mantra.
Then, one who is learned in that [Veda] should teach him while avoiding contact with the branches [of the Veda] and so forth.
Thereafter, [one should recite] "The four-wheeled" and "The eleven cities.
Then, with a white silk garment consecrated by armor-mantras, || 18.396–18.397 ||
First, one should encircle the stalk of the lotus feet with the *śikhā-mantra*.
Having balanced Agni and Soma by means of the *praṇava* at the beginning and end,
one should firmly establish the image upon the pedestal using the *mūla-mantra*.
In the rite of installing a deity, the middle of the doorway must not be abandoned.
One should not place [the deity] in front of that, nor on the side, nor behind;
the best of teachers should subsequently abandon the northwest wind [direction] from the name.
One should recite the two mantras, *pratiṣṭhā* and *liṅga*, in sequence,
while firmly maintaining one's own form as peaceful and composed of Brahman;
even in cases where the installation is said to be purely of the nature of Brahman.
Even there, one should resort slightly to the divine portion on the left,
because [the breath] has issued forth with its sixfold nature for the benefit of all;
therefore, one should lead it slightly toward the divine portion from the station of Brahmā.

Indeed, for the sake of attaining the accomplishments such as liberation and other fruits, one should— without hesitation— hold the *kautuka* (sacred thread) which is already in hand, with the heart. Having offered it upon all limbs with the *arghya-mantra*, one should then recollect the root mantra.
Then, with a vajra-paste consecrated by the recitation of the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra,
one should perform the unification of the image, the pedestal, and the stone.
Thereafter, [one should proceed] with those [waters] residing in the eye-vessel and likewise those residing in the eight vessels.
Having sprinkled the image with water clinging to the tips of the *kūrca* grass while reciting the mantra,
one should then unite the mantras residing in each respective jar with the image; at that time, one should also place the *śakti* residing in the child-image into the root [of the image].
O best of sages, O twice-born ones, in the case of the primary image fashioned from materials such as clay,
or in the ritual image (karmārcā), or on a seat made of darbha grass,
one should perform the rite of awakening and likewise the act of circumambulation.
Having entered the palace, the preeminent teacher, composed in mind, should perform all other rites in due order within the primary image; then,
having meditated upon the root mantra, which possesses the characteristics of the tranquil Brahman.
"One should remember that everything, from the foundation up to the tip of the banner, is pervaded by it"— having first performed this general visualization (*sāmānyasandhāna*),
it is then specified according to its gross, subtle, and supreme aspects; the gross aspect is sixfold, ending with the stone (*śilā*).
Likewise, one should perform the subtle placement of that supreme [deity] within the pedestal for the purpose of grasping the image;
then, at the base of the seat, one should carry out the placement of the deities.
O best of sages, these [deities] are the instruments for the sake of worldly existence.
One should never perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon the mantra-image;
O best of sages, even without such an installation (*pratiṣṭhā*),
one should place the deities of the manifestation one above the other, as before, above the pedestal.
Beginning from the designation of the jar (*ghaṭa*), one then proceeds to the supreme worship;
for in this way, by virtue of the arrangement of all the deities,
the placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*) becomes the bestower of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Then one should perform the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) upon the limbs of the image according to the rule.
One should perform the threefold placement of the Lord— namely creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—
whether he is standing, sitting, reclining, or even moving.

O twice-born ones, one should perform the three types of nyāsa upon all of these; or else, O best of the twice-born, one should practice the nyāsa of stability when standing, that called creation when sitting,
and the nyāsa of withdrawal when lying down.
One should establish the placement of the limb-mantras in the locations beginning with the heart;
having then applied the other ornaments and so forth, ending with Garuḍa,
one should thereafter worship everything there through the yoga of dissolution.
One should again worship the circle of mantras situated on the seat through the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga),
having superimposed the word "Lord" (svāmin) upon one's own name, or else [the name] preceded by Harikeśava and then conjoined with the Tāra (Om). 18.422.
The image-keepers and the others should indeed say, "May it be well-established.
(18.423) And while scattering full handfuls of flowers and unbroken rice grains in every direction, all those standing there should say, "May it be well-established. (18.424)
One should cause him to recite "ā tvāhārṣam" along with "saha vai pratiṣṭhāsi," and the mantra beginning with "viśvasya mitram," O twice-born ones, ending with "ekāyanā.
Together with those [mantras] from the Ṛgveda and the others, he should conclude with "oṃ namo 'stu" and "namaḥ."
"Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā! 'Victory!'—thus indeed [it should be].
