18.426 Accompanied by the word 'victory,' a hymn that is captivating to the minds of the listeners should be uttered with loud voices by all the preceptors together. 18.427"
"O best of Brahmins, know that everything is established by this all-pervading one who has become the living soul, whose form is the mantra; once he is installed, all is established.
Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and other rites together with the primary image (mūlabimba), [the ritual proceeds].
O twice-born ones, one should place the ritual images and so forth before the primary image;
furthermore, one should install Lakṣmī and the others according to the prescribed rite and according to one's capacity.
Then, even while standing in the middle of the pavilion facing the God of gods, at that very moment, the King of Birds (Garuḍa) should be installed—
he who was previously consecrated by his own mantra, bathed, and anointed.

O best of beings, because it always assumes the state of being an auxiliary to the power of cognition (*jña-śakti*) along with its reflection (*bimba*), whether the objects are distinct from one another, situated near that reflection, or located elsewhere;
(18.432) at that very moment, it proceeds to become a constituent part.
Having performed the oblation in its entirety, preceded by meditation and worship,
the ritual itself, in accordance with its own nature, attains a state of universality.
Therefore, having raised [the deity] from that sacrificial hall and taken it up like an image...
Having circumambulated the deity clockwise, one should place the pentad beginning with the Vajra in the single central cavity at the site of installation as previously described.
That which was declared above it is the single support.
And it should be established as before above that pedestal; then, the meditation [is to be performed].
The body should be meditated upon, and the remainder is characterized by cognition.
Likewise, one should cause the Brahmins to recite the king of mantras, "Suparṇo 'si."
Having first worshipped that very [liṅga] with weapons,
one should then place it either between Śaṅkara and Someśāna, or in a courtyard,
or in its specific location; or else, it may be placed upon a pedestal within the interior of the temple.
Having installed Viṣvaksena according to the procedure prescribed in the *Khaga* [Tantra],
the most excellent of teachers should likewise install all the deities stationed at the doors as well as those situated in the enclosures, in the same sequence as previously described.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water from the ritual jar, he should then proceed to the kitchen;
having established the fire upon the hearths, he should recite the hymn "I praise Agni" (agnim īḷe).
There, indeed, [he should prepare] various sacrificial offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like.
Then, O Brahmins, one should cause [the deity] to be cooked; thereafter, one should proceed to the abode of the gods.
Then the Lord is to be bathed with water-pots placed upon his back, together with all the image-bearers, according to the proper sequence.
With the *aghamarṣaṇa* alone, and with the *gāyatrī* repeated;
first with the *ṛṅmaya* [mantra], and thereafter with those repeated four times by himself;
and with the six [mantras] repeated from the heart (*hṛdaya*) onwards—the knower of the *yajus* should sprinkle [the disciple] with that.

Then, the knower of the Sāman hymns himself should likewise bathe [the deity] with six other jars; thereafter, the one versed in the Atharva Veda should do so himself with those very same jars, which have been consecrated by the *pavitra* mantras,
at intervals throughout.

Then, together with those belonging to the Ekāyanīya school, one should immediately perform the ceremonial bathing using a water-pot that has been consecrated many times with the mantras consisting of the four forms;
having taken the remaining water in the jar, one should indeed bathe [the deity].
Having performed one hundred rotations of that [mantra] together with the primordial form (ādyamūrti) and its root,
one should indeed engrave it upon the head of the God of Gods and cause it to be recited.
Then, with the weapon-water, one should [recite] "jitanta" over all [of them].
Having purified the temple and gone to the vicinity of the water-pot (kumbha),
one should worship the Lord of Gods there according to the previously mentioned sequence; then,
having worshipped in the mandala, one should proceed to the vicinity of the image (bimba).
There, one should especially worship the deity— excluding the ritual bathing—
with various tactile offerings such as seats and other formal services,
as well as with heart-pleasing, non-designated items, and the four kinds of food beginning with milk-rice.
O best of the twice-born, having performed the rites in due order, beginning with abundant food and other kinds of edibles and consumables, and concluding with the formal presentation of gifts;
One should especially offer [oblations] along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru and to those who bear his form;
having first offered seven pieces of fuel-wood, one should indeed satisfy [the deities] in due order within the fire.
Having likewise established the perpetual fire in the kitchen according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].
Having performed the oblation according to the prescribed method and having made the offering of the *homa*,
one should bow to the deity and inform him through action, mind, and speech:
"O Lord, you who reside within my own image, and whatever [has been offered] by me into the fire and other [elements]..."
"You have been brought before me; therefore, O Acyuta, you must forgive me.
Having thus prostrated and made his request, he stepped forward and emerged face-to-face.
From the very foundation up to the top of the banner, he beheld the palace that had been constructed of old.
Having circumambulated the deity and prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma),
and having taken up the vessel for the water offering (arghya-pātra), he should go outside the temple.
Having worshipped the vehicle, which is identical with the Blessed One, with bathing and other rites...
Then, after that, one should offer the bali-oblation in due order, as before, to the previously mentioned guardians of the directions stationed at the gates; furthermore,
one should perform the offering of bali for the multitude of spirits.
"May the beings devoted to the Blessed One who dwell outside the temple accept [this offering].
And may their followers, purified by power and mantra, likewise accept it.
Having thus given the *bali* offering in sequence for all, one should then cause them to recite [the mantra].

One should offer oblations in a clockwise direction for the sake of the ritual offerings (bali) upon all the enclosures, using respectively the *Ṛg* verses beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," the *Sāman* chants beginning with "Yā devās tvā," as well as the *Anna-sāmans* and those consisting of the "Mayā" [verses] together with the "Dhenu" [verses].
Having performed this, the preceptor should afterwards sip water (ācamana) and enter his residence.
To pacify any deficiencies or excesses, he should offer a hundred oblations ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Then, using the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) together with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), he should present the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
In this manner, beginning from that day, one should perform the worship of the God of gods for four days, proceeding in sequence at the four locations.
When the fourth day arrives, however, one should remove the garlands and other offerings.

Having first performed the worship of the jars, the mandala, and the image within the sacrificial hall according to the previous procedure, and having completed the mantra's concluding fire-offering (homa),
one should rinse the mouth, offer the bali-oblation, and then proceed to the temple of the deity.
There, having worshipped the Lord as before with offerings beginning with the seat and ending with the bath,
[they should worship] again with water well-filled in jars that have been removed from their cloths, placed upon a pedestal of grain,
and consecrated with the heart-mantra.
Together with the embodied [deities], as before, by means of their internal and intermediate conjunctions,
the rite of bathing should indeed be performed according to the ritual procedure; then, having worshipped again as previously in the waterless temple.

Having performed the offerings beginning with the seat and ending with the final gift to the Imperishable One, one should bind the mudrā and recite the mantra; then, having offered praise and asked for forgiveness, one should go outside.
One should personally offer oblations a hundred, a thousand, or eight times more, O King of Mantras.
Together with its limbs and its retinue, it should be recited according to the rules of *saṃhitā* pronunciation.
By the image-keepers (*mūrtipas*), one hundred repetitions each should be performed with the *gāyatrīs* preceded by the *praṇava*;
likewise, those who possess the single path (*ekāyana*) and the higher knowledges (*abhijñās*) should perform an equal number with their own respective mantras.
Then one should cause the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipās*)— beginning with those of the *Ṛgveda* and the others, who follow the single path— to offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
At the conclusion of that, one should then have them recite [the mantras] in sequence,
beginning with the mantra "O Full One, you are full" (*pūrṇāt pūrṇam udacyase*) and ending with "You are full" (*pūrṇam asi*).
One should personally deposit [the deity] with the mantra accompanied by the salutation and its constituent parts.
Then, one should satisfy all the spirits (bhūtas) who were previously present with offerings.
Having entered and sipped water for purification, one should subsequently ask for forgiveness from the deity residing in the jar.
As before, one should worship Viṣvaksena, who resides in the maṇḍala and subsequently in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), using the desired and remaining offerings in due order.
One should then adorn the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), beginning with the Guru, with bracelets and other ornaments.

One should offer the sacrificial materials to the Guru or to the Guru’s son. For the sake of attaining the desired goal from the forms of the Siddhas, one should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Thus has been declared for the practitioner who desires the propitiation of the mantra.

I shall briefly describe the fruit for the patron (*yajamāna*) in the consecration of the mantra-form, by means of which one attains perfection (*siddhi*) while remaining therein— from the site of the temple grounds,
O best of the twice-born, for as great a number as there would be of all atoms everywhere, including those endowed with all accessories and within all obstructions,
for that many years the doer shall dwell [in hell].
The enjoyer of pleasures goes to the world of Viṣṇu and, at the end, reaches the supreme state.
Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa who performs the rite becomes a learned sage and the master of all sciences;
the Kṣatriya who performs the sacrifice becomes the sovereign of all lands.
A Vaiśya who performs a sacrifice shall be rich in wealth and grain;
a Śūdra who performs a sacrifice shall rejoice together with his kinsmen,
and he shall likewise possess noble birth and knowledge.
One who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom.
For those devotees who are free from desire, their devotion remains unswerving, as does that eternal knowledge which exists together with its inherent nature.
The installation of images fashioned by oneself is thus proclaimed.
Having installed the image in this manner in either a temple or one's own home,
from that time forward, one should worship it every day.
For as long as the procedure for restoring what has decayed is carried out according to the rules,
one must not allow the omission of worship, whether through negligence or intentionally.
This applies equally to the goddesses such as Śrī and to the *cakras* and other such objects.
One should perform the installation for all devotees of Viṣṇu, whether in the first enclosure, in a pavilion, or in a courtyard. Through the installation of Lakṣmī, all prosperity arises for men.
By the installation of the *cakra*, the protection of the site becomes certain.
From the consecration of a devotee of Viṣṇu, there arises fruit both in this world and the next.
Therefore, the installation of Śrī and the other deities should be performed in the temple of the Lord.
Whether at the time of the installation of a deity, or at another time separately,
when these [deities] are installed together, there is no separate performance of the rites beginning with the *aṅkura* (seed-syllable ritual),
nor the construction of a sacrificial hall; rather, it should proceed as described for the retinue.
O best of sages, listen: all that must be performed there as well— namely,
the bath with the six substances beginning with *siddhārthaka*, the binding of the protective thread (*kautuka*),
and the consecration in water (*jalādhivasana*) within the five vessels beginning with the very subtle one.
Among the various ablutions, one should perform any one of them, as well as the opening of the eyes; likewise,
the consecration on the bed and the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the respective mantras and the array of their respective insignia according to the prescribed rule.

One should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a separately prepared sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) using the respective mantras for each. One should then perform the consecration of the respective seats (pīṭha) and so forth, as well as the installation of the seat itself.
Furthermore, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five [deities] beginning with Vajra, and their installation in their respective positions as previously described.
Furthermore, the placement upon its respective support, whichever has been prescribed for each, as well as the installation of the *bimba* above the pedestal according to the ritual rule—
at the time of each such installation, the recitation of the corresponding mantra must be performed. (18.500–18.501)
Having fully reflected upon all this, the best of preceptors should perform [the rite];
he should carry out every ritual action according to the rules during the separate installation,
together with the respective mantras and the respective worship of the retinue.
O twice-born ones, hear now a certain distinction regarding the installation of the wheel (cakra).
One should install there, upon the pinnacle of the temple, a wheel that is formless [in essence], having twelve spokes, or eight spokes, or six spokes. (18.503–18.504)
One should install the image in the courtyard, either with sixteen or eight arms;
at the time of its installation, one should mutter this mantra of its name.
One should cause those who know [the ritual] to recite the Vidyā beginning with "Gadā" (the Mace), and so forth.
He should cause the Bahvṛcas to recite the two verses beginning with "camūṣacchyena" and "prati viṣṇo," as well as the Śākuna Sūkta;
thereafter, he should [cause them to recite] the mantra "dhṛtordhvapuṇḍraḥ kṛtacakre."
With the mantra "pavitraṃ te vitataṃ," he [initiates] those consisting of the Yajurveda;
with "āroha" and "pavitranto agniḥ," those consisting of the Sāmaveda;
and with "ebhir vayaṃ urukramasya," the twice-born followers of the Atharvaveda.
Having thus established [the image] according to the rules, one should then bathe it with nine jars using the eight mantras residing in the *Brahma-sūkta*,
and with the mantra beginning "viśvasya vaśinaṃ devam," which was previously established.
By the outer enclosure situated in the direction of Agni, it is said "it exists";
by that situated in the south, "that which arose from the navel-lotus";
and by that located in the direction of the Yātudhānas, "one who has worn the upright sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra)."
On the right arm, O Brahmin, [the mantra] begins with "iti";
on the western side, it is "viṣṇunāttamaśnantīti"; and situated in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), it is "puṃpradhāneśvaro viṣṇur iti," located in the region of Soma (the north).
With this Great Upaniṣad, using all these mantras recited while facing the Lord (Īśāna), one should sprinkle with the central jar.
One should perform the sprinkling upon the wheel situated at the top of the temple.
One should recite the eight mantras previously mentioned that reside within the Mahopaniṣad (18.515),
or else one should recite the Puruṣasūkta for the sake of all-pervading peace; furthermore, whatever has not been stated here, one should perform it exactly as previously described (18.516).
Thus, the consecration of the Heroic Fortune (Vīra-lakṣmī) and others has been proclaimed;
now, however, the consecration of ornaments and ritual implements is being described.
For that purpose, listen here to the sequence of deities for all of them.
In the crown, the Kaustubha gem, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the forest garland, those very same deities reside; their forms have already been described.
Furthermore, in the radiance is the goddess Prabhā, and likewise Ananta and the others are present in the pedestal.
Vainateya resides in the sandals, while Sarasvatī dwells in the bell.
Likewise, in the palanquin and the vehicle, as well as in the swan and the lion,
and in the elephant, horse, and chariot, Garuḍa alone is the presiding deity.
And likewise upon the two lords of birds, Śeṣa and Garuḍa, as well as upon the orbs of the moon and the sun;
on the son of the Wind (Hanumān) are the banners, which are the deities Śeṣa and the others in person.
Having thus known those respective deities in their proper order in the past, O twice-born ones— || 18.521–18.522 ||
The preceptor should perform the respective installations with their corresponding mantras,

having performed the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurāropaṇa), whether immediately or at a later time; then, having bathed [the image] with the six substances beginning with white mustard seeds, he should perform the tying of the protective thread (kautukabandhana).
Having performed the consecration by shadow or the consecration by water,
and having opened the eyes of the embodied [image] according to the rule,
one should bathe it with jars according to the rite and perform the consecration of the bed.
Having established the pitcher there and having worshipped the respective deities upon its various parts,
and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of their respective mantras and so forth, one should worship them with those respective mantras.
O twice-born ones, one may offer oblations either in fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*), or on sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍilas*), or in a single location.
Then, at an auspicious moment, one should sprinkle water from the two jars.
One should cause the teacher and others to receive their sacrificial fees and other gifts according to one's capacity.
Thus has the general procedure for the installation of all [deities] been described.
The specific procedure for the installation of the chariot is to be understood as being like that described for the temple;
all other implements, beginning with the parasol and the fly-whisks,
as well as the divine ornaments and the incense burners and so forth, [should be prepared].
Having washed all the vessels, such as those for the *arghya* offering, as well as the various musical instruments,
and having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite;
and having consecrated them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and through the rites of burning, satiating, and so forth.
Having consecrated them, one should employ them for the worship of the God of gods.
Those who provide the Lord with armlets and other ornaments, rich with the luster of various gems and fashioned from gold and other materials, [attain great merit].
Having attained the partless body, all those whose taints have been shaken off are united with perfect knowledge; they do not fall into any state of existence,
but for their own benefit and for the cessation of all suffering.
From the tip of the big toe to the ankle, up to the knee, and reaching as far as the shoulders—
whoever, with great devotion and according to their own capacity, casts upon the arrived Acyuta armor made of gold and the like, enriched with jewels, pearls, and corals; || 18.535 ||

He goes to the supreme abode, O kinsmen of all creatures. But he who, out of delusion, removes the armlets, anklets, or other ornaments that have been fixed upon the image, his state remains fixed in the Vīci hell.
[He is the refuge] of those brahmins who are authorized, devoted to the five times,
who know the five times, and who are devotees desiring spiritual perfection.
Now, for those whose spiritual branches have been severed, yet whose souls are devoted to Nārāyaṇa—
whether they be ascetics, observers of vows, *snātakas*, or celibate students;
or for other devotees whose minds are intent upon worship— [this applies].
Having constructed [it] for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord, he duly presents it—
provided with halls and other dwellings, composed of stone and baked bricks,
filled with both cultivated and wild grains, and crowded with those of virtuous conduct. || 18.540 ||
Accompanied by merchants, family members, laborers, and guards,
he obtains inexhaustible fruit for as long as the moon and stars endure;
he shall attain an eternal station in the world and imperishable fame.

For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, one should place before the vicinity of the seat a beautiful and delightful vessel for the enjoyment of offerings, possessing the characteristics previously described; or else, for the purpose of an outer enclosure for ritual practitioners who are united with Brahman.
He is liberated from the three debts to the sages, the gods, and the ancestors.
In the middle [of the design], it is marked by Garuḍa, with the signs of the discus and the lotus;
or else, it is shaped like a quadrangle (caturaśra) or circular (vṛtta), provided with a pedestal like a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

The donor who constructs a sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) outside the abode of Acyuta goes to the station of Acyuta by means of celestial chariots (vimāna) with the brilliance of the sun. He who indeed bestows a village or a grove upon the Lord, O Lord, [attains the same].
Endowed with various flowers and fruits, crowded with ponds and trees,
possessing reservoirs of water with lotuses, and provided with Māra-khaḍga,
he enjoys pleasures in the Nandana grove and goes to the abode of Acyuta.
He who [bestowed] the earth, filled with crops and endowed with excellent fragrant rice;
Kedāra is completely covered on all sides by cascading waters;
having reached that eternal time, he goes to the source of the world.
He shall go to the brilliantly white island, where he dwells like the Blessed One himself.
Having honored a herd of cows together with a bull— the very essence of the mantras for bathing and enjoyment— he who offers this worship indeed establishes the Vaiṣṇava image;
he, freed from all defects before long, proceeds to the world of Viṣṇu.
An elephant, a chariot, and excellent horses; a lamp-stand of auspicious marks;
a fan, a fly-whisk, and a parasol; musical instruments and a troupe of courtesans; beautiful garments, eye-salves, and divine ornaments.
A canopy and a Vaijayantī banner, a multitude of variegated leafy creepers,
a sweet-sounding bell, an auspicious incense burner,
a water-pitcher, a mirror, a water-jar, and a large fragrant stone.
Whoever gives other various grains previously mentioned with devotion to Hari shall attain His world.
[He who] gazes at the face of the Lord while carrying a vessel of lamps—

O lords of sages, whoever with faith [establishes] a great lamp or a yantra in the form of a tortoise or other such shapes, situated upon the seat of the arrow-sacrifice (śara-yajñāsana) and adorned by the casket of the mind, possessing various seats of the sacred scriptures— || 18.557–18.558 ||
He who gives [to the Lord] attains the supreme abode of the God of gods. Whatever is offered with devotion, placing the Source of the Universe (Jagadyoni) at the forefront,
shall become inexhaustible for those intent on His worship.
"Thus has the procedure for the installation of [deities] preceded by the *bimba* been described.
O bulls among sages, if you wish to hear anything else beyond this, let it be told.
Thus ends the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* within the venerable *Pāñcarātra*.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Consecration.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
O venerable sage Nārada, O sages, [please explain] likewise the procedure for the restoration of the dilapidated [temple],
as well as [the rites] when the image has been touched by those who are untouchable, or when great portents and the like occur.
O Yogin, we wish to hear in its entirety the expiation for the omission of daily worship and other rites; please reveal all of that to us. (19.2) Nārada.
Listen, O twice-born ones; I shall here proclaim the restoration of dilapidated temples and related rites, by performing which the happiness of the four classes of teachers and others increases.
First, I shall describe the procedure for restoration regarding a site constructed by humans.
Whether produced from clay, stone, wood, or cast into cloth and other materials—
O lords of sages, for whichever form of the Blessed One there may be,
one should perform the restoration of minor limbs when they are broken, and the restoration of major limbs when they are shattered. (19.4–19.5)
Having abandoned that image, one should create another image once again;
therein I shall first explain the sequence of the major and minor limbs:
the head, the face, the two ears, the two hands, the chest, and likewise the abdomen.
The navel, the penis, and the feet, O best of the twice-born, are the great limbs;
likewise the eyes, ears, nose, palate, the fingers and toes, as well as the hair of the head and beard, body hair, nails, and teeth. (19.7–19.8)
O best of sages, listen further: the collection of weapons such as the discus, and ornaments such as the forest garland (*vanamālā*), are the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) on the earthen image.
That which is the primary trident therein is called the "great limb" (*mahāṅga*).
The chest-staff, the waist-staff, the arms, elbows, and forearms;
the shanks, thighs, and knees—these, O lords of sages, are the other minor limbs.
Even when a fracture of a major limb occurs in the image, O preeminent sages, [the following applies]. (19.10–19.11)
As long as there is the capacity for joining, one should never abandon it;
for its abandonment and destruction cause successive obstacles.
However, the abandonment of large objects such as statues and the like is not appropriate.
But when the face of the image is damaged, one should perform the ritual abandonment of it in every respect.
Images that have been abandoned, provided they are not made of metal or stone,
should be cast according to the prescribed rite into a deep body of water or into the ocean.

Or, O Brahmins, one should bury it in the ground according to the requirements of place and time—especially those made of superior gold, silver, or copper. Abandoning such objects is not appropriate; therefore, one should perform the rite of rejoining them.
If it is found to be unfit, one should perform its abandonment.
Having melted down the abandoned material according to the rule,
one should complete the rite by fashioning a new image with that material as before.
Alternatively, that which is made of inferior copper or brass,
or that which is made of counterfeit metal and is unfit for the process of joining— these two types should be discarded.
Once discarded, one should cast that image according to the previously mentioned method.
Then, O lords of sages, one should fashion an inner image made of silver or gold,
or produced from the most excellent material of its respective kind;
for in all ritual images, one should proceed in this very manner.
O twice-born ones, listen now to the method for joining a broken limb;
for a broken limb of metal, stone, wood, or an image, one should use strips of iron.

Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, one should carefully join a broken limb of a metal image using molten gold or other such materials. As for images made of clay or painted [materials], their broken limbs...
O best of sages,
whatever limb is broken or lost for all [beings], it should be restored with material of the same kind through diligent effort. || 19.23 || Thus again [it is restored].
O best of sages, even if a large part of a gemstone image is broken, it must be joined back together with material of the same kind through diligent effort;
it must certainly not be abandoned, just like a self-manifested stone image.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, whether during the restoration of all the constituent parts or during a new creation,
the preceptor, having invoked the Śakti residing in the worn-out image into the ritual pitcher,
should perform worship there and carry out the reintegration of the image.
If the stabilization [of the image] occurs within a month, one should worship the Śakti in the Kumbha.
If there is a delay in stabilization beyond that, until the end of twelve months,
one should construct a house for the child there and install the child-image according to the prescribed rite.
Having established that power there and having invoked [the deity], one should worship it;
O twice-born ones, when only the limbs are installed, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
If the installation of the interior image is to be performed, one should carry out the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) once again.
One should construct the children's quarters and other such structures upon the alignment of the limbs of the primary image.

But when the limbs of the ritual image (karmabimba) are broken, one should withdraw the pervasive Lord residing in each of those images into the primary image (mūlabimba) and perform the rites of reconnection and so forth.
This applies to the first case, the construction of a new temple for a child, and the last case, known as the restoration of a dilapidated temple.
"I shall proclaim the expiation; listen, O best of sages!
When the time previously requested has passed, the builder should perform the supreme consecration bath for the temple and the image, as enjoined by the scriptures. (19.32–19.33)
Afterwards, one should request the desired time for its completion. If,
without having done so, the twelve-year period elapses,
one should perform the consecration again, either at the root [shrine] or in the child-shrine (bālālaya).
If the image is lost by thieves or others due to negligence in the house of a child,
one should recover that very same image, install it according to the rules,
perform the supreme ablution, and carry out the peace-offering oblation (śāntihoma). || 19.35–19.36 ||
O twice-born ones, if the image has been stolen by thieves and is recovered again,
one should perform the rite of re-consecration, even without the ritual of opening the eyes,
provided it has not moved from its original location for whatever reason. (19.37)
Having established it as before, one should install the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
All rites—daily, occasional, and so forth—should be performed in the child’s chamber.
If the image previously installed is devoid of the [proper] characteristics, [it must be replaced].
At the time of restoring a dilapidated [shrine], one should perform [the rite] endowed with the proper characteristics;
however, one should never perform it prior to the procedure known as *jīrṇa*.
[The image may be made] of bronze, copper, or even brass.
When a sublime object of worship, such as a ritual image or the like, has been honored,
and after some time it has become worn out while a superior [image] is available,
the wise person should discard the inferior one; no fault is found in that.
When the primary image (*mūlakautuka*) has been installed using iron, stone, clay, or wood,
it must never thereafter be replaced by any other principal object. If, as in the past, it should fall into a state of decay, the primary image must be remade.
O sages, whether it be a multi-bera or a single-bera [temple] that was previously established,
it should be restored in the same manner as before during a rite of renewal (jīrṇoddhāra).
One must never effect a change between the multi-bera and single-bera forms.

In the case of restoring a dilapidated temple (jīrṇoddhāra) where Lakṣmī and other deities are absent, one should perform the rite for the two goddesses even without [the presence of] many vessels; otherwise, there would always be a loss of the abundance of vessels. 19.46. From the opposite course, such a loss would not occur.

The bed, the seat, the vehicle, or the standing place should remain exactly as they were previously situated; or else, at the time of re-creation, they may become otherwise according to his will. If the goddesses were as they were before when the god was worn out and then re-created, [then it shall be so].
This deity is to be joined with those very goddesses and not otherwise.
Thus has the restoration of a human image been proclaimed.
The same applies to self-manifested (svayamvyakta), divine (divya), perfected (siddha), and those of the sages and other non-human origins.
I shall describe the procedure for the restoration of dilapidated [images]; listen, O best of sages!

In the case of self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) and other images, whether in the primary limbs, the secondary limbs, or the minor appendages, there should only be a rejoining when they are broken; there should never be an abandonment [of the image].
O best of sages, even if it is unfit for rejoining, that Sāligrāma stone image must not be abandoned— whether it be split, broken, large,
or slightly damaged; provided it is made very firm with golden bands.

And in the same manner, one should perform the binding even upon those [images] that are self-manifested and so forth. In the case of stone images, one should join together what is split or broken with gold-encrusted plates so that it becomes more firm.
Alternatively, having fashioned that limb out of gold, one should properly join it;
this applies likewise to those made of wood or metal, and even to those that are self-manifested (*svayamvyakta*) and so forth.
Even when there is a discrepancy in the limb, the ritual application (*samādhi*) remains valid, as in the case of a stone image that is self-manifested.
In the case of a gem [image] as well, one should perform the restoration in exactly this same manner.
But when the primary image made of clay has become worn out by water and so forth,
or is deficient in its limbs, one should likewise diligently carry out the rejoining.
In this way, one should perform the joining even when the color is deficient;
one must never discard the clay, the pins, the cord, and so forth. Likewise, if a part of a painted image has fallen away, it should be restored with substances impregnated with fragrance.

O twice-born ones, artists who are experts in the scriptures should paint [the image] with purifying colors such as white and red, consecrated with mantras, according to the previous [prescribed] method;
however, O brahmins, there is this specific distinction regarding self-manifested [images] and others.
One should not create images of children, houses, and so forth right there as before;
while the worship is underway, one should perform meditative absorption and other such practices.
One should duly perform the reconnection of those [images], including the ritual sprinkling and other rites.
Or even in the case of a curiosity (kautuka) worshipped by gods and others, or one that is self-manifested (svayam-vyakta),
if it is made of clay or wood and has become worn out by worms, fire, water, and so forth,
one should construct a new house for each respective [image] and worship it as before.
Having performed another consecration in due order, one should install it according to the prescribed rite;
when the image of a child has become worn out here, one should do this again and again.
Indeed, such as the self-manifested images and others may be, [one should act accordingly].
Whether they are endowed with the correct characteristics and measurements or devoid of them,
whether produced from superior metals or arising from inferior ones— they simply remain as they are; one should not alter them otherwise.
One should not create another characteristic, nor likewise another means of knowledge;
one should not create another substance, nor should one perform another action.
One should not employ another mantra; one should do everything exactly as before.
O lords of sages, if one were to cause a reversal of the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and so forth,
there would be great misfortune for the king, the kingdom, and everyone else.
Therefore, one should not practice such a reversal in the place established by the ancients.
One should not act otherwise even regarding the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth;
for those individuals, O twice-born ones, whose signs are not manifest upon their bodies,
they [should instead place] their own signs on the forehead or on a shoulder-band.
Whether on the back, or on a cloth-wrap for the limbs, or on the palms and soles of the feet,
or on the head— one should examine it in each of those places.
Therefore, a manifestation devoid of marks (lakṣaṇa) never exists.
O lords of sages, if in images made of stone and other materials— whether self-manifested or human-made—
a deficiency of one, two, three, or even four *yava*s occurs in the nose or other limbs, [the rite of purification must be performed].
One should carefully perform [the restoration] as before with the respective sharp instruments.
Then, O best of sages, one should perform the consecration (saṃprokṣaṇa) of the deity;
likewise, even when the pedestal or other parts are broken, one should properly carry out the rejoining (sandhāna).
The image, its pedestal, the inner sanctum within the temple,
and the form of the God of gods— these four are equal.
Likewise, meditative absorption (samādhi) and peace (śānti) must always be practiced there with equanimity.
If there should be a fracture in the radiance, one should bind it with iron bands. But if the pedestal itself is broken, the wise man should always discard that pedestal;
however, if the pedestal is only slightly deficient, he should bind it with iron bands.
Having raised up and dismissed that image which has been excessively defiled by defects such as the breaking of limbs from previous worship,
one should install it upon the pedestal according to the prescribed rite, having fashioned it anew as before.
Likewise, when the pedestal is broken or another is fashioned, one should firmly join it.
Even when the eight-fold bond between the image and the pedestal has been loosened,
one should again perform the eight-fold binding and then carry out the consecration by sprinkling.
O lords of sages, whether in the case of a self-manifested image or one made by humans,
if the image has been stolen by thieves or others, one should fashion a new one endowed with all auspicious marks using those very same materials as before, and install it at that very time.
The mantra-practitioner should worship the image as before at all times and in all places.
Or, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, the preceptor may fashion it from another material.
O twice-born ones, if an image that was stolen by thieves is recovered again, [it should be treated in this manner].
O best of the twice-born, having performed the sprinkling and worship of the image made of human material,
one should perform the re-installation again, excluding the ritual of opening the eyes (nayanonmīlana).
This applies when the original image— whether made of human material or non-human material— is consumed by fire.

The ritual bath with a thousand jars (sahasrakalaśasnāna) should be performed according to the prescribed rules. When discoloration occurs in the ritual image or other [objects] due to fire, one should perform the supreme bathing ceremony upon each of those images in the proper sequence.

If the primary image, or the ritual vessel (*karmakautuka*), has its parts broken due to fire, heat, or other causes, it should be joined back together by the most excellent artisans as previously described.
After the joining is complete, one should perform a thorough consecration (*samprokṣaṇa*) in all cases.
O Brahmins, the restoration of temples and other structures belonging to the All-pervading Lord will therefore be described.
In that regard, O twice-born ones, first hear the procedure for [the restoration of] human [buildings].
When a portion of the temple, such as the pinnacle or the finial, has been broken,
one should invoke the deities residing in the temple onto the pedestal of the primary image and worship them; then, one should make the broken part of the temple firm.
O best of beings, having first addressed the deity, one should subsequently perform the sprinkling and other rites for the temple according to the path prescribed in the scriptures;
even if the celestial chariot (vimāna) is broken on all sides, one should arrange a place for the child (the deity).

O lords of sages, those deities who reside within the temple should be placed upon the pedestal of the child-form (bālabimba) and worshipped as before. In the same manner, the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and other rites should be performed for the child-form.
O best of sages, one should perform all the rites up to the *pavitrārohaṇa*,
and having reconstructed the temple and consecrated it according to the rules,
one should perform the sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*) and other ceremonies for the deity.
Thus, when a pavilion, a hall, a gate-tower, a flower-garden,
or the like has become dilapidated, one should remove all the deities residing therein to another location;
then, having renovated them as they were before, one should re-install them according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform the supreme consecration for the pacification of that defect,
if the temple or other structure previously constructed is devoid of its proper characteristics;
in such a case, one should restore it to possess those characteristics according to the section on restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*).
In the case of a temple or similar structure previously constructed of mud, brick,
or even stone that has become dilapidated, one should restore it by rebuilding with stone;
however, the restoration of a shrine that is self-manifested (svayamvyakta) and so forth will be described later.

If a portion of a temple or similar structure has collapsed, the deities residing therein should not be moved elsewhere; rather, one should worship them right there while repairing the broken part and performing a ritual consecration (samprokṣaṇa). 19.101.
Having joined the broken section back together, one should perform the sprinkling rite.

The twice-born [should act as follows]: "When a temple has collapsed on all sides, one should invoke the deities residing in that temple onto the pedestal of the primary image and worship them there. (19.102)

One should reconstruct the temple again using the same materials as before—such as bricks and other items of that same kind—whether they be old or newly acquired. Whatever material was used for the original structure and whatever characteristics it possessed, [those same should be employed]. || 19.103–19.104 ||
One should perform it exactly as before and not otherwise.
O best of sages, having again consecrated the celestial chariot and other objects according to the rules, one should perform the sprinkling and other rites for the deity.
Whether in an image that is self-manifested or fashioned by gods, siddhas, and others; or in a celestial palace, a wall, a gate-tower, a gateway, or a pavilion;
or on a pedestal, in a kitchen, a residence, a treasury, or even elsewhere—(19.106–19.107)
Whether it is endowed with the characteristic marks or even devoid of them,
one should restore it when worn out in accordance with its original form.
O Brahmins, by acting otherwise, a great transgression would occur.
In a temple that is self-manifested or otherwise established by gods and the like,
when some degree of decay has occurred over the course of time,
[restoration may be undertaken] with the permission of the devotees who maintain it and are learned in the scriptures.
For the sake of protection, both outside and inside the sanctuary, a wall-enclosure should be constructed on all sides by skilled artisans using stone and other materials.
This applies whether the temple has been consumed by fire, or is inhabited by humans or non-humans.

To pacify those defects, one should perform the ablution of the Lord. If the temple has been damaged by fire or other causes, one should have it repaired by skilled artisans as before, and then perform the consecration and other rites.
If the temple of the Blessed One falls due to the upheaval of the earth, the force of water, or other such causes,
one should relocate it from that place to another, together with its original image.
If the abode, including the image, is destroyed by divine or other forces, one should perform the rites as previously described.
But when the human image has been utterly destroyed by the force of rivers, fire, and so forth,
one should subsequently fashion another image as before, or otherwise; however,
because the original image is no longer present, there should be no installation of the deity, nor the bringing in of the child-form (bāla-arcā), and so on.
The preeminent teacher should not perform [the rite] as before; rather, having established [the deity], he should worship them.
For thus it is for all the gods, including those whose forms consist of the supreme manifestation (*paravyūha*) and so forth, as well as the host of attendants such as Viṣvaksena and Gaṇeśa.

O best of sages, for all those [deities] who have been installed in gate-towers and other locations in the form of magnificent manifestations, and who are worshipped day by day due to their extraordinary presence, the rite for the restoration of the dilapidated is prescribed.
One should perform the installation and other rites in accordance with the specific presence [of the deity];
the practitioner, having carefully deliberated, should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta).
This applies when there is damage to the limbs of the image and so forth, or to the temple and its surroundings.
But the teacher, afflicted by remorse, should recite his own mantra ten thousand times.
From that time forward, remaining established in the vow of celibacy together with the practitioners,
he should recite the mantra without weariness until the absorption into the image [is attained].
One should perform worship at the four locations for the pacification of all defects;
or, for three nights or seven nights, one should practice the giving of gifts to worthy recipients, such as cows, land, gold, and so forth, according to one's ability, O lords of sages. (19.123)

One should always feed a hundred or even a thousand Brahmins; one should especially worship the Lord until the rejoining of the image is complete. At the conclusion of the rejoining of the deity, having performed the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) and other rites—
The patron should perform the pacification oblation (śāntihoma), as well as acts of charity and the feeding of Brahmins;
he should satisfy the preceptor with sacrificial fees and other gifts.
He should gratify him according to his capacity, for by that Keśava is pleased.
"By restoring what has fallen into decay, the patron obtains a reward even greater than that of a first-time construction;
there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Thus, O tigers among sages, the restoration of ruined temples has been described by me. (19.127–128)

Therefore, O best of sages, regarding the touch of the Bimba image by those who are untouchable, I shall declare the expiation; listen with focused attention. Likewise, if a preceptor has not bathed after being defiled by a Caṇḍāla or similar person, [the following applies].
If one who has gone to a woman while touching impurities such as hair or bones fails to bathe,
and then touches an image of the Blessed One, he should bathe it with nine jars of water,
perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma), and recite the mantra one hundred times.
If these [images] enter within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),
then one should bathe the Lord with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and perform rites such as the *śānti* oblation.
This applies when they are brought by those who are uninitiated, those initiated into other tantras, or those other than the officiating priest (*arcaka*).
When the image has been touched, one should then perform a bath, which is the lowest means of attainment;
furthermore, one should perform a fire sacrifice for pacification and recitation of mantras for the sake of quelling that fault.
When these [images] enter within the inner sanctum, [the rite is performed] with nine jars.

Having bathed the Lord of the gods, one should perform the pacifying oblation (*śānti-homa*) and other rites. If the image has been touched by women, by those who have not received initiation (*anupanīta*), or likewise by Vaikhānasa Brahmins or non-Vaiṣṇavas, it is considered inferior or middling.
Having performed the ceremonial bath according to the rules, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) and other rites.
When [the deity] has entered inside the house through the lowest path by these [means],
one should bathe the deity according to the rules and perform the propitiatory fire-oblation.
Whether fallen, a sinner, or afflicted by leprosy or epilepsy;
whether one-eyed, blind, mute, deaf, or deficient in limb;

whether addicted to another's wife, or a *kuṇḍa*, or even a *golaka*— 19.138–139ab. If one should touch the image of the Blessed One— whether it be of the highest or lowest class— while being in contact with a menstruating woman, an outcaste, or an ass and the like,
one should bathe the deity according to the rules and likewise perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).

O twice-born ones, when these have entered within the sanctuary, one should perform the inferior or middling ablution (snapana) of the God of gods, and likewise carry out the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma). This may be done by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, as well as by their respective women.
When the images have been touched, one should perform the ablution (snapana) in sequence, whether it be inferior or superior;
likewise, that known as middling-inferior and middling-middling.
By means of these, O best of sages, [the rite is performed] upon entering within the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
One should perform the ritual bathing in sequence, designating it as "lowest-of-the-low," "low-and-middle," and "low-and-highest," respectively.
In every case, one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and recite the mantra a thousand times.
In the case of a favorable touch by the image, there shall be a ceremonial bath (snapana).
However, if it enters within the house or touches a celestial chariot (vimāna) with those [signs] known as middling or superior, the bath is middling-inferior. || 19.145–19.146 ||
If the image is touched by one born of an inverse (pratiloma) union, one should perform either an excellent or a middling consecration; likewise,
if they enter the inner sanctum (garbhamandira),
or even if the temple (prāsāda) is touched by them, an excellent or a lowly consecration must be performed.
O lords of sages, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and recitation (japa) everywhere as previously described.
Whether he be a thief, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra born in the natural order (anuloma), or even one born in the inverse order (pratiloma)— 19.148–149.
If one should touch the image of the deity, there shall be a gradual consecration (*snāpana*):
that which is designated as middling-inferior, likewise middling-middling, designated as middling-superior, and designated as superior-inferior. (19.150)
That middle bathing should likewise be the highest of the high.
However, regarding entry into the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), there are three types: the lowest of the high, the middle of the low, and the highest of the low. || 19.151-19.152 ||
O twice-born ones, one should then perform the intermediate ablution in due order when the image has been touched by thieves whose caste is unknown;
one should bathe the deity with a thousand jars according to the prescribed rite.

But for those who enter the interior of the sanctum sanctorum, the ablution shall be of the highest order. In all cases, however, there must be a propitiatory fire-oblation (śānti-homa) and likewise the recitation of prayers (japa), especially by men who are under ritual impurity or who are great sinners (mahāpātakin).
If the image of the Blessed One is touched by Caṇḍālas, women recently delivered, outcastes, Mlecchas, Pulkasas, or others of similar status, one should bathe it with cow-ghee,
perform the ritual sprinkling according to rule, and carry out the rite of pacification.
Likewise, one should perform the gift of cows and other such rites, and also feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Having renovated a painted image made of clay according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform the consecration again, as in the case of self-manifested images and others.

Nor should one perform the sprinkling and other rites anew for a painted image and the like as was done previously; rather, it is purified by that very same [initial] rite. When entering the inner sanctum (garbhamandira) with these aforementioned persons who are under ritual impurity, [the following applies].
Even when a celestial chariot is touched, all the vessels situated in the dwelling [must be cleaned];
having discarded the earthenware vessels, one should purify the metal vessels,
and having thoroughly cleansed the dwelling by sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, and other such means.
Having sprinkled [the Lord] everywhere with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), O best of sages,
one should bathe the Lord according to the rules by way of the most excellent path,
either within the front pavilion or in the first enclosure.
O lords of sages, having performed the purification of the abode upon entry as before,
one should bathe Puruṣottama by way of the lower and upper paths,
beginning from the second enclosure up to the western end of the street-enclosure.
Once they have entered within and performed the purification of the temple,
O twice-born ones, they should bathe the deity by means of the lowest-of-the-low path.
In every case, one should perform a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*) and provide a feast for the Brahmins.
O lords of sages, if Caṇḍālas or Śvapacas should, through negligence, reside continuously for one month in the temple of Viṣṇu,
[the priests] must abandon their earthen vessels and thoroughly sweep the house of the Lord.
Then, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should cause a herd of cows to dwell there for the pacification of all defects.
Having had the Great Peace (mahāśānti) recited by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
and having fed the twice-born there, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
In this manner, [one should perform it] for a month, or half a month, or for seven, five, or three days.
Having first purified the temple and the images with cow's ghee,
and having performed the consecration as before, one should then perform the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
O twice-born ones, this applies likewise to images made of clay or those consisting of paintings.
Having renovated it as before, one should again undertake the consecration ceremony.
If, however, out of negligence, Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, or others are authorized for work in the temple of the Lord, or if twice-born men dwell together with them, [the following applies].
Having bathed and drunk water with *kuśa* grass, and having performed the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances,
as well as the purification of the temple, followed by the feeding of the twice-born,
one should perform all the rites such as the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) exactly as before.

One should perform a great festival beforehand for the pacification of all defects. Likewise, if those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) and others are authorized for the rite, one should perform everything according to the rules, beginning with the purification of the temple as previously described.

One should perform the bathing and the festival with a thousand jars. If the image has been touched by the corpses of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those born in the natural order of castes, one should sprinkle it with cow’s ghee.
One should perform a ritual sprinkling and an ablution with a thousand jars;
one should also perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and a recitation (japa) numbering ten thousand times.
Having renovated the human image and other such representations according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
One should perform a re-consecration involving immersion in a thousand jars when the interior of the sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) or the temple (*vimāna*) has been defiled by those corpses;
one should also perform a supreme sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) and an excellent bathing (*snapana*).
In the case of an image defiled by one born of inverse-caste union (caṇḍāla), a woman who has recently given birth, or a corpse,
one should perform the consecration without the rite of opening the eyes;
furthermore, one should bathe the Supreme Person with a thousand jars.
If the palace has been defiled by those corpses, one should perform a ritual sprinkling;
one should also bathe it according to the prescribed rites with a thousand jars of water.
Beginning from the first enclosure, this extends to the western side of the street-enclosure.

If the courtyard or the field is defiled by the corpses of Brahmins and others, or even by the corpses of those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), one should dig four cubits of earth, remove the soil, and cast it outside; by this, purification is attained. (19.184–19.185)
Having filled it and leveled it, one should perform the sweeping and other rites;
if it is a stone surface, one should burn that ground without digging.
Then, having smeared it with cow dung, one should perform the proclamation of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and so forth.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should have the herd of cows stay there.
Having had the Great Peace (mahāśānti) recited, one should indeed feed the twice-born there.
Having thus performed the purification of gross impurities, one should thereafter perform the rite of pacification (śānti).
Having performed the ablution specifically for each deity in order, from the principal and highest down to the lowest and final,
one should perform the propitiatory fire-offerings (*śāntihoma*) and other rites,
O eminent sages, whether in the temple or during a birth, due to negligence.
The expiation shall indeed be performed according to the sequence of those respective enclosures:

in the *sāla*, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), or the pedestals; in the gate-towers (*gopura*) or the temples; outside the *vimāna* itself, or in the shrines of the retinue (*parivāra*) and so forth. || 19.190–191 ||

In the event of death or birth among the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, or among those born of inverse or natural order, one should perform the penance as prescribed for those respective obscurations; this applies even in cases such as touching a [defiled] image.
One should perform an expiation according to the specific proximity [of the defilement].
Likewise, whether in the kitchen or even in the sacrificial pavilion,
if there is the entry of a Caṇḍāla or others, or if it has been defiled by corpses and the like, [one should act accordingly].

Having discarded the earthen vessels and purified the surface of the earth by digging and other means, and having abandoned the fire situated in the sacrificial pit and hearth according to the prescribed rule,
one should re-establish the fire and perform the propitiatory oblations (*śāntihoma*) and other rites.
If the death of a member of the Brahmin caste should occur in a village or similar settlement that has been designated as an auxiliary to self-manifested shrines and other such sites,
O twice-born ones, for as long as the corpse remains within the center of that village— (19.196–19.197)
O lords of sages, as long as the impurity of the village persists, one should not perform the worship of the deity once the corpse has been carried out of the village; rather,
having sprinkled water everywhere throughout the village, preceded by the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha), [the rites may proceed].
Then, one should perform the worship and other rites for the God of gods.
O Brahmins, if the village becomes defiled by a corpse while the worship has already commenced,
the preceptor should quickly complete the commenced worship by means of a ritual summary (tantra).

As before, after the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the village, one should perform worship again. If indeed the death of a Śūdra or others should occur within the village, then impurity (*āśauca*) applies only to the household; there is no impurity for the entire village.
Even there, O best of the twice-born, within eleven bow-lengths of the Blessed One’s residence, if it has been defiled by the corpse of a Śūdra or others,
one should first remove that corpse and only afterwards perform the worship of the Lord.

Even if a temple for the Blessed One has been constructed as an integral part of a city, village, or the like, if there is a corpse within that village or similar area, one should not perform the worship of the deity. However, in a village, city, or the like, provided it is occupied by four hundred Brahmins...

O lords of sages, even when there is a corpse within [the village], there is no impurity for the village; however, even in that case, if a corpse remains near the house of the Blessed One or in a single path,
one should not worship the deity until after it has been sprinkled with water.
In a village or similar place prepared as part of a festival, crowded with people from the kingdom,
and occupied by outcasts (caṇḍāla), those who have fallen from their caste (patita), women in their courses (udakyā), women recently delivered (sūtikā), forest-dwellers (śabara), and others,
as well as dogs and the like, and likewise by various kinds of meat; 19.207.
If the ground is defiled by a corpse or bones, whether everywhere or in one spot,

one should dig it up, remove the earth, and cast it outside; then, having filled it back with pure soil and leveled it, one should purify it by sprinkling it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other rites.

Having performed purification, one should perform a rite for the peace of the village to pacify those defects, O lords of sages, when the image has been touched by semen, urine, excrement, and the like; by blood, vomit, or undrinkable substances; or by saliva, bones, flesh, and so forth. (19.210)

One should bathe [the deity] by means of the most excellent path and perform a rite of pacification (śānti). When there is contact with the temple by these [means], one should bathe the Lord of the Gods of gods according to the middle and most excellent paths and perform a fire-offering for pacification (śāntihoma).
When the first enclosure has been touched by those [impurities], O best of sages,
one should bathe Puruṣottama via the lower or the higher path.
But when the second enclosure and the others are defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, [the same applies].
Immediately after that, having led it outside and purified the ground by sweeping, smearing, and so forth, one should subsequently sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Then,
one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of all defects.
In the same way, when the ground in the innermost enclosure and other areas of the Blessed One’s temple was defiled by the dust of women,
one should dig the earth down to the depth of a knee and fill the surface of the ground with fresh soil.
Having smeared [the area] with cow-dung and water, and likewise performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa),
as well as the recitation for an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) and the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then address the door-panels that have been touched by women in their menses.
Having again washed them with water and having purified their path by sweeping and by smearing it with cow dung,
and having discarded the earthen vessels, [he approached] the Lord residing within the palace.

Having bathed [the image] in that same manner by means of the lower and higher paths (adhamottamamārga), and having likewise bathed the image according to the scriptures when it has been brought near a woman in her menses,
the best of preceptors should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) and recitation (japa).
O lords of sages, when the image is touched by cats, mice, snakes, frogs, chameleons, and the like, or even by female insects and fireflies,
one should bathe the God of gods with nine jars of water.
No fault is found if the image is touched by ants and similar creatures.
Likewise, if the image is touched by a cow’s mouth or by drops of rain,
one should perform a propitiatory rite after bathing it according to the lowest-of-the-low method.
If the image is touched by dogs, donkeys, camels, boars, jackals, or hares, one should bathe it according to the most excellent of superior methods;
one should perform a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*) with a thousand oblations and recite mantras.

If these [defilements] occur upon entering the interior of the sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) or even by touching it, one should bathe Puruṣottama by way of the middle or the highest path. However, upon entering the interior of the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), one should bathe him by way of the lowest or the highest [path]. || 19.226–19.227 ||
One should cause them to perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) in the second enclosure and so forth.
If they enter the presence of the God of Gods by the lowest-of-the-low path,
one should bathe him, perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma), and carry out a thousand recitations (japa).
If the image is touched by the carcasses of cats and other such animals,
the best of preceptors should perform a ritual bath and a fire-offering for pacification; however,
if the interior of the sanctum is defiled by them, he should do so with nine jars.

One should bathe the God of gods and likewise perform the *śānti* oblation; if the area is defiled by those [impurities] in the first enclosure and so forth, one should lead it outside. One should purify it with sprinklings, smearings of cow dung, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

If there is contact with the image by means of cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and so forth, or likewise by monkeys and other such animals, one should bathe it according to the most excellent of the superior methods (uttamottama-mārga).
However, if the interior of the sanctum (garbhagṛha) is defiled by these, the procedure is the middling of the superior (madhyamottama).
The most excellent of teachers should perform the ritual bathing (snapana) and the pacificatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the previously mentioned items,
such as cows and others, within the first enclosure and so forth;
and likewise, in the event of birth or death [of those animals], he should perform rites such as digging up the ground where they were located.
Having purified it, one should bathe the deity according to the lower or higher path.
However, if the image (kautuka) has been touched by the corpses of a dog, a donkey, a pig,
or the like, one should perform a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa), as well as pacifying oblations (śāntihoma) and other rites.

When these [substances] come into contact with the temple, one should bathe the God of Gods according to the highest of the high paths (uttamottama-mārga) during the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) and so forth. If they have defiled [the deity], one should bathe the God of Gods according to the middle of the high paths (madhyamottama-mārga).
The best of preceptors, having performed the ritual bathing, should carry out the propitiatory fire-offerings and other rites.
Likewise, if a dog or similar animal enters the kitchen or the sacrificial hall,
or if they have been defiled by their carcasses, one should discard the earthen vessels.
Having thoroughly cleansed the iron vessels and performed the sweeping and other rites,
and having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
O twice-born ones, this should be done when those [vessels] come into contact with the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or the like, as well as upon contact with the hearth (cullī).
O twice-born ones, having abandoned that fire, one should establish another according to the prescribed rites.
O lords of sages, [this applies] when there is contact with the image by crows, vultures, owls, cocks, pigeons, hawks and the like, or by monitor lizards.
One should bathe [the image] by means of the middle or superior path and perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*).
O best of sages, when these [images] enter the interior of the sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),
one should bathe them by means of the inferior or superior path and perform a rite of pacification.
O twice-born ones, in those places within the first enclosure where entry is forbidden,
if these [unauthorized persons] enter, one should sprinkle that spot with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should perform the fire-oblation for peace (śāntihoma) and other rites for the pacification of all defects.

If the image is touched by the corpses of crows and other such creatures, one should perform the most excellent bathing and a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of that defect. If, however, they touch the temple itself, one should act according to the middle or highest method.

One should bathe the God of gods in the first enclosure and the others. However, when that spot has been defiled by them, one should purify it through sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and other means; then, having cleansed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform sprinkling and a rite of pacification.

O twice-born ones, if those [defects] are found in a kitchen or similar place, one should perform everything as previously described; or, in the case of a dilapidated structure, a honeycomb, an anthill, and so forth,
or if the image has become sunken, one should immediately remove that [defect].
Having performed the consecration of the image with the five products of the cow according to the rule,
and having subsequently performed the ritual sprinkling, one should carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
To pacify that defect, one should give gifts such as cows, land, and sesame seeds.
O best of sages, one should feed a thousand Brahmins when looseness or other defects arise in the temple or the inner sanctum;
one should bathe Puruṣottama according to the most excellent of rites.
One should perform the pacifying oblation (*śānti-homa*) and other rites exactly as previously described,
whether in the enclosure wall, the pavilion, the gatehouse, or among the mounts, in the event of the appearance of loose soil, bees, anthills, and the like. (19.253–254)
When the parasols have arisen and the Brahmadaṇḍa has emerged,
one should immediately uproot them and sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Having bathed Puruṣottama according to the inferior or superior method, [one should proceed].

One should perform all rites, such as the propitiatory fire-offering (*śānti-homa*) and others, exactly as before. If [these items] have been placed in the temple of the Blessed One by those other than the worshippers—namely, seats, bedding, food, and so forth—[one should treat them accordingly]. (19.256–19.257)

Having sprinkled that site with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*). If the image falls upon the fire-altar, or if a limb is broken, one should repair it according to the rules, perform a sprinkling, and likewise [perform the rite] with a thousand jars.

Having bathed the deity for the sake of pacification and having performed oblations, one should provide a meal for a thousand Brahmins; at the conclusion, one should hold a great festival. In the case of a temple damaged by a lightning strike, one should repair it as before.
Having performed the sprinkling and other rites according to the most excellent path,
one should bathe the deity and subsequently perform the peace-offering (śānti-homa) and other rituals in the first enclosure,
at the gateway (gopura), or in the pavilion (maṇṭapa).
If a thunderbolt should fall from either a low or a high path,
there shall be a ceremonial bath, a fire-offering for peace, and the feeding of Brahmins;
now, O twice-born ones, listen as I describe the pacification of such portents.

When there is the falling of meteors, thunderbolts, and the like; when a constellation has fallen from the sky; when there is smoke in the quarters and the burning of the directions; when the king is possessed by spirits and the like;
when there is famine, disease in the kingdom, or likewise a crisis with enemies—(one should perform the rites).
In the event of the sun rising out of its proper course, during an earthquake or the splitting of the earth;
during excessive rain or drought, or upon the sounding of celestial drums;
when a rainbow appears at night, or likewise when fire is produced within water.
When there is moonrise in darkness, or when smoke is seen without fire;
when a mock-sun is seen, or when stars are seen by day;
when a hair or a fish is seen [in the sky], or when the sun is seen at night— 19.267.
But in dreams, O twice-born ones, [there are omens] such as the falling of the moon, the sight of fire upon the earth,
the sight of spirits and the like, the sound of a wheel-rim in the sky,
and the battle of planets in the firmament— even without any external cause. (19.268–19.269)
Likewise when a moist tree falls, or similarly when a mountain collapses;
when another fruit is seen on a tree, or likewise a sprout on a rock;
during a shower of stones from a pond or similar body of water, or upon seeing red moss.
When a tree produces a two-headed creature or blood, when humans, cattle, or birds give birth to hybrid offspring,
and when other such wonders and great portents occur; (19.272)
O best of Brahmins, the king should quickly effect the pacification of those defects within a beautiful pavilion prepared according to the prescribed rules for installation,
and within the previously arranged [mandalas] beginning with the discus and the lotus, in the proper manner.

In ten sacrificial pits, with oblations produced from the *brahmavṛkṣa* and other trees, along with sesame seeds and clarified butter accompanied by the groups of mantras previously mentioned, and mixed in due order with the five sweet substances and so forth— 275.
For the pacification of great faults, those most skilled in mantras should offer oblations—
ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, or up to ten million— as their strength permits,
together with a full oblation by ten of the most skilled mantra-knowers.
The assignment of mantras to the central and eastern pits is as follows, in order:

in the twelve-spoked lotus of the wheel, with the twelve-syllable mantra; in the eight-spoked [lotus], with the eight-syllable mantra; in the six-spoked [lotus], with the six-syllable mantra; and in the conch-like [lotus], with the *praṇava*. (19.277–278)
One should worship with the *jita* mantra in the square [mandala], with the *viśvatrātrā* in the triangle,
and with the *nṛsiṃhānuṣṭubh* in the lotus known as having thirty-two petals; likewise, one should worship with the *sudarśananṛsiṃha* in the wheel-pitcher whose spokes consist of syllables.
In the diagram called the Ardhacandra, one should place two sacrificial sites (dhiṣṇya) on the central altar using the Vārāha and Saudarśana rites, as previously described, to the south and north;
the remaining sites should be constructed all around, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Hotṛs who have mastered the mantras should be appointed for rites of pacification (śāntika).
All fire-pits (kuṇḍa) may be fashioned according to the will of the Guru for all mantras;
or rather, the mantras themselves should be so conceived, since they bestow all fruits.

The mantra should be recited by you according to the rule and with the prescribed number. Satisfaction should be provided through gifts of cattle, land, gold, sesame seeds, and food to worthy persons, and especially to the divine shrines and other sacred sites.
By a king whose nature is to protect his subjects and who desires his own welfare, such peace must be established through many branches of the scriptures and abundant wealth.
O best of the twice-born, this is the rule for the primary ritual; in the secondary ritual, it is as follows.
As before, in the sacrificial hall, one should perform [the rites] in sequence within five fire-pits (kuṇḍa) using the five pervasive mantras preceded by the eight-syllable mantra,
with the five substances such as honey, milk, and so forth, [reciting] the one called "niyuta."
The mantra-practitioner should perform the oblation according to the numerical count so that it reaches one hundred thousand;
O lords of sages, he should likewise give gifts of cows, land, sesame seeds, and so forth, as previously described.
At the conclusion of every [rite], one should conduct a festival preceded by the hoisting of a banner.
Likewise, when the image smiles, moves, weeps,
falls, revolves, perspires, or bleeds,
one should perform a sprinkling with water and then carry out the previously mentioned pacification ritual.
At the conclusion of the great festival of the Lord, for the pacification of all defects,
if heat should suddenly arise within the image situated inside the temple,
[one should perform the rite] with milk, honey, ghee, and likewise with coconut water.
One should bathe [the deity] for seven days with thousands of distinct measures of water.
Then, one should perform the previously mentioned propitiatory rite (śānti) until the conclusion of the festival,
O lords of sages, when a red rain has occurred upon the temple and other structures.
Having washed it with pure water and likewise smeared it with cow-dung,
one should perform the circumambulation with fire and the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
