Having performed the ritual sprinkling of the deity according to the rules,
one should then proceed with the bathing of the deity with honey and ghee using thousands of *prastha* measures.
One should perform the previously mentioned propitiatory rite (*śānti*) according to the prescribed method until the conclusion of the festival.
Having bathed the deity for seven days with thousands of *prasthas* of honey-rain and milk-rain respectively, as previously described, one should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*).
[This applies] when the temple suddenly collapses or when a tree falls upon it.
Having made the preliminary preparations as before, one should quickly perform the sprinkling of the Lord;
one should perform the previously mentioned propitiatory rite and conclude with a great festival.
Thus, O Brahmins, the pacification of the faults of great portents has been proclaimed.
Now, however, the expiation for the failure to perform worship and other rites shall be described.
One who has not bathed, one who does not wear the vertical *puṇḍra*, one who is impure, and one who lacks the sacred thread—
Whether naked, or wearing a single garment, or indeed wearing tattered clothes;
likewise, wearing stale clothing, or wearing blue garments, or even wearing burnt clothing, or wearing wet clothing. (19.300–19.301)

O twice-born ones, if one should worship the God while not having sipped water, devoid of meditation, with hair disheveled, with limbs perspiring, laughing, angry, panting, or talking idly; or even if accompanied by spitting and the like— (19.302)
To pacify those faults, O Brahmins, one should recite the unsurpassed eight-syllable mantra a thousand times or a hundred times, O twice-born ones;
then one should perform the worship of the God again according to the prescribed rite.

One who has touched hair, bones, clods of earth, rags, blood, or anything defiled by contact with the untouchable; likewise, one who has stepped over urine, feces, and the like, or has failed to bathe; one who has been touched by those in a state of ritual impurity (āśauca), or has been affected by the presence of a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste—[these must perform penance].
If one whose limbs are smeared with blood and the like should worship Keśava,

he should bathe him with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and perform the worship again. This applies even if he has been touched by crows, vultures, and the like, or by dogs, donkeys, and so forth.
If one should worship [the Lord] while being touched by heretics, those acting contrarily, outcasts, those of base livelihood, or even by sacred trees and the like,
one should bathe Puruṣottama according to the lowest of low methods.

If one who has had sexual intercourse with a woman while remaining unwashed after being touched by Caṇḍālas, Mlecchas, menstruating women, women recently delivered, or those guilty of mortal sins (mahāpātakin),
should nevertheless worship the Lord of Gods according to the lower or middle path; || 19.309–19.310 ||
Having bathed the deity, he should thereafter perform worship again.

One who is addicted to approaching the wives of others, or one who is afflicted with leprosy, or one who is deficient in limbs; or one who is one-eyed, blind, mute, deaf, or even lame— [should likewise bathe the deity].
O twice-born ones, if one who suffers from epilepsy or is insane should worship the God,
he should bathe the God according to the lowest or highest path.
Or even one who is in a state of ritual impurity, an outcast, a leper, or a *golaka* [illegitimate son], [may perform this].
Even one who has committed a great sin (mahāpātaka), if he should worship the God,
having bathed Puruṣottama according to the most excellent method,
should perform a fire-offering for peace (śāntihoma) and the recitation of the root mantra.
[It is defiled] by worms, insects, and the like; by grains, flowers, fruits, and the like that have been spoiled; by parts of living beings, husks, ashes, bones, hair, teeth, nails, and the like;
and by substances that have been touched [by such things], as well as by fruits and other items touched by the hands of those who are untouchable (aspṛśya). || 19.315–19.316 ||
Likewise, when worshiping the Deity with other leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth that have been kept overnight, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
[This applies even if the materials were handled by] Caṇḍālas, outcasts, women in their courses, women who have recently given birth, or those born of inverse unions.
With substances touched by Śabaras and others that are censured by the scriptures;

with leaves, flowers, and the like, or even those touched by the mouths of cows and so forth; with substances stepped over by humans, as well as by untouchable animals and the like. || 19.318–19.319 ||
O twice-born ones, [one should avoid] substances joined with worms, insects, moths, bones, teeth, hair, nails, and the like; likewise with chaff, ashes, clods of earth, and so forth;
as well as with previously offered substances and water that has stood overnight.
When the worship of the deity has been performed, having bathed [the image] with water from *kuśa* grass while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*,
one should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
or alternatively, one should perform a *śānti* oblation for the pacification of all defects.

[One should not worship] with flowers and other offerings eaten by insects, those from near low dwellings, flowers grown in another's garden, those woven together, those offered by one who is not initiated,
those brought by a Śūdra, those placed outside the flower-house, or those brought by the sick.
In the worship of Hari with leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth that have fallen upon the ground,
one should bathe the Lord of Gods with milk and recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times; then, one should worship again with pure leaves, flowers, and other offerings.
If the worship of the deity has been performed with worn-out or unwashed garments, with old umbrellas and such, or with unpurified vessels for the *arghya* offering and so forth,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and perform the worship again.
If the deity has been worshipped with garments touched by impurities such as hair or bones, or likewise by Śūdras and others,
or by dogs and the like, or by those who cause defilement such as Caṇḍālas,
[the rite must be repeated] according to the lower or higher path.
Having bathed the God of gods, one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
If the worship was performed with garments touched by a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, or a menstruating woman,
one should bathe [the deity] according to the most excellent method and perform the propitiatory rite.
O best of sages, cotton cloth that has been touched by Śūdras, such as those who eat hair or bones,
or by Caṇḍālas and others, should be purified again and offered to a deity; however,
cotton cloth touched [by them] should simply be discarded.
O twice-born ones, if fine silk cloth has been touched by Śūdras and others, one should sprinkle it with consecrated water;
however, if it has been touched by Caṇḍālas and the like, the Guru should wash it thoroughly with water.
Likewise, [it may be purified] with the clarified butter of goats, sheep, buffaloes, or camels, or with oils derived from castor seeds.

O best of sages, for the pacification of that defect, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) using oils derived from animal parts or from fruits as an digestive stimulant (*dīpana*), or by offering the milk, curd, and ghee of goats and other such animals.
During the bathing or the offering of the deity with the previously mentioned clarified butter and other substances,
one should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*) through bathing according to either the inferior or the superior method.
When the wicks for the lamps and such are made from pieces of cloth worn by men, [the rite should be performed].
One should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and carry out a thousand recitations.

If one should worship out of delusion with incenses mixed with animal parts, or those produced from oil, or even from *snuhī* plants, or with other foul-smelling substances, [the following is required]. 19.336–337.
O best of sages, having offered a thousand oblations with the ghee of a tawny cow and having worshipped the Lord with a thousand jasmine flowers,
the preceptor should again fumigate [the image] with pure camphor and agallochum.
If [the deity] has been worshipped with the remains of offerings from another deity or with impure substances,
one should perform a purification rite after bathing [the image] according to the lowest of low methods.
[This applies to images] touched by outcastes, women recently delivered, menstruating women, or defiled by corpses.
When the worship of the Lord has been performed with water drawn from a well,
one should bathe Puruṣottama by means of the most excellent method.
[This applies even if] the well is situated within a horizontal fissure or has been touched by those born of inverse unions (pratiloma).
If one should worship the deity with water drawn from a well out of delusion—

specifically from a well containing living creatures or corpses, or one defiled by excrement, urine, or undrinkable substances— one should perform either the highest or the middle-grade ritual bath to pacify that fault. (19.342–19.343)

In the worship of the God of gods, bathing with water that has been offered to another deity, or is defiled, or has been carried away [as leftovers], would be the lowest form; likewise, it would be the lowest if the water has remained inside [the vessel] containing a corpse, or has been touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and the like. (19.344)
For the worship [of the deity], water drawn from a lake is middling or excellent;
one should perform the bath of the deity with water drawn from a lake that has been stayed overnight within, or that has been touched by those moving crosswise or against the current.

When there is worship of the deity, bathing with water drawn from a pond that has been touched by outcastes (caṇḍālas) and the like, or defiled by a human corpse, constitutes a mediocre-inferior rite. However,
when there is worship [with water] drawn from such a pond, it is an inferior-superior rite.

The best of preceptors should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) of the God of gods. O lords of sages, if a well in which a corpse has remained has been touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and others, one should remove all of its water, or at least half of it.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should then sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
If the water is defiled by animal carcasses and the like, one should remove half of it;
or having removed even a quarter, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow.
If a well is defiled by the corpses, urine, or excrement of creatures such as rats, or by the ritual remains (*nirmālya*) of Śiva, one should remove that water;
or else, one should sprinkle it with *pañcagavya*, using either a quarter or half [the amount of the impurity]. || 19.351–19.352 ||
In a place defiled by contact with impure persons such as Caṇḍālas and the like, or by a human corpse,
or defiled by contact with those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), or by the carcass of an animal,
one should perform half of the penance prescribed for a pond or a well.
If a pond (taṭāka) has been defiled by the touch of a corpse or a Caṇḍāla and so forth,
one should perform half of the prescribed penance at a lake (saras). Or rather, [half] at a large lake or a very extensive pond.
One should draw out a thousand or a hundred jars of water;
during the day one should draw out the water, and at night, if possible, in the vicinity of fire.
[This applies when defiled by] Caṇḍālas, women who have recently given birth, menstruating women, Śabaras, drunkards, and others.

When food, drink, or edibles have been touched by dogs, jackals, boars, and the like, or by crows, vultures, and so forth; likewise, when food has been touched by blood, flesh, or bones, it is offered to the deity. (19.357–19.358)
If food has been offered in a house defiled by a corpse or similar impurity,
one should discard the earthen vessels and purify the metal vessels. Having performed the purification of the utensils, everyone should bathe according to the prescribed rule.
They should perform the ritual with *kuśa* grass and water, as well as the most excellent bathing ceremony.
Having performed this for the deity according to the rules, one should carry out the *śānti-homa* (propitiatory fire-offering).
This applies to those addicted to approaching the wives of others and those who lack discrimination between what is fit and unfit to be eaten.
If the sacrificial oblation has been touched by non-Vaiṣṇavas,
or if it has been discarded, or has become stale, or has been seen by unworthy humans,
or even if it has been touched by frogs, mice, snakes, or cats— [it is unfit for offering].
If food and other offerings have been touched by worms, insects, moths, and the like; defiled by hair and such; struck by breath; smelled;
or previously offered—then one should offer it again in sequence with twelve jars.
Having bathed the Lord of the gods, one should perform the peace-offering (śānti-homa).
When offering cooked food from a hearth touched by dogs, vultures, or the like,
one should bathe Puruṣottama with twelve jars as previously described.
If food cooked on a hearth touched by Caṇḍālas or others is offered,
one should bathe Puruṣottama with twenty-five jars of water.
[Water that is] too hot, too cold, or mixed with dust, chaff, and grit [is likewise forbidden].
O best of the twice-born, if one should offer an oblation (havis) that has been defiled by clay or stone, one must recite the root mantra one thousand times. Likewise,
if an oblation is offered that has been prepared with unsuitable grains such as kodrava and the like, [the same penance applies].
If one offers prohibited vegetables, roots, or fruits,
one should bathe the deity with cow’s ghee and perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
O twice-born ones, hear now the specific rule regarding the ritual of the Great Oblation (mahāhavis).
Food prepared elsewhere than in the kitchen by those other than the initiated,

food not consecrated with mantras, food that has not been distributed, food lacking auspicious marks, food looked upon by the unworthy, and food touched by flies and the like— [such food is unfit]. (19.371)

Having sprinkled the offering with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, one should present it with diligent reverence. (19.372) In other cases where the sacrificial substance (*havis*) is thus defiled, one should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*).
That which is bitten by flies, woodworms, bees, and the like, or defiled by excrement, is considered spoiled. (19.373)

Food consisting of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, which has been occupied [by spirits], must be abandoned; having sprinkled it with water consecrated by mantras, one should offer it to the deity with devotion.
However, without performing the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) or the ritual placement of mantras (*mantra-nyāsa*), etc., [the offering should not be made].

O twice-born ones, if out of delusion one should perform the worship of the deity without first worshipping the Lord in the heart, or if one should perform the sacrifice to the deity without first performing the removal of the withered garlands (*nirmālya*) and so forth, as well as the purification of the image and the purification of the site; (then there is a fault).
To pacify that fault, one should recite the root mantra one thousand times;
then, having performed the rite for the omitted action, one should perform worship again.
In the case of the omission of substances such as the *arghya* offering, [one should perform] the rites of burning, nourishing, and so forth.
Or, if [the ritual] has been omitted, having recited the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī one hundred times according to the rule (19.378),
and having performed the consecrations such as the placement of materials (dravyanyāsa) and so forth, one should worship the arghya and other offerings,
as well as the deities of the temple doors and those residing in the surrounding enclosures (19.379).
If the worship has been omitted, one should recite those respective mantras in their proper order one hundred and eight times before that [deity], and then perform the worship again—
whether for the deities of the temple gate or for the assembly of the retinue.
If there is an inversion, one should recite the root mantra a hundred times and then perform the worship in the proper sequence.
Even if the worship of the deity has been performed without first performing the worship of the *pīṭha*,
one should recite the mantra of the deities of the *pīṭha* and so forth a hundred times, as prescribed.

Having again performed the worship of the seats (pīṭha), the Guru should worship the Deity; for in the case of worshiping ritual implements, images, and so forth, as well as in the worship of the limbs and the icon (bimba), [the rite is complete] even without the invocation (āvāhana). If the worship is performed without the sacrifice of absorption (layayāga) or the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga), [it remains valid].
Having consecrated it one thousand times with the root mantra, he should worship again.

O twice-born ones, this is likewise for any deficiency in the mantra, deficiency in the ritual action, or deficiency in the mudrā, as well as for any inversion in the enjoyment, the mantra, the ritual action, and so forth.
To pacify those faults, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. However, if the bell is not rung at the time of worship,
or if it is devoid of the resonance of the Vedas, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
But if the previously prepared offerings are deficient, one should perform worship again with double the materials and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
This applies to those who are formless, whose nature consists of ritual service, touch, and the heart.
O twice-born ones, upon the loss of the three types of enjoyments,
one should offer all seeds, as well as honey, wealth, and rice cooked with ghee, to the Lord during worship, preceded by a special sacrifice. (19.389)

But in the event of a deficiency in the materials such as the *mātrā* offerings, O lords of sages, one should bathe the deity with auspicious waters and perform a *śānti*-oblation to pacify that defect. This applies even if the lamp should suddenly go out in the midst of the worship. (19.390–19.391)
Having rekindled [the lamp] for the sake of pacification and offered oblations, one should recite the Netra-mantra.
O best of sages, if the lamp of the Unextinguished One should go out,
one should bathe the Lord of Gods with milk and perform a pacificatory homa.
Having relit that lamp, one should recite the root mantra a thousand times.
When the lamps have been summoned from the kitchen for the purpose of the deity’s *nīrājana* rite,
if even a single lamp among them should go out, [the rite must be repeated].
If, due to negligence, the force of wind, or because it was not announced beforehand, the destruction of prosperity occurs first, followed by affliction from disease and the like,
then one should suddenly ignite [the fire] and recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.

Likewise, if the *nīrājana* lamp goes out before or after the final offering, one should relight it immediately and recite the mantra a thousand times. However, if that vessel has been touched by an unworthy person, one must abandon it.
Having brought another jar,
O twice-born ones, one should perform that [rite] with it; whether at the time of worship, in the incense burner, or in the lamp vessel,
or in the jar used for the *nīrājana* ceremony, should it happen to fall through negligence.
O twice-born ones, if the bell, the arghya vessel, or other items such as the parasol should fall,
one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
If the incense burner or similar objects are broken, they should be repaired as before.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should employ it at the beginning of the worship and other rites.
If any part of the worship is omitted during the prescribed times for worship,
then at the subsequent time, one should worship the deity with double the amount of materials.

O best of sages, one should worship [the Lord] two or three times a day; even if these occasions are missed, one should worship Puruṣottama with materials multiplied three or fourfold. If there is a lapse in worship for a single day, it is according to the lowest of the low paths.
Having bathed the deity according to the prescribed rite, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
One should worship with double the usual materials and likewise feed the Brahmins.
O lords of sages, in the event of a two-day period or at the end of a fortnight, or when worship has been omitted;

Having performed the ritual bathing according to the inferior or superior path, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti). Having worshipped the deity according to the rules with twice as many materials as required by the number of days, one should feed many Brahmins.
If worship is omitted for one month according to the highest of the high paths,

O best of the twice-born, one should bathe the deity according to the rules as previously described and perform the rites of pacification and so forth. This applies from before three years have passed and after one month [of omission].
But in the event of an omission of worship to the deity, one should likewise perform a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
Having worshipped the deity according to the rules with twice as many materials as the number of months [elapsed], one should feed a thousand twice-born men.
If worship is neglected for more than three years in the case of a human-made image,
one should perform a re-consecration; however, in the case of self-manifested images and the like,
one should perform a ritual sprinkling as well as a ceremonial bath with a thousand jars.
O twice-born ones, in a place fashioned by humans, if there is a lapse in worship or other duties,
one must perform an expiation before engaging in daily worship and so forth.
However, in a place that is self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) and the like, even when a lapse in worship occurs, [no such requirement applies].
While the worship is being performed, one should perform an expiation for the sacrificial fuel,

the enclosing sticks, the *darbha* grass, the ritual brooms (*kūrca*), and the oblations; likewise for the vessels such as the clarified butter pot, the fire, and the altar-mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In the absence of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, or if they lack their defining characteristics,
the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations for the sake of pacification as before, using the five pervasive [mantras].
This applies when these [utensils] have been broken, cut, or subjected to burning by fire, and so forth.
Having again entered the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), one should perform the *śānti* oblation (*homa*).
In the absence of wooden fuel-sticks (*kāṣṭha-samidh*), one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) and sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
In the absence of fuel-sticks and clarified butter, however, one should perform the oblation with sesame seeds (*tila*).
In the absence of other oblations, the wise man should offer clarified butter (*ājya*).
By all means, for the sake of the fire-offering (*homa*), one must not omit sesame seeds or clarified butter;
for in the absence of sesame and clarified butter, the sacrifice would be fruitless.
One should perform a *śānti* oblation for the removal of that defect, once the fire has followed its course in the hearth, the sacrificial pit, the ground, or the stove, and has been consecrated;
having rekindled it and performed the consecration again, one should offer the *śānti* oblation and other rites.
If the ritual for the installation of the fire and other rites are performed incorrectly due to delusion,
one should perform the pacifying oblation (*śāntihoma*) again after restoring it according to the rules.
Likewise, if the fire is touched by those who are untouchable, such as hair, bones, or nails, [the same rite must be performed].
One should offer oblations of clarified butter one hundred times with the root mantra as prescribed;
however, if one has come into close proximity with a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, or others such as these, one should offer ten thousand oblations.
If one has been touched by another [impure person], having composed oneself in meditative concentration, one should offer ten thousand oblations and likewise recite the mantra ten thousand times.
If the fire has not been properly kindled when the oblation is offered, one should perform the homa again.
In the case of occasional rites, optional rites, and especially during festivals,
one should perform the sacrifice to the fire that is part of that rite in another sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
If an inversion occurs through delusion, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*).
If the remnants of the oblation have been consumed by unworthy persons,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the root mantra ten thousand times for the donor’s pacification of sin.
If, having intended the sacrifice at times of one, two, three, four, five, or six [units], the oblation up to the end of the *homa* has been performed,
the best of mantra-knowers should perform the oblation twice, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*.
If the fire-oblation (*homa*) is omitted for one day up to the end of a month,
one should bathe Puruṣottama according to the lower or higher method and perform the rite of oblation with double the respective materials.

If the fire-oblation (homa) is omitted for more than a month but less than a year, one should perform the lowest and highest forms of ritual bathing and the pacification oblation (śāntihoma) with a thousand offerings. However, if the omission of the oblation exceeds one year, one should perform the middle and highest forms of ritual bathing.
One should perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), the gift of a cow, and the feeding of Brahmins.
In the event of the falling of the sacrificial materials, the preceptor should discard them and offer a new oblation;
having thus offered the oblation for the sake of that pacification, he should then perform the *śāntihoma*.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, upon touching objects belonging to a *balī* that are untouchable;
and likewise, when one's preferred vessel is defiled by hair, a clod of earth, or the like—
one should discard it, perform the rite with another vessel, and mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one wishes to offer a *bali* with a malevolent intent, it should be preceded by a propitiatory *homa*.
Having offered the *bali*, especially while reciting the mantra of the retinue (*parivāra*),
one should perform the mudrās, mantras, ritual actions, and meditations, which take the form of enjoyments through the various substances.
If, specifically at the time of the offering, there occurs a deficiency in the various musical notes of the songs, or in the rhythm, dance, and so forth,
the mantra-practitioner, endowed with meditative concentration, should recite the root mantra one thousand times.
If the image of the deity (balibimba) situated on the vehicle is crowded by unqualified people,
one should sprinkle it with water mixed with kuśa grass and perform a pacifying fire-offering (śāntihoma).
If the carriers of the deity's image have been touched by those who are untouchable (aspṛśya), [the same rite should be performed].
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with another pure substance, one should carry it forth.
At the time of the bali offering, if the lamp is extinguished, one should relight the lamp,
complete the remainder of the festival, and then perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
Once the image of Bali has been placed upon the palanquin and so forth, the lords of sages should install it as before; thereafter, one should carry away the remains of the offering.
To pacify any defects therein, one should bathe the Lord with nine jars.
Even when a consecrated image falls from a vehicle, one should perform the rite of pacification in this same manner.
But when an image intended for constant festivals falls to the ground from a vehicle,
the knower of mantras should immediately lift that image, bathe it while it is still intact, and perform the rite.
Following this, one should perform oblations according to the lowest-of-the-low path for the sake of pacification;
likewise, having restored the damaged image to its former state,
one should perform the rite of consecration and subsequently install it in its proper place.
For as long as the time of the ritual concentration lasts, or for that duration,
one should perform the daily festival of Hari using a lotus stalk, another image, or even by the falling of flowers and other offerings upon the head of the sacrificial image.
Furthermore, upon the falling of the crown, to pacify that fault,
one should perform a ritual bathing with nine jars and a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). Likewise,
when a courtesan falls while dancing at the time of the bali offering, [the same rites should be performed].

O best of the twice-born, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa) for the pacification of those faults. O brahmins, if the offering of the bali-oblation is omitted during a single period of worship and so forth, or if it is omitted on a single day, one should offer double the amount of the bali.
If the offering of bali has been omitted, one should then perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra;
thereafter, one should offer a hundred oblations each, using ghee mixed with sesame seeds, to the deities of each respective enclosure and gateway according to their individual names.
From two days up to the end of a month, and beyond that until the end of a year;
and after a year, if the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) is omitted, it is the lowest of the low.
The bathing (*snapana*), however, is respectively the highest, the middle, and the highest [of its own categories]. (19.450–19.451)
One should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) with double the quantity of materials for the bali offering,

if either birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtāśauca) is heard of at the time of worship. O Brahmins, the best of preceptors (deśikottama) should observe the period of impurity after the conclusion of the worship.
If, through delusion, a confusion of Siddhāntas occurs during the daily worship of the Deity and so forth,
or if a confusion of Saṃhitās arises, then for the pacification of that fault,
one should first perform a ritual sprinkling followed by an ablution with a thousand jars.
One should perform a great festival; otherwise, peace is not desired.
O lords of sages, if a teacher has been initiated into one tantra or one *siddhānta*, he should not perform worship and other rites elsewhere, O twice-born ones. (19.455)
Whether in a division of Tantras or a division of Siddhāntas, during festivals and the like,

one must not perform the office of an Ācārya or act as a sacrificial priest out of delusion; for such an act leads to fault, resulting in the destruction of the king, the kingdom, and the sacred abode.
When [the deity] has been installed and worshipped according to the path taught in the *Pañcarātra*,

or when it has been worshipped by the *Vaikhānasas*, one should perform the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) once again. Likewise, one should not practice a confusion of ritual forms (*karmabimba*) among them.
O twice-born ones, whatever ritual action has been prescribed for rites such as the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and so forth,
one should perform it upon that very image of the deity;
indeed, when that specific image representing the object of the rite is present there, one should act accordingly.
One should not perform a transposition of those various specific rites,
for in their absence there would be faults such as the destruction of the kingdom;
rather, that which is appropriate to the particular place and time should be present therein.
Whatever ritual action constitutes the form of the goal, one should perform all of that there.
This includes both types of ablutions— namely the regular and the occasional—
as well as the regulations for the regular festival and likewise the occasional festival.
The procedure for pilgrimage, and thus these five rites indeed;
then one should perform the rite of the reclining and the rising upon the *kūrca*.
Alternatively, when the consecrated image is being worshipped for the sake of beauty.
Thus it has been taught: when a single image is present, [the rite is performed as described];

but when two images are present, having performed all the other [preliminary] steps according to the requirements, one should proceed accordingly according to the distinctions of their respective activities. 19.465–466.
Having reflected thus, one should perform [the rite] once each respective image has been manifested;
indeed, this applies to all ritual images when they are present there.
At that time, one must not effect a transposition of those images.
If a reversal occurs due to negligence, one should perform the supreme ritual bathing.
Hereafter, I shall explain the expiation for the festival,
following the planting of the sprouts intended for all subsequent rites.

In those that are red or dark-colored, as well as those moving horizontally, those that are curved, those that have not fully grown, those facing south, those lacking the prescribed rites, those touched by the untouchable, and those without the appointed officiants— [these are inauspicious]. || 19.470 ||
If the *pālikā* vessels and so forth are broken, lost, or fallen,
or if they have been bitten by mice and other such creatures, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times;
having then performed the sowing of sprouts once more, one should carry out the *śānti* fire-oblation.
O twice-born ones, when seeds have been sown in earthen vessels that were used only once, no great fault arises, O Brahmins; however,
for the sake of pacifying that, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering and again sow the sprouts.
One should perform [the sowing] in earthen pots and the like produced from anthills and similar sources.
Having abandoned those, one should perform the sowing of seeds in other vessels;
likewise, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should feed a hundred Brahmins.
O twice-born ones, having prepared the sprouts for the sake of the ritual, if those rituals are not performed,
one should abandon even those sprouts and perform a *śānti* oblation. However,
if a great festival has already commenced through delusion and the sprouts have not been offered, [one must proceed accordingly].
Having performed that immediately on the following day according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform a *śānti* oblation for the removal of that defect,
O lords of sages, when a transposition of deities has occurred in the *pālikā* and other vessels.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma).
Likewise, in the event that the positions of the *pālikā* vessels and so forth are interchanged,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and re-establish them in their proper order.
O twice-born ones, if the characteristics and other qualities of vessels such as the *pālikā* are deficient,
one should mutter the eight-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times while the vessels are held in the hands of the preceptor (*deśika*) or others, or those of the God of gods.
O best of sages, if the auspicious thread (kautukasūtra) is lost or broken,
one should fasten another thread and perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
O most excellent of sages, [this applies] when beginning a rite without having performed the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha).
Having immediately bound the *pratisara* amulet, one should perform the *śāntihoma* sacrifice.
During great festivals and other celebrations, during rites such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*),
or during rituals such as ritual bathing (*snāna*), the Guru should have the *pratisara* bound [upon himself].
Likewise, even if impurity should arise during the performance, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) do not become impure; they remain so until the conclusion of each respective rite.
Whether it be impurity due to death (śāva) or birth (sūtaka), one should observe it immediately after the ritual act.

If a death occurs while one is in the midst of performing a ritual, only a bath should be performed. Or, even in the midst of a rite, impurity shall apply if one who is "connected to oneself" has died;
father, mother, eldest son, and wife are recorded as being connected to oneself.
Then, having obtained the permission of his guru, another supreme preceptor,
for the sake of pacifying that fault, shall bathe the deity according to the most excellent path and offer a thousand oblations for the sake of peace.
Having given gifts such as cows, land, and sesame seeds, one should feed many Brahmins.
Then, provided with food, one should complete the remainder of the ritual.
In this same manner, if the Guru is ill or deceased, another person should perform the rites.
O best of the twice-born, having first performed the expiation for the remainder of his karma,
[he should be placed] upon a banner with a young child as its emblem, on a cloth or a scroll that lacks any [specific] measurement,
and upon a bamboo staff marked at the top with colors, ornaments, and names.
In the case of a broken jar, a well, a seat, a water-station, or the ropes of a banner,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śānti-homa) and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
This applies when [the vessel] is cracked, split, burnt by fire, lost, or bitten by a mouse.
If [the banner] is defiled by feces, urine, blood, undrinkable liquids, semen, spittle, and so forth,
one should discard the banner and perform the rite again with another [banner] as previously described.
Then, having installed it, the lowest [class of person] should bring it to the tip of the staff.
Having bathed [the image], one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter for the sake of pacifying defects.
Then, the consecrated twice-born should perform a protective rite for the cloth of the banner at the top of the pillar;
there is no fault in their climbing it for the purpose of protection.
If the rope of the banner is severed, or if the banner is slightly torn,
or if it is deprived of its staff and bell, one should perform a *śānti* oblation.
Having discarded the old, worn-out foam-staffs and so forth, one should then install others.
Having consecrated it, one should quickly join it there after fastening the banner.
At the conclusion of the midday ablution,
one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the celestial banner whose color has faded from exposure to rain, wind, and sun.

Nothing at all undesirable would occur as long as the festival lasts, even if the cloth banner tied to the top of the pillar were to fall from the base due to the force of the wind or other causes, provided the pillar itself remains intact. However,
if the base is severed and the pillar falls along with its banner, [disaster follows].
Without causing the separation of the banner, one should promptly install the remainder;
one should perform the supreme ritual bathing and the worship of the four locations,
and carry out the giving of cows, land, gold, sesame seeds, and other gifts according to one's capacity.
Through the breaking of the festival banner, the king shall fall from his kingdom;
therefore, to avoid that, one should perform a propitiatory rite with haste.
If the banner falls to the ground due to causes such as the force of the wind, [one must act].
Having quickly lifted and bound that [image], one should perform a ritual bath with the lowest [type of materials].
For the sake of pacification, one should offer clarified butter with sesame seeds a hundred times.
When the banner has fallen or been broken, one should perform the highest type of ritual bath.
Having produced another [image], one should likewise consecrate it;

otherwise, if there were a fault, it would affect the king, the kingdom, and the ministers. At the time of the circumambulation of the village, if the banner [falls] to the ground due to the wind or other causes, [the following applies].
When that vehicle has fallen, one should place it back upon it and lead it to the temple;
then, having bathed it with the *adhamādhamena* [mantra], one should perform a *śānti-homa*.
If it was once employed at a pillar or similar structure and is employed there again, [the same rite applies].
One should perform the ritual bathing and the rite for peace according to the lowest and highest paths.
If, out of delusion, one should bind the banner and cloth in reverse order,
one must release that and bind another according to the lowest-of-the-lowest path.
One should perform a ceremonial bath (snapana) and a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the removal of defects.
[This applies] when the jar presided over by the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is lost or has fallen to the ground,
or has been touched by those who are untouchable, as well as by hair, clods of earth, bones, excrement, and so forth.
Having transferred that power residing within the jar into another jar,
and having offered oblations and recited the root mantra ten thousand times, one should perform the remaining rites.
O best of the twice-born, this applies even when the time for hoisting the banner has already passed.
One should perform either a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) or a thousand recitations; or,
when the flagstaff has been slightly scorched by fire, having repaired it as before,
one should perform the pacifying oblation for the removal of that defect.
O twice-born ones, in the event of a great fire, cutting, or breaking of a pillar,
the best of preceptors should install another pillar according to the supreme method for the deity, and perform the ceremonial bathing and the propitiatory fire-offering.
If the flagpole is defiled by contact with a Caṇḍāla, a woman in her courses, or others of that sort,
one should discard it, install another, and perform the propitiatory rite as previously described.
This also applies if it has been touched by those in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (pretaka), or by those born of inverse unions (pratiloma).
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the pacificatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
O lords of sages, if there is an omission of worship for the Lord of Birds (khageśa) on the flagstaff,
one should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) prescribed for an omission of worship, as previously stated.
In the act of striking the kettledrum for the purpose of invoking the deities,
or when the entire array of musical instruments— such as the mṛdaṅga, paṇava, and others— is not placed in its proper position, resulting in the omission of their respective worship; 19.519–19.520.

In the absence of the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should chant the *Mūlamantra* one thousand times; likewise, in the event of the omission of the sounding of the drum, one should perform those respective rites according to the scriptures. Having bathed the deity according to the prescribed rule by means of the lowest of the low methods, [one should proceed].
Furthermore, one should perform that striking again, preceded by a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa).
O best of the twice-born, at the time of striking the drum, if the corner is broken,
or if the skin is torn, [one must likewise act] preceded by a propitiatory fire-offering.
Having recited the Gārutmata mantra, one should again perform another rite:
one should strike the drum according to the rules with the *āvāhana-gāthā*.
[One should likewise act] toward the spirits together with their hosts, and in houses, on elevated places, and so forth.
In their respective directions according to rule, even when no one has been invited;
at the gates, enclosures, and streets, and in the village dwellings in due order;
likewise, where the offering of oblations is omitted, as well as in the case of cymbals, musical tones, and so forth.
When the songs and dances have failed, preceded by rites for peace and fire-offerings,
one should subsequently recite the mantra of each deity eight times.
Then, one should perform everything again, beginning with the invocation of the deities.

O best of men, if the initial ablution is deficient, one should bathe the deity preceded by a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*). If the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) is omitted, one should perform the oblation twice over, preceded by a peace-offering. (19.528–19.529)
If, through negligence, the worship of the door-keepers or of the sacrificial hall is omitted,
one should recite their respective mantras eight times and worship them once again.
O best of the twice-born, if the worship of the four stations is omitted for a single session, [the same penance applies].
One should perform worship preceded by a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*) using double the usual materials.
If there has been a lapse in worship for one day for the deity stationed in the four locations,
one should bathe the deity according to the rules following the lowest-of-the-low method.
O best of beings, having first performed a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should worship with double the usual materials if a breach or a crack occurs in the great jar (*mahākumbha*).
Likewise, if it is touched by those who are untouchable, one should [perform the rite] upon the ground of the mandala to restore its power.

Having invoked [the deity] into that jar, one should discard it and, having invoked [the deity] again as before into another jar possessing the proper characteristics, one should worship and perform the rite of pacification (śānti).
O twice-born ones, when such defects arise even in the mandala, the procedure is the same.

Having invoked the deity into the pitcher, one should perform everything as before. In the case of a mandala that is defective due to being dug up by an anthill or being loose, one should release the deities residing therein into the pitcher, dig up that altar, and fill it with sand.
Having drawn the maṇḍala again as before,

he should worship the deity there for the pacification of that fault; the best of preceptors, having bathed the deity according to the lowest-of-the-low path, should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).

In the event of the loss of the banner, the archway, the water-pots, the tufts of grass, the sprouts, the cloths, the images, the grains, the pedestals, and so forth, one should perform a rite of pacification;
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should arrange it according to the scriptures.

O lords of sages, when a fire has broken out and destroyed banners, archways, pedestals, water-stalls, pavilions, vessels, or any other such items that constitute the limbs [of the ritual site], one must have them produced once again. || 19.540–19.541 ||
O lords of sages, if by negligence the sacrificial fire of the festival should be extinguished, one should perform a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) and likewise recite the root mantra; then,
having re-established the fire and invoked the deity as before, [the rite should proceed].

One should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and feed a hundred Brahmins. O best of sages, when the lamp in the sacrificial hall has gone out, one should kindle the lamp again as before, preceded by a peace-offering.
O best of the twice-born, one should recite the Netra-mantra one hundred and eight times.
[One must avoid contact with] Caṇḍālas, women who have recently given birth, menstruating women, donkeys, dogs, pigs,
camels, and the like, as well as those in a state of birth-impurity (sūtakin) and those born of inverse unions (pratiloma).
Having entered within the sacrificial hall, and having duly invoked the deities residing in the pitcher, the mandala, and the fire into one's own heart,
one should then set aside the pitcher, the mandala, the fire, and so forth, provided they are made of metal.
Having thoroughly purified those vessels by means of wiping, sweeping, and other such methods,
and having cleansed the sacrificial hall, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Then,
having again established the jars and other implements, the deities residing in the heart [should be invoked].
Having invoked [the deity] as before, one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
Having recited the root mantra ten thousand times, one should feed a hundred Brahmins.
Every night, upon the exchange of the offering materials, there should be a hundred oblations of clarified butter.
Having offered oblations into the fire with the root mantra, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
At that time, one should offer the *bali* exactly as it is obtained at that moment.
If there is a transposition of the deities of the *bali*, the recitation and the fire-offering should be performed in the same manner.
O twice-born ones, if the village offering has not been made in the temple of the Lord of Horses,
one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of that fault.
Furthermore, during festivals, two offerings must be performed every morning and evening.

In the event of the defect of deficiency or excess [in the image], one should bathe the deity according to the rules following the inferior or superior procedure and perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). O best of men, if the vehicle occupied by the image should fall to the ground—
Having removed the remnants of the festival and bathed the Lord with new jars,
the best of preceptors should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
[This applies] when the vehicles have been occupied by the image, or in the event of a fall or other such mishap.
Even if the mounts should break down anywhere through negligence,
having placed [the deity] upon another vehicle or mount out of curiosity,
one should first perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) and then recite the root mantra a thousand times.
One should give gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth, even to the preceptor, for the sake of the Vaiṣṇavas.
When the image has fallen from its vehicle or its mount,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering after having arranged an excellent funeral rite.
Having placed that image upon a vehicle, one should perform the festival once again;
likewise, having restored the damaged image to its former state,
and having performed the ritual sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa), one should thereafter carry out the remainder of the festival.
In a long-duration meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one may perform it for the sake of beauty or as a matter of curiosity.
When the remaining rites of the great image have been completed and the rite of consecration (*sandhikarman*) has been finished,
having installed it as before, one should duly perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*).
When the vehicle has been consecrated by the image and is being carried by persons who are untouchable,
one should wash the deity’s vehicles and so forth from the lowest of low paths. When the vehicle is being carried by them, one should bathe it with pure water alone.
Having washed the vehicle according to the rules, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
When the light goes out during the festival of the deity,
or when the lamp falls, the knower of mantras should [perform the rite] with the root mantra.
Having offered one thousand and eight oblations, one should recite [the mantra] that same number of times;

but if the parasol, the fly-whisk, or other such items fall, one should recite it one hundred times. When a fire has broken out, having produced those [items] once again, [one should perform the rite].
One should perform the peaceful *homa* with recitation one hundred and eight times.
When death occurs in a village during the festival of the deity,
one should subsequently sprinkle the village according to the lowest of the low methods.
Thereafter, one should bathe the deity and perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
When the village or other areas have been defiled by a fire during the festival of the deity,
the wise man, having sprinkled the village and so forth with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [should proceed].
Having performed the *śānti* oblation, one should then perform the festival again.

(19.570) If a village or similar place has been scorched by fire, or defiled by a whirlwind, a downpour of rain, and so forth, one should first perform the *śānti* oblation and afterwards perform the festival. (19.571)
Otherwise, when a festival has been arranged according to the inferior or superior methods,
one should bathe the deity according to the rules and perform a *śānti* oblation.
One should also hold a festival in deserted villages, cities, towns, and so forth.
One should not perform the offering of a sacrificial victim (balidāna); if it is performed there, it is fruitless.
The preceptor (deśika) should perform the festival and the offering of the victim in the temple itself;
otherwise, by acting differently, one violates the most excellent path regarding the deity.

Having performed the ritual bathing, one should perform a *śānti*-oblation (*śāntihoma*) for the pacification of those defects. When the village and its surroundings have become composed, one should again hold a festival preceded by a village-purification rite (*grāmaśānti*), with the permission of the Brahmins.
O tigers among sages, if an obstacle arises due to fear of enemies, thieves, fire, rain, or the like during some festival, one should perform only the bali offering;
once the festival has passed, one should perform it on another day preceded by rites for peace (śānti).
If the offering of the bali-oblation is obstructed, then on another day— whether it be a lower or higher one—
one should perform a ceremonial bath and a pacifying fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), and having thus completed the festival that was missed,
one should perform the bali-offering for two or three days.
Or, if the festival is interrupted for four or five days,
one should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) according to the specific fault incurred,
and then conduct the festivals that were passed over as well as the offerings of oblations (balidāna) in their proper sequence.
During the festival of the deity, if the image is touched by great winds, heat, dust, rain, or frost, it becomes either inferior or superior;
for the pacification of that defect, one should perform a ritual bathing and a fire-offering for peace.
When the image has been lost by thieves or others during a great festival,
one should procure another image and re-install it as before,
performing the great consecration, the fire sacrifice, and the recitation of mantras according to the prescribed rule.
One should complete the remainder of the festival, but one should not perform rituals such as the worship of the image.
However, at the time of the chariot procession, if there is a break in the wheel, a fracture of the axle,
or even a snapping of the rope, one should join another [rope] and proceed as before.
At the conclusion of the journey, one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) for the pacification of any defects [caused by those incidents].
If the crest-pot (*śikhākumbha*) falls, or if the charioteer falls,
one should re-establish it as before and perform the *puṇyāhavācana* rite.
Having sprinkled the chariot at the conclusion of the procession, one should perform the *śānti* oblation; however,
if those unworthy have ascended the chariot, one should sprinkle the chariot with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) by way of the lowest of the low paths.

One should bathe the Lord of the God of Gods on the chariot; if it has been somewhat scorched by fire, one should restore it to its original state and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). At the conclusion of the procession, one should perform the ceremonial bath, known as either the inferior or the superior.
When the chariot has been severely burned, one should place the deity upon a palanquin and lead him to the temple by the most excellent path;
then one should perform the ceremonial bathing, the propitiatory fire-offering, and the feeding of Brahmins.
If Bimba falls from the chariot, or if a bird alights upon the chariot,
one should then place the deity back [upon it], lead him to the temple by the most excellent path, and perform the ritual bathing as well as the fire sacrifice.

Having performed ten thousand recitations of the root mantra and having given gifts such as cows, land, and sesame seeds, one should feed a thousand twice-born brahmins for the sake of pacifying that fault.
In the event of the falling of the image or the chariot itself, one should perform the rites as previously described.

O best of the twice-born, in the event of a chariot breaking, the preceptor should repair it and, having completed the remainder of the festival, perform an oblation for the sake of peace. If the chariot cannot be repaired, he should place the deity upon a bird and proceed.
Having led the deity to his abode by way of either the lowest or the highest path,
one should bathe him and perform rites such as the *śānti*-oblation for the pacification of that fault.
This applies when a human death has occurred due to being struck by a chariot wheel or similar means.

Having carried the corpse outside and performed the five purifications in sequence, such as digging at that spot, one should, at the conclusion of the procession— whether it be for the lowest or the highest [caste]—
perform the ritual bathing, the fire-oblation for peace, and the feeding of Brahmins.
In the event of the death of an animal due to a blow from a wheel or similar cause, one should perform the rites as previously described.
All procedures beginning with the purification of the ground should be carried out, but the ritual bathing is of the lowest-of-the-low order.
Likewise, during the time of a procession, [death may occur] due to mutual conflict involving weapons and the like.
In the event of a person's death near a chariot, the expiation is declared to be as previously stated.
If the chariot is touched by its blood or other such substances, one should wash the chariot with water,
sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and at the conclusion of the journey, perform the lowest of the low rites.

The most excellent of preceptors should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) at the time of the chariot festival, whether in that village or anywhere else. In the event of the death of Brahmins or others, their corpse [should be taken] outside the village.
Having cleared the village streets by sweeping, scrubbing, and other means,
and having purified them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sprinkled them with water, one should undertake the procession.
Then, one should perform the lowest-of-the-low ablution and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
When one, two, or three days have passed and the chariot has returned to its own place,
having performed the ritual bathing and the fire-oblation according to the inferior or superior path,
one should then perform the concluding festival and the bali offering.
Likewise, on a festival day of a holy site, when the chariot has not yet entered the grounds,
one should descend the deity from the chariot and place him upon the lord of birds (the Garuda vehicle),
and lead him in circumambulation of the village by way of the most excellent path.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the peace-offering (śāntihoma), and once the festival has concluded,

one should present the sacrificial offering (balidāna) and thereafter perform the pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrtha) and other rites. However, if the mounting of the chariot is obstructed, this should be done within one, two, or three days.
Having performed the ritual bathing and fire-oblation according to the inferior or superior path,
and having fed the twice-born, one should immediately perform the chariot festival. However,
if the chariot festival is obstructed for one, two, three, or four years, [the following should be done].
Having performed the supreme ablution, the fire sacrifice, the feeding of a thousand brahmins,

and the gift of cows, land, and so forth, one should perform the sprinkling of the chariot. Then, having worshipped the deities stationed upon the chariot with the Khageśa mantra, [one should proceed].
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and rice,
one should offer eight separate oblations with the mantras of the deities stationed on the chariot.
Having performed this, one should then conduct the chariot procession of the God.
O lords of sages, during the rites of the spring festival which forms part of the great festival, as well as during the swing festival, the hunting festival, and other such festivities;
at the commencement of battle, and likewise during the ceremonial sprinkling with powders by the two goddesses—
If [the timing] is lost, one should perform a *śānti* oblation for the pacification of those respective defects.

(19.615) Even when there is a lapse of a *muhūrta* during a festival or any ritual action, one should likewise perform a *śānti* oblation and a recitation (*japa*) of one hundred and eight [times]. (19.616)
One should perform the festival by day and night, from sunrise until sunset;
if the two times are reversed, one should perform the lower-grade ablution.
A pilgrimage to a sacred ford (tīrtha) should be undertaken before the setting of the sun.
One should perform the supreme ablution (uttama-snapana) either in the first part of the night or during the manifestation of one's own deity;
this should be done when the proper time for pilgrimage has passed or when the pilgrimage has been lost, after having descended from the banner of the bird (khagadhvaja).
Having raised the banner as before, one should perform a festival for the sake of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
If the sprinkling with the water-pot (*kumbha-prokṣaṇa*) is omitted, then a bath of middling or superior quality [must be performed].
If the bath at the conclusion of the great festival has not been performed, one should then cause [the deity] to bathe.
Then, for the sake of pacification, one should perform the oblation by means of the most excellent path.
One who desires all forms of pacification should do so at night; one desiring nourishment, at midday;
one desiring growth, in the forenoon; and one desiring dharma, at midnight.
Likewise, one who desires the destruction of enemies should perform a flower sacrifice;
however, one should not worship with flowers that are stale or withered.
To pacify the fault of that [offering], one should perform the lowest of the low ablution rites.
If this flower sacrifice has not been performed, one should perform the supreme ritual bathing.
On that night, having lowered the bird-banner from the tip of the flagpole,
and having offered the bali-oblation to those residing in the village and other dwellings, one should dismiss it.
If the banner is lost at the conclusion of the festival before the descent,
one should raise the banner again as before and then perform the descent once more.
Even if the descent occurs more than five days after the end of the pilgrimage site [the festival], [one should act accordingly].
One should perform the bathing ceremony for the banner in either the middling or the superior manner.
After lowering the banner, one should then dismiss the deities.
In the event of an omission regarding the dismissal offering (*udvāsanabali*), it must be preceded by a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*).
Having offered double the sacrificial fee (bali), one should perform the ritual dismissal of the deities.
If the preceptor (ācārya) lacks a sacrificial fee, that festival shall be fruitless. The same applies if the officiating priests (ṛtvij) likewise lack a sacrificial fee for the preceptor.
Whatever action is performed, all of it may lead to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying that, the patron himself should then have the preceptor perform a *śānti* oblation,
having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before the preceptor.
The wise man should cause satisfaction to be given through garments, gold, and rings;
he should give double the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and by that, peace will come.
Even in the event of the omission of feeding the twice-born, one should likewise perform this rite for peace.
Hari is never pleased when the Brahmins are dissatisfied;
but where the Brahmins are satisfied, there the God is propitiated.
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying that fault, one should feed twice as many twice-born men.
O Brahmins, if due to fate, human causes, or even disturbances in the kingdom, the great festival remains uncommenced for one, two, or three days,
one should seek permission from the Brahmins regarding the lowest or highest [status] of the Lord of Gods.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), and having fed the Brahmins;
then, preceded by the ritual sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) with double the usual quantities of materials,
and having completed the concluding festivities, one should then perform the rites that follow in due order.

If the festival has not yet commenced, one should perform the bathing for four or five days as either a middling or superior rite to pacify those defects; one should perform everything else as previously described. (19.638) If, however, [the festival] has not begun within six or seven days, [one should act accordingly].

The bathing according to the supreme-of-the-supreme path is as follows; otherwise, it is as before. Likewise, if the great festival has not yet commenced by the end of the eighth day, one should bathe the deity with a thousand pitchers and perform the remaining rites as previously described.
Alternatively, O Brahmins, the festival should be commenced on the day of the *tīrtha*;
likewise, O best of the twice-born, even when that *tīrtha* day has passed,
it should be performed according to the position of the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*) associated with the *tīrtha* during that month.
One should perform the festival once again for the pacification of all defects.
Even when that month has passed, it should be performed in the following month;
thus it should continue until the end of the year, even when the year itself has elapsed.
O twice-born ones, one should cause the bathing with a thousand jars, the fire-sacrifice for peace (*śāntihoma*), the recitation of mantras (*japa*),
and the feeding of a thousand Brahmins to be performed;
by that alone peace is attained, and one should not perform a festival for one whose life has departed.
O twice-born ones, whatever was previously resolved for the festivities preceding a wedding ceremony, lasting for as many days as the celebration, that shall remain so every year;
one should not arrange the festival for fewer or more days than that.
If the ministers should perform [the rites], one should celebrate the festival again when special occasions arise or while a great festival is underway;
on the twelfth day and so forth, one should perform all of that according to the proper rule.
A wise practitioner should not, with effort, omit that which has been specifically prescribed.
Furthermore, for the sake of pacification when [rites] have not been performed, the mantra-reciter should recite the weapon-mantra ten thousand times.
O best of sages, this applies to such and other defects.
One should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) according to the scriptures in the festival fire;
however, when the festival rites have been omitted, even the lowest of the low should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana).
One should also especially perform the offering of sacrificial oblations (havirnivedana).
If the festival of Śravaṇa and the others has been omitted, one should perform the ablution— whether it be the inferior or the superior rite—

either when the Kṛttikā-lamp has been omitted or in the month immediately following it; specifically, one should perform the ablution— whether it be the inferior or the superior rite— under the constellation of Agni (Kṛttikā).
One should perform the Festival of Lights preceded by a peace-offering oblation (*śānti-homa*);
likewise, O best of sages, in other festivals that have been omitted,
one should do so either in the month following them or on the specific day of each respective festival.
One should perform the festival as before, preceded by ritual bathing and fire oblations (homa).
O twice-born ones, I shall now declare the expiation for the Pavitrāropaṇa rite:
if the sacred thread (pavitra) is of improper measure, one should recite the Astra-mantra ten thousand times.
But during the aforementioned time, in the middle of the four-month period,
having performed the intermediate bathing, one should then perform it at another time.
[One should avoid] sacred threads, hair, stones, skins, charcoal, nails, and so forth.
If it has been defiled, burnt by fire, cut, bitten,

or excessively chewed by mice and the like, or touched by crows and other such creatures, one should discard it and then prepare another of that same kind according to the rules and perform the consecration (adhivāsana).
Thus, when the offering of impure *pavitra* has been performed out of delusion,

one should discard that [impure one] and, having bathed the Lord of Gods according to the methods for the inferior or superior [rite], and having offered oblations for the sake of pacification, one should present a pure *pavitra*.
But if the investiture with the *pavitra* for the deity is performed out of sequence,

one should then perform a *śānti*-oblation and carry out a thousand-fold recitation (*japa*). Once the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) has passed, [one should proceed] from the pure sacrificial expansion.
O lords of sages, if the pilgrimage to the sacred ford (*pavitrikī tīrthayātrā*) has not been performed, one should offer the *pavitra* to the Lord in another [image] preceded by rites for peace;
having performed the supreme ablution, one should then conduct the festival again.
When the purifier (pavitra) has been employed for those unworthy of the God of gods,
one should then perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) and carry out a thousand-fold recitation (japa).
During the Cāturmāsya period, however, one should perform the festival of the Lord’s reclining (śayanotsava).
In the event of their transposition or omission, the practitioner of mantra should perform worship at the four locations and so forth;
having recited the root mantra ten thousand times, he should likewise offer oblations for the sake of pacification.
If it is for the purpose of installing the water-pot (*kalaśa*), one need not perform the rite of sowing seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
Likewise, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times for the binding of the *pratisara*.
Having again offered those sprouts and tied the *kautuka* on the image, if one does not perform the ritual bathing—whether intentionally or unintentionally—[the following occurs]. (19.666–19.667)
Having first performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should recite the eight-syllable mantra ten thousand times;

then, preceded by the rite of the auspicious thread (kautuka) and the sprouts (aṅkura), one should perform the consecration once again. However, if one has not performed the sacrifice of the sprouts as well as the binding of the auspicious thread, [the rite must be repeated].
If the Lord of Gods has already been bathed, the bathing would be fruitless. Having performed the sowing of sprouts and the binding of the *kautuka* according to the rules,
the mantra-master should bathe him according to the two-fold rite, preceded by a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*).

If the intended ablution has not been performed, one should perform it twice over. Even if the ritual is performed with materials that have not been procured or are deficient, one should act in this same manner.
Furthermore, if the jars have been set out but are deficient, one should set them out again as before.
One should recite the mantra dedicated to the deity of the jar one hundred and eight times.
(19.672) If the jars have been lifted up and become empty due to a hole or similar defect, one should install another as before and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. (19.673)
If a water-jar has been touched or stepped over by a cat, a mouse, or the like;

or if it has come into contact with hair, bone, or a clod of earth; or if it is cracked, broken, or otherwise damaged; or if ants and such creatures have fallen into it, or if it contains cow-products and the like, or if threads or cloth have fallen into it—[it must be purified].
Likewise, in the event of a fire or when a jar has been defiled by the *kālamaṇḍala*,
one should abandon that particular jar and set up another jar again;
having worshipped the deity of the jar, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
If the bathing jar has been set down and is touched by dogs, cocks, or crows;

or even by those who are untouchable, such as menstruating women or women recently delivered; or if it is brought near to or touched by *caṇḍālas* or men in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtakin*); [then it must be purified].
Having discarded all the [old] jars and having established pure ones as before,
one should perform the rite preceded by the declaration of a holy day (*puṇyāha*), and having recited the root mantra a thousand times,
one should separately recite eight times the mantra dedicated to the deity of the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
If the deity has been bathed by the wicked, one should bathe him again with curd,
milk, ghee, and so forth derived from buffaloes, goats, or camels; or even with milk that has been kept for more than a month, mixed with curd.
With curds mixed with milk, with honey mixed with molasses,
with other such mixed substances, as well as with water that has stood overnight,
with unfiltered water, and likewise with water from puddles. || 19.681-19.682 ||
Once the Lord of Gods has been bathed, one should bathe him again and perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of those respective defects. However,
[one should first use] the waters contained in the consecrated jars.

There is no fault of being stale due to the ritual dwellings and such offerings. [But there is fault] in the non-worship of the jars, in worshipping them out of order, in their removal out of order, in their installation, and in the application of the ritual substances. || 19.684–685 ||

O lords of sages, [this applies] when the substance is deficient or excessive, or likewise in the case of a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) or a large jar (*kalaśa*); also in the case of a grass mat (*kūrca*), a cloth, a storehouse (*koṣṭha*), a pedestal (*pīṭha*), an archway (*toraṇa*), and so forth; or when it lacks the prescribed measure, or when there is an absence of a grain-pedestal (*dhānyapīṭha*).
And in the absence of cloth for the sacred thread and other such items, one should recite the mantra one hundred times,

even without songs, auspicious musical instruments, hymns, dances, and the like, as well as without the sounds of lutes and flutes, and likewise without the formal declaration of a "holy day" (puṇyāhavācana). || 19.687–19.688 ||
Without performing an ablution, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
One who seeks liberation should bathe the deity at all times according to the prescribed rule;
however, one who seeks the subjugation of enemies should always perform it during the day.

One who desires heaven should bathe the Lord in the forenoon; one seeking merit and wealth at midday; one desiring all enjoyments at the end of the day; and for those performing penances, at all times. During an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should bathe the Lord at that very moment.
During the sun's transits, both before and after [the exact moment], sixteen nāḍīs each are to be known as the time of transit.
At that time, one should bathe the deity; once it has passed, one should offer oblations with the mantra.
Thereafter, the mantra-practitioner should perform that same rite one thousand times. When the image has been secured with a protective thread (*pratisara*) for the purpose of bathing,
and another bathing occasion arises due to a cause requiring expiation (*prāyaścitta*), [the rite should be performed].
For that purpose, having tied the auspicious thread (kautuka) and completed the ritual bath,
one should perform what was previously commenced immediately after the expiation (prāyaścitta).
In other cases, one should perform it gradually after completing what was previously commenced.
O twice-born ones, if this rite should otherwise become fruitless,
then for the sake of averting that defect, the knower of mantras should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and recitation (japa) one thousand times with the root mantra.
If, however, out of delusion, one should bathe the deity outside the Devamālā before the time of the *avabhṛtha* rite, one should perform a propitiatory *śānti-homa*.
In the case of a multi-armed image, one should take that consecrated statue from the front pavilion (*agramaṇṭapa*).
If the practitioner goes outside for the purpose of bathing while [the deity] has gone out,
he should perform a *śānti* oblation to pacify that fault. Furthermore, if the image falls from its bathing seat while being consecrated, [he should likewise perform a rite].
Having performed the consecration and the ceremonial bathing, one should carry out the *śānti* oblation (*śāntihoma*).
O twice-born ones, especially when there is movement of the image at the time of bathing,
and when there is movement of the bathing altar, one should perform the *śānti* oblation.
When [the image] has been damaged by the breaking of its radiance, pedestal, weapons, garments, or limbs,

the artisans, having fixed the respective power residing within each of those forms while maintaining a sense of wonder, perform the rejoining and then immediately carry out the thorough consecration.
When the remaining ritual actions have been completed, one should perform the ceremonial bath according to the supreme procedure.
