One should offer oblations a thousand times each with sesame seeds, sacrificial porridge, and clarified butter, using the root mantra; by that, peace will be attained.
If, due to the great weight of the effort, one is unable to construct it at that time,

one should perform the remaining rites after placing a beautiful image in front; this applies likewise to images used for festivals, pilgrimages, purposes of wealth, or for lying down [in ritual sleep], and so forth.

O twice-born ones, at the time of seizing the ground, if ill omens arise, one should first perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) and then carry out a thousand-fold recitation (japa), followed by the joining of the respective limbs and so forth, as well as the installation and the subsequent union.
Likewise, when the measuring cord is extended for the purpose of measuring the field—
if that cord is snapped, or if the stakes are torn out, or if the vessel for the *bali* offering falls at the time of offering the *bali* to the spirits— [these are faults]. (19.708–19.709)
O twice-born ones, when earth is being dug up and ashes, charcoal, husks, and the like, or even worms and insects are seen, for their pacification,
one should perform oblations with sesame seeds and clarified butter by the thousands using the Nārasiṃha mantra.
O Brahmins, having first performed the selection of the preceptor (*ācārya-varaṇa*),

one should carry out the ritual acquisition of the ground (*kṣmā-parigraha*) once the temple has been constructed, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas and preceded by a propitiatory fire-offering (*śānti-homa*). || 19.711-19.712 ||
O twice-born ones, even before the foundation stone has been laid for the temple that is being constructed,
the preceptor, accompanied by the patron, should worship with devotion the Lord who resides within the solar disc prior to the installation of the primary image.
"Obeisance to you, O lotus-eyed one, who bestows grace upon your devotees!
O Lord of Gods, you ought to forgive whatever I have done improperly or what I have failed to do.
Having thus prostrated before the Lord of Gods, he took up his dwelling according to the prescribed rite.
Having fashioned a deity there and installed it, one should worship it,
O best of sages, in the excavated area in the middle of the temple site;
even without the construction of a temple, the rites such as the placement of the *kumbha* [pitcher] are to be performed.
Having obtained the permission of the Brahmins and having excavated the center of the palace,
one should perform the placement of the water-pot and other rites there as appropriate;
and one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of all defects.
Even if the ritual placement of the embryo has not been performed, one should likewise perform the placement of the embryo.
Or, if the temple is deficient in the purification of the site and other requirements, or is devoid of the proper characteristics,
one should perform the *śānti-homa* (propitiatory fire-offering) again according to the scriptures.
If the crest-pot has not been established or the temple has not been consecrated, O twice-born ones,
one should perform those respective rites again, preceded by a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa),
as well as for the walls, pavilions, gate-towers, and so forth.

O twice-born ones, when the consecration has not yet been performed, one should first perform rites for peace regarding each respective material— whether wood, metal, stone, or the like— at the time of its collection;
likewise, when ill omens arise or a bad dream is seen.
One should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) with sesame seeds and clarified butter a thousand times using the Nārasiṃha mantra for the pacification of all defects,
as well as when taking possession of wood, metal, stone, clay, cloth, and so forth.
If the substances, mantras, ritual actions, and so forth, which have been proclaimed as the respective ancillaries [of the rite],
should fail, one should perform propitiatory fire-offerings (*śānti-homa*), recitations (*japa*), and the like.
However, if the selection of wood and other materials for the mountain-shaped altar (*parvata*) and such has not yet been made, [one should act accordingly].

When the image has been brought to the site of the temple, the wise one should perform the collection of materials for the worship without fail, even by craftsmen who have not performed the consecration;
this applies when the ritual image and other objects have already been fashioned, even if the formal collection [of materials] has not yet occurred.
Furthermore, one should perform that [rite] preceded by a peace-offering (śāntihoma) regarding the measurements,
proportions, and characteristics of the image, the pedestal, the stone, and so forth; however,
if these are deficient, one should perform a peace-offering to pacify those defects.

O twice-born ones, if the pedestal stone for the image and the male stone (puṃśilā) and so forth are misplaced, one should abandon each of those and fashion [the image] again with stones as prescribed;
for an image that has been fashioned but not quickly installed in its own home [is defective].
It would bring about misfortune for the king, the kingdom, and its creator;
after twenty-one days, she will certainly become an *āsura* woman.
Having performed the great consecration and other rites, one should install her; otherwise, one should abandon her.
During the preliminary consecration of the water, the ritual bathing, as well as the opening of the eyes,
on the bed and the altar, in rites such as the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), in the worship of the jar and the mandala, and regarding the jars at the doors and archways— 19.732–19.733.
If the consecration of the home, the seats (pīṭha), and so forth has not been performed, or has been performed incorrectly,
one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) consisting of a thousand oblations. One should also perform ten thousand recitations of the root mantra and feed one hundred Brahmins.
If an image has been installed in an improper place, provided it is accompanied by a pedestal stone,
one should immediately remove it and re-install it in its own proper place;
having performed the supreme consecration bath, one should carry out the peace-offering rite (*śāntihoma*).
Once this moment for the installation has been fixed, one must not remove the image at that time.
When the ritual bathing and the fire-oblation have been performed as before, peace will prevail.
If the primary preceptor authorized for the installation falls ill, [the following should be done].
Alternatively, when the body has been cast off, or while the sequence of ritual actions is still proceeding,
the instructor of the ritual mantras remains engaged in the rite of consecration;
or the son of the preeminent teacher should perform the remaining rites for the installation.
Having first consecrated the Lord of the Gods with a thousand jars,
he should then perform the rite in the lotus-shaped fire-pit (kuṇḍa) using honey, milk, and other substances in due order.
For the sake of pacification, having offered oblations of honey, he should perform a recitation (japa) of that same number.
O twice-born ones, when a quarrel arises between the preceptor and the patron at the time of the consecration rite and so forth, or even between the officiating priest and the preceptor,
the ritual action becomes fruitless; one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
Having paid homage and honored the Guru, one should utter the words, "May you forgive me.
O lords of sages, even when such faults as these occur,
one should effect their pacification through rites such as propitiatory fire-offerings (homa) and recitation (japa).
O bull among sages,
you have described in various places all the expiations heard from the sages, as well as the rite known as sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
Furthermore, O Sage, we wish to know everything regarding the procedure for pacifying a village, the fire-oblation for pacification (śāntihoma), and the specific rules for performing them. Nārada.
O best of sages, I shall now describe the rules for the ritual sprinkling and other related rites.
Now listen all of you with attentive minds:
when the broken parts of the image, the pedestal, and the celestial chariot have been set together,
and the eight-fold binding of both the image and the pedestal has been performed once again—

When a divine image has been touched by men who are under ritual impurity, by those who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka), by Caṇḍālas, Udkyās, and the like, or by Mlecchas, Pulkasas, and so forth— including Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others— [the following applies].

O twice-born ones, if for one month continuously the Lord’s abode remains occupied, and if out of negligence Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others are authorized to perform rituals in the Lord’s house, or even if they dwell there together with them; 19.750–751.
O best of the twice-born, when an image or a portion of a temple has been touched by corpses;
or when an anthill, loose earth, or bees appear upon an image;
or when an image or a temple has been struck by lightning, O lords of sages— (19.751–19.752)
O brahmins, when the image smiles, or moves, or weeps, or likewise falls,
or wanders, or when sweat, blood, and so forth arise, as well as when it trembles,
or when there is a rain of blood and the like.
O lords of sages,

O best of the twice-born, when the propitiation has been interrupted for more than a month, or when there is a confusion of the *saṃhitās*, or likewise a confusion of the *siddhāntas*, or when the image has been buried underground and then exhumed, [the procedure must be performed] after a month has passed.
One should perform a ritual sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa) for the pacification of those respective defects,
having recognized that the temple, the image, or other such objects have been afflicted by defects.
If one performs worship without having performed the sprinkling, it quickly brings ruin upon both the king and the kingdom.
It would destroy the village and the temple; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a consecration (samprokṣaṇa) must be performed for the temples, images, and so forth.
Prior to the day of consecration, it brings about the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
Having determined [the date], on the day previously announced by those who know the proper time,
one should offer the ritual sprouts according to the rules; thereafter, in a house thoroughly purified,
one should sprinkle it everywhere with cow-dung and water, preceded by the proclamation of a "holy day" (*puṇyāha*).

Having sprinkled [the images] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with kuśa-water, and having performed the washing many times with water consecrated by mantras from the sacred thread (pavitra), using the six substances beginning with white mustard seeds (siddhārthaka) for the primary image (mūlabera) and the other icons; || 19.760–19.761 ||
On the night preceding the principal day,
in the sacrificial pavilion (maṇḍapa) adorned with arches, gates, water-pots (kalaśas), canopies, and banners,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) for initiation in the water-pot situated within the pavilion.
One should perform the worship according to one's means, ending with the recitation of mantras in the root temple;
then, one should bathe the *dhruva* and *kautuka* [images] with milk and other substances twenty-five times,
in front of the image situated on a wall or a cloth, upon an auspicious seat.
Alternatively, having bathed according to the rules with the ritual jars placed in the front pavilion the image of the rite, or its reflection in a mirror held by the *kūrca* grass-bundle,
one [performs the rite] for the festival images and so forth, which consist of the limbs that serve as their substratum.
Worship and bathing should be performed in the western sacrificial pavilion;
there, the oblation should be offered into the fire-pit marked with the signs of the conch, discus, and so forth,
using honey, milk, and other substances, in a number of one hundred thousand.
Apart from the ritual image (*karmabimba*), one should prepare a great bed for the other images, which possess the form of the [deity's] limbs, within the pavilion on the right side;
it should be provided with loads of sesame, rice, and *śāli* grain, along with garments and other such items.
Above that, one should lay the image down according to the rules with the *kautuka* thread tied;
having worshipped it, one should cover it with blankets and the like, and with white and other colors, one should draw a mandala adorned with a wheel and a lotus.
Until the time of dawn, the preceptor should pass the night in the presence of the one situated in the *bimba* by means of the recitation of the root mantra alone.
When the night has turned to dawn, the Guru, having performed the ritual of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vidhi*), [should proceed].
Having performed the worship of the four locations as before, accompanied by the ritual bathing,
and having duly completed everything including the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should dismiss the deity residing in the sacrificial pit and the deity residing in the mandala into one's own heart.
Having dismissed the deities of the door along with the offering of oblations (bali),
when an auspicious moment has arrived, [the image] should be adorned with new garments,
provided with an upper cloth and a sacred thread, and bound with the marriage-thread (kautuka).
Having worshipped, in due order, with water offerings (arghya) and other rites, that which is arrayed across all the principles (tattvas),
[one should contemplate] from the lotus of one's own heart, preceded by a handful of flowers:
that which is ungraspable, undifferentiated, formless, stainless, and great.
Eternal, pure, incomparable, extremely subtle, immovable, manifest, of the nature of existence and consciousness, unique, luminous, very firm, and great—
having thus transmitted that splendor and prostrated like a staff, [he spoke].
O best of the twice-born, having reported all the performed rites to the Lord,
they should raise up the festival image and the others along with the auspicious items as before,
while carrying the great jar in front, accompanied by the image-bearers and others.
Taking up the water-pot weapon (*karakāstra*), the Preceptor should walk in front,
sprinkling the ground with a continuous stream no thicker than a small stick; then,
O best of sages, having led him clockwise into the interior of the temple, he should enter.
One should perform the sprinkling of the water-pot according to the procedure taught for the Great Festival (mahotsava).
One should [also worship] the deities of the doors and enclosures, those residing within the temple,
and all the attendants such as Khageśa, Viṣvaksena, and others.
One should sprinkle [the area] everywhere in sequence with the water remaining in the pitcher;
one should then consecrate the remaining water from the pitcher upon the *balipīṭha*.
Having thus sprinkled according to the rule and having entered inside the temple, [one should proceed].
Then, having cast away from his heart the curiosity held in his hand,
and having given cows, land, gold, and so forth for the pacification of all defects,
he should especially worship the deity with offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial oblation (*haviranta*).
Thereafter, one should feed a thousand or even a hundred Brahmins;
or else, one may perform the entire consecration of the Lord immediately,
preceded by flowers and sprouts, for the pacification of those respective defects.
Neither the lunar day, nor the asterism, nor the specific time of day is required [for this]. O Brahmins, sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa) may be performed immediately, whether by night or by day;
however, if there is a delay in performing the expiation (prāyaścitta), one should observe the proper timing.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the entire procedure for sprinkling has been declared; however,
one must perform the expiation whenever its specific cause arises,
either immediately at the conclusion of that rite or within three days.
According to the gravity of that [offense], the commencement or completion of it may occur within five or seven days; otherwise, one should perform double the penance in all cases,
including at sites such as those self-manifested (*svayamvyakta*).
Now, therefore, O twice-born ones, I shall fully explain the ritual for the pacification of a village:
when there is turmoil in the kingdom, when the village is deserted, or for some other reason;
or when the village has been burnt by fire, or afflicted by whirlwinds, torrential rains, and the like.
Furthermore, when one has become composed in meditation, even if a village where rains of blood, honey,

and so forth have occurred, or where many killings of Brahmins and cows have taken place, or where one has stayed for many days in a village inhabited by Caṇḍālas, Śabaras, and others; || 19.793–19.794 ||
In the event of a great plague or other disease caused by the host of Māras and others,
one should perform a rite for the peace of the village for the sake of pacifying all defects.
O tigers among sages, [one should do this] upon the ground, either throughout that entire village or in a single location.
Having dug up the earth, removed it, and cast it outside with pure [hands],
and having filled [the pit] and leveled it, and having wiped it with *kuśa* grass and water,
one should have the Brahmins perform the circumambulation with fire on all sides.

Having sprinkled it with cow-dung water preceded by the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha), and having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should settle the herd of cows there.

Having fed the twice-born there, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Having thus performed the purification of the site, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) in due order in front of the temple, in the vicinity of the outer door.
One should first have a pavilion constructed, provided with four doors and other such features.
In its center, one should prepare an altar (vedikā) equipped with an upward-facing sacrificial pit (ūrdhvakunda).
Around it, one should arrange either eight or four pits.
Or, O best of the twice-born, one may perform the entire oblation in the central pit;
having gathered all the requisites for the sacrifice, one should remain well-composed.
When the onset of night had arrived, having performed his ablutions and completed his daily rites,
the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, approached the temple of the God of gods and worshipped Him, following His permission.
Having entered the sacrificial hall together with all his attendants,
he should arrange the door-vases and other items there according to the prescribed rite; specifically,
upon the altar above the fire-pit, to the south, he should place a water-pot.
Having placed the great pitcher (mahākumbha), one should place the peace-pitcher (śāntighaṭa) on the left.
Having performed everything beginning with the purification of the hands up to the final heart-sacrifice (hṛdyāga),
and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should sprinkle all the ritual materials (sambhāra) in their entirety.

Having first performed the worship of the doors according to the rule, and having worshipped the Lord in the great pitcher (mahākumbha) with offerings beginning with the arghya and ending with the oblation (havis), as well as the Weapon-mantra (astramantra);
then, O twice-born ones, [they should worship] Vāsudeva and the others around it in the peace-pitcher (śāntighaṭa).
Having duly worshipped Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi,
one should also fully honor the hosts of Vāstu deities right there;
and in the jars situated in those eight directions, one should worship Kumuda and the others.
Then, having duly installed the sacrificial fire in the upper hearth (ūrdhvakuṇḍa) and having gratified the deity there with seven pieces of fuel wood in sequence,
[he should offer oblations] with sesame seeds mixed with ghee, numbering one thousand and eight.
Having performed the libations for the sake of pacification and then extracted the group of fires,
he should distribute them in due order into the sacrificial pits of the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions;
then, having stationed four officiating priests in the cardinal directions beginning with the east, [he should proceed].
With the *vāsudeva* and other mantras, preceded by seven fuel-sticks (*samidh*),
one should satisfy the deities with sesame seeds mixed with ghee, numbering one thousand.
Even thus, through non-union (*ayoga*), [one should worship] starting from Vāyu and ending with Īśāna.
Having arranged the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, in their proper order,
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter (ājya) a thousand times, accompanied by Vaiṣṇava hymns and purifying peace-chants (śāntisūkta).
One should satisfy Śānti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, as well as the hosts of Vāstu deities and the groups beginning with Kumuda, each in due order within the central pit,
with eight oblations of a stream of clarified butter for each.
Brahmā, Marīci, Atri, Vivasvat, the Lord of the Earth,
Citra, Apavatsa, Sandhita, Savitraka,
Rudra, Rudrajaya, Indra, and likewise Indrajaya. || 19.818–19.819 ||
Īśa, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka,
Bhānu, Satya, Bhṛgu, and Antarikṣa the first;
Agni, Pūṣan, Kṛśa, Bhānu, Guha, and likewise Kṣetrādhipa.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛtyu, and likewise Antaka;
Pitṛdauvārika, Sugrīva, and Puṣpadantaka; Varuṇa, Bhṛśa, Āpa, Yakṣa, Māsa, Manojava—|| 19.821-822 ||
Yoga, Nāga, Mṛtyanta, Bhallāṭa, Soma,
Aditi, and Vāstunātha are recorded as the groups of deities of the village site (grāmavāstu).
One should offer oblations to these in sequence by their respective names, ending each with "svāhā."
Likewise, [he worshipped] the deities residing in villages, the deities residing in cities,
the deities residing with kings, and the deities of shrines and temples;
those situated in gardens and groves, and those dwelling upon mountains and trees.
One should satisfy all the assembled gods with a stream of clarified butter;
then, having collected the residual ghee (*sampātājya*), one should pour it into the *śāntikumbha*.
The preceptor, having once again worshipped the God of Gods residing within the jar, [should proceed].
One should perform the offering of the bali sacrifice throughout the interior and exterior of the village, beginning from one's own house.
Then, having completed the remainder of the night, at dawn the most excellent preceptor,
having performed his daily rites, shall go to the sacrificial hall.

Having first performed the worship of the door, one should worship in due order the deities stationed in the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*) and other vessels with offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with the sacrificial oblation (*havir*).
Then, together with the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipas*), one should proceed in sequence through the central fire-pit (*madhyakuṇḍa*) and the others.
O lords of sages, having gratified the deity according to the previously mentioned procedure,
and having performed all the rites such as the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in accordance with the rules,
one should gradually dismiss the deity residing within the fire into one's own heart.
Then, having dismissed the door-deities preceded by the offering of oblations (bali),
the preceptor, accompanied by the image-bearers and Brahmins reciting the Śānti-sūktas, should have all the great jars and other items carried away.
Accompanied by the auspicious sounds of conchs and other instruments, together with the ringing of bells.
Having reached the temple of the deity, one should worship the deity with offerings such as the *arghya*.
One should sprinkle it with water from the great jar (*mahākumbha*) while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.
Starting from the door of the palace and proceeding in order up to the final *balipīṭha* (offering altar)...
O twice-born ones, one should sprinkle [the area] with the water remaining in the pitcher as before.
Then, O Brahmins, for the pacification of all defects, one should sprinkle the village on all sides with the water from the *śānti*-pitcher while reciting the *śānti*-sūktas.
Then, having reached the temple and worshipped Puruṣottama,

and having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis), the preceptor should perform everything up to the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa). Then, the preceptor, having placed the image of the deity upon a vehicle, [should proceed].
By means of the performance of constant festivals together with the requisites for the procession,
and having especially offered oblations to the deities of the door-surroundings,
one should also duly offer the *kumuda* and other oblations in the village according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having worshipped the *balibimba* and established it in its own place,
one should worship the primary image (*mūlabimba*), prostrate, and ask for forgiveness.
At that time, one should give gifts such as cattle, land, and gold for the sake of universal peace.
He should satisfy the teacher, the officiating priests, and others with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Afterwards, he should feed a thousand or even a hundred Brahmins; bringing happiness to the king and his kingdom, he should give them sacrificial fees as well. (19.841–842)
O best of sages, this procedure for the pacification of villages has been told;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the pacificatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*),
which pacifies all defects and fills all gaps.

It bestows all sovereignty upon men and destroys all calamities; it grants the desires of both the performer and the one who causes the performance to be done, as well as for all living beings. It is effective during excessive rain, drought, famine, and the outbreak of disease.
When there are bad dreams and other such ill omens, when great portents occur, when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary components of propitiation, when the elements of the festival have lapsed,
or when a deficiency in the constituent parts of the consecration, bathing, and so forth arises— 19.846.
O bulls among sages, when the aforementioned omens occur— such as touching objects that should not be touched, including images, ritual implements,
and so forth— one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of each respective fault.
Alternatively, one should construct a pavilion provided with four doors in front of the temple, or at the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) and so forth, for that purpose;
or, O Brahmins, if a pavilion or similar structure has already been built somewhere previously.
Whether in a sacrificial hall, or even in a kitchen,
or in a cow-pen, a storehouse, and so forth, or in gardens, groves, and the like—
[the pit] should be two cubits or one cubit [in depth], and either circular or square.
Alternatively, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or perform the fire oblation (homa) upon a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
On the southern side of the pit, upon a pedestal of grain,
one should place the great water-pot (mahākumbha), which possesses the proper characteristics, together with a smaller vessel (upakumbha) and a water-jar (karaka).
Having placed the *śāntikumbha* (peace-pitcher) with its proper characteristics at its side,
O twice-born ones, and having performed the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*) up to the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) and so forth,
one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and sprinkle all the ritual materials (*sambhāra*) in their entirety.
Then, having prepared the *arghya* and other offerings, and preceded by the worship of the doors,
one should duly prepare the *yogapīṭha* upon the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*). Therein, one should invoke Nṛsiṃha, the pacifier of all defects.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa according to the rules, one should worship in sequence with the offerings of *laya*, *bhoga*, and so forth, beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with the oblation (*havir*).
One should also worship Sudarśana in the water-pot (*karaka*) and in the jars starting from the east.
Having worshipped Vāsudeva and the others according to the principle of their origin and dissolution,
one should worship Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi in the peace-vessel (śāntikumbha).
Then, having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and established the fire therein according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
There too, O best of sages, having duly invoked the god Nṛhari and having gratified him with seven fuel-sticks according to his own mantra,
one should perform a special oblation for the sake of pacifying defects.
O twice-born ones, at the beginning, the preceptor [should recite] "Oṃ Kṣrauṃ, obeisance" joined with the *cetimantra*,
and then with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Nārasiṃha," ending with "Destroy,
destroy this defect, svāhā. (19.861)

O twice-born ones, one should offer a hundred, a thousand, or eight times that number of sesame seeds mixed with honey, clarified butter, and milk, along with fruits, according to one's capacity; likewise,
[one may offer] fuel-sticks of palāśa, khadira, bilva, or udumbara wood.
O twice-born ones, one should offer eight kinds of fuel-sticks— of the *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *apāmārga*— prepared with honey, milk, and clarified butter;
one should sacrifice separately one hundred and eight times for each, using the eight-syllable mantra.
Likewise, one should offer pure clarified butter with the twelve-syllable mantra;
one should offer sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter one hundred times with the six-syllable mantra;
and having offered seeds one hundred and eight times with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
The supreme preceptor should offer the *caru* oblation with the *Puruṣasūkta*,
and then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* homa as well as the expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) oblations,
he should subsequently offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *Nārasiṃha* mantra.
Having taken the ghee from the *sampāta* offering, he should sprinkle it into the center of the pitcher.
Then, having worshipped the deity residing in the pitcher according to the prescribed rite,
the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should touch the *śānti*-pitcher.
One should consecrate [the site] with the Nārasiṃha mantra and with hymns for peace (śāntisūkta).
Then, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) to the deities of the gateway according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus performed these rites on the night of the preceding day, the best of preceptors—
Having risen early the next morning, having performed his bath and daily rites,
and having worshipped the deity situated in the jar according to the prescribed rule, he should offer oblations into the fire with the previously mentioned materials twenty-eight times.
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation and dismissed the omnipresent Lord residing within the fire,
and having dismissed the two door-keepers preceded by the offering of sacrificial food (*bali*),
he should have the Great Vase and the Peace Vase carried away together with the Brahmins.
Accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas, the sounds of musical instruments, and the ringing of bells,
having reached the divine abode and worshipped the Lord of the World,
one should sprinkle the All-pervading One with water from the great jar while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Then, for the pacification of defects, one should sprinkle with the water from the *śānti*-pitcher the deity, the temple or other structures, or even all the ritual implements that have been defiled; by using the *Śāntisūkta*, the pacification of the defect will come to pass.

The patron should satisfy the preceptor afterwards with sacrificial fees and other offerings. Even in the case of an immediate rite, one should likewise perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) according to each specific fault for the pacification of all defects.
Or, even without the worship of the water-pot (kumbha), one may perform the fire-oblation alone;
during great festivals and other celebrations, such as consecrations and ritual ablutions,
one should perform the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) in the fire that serves as a constituent part of those respective rites.
Thus everything has been fully explained; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Procedure for Expiation" in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
The nineteenth chapter;
now the twentieth chapter: The Sages.
O Blessed One, tiger among sages, expert in all scriptures,

you have previously described in various places here the specific details regarding rites such as the restoration of ruined temples, categorized according to their types, beginning with those that are self-manifested (*svayamvyakta*).
What and what on earth is self-manifested, and of what nature is its greatness?
O Treasure of Compassion, reveal all that in detail.
Nārada.

I shall proclaim in its entirety the various manifestations, such as the Self-Manifested (Svayamvyakta), and the full majesty of that [place]; listen to it with an attentive mind. In sacred fields such as Puṣkara and others, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, [resides].
Having personally manifested out of a desire for the welfare of his devotees,
the God remains present in person as Svayaṃvyakta, O lords of sages.
In certain sacred fields, the God has been installed by the most excellent of deities.
In the same way, [he was honored] by certain perfected beings (siddhas), by certain eminent sages (ṛṣipuṅgava),
and also by gandharvas, yakṣas, and the highest vidyādharas; likewise by asuras, rākṣasas, and certain lords of men (manujendra).
When the Lord, the Master of the Universe, is installed according to the prescribed rites, He becomes present.
Thus, through the forms of the Blessed One— characterized by various configurations,
diverse specific features, and for the sake of various purposes— He manifests.

The entire universe has been filled with those devoted to the worship of the Blessed One, established by lords of men out of a desire to bestow grace upon all. The greatness of [the Liṅga] installed by the Lord of Rākṣasas shall be tenfold greater than that.
Then, O twice-born ones, it is said that when the Lord was established by the Asuras, the merit was a hundredfold;
when established by the Vidyādharas, O brahmins, it is said to be a thousandfold;
and ten times greater than that, O sages, is the majesty when established by the Yakṣas.
Ten times that merit is proclaimed when [the image] is installed by Gandharvas;
it is said to be ten millionfold in the case of an Ārṣa [installation], and ten times that in the case of a Siddha [installation].
O lords of sages, in the case of a Divine [installation] or one that is self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta), the merit is ten million times ten millionfold.
"It is determined in the scriptures that its majesty is incalculable.
That [majesty] is twofold: the self-manifested image of the all-pervading Lord, in the form of *sālagrāma* stones, and others made of stone and so forth. (20.13–14)
In both cases, the supreme presence of Hari is equal;
yet, regarding the image of the Śālagrāma stone, how is the determination of each specific form made? Having recognized them by their respective established marks, one should perform the worship.
In sacred fields such as Puṣkara and others, the Lord of the World himself descends in the form of an image,
endowed with manifest marks such as the discus and other symbols,
and remains present out of a desire for the welfare of his devotees.
O lords of sages, I shall proclaim the deities residing in those various sacred fields,
by knowing whom a person in this world is liberated from all sins. (20.18) Having taken recourse to the sacred field of Puṣkara under the name Puṇḍarīkākṣa...
But the Blessed Vāsudeva remains eternally present there.
Thus, in this divine and excellent field of Śrīraṅga, as well as in the one called Naimiṣa and in other sacred fields, he abides under such names as Vāsudeva and others.
The Lord, established in four forms for the sake of protecting the world,
exists as Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, in Kurukṣetra and other places;
O best of sages, Nārāyaṇa is stationed on Mount Nārāyaṇācala.

O Lotus-born One, Mādhava resides on Veṅkaṭagiri, Govinda at Puruṣottama, and he is likewise established in the place called Nābhasa and in the region known as Bṛndāvana; thus, O Lotus-born One, he exists in two ways.
O brahmins, Viṣṇu is established in the removal of greed and also in the station of Viṣṇu;
and having reached the mountain named Mandara,
Madhusūdana descended and remained there for the sake of compassion toward all beings.
O Lotus-born one, the God of gods, Trivikrama, remains resorting to the waters of the Yamunā; O Lotus-born one, on Siṃhādri is another form known as Vāmana, which grants a good rebirth when crossed.
Having come from his own abode and rested there for the sake of quelling the sorrow of living beings,
the Lord Śrīdhara resides at the place called Narmadā, having entered its water which brings about the destruction of sins; he is likewise established at Kauṇḍala together with Śrī.
But the Blessed Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, though established in his own self upon the earth,
O Lotus-born one, remained in the field called Dhvajākhya at Kubjāmraka,
having descended as Padmanābha, the Lord of Gods.

O Brahmin, having come from his own abode, the Blessed Lord Dāmodara dwells on Mount Raivataka, situated near the ocean in the southern direction, for the sake of the welfare of those with purified souls. 20.30dāmodaras tu bhagavān hitārthaṃ bhāvitātmanām |

O best of the twice-born, this temple of the universe is pervaded by these various forms together with their manifestations; therefore, O one of great intelligence, listen with an attentive mind to the arrangement of those others as well.
Know that he is the Lord of Swans (Haṃsarāja) in Śvetadvīpa, worshipped by the Siddhas and immortals;
he is the Blessed One in the form of a Fish within the waters, and in the form of a Horse in the Submarine Fire (Vaḍavāmukha).
He is in the form of a Tortoise in the netherworld (Rasātala), and in the form of a Boar in the Vindhya forest.

The soul of the Lord of Beasts, the destroyer of the sins of all embodied beings, is to be known [there] in the form of a boar at that very sacred site (kṣetra), on the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā’s waters, frequented by gods and perfected beings. || 20.34–20.35 ||
The Lord, bearing a golden head, resides within the great Golden Mountain;
likewise, the Lord with a fish-face remains on the Nau-bandhana mountain.
The horse-headed Lord resides in Kṛṣṇāśva, and in the honored Kṣitikṣetra.
On the coastal region bordering the salt ocean, frequented by the Siddhas,
the Lord Nṛhari, whose face is like a tortoise and who bears the conch and discus in his gaze, is stationed;
and at Ujjayinī, O twice-born ones, he likewise dwells when purification has been performed.
Thus situated in three ways in the places known as Viśākha and Mūla,
[I am] at Kokāmukha, at Varāha, and at Vārāha, the best of mountains;
at Mandamāla, at Vivaitasa, at Kulakukṣi, and on the Himācala.
Vāmana, of dwarfish form, is established through his universal manifestation.
In the Middle Country, at Kurukṣetra on the banks of the Gaṅgā, and having taken recourse to the bank of the Yamunā, there is a great further manifestation [of him] at Pauṣkara.
O twice-born one, the Lord known as Trivikrama, whose body traversed the three worlds, stands upon Mahendra, the best of mountains, with an axe in his hand;
and the Blessed One known as Rāma, the ender of the Kṣatriyas, is likewise stationed there.
On Mount Citrakūṭa, the great Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas, is established;
another Rāma, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, is present there.
Yet another Rāma, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), is indeed on the Yamunā, agitating the water.
Established upon auspicious human lands and even on the island in the ocean known as Dvārakā, which is honored by the immortals,
the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa— the Self of All, the Supreme Lord— resides there.
The Lord Kalki Viṣṇu, being praised by the twice-born,
remained there with a restrained mind after reaching the river Vipāśā,
in the great forest of Dharma (Dharmāraṇya), which is honored by the gods and is the very embodiment of righteousness.
Intent on bestowing grace upon the worlds,
the Lord of the Universe, known as Nara, remains ever present in delightful regions of the earth that are worshipped by the Siddhas and honored by the world.
On the mountain named Govardhana, the Lord Hari, the sovereign of all,
resides; he is present in that consecrated place during the processions of the cows,
and also in Sālagrāma, O twice-born ones, and in the forest called Rājendra.
Likewise,
O Brahmin, the fourth form of Kṛṣṇa, known as Devavrata, having descended to the surface of the earth, remains at Piṇḍāraka on a portion of the earth, liberating people from their evil deeds.

O Lotus-born One, the Lord exists as Viśvarūpa on Śvetadvīpa, Kurukṣetra, the Himavat mountain, and even upon the sacrificial altar or its bank; as Hari, he is Padmanābha in the Ocean of Milk, reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa.
"O Lotus-born Grandfather,
since she exists within this entire universe by resorting to a fourth form,
you should indeed understand correctly how she abides for the welfare of all the worlds. (20.54)
O Brahmin, having reached his bed situated in the depths of Pātāla,
he who, at the end of time, withdraws the universe by taking up the Agni-vaṭa tree,
resorts to the root of that vaṭa tree at Prayāga, which is honored by the gods.
Having turned the entire world into a single ocean and having reached a divine tree,
that Blessed One remains upon its bank on the earth, O twice-born ones.
One should meditate upon him as reclining beneath the *nyagrodha* tree, the bestower of divine states.
On a lofty portion of the Himalayas known as Bhṛgu,
he who is the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha remains upon the surface of the earth,
in the sacred field of the land of the Milk Ocean, frequented by gods and demons.
The Lord who bears Mount Mandara dwells there, worshipped by the gods;
right there resides the Lord Amṛtacit, served by the Siddhas.
The Lord assumes a beautiful form and holds a jar of nectar.
The conqueror of death stands among the Siddhas, Munis, and gods; the Lord who rides Garuḍa, accompanied by his Gaṇas, divides himself in two and resides at Sālagrāma in the region of the Sāla tree.
On the summit of Mount Trikūṭa, which is accessible to those who travel through the sky, the Lord,
the Sovereign of Śvetadvīpa, descended and remained there under the name Aprameya, by means of the very pretext of lifting up the elephant.
At the delightful spot on earth where the Gaṅgā meets the ocean,
at Naimiṣa, which is honored by the Siddhas, the Lord, the divine enjoyer of sacrifice,
remains; and the infinite Lord has taken up residence in the Saindhava forest.
But the Lord of Gods, Śārṅgapāṇi—
the imperishable Śauri— resides in the region known as Utpalāvartaka within the Daṇḍaka forest;
he stands upon the earth at the junction of the ocean and the sea, a place frequented by the Siddhas.
The Blessed One, the teacher of knowledge, remains present for the sake of the pacification of suffering.
Having reached the field of Sūkara, the Lord whose vehicle is Garuḍa stands mounted upon Garuḍa, marked by the Pārijātaka tree in his hand.
O Pauṣkara, together with the Siddhas and the hosts of gods, the God of gods,
the Lord of the World, the granter of boons to all, remained upon the summit of Mount Hasti, having reached a certain spot in the sky.
O high-minded one, Vaikuṇṭha, with a garland in his hand, is in Māgadha; Puruṣottama, the inconceivable-souled Lord, is situated on the holy ground at Uḍḍīya and on Mount Gandhamādana.
In the region known as Śipiviṣṭa, he remained established in the conduct of Śipiviṣṭa; then,
on the auspicious coastal land extending toward the eastern ocean,
the Lord Vāsudeva took up the form of Kapila and remained there.
Having descended from his own being, the Lord of Creatures, known as Brahmā,
reached Maṇibandha and remained there eternally present,
O Brahmin, in the region of Magadha, taking refuge at Mahābodhi.

O twice-born one, Janārdana, the God of gods, whose self is the Lord of the World, exists as the embodiment of the ego-sense within the right eye of the god [Dakṣa]. That Blessed One, known as Sūrya, is situated upon the Golden Mountain.
In Ācyuta, within the left eye, is the all-pervading Lord whose body is composed of ego;
and the Lord known as Soma is likewise present in the hermitage of Somatīrtha.
Furthermore, the unconquered one exists in the form of fire within the submarine fire.
O Brahmin, the Lord, the soul of all things, shines forth as the destroyer of the Asuras;
furthermore, the God named Viṣṇu is adorned with many weapons. Known by the name Jaya, he resides in Ujjayinī, bringing victory over sin for men.
In the auspicious region of Kāśmīra, in the sacred field named Cakradhara,
the Blessed Lord Cakrapāṇi stands as the bestower of liberation upon his devotees;
and in Pauṣkara is the one named Surottama, who holds a mace in his hand.
Know that he is always present at Gaṅgādvāra together with the gods—
the eternal Lord Viṣvaksena, who stands at Piṇḍāraka, possessing four arms, four forms, four faces, and four states of existence.
Having reached an auspicious region and likewise the city of Prāgjyotiṣapura,
he took up residence in his own domain at the sacred site named Sātatranā, which is frequented by perfected beings and Vidyādharas, where the deity known as Viśveśvara resides.

The Lord of the World, known as Svāmī, resides on the bank of the Mandākinī; during the great conjunction of Bhadrātaka, he bestows liberation upon those who meditate. On the surface of the earth, at the place called Nṛsiṃha situated on the bank of the Devikā—
O Brahmin, the Lord who is the sovereign of all resides in the place called Ripukṣaya;
and in the region known as Śaṅkara, which is frequented by all the gods,
the Lord of the World, the embodiment of knowledge, dwells there, bestowing auspiciousness upon men.
O Brahmin, on this earth, in the field of the ancestors, the Blessed Lord, the Soul of the Universe, dwells under the name Janārdana, liberating beings from the three debts.
These incarnations have been described to you in brief, O Lotus-born One.
O Lotus-born One, out of a desire to favor transmigrating beings, you yourself have repeatedly pervaded the surface of the earth with these [names],
which are otherwise inaccessible even at the three junctions of the day through mere recitation.
He practiced this constantly.
(20.89) And he set his mind upon visiting and even beholding those Mlecchas who were in those regions on earth, as well as the sacred fields and other sites. (20.90)
Indeed, they should always be viewed by the seers, gods, and perfected ones as being free from confusion, within their own great hermitages,
in sacred reservoirs of water, and in various places upon the earth.
All those who have been described as having the form of the Blessed One, characterized by the manifestations of his power,
and those others whom one may perceive for oneself through the intellect—
those of true valor who have been duly installed along with their mantras— [are all present]. (20.92–20.93)
Through their persistence, they appear in various forms designated as past, future,
and so forth, according to their arrangement as gentle, fiery, or both,
and indeed through that which consists of playful delight and bestows happiness upon the mind.
Indeed, together with the various weapons held in their arms and the distinctions of their banners,
the region was likewise adorned by men in this very manner.
By the devotees, the favored ones, the Siddhas, and others, as has been declared;
these Lords of the Principles (tattveśas), beginning with Ādideva, have been described,
and they abide non-differently within the supreme reality of the Lord (bhagavattattva).
Just as the rays of the sun, just as the masses of flames from a fire, and just as the waves of the ocean, so too, O Lotus-born One,
are the Supreme Lords— identical in their consciousness, eternally pure, and all-pervading.
Relying upon the existence of reality (tattva-sattā) and adorned with knowledge and other virtues,
they abide in their own self endowed with the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
Indeed, they constantly maintain their presence throughout all the stages of the paths (adhvan).
For the liberation of all beings, especially on this earth,
from the time of universal origin until the end of dissolution,
he dwelt in sacred fields and on the banks of holy fords, his very self consisting of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
Even by means of a general mantra, through his own nature which is its manifestation,
he assumes a form both manifest and otherwise, consisting of the element earth;
he has descended as the imperishable one for the benefit of all the worlds.
In this [place] called Jagatyāyatana, yogins attain success;
for if, over the course of time, the immersion of individual beings occurs there,
they constantly maintain their presence through the state of their power (śakti).
The lords of yoga, the immortals, and the perfected ones (siddhas), recollecting that form as being of that very nature,
establish an image made of stone, clay, wood, or metal;
and those who possess the power of mantras perform the consecration (anuveda) therein.
Whatever other place is remembered by the name Acyutīya, there is the presence of the Vairūpas and of the one who bears sound as his form;
[this applies] to both those of distinct natures and to those who are unmanifest within self-manifested forms.
When the mantras have been completely restrained and have entered the power of will,
the forms and configurations [of the universe] belong to the Supreme Lord in one way;
yet in this world, they appear otherwise— as both the manifest and the unmanifest, and as eternal.
Thus, O Pauṣkara, the eternality of the sense-bases (āyatana), as well as their beginninglessness, incalculability, and greatness, have been fully revealed. In this way,
the various manifestations situated within the field (kṣetra) have been correctly proclaimed.
O Indra among kings, among these sacred fields, there is a quartet that constitutes the very essence:
Śrīraṅga, Veṅkaṭādri, Hastiśaila immediately following, and then Nārāyaṇādri; these are my four abodes.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, indeed by Nārāyaṇa himself:
"Those best of men who, endowed with great devotion, serve Puruṣottama established within these four sacred fields (kṣetra). (20.113)
The gods residing in all fields have been served by them, without a doubt;
O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, O best of all speakers, [you know] everything.
We wish to hear the greatness of the Nārāyaṇa mountain.
For although you previously described here the meditation, worship, and so forth of Nārāyaṇa himself, you did not [describe] Hari as Nārāyaṇa.
"How did he reach the best of mountains, and of what nature was its greatness?
O best among speakers, tell all of that in detail. Nārada.
"Excellent, O highly fortunate ones, you bulls among sages, that you have asked about the supreme majesty of Hari residing on Nārāyaṇācala.
I shall describe it in brief; listen with attentive concentration."

In the beginning, the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, having produced from the lotus of his own navel the four-faced one who was refined by all purificatory rites, and having made him a knower of the true meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras— (20.119–120)

Having appointed Brahmā to the task of creation, he then vanished. When that god had disappeared, Vidhi, his mind bewildered and his intellect overturned, became confused as to what ought to be done and felt distressed in spirit.
Then he performed austerities, desiring to see the Lord of the Universe.
When many periods of time had passed while the Grandfather was performing penance,
O twice-born ones, the Lord of the World appeared before Brahmā.
Seeing the beloved of Kamalā, the four-faced Brahmā was filled with supreme wonder and praised him with various hymns perfected by the Vedas.
Being thus praised by him, the Sustainer of the World, his mind full of compassion, [acted].
He spoke these words to Brahmā with a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"My child, from where have you performed such exceedingly difficult penance?
I am pleased today by your austerity; tell me, what is it that you desire?"
"O Lord, there is no other fruit for Brahmā than the sight of you;
for I was appointed by you, O All-pervading One, to create the world in the past. (20.127)
"O Mādhava, what power do I have to create this entire universe?
Tell me the means for this, O ocean of the nectar of compassion.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the Lord [revealed] the supreme eight-syllabled mantra.
Having instructed him and explained its meaning in detail, the Blessed One said:
"Constantly contemplating this eight-syllable mantra within your heart,
you shall be able to create the world through the power of this mantra."
When the work of creation has commenced through the power of this mantra,
the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa will manifest visibly before you.
O Lotus-born one, worship that Lord of Gods with this mantra.
"Then, at the end of your term of office, you shall certainly attain my state," having spoken thus,
the four-faced god, being pleased, vanished while reciting the root-mantra that consists of both the conscious and the unconscious.
O best of sages, having created this entire universe, Virañci,
desiring to see Nārāyaṇa, performed a most difficult penance.
Then, a divine celestial chariot of auspicious characteristics appeared.
From Śrī Vaikuṇṭha [he came], like a wondrous fruit of the penance of the Four-faced One (Brahmā),
enveloped by a splendor shining like many tens of millions of suns,
and preceded by Ananta, Vihageśāna, Viṣvaksena, and others.
He was closely followed on both sides by Śrī and Sudarśana,
surrounded by Kumuda and others, beautiful in every limb,
circular in form, auspicious, and adorned with all ornaments.
Seeing him, the lotus-seated one rose up suddenly, filled with joy;
his entire body bristling with horripilation and his eyes rolling with delight,
he stood with palms joined in reverence and gazed upon the celestial chariot.
Upon the pedestals and other parts up to the pinnacle, as well as on the components of the temple,
one should contemplate in sequence the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ and ending with Satya;
and among the paths, the six beginning with the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and ending with the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan).
O lords of sages, he beheld the entire multitude of principles, beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa, abiding while remaining in the form of pure existence;
thereafter, he observed the host of deities in their proper order.
Beneath the stone supporting the jar is Ananta of immeasurable luster;
above that is the Cakra, and within another stone is the Sāmarthya-śakti.
The Mantra-nāda is in the central jar, while [the others] are in the eight jars starting from the east.
And [he perceives] Vāsudeva and the others, according to their connection with origin and dissolution;
situated within their respective coverings (pidhāna), starting from the center and ending with the northeast direction;
and the ninefold group of powers (śakti) beginning with Jñānabhāsā, in due order.
Likewise, there is an octad of Dharma and the other [qualities], and an octad of foot-stones;
within that is the wheel of phonemes (varṇacakra) beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
This wheel, consisting of the support of all, rests upon the root of the branches.
O lords of sages, upon the two branches of the supreme Lord, who consists of knowledge and action,
one should place the primordial [deity] above the udumbara tree, and on its back, Dharma itself; moreover,
on the two door-panels, Kālāgni and Varuṇa.
The Śaṅkha and Padma treasures are located at the two sides of the front door;
then, upon the assembly of the shanks and likewise within the intermediate spaces,
[one should place] the deities who are the instruments of existence, beginning with Kāla and ending with Vasudhā.
On the tips of the shanks are the six deities beginning with Keśava;
on the surface of the pedestal is the collection of weapons beginning with the discus, existing in the form of their essence.
In the four locations of the nostrils are the four beginning with Varāha.
Upon the surface of the altar, adorned with leaves and other ornaments,
one should place Sudarśana together with his spear in the crest-pitcher, and Vāsudeva, who is higher than the highest, in the supreme pitcher.
In the space before that, one should place Hetīśa, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns.
O Brahmins, that celestial chariot of the Lotus-Seated One consists of the entire world, likewise consists of all the paths,
consists of all the principles (tattvas), and likewise consists of all the gods;
it is known as being composed of bliss.
Having thus gazed upon [the deity] in sequence, prostrated again and again,
and likewise performed circumambulations with the permission of Viṣvaksena,
he entered within the celestial chariot while muttering the eight-syllabled mantra.
In the interior of the celestial chariot, in the center of the inner chamber,
he beheld Puruṣottama seated upon a lotus,
his divine form radiant like a mass of clouds in the rainy season.
The god who consists of all gods, the treasury of the splendors of all,
complete with every auspicious mark, and endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
With a beautiful, divine, and manifest body,
he incessantly emitted from his form a light characterized by wisdom— a great light that destroys the ignorance of meditators even without effort. (20.159)

He was adorned by his own hair, which resembled thickly curled black lotus petals or crushed collyrium, was grey with camphor, divine, and interspersed with flowers; it was further graced by a crown and a diadem that rested upon it.
Resplendent with a tilaka mark rising upon his forehead, resembling the young moon;
with beautiful eyebrows, a handsome nose, and peaceful, playful smiles upon his lips;
his eyes were slightly reddish, like pure white cow’s milk, and like blue lotuses.
With cooling glances that bring refreshment to the world,
his broad cheeks were radiant and his earrings gleamed upon his ears;
his chin was graced by the flowing beauty of his face.
His face was a radiant orb like the stainless autumn moon;
he had a neck like a conch shell, broad shoulders, long arms, and a large chest.
He possessed four arms, noble limbs, and shining lotus-like hands.
Clad in yellow silken garments, with a deep navel and a slender waist,
she possessed a pair of beautiful thighs and lovely shanks;
her lotus-feet shone with brilliant ornaments such as jeweled anklets.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, and he wore celestial garments;
he was endowed with divine garlands and head-wraps, and adorned with divine ornaments.
He shone with a crown and tiara inlaid with many jewels.
The Supreme Lord was adorned with the Kaustubha gem worn upon his chest and the Śrīvatsa mark; he was further beautified by a forest garland composed of red flowers, gold, and fine pearls,
along with a sacred thread.
With his primary right hand he grants fearlessness to those who are afraid;
with his left hand resting playfully upon the slope of his hip,
he holds a heavy mace that rests upon the surface of the earth.
In his right hand he holds a discus with the brilliance of the fire of time,
containing within it the resonance of the *praṇava*; and in his left hand he holds a conch shell, possessing incomparable luster and more than a hundred times the size of the Himalayan mountain.
Situated in the midst of a circle of flames produced from the splendor of his own body,
his heart full of compassion, and striving for the upliftment of the world;
he is augmented by the power of the sixfold sovereign qualities (ṣāḍguṇya) which are both indivisible and complete.

Having beheld the Lord Nārāyaṇa— the object of meditation for yogis, unborn and eternal, the cause of the world's birth and so forth, the manifest husband of Lakṣmī, the one free from all ailment— he,
with a heart full of joy, prostrated himself again and again.
Brahmā praised the beloved of Kamalā with various kinds of hymns.
Then Nārāyaṇa, of noble intellect, being well-pleased by that praise,
spoke these words to the Grandfather in a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"O Creator, I am satisfied with your austerity; I am devoted to the eight-syllable mantra.
Worship me here for ten thousand ages, O Brahmā, and then I shall go to the earth for a certain purpose."
Thus addressed, the four-faced one, filled with great joy,
took that celestial chariot and, having placed it in his own abode,
[performed worship] according to the procedure taught by Sātvata, using the eight-syllabled mantra.
He worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rites with various kinds of enjoyments.
Thus, O lords of sages, after many periods of time had passed,
Sanatkumāra, the king of yogis, once [emerged] from the Ocean of Milk.
Having reached Satyaloka and beheld there the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who was endowed with Śrī and captivated the minds of all,
he stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke this to the Four-faced One:
"You are my preceptor and also my father, O ocean of affection.
There is no other refuge for me in this world than you, O bestower of all goals.
For all this time, this glorious and all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa [has been my guide]."

"O father, you have properly propitiated him with various kinds of enjoyments; today I wish to sacrifice to that Lord who was propitiated by you. O father, you ought to grant me Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World. (20.186)
Thus entreated, Brahmā, though possessed of affection for his son,
became overcome with anxiety out of fear of separation from Viṣṇu.
Then the glorious Nārāyaṇa [beheld] him whose mind was agitated by worry.
Having seen the Lotus-born one, he spoke these words with affection:
"O Greatly Intelligent One, O Lotus-born One, cast away your anxiety regarding separation from me;
even now, I shall grant you another form for my worship."
Taking me with him, this lord of sages shall reach the surface of the earth and,
having established me on the mountain named Padmakūṭa, he shall worship me constantly;
there, the lords of sages perform austerities in order to behold me incessantly.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord then bestowed upon Brahmā his own form, which had arisen from his heart and was accompanied by Śrī and Puṣṭi.
The Grandfather then accepted that form, joined with Śrī and Puṣṭi.
With a mind filled with wonder, he honored him especially with various enjoyments.
Then, O lords of sages, the lotus-born Brahmā, his eyes wide with joy, summoned Sanatkumāra and spoke to him thus: || 20.193–20.194 ||
"O Sanatkumāra, my dear child, you are a true son to me,
for the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself has shown grace toward you.
Having spoken thus to the lord of sages, [he gave him] the divine eight-syllabled mantra.
Having taught its meanings as well, he caused the yogi to grasp the great *Upaniṣad* known as the *Sātvata-tantra*,
which flowed forth from that renowned *Mūla-veda*.
O Brahmins, it bestows both spiritual perfection and liberation, and contains within it the meaning of all the scriptures;
therein lies the most peaceful array (vyūha), which is tranquil yet manifest, and immediate.
It consists of the arrays known as deep sleep, dream, and waking, as they have been described.
Likewise, there are other forms such as Keśava and others, as well as various manifestations;
[these are situated] upon the lotus-throne of the heart-lotus and so forth, together with the Śaktis such as Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi,
with emblems such as the conch and discus, and also with Garuḍa and the rest.
Worship by means of the Bhūtas, Siddhas, and so forth, up to the Śāstras, is beneficial;
likewise, for the sake of Viśvatrātṛ-Nṛsiṃha, there is the supreme [worship] preceded by initiation (dīkṣā).
[One should perform] the authority (adhikāra) known as Vibhava, Vyūha, and Sūkṣma in due order.
The consecration of the four, beginning with the *samayī* and the *putraka*; likewise, the conduct of the *samaya*, the sequence for the installation of the images,
and the characteristics of the mantras, mandalas, mudrās, the sacrificial fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), and so forth.
Wherein it was proclaimed by the Blessed One for the sake of reviving the world;
having taught its meanings, he then described the means of attaining it.
For this Sātvata Tantra [originated] from Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe.
It was obtained from him by Saṅkarṣaṇa; therefore,
it was obtained from that Saṅkarṣaṇa-self by the one named Pradyumna, and from him indeed by Aniruddha.
"O Sage, this [knowledge] has been obtained by me from Aniruddha, and likewise by Rudra and others from me. Among all divine scriptures, there is nothing superior to this;
just as among all mantras, there is none higher than the eight-syllabled one."

O sage, worship this Nārāyaṇa, the lord of the world, according to the procedure just described, with tactile and other enjoyments. There is a sacred field on the surface of the earth named Vaikuṇṭhavardhana.

There, O Sage, on the northern side of the Kāverī at a distance of one yojana, there is a certain great and preeminent mountain named Padmakūṭa. For that place is extraordinary; it is known as Bhūvaikuṇṭha.
Formerly commanded by the Blessed One, Śeṣa himself indeed assumed the state of a mountain;
now he remains there, awaiting the arrival of Viṣṇu.

The Virajā as well, by means of a portion [of that river], flows eternally pure on the northern bank of that mountain, destroying all defects. Likewise, there are many sacred bathing places (tīrthas) and various holy fields (kṣetras).
On that best of mountains, there are places to be frequented by the highest of the wise.
Even in the Kali age, those situated there are never defiled;
O Sage, even at the time of universal dissolution, there is no destruction of that mountain.
Furthermore, there is no place within the entire universe equal to that;
on that mountain, many excellent sages of rigid vows and pure intentions perform austerities in order to behold this Nārāyaṇa.

Even toward them, grace has arisen from this Lord, who is a treasury of compassion. Therefore, taking this celestial chariot with a concentrated mind and placing it upon that excellent mountain, worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Thus addressed, the best of sages was then delighted at heart,
having obtained from the Grandfather the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods;
O best of sages, this occurred on the full moon day of Phālguna under the asterism of Hasta.
Having brought it to that best of mountains, on its summit frequented by sages,
on the shore of this most excellent sacred ford, he then established that two-templed shrine of immeasurable splendor; so did the preeminent sages residing there.
Having beheld the god Nārāyaṇa, they were filled with great joy and exclaimed, "May there be welfare for us here! Welfare! (20.221).
Therefore, the wise proclaim that place as Kalyāṇatīrtha.
Then Sanatkumāra, worshipping the Lord of the World according to the procedure taught by Sātvata, became satisfied in his heart,
because Nārāyaṇa dwells there on that mountain perpetually.
From that time forth, it is called Nārāyaṇācala;
thus has the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa himself been described there.
Furthermore, that other form of worship which was proclaimed as arising from the heart of Nārāyaṇa—
And he reached that mountain for some reason in the past;
I shall relate that event here, so listen, O best of sages.
Formerly, the glorious Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of protecting the world, [resided there].
Having descended into the lineage of Raghu, Rāma, the destroyer of the race of Rākṣasas,
dwelling here and there in various hermitages for the sake of protecting the sages residing in the Daṇḍaka forest under the pretext of his father’s command.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and by Sītā, who was full of loveliness,
he reached Nārāyaṇagiri, which is frequented by sages; there,
filled with curiosity, he was received as a guest by the hosts of sages.
On the plateau of that mountain, at an exceedingly beautiful and lofty peak,
a trench was instantly dug by the son of Sumitrā with the tip of his bow for the purpose of sporting in the water of the Sītā; and immediately, water appeared therein.
Having stayed there with Sītā and immersed himself within the water,
Rāghava recited the *Aghamarṣaṇī* verses; then, after emerging from the water and reflecting, he beheld the most wonderful form of the Blessed One.
Wandering all around the mountain with a mind filled with wonder,
he beheld the god Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes were as broad as lotus petals, on the far shore of Kalyāṇatīrtha; having seen him, he bowed his head repeatedly.
Having worshipped him for several months, he dwelt there; thereafter, the Blessed One said to Rāma: "I am well-pleased with your worship.
Having granted fearlessness to the sages, you have conquered the foremost of the rākṣasas."
"Enter the city of Sāketa together with all your attendants;
I shall come there in part, and then you should offer sacrifice to me.
Thus addressed by the command of Indirā’s Beloved, that tiger among the Raghus—
Having rendered the earth free of thorns, he was consecrated in the excellent city of Sāketa for his own devoted and wise lord of the Rākṣasas,
after bestowing upon him the omnipresent Lord Raṅgeśvara, the deity worshipped by his own lineage.
When the Lord of the Stage was thus led away by him, he then became filled with anxiety.
Having understood that, the Four-faced One (Brahmā) took the Lord— who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa— along with Śrī and Bhūmi, and went swiftly to the city of Sāketa.
Having approached, he presented to Rāma the Hari whom he had propitiated.
Then, O twice-born ones, Rāma, greatly delighted, worshipped according to the prescribed rites that Lord who was accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi in his own home for a long time.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, his name became "Rāmapriya" (Beloved of Rāma).
Then Kuśa, the son of Rāma, while worshipping the Lord who had been propitiated by his father,
gave a certain daughter of his to a king of the Yadu lineage.
Having been thus entreated after he had given [the boon], he granted that Acyuta to her.
And having obtained that deity as a bridegroom, the one known as Yaduśekhara returned to the city of Mathurā and stayed right there in his own palace.
Having installed the Beloved of Kamalā, he worshipped him with devotion.
Then, having obtained that [knowledge] through his lineage,
Kṛṣṇa, born of the Yadu clan, while worshipping the Lord, the husband of Śrī, [learned it] from the son of Vinatā.

Having received the incomparable crown from that god who reclines upon the ocean of milk, he celebrated various festivals for him. Then, on one occasion, the wielder of the mace [Balarāma] set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Having gone to Nārāyaṇagiri and bathed there at the holy site named Kalyāṇa, as well as in the eight sacred fords (tīrthas) on the summit of that mountain,
[he beheld] the Lord of the World, who is the bliss of yoga, seated in a yogic posture.
The god who consists of all the gods, the treasury of all splendors,
complete with all auspicious marks and endowed with qualities such as omniscience;
possessing the luster of refined gold, with limbs fully formed and a magnificent body.
With a face like a fierce tiger and eyes like the scorching sun,
he was covered with hair resembling a mass of lightning; his arms were tawny, with the luster of lotus petals and exceeding the brilliance of diamonds.
With the mane of the lord of serpents quivering, possessing a luster that strikes against the surface of ten million moons,
emitting its own name with a roar like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution,
and stationed within a circle of flames from the fire at the end of the age.
With his two arms resting upon his knees, adorned with a yogic cloth,
and holding a discus and a conch with his two rear arms,
he shone with a crown and diadem resembling ten million suns.
The Supreme Lord was adorned with the Kaustubha gem resting upon his chest and also with the Śrīvatsa mark;
he was further graced by a forest garland composed of jewels, gold, and fine pearls,
as well as by a sacred thread.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, and he wore celestial garments;
he was endowed with divine garlands and head-dress, and adorned with divine ornaments.
He was both most terrifying and of gentle form, bestowing the fulfillment of desires upon those who take refuge in him.
Having beheld the god Narahari and bowed at his lotus feet,
Halin, with a heart full of satisfaction, praised him with various kinds of hymns;
O brahmins, he wandered here and there upon that excellent mountain.

Having beheld the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who stands in the midst of the bliss-filled [city] like an ocean of the nectar of beauty, he was submerged in an ocean of wonder. Having bowed at His lotus feet, he praised the Lord of the Universe in this manner:

Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; victory to you, O lover of your devotees! Victory to you, O beloved of Kamalā; victory to you, O Supreme Person! O Nārāyaṇa, let there be salutation to you; O Vāsudeva, let there be salutation to you!
Homage be to you, Viṣṇu; homage to you, the Lord of all.
Homage to you whose form is the Supreme; homage to you whose form is the Manifestation.
Homage to you whose form is the Power; homage to you, the Inner Self.
Salutations to you, the incarnated image; salutations to you who assume manifold forms.
For you indeed, for the sake of protecting the world, sport here upon this mountain, accompanied by Lakṣmī in the form of compassion and by the Sudarśana [discus].
Today my vision has become fruitful, for you, the ocean of the nectar of beauty and the lord of all worlds, have come within the range of my sight.
[This has happened] in all sacred fields and in all holy shrines.
O Lord of the World, I do not see any Blessed One like you. I have come to you for refuge, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek shelter;
look upon me with your side-long glances filled with mercy, O All-pervading Lord.
Thus praised with various hymns, Nārāyaṇa Hari, his mind filled with compassion, spoke to Balabhadra:
"O Balabhadra, you are my devotee; you are Śeṣa, my servant."
"Tell me what you desire; I shall grant that to you.
Thus addressed, this Balabhadra replied to the Lord of the World:
"O Nārāyaṇa, O ocean of compassion, [I desire nothing] other than service unto You."
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, is there anything desired that I may worship you here?
O Beloved of Ramā, I have a longing; please fulfill this heart's desire.
Thus entreated, the God then replied to Balarāma:
"O delighter of the Yadavas, you possess pure devotion toward me.
At first, in the form of Śeṣa, you performed service for me."
Then, having become Lakṣmaṇa, he propitiated me here.
Even now, O Balabhadra, you ought to sacrifice to me,
having once again become some preeminent brahmin, even in this Kali age.
"You shall perform my worship with various nets of enjoyments.
Thus addressed by the God of gods, Balabhadra, his mind filled with joy,
worshipped Hari according to the rules with various kinds of enjoyments.
Highly pleased by that worship, the glorious and all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa spoke thus to Bala, who desired to perform festivals and other rites:
"This form of mine, born from my heart, is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi."
"O Yādava, it is said that [the deity] is worshipped in your house in Madhurā;
therefore, O wielder of the plow (Halī), you ought to bring him here with devotion and perform various kinds of festivals and worship for me, so that I may be pleased. (20.279)
Thus addressed, the son of Rohiṇī went with haste to the city of Mathurā and reported that event in detail to Kṛṣṇa. Having heard it, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa became exceedingly astonished.
Then Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the leaders of the Yadus, having placed the Lord of Śrī—
who was adorned with all ornaments— upon a palanquin,
accompanied by all the requisites for the procession and the fourfold army, [set forth].
In the month of Māgha, under the Citrā constellation and at a charming, auspicious hour,
they led [the image] to that excellent mountain, to the ground before the city of Nārāyaṇa; having established it there with great joy, they both worshipped Hari.
Then, having installed the offerings for the sacrifice and the worship for the ritual bathing by the command of Hari, they desired to perform a great festival for the God of gods;
and having duly performed the great festival of the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow, they proceeded.
In the month of Phālguna, under the asterism of Hasta, which is associated with all sacred fords,
they celebrated the avabhṛtha festival at that Kalyāṇa lake,
because there the Lord, whose companion is Ramā, had been worshipped by the two Yādavas.
From that time forward, that mountain has been called Yādavādri;
thus has the majesty of this Nārāyaṇa been recounted by me.
O lords of sages, please tell me what is to be heard hereafter.
O omniscient one, O tiger among sages, there on that mountain of the Yādavas,
there exists the Kalyāṇa-tīrtha; such indeed is its origin.
"We wish to hear of the majesty of Nṛhari as he stands upon that mountain peak; please reveal that as well," [said] Nārada.
"Excellent is the question asked by you, O illustrious ones who are knowers of the essence!
I shall now speak of the greatness of Kalyāṇatīrtha; listen.
Long ago, the Lord Varāha [rescued] the Earth, which was submerged in the ocean."
Having lifted him up as before and established him upon the mountain,
he remained there together with the goddess Earth, who is of the nature of Śeṣa.
At that time, drops of ocean water clung to the body of the god.
O twice-born ones, as they fell there, that sacred bathing place became auspicious.
Then the gods, having showered the Lord of the World with rains of flowers,
praised him with various hymns, and the throngs of apsarases danced.
Divine drums resounded and the world became filled with joy.
Then Brahmā and all the other gods, as well as the foremost of the divine sages,
having arrived there, entreated the unshakable Varāha.
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, sole protector of all the worlds!
By you the great Daitya was slain, and the earth was uplifted.
And we have been protected, O Lord, ocean of the nectar of compassion.
O Lord of the World, it is fitting that you remain here in this very form together with the Earth, out of a desire to show grace to your devotees.
Thus entreated by the gods, the Lord Hari, in the form of the Boar,
placed the Earth upon his own lap and instructed Manu;
O lords of sages, he remains even today on the eastern part of that sacred site.
