Thereupon, the lord of birds was commanded by that boar:
"Having brought pure clay from Śvetadvīpa, deposit it on the shore of the lake;
for that clay is indeed honored by the world."
O twice-born ones, in that lake known as Kalyāṇa during the month of Phālguna,
all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā attain proximity.
Indeed, on the full moon day of that month, the supreme deities beginning with Brahmā [assemble there].
They come with devotion to bathe in the auspicious lake (Kalyāṇasaras).
Those who behold that divine Kalyāṇatīrtha, or remember it, or perform circumambulation around it, or bow down to it, or worship it—[they attain the highest goal]. || 20.304–20.305 ||
Those men who listen with devotion to the greatness of that sacred ford (tīrtha),
or who perform ablutions there, or who drink from that sacred ford;
or those who worship it with flowers and other offerings— those people are purifiers of the world.
Longevity, health, sovereignty, knowledge, splendor, victory, fame, virtuous sons, and contentment— whatever is desired here, O twice-born ones,
they obtain all that before long; there is no doubt in this.
"The majesty of that sacred ford cannot be fully known even by the gods beginning with Brahmā, much less by those such as myself. Thus,
O best of sages, has the majesty of the ford been described in brief.
Now, O twice-born ones, the majesty of the illustrious Narasiṃha shall be told.
In ancient times, Prahlāda, the most excellent of Vaiṣṇavas and a devotee of Nṛhari,
endowed with devotion, sought to propitiate the god Narasiṃha through austerity.
Searching for a pure place of asceticism upon the earth,
he reached Nārāyaṇācala; and having beheld its beauty,
he became certain that there is no place on earth superior to this.
Having bathed there in the Kalyāṇasaras lake and taken the auspicious white clay found on its bank, one should apply vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) and reach that mountain peak,
which is secluded and exceedingly pure.

Endowed with the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), focusing his mind solely on that, he performed extremely difficult austerities in order to behold Narahari again, while muttering the auspicious single-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha as well as the Anuṣṭubh mantra.

Then, gratified by that austerity, Nṛhari, the Lord of the World who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared upon the summit of that mountain. Prahlāda beheld Narahari, the ocean of compassion, who was the fruit of his own penance.

Seeing that supreme being upon the most auspicious rocky surface of that mountain peak— his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, endowed with virtuous qualities, his hands radiant with the discus and lotus, seated in the yogic posture— the best of sages, their hair standing on end with joy, danced with devotion.
And with a mind filled with wonder, he praised Nṛhari in this way:
"Salutations to you, O Śrī Nṛsiṃha; salutations to you, O slayer of the Daitya!
Salutations to you, O Lord of the worlds; salutations to you, O lover of your devotees!"
For you are indeed the protector of the world, and this universe has you as its very self.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are servants at your lotus feet;
O Supreme Person, there is no deity in the world superior to you.
The lords of sages seek You, the Eternal, within the Vedāntas;
You, O Ocean of Compassion, have now come within the range of my vision.
I have taken refuge in You; make me Your own, O All-pervading Lord.
Thus praised with various hymns, that Man-Lion spoke to the one named Prahlāda in a voice raining nectar:
"O Prahlāda, I am pleased today by your austerity; choose the boon you desire."
When addressed with the words, "Choose that which I shall grant you," the highly intelligent one named Prahlāda, having joined his palms in reverence, replied:
"O Lord, you are my teacher, my father, my mother, my friend, and my kinsman."
Since all knowledge and wealth exist in you and nowhere else,
O Lord of the Earth, I do not wish to remain on this earth for even a moment without you;
therefore, O God, grant me constant service at your lotus feet.
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to grant [this]," thus was the omnipresent one entreated. For the sake of bestowing grace upon Prahlāda,
Narahari made his dwelling on that very mountain and was intensely worshipped by him.
Even today it shines there, granting the fulfillment of the desires of those who take refuge in it.
Thus, O best of sages, I have briefly proclaimed the majesty of Nārāyaṇagiri; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Yādavācala," in the glorious Īśvara-saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, O omniscient one, best among speakers!"— thus spoke the sages.
"For those who have not received initiation, there is no entitlement to worship and so forth, as previously stated.
Therefore, O bull among sages, please explain correctly the procedure for initiation.
Nārada said:
Listen, all you sages: they become identical with the Blessed One.
O best of sages, whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra—any man who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, who is a knower, and who is exceedingly firm.
But one who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra longs for nirvāṇa;
steadfast through dispassion and free from fickleness, he remains for a long time in the house of his guru,
dwelling in the state of a servant, devoid of weariness or agitation.
Having ascertained his intention, one should certainly summon him and seat him before oneself;
he should then be questioned regarding what was done and what was left undone during that period of time.
Having correctly understood the strength of the fault, one should apply the prescribed expiations accordingly.
However, for those preceded by the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, the penis should be excised with great effort;
or, O wielder of the plow, because of the inability to endure many torments,
[the penance lasts] for a period ending when the mind is purified, or for twelve days.
He should be employed in the measurement and purification [of the site], in the preparation of food without solicitation, and in the practice of eating only at night;
likewise in the effort of offering praise, sweeping, bathing, and bringing flowers and other offerings in the hermitages of Vaiṣṇavas or in the divine temples of the Lord.
Constantly gazing upon the form of the Blessed One from its pedestal—
even one whose body was previously defiled by evil deeds now has his mind purified by devotion to the Blessed One. (21.10)
Having fasted for a day and night, with his nails and hair shorn,

he should then prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with water containing kuśa grass; having consecrated it four hundred times with the heart-mantra and other mantras, as well as those beginning with Vāsudeva.
In this manner, the wise one should bathe him for four days,
four times every day from dawn until the arrival of night. Having filled each of the four Brahma-tīrthas, he should drink [the water] equally.

Having sipped water for purification at intervals with the mantras recited in succession, one should eat a meal that is not yet satiating; finally, one should consume food prepared with milk and ghee,
or subsist on fruits and roots for four days and nights.
Thus, for those who have surrendered with devotion and have desisted from evil even for as long as they live,
this supreme rite for purifying the body has been described by me today,
together with the Brahmakūrca penance.
Having previously understood the magnitude of the three types of faults,
one should constantly perform gifts of gold and other valuables whenever possible,
according to the sequence for minor transgressors, following the two times previously mentioned.

Thereafter, one should drink the *brahmakūrca* with a reduction of one-fourth [of the dose] at each stage; this is said to be equal [in efficacy] to the passage of time and the excellence of one's complexion. Indeed, expiation is the destroyer of all sins for everyone.
Having understood the progressive severity of the first misdeed,

the king of the twice-born should extinguish it through penances lasting two, three, or four months; those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes should increase the duration by one month each in succession.
Starting from a period of one month and so forth in due order,
even one who was formerly of evil conduct, an eater of all things, ungrateful, or an atheist—
if he should take refuge with faith in the Primordial God— [he is purified].
Know that person to be faultless by virtue of the power of the Supreme Self—
how much more so one who is afflicted by remorse, established in this teaching, desisting from evil deeds, and taking refuge in the shadow of devotion? || 21.23–21.24 ||

O Great-minded One, for the sake of destroying the impurities accumulated over many births and for those whose faults have been thus completely purified, one should now perform the initiation preceded by the mantra and bestow the Nārasiṃhī [initiation].
For the propitiation of that very Lord of majesty is indeed [the goal];
both externally and internally, for four months,
eight months, or a year, one should first strengthen the power of one's disposition through the intellect.
Having recognized the supreme devotion of those with auspicious dispositions,
one should thereafter perform the initiation known as Vibhava-vyūha-sūkṣma.
Now, O best of sages, listen as I describe the ritual procedure for initiation.
And now, for the twice-born and others who have obtained the necessary conditions.
For those whose sins have been completely extinguished and who have ascended this sequence,
one should perform the ritual of seizing the site for the consecration of the devotees on an auspicious and favorable lunar mansion, lunar day, ascendant, and moment. (21.30)
In a meritorious region that is favorable, pleasing, and frequented by holy men;
one endowed with soft soil, water, fruit, and flowers, and free from noise; blessed with cattle, crops, and rice, and devoid of small creatures. || 21.31–21.32 ||
There, one should resort to ground that corresponds to the [appropriate] color and possesses the characteristics previously described—
ground that is entirely free from defects and frequented by noble birds and wild animals;
ground where there are auspicious sites for monasteries, cow-pens, marketplaces, and houses.
It was separated [from the sea] by reservoirs, hermitages, sacred fields, and those of virtuous conduct;
it was free from fear of water and enjoyed by the powerful and the righteous;
and it was surrounded by forests, groves, villages, and the components of cities.

Whether there is lack of gain or gain, one should establish ownership over Brāhmaṇas and others of one's own station by worshipping them with one's own mantra, having regard for their respective castes; provided that one knows the site has been previously excavated, dug out, or is otherwise possessed of defects. (21.36)
Having filled it with auspicious clay and small stones from within,
one should then pound it and afterwards sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having mixed it with excellent gems such as gold and the like, one should level it and smear it over.
There, one should perform the worship of the Lord, ending with the waving of lights (dhūpana) as before; then,
one should conclude there by performing the offering of bali to the spirits, the libation for the cows,
and the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born.
To the east of the directions, one should first construct a pavilion adorned with decorations (21.40),
beautified by pillars arranged in pairs at each corner,
and graced in its center by an earthen pedestal (pārthiva-pīṭha) (21.41).
In width, however, it is traditionally held that for those beginning with the twice-born and ending with the Śūdra,
it should be either octagonal or square, provided with a pedestal;
its height is marked by a decrease of one unit starting from eight finger-breadths.
One should design the pedestal-base (upapīṭha) for the sake of one's own exaltation for all [temples].
The width of the pedestal-bases should be equal to twice their height;
they should be attached to the base and elevated by that same measure.
Having prepared the pedestal-seat (āsana-piṇḍikā) consisting of water and other elements,
and having placed and set down the food offering (naivedya) upon the secondary seat (upapīṭha),
one should perform the entry into the interior on its southern side.

In a secluded place, one should construct a plastered pavilion provided with windows, adorned with altars and sacrificial pits, and equipped with doors and bolts; having smeared it with cow dung and water consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra (astra).

One should construct two such pavilions (maṇḍapas) beautifully according to the prescribed rules. If one lacks the necessary wealth, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) may be performed in the house of a Brahmin, or in the residence of the disciple or the preceptor; there one should carry out the formal taking of possession (parigraha).

As before, preceded by worship and followed by the libation to the spirits (bhūtatarpaṇa), one should offer rice saturated with curd, parched grain, clarified butter, honey, and water; this is called the libation to the spirits. Without that, they remain there incessantly.
Standing outside, they remain enraged, longing for the supreme state;
therefore, once the site has been consecrated with effort,
one should always and everywhere offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) for the sake of unimpeded success.
Having thus performed this for the sake of auspiciousness, which resembles the sound of a long bell,
he should raise [the disciple] from his own position as before, uttering the great *praṇava*,
and then cause him to enter with auspicious parched grain and white mustard seeds.

Fruits such as the *śrīphala* and others, sandalwood and the like, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), white flowers and other blossoms, the clusters of those very trees, green *darbha* grass with their tips intact, all kinds of gems, and gold.
All medicinal herbs, cinnamon, cardamom, and other auspicious collections of fragrant substances;
padmaka, śaṅkhapuṣpī, viṣṇukrāntā, and kunda;
seven each of the grains and six equal portions of seeds.
Abundant quantities of rice, *śyāmāka*, and *nīvāra* grain were collected,
as well as the five products derived from cows; these, along with many other items free from any flow of impurity, were placed upon leaves of the *udumbara* tree.

For the purpose of daily use, [one should provide] water for washing the feet, water for sipping, and water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) in new vessels; likewise, curd and other items should be presented in vessels made of gold and the like, or in cups made of soft leaves. (21.58–59)
Two pairs of new, white silk garments (dukūla),
a sacred thread with an upper cloth, two very bright washed cloths,
pure silken fabrics, a bracelet, and a finger-ring.
A rosary made of crystal, a counting-bead necklace of lotus seeds,
a wheel made of five metals with twelve spokes and accompanied by a conch shell,
a kutapa blanket, a meditation band, a cloth for the eyes, and a deerskin.

A small cloth, a garment, a silk scarf, wooden sandals, leather shoes, a staff, an alms-bowl, and an umbrella; and powders made from wheat and mung beans; and garlands of four colors that are beautiful, pure, and light. (21.63)
A collection of green leaves mixed with dark-green grass,
guggulu resin as a refined incense, lamp oil and wicks,
a mirror, an incense burner, a bell, and a tuft of darbha grass.
Dust, a pair of tongs, a small vessel, a white water-clock,
a very firm five-finger-width rod made of gold or other metal, five blades of kuśa grass, a thread dyed with lac, a very white [thread], and a pair of scissors and a razor.
The eight shafts, including their tips, should be provided with the feathers of a peacock;
they must be elevated, firm, and made of bone, iron, clay, or wood,
and those which serve as their supports should be colored with lime and other pigments.
Basins, water-jars, auspicious ewers and *karavī* vessels,
as well as the *kalaśa* jar which is free from desire, devoid of burning heat, and possesses a common base;
cooking pots, water-pots, ladles, their covers, and hearths.
A new, four-legged auspicious seat, square and long;
betel with its proper measure, a collection of tooth-sticks,
the fire-drill joined with dry cow-dung, and a jewel that produces fire.

The fuel-sticks should be made of *pālāśa* wood with their tips intact, and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) likewise; there should be abundant dry firewood smeared with clarified butter, along with sesame and rice. Also required are the previously mentioned sacrificial ladles, such as the *sruk* and *sruva*, and whatever other implements are necessary for the oblation (*homa*).
Everything up to the very edge of the eyelashes, provided with two large vessels—
knowing that all those aforementioned enjoyments enter into the state of being limbs within the worship of the sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila), one should cause them all to enter.
Having performed the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the day prior to the day of consecration (adhivāsa),
and having first performed the binding of the protective thread (kautuka) upon the child on that very day of consecration, the preceptor,
with a mind intent on bestowing grace upon his future devotees, [proceeds], O Lord.
For those who desire the fruits of divine enjoyments and those who seek the state of ultimate liberation,
one should indeed augment each individual limb of the sacrifice with the divine form,
together with the eternal, unmanifest reality, and the sacred mantra-Brahman.
The array of mantras, which is one's own self, action, tree, and substance, shall yield fruit for those with desires according to the tradition, and indeed grant liberation to those without desires.
Having bathed there suddenly as before and performed his daily rites, [he should proceed].
Having entered, even if situated in an improper direction, one should then enter facing the east;
one should proceed by way of the lotus posture (padmāsana) or others, sitting upon a skin with its neck pointing toward the east.
One should perform the grace for the disciple with whatever mantra one has authority over.

(21.80) One should perform all ritual acts with that very mantra together with its ancillary limbs; or, if the grace is to be performed, it may be done with mantras possessing their full majesty. (21.81)
Then, for the sake of propitiating all and bestowing gifts, and for the attainment of the twelve [perfections],
one should perform that pair of piercings with the Viśākhayūpa mantra;
having pervaded the body with its seed-syllable as before, with those [mantras] consecrated accordingly.
One should perform the mandala rite with offerings brought previously according to one's ability,
using ointments, garments, bracelets, and so forth, as well as finger-rings,
a great white turban, and white garlands.
Having adorned his body with mouth-fresheners, betel leaves, and an auspicious tilaka on the forehead, and having established himself in a state of composure with a meditation-band (yogapaṭṭa),
he should then place the seed-syllable of the Lord in the center of the lotus of his heart.
Then, on the two hands, one should place the seed-syllable known as Padmanābhīya and that called Dhruva;
thereafter, having touched the body from the feet to the end and from the head downwards with the remaining syllables as before,
one should deposit the Lord’s seed-syllable along with its limbs upon the hands and the body.

Having thus correctly performed the conclusion of the mudrās, one should thereafter take up the conch and the discus with both hands, consecrated by their respective mantras. Then, having become that very self, one should place those two upon the surface of the earth.
Having observed everything situated therein, one should then proceed with the ritual action.
Having consecrated the weapon-mantra and stood within the ritual chamber,
one should smear, sweep, and scrub the sacrificial site with that [substance].
Then, for the sake of increasing the splendor of those two birds called Brahmā,
having deposited seeds consisting of gold and other precious gems,
and having prepared the vessels for the *arghya* offering and so forth according to the rules as before— (21.91)

Having first sprinkled the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) contained in separate vessels with the primary arghya water, one should then prepare it as before using the heart-mantra and the others. Then,
having offered kuśa-water with the weapon-mantra and having consecrated it with the first [mantra], [one should proceed].
Then, having brought that which was previously fetched to the state of fitness by means of both hands, which consist of Agni and Soma,
one should sprinkle everything with that water using *kuśa* grass held at the tips of the seat.
Having taken all kinds of seeds and grains together with white mustard seeds,
and having consecrated them with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) while meditating upon them as being identical to that weapon,
one should scatter them in the ten directions through this yoga for the pacification of obstacles.
Having gathered [the materials] with a bundle of *barhi* grass and placed them in the eastern direction,
the King of Weapons (Indra), having enclosed that within himself, drew [the mandala] with sandalwood paste and other substances;
then, having adorned the water-pot together with the jar as before.
Having visualized [the deities] in embodied form, complete with enjoyments and down to their garments,
one should meditate upon the weapon-mantra (astramantra) in their midst and worship it according to the prescribed rite.
One should also contemplate the destruction of obstacles and Time as the conclusion of karma.
Having made this request, the Blessed One stood with palms joined in reverence;
"O Lord of the Universe, accept this sacrificial hall prepared by me.
O All-pervading One, remain present throughout its completion and attend to the constituent rites."
One should lead an unbroken stream of water along the wall;
proceeding clockwise from the eastern part, one should mentally follow it to the end of that footprint.
Having placed that [footprint] there, one should then perform a circumambulation together with the water-pot.
Having offered the *arghya* to those two, one should scatter the upward-moving offerings on the eastern side.
Having worshipped it and covered it with a cloth, one should place the wheel consecrated with mantras upon a noble throne (*bhadrapīṭha*), and then set it down upon its support.
Having worshipped and bowed to the weapon-vessel (astra-kalaśa),

one should then place the previously mentioned host of world-protectors in their respective directions; having performed their confinement and worship with the Astra-mantra along with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should perform the worship with water-offerings (arghya) and other rites for the arches and banners, preceded by the syllable Om, their respective names, and words of salutation. Then,
one should meditate upon the previously described pedestal in the center of the sacrificial ground.
There, one should perform the worship of the Lord according to the previously mentioned sequence.
One should perform the libation ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* as before, once the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) has been consecrated.
Then, [one should worship] those beings who have become the Blessed One, together with the Lord of the Field (*kṣetranātha*).

Having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth, and having taken the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) contained in a vessel, one should then cast it outside the sacrificial hall while reciting this:
"To those beings who are devoted to Viṣṇu and to those who follow them... (21.109).
May they, being satisfied, accept this offering and bestow auspiciousness upon me.
Having washed his feet and sipped water (ācamana), he should enter the sacrificial hall.
Then, having prepared the hearth situated in the eastern direction within the fire-chamber,
he should move the cooking range from its own place to the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having cleansed the vessel with the Astra-mantra and smeared the exterior with cow dung and other substances,
he should smear the interior with fragrant scents, heat it over blazing Kuśa grass,
strike it with the Flower-Astra mantra, and tie a white thread around its neck.
Having enveloped it four times with the recitation of the *varma* mantra and having worshipped it with the *arghya* offering and other rites,
one should place it on the stove and set it over the fire.
Once the milk has been thoroughly purified and boiled, one should pour rice grains into it while reciting the *astra* mantra.
One should cook it with the root mantra, having consecrated it with the eye-mantra;
one should lower it [into the vessel] with the heart-mantra, sprinkle it, and stir it with the crest-mantra;
then, having smeared it with the head-mantra and rinsed it with very pure water.

One should adorn [the deity] with vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍraka*) using abundant sandalwood paste. Then, having performed the *homa* for the sake of success, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* offering of sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should place [the deity] upon a seat elsewhere within the mandala.
One should perform the offering of the oblation with clarified butter (*ājya*), which consists of the essence of light and immortality (21.118),
using the syllable *haṃsa*— conjoined with the [syllables] *īśa*, *abja*, and *nābha*, along with the nasal bindu—
as well as with *vauṣaṭ* and *vaṣaṭ*, and two *praṇavas* (21.119).
Since stability here is cultivated without these two at present,
therefore, as previously described, one should take that food with the *sampuṭa* [mudrā] and,
having taken it into the heart, visualize it as covered from above.

Then, when the homa of the collection of substances has been performed and the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is completed, that which was contained in the three vessels is extracted by means of the sacrificial offering;
having applied it according to the rule upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), into the water-pot (kalaśa), and into the fire. || 21.121–21.122 ||

Then, having separated the remainder— which has been permeated by the clarified butter (*ājya*) and covered with *kuśa* grass— one should offer three hundred oblations in sequence with the root mantra, the weapon mantra (*astra*), and the eye mantra (*netra*). Having brought it to completion, one should indeed perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) once again.
Then, one should prepare a mandala in the northern direction using cow dung and other materials. There, within the heart-mantra, one should place a seat made of darbha grass facing east.
In the center of that, one should seat the disciple with his feet together and his body held erect.

Facing east, with his speech and mental fluctuations restrained and his hands joined in *añjali*, one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) upon him with water using the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) as before;
and with that same [mantra], one should strike him on the head with blazing white mustard seeds and sesame seeds.
And for the removal of the bonds arising from beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā), one should,
with the Astra-mantra ending in *phaṭ*, scrape [the area] from the region of the feet up to the top of the crest-lock with the tip of a blade of Kuśa grass, so that the path may proceed straight.
Having now visualized him as pervaded by a web of mantras like a net,
one should bind his eyes with a cloth using the eye-mantra. Having first made a full añjali offering of wealth, arghya-water, flowers, and perfumes, [one should proceed].
Taking him by the hand with the mantra "Cāmnī," he should place the boy—who stands before him with his head bowed and palms joined in *añjali*—into the temple of the deity;
while his eyes are kept closed so that he is not seen by other people. (21.130–131)
Having observed the characteristic signs of devotion in one who has entered the path of the wholesome—
abounding in horripilation, longing, and joy, accompanied by tears of bliss,
and joined with prostrations, cries of victory, and circumambulations— || 21.132 ||
Having realized that his inner organ is purified, he should contemplate, "This one is fit.
When he is thus favored by that intellect known as Acyuta,
he should then remember [the Lord] situated in the center of the discus and lotus in his right hand.
The host of principal deities resides within their own respective abodes in the Supreme;
he [Viṣṇu] illumines them all with his multitude of rays.
With that very hand of Acyuta, wet with water, one should touch him.
Having placed that triad upon his back, with hands full of flowers,
at the conclusion of the group of mantras, for the sake of pacifying obstacles to liberation,
one should again worship the Supreme Lord, having brought him [there] with the mantra.

Having first understood that [the intellect] abides within as the locus of support for the earth and other elements— which are grounded in the intellect— as well as for latent impressions and the selves,
one should then effect their separation through meditation, worship, and other such means.
For the wheel of karma indeed revolves by relying upon the truth of the self.
Resting upon that wheel is the group of seven whose essence is the intellect;
it possesses the quality of pervading ignorance and brings about the experience of pleasure and pain.
Because it depends upon the wheel of karma,
that wheel of karma— which is inherently unstable— continually increases.
Supported by its foundation of earth and the other elements, it remains standing for only so long.
As long as he has not awakened through the performance of action with his full power,
he is unable to effect its restraint at all times; [only] once awakened,
he can do so through action dedicated to knowledge in the form of mantra-adoration.

Therefore, that unique support—the earth and so forth—is indeed human effort (*pauruṣa*); having established it now, one should make the world devoid of sap and devoid of thieves, by which the tree of karma, its fruit being cast off, perishes. (21.144)

Therefore, for the sake of purifying oneself, one should perform the worship of the mantras of the Bhūtas and other deities in sequence before the Omniscient One on the sacrificial ground. Know that the body of consciousness is common [to all], presided over by the Lords of Mantra.
Having first meditated on the path beginning with the earth as being like a six-petaled lotus,
one should then place therein— in the center— the one whose navel is a lotus (*abjanābha*), and in the eastern sector, above the filaments,
the group of six beginning with Viśvarūpa and ending with Kṣmāhara.
Having taken the first letter of his own name, which has become the seed-syllable (*bīja*) for those ending with the earth element (*kṣmā*),
he should sequentially recollect their previous placement at the tips of the petals by means of that [seed-syllable],
while the seed of the earth element resides at the tips of the petals fixed upon the root.
Previously, everything was undivided as the support of all the senses; then,
discerning [the self] as being enclosed within its own natural aggregate of the *skandhas*,
he perceived it as present, rising higher and higher through yoga.

One should worship correctly with the vision of differentiation, and again by means of the path of withdrawal (saṃhāra). Having meditated upon the earth-element (kṣmātattva) in the center there—yellow, marked by four corners, adorned with a golden lotus, and accompanied by its own seed-syllable and the vajra—one should worship. || 21.151–21.152 ||
One should properly worship the Vārāha mantra, together with its limbs (aṅgas) and its enclosures (āvaraṇas), in due order;
having established it as resting upon its causal source and accompanied by its retinue,
[one should visualize] below [it], situated above the mandala, white and resembling the moon.
Having recollected the city marked with a lotus, which is as vast as the interior of a white lotus, one should meditate upon the lake situated within it and perform the ritual sacrifice; then,
one should contemplate that city above it as a triangle consisting of radiant light.
One should worship the Lord Nṛsiṃha there in the center, who has a red complexion and is surrounded by hosts of red flames and marked with svastikas.
Above that is a black circular city, adorned with hosts of stars.
Having recollected [the deity] seated upon a blue lotus, one should then visualize the one whose seat is the sky.
One should then meditate upon the formless sky above that, characterized solely by sound.
Within that, one should visualize a lotus, radiant as the sun, with its color as previously described.
Having worshipped the god Vāgīśvara there according to the prescribed rite, one should then proceed.

Then, within the space of the interior of its pericarp, one should contemplate that which has the form of a lotus, consisting of the fluctuations of the mind and possessing the luster of various jewels; therein,
one should worship the Lord of the Mind, who possesses a universal form.
Above that, one should visualize the Amṛtagarbha [mandala], which is like ten million rays of the moon;

and having meditated upon the Lotus [seat] supporting the Self by means of its own nature, the Lord of Wisdom (Viṣṇu), whose navel is a lotus, resides within it— thus one should worship him with the intellect.
In this same manner, having sequentially brought down the assembly of presiding deities from the Supreme [level] for smell, taste, form, touch, sound, and mental cognition, one should worship them;
and having worshipped them again and again, one should place them back in that very same place.
One should contemplate the stability of those rays, which are like lotuses and are the source of the elements and their colors, within this power (śakti) as the Tathāgata;
[one should likewise contemplate] that which has the form of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā), abiding non-differently within the self.
One should meditate upon her as arising from all the seeds without exception, bearing the form of Padmanābha;
indeed, she has emerged from the entire realm of sense-objects, rendered separated from her Lord,
throbbing in form, fallen away, and without support.
When the time for initiation has arrived, having worshipped with the *praṇava* and having thus sacrificed to the seven elements along with the presiding spirits and deities,
he should afterwards worship the disciple himself with his joined palms.
Then, having gone into the presence of the fire and meditated upon the three abodes,
he should place his own right foot upon the consecrated seat of darbha grass to the south of himself,
using his own right hand along with kuśa grass for the sake of the Guru.
Having taken hold [of the body], he indeed remains seated through the oneness of the self with touch and the other [senses];
one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, consisting of light, from the seed-syllable at the feet up to the crest-lock (śikhā),
suddenly tearing asunder that which is beginningless, arisen, and formless.
Having mentally resolved upon the unification of the channels and their convergence, [one perceives] the manifold wheel of saṃsāra that impels one along the path of suffering.

In the same manner, one should offer oblations with ghee and sesame seeds— twelve in number— in sequence for the purpose of separating [the soul] from its actions, armor, and weapons; having thus performed this,
I shall indeed unite it with the Supreme Self.
First, one should offer eight oblations with clarified butter using the root mantra,

while touching that supreme limb [of the deity] with the *sruva* ladle filled with ghee. Then, for the sake of wisdom, one should again offer oblations with that very same mantra, which is the essence of all virtues.
One should perform the oblation according to the previously stated number, by means of intermittent application.
Indeed, one should take everything from the fire up to the end of the eyes;
for it is exactly thus that when the *sampāta* oblation has been completed, [the result] arises.
He should be made complete with all the purificatory rites through the majesty of the mantra;
now follows the [attainment of] the powers (śakti) and other qualities, but later,
through the perfect propitiation of the All-pervading Lord and through appropriate practice, he becomes a fit vessel.
When the oblation of clarified butter has been offered,

one should perform the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) of the mantras with it once for each, and having performed the worship, one should cause the Lord to hear [the following] regarding this reality called "action" (*karma-tattva*), along with its bondage of action and its latent impressions (*savāsanā*).
That [obstacle], though of many kinds, was paralyzed by me through your power;
immediately thereafter, for the sake of expiation,
he offered eight oblations of wood with his own body, its internal seed-syllable restrained.
To this extent, for a being of great intelligence who has taken birth and whose nature is a mixture of what is to be abandoned, there occurs the destruction of that which is to be discarded;
thereafter, the Dharma, which yields the single fruit of liberation, is to be adopted.
When that [deity] comes face-to-face in various ways, O Acyuta, by that means ignorance which was previously latent within him suddenly goes to its destruction. Then,
having first taken a reddish thread and made it many-fold...
Having gazed upon him with a vision purified by the water of the [divine] weapon,
and having extended [that vision] from his big toe up to the crown of his head,
one should then remember that [body] as the locus of all sufferings along with their attachments.
Having entered the proximity of the consciousness of the Child (Śiśu-caitanya) by means of the path of the gods,
and having placed the disciple’s name— preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*—
enclosed within the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should proceed indeed by the way of the fathers (*pitṛvartman*).
Having brought [the thread] together with the cord, one should bring it into alignment with the eye.

(21.187) Having worshipped it with the *arghya* offering and other rites, and having bound it with the armor (*kavaca*) mantra of the Great-Souled One, one should offer seven oblations with this: *oṃ huṃ adanyai huṃ svāhā*. (21.188)
Then, having struck the body of the child with white powder consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra, one should likewise enter it up to the feet;
then one should utter the word "viśleṣaya" (separate) followed by the word for the specific [victim].
Then, having drawn that [object] out by means of a word signifying knowledge (jñāna) ending in *tva* or *ta*,
and having made it conform to one's own intellect, one should meditate upon it like a sphere of stars;
then, having joined it within the central thread by means of the syllable *haṃsa* with the bindu.

Having remembered that body known as the *ātivāhika*— which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*), whose power is obstructed within the physical form by the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) uttered not too forcefully, and which is of the nature of a thread (*sūtrātmaka*) manifested through the power of the Self— 21.192.
Then, having restrained [the breath] with the *valamantra*, one should perform oblations for that purpose;
having uttered "Oṃ ātmane svāhā" twelve times,
one takes up the future bonds which are all-pervasive and bestow pure enjoyment.
One should join those [deities] such as Jñāna and the rest, who always abide here relying upon their respective locations,
right there by means of their own mantras;
having performed the libation for them according to the proper sequence.
Now, know that the station of the wheel of formative forces (saṃskāra), which rests upon the multitude of principles (tattva) and is indeed all-pervading, is characterized by fixed limits;
and by that very [wheel], there is the pervasion of the principles within the body composed of the five elements.
From the ankles, knees, hips, chest, throat, eyebrows, and the hollows between them,
there is a sequence of seven earths for those who perceive the elements beginning with earth.
Furthermore, there is the ego and its various diverse manifestations arising from it.
Those others born of the mind who abide together with the intellect,
as well as those awakenings arising at the same time, and those others which precede them—
though divided into many different varieties, they all abide by depending upon the intellect.
The entire universe, consisting of fourteen worlds and endowed with manifold arrangements,
extending for hundreds of millions of leagues and serving the purposes of others through its eight qualities,
is always to be understood as resting upon the earth.
O Great-minded One, the fourfold group beginning with the waking state resides in the waters of the [first] plane; the establishment of thousands of millions of various mantras,
together with their yogas and accomplishments, resides in the fiery plane.

O wielder of the plow (Lāṅgalin), the arrangement of the principles belonging to the fourfold self— the knowable ones who possess isolation (kaivalya) and whose natures are quiescent or emergent— is situated in the state of Marut. This pertains to those who have become manifold powers, such as knowledge and the rest.

Space is the substratum of the time-periods; that form is not perceived. The mental phonemes (varṇas), which are established in the sixth state of mind, are free from measures (mātrās) and so forth when this is proclaimed as the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan).

Thus, for the sake of purification, the Lord remains as the master in the state of the power of intellect (*buddhi-śakti*), casting away and indeed bringing forth the principles of the nature of karma with ease;
having first entered [them], he renders them free from defect at that very moment.

Having withdrawn its own power, it attains eternal peace. Then, one should perceive seven, seven, and six [elements] within the pentad beginning with earth, starting from the one who lies in the netherworld (Pātāla) up to Madhusūdana.
For indeed, this triad that exists within the mind arises from Śakti and Īśa;
and in the intellect resides the Lord, the Self whose navel is a lotus, the Sovereign of All, the Master.
Furthermore, for all those endowed with their own perfections upon the earthly plane...
One should understand the auspicious state of being as divided into fourteen types (2 x 7).
Having discerned the disposition of those endowed with devotion— whether intense, mild, or otherwise— one should,
by means of the ritual contact (*ālambhana*), establish all beings in their own true state.
This sequence has been stated for the rite of consecration (*adhivāsana*) within the initiation of power (*vaibhavadīkṣā*);
now, however, learn that of the other [initiation].
From the feet up to the region of the navel, [one should contemplate] by means of the great elements beginning with earth.

It is pervaded up to the end of the wind [element] in four ways, and above that, it is filled with space again. Having visualized with the mind that it is pervaded by this very sequence, reaching from the heart up to the crest-lock (śikhā): || 21.214–21.215 ||

Aniruddha and the others, ending with Saṅkarṣaṇa, remain [in their respective positions]; having traversed the sixfold path, however, he who has transcended the paths resides in the intellect (buddhi).
Then, having assumed a formal embodiment as before, he reaches the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) along with Samanā.

These pervasive forms, however, are surrounded by innumerable beings who have attained liberation individually and are devoted to the Supreme; they abide upon the earth and in all the previously mentioned realms,
at all times and in all places.
Having first recollected the group of six as non-different from one another, like sweetmeats,
one should contemplate that everything is pervaded by that [group] starting with earth and ending at the crest-lock (śikhā).
One should contemplate the Unmanifest, which is fourfold in nature, having sound as its form and being devoid of shape.
One should meditate upon the void (kha) therein as distinct from the mere qualities (guṇamātra).
Indeed, by means of that which has been transferred to the intellect (buddhi), everything is gathered together;
and by one's own power, even without desire, having taken up the individual soul (jīva), it moves upward.
Having dissolved its own capacity through its own power, that tranquil Self remains;
yet it manifests everywhere for those devotees of pure intent who desire only that state and are permeated by its power.
"Therefore, whatever is perceivable, even if it is limited and fit to be abandoned,
that always comes to those whose selves are cultivated by way of their own essential nature.
In such passages, the support known as *vidyā* (gnosis) is eternal and universal.
That too must be understood, for it has proceeded from non-universality;
indeed, O Mahāmati, until liberation, it itself constitutes the limb of living beings in a subtle form like a diamond, and is worthy of worship. (21.225–21.226)
At the time of initiation, the disciples must understand [the procedure] exactly as it has been taught;
likewise, one should know this further regarding the bodily form in the Sūtra.
First, having divided [the body] into seven parts, one should indeed mark the joints with saffron and other substances.
Then, having visualized that [object] as the focus, one should string together [the mantra] beginning and ending with the *praṇava* (oṃ),
joined with the word for one's own name, by means of its own causal [syllables].
Thus, when the heart has been made full at the end with enjoyments consisting of pervasion, [the rite is complete].
Having led [the disciple] before the Lord situated within the maṇḍala, one should present him;
having covered him with the armor (varman) and placed him in front of the jar,
the teacher, together with his disciples, should then perform worship once more for the all-pervading Lord, the Soul of the Universe.
Accompanied by circumambulations, prostrations, and various words of praise,
one should place him within that area of ground which has been smeared, and outside of that, at the edge of the mandala,
stationed in their respective positions, having consecrated them with the eye- and heart-mantras.
Having employed that [tooth-stick] in the five products of the cow, in the sacrificial porridge, and in cleansing the teeth,
one should perform the deliberation on success regarding a tooth-stick discarded by a devotee,
provided it points toward the north, the west, the northeast, or the east.
Know that this indicates success; otherwise, it is the opposite.
To destroy that [obstacle], one should indeed offer oblations a hundred times with the Vīrya-mantra.
Incense, ointments, and the like, as well as powders, water-pots, and so forth—[these are the materials].
O Lāṅgalin, having removed the sesame seeds and other suitable materials mixed with clarified butter, and having placed them to the north, one should cover them with a clean, unused,
and very white cloth over which the *varma* mantra has been recited.

Having worshipped thoroughly with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) using flowers, incense, and unguents, and having asked for forgiveness, one should place the deity— whether situated on the ground, in the fire, or in the water-pot—
upon a pure spot of earth strewn with *kuśa* grass consecrated by the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).
Having placed the disciple with his head toward the east and having covered his body with a cloth over which the *hṛdaya-mantra* has been recited many times, while recollecting the principal mantra,
he should have him sleep with sesame seeds consecrated by the *hṛdaya-mantra* for the sake of obtaining a dream-vision.
One should place white mustard seeds all around its exterior;
with the mantra, one should place eight arrows with feathers on them as before, and also encircle it clockwise with a white thread while reciting the *varman* mantra.
Having encircled the pavilions in four ways, one should go outside;
having completed the rites such as the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*),
one should sleep oneself upon a bed of *darbha* grass in a *kutapa* cloth, with the head placed toward the south.
He should touch with his two feet the infant lying upon the bed.
Mentally praying to the Blessed One, the bestower of liberation:
"Oṃ! O Lord, Master of the World, Omniscient One, You who dwell in the heart;
there I unite this person with virtuous action, having You as his supreme refuge."
But having obtained permission, he should indeed perform the application for the disciples;
wherever that [application] is made for them, it shall necessarily be eternal.
Thus has the procedure for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of initiation been fully proclaimed.
Now, initiation (dīkṣā), which possesses both a single and manifold nature, is proclaimed;
by attaining which, at the end of the body, one reaches the desired state.
Indeed, one [type] bestows the fruit of absolute liberation (kaivalya), while the other bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Indeed, for those who are awakened, the third lunar day is always the deity of enjoyment;
all [these days] should be observed with the approval of the teacher for the sake of attaining the fruit correctly,
for disciples who are subject to rebirth and are permeated by a spirit of devotion.
For the elderly, for women, and for children whose minds are yet to be cultivated,
those [virtues] are difficult to practice without a full collection of proper conduct;
having reflected thus with wisdom in the past, together indeed with one who has approached [the teaching].
Having understood his intention and having fulfilled it, O high-minded one,
the teacher should then rise from his bed after the night has passed,
take up his water-pot, perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) outside, and enter [the hall].
One should visualize the Weapon-mantra (astra) before oneself, resembling the flame of a consuming fire;
one should enter [the bath] within that, and thus the mantra-bath is performed. By this, the impurity of sleep and delusion is constantly brought to total destruction.
Having taken up the pegs, the hour-line cord, and the colored powders with the supreme weapon-mantra, and having consecrated them by grinding them upon the ground smeared with dry cow-dung,
[one should draw] the mandala previously described.
For the sake of preserving its auspiciousness, stakes should be placed in the corners;
and having positioned a single lotus in the center for the purpose of achieving the rotation,
it will not experience even the slightest irregularity, just as during the night.
Since there is a great fault for a teacher together with his disciples when there is a significant deficiency [in the ritual],
therefore that must always be protected with great effort. Having first performed the bath at dawn, one should always complete the daily rites beforehand.
Having taken his disciple and urged him on, he should observe the attainment of dreams— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
as well as the assembly of the four forms situated according to their respective directions,
whether seated in rows or standing.
From among those, is it the single reality of the Blessed One, or that which has distinct characteristics; is it the multitude of manifestations and the collection of their emblems;
or is it this goddess, the host of women, or perhaps all of these as one?
Whether as the entire collection of the instruments of existence or as existing separately—
characterized by Rudra, Indra, the Moon, the Sun, Water, Fire, and Wind—
the Brahmins who know the Pañcarātra and are devoted to its worship [perceive this].
The twice-born ones proclaimed the three Vedas and recited them;
the ascetics, pure in being and established in the state of the true Brahman,
[beheld] the best of trees, fragrant with mountain garlands, sandalwood, and other scents.
A garden, a woman, a grove, a pond, a palace, or a great hall;
a fruit, a seed, a medicinal herb, or a water-pot; or one who has emerged from cooking; a cow, an elephant, a horse, a river, a vehicle, a maiden adorned with ornaments, or an infant. (21.265)
The sweet sound of auspicious songs, the kettledrum, the flute, and the lute;
a lake filled with lotuses and cranes, a spread white parasol,
metals such as gold, a net of jewels, and products derived from cattle.
A fresh mass of eyes, a multitude of white, unwashed garments,
the king’s domestic priest, a feudal lord, and the queen’s mirror;
the falling of snow, a virtuous rain, and the rising of great clouds in the sky.
Blood, fresh flesh, flying through the air, liquor and the like,
a flock of excellent birds and deer, a divine image, and a white chowrie—
know that these and other such signs grant success.
Listen briefly to those dreams which are inauspicious for me:
the withering of flowers, an earthquake, and a most terrifying eclipse; mist, the falling of meteors, and a thunderous crash that causes the mind to break.
Entering a pit, eating curd-rice and boiled meat,
dancing, the destruction of a chariot, the flowing of clarified butter from one's own body, laughing excessively at a donkey or a camel, and a forest infested with monkeys and bears. (21.272–21.273)
A place filled with smoke, burnt, or surrounded by black garments;
the drying up of rivers and the like, or their flowing in the opposite direction;
a boat-vehicle, and even the breaking of a banner, an umbrella, or a tree—these bring about failure.
Descending from a mountain or a tree, falling to the ground, seeing a hungry ghost (preta);

smearing oneself with collyrium, lampblack, oil, or ghee; standing in fresh mud; [dreaming of] a buffalo, a snake, a man, or a black cow; and coming from the southern direction while feeling hungry. (21.275–21.276)
The plucking out of nails and hair, the breaking of bones,
and other such inauspicious things, O Mahāmati,
[occur] when one has experienced auspicious or inauspicious dreams, having indeed formed an intention in the heart.
Out of eagerness, one should perform the worship and fire-oblation that destroys inauspiciousness.
Having brought down the deity according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him in due order;
having gratified him according to the proper method, one should worship again until the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
In the northeast or the north corner of the sacrificial hall,
upon the previously described mandala— whether circular or square—
one should seat the disciple, who has bathed, wears a garland and fresh garments, and has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having gazed upon it, struck it, sprinkled it with water, and touched it with *darbha* grass as before;
having consecrated it like an image, but rather having favored that which has entered the earth,
he should then touch it from the feet to the head with his mantra-hand.
He who has conquered the seeds of suffering should bestow the blazing form of the mantra-hasta;
therefore, he should perform for the disciple the five consecrations in their proper order:
heating (tāpa), the sectarian mark (puṇḍra), the name, the mantra, and the sacrifice (yāga) as the fifth.
In that regard, O best of sages, listen to the procedure for the heating [of the iron ball]:
having honored the Vaiṣṇava members of the assembly, and with their permission, the Guru,
accompanied by his disciple, goes to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit.
Having worshipped the discus and the conch, which were installed with their respective mantras and previously bestowed by one's own guru at the time of one's initiation, O twice-born ones,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter one hundred and eight times with the root mantra.
And also with the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī, namely the verse beginning "tad viṣṇoḥ," he should then cast the discus and the conch into the fire of the sacrificial pit and worship them,
O twice-born ones, using the mantra of the discus and the mantra of the conch.

Having offered one hundred and eight, or indeed twenty-eight oblations with the mantra beginning "pavitrante" and the verse "prate viṣṇo," he should then offer to the Lord of Gods and meditate upon the lineage of gurus.

O lords of sages, one should mark the disciple’s right armpit with the discus and heat the left armpit with the conch. Then, having consecrated both the discus and the conch with their respective mantras, [one should proceed].
O twice-born ones, having worshipped with the root mantra, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, O best of sages, one should apply the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra);
I shall explain the procedure for that—listen with careful attention.
Having taken pure white clay from a sacred site of Viṣṇu,
O twice-born ones, and having washed his hands and sipped water, he should sit upon a clean seat facing either the east or the north, with the palm of his left hand [turned upward].

O twice-born ones, having washed white clay there with the Astra-mantra and having applied it with the Praṇava, one should then sprinkle that clay with water while reciting the "Gandhadvārā" mantra and perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana).
Having approached with the root mantra the clay situated in his speech and hands,
the knower of mantras, having inscribed the seed-syllable of Nārasiṃha in its center,
should take the clay with his finger and apply it to his forehead and other parts.
O lords of sages, one should perform the *āyuṣkāri* [gesture] with the thumb for bestowing nourishment, with the index finger for the attainment of liberation,
with the *nāgikā* [finger] for granting desired objects,
and likewise with the middle finger.
One should hold [the clay] with these fingers, but not touch it with the nails.
The *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* should be straight, beautiful, shaped like the two feet of Viṣṇu,
with space between the lines, well-proportioned on the sides, and measuring two or three finger-breadths in width.
It should be four finger-breadths wide in its length;
one should wear it on the forehead, and it should be four finger-breadths broad at the belly.
Alternatively, it may be eight finger-breadths long or the measure of a span.
One should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) accompanied by the Mānasa [mantra]. One should wear the vertical mark on the heart, endowed with the *lakṣa* [mantra];
it should then be three finger-breadths wide and four finger-breadths long.
It is long,
O twice-born ones; the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* at the region of the throat and then on the right side of the belly is indeed equal in size to the *puṇḍra* previously mentioned for the stomach.
Then, on the middle of the right arm, one should wear an upward-pointing mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide; then,
on the right shoulder, it should be equal in size to the neck-mark (*kaṇṭhapuṇḍra*).
On the left side of the abdomen, there should be an upright *puṇḍra* equal in size to the abdominal *puṇḍra*.
On the left arm, there should be a *puṇḍra* with the characteristics described for the right arm.
Then, on the left shoulder, there should be a *puṇḍra* equal in size to the throat *puṇḍra*.

O best of sages, one should wear an upward-pointing mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) on the back, eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width; on the hump of the neck, it should be four finger-breadths long; likewise, one should wear it with a width of three finger-breadths.
Having thus applied the twelve marks (puṇḍra) in their proper sequence,
O twice-born ones, one should sprinkle the water used for washing the hands upon the head;
thereafter, in the center of the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one should apply that which is offered to Viṣṇu.
One should apply the powder of *rajanī* (turmeric) for the sake of attaining prosperity and the discovery of hidden treasures,
either in the form of a wick-lamp or in the shape of a bamboo leaf.
Indeed, when the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is worn in this manner, the Lord of the World dwells together with Lakṣmī.
O twice-born ones, he plays there constantly; therefore, with palms joined in reverence,
the wise man should meditate upon Keśava and the others, preceded by reflection on their true meaning, and remember them together with their respective Śaktis, using the names beginning with Keśava.
One should meditate on Keśava at the forehead, Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen,
Mādhava on the heart, and Govinda at the hollow of the throat.
O lords of sages, one should meditate on Viṣṇu on the right side of the abdomen.
One should meditate on Madhusūdana at his side, in the middle of the arm;
Trivikrama on his shoulder; Vāmana on the left side of the abdomen;
Śrīdhara on the left arm; and Hṛṣīkeśa on his shoulder-blade.
Others, however, should remember Padmanābha on the forehead and Dāmodara on the base of the nose.
Thus has the procedure for the upright sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) been well proclaimed. Having thus applied the upright sectarian mark upon the disciple according to the rule—
One should give a name to the disciple; the procedure for that is stated here:
taking him by the hand, one should go near the abode of the gods, placing him on one's left side and once again covering his eyes.
One should cast the water-offering (arghya) in that manner with palms joined and eyes cast down;
then, with eyes opened, one should gaze upon the supreme abode of Mantra, which bestows the fruits of one's desires.
At that moment, one should give whatever name is appropriate for the person.
Its primary name is known as the "Secret" (rahasya), while its secondary names exist according to their actual state;
or else, the general names beginning with Vāsudeva apply to all four [forms] through their own respective parts,
either specifically or according to the established sequence.
One should mark it with twelve forms ending with the Lord for Brāhmaṇas,
and for Kṣatriyas, one should likewise make it twelvefold, ending with the deities;
or else, it may rest upon the earth, ending with the hand, preceded by the emblems and weapons.
And among kings, there are those known by the marks of banners and insignia according to their respective status.

Thus, for the Vaiśyas, [the system] culminates in the *vardhana* ceremony preceded by the rites of the image and the insignia; and for those born as Śūdras, it extends down to the *dāsa* (servant) rite.
Then, having risen and paid homage to the mandala, the jar, and the guru,
the preceptor should go to the vicinity of the fire-pit together with the disciple.
This is for the sake of ensuring the completion of the performed rite without defect once the oblation has been offered.
Having become one whose nature consists of the weapon-mantra, he should enter its heart as before.
Having briefly separated him from the power of the vital breath (prāṇa) and brought him [there],
one should cause him to enter his own place; having led him there like a spark of fire,
one should thoroughly effect his separation and expel him along with the wind.
On one's own level, [the breath] is restrained from the heart to the end via the left path.
By this very rite joined with mantra, which effects the seizing of birth,
one should abandon that which consists of father and mother, as if permeated by the meditation on existence.
Then, one should give [the disciple] the sacred thread (*upavīta*) that has been consecrated seven times with the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), provided it belongs to him as prescribed; for he has,
in truth, entered into a state of servitude in every respect.
For one who does not drink intoxicants, whose lineage is pure, who has abandoned worldly customs,
who is like a trusted friend, who is established in Brahman, and who is devoted to ritual action—
for such a person of the Śūdra caste, the gift of a cow is indeed ordained, just as those other [gifts] are.

However, for those mantras that conclude with *vaiṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, or *vaṣaṭ*, the counter-measure is to perform the rite with a salutation (*namaskāra*) when the occasion for grace arises. Whatever implements for the sacrifice there may be, such as the water of honor (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth— [these belong to him].

Whether well-prepared or unprepared, [the sacrificial substance] attains fitness through devotion. For other devotees, however, the prescribed method for accomplishing the sacrifice consists of the complete withdrawal of the mind from external objects, preceded by visualization and consecration with sprinkling.
O Mahāmati, one should perform the casting of flowers before the image or at the front of the mandala;
likewise, the nocturnal rite and the *paripīḍa* are for the sake of the true reality (*bhūtārtha*).
Having first thus purified the collection of syllables through ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), [one proceeds].
With the complete [mantra] along with its limbs (sāṅga), the omnipresent one should perform that propitiatory libation (tarpaṇa) as an atonement—
one thousand times, plus a tenth part— according to the proper sequence.
Having gone there and entreated the Lord of the Pitcher (Kumbheśa), he should take the thread situated there.
Having made the thread straight like a child and having stretched it out,

one should meditate upon the Lord of Mantras in his manifest form, situated in the midst of the fire. One should clearly perceive the Child within the pervasive thread, as the path within one's own self.
Therein, one should recall the internal nature as residing within the body of the mantra;
and having brought that divine nature into one's own self,
one should [project] the threefold [nature] consisting of the elemental realm onto the thread and the body of the disciple.
At the conclusion of the root mantra, having added the word "to the Supreme Self" (parātmane) along with the salutation (namas),
one should offer four oblations.
Likewise, having uttered [the words] "to the Subtle Self" (sūkṣmātmane) and then indeed "to the Gross Self" (sthūlātmane).
Thereafter, for the sake of the Universal Self,
one should contemplate the entire collection of paths— extending from the tips of the feet to the crown of the head— residing within one's own body,
according to the prescribed sequence, even though it is divided into three types.
The arrangement and configuration of the earth and other elements, as well as their status as the objective world (*adhibhūta*),
should be understood as their respective presiding deities (*adhidevatva*) and their individual inherent capacities.
The internal state (*adhyātmatva*) is prescribed for the mantras that preside over those [elements].
Then, having abandoned the two paths, one should take recourse in the *dvādaśānta*;
having become composed of the root mantra, one should then proceed by means of one's own intellect toward the disciple’s station at the door of Brahman via the path situated between them.
Having stepped upon the earthly foot, one should bring its power under one's own control—
that which is the seed-syllable, restrained by the heart-mantra, having the form of fragrance,
enclosed within the various seeds of the cosmic egg, and endowed with manifold arrangements.
Thus, having taken up all the powers that are the culminations of the intellect,
one should place them individually and in sequence within that heart-mantra-sandwich,
by means of one's own internal group and the supreme pervasive Self.
And one should remember that body as possessing the nature of both,
as well as time ending with the exhaustion of experience; and from that time, O Great-minded One,
having thus performed the withdrawal of the powers of the elements from the form of the child—
Then, having entered the body described in the Sūtras by that very same path,
he should proceed there radiantly; and whatever he visualizes with his intellect,
he should take up those internal mantras accompanied by the elements and their constituent parts.
And having established those who abide there with the pure characteristics and mantras,
you should then emerge from the thread and proceed to the fire-shrine.
There, one should perform the binding of the limbs and the equality of the mantras.
Having established the collected mantras in their respective positions within the supreme characteristic of omniscience— which is all-pervasive and universal—
the instructor, having reached his own body through the aperture of Brahma (brahmadvāra), [proceeds].
Having taken up the *sruva* ladle and having satiated the multitude of mantras as prescribed—
including the multitude of *tattvas*— by means of their own names preceded by the *praṇava*,
and again through the method of conjunction with the number twelve.
Having drawn the disciple from the heart-lotus into [his own] heart by means of *pūraka* (inhalation),

he should then take the seed-syllable of Earth (*kṣmā-bīja*), which is characterized by the "other" (*paralaksana*) and has been rendered manifest, restrain it with the power of Earth (*bhū-śakti*) through knowledge, and draw it from the fire [element] into the heart.
Having purified [the disciple] while he rests upon the seat of the *praṇava* in the lotus of childhood,
one should then recollect the consciousness of the disciple as being singular yet possessing two forms;
one should contemplate it through the state of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and the state of power (*śakti*).
Having again emitted that [deity], who is contained within the earth-element (kṣmātattva) and possesses power (śaktimat),
from the sacrificial pit by means of its own mantra through the central path into his own body,
he should then unite it with that meditative absorption (samādhi) characterized solely by recitation and visualization.
Thus, by means of the heart-mantra and the rite of oblation, that very earthly seed should be properly led into the state of the subtle body for the sake of its benefit;
ending with *svāhā* for the attainment of enjoyment, and ending with *namaḥ* for the attainment of liberation.
Or for the attainment of both enjoyment and liberation, that very same [mantra] characterized by both [aspects] should be employed.
At the conclusion of the ritual actions, however, one should place it in the state of *sampāda*.
In this way, within that subtle body and within the lotus of the heart of that [deity], [one should perform the rite].
Having assumed authority over that [object] as it exists by means of the *śiras* mantra,
and having accomplished its enjoyment one hundred times with the *śikhā* mantra,
one should contemplate the attainment of its fruit and its state of absorption by means of the *varman* mantra.
One should perform that [act] with the very eye consisting of one's own satisfaction; by means of that, it remains established.
Its abandonment occurs through the *astra-mantra* because of separation;
then, having grasped it with the *mūla-mantra*, one should once again make it one's own.

In the same way, O high-minded one, having performed the fire-oblation with the Astra-mantra the previously stated number of times for the sake of pacifying the unique power belonging to that [deity]— characterized by pervasiveness— which resides within the *kuṇḍa* and pertains to the *kṣmātattva* (earth-principle) that is to be accomplished; || 21.370 ||
Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter and having cut out the earthen [image] according to the *Skandasūtra*,
one should dissolve it together with the full [ladle] into one's own fire at its proper place,
by means of the root mantra suddenly impelled within the heart-lotus.
Then, having projected the infantile power (*śakti*) from one's own body by means of exhalation (*recaka*),
one should meditate upon it as distinct, pervading that which stands below.
One should likewise contemplate the path of the elements (*bhauvana*), beginning with the lotus-leaf of the skull and extending to the first path.
Then, upon the seed-syllable of the earth (KṢM), which has been restrained within the body of the disciple, embraced by manifestation, and filled with its own power,
one should likewise expel the possessor of power by means of the previously mentioned method of separation.

At that moment, for the sake of his accomplishment, he should meditate with his intellect upon the disciple— who is composed of consciousness, detached from worldly existence, and who out of compassion reveals the path as it truly exists, abiding within the seed— as being his own Lord.
This is that very nature of the earth—a cage of suffering indeed, acquired in vain. Its capacity for endurance has now vanished along with its appearance;
how could I have remained here, when these [limbs] of mine are no longer extended?
Just as a bird released from a cage remains at ease,
flying upward, so too does the child, mounted [upon the body] by the power of the mantra. Then,
having informed the assembly, he remained there by virtue of his authority over them.
Indeed, it would be completely restrained for him at all times from every side.
By the power of your grace, the quality of earth remains exactly as it is until the end of the body; for him who is seated, the subtle element of smell indeed persists.

O Lord of the Earth, O Protector, from this day forward, you must act for the destruction of those obstacles to liberation and for the sake of the karma within the supreme teaching of the Lord, for one who has correctly entered upon the path.
Having thus informed and commanded, one should offer oblations in sequence;
then, having drawn [the consciousness] together with the Śakti by means of the *pūraka* breath,
one should again place the watery seed-syllable along with its support within that body, as before.
Having placed the vital energy (jīva-śakti) within the center of the vessel as before,
and having exhaled that energy, one should then fix it there;
O Great-minded One, by means of the breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should remain in that meditative absorption (samādhi) just as previously described.
Then, having attained this body through [the practice of] fire-offerings, meditation, and so forth,
and having indeed completed everything there according to his qualification,
he casts down the full [body] together with the aqueous thread and the aggregate.
One should likewise remember the state of authority (*āptatva*) conjoined with the word (*pada*), pervaded by that [authority];
and indeed, one should cause the collection of mantras situated therein, together with its Lord,
to be heard as before, having made known the flavor (*rasa*) like a fragrance.
Having thus brought the mind to its conclusion within the sphere of the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the upward movement,

O Greatly Wise One, one should then, by means of the weapon of the fire-syllable (tejasāstra) belonging to the final limb, extract [the consciousness] according to one's will and join it, as before, to the sphere of the Buddha.
Having remembered that disciple— who was previously bound by the six paths,

who has now attained consciousness, who is freed from the sheath of the *tattvas*, and who has reached unity within the peaceful Self— as having acquired the defining characteristics in the fire of the nature of Śakti at the supreme level; || 21.391 ||
But by means of the seed-syllable of Īśvara, which is said to be endowed with sattva,
one then experiences [the state] and, having enjoyed it, applies oneself to samādhi;
there, being fully absorbed, one does not perceive even the mere duality of one's own bliss.
Having offered a hundred oblations in that rite for attaining that state,
he brought everything— including the entire web of objects of cognition along with the continuous flow of speech— into equality with that very [reality] through his own wisdom. (21.394)

Becoming composed and free from mental fluctuations, he should offer the supreme full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Then, having attained the state of "I-am-ness" (asmitā), the Guru should again offer an oblation by means of the Lord of the Seed-syllable (bījanātha) for the sake of the disciple’s liberation from bondage.
With his mind fixed on the state of the syllable *pada* while the *padās* are restrained by the *oṃkāra*,
and having said, "Become omniscient," he should offer twelve oblations.
"May you be thus, O Blessed One— faultless and without support."
Hari is the Lord of all, possessed of all powers, perfectly complete, and infallible;
he is all-pervading, with his six attributes restrained, changeless, and stainless;
he is eternal, eternally manifest, never deficient, eternally blissful, and perfectly partless.
Vāsudeva is indeed without beginning or end, and without destruction; he is the possessor of all glory.
Having thus offered the oblation, one should then perform the *pūrṇāhuti* once again.
Thus established in the initiation of his own glory, the seeker of liberation stands upon the sovereign plane.
Established there, one indeed attains the abode of the Supreme Lord without delay (21.401).
O Great-minded One, by the power of the Lord’s will alone, [this occurs] upon the falling away of the body for one who desires enjoyment,
and for one who desires both, in the two states belonging to Padmanābha (21.402).
Now, by means of the union of the possessor of power and power, one should be established on the path consisting of the intellect (*buddhimaya-adhvā*),
having been extracted from that state for the duration until the fall of the body;
just as fire is hidden within wood yet becomes separated from it.
A person does not again attain identity with wood as before;
once joined within the path, he does not thereafter return to that state.
Having brought about a withdrawal from meditative absorption, he establishes himself before [the object].
The path, both white and black, must be taught to him exactly as it is;
for that which exists undivided within the Supreme Self appears as if divided.
It is the supreme, imperishable Brahman, free from the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower.
Indeed, by His own power and through the state of being that Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman),
the Supreme Lord Himself arises for the liberation of all living beings.
Know Him to be the unmanifest Imperishable (Avyaktākṣara), just as the word "tantra" is a derivative of the root *kal*.
It does not proceed by itself toward stability through the nature of distinct castes;
nor do they reach certainty therein because of the grace of the fourfold self,
except for those Brahmins who know the Veda regarding this first syllable.
That Blessed One, whose form is sound, approaches in the form of a *kalā*;
for his abode is attained through those actions dedicated to him.
And that stainless form, which arises from the *kalā* of the six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), [is reached] until [the end].
Speak, for otherwise that which is material is employed to be grasped.
All the principles consist of the *kalās* and are characterized by origination and dissolution;
