they are the previously mentioned [entities] beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with the Adhyakṣa, as they have been described.
The mantras have emerged from the principles (tattvas) and are endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest;
they are joined with the six parts of the plowshare (ṣaṭkalāṅgalavas), and their number is not known.
By them, the manifestation of sound is revealed, which is designated as the state beginning with the fourth (turya).
For the sake of the manifestation of karmas, for the sake of delusion, and for their destruction,
there exists this universe consisting of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) and comprising fourteen worlds (*dvisaptabhuvana*).
It is indeed impure, insentient, eternal, an object of experience (*bhogya*), all-pervading, and situated separately.
Thus has the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan), characterized by what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, been described.

Excluding the fourth state (turyapada), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and the path of words (padādhvan) constitute the remainder of what is to be abandoned; in relation to that [fourth state], they are to be accepted through ritual action (karman).
Even through dependence, that which is to be attained falls into the category of what is to be abandoned; however,
for one established in the state of discernment and refined by initiation, there is indeed the means for attaining that waveless, supreme state.
When investigated in this manner, that wherein rest indeed becomes clearly manifest is the Supreme Brahman, known as Vāsudeva, the imperishable;
it is like the ether that is the locus of atoms and sacrificial ladles.
Thus, this is to be known as the primary abode of awakened living beings,
and that which is the interval between the worlds and the planes,
by whose will those mantras indeed sport.

In that non-dual state of Māyā, for those devotees of the Supreme Lord who are permeated by the will of the Lord— namely, the gurus and the initiated whose souls are intent on propitiation— the fruits consisting of pleasure and pain [do not arise]. || 21.422–21.423 ||
The mantras residing in the two paths above [the Māyā-tattva] await the command;
they lead the practitioners correctly by force from the two paths of Māyā to their own abode for the attainment of the enjoyments such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
(21.424) Indeed, it is for the sake of attaining these enjoyments.
And for one who is dispassionate, they do not impel him toward the enjoyment of those [powers] by their own power;
even by virtue of their own activity on the path of the principles (tattva-adhvan), which is like nectar,
he remains there where [powers] such as atomization (aṇimā) consider themselves as if they were mere blades of grass.

The stainless ones, such as Tattvādhyakṣa and the rest, intent on bestowing grace upon him, lead him— even if he is effortless— perfectly along the eternal path of the Sakala. He is Brahman consisting of the six qualities, Vāsudeva, who bears the form of the path.
In the eternal Self, within the connection designated as the Śabdabrahman on the path,
he who remains there himself indeed effects the union with that [Supreme].
Through the thorough knowledge of that, he attains the utterly peaceful state of the Blessed One.
O Saṅkarṣaṇa, O God, tell me what the characteristics of the knowledge of the path of the castes are,
by the thorough understanding of which one attains the true state of Vāsudeva within the path.
The Blessed One is he who,
assuming the form of a continuous stream of descent, reaches the state of direct experience for the Self that has been liberated from the sheath of the five paths and has attained its true being.
Sound, consisting of various colors and characterized by the previously mentioned marks,
should be understood as being of the nature of that [consciousness] within the collection of the fourfold self.
Through the union of origin and dissolution, it possesses the characteristic of luminous sound.
Indeed, from the letter *sa* ending and the letter *ha* ending in *a*, there arises the end of the twelve; for the letters *ha* belong to those whose nature is fourfold.
Moreover, the letter *a* is at the point of dissolution (*apye*), and thus an equality between these two is recorded.
In this collection of the array of phonemes (varṇavyūha), that which is to be known is through the meditative absorption of gnosis (jñānasamādhi):
the universal manifestation, the arising, the pervasion, the manifestation, and the sovereign Vāsudeva.
Here, each individual form is indeed to be thoroughly understood in this very manner.
In brief, it is joined with a group of four preceded by rest;
indeed, it is established in this very manner through an arrangement like a staff.
There are twelve *dhāraṇās*, beginning with the characteristic of the Self.

Having led [the disciple], who has become manifest, by means of this which serves as a staircase, one should cause him— who stands as the Śabdabrahman— to enter the supreme Dvādaśānta after having first established him within the heart-lotus; such is the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) for the initiated.
Having attended to the sacrificial ground with excellent water,
together with his disciple, he should perform the rite for the sake of unbroken success as before, using the *bhūti* ashes, marking the site, and bowing to the fire.
Having risen from there, one should depart, taking him to the abode of the Imperishable;
having worshipped the Lord of the World, one should offer [the initiation] to the child according to the rules,
whether with specific details or in brief, according to his capacity and the presence of obstacles.
It should be taught exactly as it is; then, his worship is performed within the heart.
The mantra, accompanied by mudrās and preceded by ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation, as well as the procedure—both concise and detailed according to the scriptures—should be explained.
By that [water], which is equal and continuous, every ritual act is performed as it stands;
then one should perform the worship of the Guru for oneself with wealth and other offerings.
Having filled the right hand with water from the arghya-vessel—
One should cast [the water] consecrated with the six-limbed mantra upon his head.
Then, one should visualize the maṇḍala on the hand as having the radiance of the sun by means of the *praṇava*;
there, one should install the host of deities in their full majesty, inseparable [from it], as before.
Having performed this with a focused mind, one should offer it upon his head;

then, O son, may that which is as described and as desired come to you without delay— may you possess the power of sovereign success (*vaibhavī-siddhi*) together with the fortune of liberation (*mokṣalakṣmī*).
Thus has the definition of the Vaibhava initiation been fully proclaimed.
It is common to all groups of mantras employed therein;
for by whichever specific mantra the initiation of anyone is to be performed, [that same procedure applies].
For each of those [limbs] belonging to him, the application of the parts should be performed according to the previously indicated path, as it has been described;
one should perform it for the heart and the rest, ending with the root, as if they were a collective whole.
Having correctly grasped the state of being entirely internal along with the collection of principles (tattvas),
one should then perform the worship as before;
the rites for the eyes, the heart-seed syllable, and the five limbs are prescribed.
For those mantras that lack constituent parts (niraṅga), but whose ritual actions are prescribed by the mantras of their constituent parts,
the *praṇava* should be employed together with the word for the action.
By this procedure, that [initiation] is to be accomplished for those who desire the initiation of the *vyūha*.
However, in each individual rite,
one must indeed apply the fourfold group beginning with Vāsudeva, which was previously taught as the seed-syllables;
for in this very way, the primary mantra is employed in its entirety throughout the collection of rites.
In the initiation of Brahman, one should perform the rite by dividing it into six parts as before;
[this applies] to those who have been liberated according to their own nature and at the appropriate occasions.
However, in this case, the prayer to the gods is intended to be expressed in the singular.
The application (*yojanā*), however, should be understood in brief as that which was described regarding the consecration (*adhivāsa*).
For this twofold perpetual initiation (*nityadīkṣā*), there is no fruit other than liberation.
And even therein, O lotus-eyed one, the initiation is fourfold in nature, as previously [stated].
By force, it bestows upon those of purified soul the attainment of the enjoyment of the sixfold qualities;
yet the fruit of garlands, sandalwood, and even the materials for fire-offerings,
naturally and suddenly undergoes dissolution through the initiation into Brahman.
O best of sages, one should likewise bestow these three initiations either upon a single person or sequentially, for the sake of achieving fitness for all forms of worship;
or else, O twice-born ones, [they are bestowed] upon the eight-syllable mantra and so forth, and upon the triad of pervasive [mantras].
With one [mantra], he should perform the initiation common to all according to the rule;
with that very same [mantra], accompanied by its ancillaries, he should perform every ritual act.
At that time as well, O twice-born ones, there are the arrays of manifestations and the supreme mantras.
The Guru should also instruct [the disciple] in the mantras of the weapons, the vehicles, and the ornaments of Śakti.

(21.463) Thus, O best of sages, the procedure for initiation has been correctly proclaimed; now follows [the description of the rite] for one who has beheld the mandala and knows the scriptures according to their true meaning. (21.464)
For one who is devoted to propitiation and has attained the status of a "spiritual son" (putraka),
whether for the sake of attaining the accomplishment (siddhi) of all mantras or to obtain the requisite authority (adhikāra),
the Guru must at that time perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the disciple.
In the presence of those who know the reality of the Blessed One, whose souls delight in the five-fold ritual (pañcakāla),
who have mastered the Saṃhitās, and who are teachers; and in the presence of ascetics of fixed aim, great-souled enlighteners.
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the deity,

equipped with all necessary implements and furnished in its center with an auspicious throne (bhadrāsana). Upon that [throne], one should perform the ritual union (sandhāna) beginning with Ananta, consecrated by the prescribed seating.
Having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and other items before the presence of the God,
he should place the disciple there, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) with palms joined in reverence,
while beautiful women sing and bards offer hymns of praise.
While conch shells and other instruments were being blown and auspicious hymns were being recited,
he was chanting the supreme mantra and meditating, as it were, upon Acyuta.
Having worshipped with the eight-limbed rite, he took up the Vaiṣṇava water-pot.
Remaining there, with the expectation of perfect accomplishment, having recited the mantra a thousand times or even a hundred times,
and having visualized him as radiant as molten gold for the sake of success, he should consecrate him.
Having uttered the mantra ending with *svāhā* in a protracted tone from the interior of the heart-lotus,
and having spoken thus, one should meditate upon that [deity] as pure as crystal, ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, having projected [the deity] through the aperture of the palate, one should remember it as residing within his own heart-lotus.
Having correctly established in one's intellect Brahman— which is devoid of form and incapacity, and characterized by exhilaration and bliss— and having fully assumed all one's own duties,
one should approach and worship the pure, divine collection of scriptures.
A beautiful support for worship, a rosary, and a small bell;

a *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a meditation band (*yogapaṭṭa*), and a conch, a discus, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); then a sacrificial cup, flowers, an offering vessel (*arghyapātra*), and a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*).
The two sandals, the footstool, the parasol, the seat, the mirror,
the peacock-feather fan, the white chowrie, the banner of the Blessed One together with its appropriate staff, and the two garments— one of saffron and one of linen.
Having risen from his seat and gathered all the water used for bathing,
he should pour it out in a pure place; then, having worshipped the deity,
he should satisfy [the ancestors] with that same intent, ending with the full oblation within the fire.

Having performed the propitiation according to the previously stated procedure, one should offer the bali-oblation from the collection of *arghya* vessels and from within the mandala along with the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
using boiled rice mixed with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Having prepared a sacrificial circle outside the sacrificial hall,
and having first performed the internal offering by circumambulating clockwise,
one should then say this aloud and place the remainder outside that mandala.

Salutations indeed to all those who are imperishable at all times. Having performed the worship and other rites for the sake of the peace of his own child, he should offer [the remainder] as before with what is left over from the offering.
Then, within the center of the circular enclosure, upon the interior of a white lotus,
one should worship the Lord, the master and teacher of all gods, with the remnants of what was offered.
Having gratified him within the fire, one should perform his ritual dismissal.
Then, having placed that [disc] upon the surface of the earth, or within the water of a boat,
or upon the sacrificial ground, one should contemplate that twelve-spoked disc;
having deposited it within oneself and worshipped it with offerings such as *arghya* and flowers, one should [perform the rite] therein.

Having taken a vessel filled with water and placed it there, one should worship within it with the Vīrya-mantra; in its center is the supreme Mantrāmla. Another auspiciously marked vessel is filled with honey, water, and milk.

In front of that, one should place the arghya-vessel, and in its center, the weapon (astra) residing within the discus. Having worshipped that according to the rule and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with the root mantra restrained by the word "vaṣaṭ," one should do so again.
One should offer that [liquid] within [the vessel] with the mantra as before, maintaining the flow of nectar;
one should perform the "devoiding of faults" (*nirvajrīkaraṇa*) for all [the substances] with the water of the mantra.
This is done by bestowing a stream of that water, accompanied by meditation and recitation.
Then, having distributed among them the nectar-like drink of mantra,
and having prepared the supreme weapon, he should subsequently place it around the perimeter of the wheel.
Then, taking up that water-pot while reciting the weapon-mantra, [he should proceed].
One should maintain the stream as before; then, having placed that [vessel] in the center,
having filled it completely with water and endowed it with fruit,
the disciple, with a disciplined mind, should then perform the guru-yāga.
With devotion equal to that for a sacrifice to the Blessed One, through action, mind, and speech,
having offered all the materials required for the sacrifice to him, and placing his head and both hands at his feet— 21.496–497.
One should show forbearance with a mind that is very serene and purified by faith;
likewise toward those learned in the *Pañcarātra*, ascetics, and those who have completed their Vedic studies (*snātaka*).
Having honored them according to the rule, one should give them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability.
Having obtained the respectful permission from the time devoted to massaging [the feet],
he should eat together with his many brothers who have been previously initiated,
as well as with other devotees of the Lord, friends, relatives, and kinsmen.
When he is departing with his disciples at another time or place,
one should follow him for as long as one wishes,
and then indeed turn back after performing many prostrations at his feet and circumambulating him to the right.

For devotees of purified soul, the Guru is the supreme goal because he grants all accomplishments until liberation; therefore, he alone is to be propitiated. Thus, this consecration (abhiṣeka) is for those who possess primary eligibility.
Those who are qualified for both [types of] sacrifice— for their own sake and for the sake of others—
as well as other eminent sages, are to be consecrated by initiation alone. 21.504 The Sages.
"What is for one's own benefit and what is for the benefit of others? And who are those authorized therein? O tiger among sages, best of speakers, please explain this. Nārada.
A deity installed in one's own home is designated as "for one's own sake" (svārtha).
[One may also install a deity] on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, on the shore of the ocean, in a forest,
or likewise in a village or a city, according to the distinctions such as those that are self-manifested (svayam-vyakta) and so forth.
O Brahmins, the Blessed One is said to be established for the sake of others (*parārtha*).

The welfare of others is like the sun, whereas one's own welfare (*svārtha*) is like a lamp in a house. This word "other" (*para*) is preeminent; its meaning is characterized by liberation and so forth.
Because that which is obtained from him is proclaimed as this supreme goal (*parārtha*),
and because he alone, O twice-born ones, bestows all fruits upon everyone;
therefore, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who is the supreme goal, should be served by all people.

One's own deity (svārtha) should be worshipped in one's respective home; it bestows the fruits desired by each individual. Those who are qualified for the worship of both their own deity and the deity of others are born in lineages such as that of Śāṇḍilya and have received consecration from their guru.
But others, such as the sages Śāṇḍilya and the rest, are indeed qualified only for worship for their own sake; who else are the yogis? They are simply those born of that same lineage.
"How indeed do people become qualified for performing sacrifices for the sake of others?
O bull among sages, tell us all that in detail.
Nārada said:
O twice-born ones, hear the majesty of the lords of sages, Śāṇḍilya and the others.
Formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person,
[descended] for the sake of his own worship and for the promotion of the true dharmas in the world of mortals.
And for the sake of protecting the world, having observed your own five lords of weapons,
you shall today descend to the surface of the earth;
[you shall manifest] the primordial *Ekāyana* Veda, which is characterized by liberation as its sole fruit.
Proclaim the true Dharma to all, especially me,
who have appeared in various places through different manifestations such as the self-manifested ones. Worship me on this earth for the sake of all to attain liberation.
Having been thus commanded,

those lords of weapons, Sudarśana and the others— five in number— who were obedient to the command of Viṣṇu, were born upon the surface of the earth in the form of brahminical sages in places such as Pauṇḍravardhana.

Those five parts of Pañcāyudha were Śāṇḍilya, Aupagāyana, Mauñjāyana, Kauśika, and Bhāradvāja—these were the yogins. Having gathered together and deliberated with the desire to worship Viṣṇu, they... [21.519]

Having approached Mount Totā, they performed a most difficult penance. Pleased by their austerity, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World and ocean of compassion, mounted the king of birds together with Lakṣmī.
He arrived at the best of mountains where the lords of sages were present.
Then those tigers among sages, seeing the Lord of the World approaching—
his hands marked with the conch and discus, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns— [stood there].
With all their limbs marked by horripilation and filled with tears of joy,
they danced, praised, and sang to one another;
performing circumambulations, they bowed down to Puruṣottama.
Beholding them submerged in an ocean of bliss,
the Lord of Śrī spoke these compassionate words in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed One said: "O sages, I am satisfied and pleased by your long life produced through austerity and by your single-minded devotion; choose whatever you desire."
Having heard those words, all the sages, their minds filled with joy, replied with humility and palms joined in reverence:
"All the Vedas and various scriptures have been studied by us."
"We do not know the means to liberation; therefore, we have come to you for refuge.
O ocean of compassion, it behoves you to bestow your grace upon us right here.
Thus entreated, the Lord, who is an ocean of the nectar of mercy, [responded].
At that very moment, the Lord of the Universe himself, having consecrated and initiated Śāṇḍilya and other lords of yogins,
[bestowed upon them] the primordial Ekāyana Veda, known as the Rahasyāmnāya.

Endowed with divine mantras and rituals, and characterized by liberation as its sole fruit, the Lord of the World taught each of these five [teachings] separately for one day and night; from that source, O best of sages, they [spread]. (21.531–21.532)
The scripture is called *Pañcarātra* by all people in the world;
having taught its meanings, Acyuta then said this to them:
"O twice-born ones, this Veda of the single path has been taught by me."
"Indeed, this is the path for the sake of liberation; no other exists.
Therefore, the wise call it the 'Single Path' (ekāyana).
Abiding in divine fields and other such places according to the prescribed method, one follows this."
"O best of sages, perform the sacrifice in the form of the Self-Manifested (Svayaṃvyakta) and others;
you are the primary authorities for both sacrifices for your own sake and for the sake of others.
And those brahmins who belong to your lineage shall be consecrated according to the prescribed rites."

They too shall become qualified for their own welfare and the welfare of others. O lords of sages, this Dharma of the Kṛtayuga, practiced by the awakened ones, will have its movement become sluggish at the beginning of the Tretā age.
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, all beings, endowed with various desires and becoming performers of mixed sacrifices, abandon the primordial, eternal [Veda].
This entire Veda, known as Ekāyana, then disappears.
"Then the Blessed One himself manifests [himself] for the worthy one.
Having spoken thus, the eternal Lord Vāsudeva vanished.
From that time forward, all those lords of sages, beginning with Takṣa and Śāṇḍilya, [attained their goal].

In the Kṛta Yuga, which was the first of ages, all human beings and the lords of sages practiced the dharma of the Bhagavata. Then, when the Tretā Yuga had arisen, people [acted] under the influence of various desires.
Having abandoned the Bhāgavata dharma, they became performers of mixed sacrifices.
Consequently, the Ekāyana Veda became slow in its course.
At that time, the lord of sages, Śāṇḍilya, saw people devoted to sensual desires.
For the sake of protecting the world,
he performed extremely difficult austerities for many thousands of years at the end of the Dvāpara Yuga and the beginning of the Kali Yuga.
The god Saṅkarṣaṇa himself, having attained visibility before the sage, [spoke].
For those who have abandoned the supreme Dharma and adopted a mixed Dharma,
yet still desire that state and possess faith and devotion—
for the sake of favoring these castes and for the purpose of bringing them to spiritual fitness— [he appeared]. 21.547.
Likewise, for the sake of accomplishing the desired fruits of all people,
Hari himself, having extracted the essence from everywhere in accordance with the Root Veda (Mūlaveda),
proclaimed [these teachings] in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Having instructed him in the Sātvata and other scriptures which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, the wielder of the mace (Musalī) vanished right there.
Having thus obtained the Sātvata and other scriptures, O best of sages...
Śāṇḍilya taught the sage Aupagāyana,
as well as the Mauñjyāyanas and others, and the yogis such as Sanaka and his brothers.
From that time forward, all those lords of sages were known as the Śāṇḍilyas and so forth.
Performing the worship of Hari and other rites according to the path prescribed by the Sātvatas,
they [instructed] their own kinsmen and disciples by the thousands—
those who studied the Kāṇva recension and had reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta.

Having consecrated them all through initiation according to the path properly prescribed by the Sātvatas and others, and having established those brahmins as qualified to perform worship for both their own benefit and the benefit of others, he [instructed] them in this Sātvata system and so forth.
"Indeed, they are the primary qualified recipients;
thus spoke the tiger-like sages regarding the greatness of the high-souled ones, beginning with Śāṇḍilya, here only in brief, in connection with the discussion of their qualification. (21.556)
Thus, initiation and consecration, which were previously obtained according to the Siddhānta,
should be performed by that very same path and not according to what is stated in other [traditions].
One who is learned in the scriptures should never cause a confusion of the Siddhāntas.
O Lord of Sages, O best among speakers, what indeed is that which is called the Siddhānta, and what is its distinction? Tell me all of that in detail.
O Nārada, this scripture known as the Pāñcarātra is divided into four parts:
first is the Āgamasiddhānta, and the second is designated as Mantra. (21.560)
It is said that the third is the Tantra; another would be the *Tatrāntara*.

The first reveals the establishment of the eternally manifest array (*nityoditavyūha*) and so forth for those who sacrifice to the True Brahman known as Vāsudeva, which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). (21.561)
It is the object of focus for the best of the twice-born, residing in the hearts of those who possess the requisite qualification;
it is the supreme scripture known as the Brahmopaniṣad, endowed with divine mantras and ritual actions, which bestows discernment and grants liberation even to those who do not seek it.

Thus, know that the primary characteristic of the Lord— named Vāsudeva, who is eternally manifest, whose form is eternal, and who is an ocean of qualities such as the six divine attributes— is like the term "heart" used for the limbs [of the body]. 21.564
Know this to be the established doctrine of the Āgamas, which is of the nature of Śruti.
This is remembered as the Dharma of the Kṛtayuga, the highest of all Dharmas;
thereafter, at the beginning of the Tretāyuga, for the sake of attaining both enjoyment and liberation.

Therefore, that which has emerged from the established tenets of the Āgama, characterized by many divisions and known as the Mantra-siddhānta, was engraved by the Great Soul Sātvata— the second [incarnation]— in his form as the Jāgrat-vyūha and others.
By that [power], it was transmitted to the one known as Pradyumna, by that to the pervasive Turyātman,
by that to the one called Vāgīśvara; from him, it then passed into the embodied forms known as the continents (dvīpas), and subsequently into Rudra, Indra, Āditya, and Vahni.
In the very same way, among the hosts of deities beginning with Nārada,
the established doctrine of mantra was transmitted in many ways, divided by various distinctions;
therein lies the most peaceful manifestation, which is both quiescent and immediately emergent.
The state known as deep sleep (*suṣupti*), that called dream (*svapna*), and the waking array (*jāgrad-vyūha*) as previously described;
likewise, the other forms beginning with Keśava, and the various manifestations (*prādurbhāva*);
[all these are situated] within the lotus-heart, upon the lotus-throne and so forth, together with the powers (*śakti*) such as Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi.
Worship with the marks such as the conch and discus, as well as with [the symbols] headed by Garuḍa,
and with those beginning with the Bhūtas and Siddhas up to the Teacher, is beneficial.
For Viśvatrātṛnṛsiṃha, there is first initiation and then the other.
The section titled *Vibhavavyūhasūkṣma*, in due order,
[describes] the consecration of the four, beginning with the *sāmayī* and the *putrikā*,
as well as the conduct of the pledges (*samayācāra*) and the sequence for the installation of the images.
That which contains the full ritual procedures for the characteristics of mantras, maṇḍalas, mudrās, and the *khaṇḍas* and so forth, as well as for such actions,
is known as the *Mantrasiddhānta*, endowed with many divisions.

Without the distinctions of the external array (paravyūha) and so forth, yet with each individual form— whether accompanied by its limbs, alone, or surrounded by a beloved array, ornaments, and likewise weapons joined with a body—
that which is designated as the Tantra is thus encompassed.
Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, Kroḍa, Haṃsa, Vāgīśvara, and others—
distinguished by their primary and secondary forms— are joined with their respective side-glances alone,
as well as with excellent weapons such as the discus and ornaments such as crowns.
Where she is worshipped according to the prescribed rites by hosts of consorts such as Lakṣmī, and by attendants such as the celestial beings (khaga), that other tantra has been proclaimed;
those who have attained perfection through ten million births, their final abode is established here.
Therefore, this which is called the established doctrine was understood by him according to reality:
[the nature] of the scriptures, mantras, rituals, and so forth, as well as the manifestation of forms and the acceptance of a noble teacher as before.

In that very manner, it must not be practiced otherwise for as long as time lasts; for if it is performed contrarily here, it causes harm to the king, the kingdom, and so forth. Therefore, those of perfected self should not practice a confusion of established doctrines (*siddhānta*).
Whatever is most desired in the world that does not contradict established tradition should be accepted;
therefore, a wise person should abandon what is mutually contradictory.
This applies to the Vaikhānasa tantras as well as those of the Śaiva and Pāśupata schools.
"What more need be said of those things that, though prescribed here, have arisen as contradictions?
Thus has this difference of established doctrines been proclaimed according to what was heard.
O bulls among sages, if you wish to hear anything else beyond this, let it be told."
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation," in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter:
"O Sage, you previously stated that the observances (niyamas) must be taught to the disciple."
"For it has been declared, O tiger among sages, that those observances must be revealed.
Nārada replied: "Indeed, in former times, the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa was asked this very same thing."
The Blessed One spoke: "O lords of sages, I shall now declare those observances.
For when each observance has been received from the mouth of the guru..."

The disciple should indeed say "So be it" in order to extinguish the fire of grief. The shadow cast by one who possesses dignity must not be stepped over, even if that person is a divinity traveling in a vehicle; for the group of preceptors must always be regarded exactly as the preceptor himself.
One should pay homage to his bed, seat, vehicle, and so forth;
unwearied, one should always perform every task in his house. One should not practice yoga or concentration on a seat in his presence.
Well-restrained, with speech controlled, he should await his command.
In his presence, however, he should not rise for others.
He should resolve his doubts, but not apart from his instruction.
The exposition of the scriptures, the practice of yoga, and meditative concentration—
these must necessarily be performed in one's own home, not in the house of the guru. Furthermore,
one must certainly not eat from a vessel marked with the signs of the conch, the discus, or the lotus.
A tall mark, a stone, a piece of wood, a clod of earth, or a plank and the like—
these must not be stepped over with the foot, nor should they be used for the purpose of a seat by those who know the teaching of the Blessed One and whose souls are devoted to his service.
Indeed, worship should always be performed as is appropriate and according to one's capacity;
[one should honor] the temple of the God of gods, this Goddess, the Ācārya who follows the Pāñcarātra, the Aśvattha and Vaṭa trees, the assembly of the virtuous, and the house of the Guru.
One should perform circumambulation from a distance when near an image of the Lord;
one should pay homage by prostrating like a staff toward the four directions,
neither mounted on a vehicle nor wearing sandals.
One should not enter the house of the Blessed One with a distracted mind;
nor should one fail to rise and offer salutation when there is an occasion for exposition.
This applies especially to those who lack devotion, to the foolish, and particularly to the nihilists.

It should be given and bestowed, but not upon those whose minds delight in mockery. The supreme teaching of the Lord must not be opened up if it has not been honored; it should not be revealed in the presence of those devoted to other [deities], nor for the sake of allaying their doubts.
One should not disclose that which is to be revealed out of greed, nor by unjust means, nor for both reasons;
likewise, one should avoid fragrant fruits, flowers, and the like that are unprecedented or improper,
as well as food unfit for consumption, and that which has been offered to a guru, a deity, or the sacred fire.

One should not accept wealth from a thief, from one who causes distress, from one who is fierce, or from one possessed by deceit, greed, and pride; nor from one who lacks devotion, even if it is offered with formal courtesy.
For he who wanders about for the sake of a livelihood while carrying an image of the Blessed One [is to be avoided].

One should never look upon, touch, or even converse with that temple-attendant (devalaka) in the streets and marketplaces of the city. However, one may sing the verses of the Blessed One within a village or inside a city.
The Lord should always honor that devotee of yours who is devoted to the vow of Viṣṇu, who dwells in the temple of Viṣṇu,
who is intent on conversations and discourses concerning Viṣṇu, and who cleanses the temple of Viṣṇu. || 22.21–22 ||
A disciple of the Vaiṣṇavas who is devoted to the dharma of Viṣṇu,
who seeks out the Vaiṣṇavas, and who is always honored like Viṣṇu himself—
having risen in the morning, he should indeed gather [flowers] from his own garden by his own hand.

For the sake of worship, one who is self-restrained should always take flowers and other materials with the *astra-mantra*; or else, one should go to a forest where there is no obstruction in their collection—
whether they originate from thornless trees or even from thorny ones.
All [roots], such as those that are white and so forth, which are pleasing to the heart, fragrant, fit for ritual action, and easily grasped, are acceptable;
whereas those with a pungent odor, those unfit for ritual action, and likewise those that are unknown [should be avoided].
[One should also avoid roots] growing at crossroads, in the abodes of Śiva, in cremation grounds, or in the middle of a forest.
Leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like that are damaged by lightning strikes and the like, or infested with worms and insects, should be carefully avoided.
So too should lotuses, whether fragrant or white, red, and so forth.
Indeed, purifying items must always be employed in worship;
likewise, sprouts and leaves that have fallen to the ground are prescribed for constant adoration,
according to the season in which they arise.

Worship performed in the home with flowers derived from the *karavīra* is not beneficial, especially for one who possesses desire or is engaged in the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*). Otherwise, there is no fault; however, there is a fault [if worship is done] with [flowers from] the *unmattaka* and other such plants.
Just as the purchase of flowers that have been recently plucked is prescribed for those that have already begun to wither,
one should perform the offering of those flowers once they have been sprinkled with water, and not otherwise.
By the inspection of the ministers, they quickly attain freedom from defects.
The hearts of those whose souls are devoted to the mantra become purified by devotion.
One should not eat from a bell-metal vessel, nor should one offer the *madhuparka* and other gifts to the deity from such a vessel, even if it is available.
One should not burn even incense in vessels made of clay or iron.
For the purpose of incense, guggulu mixed with clarified butter should be offered; in its absence, another substance may be used. One should avoid using lamps accompanied by the ringing of bells.
Medha, marrow, linseed oil, ghee mixed with oil, *nāvika* for the purpose of the *madhuparka*, and auspicious items such as curd and milk;
likewise, *kaulastha*, *kodrava*, black rice, and boiled *śāli* rice are beneficial. (22.36–22.37)
He should not eat uncooked food, nor meat colored by the *arā* stalks;
nor, at the time of the propitiation, should he rise up in haste. And until the completion of the rite, he should remain free from any interruption.
The removal of impurities from the Lord’s image, the support,
and the auspicious pedestal must not be performed with iron thorns, except by means of soft brushes and the like.
One should not bathe, sleep, or utter the Name while facing the Guru, nor should one observe silence in his presence.
One should not touch anything that is leftover, nor should one eat in the house of the Blessed One;
nor should one do so in proximity to fire, nor in a house where liquor is kept.
For those devotees who have received initiation, the meaning of the scriptures alone is indeed what must be manifested;
for others, however, it is the Dharmaśāstra. With a mind free from greed, he should constantly engage in the gathering of disciples who are devotees of Viṣṇu. (22.42)
All qualities such as pride, envy, miserliness, greed, and delusion must be gradually reduced to insignificance throughout the course of one's life,
even when they suddenly arise in those residing in other lands. || 22.43–22.44 ||
Instruction should be given to those whose souls are devoted to Nārāyaṇa;

however, he who does not know the reality of Acyuta and the meaning of the Pañcarātra, as well as the Vaiṣṇava initiation characterized by various scriptural descriptions—[to him it should not be given]. (22.45)
The connection should be made with "bhānena" by shifting the word order.
There is no intentional subversion of the meaning of the scriptures or of the scriptures themselves;
[such deviation] occurs here only through ignorance, lacking the traditional lineage of transmission.

One who is a devotee of the Blessed One, trustworthy, skilled in the characteristics [of things], renowned for his integrity, mature, and free from doubt regarding the seals (*mudrā*), mandalas, and mantras, should be questioned concerning the lost meaning and characteristics of the scriptures. (22.48)
Indeed, one must always remain in the presence of the gurus.
Furthermore, without a portion of meditative cultivation (*bhāva*), one should not seek favor regarding the mantras of the Omniscient One,
except through the vision of the mandala.

The King of Mantras, resembling the sun, should be remembered in these locations: at the navel-cakra, in the heart-lotus, at the root of the kanda, in the pit of the throat, between the eyebrows, and in the aperture of Brahmā—whether during travel, while sleeping, or on the road. (22.51)
One should not eat the meat of deer or boars, nor that arising from fish; nor that of swans or tortoises, nor the fruits of the *śṛṅgāṭa*,
nor likewise the seeds of the lotus, nor should one climb to the top of a banyan tree.
One should not see that [place] being cut, nor touch its leaf with speech or foot;
it is a field of merit, a great holy site, the unsurpassed Siddhāśrama,
as well as the assembly of Vaiṣṇavas and the manifest abode of Acyuta.
O Great-minded One, having approached the mandala and having fashioned a twelve-spoked wheel, the Cāturmāsya rite should be performed according to the rules;
or else, within the house, having first practiced self-restraint, one should fashion a wheel fixed upon the wall.
Then, before the image, the Guru should always bestow these commitments (samayas), which are joined with the fourfold passion previously mentioned,
upon the devoted disciples who are capable of fulfilling them.
Having first identified a devoted disciple capable of carrying out the task,
the teacher should designate him for all those duties in which he is competent, so that he does not fall away from them again. (22.58–59)
For one who abides by the observance, obstacles and destroyers run forth;
the accomplishments turn away and calamities indeed arise.
Knowing this, one must certainly remain vigilant toward them.
Having churned the ocean of restraints with the intellect and extracted its essence,
the Guru should compassionately bestow this purifying [knowledge] upon those who are free from deceit.
Devotion toward the fire, the Guru, the mantra, the scripture, and the one authorized therein [is required].
Successes desired by the minds of devotees surely come to pass through the proper preservation and practice of these five, and not through others independently or according to one's own whim. (22.63)
But those who, due to the obstruction of an impure mind,
fail to observe the rules of conduct, they suffer on the dark path;
whereas this [path] is maintained with a perfectly serene mind.
In this way, one's own self attains clarity for those who desire their own welfare,
provided they are free from turbidity and remain established here on the path of the virtuous.
May there be auspiciousness for the initiates, practitioners, teachers, and spiritual sons.
"Thus have the observances been declared; what do you wish to hear from here on?
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Prescription of Observances" in the *Īśvara-saṃhitā* of the venerable *Pāñcarātra*.
The twenty-second chapter;
now the twenty-third chapter: The Sages.
O Blessed One, O Sage Nārada, omniscient one, best among speakers!
[Please describe] the essential nature of the divine scriptures and so forth, as well as the characteristics of mantras;
the characteristics of mudrās, the meditation on the forms [of the deities], and the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and other such matters.
"Please explain in full detail, out of your grace, the injunctions regarding the sacrificial oblation and whatever else is required here. Nārada said:
The scripture is indeed threefold: divine, that spoken by sages, and human.
O lords of sages, I shall explain the specific nature of each.
That which has its primary purpose clear, free from doubt, lucid, concise in syllables, and stable—[is the divine scripture].
Of the all-pervading Lord who eternally abides in the form of the fourfold self,
wherever his inherent supremacy is proclaimed, and wherever that of other mantra-forms is conditional, [it is understood]. 23.4–23.5.
The distinction between the states beginning with the Fourth (turya) and ending with the waking state has been revealed there,
out of compassion for devotees, wherein the majesty of the all-pervading Lord of Power, who possesses four aspects, is fully manifested.

Wherein the essential nature of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), adorned with the marks and ornaments of his limbs and possessing various powers, is described as being divided by the distinctions of *laya* and other states.

O noble ones, wherever mantras are set forth through the fourfold method beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the cluster (*piṇḍa*), the word (*pada*), and so on— for the purpose of the rite of inducing sleep (*svāpana*)—
therein the ritual of binding (*anuveṣṭha*) is prescribed, as well as the perpetual worship (*nityapūjana*).
O twice-born ones, it is taught that the complete [ritual] is performed first upon the primary image;
however, whatever among those rites, such as the ritual bathing and so forth, is impossible to perform there,
that much alone [is performed] within the secondary image (bimba), preceded by the action-image (karmabimba).

O Great-minded One, that [reflection] is prescribed for mirrors and the like; however, O twice-born ones, due to the absence of such [reflective surfaces], it is accomplished through the five-fold concentration on earth, water, fire, air, and ether, as well as by means of the two-fold concentration. || 23.11–23.12 ||
Wherein purification of the physical body occurs through what is called burning and nourishing,
and wherein its own basis in the sacred scriptures and traditional revelation is established— that is the word of the Supreme Lord; for it is established by His command and bestows liberation.
O Mahāmati, know that such an Āgama, whose meaning is authoritative,
is the complete vision of the true path and constitutes the foundation of the ritual injunctions;
for by its authority, whatever is inferred should be understood according to reality.
Without contradiction between what precedes and what follows, it should be established through non-investigation;
it must be pleasing to all, subtle, and capable of providing certainty.
Thus stands the network of meanings spoken in the words of the Supreme Lord.

Whatever was spoken by the sages that was sattvic, which praised the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) and even set them in motion—he made all of that known [to others]. Yet, disregarding the primary form, he was fully devoted to the ritual worship of the image. (23.17–18)
It is declared that the daily worship is primarily performed there,
as well as the measurements and characteristics of the images of Brahmā, Rudra, and the others,
and where the installation of the Lord of the worlds is prescribed.
But worship is prescribed for those who are ordinary and dull-witted.
O best of Brahmins, it is performed with the five mantras beginning with Parameṣṭhin, which respectively denote the principles (tattvas), the directions, and time. || 23.21 ||
The fivefold [rite] beginning with *sthāpana* and ending with *pratiṣṭhā* has been proclaimed;
seven [rites] beginning with *yāga* and ending with *haristoma* have been celebrated.
Where there are these seven sacrifices (*yāgas*), the qualified practitioners (*adhikāriṇas*) follow that sequence accordingly.
It has been stated that in which *pratiṣṭhā* there is the conceptualization of sixteen placements (*nyāsa*).
Know all this to be of a *rājasa* nature as spoken by the sages;
for it is directed toward the Blessed One without, however, [regarding Him] as having the status of a limb (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, where there is indeed the independent mantra, meditation, authoritative scripture, characteristics, and installation of the gods headed by Brahmā and Rudra, as well as of the Mothers and Durgā; 23.25.

Know that to be the speech of a sage which is designated as "tāmasa" (dark). That human speech is remembered as being useless, incoherent, trivial in meaning, mere verbal ostentation, and unable to carry through the initial statement. || 23.26–23.27 ||
O twice-born one, that which contradicts the meaning of the supreme Lord's words should be abandoned; for it is a mine of misfortunes, leads to hell,
and is not to be accepted even with effort among the words of sages, even when they are characterized by sattva and other qualities.

O Brahmin, whatever is required should be accepted provided it is not contradictory; O high-minded one, this should be inferred among those [meanings] according to the sequence of *sāttvika* and the other qualities,
by adopting well-known meanings while maintaining consistency with the context and distinguishing them from others.
Moreover, if human speech is to be accepted, it should be accepted like the words of a sage.

Thus, having understood the distinction between the divine scriptures and others, one should worship Hari. But he who, without understanding this, performs worship and other rites with confusion [of traditions], [is at fault].
For he always causes confusion for the entire world,
and especially for his own lineage; therefore, O twice-born ones, even in times of distress,
one who desires his own welfare and is skilled in the scriptures must not cause confusion regarding the sacred texts.
It is self-manifested, likewise established by the perfected ones (siddhas),
and installed by the foremost sages, as well as by gandharvas, yakṣas, and even vidyādharas;
it was established as a mantra-embodiment by rākṣasas and chief asuras.

One who is learned in the scriptures should worship [the deity] according to the procedure prescribed in the divine scriptures. O twice-born one, one should also worship a deity installed by men there, following the path described in the words of the sages, by those possessed of knowledge who perceive the ultimate reality.

But that which has been established by lords of men who are devoted solely to Vāsudeva, who exclude other deities, who have abandoned the teachings of mixed scriptures, and who are endowed with intense devotion, as well as those skilled in the *anuvedha* and other rites— [that alone is the true image]. || 23.37 ||
One should worship the Lord of the gods according to the path taught in the divine scriptures.
Even where worship is performed according to the path spoken by the sages,
if one desires to perform the worship there as well according to the divine path, [one should do so].
Having abandoned the path of the sages, one should worship by way of the divine path;
there shall be the majesty of his presence for a duration until the end of the kalpa.
O high-minded one, wherever one constantly performs worship and other rites through the divine path, there the divine [path] must never be abandoned.
One should not perform worship and so forth by means of the path spoken by the words of the sages.
If a twice-born man, his mind deluded, should perform [these acts] out of confusion,
his devotion— along with its seed— will soon depart from him;
together with his ritual procedures and their mantras, even the supernatural accomplishments (siddhis) will turn away from him.

Right here, O best of Brahmins, at the end of the body, one whose lineage has perished quickly goes to a terrible hell; both the king and the kingdom perish. Therefore, with every effort, one must not abandon the divine path.

Even where worship is performed by means of a *tāmasa* path, there too worship performed by means of a *rājasa* path shall be the bestower of success. Wherever worship and other rites are performed constantly by means of a *rājasa* path, [it is likewise effective].
Even there, worship performed with a *sāttvika* disposition always bestows auspiciousness.
Wherever the *sāttvika* mode of worship and so forth prevails daily,
one should not perform worship or other rites by way of the *rājasa* path.
Where worship and other rites have been undertaken by way of the *rājasa* path, one should not perform worship and so forth by way of the *tāmasa* path.
There shall be no mutual confusion among the various *rājasa* types. (23.48–23.49)
In all human speech, that which is non-contradictory should be accepted;
one should not, however, perform installations and the like merely by means of such [human] injunctions.
Thus has the nature of the divine scriptures and so forth been described by me.
O best of sages, the nature of the mantras is now being told.
Among all Viṣṇu-mantras, there are three that are all-pervasive:
the first is the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa mantra, and the second is the twelve-syllabled one.
Then there is the six-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu for Vāsudeva;
these three mantras are common to all forms [of the deity]. Other mantras, however, are devoted exclusively to their respective individual forms.
All forms are to be worshipped with the three pervasive [mantras];
however, those specific individual forms are to be fully honored with other mantras.
Therefore, among all mantras, the triad of pervasive [mantras] is supreme.
Among these three pervasive [mantras], the eight-syllable mantra is indeed superior.
Listen with reverence to the extraction of the mantras beginning with the eight syllables:
one should extract the *praṇava* first, followed immediately by the word *namaḥ*.
Then there is this eight-syllabled mantra: *nārāyaṇāya*.
At the end of the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should place the word *namaḥ*; at the end of the fourth [syllable], the word *bhagavat*; and then the five-syllabled word *vāsudevāya*. (23.57–58)

This twelve-syllable mantra of the divine Vāsudeva consists of the word "Viṣṇu" in the dative case, joined with the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and the word "namaḥ. This six-syllable mantra is said to be recited both at the beginning and at the end of it.

O twice-born ones, the arrangement of the limbs, beginning with the heart, should be performed using syllables endowed with qualities such as knowledge and adorned with *bindus*; the remaining letters should likewise be joined with the *netra*. Thus is the arrangement of the limbs proclaimed.
Next, the sequence for extracting the mantras of the embodied forms is described:
on a praiseworthy, secluded, and protected patch of ground smeared with fragrant paste,
well-perfumed and enriched with water-offerings (arghya) and flowers, one should spread out the wheel of letters (varṇacakra).
In which the entire universe, beginning from the world of Brahmā, is established;
by whose arising the creation of the world immediately follows, and upon whose ceasing within itself dissolution occurs. (23.63–64)
That which impels through both the moon and the sun, existing both externally and internally,
eternally arisen, situated as it were within the senses, is the phoneme that expresses the Lord (Īśvara).
Therein, the Blessed One, whose essence is the phonemes, abides according to the division of locations.

The collection of solar and lunar digits, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the *visarga*, numbering sixteen (two times eight), is situated at the navel according to the division of short and long vowels. Furthermore, the aggregate of primordial principles (*tattva*), beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*, is located upon the spokes [of the wheel]. (23.66–23.67)
From Earth up to Primordial Nature (Prakṛti), O wielder of the plow, through their union in pairs;
Time, the sustainer of the body, moves upon the wheel with nine characteristics.
Wherein, within the group beginning with *ma* and ending with the *ha*-class, he himself resides.
The Lord Kālavaiśvānara himself, possessing the radiance of ten thousand suns,
stands at the end of the phonemes, enriched by thousands upon thousands of flames.
[He pervades] the series of phonemes from the beginning up to the middle, ending with the word "namas."
Having uttered [the syllable] and worshipped it with the *arghya* offering and other rites, one should indeed extract the seed-syllable of the Vidyā, which is the king of wheels;
from that, one should then extract the mantra that denotes the Supreme Self—
a mantra that flows like nectar and swiftly bestows the attainment of liberation.
One should first extract the letter situated on the axle, and immediately thereafter the sixth from the rim (nemi). This second syllable is that which is stepped upon by the second navel.
It is the second from the number ten, and below that, it is beyond the eighth.
This third syllable is the letter following the navel (the thirteenth), endowed with the third vowel.
Then the second [syllable] is the ninth from the navel, joined with the fourth vowel. Know the fifth [syllable] to be simply the eighth letter from the second.
Having taken the word *vijñāna*, which consists of three syllables immediately following that;
one should place the first syllable, split by the letter after the eleventh [consonant], and then place it above the third syllable of *neme*. (23.75–23.76)
This is indeed the ninth syllable of the mantra; now learn from me the tenth.

It is the eighth vowel, preceded by the second vowel of the navel (the letter *i*), and conjoined with the second of the rim (*e*). Following that, take the eighth [vowel] from the beginning of the rim (*ai*).
Designated by that [term], the third [vowel] is situated above the fifth;
know this to be the thirteenth, following the ninth.
One should place those three above the sixth, which has the color of a rim (*nemi*).
Then, the sixteenth [vowel] joined with the third from the navel (the letter *u*) is said;

the second [consonant] joined with the tenth letter from the navel (the letter *ṭa*) and the eleventh [vowel] (*ū*). After that, one should give the word for consciousness (*caitanya*) along with a salutation (*namaḥ*). 23.80.
This mantra consists of twenty-two syllables and is adorned with six words.
Among them, the single-syllable word is knowledge, the four-syllable word is power,
the six-syllable word is sovereignty, and the supreme five-syllable word is valor.
The four-syllabled word is the splendor of Śakti, which consists of three syllables;
it is splendor, heroism, strength, power, sovereignty, and knowledge itself.
The eye-weapon, armor, conch, head, heart, and the six [limbs] follow in due order.
The mantra, regarding the domain of meditative absorption and the conquests of various stages,
is to be remembered as formless and unconditioned, characterized by Brahman; yet,
in the first means for attaining that— namely, sacrifice, fire-oblation, and so forth— it is indeed otherwise.
One should recollect [the Lord] with his form, his limbs, and surrounded by his retinue—
by whom the qualities such as knowledge themselves have been brought to manifestation—
for the sake of the perpetual completion of sacrifices and out of compassion for ritual acts.
Thus, when the mantra of Anaṅga is recollected through the power of devotion and faith,
it surely bestows its fruit upon those whose selves are constantly permeated by it;
for while sovereignty is attained primarily, liberation follows as a secondary consequence.
In that regard, know that for the sake of pacifying those obstacles, the mantra ends with the weapon-syllable (*astra*);

however, O Great-minded One, in the case of the opposite, the mantra ends with the eye-syllable (*netra*), because for those whose minds are tranquil and who have attained the path of purity in vision and insight, where could there be obstacles? (23.89)
One's own internal radiance is projected outward through one's sovereignty.
For by whichever mantra it is accompanied, that [mantra] is considered to be endowed with the eyes;
and by whichever [mantra], it is the incomparable self-luminous [reality] within the heart.
The white and the black are to be drawn together; each is accompanied by its own designator.
Now, understand that the fourfold mantra, which expresses the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) in its distinct forms, is the eternal bestower of liberation from karmas, as previously indicated.
Having first taken the seed-syllable located at the axle, one should thereafter place it below that, prior to the eleventh spoke;
this syllable is the third of the third [group], which belongs to the rim (nemi). 23.93–94.
Know that the second [syllable] is the eighth letter from the navel, joined with the fourth vowel and so forth;
then the ninth from the rim is the fifth [letter] alone.
The letter following the eighth is joined with the second vowel.
One should know this as the sixth; the seventh is beyond the tenth.
(23.96) Now, taking the second from the tenth, one should place it above.
From the eighth, however, [comes] the second; this is the eightfold mantra-syllable. (23.97)
From the second [vowel] the first letter, and from the eighth the next;
joined with the eleventh from the navel (the letter *u*), this is the second [syllable] from the circle of the rim (*nemi*).
From the eleventh [vowel] the pure [letter], and likewise the third from the rim.
First the rim, and following that, the navel marked with eleven;
then taking the sixth from the rim, it stands above the fifth;
then, joined with the second from the navel, the third from the rim is remembered.
O Mahāmati, having taken only the second syllable of *nemi*,
one should subsequently join the four-syllabled word *namaḥ* to the maker [of the wheel].
This mantra is declared to consist of twenty-one syllables.

It remains undivided by the distinction of words, yet it indeed consists of one more [syllable]. The first word is preceded by a vowel; there should be two [words] of five syllables each, while the third is of six syllables, and the fourth is exactly like that.
Know that the fifth consists of two syllables; likewise, O Mahāmati, the sixth.
Now, attend to another great mantra, the second, by knowing which there is no further rebirth for the practitioner.
Having taken the middle [syllable] of *akṣa*, preceded by the navel (*nābhi*), and beyond that;
first, the eye (*nebh*) of that very [word] should be joined with the thirteenth navel.
The syllable following the second is the *ātmanepada* ending for all powers.
The second [syllable] from the twelfth letter, then the first from the second,
and the fifth from those situated outside— know these three to be pure.
Then the second conjoined with the eleventh from the navel, and then the eighth from that.
The eighteen-syllable mantra consists of the word *namo namaḥ* joined [to the rest].
Of this, the first part consists of one syllable, followed by a three-syllable part;
the third is six syllables, and the fourth is four syllables.
The second [mantra] is proclaimed to consist of two syllables for each of the two feet;
now, O best among those who know mantras, I shall declare the third mantra,
by knowing which practitioners attain supreme purity of mind.
Taking the seed-syllable situated in the middle, then the first from the eleventh;
then the third of *nemi*, and above that, the one following *nābhi*;
then the first letter from the eighth, conjoined with the second vowel.

Then, one should take the first syllable from the eleventh [position] and another from the tenth; finally, the eighth syllable from the rim (*nemi*) is joined with the second syllable of the hub (*nābhi*),
which is the first syllable of the rim.
Taking the letter following the tenth, which is endowed with the three *nābhis*,
and the second letter from the ninth, joined with that which follows the *nābhi*— that being the same number [as the first], pure from the tenth— and then the fifth from the exterior; 23.115–115.
The second [syllable] from *nema* is joined below that, but beyond the *nābhi*;
one should take the second syllable from the tenth [letter], a three-syllabled word for the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Then, one should likewise extract the first [syllable] from the eleventh, taken alone.
Then, one should place the third *nemi* joined with the second *nābhi*;
thereafter, another [should be placed] among the outer ones, joined with the thirteenth *nābhi*.
One should then set down two [units] from the third *nemi*, and another from the ninth.
Then, from the second [syllable] joined with the navel up to the circle of the front rim,
the second [part] is indeed entirely accompanied by the *namas* outside;
this king of mantras is endowed with twenty-three syllables.
Now their divisions are also stated by means of the previously mentioned number of feet:
know that the first has one syllable, the second has nine syllables,
the third has two syllables, and the fourth is recorded as having three syllables.
First is the six-syllabled [mantra], then the one situated above which consists of two syllables;
now learn from me as I speak the fourth mantra, by the mere knowledge of which the supreme consciousness arises. (23.122)
First, having taken that which stands in the axle before the navel,
and then having taken the letter following the third from that, O wielder of the plow;
then the second of the rim below that, and the fifth below the navel.

Taking the second letter from the eighth [group] and the same number [of letters] from the rim-circle (nemimaṇḍala), one should form this pair joined with that which follows the hub (nābhi). Then, [taking] the fifth [letter] from the outside, joined with the third of the hub—
First, having taken the letter from the beginning (the first) joined with the seventh from the navel (the seventh),

one should take the second letter from the eighth [position] and the second from the circle of the rim (the tenth); these two should be employed, along with the second from the range of the navel (the sixth).
Then one should take the second letter from the tenth;
the second letter from the eighth, and above that, the one following the tenth.
One should then join the second letter of the navel immediately thereafter.
Then one should extract only the syllable located on the rim (*nemi*).

Next, from the center (*nābhi*), one should respectfully take the first syllable situated before the tenth; then the pair below that from the exterior, followed immediately by the syllable *pra*. 23.129–130.
It is joined with "nābhi" as its second member, and immediately following that, it takes "nemidvitīya" as its number; then comes the word of salutation (*namaskāra*).
Thus, this [mantra] consists of eighteen syllables, exceeding [the previous count] by two due to the number of words.
The first word consists of a single vowel; the second has four syllables;
the third has five syllables; and the fourth has four syllables.
Know that the fifth is likewise, while the one situated at the end is recorded as having two syllables.
Wherever an excess of syllables in the words has been illustrated,
there one should first place the word beginning with "vyāhṛti" preceded by the navel;
then follows the mantra of this great-souled deity whose body is indivisible.
I shall describe [the ritual] known as Viśākhayūpa, which bestows discernment regarding the procedure:
having taken the first letter situated on the axle, then the eleventh;
the second is distinct from the second of the navel, and the third from the circle of the rim.
The second [syllable] is indeed the state belonging to the external form of fire alone;
then, one should extract the eleventh [syllable] from before it, which is also alone. The third syllable is joined with that which is external and situated above the navel.

Then one should extract the letter following the tenth, and from there the one preceding the eleventh; immediately thereafter, one should extract that which is conjoined with the eleventh vowel, and then that which is the second letter after the navel (the letter *ya*). || 23.138-23.139 ||
Only the first two [letters] are from the exterior; likewise, the first [of the remaining] is from the single [unmanifest] source.
The third is from *nemi*, followed by that joined with the second vowel.
Then, the other pure [letter] is from the tenth, and the former is from the eleventh.
O one of stainless vision, at the end of that [is] the letter joined with the eleventh of the navel (nābhi).
One should take the first letter joined with the third of the navel; then, that which follows the eighth, joined with the second of the navel.
Following that, the second [part] is accompanied by a salutation;
this great mantra consists of twenty-four syllables.
Its first word is traditionally known as the single syllable [Oṃ], which is the Praṇava.
The second is said to consist of three syllables, and immediately after that, one of five syllables.
The fourth consists of six syllables, while the fifth here consists of seven.
The sixth word of this mantra, O great-minded one, consists of two syllables.
For the Supreme Lord, the Primordial God, exists at all times as the very nature of various mantras, abiding always at the beginning, middle, and end of everything;
He resides within His own fourfold manifestation of the four vyūhas, characterized by the states of the tranquil and the manifest.
And it abides preeminently within three deities.
Just as the sun, though singular, O high-minded one, while stationed in the sky, manifests its own nature by resorting to various reservoirs of water. || 23.147–23.148 ||
Thus, although the Blessed One is one, he assumes plurality within the various bases of mantras and within those established in the states beginning with the fourth (turya),
for the sake of favoring his devotees according to their diverse inclinations. 23.149
Now, listen as I speak of the fourfold group of mantras,
which serve as the expressive designators for the distinct colors beginning with white, in their proper sequence:
the syllable situated on the axle, the one preceded by the navel, and the syllable that follows the tenth.

Then, know these three syllables alone: the one preceding the rim (nemipūrva), then the one from the nave (nābhi) combined with the thirteenth; the second syllable from the twelfth, then the first from the second; and the fifth from those on the outside. 23.152.
Then, from the eighth [syllable], the second [part] consists of the navel [syllable] modified by the eleventh;
immediately after that is the five-syllabled word *vāsudevāya*.
This is indeed proclaimed as the first [mantra], consisting of thirteen syllables.
I shall explain in due order the extraction of the others as they stand:
the syllable situated on the axle, and immediately after that, the second from the navel;
then, following the previous mantra, one should provide three words.
Now, know that the fifteenth [mantra] here, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* at the navel, is a mantra consisting of three words joined with that very same [syllable].
Then, there is the sixteenth in number, which is preceded by the *praṇava* at the navel.
One should first place those words possessing the previously mentioned characteristics;
know that from these three mantras, two are according to the number of the preceding mantras. One is devoid of a single syllable; therefore, hear the distinction between the words.
Of all [the names], the first pair is remembered as having one syllable;
the third has two syllables, the fourth has four syllables,
and the fifth indeed has five syllables for three [of them].
Thus it has been proclaimed, O wielder of the plow:
that single [reality] consisting of the four castes, belonging to the one named Pradyumna who abides in the state of dream, has been described in brief. || 23.160-23.161 ||

I shall now describe the sequence of the four; listen to the collection of mantras. Having taken that which is within the axle, it follows the navel; thereafter, it is split by the second navel, immediately preceded by the rim.
Having taken the fifth from the navel, then the first from the ten, the third, and the second from the navel, one should mark them;
then, with the second seed-syllable of the navel, [one takes] the one following the ninth.
That which is the second [part] from the twelfth should be applied below that;
then, immediately thereafter, one should join it with the fifth [part] from the navel.
Furthermore, the pure [portion] following the eighth, as well as the one preceding the rim (*nemi*), should be made in the same manner.
The second [syllable] joined with the second [vowel] from the circle of the rim (nemimaṇḍala) should indeed produce only that which is the word for the Lord of Yoga (yogeśvara).
At the end of that is the word for the Wielder of the Discus (cakrin), and then the eighth [syllable] from the rim.
Having placed that which is joined with the fifth [vowel] at the end of the navel, one should then set down the word *dhvajāya*—
the first [syllable] being pure and preceding the eleventh, followed by the third [vowel] from the eighth [consonant],
and the latter [syllable] being overlapped by the third [vowel] from the navel.
The first [syllable] is split before the eleventh, and then by a fourth part from the navel;
the subsequent pure fifth [syllable] is from the rim of the circle,
joined with the second vowel, and the word consists of two syllables including "sa" and "iti."
Following that, there should be the word "vāsudevāya" with a prostration (namaskāra);
this thirty-six-syllable mantra is now described in its divisions.
First, the eleven-syllable word is proclaimed.
The second consists of five syllables, while the third is known to have three syllables.
Know, O best among those who know the words, that the fourth has six syllables, the fifth has five phonemes, and the sixth has seven syllables. (23.172–173)
Then, having taken up the second [syllable] from the circle of the navel at the end of the *praṇava*,
one should then join the eight spokes of the rim with the fourteenth [vowel] from the navel.
Furthermore, one should again duly take up the second [syllable], purified from the tenth.
Below that, from the ninth [letter] to the last, joined with the fourth and so forth;
the second [syllable] is conjoined with the eleventh vowel, and from there,
the eighth from the outside, joined with the fifteenth [vowel] from the navel.
One should extract this syllable: the fifth [consonant] alone, then the second from the eighth [vowel], and that which is occupied by the third of the *nemi* [vowels];
it is joined with the third of the *nābhi* [vowels], and indeed the first [vowel] before the *ārā*.
The second [syllable] is the tenth letter from the [first], marked with the eleventh [vowel] at the navel;
one should give this five-syllabled word, and at its end, to the one whose banner is a palm tree (Tālaketu).
Furthermore, at the conclusion of that, one should give the five-syllabled [word] to the one clad in blue (Nīlavāsas).
First, from the first [syllable], and then the second joined with the second vowel;
then the first alone preceded by *nemi*; then from the eleventh;
then the fourth from the outer ones; one should place that which follows the two from the *nābhi*.
One should take only the second syllable from the outside for Saṅkarṣaṇa;
then the third, which is the first of the rim (nemi), joined with the vowel 'ā';
then the second [syllable] from the outside, pure, followed by "namaḥ."
O Mahāmati, this mantra consists of thirty-six syllables.
Its first word has six syllables, and the one immediately following it has five.
The third word has ten syllables, and after that there are three words of five syllables each. (23.183)
Then, having taken the seed-syllable located on the axle, followed by the fifteenth [vowel] from the navel,
one should then give the four-syllabled word held by Śārṅgin;
thereafter, having taken the one preceded by the rim (nemipūrva), then the first [syllable] from before the spoke (prāgarāt).
And the third [syllable], consisting of three phonemes, is for the Banner (Dhvaja) from the outermost [group].
Then, from the third [group] outward, one takes the first [phoneme] from the first [group];
that should be applied below it, as the second phoneme from the eighth [group].
Then, the fifth from the outside conjoined with the second vowel;
then the eighth according to that same sequence, and again that very same one alone;
then the eleventh from the navel, followed immediately by the six-syllable mantra.
The word "sanatkumārāya" follows immediately with the five syllables;
then the word "jagatpriyāya," and thereafter "pradyumnāya namaḥ.
This mantra consists of thirty-four syllables; now hear its constituent words as well.

The first is to be known as having six syllables; the second is indeed exactly like that. Know the third to have five syllables, the fourth to have six syllables, the fifth to have five letters, and the sixth to have six letters.
For it is thus:
the sixteenth [vowel] resides in the axle; the second from the navel is indeed from the tenth.
Then, by that alone, the ninth beyond is completely traversed.

Then, having taken the first [syllable] from the very beginning and the first from the end, this syllable is joined with the second [syllable] of the navel, O Mahāmati. These two syllables are at the beginning of the word; indeed, that same [word] exists for him once again.
Then the second [syllable] from the ninth, the first from the first;
then the third from the rim (nemi), conjoined with the second vowel;
the second alone from the exterior, and the seventh from the navel-circle.
Then, one should place two syllables traversed by the sixth [vowel] upon the rim (*nemi*);
likewise, the tenth syllable from the rim and the fifth syllable situated above it;
and the syllable following the fourth, which is the second from the circle of the rim.
Immediately after that, one should join the second [syllable] with two [consonants].
Then, the syllable following the tenth, conjoined with the third vowel, and then the third [syllable] of the rim (nemi), conjoined with the fifth of the hub (nābhi). || 23.197–23.198 ||
The second [vowel] joined with the second [consonant], the ninth [letter] with devotion;
then the first of the tenth [group] should be applied to this very [mantra].
The pure second word of the rim, however, belongs to the one clad in black.

Following that, it is accompanied by a salutation to Viṣvaksena. Indeed, this thirty-two-syllable mantra, when further divided according to its constituent words, becomes one syllable more; now learn from me those words.
The first word consists of two syllables, while the second has eight syllables;
three other words have five syllables each, and the sixth is recorded as having seven syllables.
This [mantra] is for the occasion of dissolution, and for the recollection and worship of the Lord.
Listen now to another fourfold mantra in brief:
the first syllable is the eleventh letter [na] joined with the fifth vowel [u]; the third is joined with that same vowel from the circle of the rim [ṇa]. (23.203–204)
Then, the second [vowel] conjoined with the seventh from the outside;
then the second [vowel] alone [is placed] at the beginning and end of the rim (*nemi*). [The mantra is: *Oṃ*, *namaḥ*.
Then the pure eighth [vowel] from the outside, and then the second from the eighth.
Then, the second [syllable] joined with the rim (nemi), but following the nave (nābhi);
then the pair alone, followed by the outer [syllables] as a salutation;
then the syllable preceded by the nave, and the second [syllable] out of reverence for the triad.
Below that, the pair from the outside joined with the fifth from the navel; then that which follows the eighth, joined with the second from the navel;
then the simple pair from the outside; and after that, the salutation.
Then, from the axle, the second seed-syllable;
with devotion, from the twelve-spoked [rim], the first from the second, and then the fifth from the circle of the felly.
