Indeed, this is the triad alone, and likewise the second from the eighth.
"Salutation indeed to Vāsudeva, pervaded by the eleven vowels.
The first mantra consists of seven syllables, while the second has six syllables.
The third is equal to the first, but the fourth has twelve syllables.
This group of four mantras, free from the division of individual words,
should be guarded with great effort by those who know the ritual procedures and desire spiritual accomplishment.
It ends with the letter *sa*, is mounted upon the sixth vowel, and is adorned with the *anusvāra*.
The seed-syllable of the first, the all-pervading Vāsudeva, has been proclaimed;
that very same seed-syllable, situated as a seed, is deprived of the sixth vowel.
When conjoined with the second vowel, it is the king of seed-syllables belonging to Saṅkarṣaṇa.
One should join the letter *ra* between the two, [placing it] after the first seed-syllable.
This is the third seed-syllable of Lord Pradyumna, which grants all desires.
One should place the letter *ha*, mounted upon *jīva*, above the end of the scale (*tulā*).
The seed-syllable accompanied by the *visarga* is the designator of Aniruddha.
Having placed the letter *ha* within the letter *sa*, and having arranged it in six ways,
[one should apply] the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, and tenth [vowels] in sequence.
Know that one should always employ all [the mantras], beginning with the heart and ending with the eyes,
as the means for accomplishing the fourfold self-mantras.
Therefore, listen now with reverence to the mantras of the regional deities and others.
Having first written the syllable *ha* three times, and likewise the seed-syllable of the living soul (*jīvabīja*),
one should write the syllable *ka* and the syllable *kṣa* in the same way, three times each.
Thus, having placed twelve seed-syllables in sequence at the beginning, [one proceeds].

Then, one should repeatedly apply the three syllables known as "the water of the cloud-holder" at the end of all [the preceding names]. All [these syllables] are mounted upon the sixth vowel and adorned with the *anusvāra*.
These seeds of Keśava and the others are to be understood individually,
together with their respective names beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, followed by the fourth case endings.
Keśava is the first name, and after him comes Nārāyaṇa.
Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana,
Trivikrama, he who is called Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Padmalocana,
Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and the one known as Dāmodara. || 23.224–23.225 ||
One should fashion the limbs (aṅgas) as before, joined with the seed-syllables and the long vowels.
Now, O twice-born ones, listen to the mantras of the goddesses beginning with Keśava. One should indeed write this triad of *kṣaha-sat* in sequence four times.
Then, having placed those twelve seed-syllables upon it,
one should [place] in sequence the second and fourth from the seventh group,
and again the third, the fourth, the second, and the third.

One should perform this specific distinction by taking the second and the fourth, then the fourth immediately after that; then the third from the eighth, and again the third from the seventh; finally, from the ninth and the twelfth. (23.229)
Then one should join the letter *repha* (ṛ) to the head of those three;
one should place the vowel *ī* above those known as the sixth, seventh, and eighth,
along with the *anusvāra*, for all of them and for the host of goddesses.
The twelve seed-syllables have been declared according to their proper sequence;
they should be addressed by their respective names joined with the seed-syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and *namaḥ*.
[These are: Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śānti, and Vibhūti.
*Ichā*, *prīti*, and *rati*, as well as *māyā*, *dhī*, and *mahimā*;

the seed-syllables (*bījas*) associated with their respective classes of vowels and so forth, beginning with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*)—thus are the goddess-mantras of Keśava and the others proclaimed. (23.233–234)
Then, O lords of sages, I shall declare the mantras for those weapons:

"To the one whose form is the ocean, svāhā"—this mantra for the lotus begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with "to the one who moves within all. Then, [the mantra] for the one whose form is the sky: ||| 23.235 ||| Having performed [the rite] for the one who moves within all, then [one proceeds] for the one whose form is the sky.
The mantra of the conch is proclaimed to begin with the syllable *oṃ* and end with *svāhā*. Furthermore, in the Veda-mātṛ, the *vidyā* consists of the word *svāhā*.
This is declared to be the mantra of the mace; now the mantra of the discus is being described.
At the end of the syllable *oṃ*, one should place the five-syllabled word for the "All-Powerful One" (*prabhaviṣṇave*);
at the end of that, the word "Time" (*kāla*), then "to the Form" (*mūrtaye*), followed by *huṃ* and then *phaṭ*.
These four constitute the four mantras of the lotus and the other [three] seats.
Thereafter, O twice-born ones, I shall declare the mantras of those whose forms are dissolution (vibhava).

Indeed, for the purpose of propitiation, the designator is prescribed as fourfold: that consisting of names, that consisting of words, that called the "lump" (piṇḍa), and that characterized by the seed-syllable (bīja). (23.239–23.240)
From among these, one should address even a single person with devotion;
then, by means of the mantra arising from the "single-piṇḍa" formula, or by that which pertains to both,
one should perform the ritual arrangement for those two according to this very procedure.
Or, that which is to be expressed, being of undifferentiated characteristic, is metaphorically designated as one alone.
Whether it be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) or the composite syllable (*piṇḍākṣara*) of the name-mantra in the *kṛt* and other [categories],
one should bring that which is to be expressed face-to-face by means of it, either through its initial or its final [letter].
Then, he should indeed perform the placement of the mantra there according to this rite: situated upon the seat of the *praṇava* (Om) and endowed with the banner of salutation (*namaskāra*).
For it is precisely because of these two that there is oneness, owing to their nature of being peaceful.
The term *saṃjñā* refers to the word-mantra (*padamantra*), which is characterized by the accomplishment of the ritual procedure.
A single-syllable seed-syllable (*bīja*) is known to arise from either a vowel or a consonant;
through the conjunction of vowels and consonants, it becomes a multi-syllabled king of *piṇḍa*-mantras.
O Mahāmati, from both the first and likewise the last [syllables], one's own heaven arises;
for the nature of mantra belongs to others together with the *bindu*,
whether joined with a single vowel or endowed with a pair of vowels.
O Lāṅgalin, know that even a consonant accompanied by an anusvāra possesses the nature of a seed-syllable (bīja).
Know that the manifestation (vivarta) of the word called "sakhaṃkāra" is the radiance of light;
it is endowed with excellent characteristics yet formless, and understand its expression to be threefold.

In some places it is a mass, in some a seed-syllable, and in some the unstruck sound (*anāhata*). Indeed, the clear measure of that which is being sung aloud consists of many syllables and many words, characterized by praise and awakening.
The indestructible *sakhaṃkāra* bestows great supernatural power (*mahardhi*) upon the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and so forth.
First, one should offer the great seat with the *praṇava* and then with that which is called *satya*;
thereafter, one should place the seed-syllable, distinct from *satya*, upon it.
One should conceive the emergence of the form from the seed by means of its own manifestation;
when the occasion for sacrifice has arrived and the ritual is completed,
one should contemplate dissolution just as water [evaporates] upon a heated stone.
O Mahāmati, this is like the expansion and contraction of the sun's rays;
however, due to the influence of activity (kriyā), there is here merely the perception of difference.
Where there is neither seed nor mass, there indeed follows from the *praṇava* [the realization of non-duality].
The first syllable of the word-mantra (padamantra) is that which expresses the light;

from that, one should raise up the remaining body by means of the syllables, like a tree. Where there is only the seed-syllable (bīja) or the cluster-syllable (piṇḍa), devoid of the word, [that is the case].
In that regard, the status of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is prescribed for the phoneme known as *a*;
the status of the Field (kṣetra) belongs to the remaining phonemes in their embodied form.
For the self-abiding state of the seed alone is the nature of the Brahman-phoneme (*brahmavarṇatā*).
The falling away from intrinsic nature is the seed; likewise, the utterance of the seed is the ritual action.
One should fully understand that the mass-mantras (piṇḍamantra) possess seeds and are ever-arisen.
That mantra which possesses the characteristics of a seed has indeed the great power of Viṣṇu.
Of the innumerable and countless objects of expression, which possess diverse forms—
through their thorough knowledge as they truly are, through recitation, meditation, worship,
oblation, and becoming one with them— one attains the seedless state.
For indeed, for practitioners who have always accomplished their desired goal, O Blessed One, it is exactly thus regarding the mantra-forms consisting of the *piṇḍa* and so forth;
however, through thorough knowledge of the *piṇḍa*, there arises supreme stability in that [mantra]. (23.262)
Diversity arises from the various names and mantras, and from the emergence of various other worlds.
Through the thorough knowledge of the designations of the stages (*pada*), there is the attainment of all stages.
Whether with seed (*sabīja*) or as a condensed essence (*sapiṇḍa*), that which is the supreme duality of mantras— || 23.263–264 ||
Each [deity] bestows its own respective fruit; however, one should meditate upon the primordial state,
because Acyuta, the Lord of All, exists in the form of both the mantra and the Kṣetrajña,
pervading [all things] through his will to bestow grace.
Beginning with all enjoyments from the world of mortals in their pervasive form,
up to the greatness of the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), he bestows the supreme fruit upon the practitioner who possesses a divine body and is weary of worldly enjoyment, granting his own abode.
The self, consisting of the field-knower and the seed-mass, is characterized by being free from obscuration;
it bestows the attainment of the Self through that stainless, pure knowledge which restrains [the mind].
Furthermore, for the self that has assumed the state of the waking function, there is the nature of being composed of power and manifestation.
In this way, O Mahāmati, there is indeed the unity of the state of dream belonging to the self of ideation (saṃjñātman), and likewise for the state of deep sleep belonging to the mantra called Piṇḍa;
and for the state of the fourth (turya) belonging to the seed-self (bījātman), there is indeed the manifestation of power (śakti). || 23.269–23.270 ||
Although it is traditionally held that [the visualization] is restricted and endowed with the fruit of individual knowledge,
nevertheless, for the mantras and forms of the Lord,
as well as for the Primordial One, the Fourfold Self, or the Sovereign alone— || 23.271 ||
Know that mantra which is of four kinds bestows liberation and prosperity. Whatever else is prescribed— whether unmixed or indeed mixed—
know that its fruit is exactly according to one's state of being and not otherwise.
Now listen with an attentive mind to the seed-syllables:
in a pure, pleasing place, well-smeared and adorned with flowers,
mixed with powdered sandalwood and perfumed with excellent incense.
Having again inscribed the wheel of the Mātṛkās according to this division,
by the mere sight of which sin is shattered into a hundred pieces—
one should write the five groups of consonants starting from the letter *pra* (the first) at the end of each row, and the final letter of the middle group in the center.
The nine letters beginning with *ña* are situated at the navel; those beginning with *ca* occupy the sixteen spokes;

and all those beginning with *ka* reside on the rim. Whatever was located on the axle in the previous wheel, that is manifested here as the hub (*prathi*), which one should then worship according to the prescribed rite.

The wheel consisting of the Śabdabrahman should be worshipped in sequence with offerings such as water for the feet and flowers. From the center of that, one should first extract that which is the cause of all things: the syllable situated above, adorned with the letter 'a' at its beginning and the letter 'ya' at its end.

Know this to be the seed-syllable of the Lord of All, the cause that is itself without seed. This very syllable, joined with the Visarga, is remembered as belonging to the One whose navel is a lotus (Viṣṇu). It is indeed the second letter from the group beginning with *na*, and from that, the sixth vowel.
The eighth [mark] is from the region of the navel, and that same number [of marks] is from the circle of the rim. From the rim toward the navel, the seventh mark proceeds to the fifth spoke;
and from the spoke, the fourteenth mark is indeed that which has gone toward the western direction from the axle.
Then the eleventh from the rim, the sixteenth, and the thirteenth;
the fifth from the region of the navel, and the nineteenth from the rim;
its end, the seventh, and indeed the ninth, O Mahāmati.
The third from the *nābhi*, and immediately after that, the same number [third] from the *nemi*;
the twelfth from those situated on the outside, and the tenth beyond the sixteenth;
then the syllable preceding the *nābhi*, which is indeed the fifteenth from the *nemi*.
From the fourth syllable of the enemy [mantra], one takes the seed-syllable; then the fourth from the navel;
the sixth from the rim (nemi), and likewise the fourth from the middle letter. In that very place, one takes that which stands in the eastern direction, and then the fifth from the exterior.
From the axle, one should draw [the line] situated in the southern direction, being the eighteenth from the rim;
then, from the region of the nave, the second [line], at the end of which is the seventh spoke.
From there, the fourteenth from the rim, and then the sixth from the nave, one should draw.
In brief, all [the mantras] should be joined with the head [of the deity], beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *namaḥ*. They are intensely radiant, like fire.
Padmanābha and the other deities are to be designated for them in their respective order.
Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktyātman, Madhusūdana,
Kapila the presiding deity of knowledge, Viśvarūpa, Vihaga,
Kroḍātman, Vaḍavāmukha, Dharma, and likewise Vāgīśvara. || 23.290–23.291 ||
O Lord, you are the tortoise reclining upon the single ocean who supports the netherworld (pātāla);
you are the boar and the man-lion, and indeed the one who brought back the nectar of immortality.
You are the Lord of Śrī with a divine body, the beloved soul, and the bearer of the stream of nectar.
The conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, the great harer of the Pārijāta tree;
the protector of the worlds, the peaceful-souled Dattātreya, the great lord;
the Blessed One who sleeps upon the banyan tree, and thereafter he whose body has a single horn.
The god who has a dwarf body, yet is all-pervading as Trivikrama;
likewise Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa;
Rāma of the flaming axe, and another Rāma who is a wielder of the bow.
The Lord Kalkī, the knower of the Vedas, the Lord who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla)—
this group of primary incarnations has thus been described to you in brief.
Now, however, learn of the gods who have been mentioned in their proper order.
With an attentive mind, [one should contemplate] the group of *piṇḍa* mantras from me:
that which is the eighth seed-syllable situated above the seventh,
and below that, one should adorn it with the subsequent syllable, like a spoke within a wheel.
Then, taking the subsequent [syllable] from the region of the eye (akṣa), one should place it below that.
The seed-syllable with the second *nemi* (rim) is in the center; that which is in the middle of the middle is on the seat.
Then, one should indeed make the seventh [syllable], the navel, conjoined with the sixth spoke (*āra*).

Know that the eighth is above that, and this is the third [stage]. Then, taking the eighth from the navel, it is situated as the sixth from the enemy (the lower end). Then, having placed it in sequence upon the second navel— 23.301 —and then having established it there.
Then, having taken the third, the seventh, and the fourth from that same point;
and then, having first taken [the point] below the navel, and then the seventh from the navel;
and having likewise established the third below that as well.
Then one should place the ninth [syllable] from the navel, extending both upward and downward;
know that the second [syllable] in that very place is the seventh *piṇḍa*.
One should then place [the syllable] above the sixth *ar* and prior to the navel.
The seventh and the eighth [cakras] are indeed situated one above the other in sequence.
Then, the eighth has ascended from the region of the navel to the top of the seventh;
that is situated in the middle and is proclaimed as the ninth, the *akṣa*.
Again, from the fifth [circle] upwards, one should place [the mark] at the third [point] above the navel;
the third from the outside, upon that, is this tenth *piṇḍa*. From the region of the navel, the second [is placed], and the third is situated above that.
This eleventh [syllable] is recorded as being at the top of the *nemi* (rim), at the beginning and the end.
Then, having placed the seventh [syllable] of the fourth *nābhi* (navel),
that which follows the *nemi* is recorded as the twelfth.
O Great-Minded One, having taken the third letter from the end, one should join it below that in sequence; likewise the seventh and the fourth, which are above the navel.
All these, together with the sixth and the seat (the vowel), constitute this thirteenth syllable-group.
Taking the fourth from *nābhi*, one should place it above that;
likewise, the ninth upon its head—know this to be the fourteenth.
Having placed [the letters] above and below that which is designated as the fourth from *nemi*...
One should take the second letter from the group of consonants (*varṇa*), which is remembered as the fifteenth;
then, taking the twentieth letter from the external circle known as *Āra*, one should immediately join it with the sixth letter ending in *s* (*sa*). (23.313)
Having placed [the letter] above and below the seventh consonant *na*,
know that the second [vowel] from the region of the navel is the seventeenth;
one should place the ninth [vowel] from the region of the navel above the seventh [consonant].
Then, from the region of the navel, one should perform the eighth [breath] going upward to the seventh [digit];
the second [breath] likewise below that, from the circle of the navel. The thirteenth is upward from the enemy (the sixth), for that is the nineteenth.
The fourth from the navel, its third above that, and the one situated further up;
know that this is indeed the seventh in that very place and the twentieth here.
Having joined the eighth of the second [group] with the letter above the navel. (23.317–318)
Sixth from that, one should place [the letter] below it; thereafter, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) [should place the seventh].
From the region of the navel, one should place the ninth above the third.
One should place the second below that; now hear about the twenty-third.

One should apply the eighth, the seventh, the second from the navel, and then the first; these should be joined in sequence up to the sixth on the head. Taking the seventh from the navel (nemi), one places it below that, at the seventh from the navel.
That third [line] is remembered as being twenty-fourth below it;
the third from the navel is above that, and the second is above that.
Having established the one preceded by the rim (nemi), the twenty-sixth is now described.
One should make the sixth seat from the rim, its color being the third from the navel.
Above that is the seventh; understand the rest from this point.
One should place [the mark] twenty units below the rim, extending both upward and downward from it.
Taking the seventh from the letters of the *nābhi* group and the fifth from the letters of the *tvara* group,
and taking the first and second from the *nemi* group, one should place them below that.
O Great Buddha, the middle syllables are known as the twenty-eighth.
The ninth, the seventh, the third from the navel, and the second;
then, having taken that which is situated above the vowel *a*, one should place it below;
and immediately after the region of the navel, the third and the second.
Taking the second from the navel and the seventh as well as the fourth,
then from the exterior of the third navel, one proceeds upward from the beginning to the end.
Then, from the ninth navel, one proceeds upward, situated in the middle of the axle.
Then, from the eighth [digit], one should place the second [digit] above the navel;
immediately following that, the sixth [digit] is indeed situated below it.
Then, above the sixth [digit], one places the one preceding the navel, and that which follows it.
Having fixed the eighth, understand the thirty-sixth;
and having joined the seventh, the third, and the fourth from the navel-circle,
one should place the thirteenth spoke above that.
Now, know that which is the ninth from the navel, the third, and the second; that is the thirty-seventh. Then one should bring it forth from the region of the navel:
first the seat of the sixth, and the second above that.
And the ninth [syllable] above that, excluding the first [syllable] beginning with *piṇḍās*,
should indeed be struck by the spokes with the head; all [these] should be well-adorned,
ending with *namaḥ* and preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), joined with their respective names.
Having removed the spokes, that which remains above, or below, or together with the navel, or alone, is beneficial;
having set that aside, one should perform [the rite] for the worship of all. || 23.335–23.336 ||

However, according to their respective physical bodies, one should conceive of the limbs like a lion; then, enriched by the name and the *praṇava* (OM), the caste [is determined] again by the power of karma.
Until the aforementioned secondary sacrifices are completed, one who is intent on liberation should perform them.
Furthermore, one should employ the entire application of the seed-syllables, the clusters,
and the words; however, for the rite of offering and propitiation, the Vaibhava-mudrā of these [deities] should be used,
and the limb-mudrās of their members should be joined with their respective mantras.
I have taught all this common foundation along with these mantras;
for the accomplishment of the four aims of mantras is preceded by initiation.
Now, listen to the characteristics of the words and mantras.
For without them, the worship of those beings who have attained existence does not occur.
Immediately thereafter [one should offer salutation] to the one who transcends the universe, the bestower of the stainless state, the knower of wisdom,
Padmanābha, and the one who pervades the universe.
Know this to consist of twenty-four syllables; now hear the supreme number [of the next].
One should give the five-syllable word "jyotīrūpāya" and the word "gaganamūrtaye," then to Dhruva, and after that, the supreme three-syllable [mantra].

The three-syllable mantra is for the sake of the four castes who have attained their respective stages. One should then give the word *anantāya* (to the infinite), followed by *aparimitāya* (the immeasurable),
then *sarvāśrayāya* (the support of all), and at the end, *dhūtaśaktaye* (to the power of purification).
This [mantra] consists of twenty syllables; therefore, hear the one of twenty-two syllables:
having first uttered "namo bhagavate vāsudevāya," then follow with the words "sarvaśaktyātmane 'nantamūrtaye."

The word *mahāśabda* belongs to the Person whose nature is vigor; that is his station. Then there is the station of *moha*, *māyā*, and *pada*; then indeed to the Destroyer, the word *sadodita*; and after that, the station of *sarvaśakti*.
The one consisting of twenty-seven syllables is traditionally taught as being composed of four classes (caturvarṇa) to be employed.
Then there should be the word "viśvarañjakāya" for the knower of the Vedas;
at the end of that, "viśvapataye," and then indeed "paramātmane."
Listen to this seventeen-syllable [mantra] consisting of twenty phonemes:

one should form the word *jñānātmane* (to the self of knowledge), followed by the word *saṃvit* (consciousness), and then the word *prakāśāśayāya* (to the one whose nature is peaceful light). 23.350–351.
Immediately after that, [the word] for the one of infinite power, the all-pervading;
then, for the one consisting of the world; and then, indeed, the word for the one whose form is the universe—this has been stated in twenty-one syllables. Listen now to the next.
Having first taken the six-syllable word, then the word *guhāśaya*,
then for the *paramahaṃsa*, then for the one who moves in the mind (*mānasacārin*);
and then, consisting of nineteen syllables, [the name] for *yajñamūrti*.
Then, taking the word *pada*, followed by *viśvāntarvartine*,
then the word *bhuvana*, then the word *varāhāya*,
and finally *vibhūtisvāmine*— this [mantra] consists of twenty-four syllables.
One should offer salutations to the Blessed One and then indeed to the Mare’s Fire (vaḍavāgni).
The state that is the fuel for the waters of the world is the blazing state itself;
with "vīryāya phaṭ" at its end, this is remembered as having such a number [of syllables].
One should give the word *sarvāntaścāriṇe* and also the word *prasannapada*;
then one should give the word *mūrtaye* and the word *dharmātmane*.
This indeed consists of sixteen syllables; therefore, listen now to what is secret.
Then one should offer [the mantra] to Sarvavidyeśvara, and thereafter to Vākpati;
taking the word "pada" along with its case-ending, one then says "vāgvibhavam. This indeed consists of nineteen syllables; now I shall tell you another.
Then, one should offer a foot [of land] to the one who bestows the sovereignty of yoga, to the essence of yogic sleep, to the cloud-like one, the Blessed One who reclines upon the waters.
This [mantra] consists of twenty-four syllables, plus one more.

Taking the word *bhagavat-pada* for the one of infinite strength and power, then for the one consisting of splendor who upholds the world; thereafter, the two-syllabled word should be employed at the end,
namely the word for the one whose self is the tortoise (*kacchapa*).
O best among those who know mantras, know that the mantra consists of twenty-six syllables;
having first taken the body of the sacrificial limbs, thereafter [one should give] the great state (mahāpada) to Varāha, the Ancient Puruṣa.
Then one should add the word *prajā* and at its end the word *pataye*.
O best among those who know mantras, this is the twenty-four-syllable mantra; having first uttered "namo bhagavate," one should then say "nārasiṃhāya. (23.365–23.366)
One should give the word *tejonidhe*, then *padaṃ dadyāt*, and then *padaṃ hana hana*.
Following that, the five-syllable mantra *vikarmajātyai śadaṃ* arises. Indeed, at the end of that is *duṣkṛtaṃ*; thus, this [mantra] consists of twenty-seven syllables.
"O you who are the embodiment of nectar, O Supreme Self of knowledge!
O Blessed One, Lord of All, this [mantra] consists of nineteen syllables.
O Lotus-eyed One, O Supreme Lord, take up the word 'Ādāya'! (23.368–369)
Then the word "sakala," which is indeed a term for happiness and good fortune; then the word "nidhi," which is the sound of one's desire; then the word "siddhiprada" (bestower of perfection);
and then the word "akhiladuḥkha" (all suffering), followed by "śamanāgnaye" (to the fire of pacification).
Then one should place the word *ānandasundara*, followed by the word *lakṣmī*. Having uttered the word *pataye*, one should then utter the fifty-syllable [mantra] three times.
Next, having taken the word *sadasat*, one should then add *mūrtaye*.
Then, for Puruṣottama, and thereafter for Amṛtanidhi,
this sixteen-syllable mantra of the Lord, whose nature is splendor, is declared:
"To Puruṣottama," and then "the Unobstructed."
Then one should give the word *śaktaye*, and after that the word *sarveśvara*.
Following that, at the point where [the phrase] *samagrograhaya* occurs, there is the warding off (*nivāraṇa*).
This is said to be the twenty-seven-syllable mantra; listen further to what follows.

Having extracted the *niyantra* word, at its end [one places] "for the cause of the universe" (*viśvahetave*), followed by "to the bridge" (*setave*) joined with the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma*), and immediately after that, *oman*.
This mantra consisting of sixteen syllables is thus described; beyond that—
In the passage beginning with "the peerless state" (padam apratima), one should first [worship] Prabhāva; immediately after that, Mahāvibhūti; following that, the state of Mahāmāyā;
and then the word Darśaka for Tālaketu at the end of that.
This twenty-four-syllable mantra has been taught in brief. One should give the word *śāntātmane* (to the peaceful self), and at its end, one should place this [syllable].
One should give that for the sake of taking refuge in the observances (*niyama*), and also for the supreme gift.
The word "Nārāyaṇāya" is traditionally taught as being equal in syllables to the preceding number;
immediately after that, the word "Bhavabhaṅgapadāya," and then the word "Kāriṇe"; thereafter, the word "Bhagavate," and then indeed "Ataryāya."
Then the word *varṇāśramapadam*, followed by the word *dharma*; for the sake of inclusion, the syllable *praṇava* (om) is traditionally taught as the twenty-eighth.
Then the words *salokamāyāmāya* and thereafter the word *sarvajñāya*.
Then [the word] "Śabda" for the Universal Self, and then the word "Vimala";
then the word "Sarveśvarāya" (to the Lord of All) and the word "Nyagrodhaśayanāya" (to Him who reclines on the banyan tree).
Now, learn another [mantra] consisting of twenty-three syllables.
Then, taking the word *bhūta*, followed by the word *bhāvanāya*;
then the word *śabda* for the Universal Self (*viśvātman*), and then the word *vimala*;
then the word *niketanāya*, and after that the word *kaṇṭharāya*.
This king of mantras is remembered as having twenty-two syllables.

Having first uttered the word "to Viṣṇu," then "to the one who is both weaponless and armed with weapons," then the word "to Brahman," then "to the one with matted hair" and "to the one with a staff."
One should indeed utter the word *vidita* at the end of that for the sake of prosperity;
this mantra consists of twenty-six syllables—now listen to it from me:
*sarvaśabdam*, then *athādāya*, and immediately after that, *vyāpine*.
One should offer the auspicious five-syllable mantra to Sahasrārcis;
then the word to Trivikrama, and then indeed to Aparimita.
One should offer the word to Prabhāva; this is remembered as consisting of twenty-three syllables.
Then, for the Lord of Men, the foremost of persons, who is intent on meditation upon the Self, there is the two-syllable mantra "Nā-ya. Next,
listen to another mantra consisting of twenty-one syllables.
One should offer the word "to Nārāyaṇa," which is indeed the state of Nirati;
then the word "to Him who consists of bliss," which is indeed the state of Nirabhimāna;
and thereafter, the word "to Him who is attached to the state," which consists of twenty-five syllables.
Taking the word *parāya* [as the first],
this sixteen-syllable mantra is for Hari, the Lord of Yoga, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Having first taken the seven-syllable word *namaḥ paramātmane*, [the mantra follows].
Then the word *kṛṣṇāya*, followed by the lotus (*kamala*), and then the three-syllable [word];
then the expanded word *dala*, followed by *netrāya*; then *bṛhmiṣṭhāya* and *brahmaṇe vā*—this [mantra] consists of twenty-eight syllables. (23.395–396)

Taking the word *bhagavatpada* and [the word] *yugāntadahaneti*, one should then give the word *dṛptaye*; for this is indeed the word *saṃsārapada*. This [mantra], consisting of twenty-two syllables, is remembered as the one that effects the severance of bondage.

One should indeed utter the clear-sounding "pada," which is the word for the ultimate reality (paramārtha). One should offer [the mantra] to the one who possesses four forms, who consists of the four states of existence,
and who bears the arrow and the bow, possessing the luster of an autumnal blue lotus.
Then one should offer the "Delightful Foot" (*abhirāmapada*) to the Blessed One;
thereafter, the "Body Foot" (*śarīrāyapada*) is remembered as consisting of thirty-eight syllables.
One should indeed offer the "Two-Ten Sound" (*dviśadaśabda*), and then the "Ultimate Reality Foot" (*paramārthapada*).
Then, O Lord, one should give the word "to the knower of the Vedas," "to the wise one," and "to the pervasive one. Thereafter, one should indeed give another word consisting of three syllables.
This [mantra] has been described as having twenty syllables; now hear another from me.
One should utter the word "Garuḍa," followed by "vāhana" at its end;
then "sarvaśastrāstrodyata" and likewise "śamaya-aśubham. Thereafter, one should recite "adhunādhunādāya karmabandhān."
Protect the Dharma; thereafter, one should bestow it. Abandon unrighteousness; thereafter, one should uplift it. This is the thirty-four-syllable mantra; hereafter I shall speak [of it]:
"To the form of withdrawal (saṃhāramūrtaye)," the word, "to the flame of the fire of time (kālavaiśvānarārciṣe)."
"Obeisance to him who reclines in Pātāla"—this is indeed the "flow of ignorance.
Recite "Destroy the accumulation" with repetition, and immediately after that, the *praṇava*.
This mantra of thirty-five syllables is remembered as the granter of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
All [mantras] adorned with the *praṇava* and embellished with the word of salutation (*namaskāra*),
when consecrated, worshipped, and especially meditated upon and recited (*japta*),
there is nothing on earth that they do not bestow through devotion for those of virtuous deeds.
Now listen to the characteristics of the treatises on the mantras of the sectarian marks (lāñchana):
one should first place the word "sahasradīdhiti" and then add "śurita. (23.409)
For the sake of conflict, one should take from Daśārṇa the three [syllables] exceeding those of the *makuṭa*;
having taken that which bestows the desired state,
one should then give the station of great contemplation (*mahācintā*) to the *maṇi*.
Know that it consists of fifteen syllables; now hear another of ten syllables:
[the word] *sarvalakṣaṇa*, followed by *sampatpradāya*, then taking the word *saubhāgya*, and finally the three-syllable [word] *janani*. (23.411–23.412)
But in every case, this very [mantra] consists of ten syllables.
Know that "prāṇātmane atha satyāya" consists of seven syllables.
Furthermore, "kālakartre atha cakrāya phaṭ" is proclaimed to consist of eight syllables.
One should offer a seat to the Soul of the Universe, and then to the Giver of the Universe.
Know this to be the nine-syllabled mantra; now hear the supreme eight-syllabled one.
Having taken up the word "Vidye," it is then honored by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
One should first perform [the offering] to the form of sound; this is remembered as the eight-syllable mantra for the conch.
One should then utter the word "O treasure of taste," and after that, the word "Bhīma.
At the end of that, one should say "to the Terrifying One" (bhīṣaṇāya); this is remembered as the ten-syllable mantra.
Know that "to the Lord of the World in the East," which consists of thirteen syllables, is for Stambha; understand the next one:
"to the Treasury of the Senses" (indriyakośāya), which consists of ten syllables, is for Iṣvāstra.
To the one whose voice is like the wind at the end of an eon, whose state is like the flash of lightning,
and who is radiant— listen now to the sixteen-syllable mantra, and thereafter the nine-syllable one.
One should then bestow the word *mahāmāyā* followed by two syllables for binding.
Having taken up the word for the destroyer, hear this supreme number next:
"the devourer of all missiles," followed by "the supreme," then "the one who causes torment," and then "the destroyer of pride."
Know that there is one of eleven syllables, and then another of nine syllables is spoken;
immediately after that is the phrase "for the destruction of ignorance," and for the Supreme (Parā) follows the nine-syllable phrase "for the form that fascinates the three worlds."
The phrase "the performer of all attractments" and "consisting of the great illusion" indeed [form the mantra].
One should then extract the twelve-syllable count and the nine-syllable [mantra], and having joined them, one should apply that at the end, with the word "unbroken" placed first.
Now hear from me the seven-syllable mantra for valor;
and indeed, understand the five-syllable mantra for the subduer of pride.
"O you who are garlanded with splendor"—these are proclaimed as twenty-two [mantras].
As before, [the mantras] are enclosed at the beginning and end and adorned with their own names;
one should always place the word of the name at the end of the syllable that concludes the number.
For the weapon-mantras, one should form them like a wheel, ending with the name.
In due order, there are fourteen [syllables] ending with Śakti, and the six-footed [mantra].
Now I shall declare the supreme mantra of Nṛsiṃha, the protector of the universe;
indeed, the previously mentioned wheel of letters should be kept well-concealed beneath the surface of the earth.
Having smeared [the surface] and then drawn [the design], and having worshipped it according to the ritual rule,
one should then extract the mantra of manifold and wondrous power;
taking the *praṇava* (oṃ) first and joining it at the end.
The ninth [syllable] is from the nasalized vowels (*nābhivarṇa*); the fourteenth is from above that.
Above that, one should place the semi-vowel (*antasthavarṇa*) within it like a sphere.
This syllable, ending with *namaḥ*, is indeed the designator (*vācaka*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The six qualities beginning with knowledge, as previously mentioned, correspond to the heart and the other [centers].
For that very purpose, one should simply write that syllable in six ways, using the second, fourth, sixth, twelfth, and final [vowels]. (23.432–23.433)
One should duly apply [the mantras] from the fourteenth group onwards in sequence;
one should mark all of them with the seed-syllable at the head, except for the fifth.
Having first placed the *praṇava* (oṃ) before all of them, one should then join it at the end of their respective names.
And at the end, one's own mantras should likewise conclude with *vauṣaṭ* in their proper order.
Then, having remembered the twelve-syllable mantra—"Oṃ namo bhagavate nārasiṃhāya"—as if it were embodied in form, as before. (23.435–23.436)
One should worship with the primordial [deity] together with its limbs, abiding both externally and internally.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Extracting Mantras," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter. Nārada said:
"O best of sages, listen as I now describe the ritual procedure for the mudrās."
It bestows the state of immortality upon those who have performed the stainless sacrifice regarding the true nature of the self and its actions;
it dissolves the defects that move within and without,
and for this reason it is called *mudrā*, as well as because it seals (*mudraṇāt*) what has been accomplished.
Therefore, having first established either the natural state or the mental bond,
one should indeed always meditate upon it as pervaded by its respective mantra. Even though the entire collection of branches is permeated by consciousness, [it remains so].
There too, the superintendent of the mantra-recitation shall perform that duty. Having smeared his hands with fragrant substances, he should perform the binding of the mudrā;
specifically, from both hands joined in pairs, [he should form it] with the middle and ring fingers.
Having made them clearly face away from each other,
they should be joined together with effort, continuously from the roots to the tips of the nails.
Likewise, the remaining fingers should be placed upon the upturned palms.
By means of the lower and upper [positions] on the left and right respectively; likewise,
having extended the index finger upward toward the thumb and facing it.
O best of sages, this mudrā should be fixed in the heart;
it should be employed in the worship of the Fourfold Self (Cāturātmya), for it bestows all perfections.
The two hands, remaining open, should be joined at the wrists.
Having restrained both elbows at the sides and the two [hands] at the navel like a staff, one should sway them slightly;
afterwards, those two hands should be moved downward and upward.
Having established this protection, it is to be employed in the rite of worship with the mudrā.
O twice-born ones, hear now from me another [mudrā] of the forms beginning with Keśava:
having joined the two palms together, one should form a cluster of creepers (latāgaṇa) while bowing forward;
then, releasing them, one should place them inside along with both thumbs.
One should make the two wrists well-joined and extremely steady;
holding both hands with the palms hollowed, one should maintain them immovably by one's own intellect.
Then, while seated between the thighs, one should place the elbows upon the thighs.
Having concealed it with effort, one should perform its binding.
O twice-born ones, this is the single Vaibhavī mudrā of the gods of power;
when employed with the *praṇava*, it possesses a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun.
Now the two mudrās of Viśvatrātṛ Nṛsiṃha are described.

Having meditated upon the three fingers of the right hand as having the form of the three sacrificial fires, they are clearly turned upward; that same [finger] is the Jyeṣṭhā, while the little finger is the Kanīyasī.
Then [he is] the form of all sacrifices, yet he is beyond the path, assuming the form of fire;
the Lord who transcends the three qualities and likewise transcends the three paths,
who is liberated from the grossest attributes, and who is this manifest one worshipped by the intellect.

With their faces turned toward one another and their arms interlaced, they are joined by their branches; however, each raises his own right hand upward. This mudrā, previously described, is known as the Avidhyādalanī.

Next, the six mudrās of the heart-mantra and the others are described. Having formed the *sampuṭa* (enclosed) mudrā at the region of the heart with both hands, with the fingers held close together— this mudrā is known as *hārdradhī*.

The two pairs of fingers, beginning with the thumbs and ending with the little fingers, should be held separately with intervals from this *sampuṭa* mudrā; likewise, it should be so for the little fingers and the rest.
The mudrās for the head, the crest, the armor, the weapon, and the eyes follow in due order.
Having formed the hands into a bud-like shape, one should place them upon the head with the mantra.
This is to be known as the kirīṭa-mudrā (crown mudrā), which resembles ten thousand suns.
Then follows the śrīvatsa-mudrā, which is indeed proclaimed to be the padma-mudrā (lotus mudrā).
With the middle and ring fingers shortened,
placed in the center of the palms like two fists, O Brahmin, one should then join the two fists together with their openings aligned and extend both index fingers.
Then one should join them from the tips, placing the two thumbs at their tips;
by means of the two middle fingers, however, they should be joined to each other in sequence.
This is declared to be the mudrā of the Kaustubha gem; now hear about the garland mudrā.

O Brahmin, whether sitting or standing, one should hold the eight branches with both hands, grasping them from the tips forward; then, with the arms held close together and hanging down, one should let the two arms hang down between the thighs.
The Mālāmudrā is proclaimed as being correctly formed when [the hands] reach as far as the wrists. When the two thumbs are joined together and the fingers are held apart,
this is indeed the Pādmī mudrā, which bestows nourishment and good fortune.
One should grasp the left thumb with the right hand,
and place the fingers from the left hand upon the right [hand]. Then,
one should join the tip of the left index finger with the tip of the right thumb.
One should join them firmly together, facing each other; this is the Śaṅkha mudrā when held with the palms turned upward. With both hands clearly extended and joined to one another— || 24.32–24.33 ||
From its rotation, it is celebrated as the Cakravartinī;
it is the destroyer of all sufferings and the supreme among seals that pierces [obstructions].
Having formed a fist with the right hand, one places it upon the top of the left thumb.
Having performed this, one should display the very beautiful Kaumodakī.
Known as the Gada-mudrā, it crushes the armies of faults.
The left hand should be extended upward with the fingers spread apart.
The fingers should be slightly contracted at their tips like a bridge,
meeting one another with the thumb in the middle among the finger-tips.
Facing the heart, one should bind this Śakti-mudrā, which bestows happiness.
Know that, beginning with the *prādiśinī* [mudrā] and ending with the *kaniṣṭhā*, these are used for the *śrī* and other [deities].
O twice-born one, having first extended and joined the two hands together,
one should place the tips of the two thumbs upon the root-regions of the ring fingers.
Facing downward, fallen directly in front of the wrist,
clearly raised and joined like a tail with the pair of little fingers—
this is the seal of the Great-Souled One alone, the King of Birds.
The single *añjali* gesture is known as common to all mantras.
One should employ it conjoined with its respective mantra,
while visualizing a red lotus and the sun upon the palm of the right hand.

One should touch the substances with that [hand]; thus, this mudrā is of the nature of burning. Recalling the moon within a white lotus on the palm of the left hand, one should touch the substances with that [hand]; thus, this mudrā is also of the nature of nourishing.
Having joined the two hands together so that they are well-locked and facing downwards,
one should then apply the little fingers and thumbs in close contact,
while the pair of middle fingers are placed upon the backs of each other's hands.
The two ring fingers extended and likewise the pair of index fingers—
this is the mudrā of the Wish-Fulfilling Cow (Kāmadhenu), which completely fulfills all desires. Now, the binding of the mudrās for the mantras of the seats will be described.
Of the left hand facing downward, both the ring finger and the index finger [should be bent];
having bent them so that they rest against the back [of the hand], one should place them upon the middle finger;
below those two, with the two middle fingers straight, one should form [the mudrā] facing downward.
O Sage, that *phaṇiṣṭhikā* [mudrā] should be formed with the thumbs well-extended;
this is the *anantāsana-mudrā*, O twice-born one, for there is no mantra superior to it.
Indeed, this [mudrā] exists having embraced this entire world.
Having placed the two hands so that they do not touch, one should then join them:
the mouth [of one hand] with the mouth [of the other], and not release [the grip] with the two index fingers;
then, one should form such a binding, and having released that, [one does the same] with the two ring fingers.
Having withdrawn that as well, one should apply the two little fingers;
one should place the pair of thumbs joined together in each individual bond.
These are the four mudrās for Dharma and so forth, and Adharma and so forth.
For the lotus situated above that, the previously mentioned [application] is performed through the yoga of mantra (24.53). Having joined the index finger and thumb of the right hand,
one should then gradually open that bond (24.54).
One should perform the separate emanation (*samutthāna*) and keep the assembly of branches (*śākhā-saṃgha*) situated separately;
this is said to be the mudrā for the three abodes (*dhāmatraya*) of Gaṇeśa and the others.
The three fingers beginning with the little finger of the left hand are placed in the middle of one's own palm.

From the thumb, the index finger should be raised behind them. Then, with the right hand, one should form a fist as before, placing it against the region of the bridge of the nose using three fingers.
Having doubled the index finger, one should join it at the tip of the thumb;
the right arm raised like that which is uplifted for hurling a discus—
this is the mudrā of Viṣvaksena, which severs all bonds.
Having joined the two hands together in front and extended them,
they should be applied to the forehead; with the head bowed,
this is the mudrā for the triad beginning with the Guru, which clarifies the mind.

One should place both hands palm-upward at the region of the navel, with the right hand behind the left; this is the mudrā of the lineage of the Siddhas (24.61). But for all others, O twice-born ones, the mudrā should be the añjali.
In the same way, for the retinues and those dwelling at the gates and enclosures,
as well as for others who have been worshipped, the mantras should be applied again and again according to their sequence, by one whose mind is full of devotion, together with the *śiras* [mantra].
Having formed the hands into the shape of a lotus, with the thumbs and little fingers joined together at their tips like the pericarp of a lotus, O twice-born ones,
the remaining three fingers beginning with the index fingers should extend upward from both hands.
But by placing them unjoined, it is proclaimed as the mudrā of the fire.
Slightly contracting the right hand and bringing it toward the heart,
with the two thumbs clearly separated, this is remembered as the mudrā for invocation.
Having joined the two palms with the fingers extended upward, one should release each respective little finger with the two thumbs; this is the *sannidhi-mudrā*.
Then, one should perform the wiping (*unmārjana*) between the ring fingers and the middle fingers.
Likewise, the two [hands] are made to be in a state of firm rigidity and complete stillness.
O twice-born ones, one should form the añjali with the hands slightly opened;
this is indeed the Saṃmukhī-mudrā, for it brings the Lord face-to-face.
Having made both thumbs straight like a staff with the fingers spread apart like the edge of a sword, one should gradually form a fist starting from the little fingers;
this mudrā is for dismissal.
By this method, he who knows the ritual procedure and binds the mudrā—
by him this entire universe is sealed, and it once again becomes a bestower of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
Now, O twice-born ones, I shall describe in due order the meditations (dhyāna) upon the mantras previously mentioned.
First, listen to the supreme meditation upon the single-formed [Lord]:
the Supreme Lord of the World, our God, should be meditated upon as accompanied by Śrī, and bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, marked with the conch and the discus. (24.73)
Endowed with two hands capable of uplifting the three worlds,
he is peaceful and the very nature of consciousness; yet, out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees,
he has assumed a formal embodiment through a form that is beyond comparison, though he is in truth formless.
Causing the entire universe to swell with his splendor, which was equal to ten thousand full moons,
Filled with all ornaments, radiant yet formless, and surging with waves of nectar, his body and feet remain changeless. Next, I shall describe the unsurpassed meditation upon the Suṣupti-vyūha.
As the knower, the Blessed One, whose form is permeated by Brahman,
remains like a pillar in the center of the pericarp and thus becomes the object of knowledge;
he does so of his own accord for the benefit of those performers of ritual action who sacrifice to Brahman.
From the eastern portion up to the northern one,
the supreme Lord Vāsudeva, O wielder of the plow, divides his own measure according to the distinction of qualities;
yet, without abandoning his essential nature, he remains in the eastern portion as the sixfold self.
Then, the Supreme Lord abides in the southern quarter with knowledge conjoined with power (*bala*),
and is established in the western portion through sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and valor (*vīrya*).
He is situated in the northern quarter as splendor (*tejas*) in the form of potency (*śakti*).
"Even though the Blessed One is formless, consisting of manifestations and characterized by qualities, it was already stated previously that 'form' is used here figuratively. However,
O auspicious lady, [this applies] specifically to the two palms of his second form."

The right hand of the third was clearly marked with a beautiful arrow, while the fourth [hand] bore a large, distinct conch shell and a very evident plow; by these two, both hands were marked with excellent swords.
With his face turned downward by the power of his hands, yet upward by his very nature;
by this much of a characteristic, and by having attained a state of manifestation,
he establishes the stability of the emotional state (*bhāva*) for the practitioner within this ritual array.
Because of their similarity, because they possess six qualities, because of their equality,
and specifically because of their tranquility and inactivity, a distinction exists;
even though I have previously described them by means of two pairs of qualities each.
For although each individual form of the Blessed One is primary,
there remains a quartet of qualities that abide together;
one should always attend to the continuity of each one of these.
Now listen, O best of sages, to the meditation on the array of dreams, by which the Self— out of compassion for those engaged in action—
is gradually led to manifestation upon the lotus of the syllables of speech. 24.91
He was augmented by the undivided and complete majesty of the six royal qualities;
he beheld the stainless God, blazing with continuous rays of light such as white and others, and radiant with the splendor of his risen state.
Then, relying upon the tip of the pericarp, one should perceive for oneself by means of one's own power that divine body consisting of mantra, which is invisible in form due to time;
and one should perceive that manifest form, possessing the characteristics previously described, as it is being withdrawn.
Having thus withdrawn the body consisting of mantra, O wielder of the plow,
you shall fill it from the base to the tip of the pericarp with your own splendor;
then, O high-minded one, having ascended it in the form of the sacrificial post of Brahmā, you shall proceed.
The fourfold gentle form, which extends in all directions,
manifests itself in the east through the Lord himself in the form of Vāsudeva, with a white body that surpasses the brilliance of the sun.
Immediately thereafter, with a splendor like that of a ruby,
that Lord indeed rises in the southern quarter in the form of Saṅkarṣaṇa,
possessing a hundredfold radiance exceeding even the sun, which is heated by its own rays.
And in the western direction, the Supreme Lord is clearly manifest in the form known as Pradyumna,
with a complexion resembling the autumnal sky. || 24.99 ||
Then, he was also absorbed into Aniruddha in the northern quarter;
indeed, that primordial form is remembered as being equal for all.
O lotus-eyed one, they all possess the splendor of ten million suns in their radiance.
With the canopies of moonlight from their teeth, they illuminate the quarters of the sky;
resembling ten thousand full moons, they are adorned with pearl necklaces and other ornaments,
and are clothed in radiant garments like nectar, accompanied by excellent garlands.
With their hands raised holding excellent weapons, they were not bereft of their own respective emblems; marked by the soles of their feet with lotuses that had arisen from the drawings,
their faces were intent upon allaying the suffering of the submerged people.
With hearts full of compassion, they are intent on rescuing the world;
standing in the midst of a circle of flames produced from the splendor of their own bodies,
this Blessed One is to be thus gratified through the preliminary practice.
O Great-minded One, by means of each individual portion in succession according to its power,
one should again worship the Supreme Lord— beginning with Aniruddha and ending with the Primal Form (Vāsudeva)— through continuous offerings in due order.
By means of the two *praṇavas* alone, with a perfectly purified intellect, according to the procedure known as *apya-ya*, by the wise who are devoted to the heart-sacrifice (*hṛdayāga*),
O twice-born ones, I shall then describe the sequence of meditation upon the waking manifestation (*jāgrad-vyūha*).
O Great-minded One, that which rests within the expanse of the infinite ocean,
whose root is the syllable *A*, is the eternal lotus that is the support of all.
Its stalk is the syllable *A*, and its leaves are all the remaining letters.
That which stands like a wheel, resting upon the eight directions—
within its petals, at the station known as "the waking state," the Blessed One is to be worshipped and meditated upon; how this is to be done is now described.
The other [deity] is completely filled with his own splendor by means of the seed-syllable *praṇava*;
he stands from above the pericarp down to the interior of the filaments, and having been thus beheld,
[one should proceed] then from the four Brahma-seed syllables preceded by the *praṇava*.
One should meditate upon the fourfold form of the Lord as it arises in the sequence of the directions, resembling *kadamba* flowers and crowded with hundreds of rays;
the mantra-form is clearly defined in its characteristics, while the external form is enveloped by the vibhava-form.
Arising from the Supreme, resembling a spark of fire,
entered within the expressive word (*vācaka*), and having attained manifestation—
therein is the first form of the Blessed One, possessing the luster of snow, the *kunda* flower, and the moon.
Four-armed, with a gentle face and eyes like white lotuses,
clad in yellow silk garments and adorned with a golden banner;
with his primary right hand, he bestows fearlessness upon those who are afraid.
The king of conchs, the treasury of knowledge, was grasped by his left hand;
on the other side at his back, the mace was raised aloft by his right hand,
while likewise a mace rested upon the surface of the earth in his left.
Having the form of a peak of vermilion, with one face and four arms,
wearing garments resembling the flax flower and marked by the crescent moon;
his two principal hands are indeed equal to those of the Primordial Lord.
The plow was in his hand, while the pestle was in the hand that held the mace;
it possessed the luster of a multitude of fireflies appearing at night during the rainy season,
was clothed in red silk garments, and was adorned with the dolphin-bannered god of love.
The third supreme lord has one face and four arms.
O high-minded one, his two principal hands should be meditated upon as before;
in the left [hand] is the Śārṅga bow, and in the right are five arrows.
Resembling the mountain of collyrium, draped in pure white garments,
four-armed, large-eyed, and adorned with the mark of the moon.
The pair of hands of the first [deity] is proclaimed to be the same for this one as well;
then, in order from the right, he holds a sword and a shield with two hands.
All of them wear forest garlands and are marked with the Śrīvatsa.
They were adorned upon their chests with the Kaustubha, the king of jewels;
with beautiful crowns and diadems, necklaces, armlets, and anklets; with variegated tilakas on their foreheads, and shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings.
They should always be visualized as adorned with various beautiful garlands, wreaths, and ointments such as camphor;
furthermore, by means of the yoga of reabsorption, they are to be placed upon the eastern, northern, and central petals.
One should meditate on the Lord Aniruddha with a white and black body.
One should contemplate Pradyumna in the petal situated between the north and the west,
with a form that is black and yellow at the time of dissolution.
In the rite of the counter-current (pratisrota), one should meditate upon the god Saṅkarṣaṇa, who abides in the middle between the west and the south, and who bears a body of yellow and red hue;
in the center and between the east and the south, he shines with white and red splendor.
"O high-minded one, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, is to be meditated upon. Then, by virtue of his pure intention, the All-pervading One— like a crystal stone—
having attained a distinction of location through the two [reflections] of his own splendor, indeed..."
It grasps a variegated form characterized by withdrawal,
existing non-differently from the primordial source like the seed of a banyan tree; yet,
in the ultimate sense, it is devoid of all activity and is formless.
That primordial Cāturātmya is indeed great, consisting of pure consciousness;
it possesses the luster of a thousand fires, suns, and moons, and is characterized by the vibration of bliss.
It is the seed of all actions and the locus of all conceptual constructions.
Know that, O fair-eyed one, it is the fourfold self, the second [form],
which is eternal, possessing an eternal form, and brilliant with the splendor of the sun;
it is divided by the distinctions of white and other colors, and situated above and below.
It bestows the fruit of liberation and enjoyment, and brings about the conquest of the seed of worldly existence.
The third [form] is the Cāturātmya, beautiful with a mass of nectar,
performing maintenance, creation, and dissolution, and endowed with all necessary instruments.
Presiding over his own nature, he rises and sets;
know that to be the fourth [state], by whose command the universe abides. That form which is white and so forth, which exists in the fourth age (the Kṛtayuga), [is that].
O Great-minded One, in the Tretā age, [the sequence] begins with red and ends with white;
when the Dvāpara age arrives, it is yellow, black, white, and red;
and in the Kali age, it is black, white, red, and yellow, respectively.
Now learn from me that form which the Supreme Lord assumes during the four junctions of the ages (*yugasandhyā*), a form characterized by a commonality of diverse manifestations:
at the end of the Kṛta age it is yellow-red, and after that, red-yellow.
Next is yellow and black, and immediately after that, black and white;
the distinction between these is to be known by the previously mentioned weapons, garments, and emblems.
Otherwise, by what means could the division here be determined, given their similarity?
Thereafter, O lords of sages, I shall describe the meditation upon Keśava and the others;
for that which is all-pervading, the supreme light, formless and stainless—
considering that very [light] to be Vāsudeva, one should then worship him correctly.
[He worshipped] the Lord with all [offerings], such as flowers, which were like nectar to the mind.
Afterwards, one should meditate upon that supreme, stainless, and imperishable abode in embodied form—
compassionate, incomparable, with his hand resting upon the slope of his hips,
bestowing fearlessness upon his devotees with his right hand. (24.149)
One should then meditate upon that which has simultaneously emerged from that abode— richly adorned with flowers, ornaments, and garments, endowed with a pair of conchs and discs,
resembling a great mass of sparks, and eternally radiant.
And by that, one should visualize the host of wheels being completely overcome;
then, one should visualize [the deities] arising sequentially from each portion of light,
three in number, beginning with white, and Keśava and the others, four-armed.
With the right and left hands behind [the back], one should recognize the pairs [of attributes] among Keśava and the others in sequence, moving upwards:
the conch and discus, the lotus and the mace, and the conch and the lotus.
That [hand] has the conch, the lotus, the discus, and the mace; then the conch, the discus, the lotus, the discus, the conch, and then the mace. (24.155)
Similarly, for each of the twelve [deities] ending with Dāmodara, one should know that the two lower [parts] correspond respectively to the two upper [parts]. Listen to this:
[the sequence is] the lotus, the mace, the sound, the discus, that lotus, the supreme weapon, and the sound.
The mace, the discus, that knowledge, the lotus, and the conch—that is the lotus;
the mace, the lotus, the mace, and the conch—that is the knowledge-lotus for you.
Furthermore, one should remember that great [emanation] which has issued forth from that host of abodes.
The triad beginning with Śrī and the triad beginning with Keśava are each marked by their mutual relationship with the triad beginning with Kamalā;
they are seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and face toward the cardinal and intermediate directions.
And out of modesty, she fanned him with a white yak-tail whisk.
Now, the form of those twelve goddesses is described:
they all had faces like the full moon and were adorned with flowers from every season.
Complete with all the marks and adorned with all ornaments,
the first triad has the luster of coral, while the other has the radiance of the campaka flower;
the third deity is dark like a cluster of priyaṅgu blossoms.
One should meditate on the fourth triad as having a radiance like the *jāti* flower.
One should meditate on a lotus in the hand of the first [deity], the king of weapons in the hand of the second, and a conch in the hand of the third; thus one should meditate upon each triad.
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the meditation of the Vibhava deities.
That great assembly of deities belonging to the Vaibhava realm,
which was previously described to you by me, know each one of them to be threefold.
It was indeed prepared for the destruction of the defects of universal dissolution throughout the four junctions of the ages and the ages themselves;
it was marked by hands holding blazing weapons and appeared in forms such as white and red.
At the beginning, middle, and end of every undertaking,
he alone, though one, assumes his own form in manifold ways;
for the welfare of all worlds, he takes on a gross form at will.
With a body unassuming yet as white as a kunda flower or the moon,
he remained with a joyful mind in the vīrāsana and other postures;
holding all weapons with effortless ease, his face was gentle and composed.
O best among those possessed of form, that manifest form known as "Peace," which destroys the entire multitude of defects for those seeking liberation through wisdom,
illuminates the true path for those whose souls are devoted to meditative absorption.
That form which consists of splendor is the manifestation known as Śānta.
All [these forms] bestow every fruit upon the devotees who worship them.
The Blessed Lord Viśākhayūpa himself, out of a desire to create the universe, [manifested].
For indeed, by its presiding essential nature, it arises as one alone;
having taken up the entire, pure majesty preceded by consciousness, it belongs to the all-pervasive Lord who abides in the primordial state and possesses the fourfold nature.

And thus, O high-minded one, the activities of the gods are indeed primarily based upon that foundation; for the splendors such as whiteness and so forth, as well as the [qualities] beginning with glory (śrī),
along with the marks, the manifestations of power, and the weapons, are merely the seed itself.
The sixfold group beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*), all the powers (*śakti*) mentioned therein,
the eightfold group beginning with atomization (*aṇimā*), as well as the emergence of maintenance, creation, and dissolution—
this power belonging to the fourfold Self is designated as "the Sovereign" (*aiśvarī*).
Just as a great spark of light, having abandoned the mass of the sun's rays,
fills its entire range of perception without its own cause,
so too does that Supreme Lord, by virtue of His sovereignty and perfection.
Setting aside the fourfold branch of forms beginning with Vāsudeva,
he remains as the lord of the Vaibhava host,
characterized by origination, maintenance, dissolution, enjoyment, and liberation.
Impelling with his intellect this supreme five-spoked wheel,
he— remaining in his own station— should be remembered by means of his own seed-syllable, which is pure in nature;
[he should contemplate] that entire sphere of his limbs from the head down to the feet.
It should be visualized as adorned with seed-syllables of the nature of splendor, like jewels;
by their being uttered in succession, as before, with a flood of nectar,
worship bestows the state of the Supreme Lord in no time at all.
In this manner, the Supreme Lord exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all future beings, having assumed a partless form;
that Blessed One, though his desires are fulfilled, acts by virtue of his own inherent activity.
Relying upon his own power, he once again, in the form of Padmanābha, [appeared] within a lotus composed of the four elements—
earth, water, fire, and air— with its root, stalk, and petals,
inside the single ocean of the sky.
In the mind, upon the couch of Ananta, the all-pervading Lord, whose body is divine awakening,
lies reclining at ease like the sun with its thousandfold radiance;
then, within the illusory lotus of his navel, which possesses the luster of various jewels.
But Pradyumna, by his own power, [bore] the Vidyā embodied in her full capacity,
surrounded by all the personified forms such as the banners and others who were devoted to her;
such was the manifestation of the Lord, the Self of Īśvara, whose activity is infinite.
One should meditate upon that form which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, which is peaceful, manifest,
and majestic; established as before in the state of the fourth (turya) within the sky of the heart-lotus,
illuminating the ten directions and adorned with various limbs and members.
One should meditate upon the gentle Lord, who is sixteen years of age, whose eyes are like lotus petals,
who holds the wheel of the stellar sphere (bhacakra) and likewise possesses a body [marked by] the mace (gadā),
and who firmly wields the spear known as the Foundation (ādhāra).
He who stands as the pillar within this temple of the universe,

characterized by the distinct natures of earth, water, fire, air, and ether— thus has been proclaimed the description of the primary elements, beginning with the former and ending with the fixed point (dhruva).
Now, ascertain the meditation as it truly is, extending down to the abodes of Pātāla, for Śeṣa and all the others who remain;
O Lord of the World, you alone [manifest] through your powers such as Svarūpa and the rest.
Listen now to the conceited form of that Lord of All, who, though infinite even in his manifold manifestations, assumes this out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees:
resembling the snowy mountain, with a face like the full moon.
He was indeed joined by a multitude of hoods adorned with his own jewels,
and he bore a plow and a discus with his two right hands,
while with his two left hands he held a conch shell and a mace.
One should meditate upon Him who is eternally present, the power of Śeṣa, the omniscient and infallible;
for those performers of ritual action whose minds are turned inward, He fulfills their desires. Furthermore, the Lord of Power (Śaktīśa), whose eyes resemble a lotus, should also be contemplated.
Assuming a form at will, gentle and with a smiling countenance,
he pressed down upon the earth with his two feet and both hands for the sake of manifesting fruits and other offerings out of compassion for his devotees. (24.201)
Possessing a splendor in accordance with the age, he has four faces and four arms;
from his own form, which holds a discus and a mace in its hands, he emerges marked by a lotus.
With that lotus, radiant as the moon, he brings relief to all suffering.
He reveals the knowledge consisting of various mantras to those of pure soul,
by means of Kambū, the Lord of Speech, who is the very embodiment of sound; and likewise,
by means of the two, the mace and the discus, which await his command.
Impelled by him, [the Lord] swiftly slays the one who causes distress to the virtuous with his Man-Lion (Nārasiṃha) face; he, the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence,
nourishes all beings with his Boar (Vārāha) form, which is of the nature of nectar.
One effects withdrawal by means of the tawny [fire] situated in the west;
indeed, for those devoted to and endowed with faith, it occurs simply upon being remembered— at all times—
within the center of the heart, in the sky, on the earth, in the midst of fire, or within water.
Out of compassion for the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas,
he himself manifests in a fourfold form according to the nature of the four classes;
indeed, he appears with bodies identical to his own, marked by the conch and the lotus.
But [the mantra] should be joined with the embodied [deities] such as Halāhala and others, though without faces;
it may consist of syllables that correspond in color, whether they are equal or unequal,
provided they follow one another exactly as previously specified and not otherwise.
Madhusūdana, who possesses the splendor of the sun at the time of universal dissolution, should be meditated upon;
he has eight arms, is vast in form, is marked with the sign of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice,
and likewise holds a conch and a discus, as well as an arrow and a bow.
The two hands of the Lord, placed upon the pedestal of the ears for the sake of engagement with and withdrawal from the embodied forms of *rajas* and *tamas*, should be meditated upon;
O Blessed One, [he should be visualized as] the presiding deity of knowledge (*vidyādhideva*), four-faced and four-armed.
One should then meditate upon him with a long beard, wearing matted locks, a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary;
possessing the luster of a full-blown red lotus, marked by white lotuses held in his hands,
and emitting from his mouths the Ṛgveda and other scriptures.

One should meditate upon that Kapila, the treasury of splendors, who has the luster of smokeless embers, who holds a conch, a lotus, and a rosary, whose glory is the radiance of full-blown red flowers, who possesses the sacred thread of the deities and the inner self, and who holds the gesture of fearlessness in his hand.
That God who is the Lord of all within, established as the witness,
sustains objects through His own power like a crystal stone,
for the sake of His devotees transformed by ignorance to attain the state of Reality.

Therefore, one should meditate upon the Lord of the World, whose beginning is the forest [of creation], who exists externally in a grosser form, yet dwells within heaven and earth as the Universal Form (viśvarūpa),
possessing many faces, feet, eyes, and marked by manifold hands.
Although he possesses many faces and is adorned with many arms,
he is indeed endowed with thirty-three diverse divine faces and forty great arms exceeding four.
Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Dakṣa, Arka, Candra, and the Siddhas, as well as the Śruti—
these abide in the upper face of the Puruṣa.
[The lower faces consist of] Piśācas, Agni, Marut, Śaila, Dvīpa, Gandharva, and Vāri.
One should meditate upon the southern face of the All-pervading Lord with mouths situated facing upwards;
and one should meditate upon the western face with mouths directed toward the great clouds of the netherworld and the world-realm of the quarters, accompanied by the syllable *Tāra*.

One should meditate upon the auspicious faces above the boar-face, [consisting of] the Yakṣas, Antakas, Ambus, Nāgas, and so forth, along with the Vasus, Nakṣatras, and groups of cows (the seven Ṛṣis). Furthermore,
there is the great group of ten mantras of one's own fourfold nature beginning with Padma.
For that fourfold set of emblems, beginning with gold, is raised high;
likewise in the world, there is the eightfold scripture, a book, a rosary,
a golden ladle, a water-pot, the gesture of fearlessness, and the granting of boons.
Then there was a seat of darbha grass and deerskin, a most beautiful umbrella, and a white fly-whisk;
also the *sruva* and *sruva* ladles, two water-pots, and an altar provided with fire.
There were the full orbs of the moon and the sun, and the lord of serpents as a jeweled mirror.
A divine garland of flowers, a fan, and likewise a creeper with all its leaves—
these should be visualized upon the arms of the Lord in their respective positions,
following the stated sequence so that no transposition occurs.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the World within the lotus of the heart and other loci, illuminating this entire universe with various kinds of radiance arising from his body;
then, one should meditate upon oneself as having the form of a swan, the enjoyer of the sacrifice of knowledge.

One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord as a physical form consisting of fire and moon, possessing a luster as smooth as jasmine or the moon, with a golden beak and a massive body; a form that dispels passion and darkness and is composed of pure goodness, observing both merit and demerit. (24.232–24.233)
It was adorned with a pair of wings extending to the south and north;
though situated outside, it appeared as if standing in water, resembling a mountain of gold.
Having meditated, one should worship Acyuta in the form of a swan according to the prescribed rule.

One [form] consists of external substances, while the other is characterized by the single common feature [of the mind]. This has been correctly described; for those who desire it, it first leads to heaven.
Within the sacrificial altar, he who is indeed one alone,

consisting of the nature of austerity, sacrifice, recitation, and meditation, is the great sacrifice itself; for by its completion, he eternally bestows liberation upon those who perform the sacrifice.
One should meditate upon that Lord of Sacrifice, Brahman, Vāsudeva, the unborn Hari,
who has assumed the form of a boar, possessing a luster like the Añjana mountain,
whose feet are marked by the limbs of sacrifice, and whose tusks are the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti).
The body— Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar— is a single mind whose essence is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
It swiftly washes away the mire of ignorance for those who have sought refuge,
using the physician’s eternal and stainless boat-paddle.
And for the sake of bringing peace to the existence of living beings who are permeated by latent impressions (vāsanā),
