the Blessed One— whose form consists of the six perfections in their fullness and who possesses great majesty—
took a handful [of water] from his own most tranquil Brahman-reality.
And by his own splendor, he performs a sprinkling upon those consumed by defects.
In the rite of external propitiation, that unborn one appears in a gross form,
like a mountain of smokeless embers fanned by the wind.
In that same manner, one should meditate upon the greatly radiant horse-faced one,
marked by the absence of a mane, standing with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, his eyes like molten gold,
and drawing up as fuel for the waters the moisture arising from the three worlds with the tip of his snout.
Having completely reduced that to ashes while blowing from his mouth,
[he spoke of] the universal, stainless, beginningless and endless, all-pervading Dharma—
which is difficult to attain for those who are awakened without a mind of grace toward it.
Hear now of its grosser form, which is supreme for attaining that [subtle state]:
resembling the snowy mountain (Himālaya), with a gentle face and four arms,
it bears the objects of desire and wealth under the guise of a conch and a lotus.
One should then meditate on him whose hand holds a boon-granting gesture and contains a white rosary, who restrains those standing on the path of the virtuous with his intellect,
and for whom the entire collection of speech is an imperishable reality.
One should meditate upon the Lord Vāgīśvara, who is the nature of consciousness abiding as power (*śakti*), possessed of immeasurable luster, with the face of an excellent horse,
resembling the sun in brilliance, and adorned with many arms. (24.250)
A lotus, a rosary, an altar adorned with the three sacred fires,
the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles filled with clarified butter, a seat together with the *soma* vessel,
darbha grass, a deerskin, and girdles— these six are likewise present on the left side.
One should visualize in his left hands a book and a conch shell;
in one hand, a staff, a water-pot, and a ladle—these three together;
and in the fifth, a vessel filled with sacrificial offerings consisting of both cultivated and wild grains.
With scales, roots, fruits, and vessels, along with sacrificial materials and ritual fees (dakṣiṇā),
and equipped with all the requisites for the stages of life (āśrama),
he should meditate upon him [Viṣṇu] on his sixth arm, surrounded by the personified Ṛgveda and the other Vedas.
Together with the Vedāṅgas, the Upavedas, the Saṃskāras, and the Samakhās,
within the support of the earth of transformations, yet in the absence [of duality] within the ocean of qualities—
having first made the fourfold [mind] permeated by its own power.

One should meditate upon the omniscient Lord, who dwells within primordial nature (prakṛti) by means of the Puruṣa-self; he who possesses the luster of refined gold, reclines upon the couch of the serpent-king,
and is surrounded by his embodied forms such as the Discus (Cakra) and others— this deity known as Arṇavaśāyin.
Being massaged by Lakṣmī, yet overcome by sleep,
being fanned with affection and indeed sung to by the Vidyās—
the Lord, whose self is the tortoise, should then be meditated upon as having the form of a tortoise, O wielder of the plow.
The eternal one, possessing the luster of molten gold, whose abode is the water of his own power,
has two pairs of feet consisting of the group of kalās beginning with Śakti.
Rich in the arts of peace and the rest, emitting the three Vedas,
resembling an *atasī* flower in hue, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
with the implements of sacrifice as his limbs, he is capable of lifting up those who have sunk [in the ocean].
Supported by the manifestation of its own power, with rays of will, knowledge, and action, and constantly arising with waves of sparks consisting of various specific cognitions—
[it stands] tearing asunder the dense and unabated delusion residing within the heart.
One should meditate upon that unborn Supreme Lord, the man-lion (Nṛkesarin), who is beyond hunger and beyond description, possessing the luster of molten gold,
and enveloped by sparks of blazing fire arising from his own body.
Holding the discus and the conch, most terrifying in his Brahma-form,
with both hands illuminated by the rows of rays from his virtuous palms, he perfectly restrains living beings with his wisdom, bestowing supreme fearlessness.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, who resembles a cloud filled with nectar, who brought down the nectar,
who wears yellow garments, has one face and four arms,
places his hand upon the slope of his hips, and is adorned with the conch and the discus.
Flowing from the center toward the south, bearing the form of a mountain,
it is permeated by pure knowledge and destroys the fear arising from karma.
He who, out of affection for his devotees, correctly instructs them through his own wisdom;
he who was manifested after churning the ocean of milk with his illusory power (māyā);
he who is the nectar that is the antidote to hunger, thirst, and other ailments, and is free from all disease.
In this way, one should meditate upon that which is imperishable, situated in the midst of the ocean called illusion—
the immortal Self, beyond comparison, by means of the practice of destroying the day [of worldly activity].
One should contemplate the God of gods, the Lord of Śrī, who shines like the interior of a lotus.
Offering his two hands— adorned with the abode of Lakṣmī (the lotus) and the weapon of Śiva (the trident)—
as if in sport during the marriage of the Goddess,
he manifested the beginninglessness of the Self together with primordial nature.
This primordial nature (prakṛti) is permeated by my rays, and I am the source of that nature;
for I am its substratum within this form, and by relying upon me,
one easily crosses the difficult-to-traverse ocean of the qualities (guṇas).
Devoted to manifest meditation, they cross over in no time at all—
[seeing] the god whose eyes were unsteady with intoxication and who had reached the bloom of youth,
shining like a full-blown red lotus, yet not abandoning his own mindfulness.
One should meditate upon him who causes wonder in the three worlds, who bears a lovely form,
and who is resplendent with a face full of the nectar of bliss, possessing the luster of the moon, and adorned by a vessel in the shape of a jar held in his hand.
He was slaying the enemy of the gods with the arrows of his playful side-glances and words;
his hand held a mango creeper swarming with a multitude of bees.
He was the extremely terrifying one known by the name Rāhu, whose very self was designated as the embodiment of a digit (of the moon).
Indeed, he incessantly devours [the world] through his forms of the manifest and the unmanifest—
his form consisting of Agni and Soma, which is beneficial for ritual actions;
existing internally in the form of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and externally as the nature of the moon and the sun.
Established as the overseer in that victory over those whose souls delight in truth and meditation,
he should clearly contemplate that [deity] externally through a state of motionless awareness—
one who has the luster of the color of a dark blue cloud and eyes like lotus petals. (24.282)
Having the form of the midday sun, with twelve spokes radiating forth,
he playfully holds a heavy mace with his left hand resting upon the slope of his hip, while it lies settled upon the surface of the earth.
And that rim of the wheel of time called ignorance, which is difficult to restrain,
shakes off the body by relying upon the power of the *sāmāyīya* [state] and through the force of darkness (*tāmasa*) regarding recitation, sacrifice, ritual acts, and the like. (24.285)
One should meditate upon the Lord, who has the luster of a royal sapphire, who obstructs the expansion of that [demon],
who blazes with rays of higher knowledge, whose throne is the Garuda of pure being,
whose self consists of various forms of weapons, and who is adorned with the arms of true wisdom.
In his six right hands, he holds a discus, a sword, a mace, an arrow, a goad, and a spear; and in his left arms, a trident, a bow, a large bow, a club, a terrible mallet, and a shield.
O Lord, he who resembles a ripe mango fruit and has surpassed the *pārijāta* tree should be remembered;
for the Lord of Gods, whose deeds are unimpeded and whose prowess over beings is manifold,
[is the refuge] even for embodied beings who have attained devotion through continuous practice.
That which is firmly rooted in the ground of awakening, yet is impermanent and full of attachment;
though it has the form of a banyan tree, it is characterized by the bondage of ignorance.
This vast tree of karma is covered with the fruits of delusion and illusion.

For the sake of accomplishing their uprooting, that Lord of the World always remains present, out of compassion, having entered those people to be favored merely by his presence. Having become one whose self is discernment, he bears the outspread arms of knowledge.
Bearing the power of stability in sovereignty, dharma, dispassion, and tranquility,

and having taken up the flood of weapons consisting of the *saṃyamas* as well as the multitude of weapons that are the *niyamas*, he conquered the host of enemies that are the senses— he who indeed inflicts the penalty upon those who act with fault.
One should meditate upon that form of his which is victorious over the gods, possessing twelve arms,
wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial ornaments,
four-faced, with beautiful eyes, and with his beloved placed upon his left lap. (24.295–24.296)
In his six right hands, the Lord holds a sword, a discus, a mace, an arrow, a pestle, and an excellent tree; and in his left hands, he holds a conch, a goad, a bow,
an umbrella, and a serpent-noose.
The goddess was embraced by his left arm, which bore a lotus; while she,
her hand resting upon his shoulder, fanned him with a white yak-tail whisk out of modesty, her mind constantly fixed upon him.
The Lord of the World, large-eyed and saluted by all the gods,
seated upon an excellent lion-throne with eyes opened in meditation,
sitting in the lotus posture with a radiance like the interior of a lotus.
One should then meditate upon the one named Datta, whose intellect is permeated with compassion, who is marked by hands holding a conch and a lotus,
who demonstrates the three paths of knowledge, dispassion, and the true Dharma,
and who is the embodiment of gnosis, free from all taints.
These [beings] were in the minds of the gods, whose souls were absorbed in meditative concentration,
who had slightly attained the flavor [of liberation], and who followed the path of Brahman;
they illuminated the true path by means of their own mass of radiance.
Together with the mind and the vital airs, he effects the cessation of rebirth;
likewise, [he is the source] of the Vedas, the scriptures, and their ritual applications,
as well as of the social classes, the stages of life, and their respective conducts.
For he is indeed the protector of the social classes and the stages of life;
even while standing within the single ocean of the mind, he should remain mindful of that which is situated above the unmoving tree of the intellect,
though it be rich with the creepers of verbal expression.
Dark as a mountain in the rainy season and blazing with splendor like fire,
he was the destroyer of the multitude of obstacles and the mass of sleep and indolence;
appearing in the form of an exalted twice-born, he possessed the likeness of a blooming lotus.
He alone should be meditated upon as having two arms, holding a staff and a rosary of darbha grass;
the all-pervading Lord, who has conquered ignorance with the moonlight of his teeth, reclining upon a bed of *nyagrodha* wood,
seated slightly supine, possessing two arms, and appearing in the form of an infant.
In this very way, with his weapons cast aside and established in the savor of peaceful sleep,
yet not abandoning his essential nature through the power of yogic illusion,
he both exhaled and inhaled with a pair of breaths.
Indeed, everything up to the realm of Brahmā is dominated by karma;
it exists in an impersonal form, with its constituent parts concealed.
Then, one should meditate upon the central observer situated in the midst of the waters of one's own *māyā*.
One should meditate upon the single Brahman, adorned by the multitude of qualities such as knowledge which serve as its wings, emerging from itself and radiating forth, shining with a single horn,
even at the time of the dissolution of the aeon.
Then the Blessed One, whose nature is like that of a noble fish, with eyes unblinking and a body as stainless as a pearl, beheld the vast earth spread out, filled with the hosts of Prajāpatis.
He who, out of compassion for the wise who are perpetually afraid of worldly existence,
dwells within their hearts by means of the rod of self-restraint— resembling ten thousand suns and having conquered the terrible power of ignorance along with the host of enemies that are the senses.
He quickly restrains himself for the sake of true bliss, rejoicing in the Brahman;
he should meditate upon Him alone—the short-limbed one, peaceful, with eyes like lotus petals, who has entered within the worlds and is adorned with matted hair and bark garments. (24.318)
In his left hand he holds a parasol, and elsewhere a bamboo staff.
Having stepped upon the splendors of the waking sun, the moon, and fire,
the Lord Ananta stands, known as the Fourth (turya), bearing the manifestation of consciousness.
Impelling from his own station the light of immortality—
the power that generates delight— for those performers of action whose souls are purified,
he meditated upon that very one who possesses the luster of a green gem and fills the three worlds.
Adorned with a multitude of arms equipped with various seals and weapons,
he bore the enemy-destroyer [Viṣṇu] with his staff-like leg extended through the sky,
as well as the celestial river Gaṅgā together with the Vaijayantī banner for the gods seeking victory.
A sword, a discus, a mace, a staff, an arrow, a goad, a hammer, a spear,
an axe, and the king of mountains— these ten are in his right arms;
[and] a conch, a javelin, a bow, a noose, a trident, and a tree.
A vajra, a razor, a plough, and a great pestle—
these ten, along with other mudrās, are to be meditated upon in the left hands;
they are characterized by fear, wonder, the heart, the braid of hair, and the seizing of the ear.

One should meditate upon the five mudrās of the All-pervading Lord, all of which are located on the five hands: the one called Varā (the Boon), the one named Bhūti (Prosperity), the one joined with Abhaya (Fearlessness), and the Gopanī (Secret) mudrā; these one should visualize on the right hands, numbering as many as those [five].
He by whom the thread of the world was spun together with the [five] senses, that one of immeasurable self,
who consists of the nature of the six qualities and is devoid of the previously mentioned forms— he indeed should be remembered as fourfold, free from marks and weapons.

Always protecting [the self], one should first perform the fourfold recitation (*japa*), ending with yoga-practice and austerity; this bestows true prosperity and liberation. Whether as a human being or one devoted to Kṛṣṇa, one may practice these either separately or together, according to one's desire.
There he saw a man with the luster of coral, his eyes half-open,
whose inner being was absorbed and whose mind was fixed solely on the Śabdabrahman;
he was softly reciting an imperceptible mantra characterized by the syllable *yadom*.
Adorned with a crystal rosary held in his hand,
counting the beads of the rosary with his left hand,
he should then meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa, white as a water-lily.
With his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, peaceful, and with his mind fixed upon the lotus of his heart.
One should meditate upon Hari, who is golden-hued, holding a water-pot in his hand, uniting his own self with the supreme, imperishable state, seated upon a mat,
and demonstrating the ritual section of the Vedas. 24.335
Constantly reciting the scripture preceded by the Pañcarātra,
[they saw] Kṛṣṇa, dark as a blue lotus, with arms raised, wearing matted hair,
standing on one foot and drawing in the wind.
One should contemplate him teaching the one-night, three-night, six-night, and twelve-night fasts, as well as the *atikṛcchra* penances, and the fortnightly and monthly fasts;
all of them wearing black antelope skins as upper garments and clad in saffron robes. (24.338)
All of them bore the marks of Brahman; all were devoted to Brahman.
Having transcended primary ritual actions for the sake of inspiring the virtuous, they all remained devoted to their supreme goal, acting in accordance with the times.

One should meditate upon that very same two-armed Lord, radiant as the rising sun, who, by means of his unimpeded power known as the "axe," cuts away the roots of bondage— the trees of karma— of those engaged in action. (24.341)
Clad in the skin of a black antelope, marked by a fine axe in his hand,
with ten sense-organs for faces, he is the terrible night-stalker of the mind;
he brings to peace that [mind] of yogis through a net of arrows of discernment.
He alone is the Supreme, the Soul of the Universe, possessing the luster of a water-laden cloud;
his eyes are like red lotuses, and he is marked by hands holding a bow and arrows.
He is indeed the Veda of Speech, the Maṇḍala, characterized by the splendor of his own essential nature.

One divides that which arises from oneself into three parts, perceiving the former as it sequentially emerges in the locations of the heart, the wind, and the awakening. That Blessed One, who has the luster of an *atasī* flower, is also to be remembered.
Carrying in his left hand the book containing the meaning of all the scriptures, and with his right hand pointing out the meaning of the scriptures exactly as it stands,
he did so for the sake of generating tirelessness among those who distinguish according to the divisions of the ages.
But he, the knower of the three times, divided that single Veda into four parts for those devoted to the duty of giving, for those who perform sacrifices and follow the path of ritual worship,
for those intent on austerity and sacred study, and for those seeking liberation from rebirth.
And for the sake of protection and to manifest their knowledge of fitness,
the Lord of the World arises from the forest of their heart-lotuses;
having seized the horse of the mind and taken up the weapons of his own qualities.

Surely he swiftly uproots the web of latent impressions (*vāsanājāla*) arising from hundreds of previous births, which pertains to the realm of sense-objects, for the sake of attaining pure consciousness (*śuddhavijñāna*). One should meditate upon that [deity] mounted on a noble horse, his body enveloped in armor.
His forehead was adorned with a white turban, and he wore matted locks that were not overly long;
he possessed the luster of molten gold and stood between two quivers,
his hands busily holding an arrow and a bow, while wielding a sword, a spear, and an axe.
Indeed, he was protecting the performance of sacrifices, Vedic study, charity, and other such acts;
he was bringing peace to those of low caste who were devoted to unrighteousness;
he was the all-pervading Lord, the reality that is the refuge of all principles and composed of all powers.

Manifesting the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses; it should be meditated upon as situated below, resting upon the couch of Ananta, with the brilliance of the fire at the end of an aeon. 24.356
Endowed with rows of blazing flames and illuminated by the rays of fire,
he was surrounded by a multitude of personified weapons beginning with the discus;
Lakṣmī stood at the region of the feet of the Lord, positioned to his right.
Sleep resides in the region of the crown of the head, while nourishment is situated to its left.
This has been stated in brief as the meditation on the principal deity,
by knowing which birth, death, old age, and disease are brought to an end.
Even those whose identity is clearly manifested throughout the three worlds by means of weapons, garments, and banners,
bear a multitude of marks upon the soles of their feet,
on a decorative plaque on their foreheads, on their backs, and on the palms of both hands.

Even for a transmigrating being who is by nature a Vaiṣṇava, the mark of Acyuta does not leave the two hairs on the head for the sake of performing ritual acts; how much less so for one whose form is that of the Vibhava [incarnation]?
Regarding what was previously stated by me— that all possess the freedom of their own movement—
[it is seen that] the visible world, characterized by large and small feet, arms, colors, faces, and middles, exists everywhere and at all times in both singular and manifold numbers.
But one should not effect a change of form; rather, the instrument is the capacity for assuming any form at will.
For within this temple of the universe, during the times of the maintenance, withdrawal, and creation of the gods, each possesses its own distinct function. (24.365)
Even though this rule is thus established, nevertheless, by the power of the Blessed One,
that which is situated upon the lotus-petal ground from the assembly of the fourfold self,
and likewise from among the gods of manifestation, has eyes like lotus petals.
But the one whose essence is power, for the sake of bestowing grace upon those of purified soul,
assumes a form arising from many divisions while stationed upon his excellent vehicle;
by the recollection, meditation, and worship of which, a person [attains liberation] before long.
One attains whatever is desired by the mind; listen as I declare that to you.
Satya, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya are the lords of birds.
These are the fifteenfold modifications of the fivefold vital breath (prāṇa).
He whose entire body is human in form, yet extends as far as the range of his feet,
who has two arms, is white as snow, and is the true deity of the vital breaths; he is Suparṇa, radiant like a ruby, stainless, and with eyes of gold.
Garuḍa was golden-hued, with curved eyebrows and reddish eyes;
Tārkṣya indeed had squinting eyes and resembled a rain-cloud;
Dravatkanakanetra was the fifth, having a variegated luster.
The four-armed ones, Suparṇa and the others, are of gentle form and composed;
all have feet like those of birds and are adorned with circles of feathers.
They have pendulous bellies, well-nourished limbs, and are decorated with earrings and other ornaments.
With curved eyebrows and well-rounded eyes, they have crooked snouts and smiling faces;
established through their lordship over the vital winds such as the *apāna*,
they are of great strength and massive bodies, and among them, the fifth has a red snout.

The left hand of the first [deity] rests below the foot that is to be placed; the right hand is illuminated by a very white rosary. In this very manner, the two arms of the golden one are to be understood.
At the navel, the left [hand] is supreme and upturned with wonder;

the right [hand], facing upward and filled with clusters of flowers—know these two to be the form of Garuḍa in the region of the heart, in the shape of a joined palms gesture (añjali). || 24.378–24.379 ||
In that very place, the two hands of the fourth [deity] are in the *sampuṭa* (joined) gesture;
in the right is an amṛta-pitcher, while in the left is a venomous serpent.
His [the first deity’s] leaves are double, and for the remaining three, they are equal to those of the first two.
If indeed the right hand is pressed down by the foot to be placed upon it,
then the movement of the rosary is prescribed on the left;
[this applies] when both palms of the hand are situated beneath the foot to be placed.
Know that vehicle, which has cast off its reins, to be composed of the Blessed One;
intent on bestowing grace, he remains seated upon a lotus throne formed by the wings of birds,
endowed with his own splendor and innate power, accompanied by the foremost of the Asuras.
Know that he who is endowed with splendor, seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or any other,
with the configuration of his limbs clearly manifest, is Garuḍāsana;
he is the son of Bhadra, born from the same womb as the one who moves with speed and is hidden.
Because he travels with his own head due to the descent of his vigor,
and because he meditates with affection for the sake of the welfare of the worlds between [the cosmic eggs], even for those who contemplate him;
and for the purpose of being seen directly, he is remembered as having Garuḍa as his vehicle.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining success, one should meditate upon the Blessed Viṣṇu, who assumes such a form; whether he is seated or standing,
having withdrawn his left foot, he may be situated upon a lotus or perched upon a bird.

The left [channel] is that which destroys the fruits of one's desires when another thought arises; O Acyuta, thus it is remembered as being until the knees for those whose minds are undistracted. For those who meditate, the right [channel] shall lead to all perfections until final liberation.
It is traditionally held that everything remains perfectly upright for those who seek [the truth].
However, even for one seated upon a throne fashioned from lotus pedestals and marked with *svastikas*, this occurs only when they are without a vehicle. (24.390–24.391)
And here, by virtue of his mastery of yoga, the Lord of Birds assumes a multitude of faces and a multitude of arms, equipped with the best of weapons and the lords of serpents,
either by the power of the All-pervading One’s command or for the sake of the All-pervading One’s own satisfaction.
For the sake of the world’s victory and for the peace of those seeking refuge,
the Hero indeed wanders alone, his movement unimpeded, through various other worlds in diverse forms. (24.393–24.394)
Now, learn from me as I speak of the nature of Śaktīśa as he is currently mounted [upon that], which is indeed divided into many varieties:
he who is ever tranquil, yet restrains those subject to existence with his right hand.
And with his left hand, he bears a conch shell possessing the characteristics previously described.
This is the form of the two-armed Śaktīśa alone;
furthermore, by means of this very form, he manifests in six ways.
That which is together with the group of consorts, or separately as the first one alone,
joined with Lakṣmī as before— that is the one form of the Lord.
Then, that which stands between Śrī and Puṣṭi is proclaimed as the second.
Know that the supreme [wheel] is surrounded by a group of four beginning with Śrī and ending with Māyā;
now understand the fourth to be surrounded by a group of six beginning with Śuddhi;
and the fifth by a group of eight beginning with Śrī and ending with Puṣṭi.
Know that the sixth [tattva] is endowed with a group of twelve beginning with Lakṣmī:
Śrī, Vimalā, Kīrti, Jayā, Lakṣmī, Halāyudhā,
and fourthly, Bhagavan-māyā, which binds this entire universe.
Purity is stainless and eternal, O unconquered one, whose power of knowledge is supreme.
Nature (prakṛti) is beautiful; this is called the "group of six" (ṣaṭka), which bestows all accomplishments.
She is the treasury of the word "Lakṣmī," the granter of all desires, and the increaser of joy.
That which is proclaimed as the group of eight goddesses— Yaśaskarī, Śāntidā, Tuṣṭidā, and Puṣṭidā—
within the yoga of the twelvefold majesty,
should be understood as beginning with Lakṣmī and ending with [Puṣṭi] in this division of the Pārameśvara [Tantra].
Furthermore, the sevenfold classification of the four-armed [form] should be understood in this way:
however, with the two left hands, he bestows upon this world eternal peace through the primordial [state], [holding] the conch and the discus. (24.405–24.406)
With the second [hand], one should indeed brandish a mace in the counter-clockwise direction;
furthermore, with the four hands according to the previously mentioned sequence,
one should hold the four [implements] beginning with the lotus, each in its respective position.
That form of yours which is twelvefold and entirely devoid of power,
O lotus-eyed one— that same twelvefold [form] exists again together with two powers, increased by one, as sixfold. (24.408–409)
Thus, the Lord exists in many ways with a four-armed body alone,
or again in seven ways with six arms and so forth, or with an even greater number of arms; understand how he is thus situated in manifold forms.
He has six arms, eight arms, ten, twelve, fourteen,
sixteen, and likewise eighteen adorned hands;
he is the primordial one among all, and as before, his division is sevenfold.
Listen to me as it truly is, marked by the arrangement of his weapons:
with six arms, he holds in his right hands a sword, a lotus, and a mace;
and in his left hands, a bow with an arrow, a conch, and three supreme missiles.
He has eight arms; with his right hands he holds a mace, a club, a discus, and a sword, while with his left hands he holds a conch, a goad, and a noose, as well as a bow with an arrow.
Furthermore, his right hands are equipped with a sword, arrows, a mace, a lotus, and a spear.
On his ten arms are the bow, conch, discus, sword, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
adorned with twelve arms, he holds in his six right hands the lotus,
his own sword, discus, arrow, mace, and goad.
He possesses fourteen arms; with his seven right hands he holds the conch, the noose, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the spear, the mace, and the bow;
while with his seven left hands he holds the conch, the mallet, the goad, the noose, the pestle, the hammer, and the plow.
He should bear a staff, a lotus, a vajra, a wheel, a sword, a spear, and an axe; with sixteen arms, his principal hands hold a mallet.
[The other hands hold] the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a lotus, a sword, a spear, a staff, an arrow, and a goad.
With your eight hands, you hold the conch, discus, mace, vajra, plow, and bow; and with your right hand, O Conqueror of All, you hold the boon-granting gesture,
as well as the lotus, sword, mace, vajra, discus, arrow, and goad.
Holding a staff in his right hands, the Lord, who possesses eighteen arms,
bears with his left arms these: the conch, the gesture of fearlessness, the plow, the spear, the mallet, the club, the bow, and the incomparable axe, as well as the noose.
He bears these very forms in their specific manifestations for the sake of pacifying the wicked and for the protection of the virtuous;
specifically,
by means of his two excellent faces alone, he displays immeasurable valor.

For the benefit of those who have withdrawn their vital energy, who are unable to endure [the world], whose souls are intent on the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), and who are afraid of the company of women and the like,
[this is taught] regarding the immortal portion within the house, which is the eternal sacrificial fee for the sake of spiritual luster (tejas).
The Lord, the lotus-eyed one, should indeed perform a reversal with his left and right faces for the sake of increase as well as for the sake of pacifying his splendor; by that means,
the Blessed One is truly both external and internal.
Having unified Agni and Soma, he abides with a common nature;
yet, having brought [the power] into manifestation above the head at the mouth of Vāgīśa,
he proceeds in manifold ways from the root upward through his five-faced body.
And for the sake of the self-realization of those meditators devoted to the Śabdabrahman,
and for the filling of all the worlds down to the netherworld (Pātāla),
he assumes various bodies and proceeds again one by one.
Relying on differentiated forms such as white and so forth,
and through his manifestation, he possesses the majesty of omniscience even without faces like those of Nṛsiṃha and others;
yet it is Aniruddha, in the form of Tārkṣya, who bears these various forms.
Having thus mounted Garuḍa, Pradyumna assumes that body;
and Saṅkarṣaṇa, having entered Suparṇa, likewise undergoes manifoldness.
The divine Satya, the soul of all, remaining as Marut, proceeds in many ways.
For the sake of pacifying the suffering of gods, siddhas, humans, and other beings,
those who are the innate castes of the four [classes] exist within the various forms [of the deity]. This applies both to Viṣṇu, whose first form has four arms, and to his other forms as well.
When there is equality in the possession of excellent marks, the two banners serve as the differentiators. By means of that banner called Tāla, which stands to the right (apasavya),
one attains a distinction of form at all times along with one's own body.

"Because, by the power of their respective functions, even the embodied forms [of the deities] possess hands bearing four lotuses and so forth; likewise, the peaceful forms, whether with or without bodies, are thus uplifted.
O lords of sages, such is the meditation upon the Lord in all his embodied forms.
O twice-born ones, the meditation for certain divine weapons has already been described; now I shall describe the meditation for the remaining weapons:
the ploughshare, resembling an evening cloud, with terrifying eyes.
One should meditate upon Nandaka, who possesses the limbs of forbearance, elevated shoulders, a body like a diamond, and is preeminent in strength; he is inlaid with rays of light and is dancing,
displaying a row of teeth that resembles the autumn sky.
Resembling the orb of the sun,
with a gentle form,
he incessantly and forcefully devours multitudes of missiles with his own mouth.
One should meditate upon Balamuṣṭi as a staff with a red body and red eyes,
an embodiment of wrath who bites his own lower lip with his teeth,
possessing the color of Indra’s bow and a terrifying form with an axe.
With eyes like molten gold, bearing matted locks of blazing flames,
holding a mallet with the brilliance of a hundred suns, he had broad shoulders and a large body;
gentle, wearing a mass of matted hair, his eyes resembled white lotuses.
The vajra, resembling a diamond-stone, stood marked with long claws;
its face was terrifying with fangs, and its eyes were blazing golden.
It bore a spear with the brilliance of lightning, possessing a mouth and eyes like extinguished fire.
O lords of sages, they repeatedly emit a deep and rumbling roar; however, everything else regarding their meditation is as previously described.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, the sequence of presiding deities for these [mantras] consists of medicinal herbs and the plough.
Nandaka is known as all the scriptures, and the shield is remembered as the earth.
Indeed, the staff should be understood as destiny, and detachment is remembered as the axe.
O lords of sages, the mallet is to be recognized as the ego.
The maṇḍala of consciousness is the vajra; samādhi is said to be the śakti.
Now hear in sequence the meditation upon the host of beautiful goddesses who have been described as belonging to the omnipresent Lord in his differentiated form—both common and uncommon.
Cintā has the luster of Indra’s bow; Lakṣmī has the radiance of a red lotus;
Puṣṭi is fair as gold; Kīrti is white as a water-lily;
Jayā resembles the brilliance of the sun; and Māyā is known to be like collyrium.
Śuddhi is like the kiṃśuka flower; Nirañjanā has the luster of a kunda flower; Bandhujīvā is eternally radiant; Jñānaśakti is white and red;
and Parājitā should be known as having the color of a full-blown blue lotus.

Sarasvatī is naturally white and yellow, with the luster of a red lotus; she is the perfection that grants all desires. She who has a radiance like a sapphire should be known as the one who increases joy, possessing a complexion like a mass of vermilion.
Yaśaskārī is the luster of milk, Śāntidā is radiant as coral; Tuṣṭi resembles snow, Dayā is like lapis lazuli, Nidrā is similar to a magnet, and Kṣamā has a yellowish-red radiance.
Radiance resembles a mirror; fortitude is as brilliant as yellow orpiment;
friendliness has the luster of the bandhūka flower; love is like red ochre;
and intelligence indeed has the hue of emerald—all these qualities are exceedingly joyful.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with various ornaments,
and endowed with celestial wreaths and attire, they gazed upon their own lord as he lay upon his bed. These were the four Śaktis belonging to the Lord who had gone to rest.
The previously mentioned [deities] situated in the eastern direction impel the Unborn there.
As for the triad located in the three directions, it is intent upon that conveyance;
where Śrī is one, there the arrangement of the Lord is placed in front.
Wherever there is one Śrī of the Lord, whether on the left or even on the right,
wherever there is the pair known as Śrī and Puṣṭi, there [the others] are to their right and left;
they are seated in the lotus posture with two wings.
One [hand] holds a lotus stalk, while another holds a jar of nectar.
The primordial body of the All-pervading One consists of fire and moon;
His two powers are likewise of such a nature, unmixed and possessing distinct characteristics.
The power of the enjoyer is known as Lakṣmī, while that called Puṣṭi is designated as the agent;
these two imperishable powers arose together with him who descended for the sake of enjoyment out of compassion for the worlds. (24.465)
For indeed, its transformation is manifested through diversity.
That which resides within the four directions as its petals consists of the four goddesses;
in their hands, there are respectively the spear, the axe, the weapon, and the goad.
A group of six [weapons] is situated within a network of filaments; among them, two are in the east and west, and two each are in the north and south. And upon their left hands [are placed]:
the conch, the discus, the mace, the plow, the bow, the sword Nandaka, and the white [spear].
Regarding that supreme group of eight beloved women situated within the petals, their first eight [attributes] on the left hands should be understood as follows:
the bilva fruit, the rosary, the garland, the mirror, and the cluster of flowers. (24.469–24.470)

O lotus-eyed one, the seat, the small bell, and the collection of weapons are to be known; the hand granting power, along with the one showing the gesture of fearlessness, belongs to the twelve [deities].
By means of their alternating arrangement, all [the goddesses] are marked by chowries.
Seated upon svastikas with their minds filled with inner joy,
O wielder of the plow (Balarāma), [they represent] this Saṃgha beginning with two and ending with twelve,
by means of colors beginning with white and by the reversal of their emblems.
When that [duality] has indeed been dispelled through the application of identical marks,
then— due to the hands being joined by the gestures of boon and fear, or even from their mere presence—
the multitude of various distinctions is to be understood as before.
What is the remainder? It is indeed the collection of the gods who provide the requisites for existence.
O Greatly Wise One, this is well known; however, as before, all the marks beginning with the lotus should be meditated upon on the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and so forth.
He who is always devoted to all beings through devotion, faith, and vows,
and who performs worship after meditating [upon them] with offerings preceded by physical contact,
shall before long attain his desired fruit, which is established in liberation.
Surrounded by an entourage ending with the crown and other weapons,
or else the desired form should be worshipped with devotion; or again, it may be characterized by its own meditative visualization, even if devoid of an entourage.
He surely ordains worship that brings his own state, joined with its fruit;
knowing this, the practitioner should perform worship according to his desire, with all enjoyments equal to his own power, he whose body is entirely pure. (24.480)
In the heart, on the altar, in an external image, in a temple, or in one's own home; in a shelter free from many distractions, devoid of smoke, fire, and the like,
beautiful and meditated upon as being free from contact with others.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Method for the Characteristics of Mudrās, Meditation on the Lord, and so forth," in the glorious *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Nārada said: Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and other such features.
Listen with an attentive mind, O bulls among sages!
(25.1) Just as the field was divided for the sake of accomplishing the *puramaṇḍala*,
so too, O great-minded one, from that divided field, [construct] squares.
Listen now to how the previously mentioned sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇyas) are to be prepared:
the fifth, beginning with the Brahmakarma, is situated in the eastern direction at the vital point;
one should make a mark there with a thread placed along the length of the *aṃśa* [unit]. 25.2
Between the two sections, one should fashion two marks shaped like half-moons; likewise,
below those, one should place two marks positioned horizontally and well-aligned with their respective southern and northern parts.
Just as there would be a unification of twelve parts from two rows,
so too the fourth [part] consisting of Brahma and Karma, its numerical measure being as before;
and its vital point (marman) situated on the wings is made into a single interval between vital points.
By means of those two, through the very thread already established, this is produced:
again, from the middle, that second action which proceeds upwards;
therefore, indeed, the third has become intermediate between the two sides of the fourth.
One should draw a circle with a thread placed at that *marman* as before.
Then, for the ritual of Brahmā, having made a thread from the sixth *marman* situated in the western direction and having extended it, [one should proceed]. || 25.7–25.8 ||
Up to the middle of the base of the circle, reaching the vicinity of the tip of the horn—

when two such lines have been drawn, the sacrificial altar (dhiṣṇya) shall take the shape of a conch shell. Its outer girdle (mekhalā) should be made with divisions equal in size and marked with signs.
Understand correctly, according to the previously mentioned rules for the vital points (*marmaga*), as follows:
With a cord twice as long [as the side], equal to nine moon-phases (*navacandrakalā*), one should make a mark in the eastern direction at the interval of four parts. (25.10–25.11)
From the center, at a distance of one-fourth of the diameter measured from the points of the *īśa* (northeast) and *vahni* (southeast),
one should mark two equal points. Then, from those [points],
one should mark two other points at the same distance, which serve as the marks for the [subsequent] markings.
One should cast two threads from the wings toward the southern and northern parts.
Having established seven vital points (marmas) according to the previously mentioned sequence,
they should be situated on both sides in the western portion of the life-thread (jīvasūtra).
Having marked two parts each, and like a half-circle for the other portion,
one should place a cord at the tips of those horns and stretch them out as far as the excavated area of the ground; from that base, it should be shaped like a banyan leaf.
Such is the auspicious womb (yoni) that arises for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Furthermore, within the womb, one should draw two semicircles using a cord measuring half a portion,
provided with two cords in the same manner.

The fourth part from the corner of the pit should be avoided; one should bury the remainder for the sake of the rim, or as previously stated, it should be equal to that. The vulva should be made one-quarter of the length and elevated at the back.
And [the lines] resembling the lips of an elephant touch the lip from the front.
Having extended [lines] from the front of the yoni for one-fourth of the anterior portion,
one should apply two threads connected to the eastern thread.
Beyond that, one should indeed perform the contraction from the top by means of those two [proportions] through multiplication;
the three girdles on the outside are formed by three rows of parts. || 25.20–25.21 ||
Having fashioned a square conch upon those three [levels],
the height and width of the conchs relative to the girdles [should be determined].
Regarding the four corners in the middle of the conchs among the girdles:
One should mark it with that wheel; now its characteristics are described.
O Great-minded One, one should first draw a circle in the center of the field for the purpose of digging, using a cord equal to one-fourth [of the side] fixed by the Brahma-line.

Equal to its outer portion, the field of spokes (*arākṣetra*) extends outward by two parts; its rim (*nemi*) is equal to one part on the outside. Beyond that, there is one square girdle (*mekhalā*) consisting of one part.
Then, having again surrounded the area of the spokes from the center with a single circle,
one should first lay down eight lines situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Thereafter, one should drop another set of eight lines within that [circle].
Then, O one of stainless eyes, having brought about their equality,
one should make a mark with the thread at the interval between the two sides of the counter-thread, which is restricted by the internal movement, extending from the navel to the limit of the rim.
One should measure half of one part within the interval of the circular rim;
between each pair of spokes, one should fashion a felly.
The hub should be wide and high, shaped like the back of a tortoise.
The rim should be made like a mirror, slightly depressed at its edge; everything else has been previously described. Now hear concerning the lotus-shaped [mandala]:
one should draw a circle outside the nave for the sake of the petals, in order to establish the filaments.
One should rotate the other half outside the field of the spokes;
having brought it to completion by this very method, one should fashion the circle of the rim and,
within it, eight lotus petals following the rotation of the spoke-line.
With a thread obstructed by the filaments and bees, one should mark the half-moon;
then, with two threads situated at the tips of its horns and extending outside the circumference, one should form the tips of the petals on the ground of the outer circle.
O Mahāmati, one should clearly effect the division of the continuous filaments from the base up to their tips, which are equal in height to the pericarp;
then, in the four corners of the conch-shaped [mandala], one should perform the remaining procedure as before.
One part is the *yoni*, and with four parts is the group of girdles (*mekhalā*).
The excavation is equal to the former [dimensions], but in the case of a circular [pit], the girdles are circular;
in the case of a square [pit], they are of that same shape—thus the five types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) have been described.
The time, the number of oblations, and the abundance of the sacrificial materials.
Having understood this, one should fashion [the ladles] starting from one cubit up to eight cubits.
Then, O twice-born ones, the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* are described.
First, the knower of mantras should fashion them according to the measure of his own forearm.
For the sake of accomplishing the divine ladle (*daivī-sruk*), [the wood] should be six finger-breadths wider than its thickness.
Then, the handle (*daṇḍa*) is said to be two parts in length and octagonal in shape; having made it one and a half finger-breadths in measurement, one should subtract the remainder.
At the base of the staff, one should fashion a beautiful lotus face,
O best of sages, so that the staff appears as if situated within its pericarp;
or alternatively, there may be three folds or a conch, positioned at the mouth of the staff.
Having carefully divided the portion at the tip into two equal parts,
the width of the portion at the front should gradually increase by two finger-breadths;
for the portion situated as a staff, it should be three finger-breadths wide all around.
Having given [the measurement], one should then fashion the circumference, making it low, self-contained, and well-characterized.
In its center, one should fashion a lotus, fully blossomed with upward-pointing petals.
Know that this vessel of clarified butter (ājyakośa) is like five or seven fruits.
The pericarp, together with its filaments, is indeed submerged in the center of the lotus.
Outside the eight-petaled lotus, there is a twelve-spoked wheel;
outside the lotus, a conch shell should be drawn in each of the four corners.
Then, O Sage, having divided both sides of the upper portion into three parts each, one auspicious mark (maṅgala) should be cleared away by means of one part,
while two [marks] should be cleared in the middle by means of two parts.
The middle [part] should be separated from the two mouth-fleshes by one finger-breadth.
Having first avoided a width equal to the ears,
one should then clear away the remainder, beginning from the region of the ears.
Following the sequence of the sūtra, it should be like the face of a boar;
then, from the lotus leaf up to the tip of the mouth,
O Sage, one should fashion the channel for the clarified butter with its dimensions neither exceeding nor falling short by even a single finger-breadth.
Just as clarified butter does not flow too quickly when the stride is slightly subtle,
so too should the Brahmin fashion a beautiful *sruva* ladle measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in length;
the wood should be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width and half of that in thickness.
From the measurement of its width, one should first make it circular with a thickness of two finger-breadths;
then, gradually making it a hollow depression, one should seal it with a spherical mold (golaka).
It should be adorned in the middle with a mark in the shape of a deer's footprint.
The neck, measuring three finger-breadths with a slight taper, shall be one-third of the width.
At both ends of its base, one should fashion a svastika two finger-breadths long;
the handle should be provided with various artistic designs or be smooth.
The practitioner should fashion the *sruva* ladle in this manner for the act of oblation;
thereafter, O twice-born ones, hear the means for preparing the *prāpaṇa* and other offerings:
rice, barley, beans, wheat, and millet.
These seven types of sesame are to be taken for the preparation of the *caru* when using cultivated varieties:
bamboo-seed, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, wild sesame, *gavīdhukā*, *karkaṭa*, and *kanaka*; these seven are to be known as those produced in the forest. (25.58–59)
Among these, the *śāli* rice varieties are the foremost; in their absence, others may be used.
These include the red *śāli*, the great *śāli*, the *kalama*, the fragrant *śāli*, the white *śāli*, the awned *śāli*, the golden-hued, and the *garbha-śāli*.
These ten types of *śāli* rice are known as tender and delicate. Furthermore, there are many internal subdivisions; seven varieties of mung beans (*mudga*) are enumerated:
black, golden, white, yellow, and large ones.
And these seven varieties with the luster of collyrium are declared to be internal divisions:
white, black, yellow, variegated, and the great sesame (mahātila). These five types of sesame seeds are proclaimed as those that should be accepted.
Bringing forth from the fields and from the divine [gardens], the farmers offered varieties such as *āli* and mung beans,
which were fit for the ritual worship of Hari and free from the eight defects beginning with *avapanna*.
One should first bring [the grain] into the threshing room for the purpose of threshing— a room smeared with cow dung and adorned with lime-wash and other materials—
after it has been purified with water mixed with *kuśa* grass and filtered through a hundred-holed strainer.
Having pronounced [the mantra] directed toward dry land, facing either east or north,

[he should perform the rite] surrounded on all sides by initiated and self-restrained Brahmins who bear the marks of the discus and other symbols, and who are well-bathed, using vessels made of iron, wood, stone, or clay.
Having set out mortars made of firm *khadira* wood and washed them,
they should pound [the grain] with pestles using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Having made the rice free of husks and debris by means of the hollows of winnowing baskets, [they should proceed].
They should first be pounded until they possess the luster of pearls;
they must be unbroken, not too small, and free from black spots. Likewise, they should be made into mung-bean-sized pieces, substantial, and free of husks.
In the absence of virtuous Brāhmaṇa women who have been initiated,

or of Śūdras who have been initiated, the act of threshing should be performed by temple-servant women (devadāsīs) in the temple for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial oblation and other rites. (25.72)
In the pure house of Vaiṣṇavas, or even in the house of those who have received initiation,
the preceptor should take rice grains that have been husked twice,
which are successively free from the red powder, the husks, and even insects.
However, those [grains] that are devoid of husks or stones, likewise free from living parts,
and devoid of ash or charcoal— even if they are unbroken, not light,
and [otherwise perfect]— if they have broken kernels, there will be disease; if they have chaff, there will be poverty.

With worms, there will be the loss of a son; with hair, the destruction of one's wife. Know that with stones there is death, and with lightning, fire, or water [the same]. With parts of living beings, diseases are declared; with ashes, strife is certain.
In battle, there is affliction by embers and fire from those that are broken, but defeat comes from those that are shattered;
furthermore, with small ones, there is exile. Therefore, one should avoid them.
Thus, all the equipment previously planned and approved [should be prepared].
Having gathered together with the instructors, the practitioners, and even the cooks,

the preceptor should go to the threshing house and, looking at the rice and other grains situated there, gaze upon them with his eyes alone, saying, "This is like the semen of Brahmā. || 25.79-25.80 ||
One should purify them as before by means of burning, moistening, and other such methods.
Even when vessels made of split bamboo or similar materials are impure, one should remove all that rice and so forth from them for the purpose of cooking. (25.81)
Skilled attendants,
having bathed well, dressed elegantly, and covered their faces with cloths,
should bring [the food] to the kitchen while auspicious sounds such as conchs and trumpets are played. || 25.82-25.83 ||
On the northern side of the door, in a place smeared with cow dung,
one should place those vessels in their proper order,
containing salt and other flavorful substances along with pieces of jujube as accompaniments.
One should place curd, milk, and ghee in the direction of the door;
one should also set down the implements for the fire-oblation (homa) in the south-western quarter.
Then, with water purified by a cloth, [one should sprinkle] using the four all-pervading mantras.
Having washed it four times, as is done with rice and other grains,
so that it is freed from fragments of stone, dehusked, and free of the red coating;
[the offering] is prepared using only rice grains of unripe paddy.
Sprinkled with cow’s milk and clarified butter, and provided with jaggery, sugar-candy, and fruit,
along with non-alkaline salt, this is called the oblation for the gods; that very same offering, when cooked with milk, clarified butter, and jaggery, becomes *paramānna*.
Cooked food sprinkled with ghee is called an oblation (*havis*) when other offerings are unavailable;
it should be prepared without pungent salt, and may include molasses, milk, and fruit.
This supreme oblation is to be accomplished for the sake of pacification during vows and sacrifices.
Milk-rice, rice with jaggery, rice with mung beans, plain rice,
rice with curd, rice with sesame seeds, rice from the night, and rice mixed with all [the above]—
these eight kinds are declared as the oblation approved for the God.
One should begin the cooking of the oblation by the method to be described hereafter:

having brought the fire for cooking the rice from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or from the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), one should place it upon the hearth while reciting the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) and the mantra "O Agni, seven are your... (*saptate agne*).
Having cast in the sacrificial wood fuel,
which is free from worms, insects, and the like, he kindles it with a fan using the mantra "jyotī rātri," and then [places] the copper vessels.
Then, having washed the earthen vessels with pure *tintriṇī* juice,
the knower of mantras should wash them with the twelve-syllable *vīryamantra*.
He should then anoint their interior with clarified butter using the *vyūhavidyā*.
One should pour rice into those [vessels] with the Gāyatrī preceded by Viṣṇu (Tad Viṣṇoḥ),
and again with the mantra "ambhasy apāre" recited with devotion;
one should fill them to the top with water so that there is rice in each vessel.
For a measure of rice exceeding one *taṇḍula*, there should be six *prastha*s of water.
Then, at the commencement of the rite, one should place those pots upon the hearth.
Having covered them with lids according to the sequence, using the *cakra* mantra, [one should proceed].
When it is time for cooking, having uncovered [the vessel] with the *vīrya* mantra,
one should gaze at its sound with the *netra* mantra; then, lifting the base of the ladle,
one should stir it four times and cover it again with the *cakra* mantra.
Once it is cooked, even the water should be drained away while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra; then,
having sprinkled it with melted cow-butter (gavya-havis),
one should place [the vessel] behind the support (ādhāra) with the mantra beginning "śucīṃ satkṛtayate."
O Lord, when the ground has been purified or strewn with rice grains,
one should thus deposit the prepared sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) with both hands,
and wash them externally with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Then, one should wrap [the vessel] with a pure cloth consecrated by that mantra; subsequently,
using churned ashes while reciting the names of Vāsudeva and the other [Vyūhas],
one should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks in the various directions with the fingers beginning with the index finger.

Then, having covered [the vessel] with garments that have been washed according to the prescribed rites— thus has the proper preparation of pure food been specifically described. I shall now describe the preparation of other foods, beginning with *paramānna*.
One-fourth part of rice should be added as the essence of mung beans to the milk-rice (pāyasa);
the amount of ghee prescribed is equal to that, and the milk should be four times that amount. Alternatively, coconut water may be used, which is said to be equal in measure to the milk.
One should prepare four times as much sugar-candy powder as rice, combined with the aforementioned mantra, according to the prescribed method, over plain boiled rice; then,
while reciting the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," one should sprinkle the food with cow's milk.
In its absence, coconut water should be employed;
it is called *abjāgoja*, and it serves as a substitute for cow’s milk when used in cooking.
When cooking rice with molasses (*gulānna*), one should omit milk and use sugarcane juice instead.
One should administer jaggery or sugar-candy according to the quantity of milk.
One should add the jaggery and other ingredients while reciting the mantra for adding milk.
In a dish of mung-bean porridge, one should properly incorporate rice and the essence of the mung beans.

Regarding pure food, it was previously stated that it should especially be saturated with ghee; it may consist of rice with curd, or rice with a portion of curd, or rice measured by half a portion of milk.

In *kṛsarā* rice, one should include plantains, breadfruit, mangoes, and the like, along with balls (*guḷa*) and sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), as well as powdered sugar. In *haridrānna*, there should be a *mudga* bean for every *āḍhaka* measure, and the fruit should consist of ground turmeric (*niśā*).
One should add a small amount of rice mixed with mung beans and combined with pure sugar-candy and other ingredients; it should be saturated with milk and clarified butter.
For the purpose of pacification, it should be mixed with milk, and for the purpose of nourishment, it should be mixed with jaggery.
For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), [an offering] made of mung beans and sesame; for attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), mixed with curd;

for the sake of affection (*prīti*), as well as for killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*), one should use *kṛsarā* rice; for paralyzing (*stambhana*), turmeric rice; and mixed rice serves for bewitching (*mohana*).
Plain, pure rice is common for journeys, hunting expeditions, and the like;
however, curd-rice served in vessels of gold or silver, mixed with the juices of long pepper, ginger, *likuca*, and *tintriṇī*, is especially recommended.
One should prepare [the medicine] with liquid substances derived from *jīraka* grown in *jīrṇa*;
those arising from the varieties of *rasa*, and that produced from two kinds of *panasa*.
[One should also use] those originating from the region of *cūta* which are not over-ripe due to the passage of time.
And those originating from the *bṛhatī*, the *urvāru*, the *vārtāka*, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa*; those arising from the *kāravallī* creeper and those originating from the *kārkoṭa*;
those produced from the two types of *paṭola*, and those born from the *kośātaka*. || 25.122–25.123 ||
The fruit of the bottle-gourd (*alābu*), the *karkārī*, the *nimba*, and the *bhadra*; the *tintriṇī* fruit together with the small tuber; likewise the two types of vine-tubers;
the two types of *sūraṇa* tubers; and similarly the two types of *piṇḍāraka*.
And especially that sacrificial offering produced from lotuses and water-lilies;
likewise, that which is leavings, defiled by worms, or bitten by jackals and the like;
and ghee touched by saliva or water, or originating from an impure place.

The mantra-practitioner, having examined it in many ways, should avoid in the act of cooking that which has been touched by a foot, that which has risen out of season, that which has been brought from an impure place, the remains of what has been eaten, as well as that which has been touched by one who is untouchable or left over after being offered. || 25.127 ||
Jīvantī, vāstuka greens, kāravallī leaves,
as well as tumbī leaves, piṇḍī, the leaves of cuccu and mudga, śākinī, śataparvan, and likewise śvāsamardita; ||| 25.128–25.129 |||
One should cook the *āgastya* vegetable, which is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
one may also take other vegetables and roots provided they are not prohibited,
having cut them with a sickle while reciting the *vīrya-mantra*.
Having inspected them for worms, insects, and the like, and having washed them many times with water,
one should place them as before into pots— either individually or mixed together— with *sendava* salt, black pepper, mustard seeds, and cumin.
With milk mixed with the leaves of *śrīparṇī*, with coconut water,
and also with those fruits rubbed together and combined with honey and ghee;
along with *masūra*, *māṣa*, *nimba*, and various types of *mudga* beans.

Immediately thereafter, one should prepare soups (*yūṣas*) such as those made from split mung beans (*mudgabhedādi*), and non-soups (*ayūṣas*) combined with various flavorings (*rasabheda*) like salt and so forth. Having removed the skins, one should cook them with the essences (*sāra*) derived from mung beans and with milk. || 25.134–25.135 ||
One should prepare the gulmāṣa so that it is flavorful, by rubbing together black pepper, cumin, and salt mixed with ghee,
and seasoning it with curd and other ingredients;
these should have been cooked previously in vessels filled with a cooking-pot and a shallow dish.
Plantains, jackfruits, and so forth, as well as coconut fruits;
pumpkins, brinjal, betel nuts, and the fruits of the kāravallī;
along with small tubers and the piṇḍāraka creepers. || 25.137–25.138 ||
Having placed [the meat] upon vessels such as those of Ambarīṣa, which are spread out on all sides,
smeared with ghee, and heated, and having spread it out,
[one seasons it] with powdered black pepper, cumin, and ghee.
Having repeatedly stirred with a ladle those heated and softened fruits,
they should be placed in vessels and covered with cloths and the like;
this applies to mangoes and other fruits, whether dry or fresh.

One should set aside the essence derived from oneself, mixed with *tintriṇī* and *gulā*, as well as black pepper and cumin, along with coconut milk and nourished with mustard seeds, combined with salt. || 25.142 ||
And ginger, or split and green wood-apple, scented with the juice extracted from wood-apple and mixed with salt;
as well as the fruits of plantain, jackfruit, and mango, taken alone. || 25.143–25.144 ||
One should cook cakes in ghee using flour made from wheat and *śāli* rice, mixed with molasses syrup,
cooked with the essence of mung beans, and pieces of coconut,
along with cumin and black pepper.
They were well-rounded like mangoes, equal to *dhātrī* fruits, and like the fruits of the *nyagrodha*; they had the shape of *likuca* and other such fruits,
with mung beans placed inside, and were flavorful throughout.
One should prepare cakes (*apūpa*) made from various types of flour mixed with molasses, shaped like coconuts and bound together, and fried in ghee;
as well as those made from *śāli* and *vrīhi* rice, which have been split open in cooking pots.
One should prepare *pṛthuka* grains that are small, heated in fire,
and cooked in molasses, along with powdered black pepper, cumin seeds, and even broken pieces of sugar, as well as dried coconut fruits. (25.149–150)
Saktu is prepared from roasted *śāli* rice flour mixed with cumin and other spices,
stirred with molasses until it forms separate lumps;
likewise, a ball (*piṇḍa*) may be made from well-roasted sesame seeds.
Known as *tilapiṇḍa*, it is always favored by the God.
It is well-boiled and thickened, mixed with powdered sugar,
and combined with milk, honey, and clarified butter, becoming a very dense curd.
Young pieces of cucumber and mango,
mixed with dry *sarṣapa* seeds and likewise with black pepper and curd.
Pure, strained honey from *mākṣika* bees, contained in a separate vessel,
is stirred with the crushed juices of grapes, jackfruit, breadfruit, and mango, along with jaggery,
sugar-candy, and *jīraka* and other spices.

This should be known as *rasāla*; when mixed with curd, it is called *pānaka*. When water mixed with curd alone, in equal measure, is churned, along with black pepper and seasoned with salts, [it is likewise called *pānaka*]. || 25.156–25.157 ||
A drink mixed with sugar-candy and powdered sugar brings relief from fatigue;
furthermore, mantras were previously proclaimed for the consecration of foods.
For other items, however, the consecration is performed with either the twelve-syllable mantra or the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Or one may accomplish everything with the root mantra together with its ancillaries (sāṅga);
or else with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, or with the Pañcopaniṣad.
Having thus accomplished it, one should partake in due order of the supreme food accompanied by side dishes.
Having established [the deity] within the fruit-offerings and so forth, and adorned with the vertical *puṇḍra* marks and other ornaments,
[one proceeds] from the ground of the kitchen door to the western side of the temple door,
which is smeared with cow dung and beautified by white lime powder.
Preceded by a stream of water consecrated with mantras,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, as well as auspicious songs,
and attended by those intent on maintaining the sacrificial oblation, provided with lamps and umbrellas. || 25.162–25.163 ||
Other people, with canes in their hands and intent on clearing away the atheists,

were bathed, dressed in white garments, skillful, and had washed their feet in the forest; they had sipped water for purification and held *kuśa* grass in their hands, or [smeared themselves] with clay, sandalwood, and so forth.
Wearing upright sectarian marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and restrained in the actions of mind, speech, and body, the attendants,
wearing white tunics with their mouths and noses covered,
should carry the vessels while reciting the *bala-mantra*.
Then, in a pavilion situated at the root-abode or the upper region,
or else in the first enclosure of the temple to the south in a grove of *mālikā* trees—
well-concealed, richly provided with canopies, and adorned with rows of lamps and other ornaments— [one should perform the rite].
They should be placed on a plank or similar surface in a spot covered with cloth.

The vessels made of gold, silver, and copper should be equal in size to the quantity of the oblation; having been smeared [with ghee] as appropriate, they are to be washed with water while reciting the Astra mantra.
Then, having touched them with his right hand and having placed [the portions] into those [ladles] with the *tāra* mantra,
he should take [the oblation] from the cooking pots all around the supporting ghee using a ladle fashioned of gold or other precious materials.
Remaining silent, he should place above that, in due order, milk-rice and other offerings (25.171).
Having drenched the sweet side-dishes all around with ghee,
he should set cups filled with curd, milk, and so forth upon them (25.172).
There were various kinds of prepared cakes, such as *pṛthuka* and others,
as well as diverse beverages placed in separate vessels,
all perfumed with camphor, sandalwood powder, and flowers.
Cool water, covered with cloth, contained in jars and other vessels,
mixed with cardamom, cloves, *takola*,
jasmine, and betel nuts, blended with camphor oil, and cut with razors and such implements.
Having placed betel-leaf together with lime, powdered nutmeg,
and camphor, as well as betel-nut, in vessels shaped like lotuses,
[one should offer] sandalwood and other fragrant substances, as well as various kinds of garlands.

Having established [the items] in their proper places, the attendants (*ārādhaka*) should inform the Lord, through the mouth of the presiding official (*karmādhikārin*), concerning each respective matter.
When the Lord has ascended his seat for the meal, the attendant himself [should serve].
Having worshipped [the deity] as before with the *arghya* and other offerings, ending with the seed-syllable of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
on the ground situated inside the door in front of the deity—
which has been purified with water from the *astra-mantra* and adorned with sandalwood paste and other substances— [one should proceed].
Having strewn rice grains upon the mandala according to one's preference,
and having spread out a washed piece of cloth over it,
one should place a vessel for the food made of metal upon that.

Above that, for the purpose of clothing, one should place vessels containing supreme food and other offerings, one by one in sequence, upon the stream overflowing above. Then, having established the libation (tarpaṇa) with water for washing the hands, [one should proceed].
In the rite for the gods (*daiva*), one should perform the preliminary spreading and honoring with the right hand.
Then, one should place the sacrificial offerings before the images of the deities and others:
first milk-rice (*pāyasa*), followed by rice cooked with jaggery and split mung beans.
One should offer pure rice mixed with sesame, food from the night mixed with curd,
and mixed food in sequence, and at the end of that, cakes (apūpa),
flattened grains (pṛthuka), and parched barley flour (saktu) accompanied by balls of sesame.
Various fruits such as plantains and jackfruit, refreshing drinks endowed with diverse flavors, and coconut juice for rinsing the hands; thereafter, the water for sipping. || 25.186–25.187 ||
Having offered water for sipping and betel, one should perform the previously mentioned rites.
When an abundance of sacrificial offerings has been prepared by kings,
they should be placed upon their bases within the spacious inner sanctum.

The offerings should be presented as appropriate; otherwise, they may be placed on the ground in times of difficulty. Having placed them one by one in due order upon a single firm support covered with cloth, and having made the offering, one should then remove them.
Once it has been sprinkled with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), another oblation should be offered;

one should present it as before, for this specific distinction has been proclaimed here. [25.191] Furthermore, that which is devoid of mantra-rites, tainted by odor, or discolored [should be avoided].

Food that is overcooked, undercooked, or from which the water has not been drained; that which has been looked upon by those who are uninitiated, by outcasts, or by those born of inverse unions (pratiloma);
as well as food that is too hot, too cold, or lacking in the proper measure—[these should be avoided].
That which has been completely removed, that which is defiled by the breath from the mouth and the like,
that which is devoid of condiments and so forth, that which is placed in an unworthy vessel, that which is not protected,
that which contains rice inside [the husk], and likewise that which is contained in a broken vessel— [these are to be rejected].
That which is without a base, touched by another, or struck by breath;
likewise that which is mixed with charcoal or chaff, joined with hair or stones, infested by worms, clods of earth, and the like, or provided with parts of living beings and so forth. (25.195–196)
Unripe, lacking the *āghāra* libation, devoid of condiments, and free from cow-ghee and curd—yet desired by other people;
uncovered and equated with another deity. (25.197)
Having thus recognized the oblation as defiled, one should discard it into the middle of the water.
If, out of delusion, one offers that oblation which was intended for Viṣṇu as an act of worship,
it shall be fruitless for the performers and their destruction will certainly occur.
Therefore, at that very time, one should perform a thousand recitations of the root mantra;

then, according to the prescribed ritual, [one should do so] for the deities who have been installed there as the constituent forms of the manifestation of power (*vibhava-vyūha*) within the pavilion, the gate-towers, and so forth.
And for the installed images, even those whose nature is manifestation;
for Satya and the others whose nature is the sky, when they have been worshipped according to rule;
and for the lords of the hosts such as Kumuda, who stand at the doors in the temple—[one should perform the rites].

One should sequentially arrange the sacrificial offerings, such as milk-rice and others, which have been separately prepared according to the rules for each respective mantra, for the devotees previously mentioned who are established in their practice.
One should prepare the sacrificial oblation (havis) for the purpose of the bali offering using the Gāruḍa mantra itself;
for others, one should present the prepared food using the Praṇava alone.
The oblation for the fire-rite (agnikārya) is to be prepared according to the form of the root-mantra of the temple.
Indeed, none of the various types of cakes are suitable for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*); however,
other items such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and various fruits should especially be offered regularly and on occasional occasions.
In the offerings to the spirits (bhūtas), one should constantly present milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like,
as well as cakes, parched grain flour (saktu), flattened rice (pṛthuka), and fruits—
either combined with balls of sesame (tilapiṇḍa) or mixed together, or else separately.
For they must be given according to the rule, since they bring satisfaction to them;
therefore, O Brahmin, in rites such as festivals and the like,
one should procure the materials for the bali-offerings at each respective place according to the prescribed injunctions, even when using cruel substances and the like.

In the absence of all ritual substances, one should give only rice with water, or even rice alone with water, by those most skilled in the mantras. Thus has the preparation and so forth of the sacrificial offerings been correctly explained.

Thus, O tigers among sages, whatever has been requested by you has all been revealed in full detail and according to the truth. This compendium is the most excellent, illuminating the true meaning of the Sātvata doctrine.
It should not be told to those of wicked intellect who lack devotion for Janārdana,
especially to those who, out of pride, revile the true scriptures and the true reality, to those who disparage the scriptures, or to those whose minds are conditioned by other philosophical systems.

This scripture should be fully explained after performing the initiation according to the prescribed rule for those great-souled ones who have taken refuge, whose intellects are devoted to the gods, whose minds are intent upon their own duty, and who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra.
And the meaning of the scripture should be recited, together with the meanings of the mantras.
That best of the twice-born who worships the omnipresent Acyuta according to the procedure prescribed in this scripture quickly obtains all his desired goals.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fire-pits, the Sruk and Sruva Lladles, and the Rules for Cooking the Oblation," in the *Īśvarasaṃhitā* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The Īśvarasaṃhitā is completed.
